# Simple methods for large-scale problems

## 5.1 Motivation: Why simple methods?

The polynomial time Interior Point methods, same as all other polynomial time methods for Convex Programming known so far, have a not that pleasant common feature: the arithmetic cost C of an iteration in such a method grows nonlinearly with the design dimension n of the problem, unless the problem possesses a very favourable structure. $\mathrm{E.g.}$ , in IP methods, an iteration requires solving a system of linear equations with (at least) n unknowns. To solve this auxiliary problem, it costs at least $O(n^{2})$ operations (with the traditional Linear Algebra – even $O(n^{3})$ operations), except for the cases when the matrix of the system is very sparse and, moreover, possesses a well-structured sparsity pattern. The latter indeed is the case when solving most of LPs of decision-making origin, but often is not the case for LPs coming from Engineering, and nearly never is the case for SDPs. For other known polynomial time methods, the situation is similar – the arithmetic cost of an iteration, even in the case of extremely simple objectives and feasible sets, is at least $O(n^{2})$ . With n of order of tens and hundreds of thousands, the computational efort of $O(n^{2})$ , not speaking about $O(n^{3})$ , operations per iteration becomes prohibitively large – basically, you never will finish the very first iteration of your method... On the other hand, the design dimensions of tens and hundreds of thousands is exactly what is met in many applications, like SDP relaxations of combinatorial problems involving large graphs or Structural Design (especially for 3D structures). As another important application of this type, consider 3D Medical Imagingg3 problem arising in Positron Emission Tomography.

Positron Emission Tomography (PET) is a powerful, non-invasive, medical diagnostic imaging technique for measuring the metabolic activity of cells in the human body. It has been in clinical use since the early 1990s. PET imaging is unique in that it shows the chemical functioning of organs and tissues, while other imaging techniques - such as X-ray, computerized tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) - show anatomic structures.

A PET scan involves the use of a radioactive tracer – a fluid with a small amount of a radioactive material which has the property of emitting positrons. When the tracer is administered to a patient, either by injection or inhalation of gas, it distributes within the body. For a properly chosen tracer, this distribution “concentrates” in desired locations, e.g., in the areas of high metabolic activity where cancer tumors can be expected.

The radioactive component of the tracer disintegrates, emitting positrons. Such a positron nearly immediately annihilates with a near-by electron, giving rise to two γ-quants flying at the speed of light of the point of annihilation in nearly opposite directions along a line with a completely random orientation (i.e., line’s direction is drawn at random from the uniform distribution on the unit sphere in 3D). The γ-quants penetrate the surrounding tissue and are registered outside the patient by a PET scanner consisting of circular arrays (rings) of gamma radiation detectors. Since the two gamma rays are emitted simultaneously and travel in almost exactly opposite directions, we can say a lot on the location of their source: when a pair of detectors register high-energy γ-quants within a short $(\sim 10^{- 8} \mathrm{sec})$ time window $(^{66} a$ coincidence event”), we know that the photons came from a disintegration act, and that the act took place on the line (“line of response” (LOR)) linking the detectors. The measured data set is the collection of numbers of coincidences counted by different pairs of detectors $\left({\sqrt[[objectObject]]{\cos^{2}}} \right)$ , and the problem is to recove from these measurements the 3D density of the tracer.

The mathematical model of the process, after appropriate discretization, is

$$
y = P \lambda + \xi,
$$

where

$\lambda \geq 0$ is the vector representing the (discretized) density of the tracer; the entries of λ are indexed by voxels – small cubes into which we partition the field of view, and $\lambda_{j}$ is the mean density of the tracer in voxel $j.$ . Typically, the number n of voxels is in the range from $3 \times 10^{5}$ to $3 \times 10^{6}$ depending on the resolution of the discretization grid;

- y are the measurements; the entries in y are indexed by bins – pairs of detectors, and $y_{i}$ is the number of coincidences counted by i-th pair of detectors. Typically, the dimension m of y – the total number of bins – is millions (at least $3 \times 10^{6})$ ;

- P is the projection matrix; its entries $p_{ij}$ are the probabilities for a LOR originating in voxel j to be registered by bin i. These probabilities are readily given by the geometry of the scanner;

- ξ is the measurement noise coming mainly from the fact that all physical processes underlying PET are random. The standard statistical model for PET implies that $y_{i}, i = 1,..., m$ , are independent Poisson random variables with the expectations $(P \lambda)_{i}$

The problem we are interested in is to recover tracer’s density λ given measurements y. As far as the quality of the result is concerned, the most attractive reconstruction scheme is given by the standard in Statistics Likelihood Ratio maximization: denoting $p(\cdot | \lambda)$ the density, taken w.r.t. an appropriate dominating measure, of the probability distribution of the measurements coming from λ, the estimate of the unknown true value $\lambda_{*}$ of λ is

$$
\widehat{\lambda} = \underset{\lambda \geq 0}{\operatorname{argmin}} p(y | \lambda),
$$

where y is the vector of measurements.

For the aforementioned Poisson model of PET, building the Maximum Likelihood estimate is equivalent to solving the optimization problem

$$
\begin{array}{rl} \min_{\lambda} \left\{\sum_{j = 1}^{n} \lambda_{j} p_{j} - \sum_{i = 1}^{m} y_{i} \ln(\sum_{j = 1}^{n} \lambda_{j} p_{ij}): \lambda \geq 0 \right\} & \\ \left[p_{j} = \sum_{i} p_{ij} \right] &.\end{array}\tag{PET}
$$

This is a nicely structured convex program (by the way, polynomially reducible to CQP and even LP). The only dificulty – and a severe one – is in huge sizes of the problem: as it was already explained, the number n of decision variables is at least 300, 000, while the number m of log-terms in the objective is in the range from $3 \times 10^{6}$ to $25 \times 10^{6}$

At the present level of our knowledge, the design dimension n of order of tens and hundreds of thousands rules out the possibility to solve a nonlinear convex program, even a well-structured one, by polynomial time methods because of at least quadratic in n “blowing $\mathrm{up}^{\mathrm{,}}$ the arithmetic cost of an iteration. When n is really large, all we can use are simple methods with linear in n cost of an iteration. As a byproduct of this restriction, we cannot utilize anymore our knowledge of the analytic structure of the problem, since all known for the time being ways of doing so are too expensive, provided that n is large. As a result, we are enforced to restrict ourselves with black-box-oriented optimization techniques – those which use solely the possibility to compute the values and the (sub)gradients of the objective and the constraints at a point. In Convex Optimization, two types of “cheap” black-box-oriented optimization techniques are known:

- techniques for unconstrained minimization of smooth convex functions (Gradient Descent, Conjugate Gradients, quasi-Newton methods with restricted memory, etc.);

- subgradient-type techniques, called also First Order algorithms, for nonsmooth convex programs, including constrained ones.

Since the majority of applications are constrained, we restrict our exposition to the techniques of the second type. We start with investigating of what, in principle, can be expected of blackbox-oriented optimization techniques.

## 5.1.1 Black-box-oriented methods and Information-based complexity

Consider a Convex Programming program in the form

$$
\min_{x} \left\{f(x): x \in X \right\},\tag{CP}
$$

where $X$ is a convex compact set in a Euclidean space (which we w.l.o.g. identify with $\mathbb{R}^{n})$ and the objective $f$ is a continuous convex function on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ . Let us fix a family ${\mathcal{P}}(X)$ of convex programs (CP) with X common for all programs from the family, so that such a program can be identified with the corresponding objective, and the family itself is nothing but certain family of convex functions on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ . We intend to explain what is the Information-based complexity of P(X) – informally, complexity of the family w.r.t. “black-box-oriented” methods. We start with defining such a method as a routine B as follows:

1. When starting to solve (CP), B is given an accuracy $\epsilon > 0$ to which the problem should be solved and knows that the problem belongs to a given family ${\mathcal{P}}(X)$ . However, B does not know what is the particular problem it deals with.

2. In course of solving the problem, B has an access to the First Order oracle for $f.$ This oracle is capable, given on input a point $x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ , to report on output what is the value $f(x)$ and a subgradient $f^{\prime}(x)$ of $f$ at x.

B generates somehow a sequence of search points $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots$ and calls the First Order oracle to get the values and the subgradients of $f$ at these points. The rules for building $x_{t}$ can be arbitrary, except for the fact that they should be non-anticipating (causal): $x_{t}$ can depend only on the information $f(x_{1}), f^{\prime}(x_{1}),..., f(x_{t - 1}), f^{\prime}(x_{t - 1})$ on $f$ accumulated by $\boldsymbol{B}$ at the first t − 1 steps.

3. After certain number $T = T_{B}(f, \epsilon)$ of calls to the oracle, B terminates and outputs the result $z_{B}(f, \epsilon)$ . This result again should depend solely on the information on $f$ accumulated by $\boldsymbol{B}$ at the T search steps, and must be an $\epsilon$-solution to (CP), i.e.,

$$
z_{\mathcal{B}}(f, \epsilon) \in X \& f(z_{\mathcal{B}}(f, \epsilon)) - \min_{X} f \leq \epsilon.
$$

We measure the complexity of ${\mathcal{P}}(X)$ w.r.t. a solution method B by the function

$$
\mathrm{Compl}_{\mathcal{B}}(\epsilon) = \max_{f \in \mathcal{P}(X)} T_{\mathcal{B}}(f, \epsilon)
$$

– by the minimal number of steps in which B is capable to solve within accuracy $\epsilon$ every instance of ${\mathcal{P}}(X)$ . Finally, the Information-based complexity of the family ${\mathcal{P}}(X)$ of problems is defined as

$$
\operatorname{Compl}(\epsilon) = \min_{\mathcal{B}} \operatorname{Compl}_{\mathcal{B}}(\epsilon),
$$

the minimum being taken over all solution methods. Thus, the relation $\mathrm{Compl}(\epsilon) = N$ means, first, that there exists a solution method B capable to solve within accuracy $\epsilon$ every instance of ${\mathcal{P}}(X)$ in no more than N calls to the First Order oracle, and, second, that for every solution method B there exists an instance of ${\mathcal{P}}(X)$ such that B solves the instance within the accuracy $\epsilon$ in at least N steps.

Note that as far as black-box-oriented optimization methods are concerned, the informationbased complexity $\mathrm{Compl}(\epsilon)$ of a family P(X) ${\mathcal{P}}(X)$ is a lower bound on “actual” computational efort, whatever it means, sufficient to find $\epsilon$-solution to every instance of the family.

## 5.1.2 Main results on Information-based complexity of Convex Programming

Main results on Information-based complexity of Convex Programming can be summarized as follows. Let X be a solid in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ (a convex compact set with a nonempty interior), and let ${\mathcal{P}}(X)$ be the family of all convex functions on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ normalized by the condition

$$
\max_{X} f - \min_{X} f \leq 1.\tag{5.1.1}
$$

For this family,

I. Complexity of finding high-accuracy solutions in fixed dimension is independent of the geometry of X. Specifically,

$$
\begin{array}{ll} \forall(\epsilon \leq \epsilon(X)): & O(1) n \ln \left(2 + \frac{1}{\epsilon}\right) \leq \mathrm{Compl}(\epsilon); \\ \forall(\epsilon > 0): & \mathrm{Compl}(\epsilon) \leq O(1) n \ln \left(2 + \frac{1}{\epsilon}\right), \end{array}\tag{5.1.2}
$$

where

$O(1)$ ’s are appropriately chosen positive absolute constants,

$\epsilon(X)$ depends on the geometry of X, but never is less than $\textstyle{\frac{1}{n^{2}}}$ , where n is the dimension of X.

II. Complexity of finding solutions of fixed accuracy in high dimensions does depend on the geometry of X. Here are 3 typical results:

(a) Let X be an n-dimensional box: $X = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^{n} : \| x \|_{\infty} \leq 1\}$ . Then

$$
\epsilon \leq \frac{1}{2} \Rightarrow O(1) n \ln(\frac{1}{\epsilon}) \leq \operatorname{Compl}(\epsilon) \leq O(1) n \ln(\frac{1}{\epsilon}).\tag{5.1.3}
$$

(b) Let X be an n-dimensional ball: $X = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^{n} : \| x \|_{2} \leq 1\}$ . Then

$$
n \geq \frac{1}{\epsilon^{2}} \Rightarrow \frac{O(1)}{\epsilon^{2}} \leq \operatorname{Compl}(\epsilon) \leq \frac{O(1)}{\epsilon^{2}}.\tag{5.1.4}
$$

(c) Let X be an n-dimensional hyperoctahedron: $X = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^{n} : \| x \|_{1} \leq 1\}$ . Then

$$
n \geq \frac{1}{\epsilon^{2}} \Rightarrow \frac{O(1)}{\epsilon^{2}} \leq \operatorname{Compl}(\epsilon) \leq \frac{O(\ln n)}{\epsilon^{2}}\tag{5.1.5}
$$

(in fact, $O(1)$ in the lower bound can be replaced with $O(\ln n)$ , provided that $\begin{array}{r}{n \gg \frac{1}{\epsilon^{2}})} \end{array}$

Since we are interested in extremely large-scale problems, the moral which we can extract from the outlined results is as follows:

- I is discouraging: it says that we have no hope to guarantee high accuracy, like $\epsilon = 10^{- 6}$ when solving large-scale problems with black-box-oriented methods; indeed, with $O(n)$ steps per accuracy digit and at least $O(n)$ operations per step (this many operations are required already to input a search point to the oracle), the arithmetic cost per accuracy digit is at least $O(n^{2})$ which is prohibitively large for really large n.

- II is partly discouraging, partly encouraging. A bad news reported by II is that when X is a box, which is the most typical situation in applications, we have no hope to solve extremely large-scale problems, in a reasonable time, to guaranteed, even low, accuracy, since the required number of steps should be at least of order of n. A good news reported by II is that there exist situations where the complexity of minimizing a convex function within a fixed accuracy is independent, or nearly independent, of the design dimension. Of course, the dependence of the complexity bounds in (5.1.4) and (5.1.5) on $\epsilon$ is very bad and has nothing in common with being polynomial in ln $(1 / \epsilon)$ ; however, this drawback is tolerable when we do not intend to get high accuracy. Another drawback is that there are not that many applications where the feasible set is a ball or a hyperoctahedron. Note, however, that in fact we can save the most important for us upper complexity bounds in (5.1.4) and (5.1.5) when requiring from X to be a subset of a ball, respectively, of a hyperoctahedron, rather than to be the entire ball/hyperoctahedron. This extension is not costless: we should simultaneously strengthen the normalization condition (5.1.1). Specifically, we shall see that

B. The upper complexity bound in (5.1.4) remains valid when $X \subset \{x : \| x \|_{2} \leq 1\}$ and

$$
\mathcal{P}(X) = \{f: f \text{is convex and} | f(x) - f(y) | \leq \| x - y \|_{2} \forall x, y \in X\};
$$

S. The upper complexity bound in (5.1.5) remains valid when $X \subset \{x : \| x \|_{1} \leq 1\}$ and

$$
\mathcal{P}(X) = \{f: f \text{is convex and} | f(x) - f(y) | \leq \| x - y \|_{1} \forall x, y \in X\}.
$$

Note that the “ball-like” case mentioned in B seems to be rather artificial: the Euclidean norm associated with this case is a very natural mathematical entity, but this is all we can say in its favour. For example, the normalization of the objective in B is that the Lipschitz constant of $f$ w.r.t. $\| \cdot \|_{2} \ \mathrm{is} \leq 1, \mathrm{or}$ , which is the same, that the vector of the first order partial derivatives of $f$ should, at every point, be of $\lVert \cdot \rVert_{2^{-} \mathrm{{norm}}}$ not exceeding 1. In order words, “typical” magnitudes of the partial derivatives of $f$ should become smaller and smaller as the number of variables grows; what could be the reasons for such a strange behaviour? In contrast to this, the normalization condition imposed on $f$ in S is that the Lipschitz constant of $f$ w.r.t. $\| \cdot \|_{1} \ \mathrm{is} \leq 1$ , or, which is the same, that the $\| \cdot \|_{\infty} \mathrm{- norm}$ of the vector of partial derivatives of $f{\mathrm{~ is ~}} \leq 1$ . In other words, the normalization is that the magnitudes of the first order partial derivatives of $f \{\mathrm{should ~ be}} \leq 1$ and this normalization is “dimension-independent”. Of course, in B we deal with minimization over subsets of the unit ball, while in $S$ we deal with minimization over the subsets of the unit hyperoctahedron, which is much smaller than the unit ball. However, there do exist problems in reality where we should minimize over the standard simplex

$$
\Delta_{n} = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}: x \geq 0, \sum_{x} x_{i} = 1\},
$$

which indeed is a subset of the unit hyperoctahedron. For example, it turns out that the PET Image Reconstruction problem (PET) is in fact the problem of minimization over the standard simplex. Indeed, the optimality condition for (PET) reads

$$
\lambda_{j} \left(p_{j} - \sum_{i} y_{i} \frac{p_{ij}}{\sum_{\ell} p_{i \ell} \lambda_{\ell}}\right) = 0, j = 1,..., n;
$$

summing up these equalities, we get

$$
\sum_{j} p_{j} \lambda_{j} = B \equiv \sum_{i} y_{i}.
$$

It follows that the optimal solution to (PET) remains unchanged when we add to the nonnegativity constraints $\lambda_{j} \geq 0$ also the constraint $\sum_{j} p_{j} \lambda_{j} = B$ . Passing to the new variables $x_{j} = B^{- 1} p_{j} \lambda_{j}$ , we further convert (PET) to the equivalent form

$$
\min_{x} \left\{f(x) \equiv - \sum_{i} y_{i} \ln(\sum_{j} q_{ij} x_{j}): x \in \Delta_{n} \right\}, \left[q_{ij} = \frac{Bp_{ij}}{p_{j}} \right]\tag{PET'}
$$

which is a problem of minimizing a convex function over the standard simplex.

Another example is $\ell_{1}$ minimization arising in sparsity-oriented signal processing, in particular, in Compressed Sensing, see section 1.3.1. The optimization problems arising here can be reduced to small series of problems of the form

$$
\min_{x: \| x \|_{1} \leq 1} \| Ax - b \|_{p},
$$

$$
[A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}]
$$

where $p = \infty \ \mathrm{or} \p = 2$ . Representing $\boldsymbol{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ as $u - v$ with nonnegative $u, v.$ , we can rewrite this problem equivalently as

$$
\min_{u, v \geq 0, \sum_{i} u_{i} + \sum_{i} v_{i} = 1} \| A[u - v] - b \|_{p};
$$

the domain of this problem is the standard 2n-dimensional simplex $\Delta_{2n}$

Intermediate conclusion. The discussion above says that this perhaps is a good idea to look for simple convex minimization techniques which, as applied to convex programs (CP) with feasible sets of appropriate geometry, exhibit dimension-independent (or nearly dimensionindependent) and nearly optimal information-based complexity. We are about to present a family of techniques of this type.

## 5.2 The Simplest: Subgradient Descent and Euclidean Bundle Level

## 5.2.1 Subgradient Descent

The algorithm. The “simplest of the simple” algorithm or nonsmooth convex optimization – Subgradient Descend (SD) discovered by N. Shore in 1967 is aimed at solving a convex program

$$
\min_{x \in X} f(x),\tag{CP}
$$

where

$X$ is a convex compact set in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ , and

- f is a Lipschitz continuous on $X$ convex function.

SD is the recurrence

$$
x_{t + 1} = \Pi_{X}(x_{t} - \gamma_{t} f^{\prime}(x_{t}))[x_{1} \in X]\tag{SD}
$$

where

$\gamma_{t} > 0$ are stepsizes

$\Pi_{X}(x) = \underset{y \in X}{\operatorname{argmin}} \ : \| x - y \|_{2}^{2}$ is the standard metric projector on $X$ , and

$f^{\prime}(x)$ is a subgradient of $f$ at x:

$$
f(y) \geq f(x) +(y - x)^{T} f^{\prime}(x) \quad \forall y \in X.\tag{5.2.1}
$$

Note: We always assume that int $X \neq \emptyset$ and that the subgradients $f^{\prime}(x)$ reported by the First Order oracle at points $x \in X$ satisfy the requirement

$$
f^{\prime}(x) \in \operatorname{cl} \left\{f^{\prime}(y): y \in \operatorname{int} X \right\}.
$$

With this assumption, for every norm $\| \cdot \|$ on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ and for every $x \in X$ one has

$$
\| f^{\prime}(x)\|_{*}\equiv \max_{\xi :\| \xi \| \leq 1}\xi^{T}f^{\prime}(x)\leq L_{\| \cdot \|}(f)\equiv \sup_{\substack{x\neq y,\\ x,y\in X}}\frac{|f(x) - f(y)|}{\|x - y\|}.\tag{5.2.2}
$$

When, why and how SD converges? To analyse convergence of SD, we start with a simple geometric fact:

(!) Let $X ~ \subset ~ \mathbb{R}^{n}$ be a closed convex set, and let $x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ . Then the vector $e =$ $x - \Pi_{X}(x)$ forms an acute angle with every vector of the form $y - \Pi_{X}(x), y \in X$

$$
(x - \Pi_{X}(x))^{T}(y - \Pi_{X}(x)) \leq 0 \quad \forall y \in X.\tag{5.2.3}
$$

In particular,

$$
y \in X \Rightarrow \| y - \Pi_{X}(x) \|_{2}^{2} \leq \| y - x \|_{2}^{2} - \| x - \Pi_{X}(x) \|_{2}^{2}\tag{5.2.4}
$$

Indeed, when $y \in X$ and $0 \leq t \leq 1$ , one has

$$
\phi(t) = \| \underbrace{[\Pi_{X}(x) + t(y - \Pi_{X}(x))]}_{y_{t} \in X} - x \|_{2}^{2} \geq \| \Pi_{X}(x) - x \|_{2}^{2} = \phi(0),
$$

whence

$$
0 \leq \phi^{\prime}(0) = 2(\Pi_{X}(x) - x)^{T}(y - \Pi_{X}(x)).
$$

Consequently,

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \| y - x \|_{2}^{2} & = & \| y - \Pi_{X}(x) \|_{2}^{2} + \| \Pi_{X}(x) - x \|_{2}^{2} + 2(y - \Pi_{X}(x))^{T}(\Pi_{X}(x) - x) \\ & \geq & \| y - \Pi_{X}(x) \|_{2}^{2} + \| \Pi_{X}(x) - x \|_{2}^{2}.\end{array}
$$

Corollary 5.2.1 With $x_{t}$ defined by (SD), for every $u \in X$ one has

$$
\gamma_{t}(x_{t} - u)^{T} f^{\prime}(x_{t}) \leq \underbrace{\frac{1}{2} \| x_{t} - u \|_{2}^{2}}_{d_{t}} - \underbrace{\frac{1}{2} \| x_{t + 1} - u \|_{2}^{2}}_{d_{t + 1}} + \frac{1}{2} \gamma_{t}^{2} \| f^{\prime}(x_{t}) \|_{2}^{2}.\tag{5.2.5}
$$

Indeed, by (!) we have

$$
d_{t + 1} \leq \frac{1}{2} \|[x_{t} - u] - \gamma_{t} f^{\prime}(x_{t}) \|_{2}^{2} = d_{t} - \gamma_{t}(x_{t} - u)^{T} f^{\prime}(x_{t}) + \frac{1}{2} \gamma_{t}^{2} \| f^{\prime}(x_{t}) \|_{2}^{2}.
$$

Summing up inequalities (5.2.5) over $t = T_{0}, T_{0} + 1,..., T$ , we get

$$
\begin{array}{c} \sum_{t = T_{0}}^{T} \gamma_{t}(f(x_{t}) - f(u)) \leq \underbrace{d_{T_{0}} - d_{T + 1}}_{\leq \Theta} + \sum_{t = T_{0}}^{T} \frac{1}{2} \gamma_{t}^{2} \| f^{\prime}(x_{t}) \|_{2}^{2} \\ \left[\Theta = \max_{x, y \in X} \frac{1}{2} \| x - y \|_{2}^{2} \right] \end{array}
$$

Setting $u = x_{*} \equiv$ argmin $f,$ we arrive at the bound X

$$
\boxed{\forall(T, T_{0}, T \geq T_{0} \geq 1): \epsilon_{T} \equiv \min_{t \leq T} f(x_{t}) - f_{*} \leq \frac{\Theta + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{t = T_{0}}^{T} \gamma_{t}^{2} \| f^{\prime}(x_{t}) \|_{2}^{2}}{\sum_{t = T_{0}}^{T} \gamma_{t}}}\tag{5.2.6}
$$

Note that $\epsilon_{T}$ is the non-optimality, in terms of $f,$ of the best (with the smallest value of $f)$ solution $x_{\mathrm{bst}}^{T}$ found in course of the first $T$ steps of SD.

Relation (5.2.6) allows to arrive at various convergence results.

Example 1: “Divergent Series”. Let $\gamma_{t} 0 \mathrm{\as \} t \infty$ , while $\sum_{t} \gamma_{t} = \infty$ . Then

$$
\lim_{T \to \infty} \epsilon_{T} = 0.\tag{5.2.7}
$$

Proof. Set $T_{0} = 1$ and note that

$$
\frac{\sum_{t = 1}^{T} \gamma_{t}^{2} \| f^{\prime}(x_{t}) \|_{2}^{2}}{\sum_{t = 1}^{T} \gamma_{t}} \leq L_{\| \cdot \|_{2}}^{2}(f) \frac{\sum_{t = 1}^{T} \gamma_{t}^{2}}{\sum_{t = 1}^{T} \gamma_{t}} \to 0, T \to \infty.
$$

Example 2: “Optimal stepsizes”: When

$$
\gamma_{t} = \frac{\sqrt{2 \Theta}}{\| f^{\prime}(x_{t}) \| \sqrt{t}}\tag{5.2.8}
$$

one has

$$
\epsilon_{T} \equiv \min_{t < T} f(x_{t}) - f_{*} \leq O(1) \frac{L_{\| \cdot \|_{2}}(f) \sqrt{\Theta}}{\sqrt{T}}, T \geq 1\tag{5.2.9}
$$

Proof. Setting $T_{0} = \lfloor T / 2 \rfloor$ , we get

$$
\epsilon_{T} \leq \frac{\Theta + \Theta \sum_{t = T_{0}}^{T} \frac{1}{t}}{\sum_{t = T_{0}}^{T} \frac{\sqrt{\Theta}}{\sqrt{t} \| f^{\prime}(x_{t}) \|_{2}}} \leq \frac{\Theta + \Theta \sum_{t = T_{0}}^{T} \frac{1}{t}}{\sum_{t = T_{0}}^{T} \frac{\sqrt{\Theta}}{\sqrt{t} L_{\| \cdot \|_{2}}(f)}} \leq L_{\| \cdot \|_{2}}(f) \sqrt{\Theta} \frac{1 + O(1)}{O(1) \sqrt{T}} = O(1) \frac{L_{\| \cdot \|_{2}}(f) \sqrt{\Theta}}{\sqrt{T}}
$$

Good news: We have arrived at eficiency estimate which is dimension-independent, provided that the ${\sqrt[6]{1 \cdot | |_{2}}}.$ -variation” of the objective on the feasible domain

$$
\operatorname{Var}_{\| \cdot \|_{2}, X}(f) = L_{\| \cdot \|_{2}}(f) \max_{x, y \in X} \| x - y \|_{2}
$$

is fixed. Moreover, when X is a Euclidean ball in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ , this eficiency estimate “is as good as an eficiency estimate of a black-box-oriented method can $\mathrm{be}^{\mathfrak{N}}$ , provided that the dimension is large:

$$
n \geq \left(\frac{\operatorname{Var}_{| | \cdot | |_{2}, X}(f)}{\epsilon}\right)^{2}
$$

Bad news: Our “dimension-independent” eficiency estimate

- is pretty slow

- is indeed dimension-independent only for problems with “Euclidean geometry” – those with moderate k · k<sub>2</sub>-variation. As a matter of fact, in applications problems of this type are pretty rare.

A typical “convergence pattern” is exhibited on the plot below:

## 5.2.2 Incorporating memory: Euclidean Bundle Level Algorithm

An evident drawback of SD is that all information on the objective accumulated so far is “summarized” in the current iterate, and this “summary” is very incomplete. With better usage of past information, one arrives at bundle methods which outperform SD significantly in practice, while preserving the most attractive theoretical property of SD – dimension-independent and optimal, in favourable circumstances, rate of convergence.

Bundle-Level algorithm. The Bundle Level algorithms works as follows.

- At the beginning of step t of BL, we have at our disposal

- the first-order information $\{f(x_{\tau}), f^{\prime}(x_{\tau})\}_{1 \leq \tau < t}$ on $f$ along the previous search points $x_{\tau} \in X, \tau < t;$

- current iterate $x_{t} \in X$

- At step t we

1. compute $f(x_{t}), f^{\prime}(x_{t})$ ; this information, along with the past first-order information on $f,$ provides is with the current model of the objective

$$
f_{t}(x) = \max_{\tau \leq t}[f(x_{\tau}) +(x - x_{\tau})^{T} f^{\prime}(x_{\tau})]
$$

This model underestimates the objective and is exact at the points $x_{1},..., x_{t};$

2. define the best found so far value of the objective $f^{t} = \operatorname{min}_{\tau \leq t} f(x_{\tau})$

3. define the current lower bound $f_{t}$ on $f_{*}$ by solving the auxiliary problem

$$
f_{t} = \min_{x \in X} f_{t}(x)\tag{\((\mathrm{LP}_t)\}
$$

Note that the current gap $\Delta_{t} = f^{t} - f_{t}$ is an upper bound on the inaccuracy of the best found so far approximate solution to the problem;

4. compute the current level $\ell_{t} = f_{t} + \lambda \Delta_{t} \(\lambda \in(0, 1)$ is a parameter)

5. build a new search point by solving the auxiliary problem

$$
x_{t + 1} = \underset{x}{\operatorname{argmin}} \{\| x - x_{t} \|_{2}^{2}: x \in X, f_{t}(x) \leq \ell_{t}\}\tag{\((\mathrm{QP}_t)\}
$$

and loop to step $t + 1$

Why and how BL converges? Let us start with several observations.

- The models $f_{t}(x) = \operatorname{max}_{\tau \smile t}[f(x_{\tau}) +(x - x_{\tau})^{T} f^{\prime}(x_{\tau})]$ grow with t and underestimate $f,$ while the best found so far values of the objective decrease with t and overestimate $f_{*}$ . Thus,

$$
\begin{array}{l} f_{1} \leq f_{2} \leq f_{3} \leq \ldots \leq f_{*} \\ f^{1} \geq f^{2} \geq f^{3} \leq \ldots \geq f_{*} \end{array}
$$

$$
\Delta_{1} \geq \Delta_{2} \geq \ldots \geq 0
$$

- Let us say that a group of subsequent iterations $J = \{s, s + 1,..., r\}$ form a segment, if $\Delta_{r} \geq(1 - \lambda) \Delta_{s}$ . We claim that

$IfJ = \{s, s + 1,..., r\}$ is a segment, then

(i) All the sets $L_{t} = \{x \in X : f_{t}(x) \leq \ell_{t}\}, t \in J$ , have a point in common, specifically, (any) minimizer u of $f_{r}(\cdot)$ over $X_{i}$ ;

(ii) For $t \in J$ , one has $\begin{array}{r}{\| \boldsymbol{x}_{t} - \boldsymbol{x}_{t + 1} \|_{2} \ge \frac{(1 - \lambda) \Delta_{r}}{L_{\| \cdot \|_{2}(f)}}} \end{array}$

Indeed,

(i): for $t \in J$ we have

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} f_{t}(u) & \leq & f_{r}(u) = f_{r} = f^{r} - \Delta_{r} \leq f^{t} - \Delta_{r} \leq f^{t} -(1 - \lambda) \Delta_{s} \\ & \leq & f^{t} -(1 - \lambda) \Delta_{t} = \ell_{t}.\end{array}
$$

(ii): We have $f_{t}(x_{t}) = f(x_{t}) \geq f^{t}$ , and $f_{t}(x_{t + 1}) \leq \ell_{t} = f^{t} -(1 - \lambda) \Delta_{t}$ . Thus, when passing from $x_{t}$ to $x_{t + 1}$ , t-th model decreases by at least $(1 - \lambda) \Delta_{t} \geq(1 - \lambda) \Delta_{r}$ . It remains to note that $f_{t}(\cdot)$ is Lipschitz continuous w.r.t. $\| \cdot \|_{2}$ with constant $L_{\parallel \cdot \parallel_{2}}(f)$

## • Main observation:

(!) The cardinality of a segment $J = \{s, s + 1,..., r\}$ of iterations can be bounded as follows:

$$
\operatorname{Card}(J) \leq \frac{\operatorname{Var}_{\| \cdot \|_{2}, X}^{2}(f)}{(1 - \lambda)^{2} \Delta_{r}^{2}}.
$$

Indeed, when $t \in J,$ the sets $L_{t} = \{x \in X : f_{t}(x) \leq \ell_{t}\}$ have a point u in common, and $x_{t + 1}$ is the projection of $x_{t}$ onto $L_{t}$ . It follows that

$$
\begin{array}{ll} & \| x_{t + 1} - u \|_{2}^{2} \leq \| x_{t} - u \|_{2}^{2} - \| x_{t} - x_{t + 1} \|_{2}^{2} \forall t \in J \\ \Rightarrow & \sum_{t \in J} \| x_{t} - x_{t + 1} \|_{2}^{2} \leq \| x_{s} - u \|_{2}^{2} \leq \max_{x, y \in X} \| x - y \|_{2}^{2} \\ \Rightarrow & \operatorname{Card}(J) \leq \frac{\underset{x, y \in X}{\max} \| x - y \|_{2}^{2}}{\underset{t \in J}{\min} \| x_{t} - x_{t + 1} \|_{2}^{2}} \\ \Rightarrow & \operatorname{Card}(J) \leq \frac{L_{\| \cdot \|_{2}}^{2}(f) \underset{x, y \in X}{\max} \| x - y \|_{2}^{2}}{(1 - \lambda)^{2} \Delta_{r}^{2}} \end{array}\tag{[by(ii)]}
$$

Corollary 5.2.2 For every $\epsilon, 0 < \epsilon < \Delta_{1}$ , the number N of steps before a $gap \le \epsilon$ is obtained (i.e., before an $\epsilon$-solution is found) does not exceed the bound

$$
N(\epsilon) = \frac{\operatorname{Var}_{\| \cdot \|_{2}, X}^{2}(f)}{\lambda(1 - \lambda)^{2}(2 - \lambda) \epsilon^{2}}.\tag{5.2.10}
$$

Proof. Assume that N is such that $\Delta_{N} > \epsilon,$ and let us bound N from above. Let us split the set of iterations $I = \{1,..., N\}$ into segments $J_{1},..., J_{m}$ as follows:

$J_{1}$ is the maximal segment which ends with iteration $N{:}$

$$
J_{1} = \{t: t \leq N,(1 - \lambda) \Delta_{t} \leq \Delta_{N}\}
$$

$J_{1}$ is certain group of subsequent iterations $\{s_{1}, s_{1} + 1,..., N\}$ . If $J_{1}$ difers from $I{:}$ $s_{1} > 1$ , we define $J_{2}$ as the maximal segment which ends with iteration $s_{1} - 1$

$$
J_{2} = \left\{t: t \leq s_{1} - 1,(1 - \lambda) \Delta_{t} \leq \Delta_{s_{1} - 1} \right\} = \left\{s_{2}, s_{2} + 1,..., s_{1} - 1 \right\}
$$

If $J_{1} \cup J_{2}$ difers from $I \colon s_{2} > 1$ , we define $J_{3}$ as the maximal segment which ends with iteration $s_{2} - 1$

$$
J_{3} = \left\{t: t \leq s_{2} - 1,(1 - \lambda) \Delta_{t} \leq \Delta_{s_{2} - 1} \right\} = \left\{s_{3}, s_{3} + 1,..., s_{2} - 1 \right\}
$$

and so on.

As a result, I will be partitioned “from the end to the beginning” into segments of iterations $J_{1}, \J_{2},..., J_{m}$ . Let $d_{\ell}$ be the gap corresponding to the last iteration from $J_{\ell}.$ . By maximality of segments $J_{\ell},$ , we have

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} d_{1} & \geq & \Delta_{N} > \epsilon \\ d_{\ell + 1} & > &(1 - \lambda)^{- 1} d_{\ell}, \ell = 1, 2, \dots, m - 1 \end{array}
$$

whence

$$
d_{\ell} > \epsilon(1 - \lambda)^{-(\ell - 1)}.
$$

We now have

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} N & = & \sum_{\ell = 1}^{m} \mathrm{Card}(J_{\ell}) \leq \sum_{\ell = 1}^{m} \frac{\operatorname{Var}_{\| \cdot \|_{2}, X}^{2}(f)}{(1 - \lambda)^{2} d_{\ell}^{2}} \leq \frac{\operatorname{Var}_{\| \cdot \|_{2}, X}^{2}(f)}{(1 - \lambda)^{2}} \sum_{\ell = 1}^{m}(1 - \lambda)^{2(\ell - 1)} \epsilon^{- 2} \\ & \leq & \frac{\operatorname{Var}_{\| \cdot \|_{2}, X}^{2}(f)}{(1 - \lambda)^{2} \epsilon^{2}} \sum_{\ell = 1}^{\infty}(1 - \lambda)^{2(\ell - 1)} = \frac{\operatorname{Var}_{\| \cdot \|_{2}, X}^{2}(f)}{(1 - \lambda)^{2}[1 -(1 - \lambda)^{2}] \epsilon^{2}} = N(\epsilon).\end{array}
$$

Discussion. 1. We have seen that the Bundle-Level method shares the dimensionindependent (and optimal in the “favourable” large-scale case) theoretical complexity bound

For every $\epsilon > 0$ , the number of steps before an $\epsilon$-solution to convex program min f(x) x∈X

is found, does not exceed $O(1) \left(\frac{\operatorname{Var}_{\parallel \cdot \parallel_{2}, X}(f)}{\epsilon} \right)^{2}$

There exists quite convincing experimental evidence that the Bundle-Level method obeys the optimal in fixed dimension “polynomial time” complexity bound

For every $\epsilon \in(0, \operatorname{Var}_{X}(f) \equiv \operatorname{max}_{X} f - \operatorname{min}_{X} f)$ , the number of steps before an $\epsilon$-solution

to convex program $\operatorname{min}_{x \in X \subset \mathbb{R}^{n}} f(x)$ is found does not exceed n ln $\left(\frac{\operatorname{Var}_{X}(f)}{\epsilon} \right) + 1$

Experimental rule: When solving convex program with n variables by $BL,$ , every n steps add new accuracy $digit$

Bundle-Level vs. Subgradient Descent

2. In BL, the number of linear constraints in the auxiliary problems

$$
f_{t} = \min_{x \in X} f_{t}(x)\tag{\((\mathrm{LP}_{t})\}
$$

$$
x_{t + 1} = \underset{x}{\operatorname{argmin}} \left\{\| x_{t} - x \|_{2}^{2}: x \in X, f_{t}(x) \leq \ell_{t} \right\}\tag{\((\mathrm{QP}_t)\}
$$

is equal to the size t of the current bundle – the collection of Affine forms $g_{\tau}(x) = f(x_{\tau}) +$ $(x - x_{\tau})^{T} f^{\prime}(x_{\tau})$ participating in model $f_{t}(\cdot)$ . Thus, the complexity of an iteration in BL grows with the iteration number. In order to suppress this phenomenon, one needs a mechanism for shrinking the bundle (and thus – simplifying the models of $f)$

- The simplest way of shrinking the bundle is to initialize d as $\Delta_{1}$ and to run plain BL until an iteration t with $\Delta_{t} \leq d / 2$ is met. At such an iteration, we

- shrink the current bundle, keeping in it the minimum number of the forms $g_{\tau}$ sufficient to ensure that

$$
f_{t} \equiv \min_{x \in X} \max_{1 \leq \tau \leq t} g_{\tau}(x) = \min_{x \in X} \max_{\text{selected}} \tau g_{\tau}(x)
$$

(this number is at most n), and

- reset d as $\Delta_{t}.$

and proceed with plain BL until the gap is again reduced by factor 2, etc.

Computational experience demonstrates that the outlined approach does not slow BL down, while keeping the size of the bundle below the level of about 2n.

What is ahead. Subgradient Descent looks very geometric, which simplifies “digesting” of the construction. However, on a close inspection this “geometricity” is completely misleading; the “actual” reasons for convergence have nothing to do with projections, distances, etc. What in fact is going on, is essentially less transparent and will be explained in the next section.

## 5.3 Mirror Descent algorithm

## 5.3.1 Problem and assumptions

In the sequel, we focus on the problem

$$
\min_{x \in X} f(x)\tag{CP}
$$

where X is a closed convex set in a Euclidean space E with inner product $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ (unless otherwise is explicitly stated, we assume w.l.o.g. E to be just R<sup>n</sup>) and assume that

(A.1): The (convex) objective f is Lipschitz continuous on $X$

To quantify this assumption, we fix once for ever a norm $\| \cdot \|$ on E and associate with f the Lipschitz constant of $f |_{X}$ w.r.t. the norm $\| \cdot \|$

$$
L_{\| \cdot \|}(f) = \min \left\{L: | f(x) - f(y) | \leq L \| x - y \| \forall x, y \in X \right\}.
$$

Note that from Convex Analysis it follows that $f$ at every point $x \in X$ admits a subgradient $f^{\prime}(x)$ such that

$$
\| f^{\prime}(x) \|_{*} \leq L_{\| \cdot \|}(f),
$$

where $\| \cdot \|,$ <sub>∗</sub> is the norm conjugate to $\| \cdot \|$ :

$$
\| \xi \|_{*} = \max \{\langle \xi, x \rangle : \| x \| \leq 1\}.
$$

For example, the norm conjugate to $\| \cdot \|_{p}$ is $\| \cdot \|_{q}$ , where $\begin{array}{r}{q = \frac{p}{p - 1}} \end{array}$

We assume that this “small norm” subgradient $f^{\prime}(x)$ is exactly the one reported by the First Order oracle as called with input $x \in X$ :

$$
\left\| f^{\prime}(x) \right\|_{*} \leq L_{\| \cdot \|}(f) \forall x \in X;\tag{5.3.1}
$$

this is not a severe restriction, since at least in the interior of X all subgradients of f are “small” in the outlined sense.

Note that by the definition of the conjugate norm, we have

$$
| \langle x, \xi \rangle | \leq \| x \| \| \xi \|_{*} \forall x, \xi \in \mathbb{R}^{n}.\tag{5.3.2}
$$

## 5.3.2 Proximal setup

The setup for the forthcoming generic algorithms for solving (CP) is given by

1. The domain X of the problem,

2. A norm $\| \cdot \|$ on the space $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ embedding $X;$ this is the norm participating in (A.1);

3. A distance generating function (DGF for short) $\omega(x) : X \mathbb{R} - \mathbf{a}$ convex continuously diferentiable function on X which is compatible with $\| \cdot \|.$ , compatibility meaning that $\omega$ is strongly convex with modulus of strong convexity 1 w.e.r. $\| \cdot \|$ , on X:

$$
\forall x, y \in X: \langle \omega^{\prime}(x) - \omega^{\prime}(y), x - y \rangle \geq \| x - y \|^{2},
$$

or, equivalently,

$$
\omega(y) \geq \omega(x) + \langle \omega^{\prime}(x), y - x \rangle + \frac{1}{2} \| x - y \|^{2} \forall(x, y \in X).\tag{5.3.3}
$$

Note: When $\omega(\cdot)$ is twice continuously diferentiable on $X$ , compatibility $\mathrm{~ f ~} \omega(\cdot)$ with $\| \cdot \|$ is equivalent to the relation

$$
\langle h, \omega^{\prime \prime}(x) h \rangle \geq \| h \|^{2} \forall(x \in X, h \in E),
$$

where $\omega^{\prime \prime}(x)$ is the Hessian of $\omega$ at x.

The outlined setup (which we refer to as Proximal setup) specifies several other important entities, specifically

- The ω-center of $\underline{{\boldsymbol X}} -$ the point

$$
x_{\omega} = \operatorname{argmin}_{x \in X} \omega(x).
$$

This point does exist (since X is closed and convex, and $\omega$ is continuous and strongly convex on $X)$ and is unique due to the strong convexity of ω. Besides this, by optimality conditions

$$
\langle \omega^{\prime}(x_{\omega}), x - x_{\omega} \rangle \geq 0 \forall x \in X.\tag{5.3.4}
$$

Note that (5.3.4) admits an extension as follows:

Fact 5.3.1 Let $X, \parallel \cdot \parallel, \omega(\cdot)$ be as above and let U be a nonempty closed convex subset $ofX$ . Then for every p, the minimizer x<sub>∗</sub> of $h_{p}(x) = \langle p, x \rangle + \omega(x)$ over $U$ exists and is unique, and is fully characterized by the relations $x_{*} \in U$ and

$$
\langle p + \omega^{\prime}(x_{*}), u - x_{*} \rangle \geq 0 \forall u \in U.\tag{5.3.5}
$$

The proof is readily given by optimality conditions.

- The prox-term (or local distance, or Bregman distance from x to y), defined as

$$
V_{x}(y) = \omega(y) - \langle \omega^{\prime}(x), y - x \rangle - \omega(x);
$$

$$
[x, y \in X]
$$

note that $0 = V_{x}(x)$ and $\begin{array}{r}{V_{x}(y) \geq \frac{1}{2} \Vert y - x \Vert^{2}} \end{array}$ by (5.3.3);

- The quantity

$$
\Theta = \sup_{x, y \in X} V_{x}(y) = \sup_{x, y \in X} \left[\omega(y) - \omega(x) - \langle \omega^{\prime}(x), y - x \rangle \right] \geq \frac{1}{2} \sup_{x, y \in X} \| y - x \|^{2},
$$

where the concluding inequality is due to (5.3.3). Note that Θ is finite if and only if X is bounded. For a bounded X, the quantity

$$
\Omega = \sqrt{2 \Theta},
$$

will be called the ω-diameter of X. Observe that from $V_{x}(y) \geq \frac{1}{2} \| y - x \|^{2}$ it follows that $\| y - x \|^{2} \leq 2V_{x}(y)$ whenever $x, y \in X$ , that is, Ω upper-bounds the k · k-diameter $\operatorname{max}_{x, y \in X} \| x - y \|$ of X.

Remark 5.3.1 The importance of ω-diameter of a domain X stems from the fact that, as we shall see in the mean time, the eficiency estimate (the dependence of accuracy on iteration count) of Mirror Descent algorithm as applied to problem (CP) on a bounded domain X depends on the underlying proximal setup solely via the value Ω of the ω- diameter of X (the less is this diameter, the better).

- Prox-mapping

$$
\operatorname{Prox}_{x}(\xi) = \underset{y \in X}{\operatorname{argmin}} \left\{V_{x}(y) + \langle \xi, y \rangle \right\} = \underset{y \in X}{\operatorname{argmin}} \left\{\omega(y) + \langle \xi - \omega^{\prime}(x), y \rangle \right\}: \mathbb{R}^{n} \to X.
$$

Here the parameter of the mapping — prox-center x – is a point from X. Note that by construction the prox-mapping takes its values in X.

Sometimes we shall use a modification of the prox-mapping as follows:

$$
\operatorname{Prox}_{x}^{U}(\xi) = \underset{y \in U}{\operatorname{argmin}} \left\{V_{x}(y) + \langle \xi, y \rangle \right\} = \underset{y \in U}{\operatorname{argmin}} \left\{\omega(y) + \langle \xi - \omega^{\prime}(x), y \rangle \right\}: \mathbb{R}^{n} \to U
$$

where U is a closed convex subset of X. Here the prox-center x is again a point from X. By Fact 5.3.1, the latter mapping takes its values in U and satisfies the relation

$$
\langle \xi - \omega^{\prime}(x) + \omega^{\prime}(x_{*}), u - x_{*} \rangle \geq 0 \forall u \in U.\tag{5.3.6}
$$

Note that the methods we are about to present require at every step computing one (or two) values of the prox-mapping, and in order for the iterations to be simple, this task should be relatively easy. In other words, from the viewpoint of implementation, we need X and ω to be “simple” and to “match each other.”

## 5.3.3 Standard proximal setups

We are about to list the standard proximal setups we will be working with. Justification of these setups (i.e., verifying that the DGFs ω listed below are compatible with the corresponding norms, and that the ω-diameters of the domains to follow admit the bounds we are about to announce) is relegated to section 5.9

## 5.3.3.1 Ball setup

The Ball (called also the Euclidean) setup is as follows: E is a Euclidean space, $\| x \| = \| x \|_{2} : =$ ${\sqrt{\langle x, x \rangle}}, \omega(x) ={\textstyle{\frac{1}{2}}} \langle x, x \rangle$

Here $\begin{array}{r}{V_{x}(y) = \frac{1}{2} \| x - y \|_{2}^{2}, ~ x_{\omega}} \end{array}$ is the $\| \cdot \|_{2}$ -closest to the origin point of $X$ . For a bounded $X$ , $\Omega = \operatorname{max}_{y \in X} \| y - x_{\omega} \|_{2}$ is exactly the $\| \cdot \|_{2}$ –diameter of X. The prox-mapping is

$$
\mathrm{Prox}_{x}(\xi) = \Pi_{X}(x - \xi),
$$

where

$$
\Pi_{X}(h) = \operatorname{argmin}_{y \in X} \| h - y \|_{2}
$$

is what is called the metric projector onto X. This projector is easy to compute when X is $\| \cdot \|_{p^{-}} \mathrm{ball}$ , or the “nonnegative part” of $\| \cdot \|_{p^{-}} \mathrm{ball} -$ the set $\{x \geq a : \| x - a \|_{p} \leq r\}$ , or the standard simplex

$$
\Delta_{n} = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}: x \geq 0, \sum_{i} x_{i} = 1\},
$$

of the full-dimensional standard simplex

$$
\Delta_{n}^{+} = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}: x \geq 0, \sum_{i} x_{i} \leq 1\}.
$$

Finally, the norm conjugate to $\| \cdot \|_{2}$ is $\| \cdot \|_{2}$ itself.

## 5.3.3.2 Entropy setup

For Entropy setup, $E = \mathbb{R}^{n}, \parallel \cdot \parallel = \parallel \cdot \parallel_{1}$ , X is a closed convex subset in of the full-dimensional standard simplex $\Delta_{n}^{+}$ , and $\omega(x)$ is the regularized entropy

$$
\omega(x) =(1 + \delta) \sum_{i = 1}^{n}(x_{i} + \delta / n) \ln(x_{i} + \delta / n): \Delta_{n} \to \mathbb{R},\tag{5.3.7}
$$

where the “regularizing parameter” $\delta > 0$ (introduced to make ω continuously diferentiable on $\Delta_{n}^{+})$ is small; for the sake of definiteness, from now on we set $\delta = 10^{- 16}$

The ω-center can be easily pointed out when X is either the standard simplex $\Delta_{n}$ , or the full-dimensional standard simplex $\Delta_{n}^{+}$ ; when $X = \Delta_{n}$ , one has

$$
x_{\omega} =[1 / n; \dots; 1 / n],
$$

when $n \geq 3$ , the same holds true when $X = \Delta_{n}^{+}$ and $n \geq 3$

An important fact is that for Entropy setup, the ω-diameter of $X \subset \Delta_{n}^{+}$ is nearly dimensionindependent, specifically,

$$
\Omega \leq O(1) \sqrt{\ln(n + 1)},\tag{5.3.8}
$$

where $O(1)$ is a positive absolute constant. Finally, note that the norm conjugate to $\| \cdot \|_{1}$ is the uniform norm $\| \cdot \|_{\infty}$

## 5.3.3.3 $\ell_{1} / \ell_{2}$ and Simplex setups

Now let $E = \mathbb{R}^{k_{1} + \ldots + k_{n}} = \mathbb{R}^{k_{1}} \times \ldots \times \mathbb{R}^{k_{n}}$ , so that $x \in E$ can be represented as a block vector with n blocks $\boldsymbol{x}^{i}[\boldsymbol{x}] \in \mathbb{R}^{k_{i}}$ . The norm $\| \cdot \|$ is the so called $\ell_{1} / \ell_{2}$ , or $block – \ell_{1}$ , norm:

$$
\| x \| = \sum_{i = 1}^{n} \| x^{i}[x] \|_{2}.
$$

Bounded case. When X is a closed convex subset of the unit ball $Z = \{x \in E : \| x \| \leq 1\}$ , which we refer to as bounded $case^{1}$ , a good choice of ω is

$$
\omega(x =[x^{1}; \dots; x^{n}]) = \frac{1}{p \gamma} \sum_{j = 1}^{p} \| x^{j} \|_{2}^{p}, p = \left\{\begin{array}{ll} 2, & n \leq 2 \\ 1 + \frac{1}{\ln n}, & n \geq 3 \end{array} \right., \gamma = \left\{\begin{array}{ll} 1, & n = 1 \\ \frac{1}{2}, & n = 2 \\ \frac{1}{e \ln(n)}, & n > 2 \end{array} \right.\tag{5.3.9}
$$

which results in

$$
\Omega \leq O(1) \sqrt{\ln(n + 1)}.\tag{5.3.10}
$$

General case. It turns out that the function

$$
\widehat{\omega}(x =[x^{1}; \dots; x^{n}]) = \frac{n^{(p - 1)(2 - p) / p}}{2 \gamma} \left[\sum_{j = 1}^{n} \| x^{j} \|_{2}^{p} \right]^{\frac{2}{p}}: E \to \mathbb{R}\tag{5.3.11}
$$

with p, γ given by (5.3.9) is a compatible with k · k-norm DGF for the entire $E,$ so that its restriction on an arbitrary closed convex nonempty subset X of E is a DGF for X compatible with $\| \cdot \|$ . When, in addition, X is bounded, the ${\widehat{\omega}} |_{X}$ -radius of X can be bounded as

$$
\Omega \leq O(1) \sqrt{\ln(n + 1)} R,\tag{5.3.12}
$$

where $R < \infty$ is such that $X \subset \{x \in E : \| x \| \leq R\}$

Computing the prox-mapping is easy when, $\mathrm{e.g.}$ ,

A. $X = \{x : \| x \| \leq 1\}$ and the DGF (5.3.9) is used, or

B. $X = E$ and the DGF (5.3.11) is used.

Indeed, in the case of $\mathrm{A},$ computing prox-mapping reduces to solving convex program of the form

$$
\min_{y^{1}, \dots, y^{n}} \left\{\sum_{j = 1}^{n}[\langle y^{j}, b^{j} \rangle + \| y^{j} \|_{2}^{p}]: \sum_{j} \| y^{j} \|_{2} \leq 1 \right\};\tag{P}
$$

clearly, at the optimum $y^{j}$ are nonpositive multiples of $b^{j}$ , which immediately reduces the problem to

$$
\min_{s_{1}, \dots, s_{n}} \left\{\sum_{j} \left[s_{j}^{p} - \beta_{j} s_{j} \right]: s \geq 0, \sum_{j} s_{j} \leq 1 \right\},\tag{\((P')\}
$$

where $\beta_{j} \ \geq \0$ are given and $p > 1$ . The latter problem is just a problem of minimizing a single separable convex function under a single separable constraint. The Lagrange dual of this problem is just a univariate convex program with easy to compute (just $O(n){\mathrm{~ a.o.}})$ value and derivative of the objective. As a result, $(P^{\prime})$ can be solved within machine accuracy in $O(n)$ $\mathrm{{a.o.}}$ , and therefore $(P)$ can be solved within machine accuracy in O(dim E) a.o.

In the case of B, similar argument reduces computing prox-mapping to solving the problem

$$
\min_{s_{1}, \dots, s_{n}} \left\{\|[s_{1}; \dots; s_{n}] \|_{p}^{2} - \sum_{j} \beta_{j} s_{j}: s \geq 0 \right\},
$$

where $\beta \geq 0$ . This problem admits a closed form solution (find it!), and here again computing prox-mapping takes just O(dim E) a.o.

Comments. When $n = 1$ , the $\ell_{1} / \ell_{2}$ norm becomes nothing but the Euclidean norm $\| \cdot \|_{2}$ on $E = \mathbb{R}^{m1}$ , and the proximal setups we have just described become nothing but the Ball setup. As another extreme, consider the case when $m_{1} = \ldots = m_{n} = 1$ , that is, the $\ell_{1} / \ell_{2}$ norm becomes the plain $\| \cdot \|_{1^{-}} \mathrm{norm}$ on $E = \mathbb{R}^{n}$ . Now let X be a closed convex subset of the unit $\| \cdot \|_{1^{-}} \mathrm{ball} \mathrm{of} \mathbb{R}^{n}$ ; restricting the DGF (5.3.10) for the latter set onto $X$ , we get what we shall call Simplex setup. Note that when X is a part of the full dimensional simplex $\Delta_{n}^{+}$ , Simplex setup can be viewed as alternative to Entropy setup. Note that in the case in question both Entropy and Simplex setups yield basically identical bounds on the ω-diameter of X (and thus result in algorithms with basically identical eficiency estimates, see Remark 5.3.1).

## 5.3.3.4 Nuclear norm and Spectahedron setups

The concluding pair of “standard” proximal setups we are about to consider deals with the case when E is the space of matrices. It makes sense to speak about block-diagonal matrices of a given block-diagonal structure. Specifically,

- Given a collection $\mu, \nu$ of n pairs of positive integers $\mu_{i}, \nu_{i}.$ , let $\mathbf{M}^{\mu \nu}$ be the space of all real matrices $x = \mathrm{Diag} \{x^{1},..., x^{n}\}$ with n diagonal blocks $x^{i}$ of sizes $\mu_{i} \times \nu_{i}, i = 1,..., n$ . We equip this space with natural linear operations and Frobenius inner product

$$
\langle x, y \rangle = \operatorname{Tr}(xy^{T}).
$$

The nuclear norm $\| \cdot \|_{\mathrm{nuc}}$ on $\mathbf{M}^{\mu \nu}$ is defined as

$$
\| x = \operatorname{Diag} \left\{x^{1}, \dots, x^{n} \right\} \|_{\text{n u c}} = \| \sigma(x) \|_{1} = \sum_{i = 1}^{n} \| \sigma \left(x^{i}\right) \|_{1},
$$

where $\sigma(y)$ is the collection of singular values of a matrix $y.$

Note: We always assume that $\mu_{i} \le \nu_{i}$ for all $i \leq n^{\mathrm{~ 2 ~}}$ . With this agreement, we can think of $\sigma(x), x \in \mathbf{M}^{\mu \nu}$ , as of $\textstyle m = \sum_{i = 1}^{n}$ -dimensional vector with entries arranged in the non-ascending order.

- Given a collection ν of n positive integers $\nu_{i}, i = 1,..., n$ , let $\mathbf{S}^{\nu}$ be the space of symmetric block-diagonal matrices with n diagonal blocks of sizes $\boldsymbol{\nu}_{i} \times \boldsymbol{\nu}_{i}, i = 1,..., n.\ \mathbf{S}^{\nu} = \mathbf{S}^{\nu_{1}} \times...\times$ $\mathbf{S}^{\nu_{n}}$ is just a subspace in $\mathbf{M}^{\nu \nu}$ ; the restriction of the nuclear norm on $\mathbf{M}^{\mu \mu}$ is sometimes called the trace norm on $\mathbf{S}^{\nu};$ ; it is nothing but the $\lVert \cdot \rVert_{1^{-} \mathrm{{norm}}}$ of the vector of eigenvalues of a matrix $x \in \mathbf{S}^{\nu}$

Nuclear norm setup. Here $E = \mathbf{M}^{\mu \nu}, \mu_{i} \leq \nu_{i}, 1 \leq i \leq n$ , and $\| \cdot \|$ is the nuclear norm $\| \cdot \|_{\mathrm{nuc}}$ on E. We set

$$
m = \sum_{i = 1}^{n} \mu_{i},
$$

so that m is thus the smaller size of a matrix from $E.$

Note that the norm $\| \cdot \|_{*}$ <sub>∗</sub> is the usual spectral norm (the largest singular value) of a matrix. Bounded case. When X is a closed convex subset of the unit ball $Z = \{x \in E : \| x \| \leq 1\}$ which we refer to as bounded case, a good choice of ω is

$$
\omega(x) = \frac{4 \sqrt{e} \ln(2m)}{2^{q}(1 + q)} \sum_{i = 1}^{m} \sigma_{i}^{1 + q}(x): X \to \mathbb{R}, q = \frac{1}{2 \ln(2m)},\tag{5.3.13}
$$

which results in

$$
\Omega \leq 2 \sqrt{2 \sqrt{e} \ln(2m)} \leq 4 \sqrt{\ln(2m)}.\tag{5.3.14}
$$

General case. It turns out that the function

$$
\widehat{\omega}(x) = 2 e \ln(2m) \left[\sum_{j = 1}^{m} \sigma_{j}^{1 + q}(x) \right]^{\frac{2}{1 + q}}: E \to \mathbb{R}, q = \frac{1}{2 \ln(2m)}\tag{5.3.15}
$$

is a DGF for $Z = E$ compatible with $\| \cdot \|_{\mathrm{nuc}}$ , so that the restriction of $\widehat{\omega}$ on a nonempty closed and convex subset X of E is a DGF for X compatible with $\| \cdot \|_{\mathrm{nuc}}$ . When X is bounded, we have

$$
\Omega \leq O(1) \sqrt{\ln(2m)} R,\tag{5.3.16}
$$

where $R < \infty$ is such that $X \subset \{x \in E : \| x \|_{\mathrm{nuc}} \leq R\}$

It is clear how to compute the associated prox mappings in the cases when

A. $X = \{x : \| x \| \leq 1\}$ and the DGF (5.3.13) is used, or

B. X = E and the DGF (5.3.15) is used.

Indeed, let us start with the case of A, where computing the prox-mapping reduces to solving the convex program

$$
\min_{y \in \mathbf{M}^{\mu \nu}} \left\{\operatorname{Tr}(y \eta^{T}) + \sum_{i = 1}^{m} \sigma_{i}^{p}(y): \sum_{i} \sigma_{i}(y) \leq 1 \right\}\tag{Q}
$$

Let $\eta ~ = ~ uhv^{T}$ be the singular value decomposition of $\eta,$ so that $u \in \mathbf{\partial} \mathbf{M}^{\mu \mu}, \v \in \mathbf{\partial} \mathbf{M}^{\nu \nu}$ are block-diagonal orthogonal matrices, and $h \in \mathbf{M}^{\mu \nu}$ is block-diagonal matrix with diagonal blocks $h^{j} =[\mathrm{Diag} \{g^{j}\}, 0_{\mu_{j} \times[\nu_{j} - \mu_{j}]}], g^{j} \in{\bf R}_{+}^{\mu_{j}}$ . Passing in (Q) from variable y to the variable $z = u^{T} yv$ 2 the problem becomes

$$
\min_{z^{j} \in \mathbf{M}^{\mu_{j} \nu_{j}}, 1 \leq j \leq n} \left\{\mathrm{Tr}(z^{j}[h^{j}]^{T}) + \sum_{j = 1}^{n} \sum_{k = 1}^{\mu_{j}} \sigma_{k}^{p}(z^{j}): \sum_{j = 1}^{n} \sum_{k = 1}^{\mu_{j}} \sigma_{k}(z^{j}) \leq 1 \right\}.
$$

This (clearly solvable) problem has a rich group of symmetries; specifically, due to the diagonal nature of $h^{j}$ , replacing a block $z^{j}$ in a feasible solution with Diag $\{\epsilon\} z^{j} \mathrm{Diag} \{\epsilon^{\prime}\}$ , where $\epsilon$ is a vector of ±1’s of dimension $\mu_{j}$ , and $\epsilon^{\prime}$ is obtained from $\epsilon$ by adding $\nu_{j} - \mu_{j}$ of ±1 entries to the right of $\epsilon$. Since the problem is convex, it has an optimal solution which is preserved by the above symmetries, that is, such that all $z^{j}$ are diagonal matrices. Denoting by $\zeta^{j}$ the diagonals of these diagonal matrices and setting $g =[g^{1};...; g^{n}] \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$ , the problem becomes

$$
\min_{\zeta =[\zeta^{1}; \dots; \zeta^{n}] \in \mathbb{R}^{n}} \left\{\zeta^{T} g + \sum_{k = 1}^{m} | \zeta_{k} |^{p}: \sum_{k} | \zeta_{k} | \leq 1 \right\},
$$

which, basically, is the problem we have met when computing prox–mapping in the case A of $\ell_{1} / \ell_{2}$ setup; as we remember, this problem can be solved within machine precision in $O(m)$ a.o.

Completely similar reasoning shows that in the case of ${\mathrm{B}},$ computing prox-mapping reduces, at the price of a single singular value decomposition of a matrix from $\mathbf{M}^{\mu \nu}$ , to solving the same problem as in the case B of $\ell_{1} / \ell_{2}$ setup. The bottom line is that in the cases of $A,$ , B, the computational efort of computing prox-mapping is dominated by the necessity to carry out singular value decomposition of a matrix from $\mathbf{M}^{\mu \nu}$

Remark 5.3.2 A careful reader should have recognize at this point the deep similarity between the $\ell_{1} / \ell_{2}$ and the nuclear norm setups. This similarity has a very simple explanation: the $\ell_{1} / \ell_{2}$ situation is a very special case of the nuclear norm one. Indeed, a block vector $y =[y^{1};...; y^{n}]$ 2 $y^{j} \in \mathbb{R}^{k_{j}}$ , can be thought of as the block-diagonal matrix $y^{+}$ with n diagonal blocks $[y^{\dot{j}}]^{T}$ of sizes $1 \times k_{j}, j = 1,..., n$ . With this identification of block-vectors y and block-diagonal matrices, the singular values of $y^{+}$ are exactly the norms $\| y^{j} \|_{2}, j = 1,..., m \equiv n$ , so that the nuclear norm of $y^{+}$ is exactly the block- $\mathbf{\nabla} \cdot \mathbf{\rho}_{1}$ norm of $y.$ Up to minor diferences in the coeficients in the formulas for DGFs, our proximal setups respect this reduction of the $\ell_{1} / \ell_{2}$ situation to the nuclear norm one.

Spectahedron setup. Consider a space $\mathbf{S}^{\nu}$ of block-diagonal symmetric matrices of blockdiagonal structure $\nu,$ and let $\Delta_{\nu}$ and $\Delta_{\nu}^{+}$ be, respectively, the standard and the full-dimensional spectahedrons in $\mathbf{S}^{\nu}$ :

$$
\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{\nu} = \{x \in \mathbf{S}^{\nu}: x \succeq 0, \operatorname{Tr}(x) = 1\}, \boldsymbol{\Delta}_{\nu}^{+} = \{x \in \mathbf{S}^{\nu}: x \succeq 0, \operatorname{Tr}(x) \leq 1\}.
$$

Let X be a nonempty closed convex subset of $\Delta_{\nu}^{+}$ . Restricting the DGF (5.3.13) associated with $\mathbf{M}^{\nu \nu}$ onto $\mathbf{S}^{\nu}$ (the latter space is a linear subspace of $\mathbf{M}^{\nu \nu})$ and further onto $X,$ we get a continuously diferentiable DGF for $X$ , and the ω-radius of X does not exceed $O(1) \sqrt{\ln(m + 1)}$ 2 where, $m = \nu_{1} + \ldots + \nu_{n}$ . When $X = \Delta_{\nu}$ or $X = \Delta_{\nu}^{+}$ , the computational efort for computing prox-mapping is dominated by the necessity to carry out eigenvalue decomposition of a matrix from $\mathbf{S}^{\nu}$

## 5.3.4 Mirror Descent algorithm

## 5.3.4.1 Basic Fact

In the sequel, we shall use the following, crucial in our context,

Fact 5.3.2 Given proximal setup $\| \cdot \|, X, \omega(\cdot)$ along with a closed convex subset U of X, let $x \in X, \xi \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $x_{+} = \mathrm{Prox}_{x}^{U}(\xi)$ . Then

$$
\forall u \in U: \langle \xi, x_{+} - u \rangle \leq V_{x}(u) - V_{x_{+}}(u) - V_{x}(x_{+}).\tag{5.3.17}
$$

Proof. $\mathrm{By}$ Fact 5.3.1, we have

$$
\begin{array}{rl} & x_{+} = \operatorname{argmin}_{y \in U} \{\omega(y) + \langle \xi - \omega^{\prime}(x), y \rangle\} \\ \Rightarrow & \forall u \in U: \langle \omega^{\prime}(x_{+}) - \omega^{\prime}(x) + \xi, u - x_{+} \rangle \geq 0 \\ \Rightarrow & \forall u \in U: \langle \xi, x_{+} - u \rangle \leq \langle \omega^{\prime}(x_{+}) - \omega^{\prime}(x), u - x_{+} \rangle \\ & \qquad =[\omega(u) - \omega(x) - \langle \omega^{\prime}(x), u - x \rangle] -[\omega(u) - \omega(x_{+}) - \langle \omega^{\prime}(x_{+}), u - x_{+} \rangle] \\ & \qquad -[\omega(x_{+}) - \omega(x) - \langle \omega^{\prime}(x), x_{+} - x \rangle] \\ & \qquad = V_{x}(u) - V_{x_{+}}(u) - V_{x}(x_{+}).\quad \square \end{array}
$$

A byproduct of the above computation is a wonderful identity due to Marc Teboulle:

Magic Identity: Whenever $x_{+} \in X, x \in X$ and $u \in X$ , we have

$$
\langle \omega^{\prime}(x_{+}) - \omega^{\prime}(x), u - x_{+} \rangle = V_{x}(u) - V_{x_{+}}(u) - V_{x}(x_{+}).\tag{5.3.18}
$$

## 5.3.4.2 Standing Assumption

From now on, if otherwise is not explicitly stated, we assume that the domain X of problem (CP) in question is bounded.

## 5.3.4.3 MD: Description

The simplest version of the construction we are developing is the Mirror Descent (MD) algorithm for solving problem

$$
\min_{x \in X} f(x).\tag{CP}
$$

MD is given by the recurrence

$$
x_{1} \in X; x_{t + 1} = \mathrm{Prox}_{x_{t}}(\gamma_{t} f^{\prime}(x_{t})), t = 1, 2, \ldots\tag{5.3.19}
$$

where $\gamma_{t} > 0$ are positive stepsizes.

The points $x_{t}$ in (5.3.19) are what is called search points – the points where we collect the first order information on $f.$ There is no reason to insist that these search points should be also the approximate solutions $x^{t}$ generated in course of $t = 1, 2, \dots$ . steps. In MD as applied to (CP), there are two good ways to define the approximate solutions $x^{t}$ , specifically:

— the best found so far approximate solution $x_{\mathrm{bst}}^{t} ~ \mathrm{-}$ the point of the collection $x_{1},..., x_{t}$ with the smallest value of the objective $f,$ and

— the aggregated solution

$$
x^{t} = \left[\sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau} \right]^{- 1} \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau} x_{\tau}.\tag{5.3.20}
$$

Note that $x^{t} \in X$ (as a convex combination of the points $x_{\tau}$ which by construction belong to X).

Remark 5.3.3 Note that MD with Ball setup is nothing but SD (check $\it{it !}$

## 5.3.4.4 MD: Complexity analysis

Convergence properties of MD are summarized in the following simple

Theorem 5.3.1 For every $\tau \geq 1$ and every $u \in X$ , one has

$$
\gamma_{\tau} \langle f^{\prime}(x_{\tau}), x_{\tau} - u \rangle \leq V_{x_{\tau}}(u) - V_{x_{\tau + 1}}(u) + \frac{1}{2} \| \gamma_{\tau} f^{\prime}(x_{\tau}) \|_{*}^{2}.\tag{5.3.21}
$$

As a result, for every $t \geq 1$ one has

$$
f(x^{t}) - \min_{X} f \leq \frac{\frac{\Omega^{2}}{2} + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau}^{2} \| f^{\prime}(x_{\tau}) \|_{*}^{2}}{\sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau}},\tag{5.3.22}
$$

and similarly for $\boldsymbol{x}_{\mathrm{bst}}^{t}$ in the role $ofx^{t}$

In particular, given a number T of iterations we intend to perform and setting

$$
\gamma_{t} = \frac{\Omega}{\| f^{\prime}(x_{t}) \|_{*} \sqrt{T}}, 1 \leq t \leq T,\tag{5.3.23}
$$

we ensure that

$$
f(x^{T}) - \min_{X} f \leq \Omega \frac{\sqrt{T}}{\sum_{t = 1}^{T} \frac{1}{\| f^{\prime}(x_{t}) \|_{*}}} \leq \frac{\Omega \max_{t \leq T} \| f^{\prime}(x_{t}) \|_{*}}{\sqrt{T}} \leq \frac{\Omega L_{\| \cdot \|}(f)}{\sqrt{T}},\tag{5.3.24}
$$

$(L_{\parallel \cdot \parallel}(f)$ is the Lipschitz constant of f w $.r.t.\parallel \cdot \parallel)$ , and similarly for $x_{\mathrm{bst}}^{T}$

Proof. ${\bf 1}^{0}$ . Let us set $\xi_{\tau} = \gamma_{\tau} f^{\prime}(x_{\tau})$ , so that

$$
x_{\tau + 1} = \operatorname{Prox}_{x_{\tau}}(\xi_{\tau}) = \underset{y \in X}{\operatorname{argmin}} \left[\langle \xi_{\tau} - \omega^{\prime}(x_{\tau}), y \rangle + \omega(y) \right].
$$

We have

$$
\begin{array}{ll} & \langle \xi_{\tau} - \omega^{\prime}(x_{\tau}) + \omega^{\prime}(x_{\tau + 1}), u - x_{\tau + 1} \rangle \geq 0[\text{by Fact 5.3.1 with} U = X] \\ \Rightarrow & \langle \xi_{\tau}, x_{\tau} - u \rangle \leq \langle \xi_{\tau}, x_{\tau} - x_{\tau + 1} \rangle + \langle \omega^{\prime}(x_{\tau + 1}) - \omega^{\prime}(x_{\tau}), u - x_{\tau + 1} \rangle \\ & = \langle \xi_{\tau}, x_{\tau} - x_{\tau + 1} \rangle + V_{x_{\tau}}(u) - V_{x_{\tau + 1}}(u) - V_{x_{\tau}}(x_{\tau + 1})[\text{Magic Identity (5.3.18)}] \\ & = \langle \xi_{\tau}, x_{\tau} - x_{\tau + 1} \rangle + V_{x_{\tau}}(u) - V_{x_{\tau + 1}}(u) -[\underbrace{\omega(x_{\tau + 1}) - \omega(x_{\tau}) - \langle \omega^{\prime}(x_{\tau}), x_{\tau + 1} - x_{\tau} \rangle}] \\ & \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \\ & = V_{x_{\tau}}(u) - V_{x_{\tau + 1}}(u) +[\langle \xi_{\tau}, x_{\tau} - x_{\tau + 1} \rangle - \frac{1}{2} \| x_{\tau + 1} - x_{\tau} \|^{2}] \\ & \leq V_{x_{\tau}}(u) - V_{x_{\tau + 1}}(u) +[\| \xi_{\tau} \|_{*} \| x_{\tau} - x_{\tau + 1} \| - \frac{1}{2} \| x_{\tau + 1} - x_{\tau} \|^{2}][\text{see (5.3.2)}] \\ & \leq V_{x_{\tau}}(u) - V_{x_{\tau + 1}}(u) + \frac{1}{2} \| \xi_{\tau} \|_{*}^{2}[\text{since} ab - \frac{1}{2} b^{2} \leq \frac{1}{2} a^{2}] \end{array}
$$

Recalling that $\xi_{\tau} = \gamma_{\tau} f^{\prime}(x_{\tau})$ , we arrive at (5.3.21).

$\mathbf{2}^{0}$ . Denoting by x<sub>∗</sub> a minimizer of $f$ on X, substituting $u = x_{*}$ in (5.3.21) and taking into account that f is convex, we get

$$
\gamma_{\tau}[f(x_{\tau}) - f(x_{*})] \leq \gamma_{\tau} \langle f^{\prime}(x_{\tau}), x_{\tau} - x_{*} \rangle \leq V_{x_{\tau}}(x_{*}) - V_{x_{\tau + 1}}(x_{*}) + \frac{1}{2} \gamma_{\tau}^{2} \| f^{\prime}(x_{\tau}) \|_{*}^{2}.
$$

Summing up these inequalities over $\tau = 1,..., t$ , dividing both sides by $\begin{array}{r}{\Gamma_{t} \equiv \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau}} \end{array}$ <sub>τ</sub> and setting $\nu_{\tau} = \gamma_{\tau} / \Gamma_{t},$ , we get

$$
\left[\sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \nu_{\tau} f(x_{\tau}) \right] - f(x_{*}) \leq \frac{V_{x_{1}}(x_{*}) - V_{x_{t + 1}}(x_{*}) + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau}^{2} \| f^{\prime}(x_{\tau}) \|_{*}^{2}}{\Gamma_{t}}.\tag{\( \left(*\right)\}
$$

Since $\nu_{\tau}$ are positive and sum up to 1, and $f$ is convex, the left hand side in $(*)$ is $\geq f(x^{t}) - f(x_{*})$ (recall that $\begin{array}{r}{x^{t} = \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \nu_{\tau} x_{\tau}) \mathrm{;}} \end{array}$ ; it clearly is also $\geq f(x_{\mathrm{bst}}^{t}) - f(x_{\ast})$ . Since $\begin{array}{r}{V_{x_{1}}(x) \leq \frac{\Omega^{2}}{2}} \end{array}$ due to the definition of Ω and to $x_{1} = x_{\omega}$ , while $V_{x_{t + 1}}(\cdot) \geq 0$ , the right hand side in (∗) is $\leq$ the right hand side in (5.3.22), and we arrive at (5.3.22).

${\bf 3}^{0}$ . Relation (5.3.24) is readily given by (5.3.22), (5.3.23) and the fact that $\| f^{\prime}(x_{t}) \|_{*} \ \leq$ $L_{\parallel \cdot \parallel}(f)$ , see (5.3.1). ✷

## 5.3.4.5 Refinement

We can slightly modify the MD algorithm and refine its complexity analysis.

Theorem 5.3.2 Let X be bounded, so that the ω-diameter Ω of $X$ is finite. Let $\lambda_{1}, \lambda_{2},..$ . be positive reals such that

$$
\lambda_{1} / \gamma_{1} \leq \lambda_{2} / \gamma_{2} \leq \lambda_{3} / \gamma_{3} \leq \dots,\tag{5.3.25}
$$

and let

$$
x^{t} = \frac{\sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \lambda_{\tau} x_{\tau}}{\sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \lambda_{\tau}}.
$$

Then $x^{t} \in X$ and

$$
f(x^{t}) - \min_{X} f \leq \frac{\sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \lambda_{\tau}[f(x_{\tau}) - \min_{X} f]}{\sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \lambda_{\tau}} \leq \frac{\frac{\lambda_{t}}{\gamma_{t}} \Omega^{2} + \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \lambda_{\tau} \gamma_{\tau} \| f^{\prime}(x_{\tau}) \|_{*}^{2}}{2 \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \lambda_{\tau}},\tag{5.3.26}
$$

and similarly for $\boldsymbol{x}_{\mathrm{bst}}^{t}$ in the role $ofx^{t}$

Note that (5.3.22) is nothing but (5.3.26) as applied with $\lambda_{\tau} = \gamma_{\tau}, 1 \leq \tau \leq t.$ Proof of Theorem 5.3.2. We still have at our disposal (5.3.21); multiplying both sides of this relation by $\lambda_{\tau} / \gamma_{\tau}$ and summing up the resulting inequalities over $\tau = 1,..., t$ , we get

$$
\begin{array}{l} \forall(u \in X): \\ \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \lambda_{\tau} \langle f^{\prime}(x_{\tau}), x_{\tau} - u \rangle \leq \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \frac{\lambda_{\tau}}{\gamma_{\tau}}[V_{x_{\tau}}(u) - V_{x_{\tau + 1}}(u)] + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \lambda_{\tau} \gamma_{\tau} \| f^{\prime}(x_{\tau}) \|_{*}^{2} \\ = \frac{\lambda_{1}}{\gamma_{1}} V_{x_{1}}(u) + \underbrace{\left[\frac{\lambda_{2}}{\gamma_{2}} - \frac{\lambda_{1}}{\gamma_{1}} \right]}_{\geq 0} V_{x_{2}}(u) + \underbrace{\left[\frac{\lambda_{3}}{\gamma_{3}} - \frac{\lambda_{2}}{\gamma_{2}} \right]}_{\geq 0} V_{x_{3}}(u) +...+ \underbrace{\left[\frac{\lambda_{t}}{\gamma_{t}} - \frac{\lambda_{t - 1}}{\gamma_{t - 1}} \right]}_{\geq 0} V_{x_{t}}(u) \\ - \frac{\lambda_{t}}{\gamma_{t}} V_{x_{t + 1}}(u) + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \lambda_{\tau} \gamma_{\tau} \| f^{\prime}(x_{\tau}) \|_{*}^{2} \leq \frac{\lambda_{t}}{\gamma_{t}} \frac{\Omega^{2}}{2} + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \lambda_{\tau} \gamma_{\tau} \| f^{\prime}(x_{\tau}) \|_{*}^{2}, \end{array}
$$

where the concluding inequality is due to $\begin{array}{r}{0 \leq V_{x_{\tau}}(u) \leq \frac{\Omega^{2}}{2}} \end{array}$ for all $\tau$ . As a result,

$$
\begin{array}{c} \max_{u \in X} \Lambda_{t}^{- 1} \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \lambda_{\tau} \langle f^{\prime}(x_{\tau}), x_{\tau} - u \rangle \leq \frac{\frac{\lambda_{t}}{\gamma_{t}} \Omega^{2} + \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \lambda_{\tau} \gamma_{\tau}}{2 \Lambda_{t}} \\ \left[\Lambda_{t} = \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \lambda_{\tau} \right].\end{array}\tag{5.3.27}
$$

On the other hand, by convexity of $f$ we have

$$
f(x^{t}) - f(x_{*}) \leq \Lambda_{t}^{- 1} \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \lambda_{\tau}[f(x_{\tau}) - f(x_{*})] \leq \Lambda_{t}^{- 1} \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \lambda_{\tau} \langle f^{\prime}(x_{\tau}), x_{\tau} - x_{*} \rangle,\tag{5.3.28}
$$

which combines with (5.3.27) to yield (5.3.26). Since by evident reasons

$$
f(x_{\mathrm{bst}}^{t}) \leq \Lambda_{t}^{- 1} \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \lambda_{\tau} f(x_{\tau}),
$$

the first inequality in (5.3.28) is preserved when replacing $x^{t}$ with $\boldsymbol{x}_{\mathrm{bst}}^{t}$ , and the resulting inequality combines with (5.3.27) to imply the validity of (5.3.26) for $\boldsymbol{x}_{\mathrm{bst}}^{t}$ in the role of $\boldsymbol{x}_{t}.\quad \boxed{}$

Discussion. As we have already mentioned, Theorem 5.3.1 is covered by Theorem 5.3.2. The latter, however, sometimes yields more information. For example, the “In particular” part of Theorem 5.3.1 states that for every given “time horizon $^{\textit{v}} T$ , specifying $\gamma_{t}, t \leq T$ , according to (5.3.23), we can upper-bound the non-optimalities $f(x_{\mathrm{bst}}^{T}) \ –$ min<sub>X</sub> f and $f(x^{T}) - \operatorname{min}_{X} f$ of the approximate solutions generated in course of T steps by $\frac{\mathbf{\bar{\Omega}}_{\bar{\Omega} L_{\| \cdot \|}(f)}}{\sqrt{T}}$ , (see (5.3.24)), which is the best result we can extract from Theorem; note, however, that to get this “best result,” we should tune the stepsizes to the total number of steps $T$ we intend to perform. What to do if we do not want to fix the total number $T$ of steps in advance? $\mathrm{A}$ natural way is to pass from the stepsize policy (5.3.23) to its “rolling horizon” analogy, specifically, to use

$$
\gamma_{t} = \frac{\Omega}{\| f^{\prime}(x_{t}) \|_{*} \sqrt{t}}, t = 1, 2, \dots\tag{5.3.29}
$$

With these stepsizes, the eficiency estimate (5.3.24) yields

$$
\begin{array}{c} \max[f(x^{T}), f(x_{\mathrm{bst}}^{T})] - \min_{X} f \leq O(1) \frac{\Omega L_{\| \cdot \|}(f) \ln(T + 1)}{\sqrt{T}}, T = 1, 2, \ldots \\ \left[x^{T} = \frac{\sum_{t = 1}^{T} \gamma_{t} x_{t}}{\sum_{t = 1}^{T} \gamma_{t}} \right] \end{array}\tag{5.3.30}
$$

(recall that $O(1){}^{:}$ ’s are absolute constants); this estimate is worse that (5.3.24), although just by logarithmic in $T$ factor. On the other hand, utilizing the stepsize policy (5.3.29) and setting

$$
\lambda_{t} = \frac{t^{p}}{\| f^{\prime}(x_{t}) \|_{*}}, t = 1, 2, \ldots\tag{5.3.31}
$$

where $p > - 1 / 2$ , we ensure (5.3.25) and thus can apply (5.3.26), arriving at

$$
\begin{array}{c} \max[f(x^{t}), f(x_{\mathrm{bst}}^{t})] - \min_{X} f \leq C_{p} \frac{\Omega L_{\| \cdot \|}(f)}{\sqrt{t}}, t = 1, 2, \ldots \\ \left[x^{t} = \frac{\sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \lambda_{\tau} x_{\tau}}{\sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \lambda_{\tau}} \right] \end{array}\tag{5.3.32}
$$

where $C_{p}$ depends solely on $p > - 1 / 2$ and is continuous in this range of values of $p.$ Note that the eficiency estimate (5.3.32) is, essentially, the same as (5.3.24) whatever be time horizon t. Note also that the weights with which we aggregate search points $x_{\tau}$ to get approximate solutions in (5.3.30) and in (5.3.32) are different: in (5.3.30), other things (specifically, $\| f^{\prime}(x_{\tau}) \|_{*})$ being equal, the “newer” is a search point, the less is the weight with which the point participates in the “aggregated” approximate solution. In contrast, when $p = 0$ , the aggregation (5.3.32) is “time invariant,”, and when $p > 0$ , it pays the more attention to a search point the newer is the point, this feature being amplified as $p > 0$ grows. Intuitively, “more attention to the new search points” seems to be desirable, provided the search trajectory $x_{\tau}$ itself, not just the sequences of averaged solutions $x^{\tau}$ or the best found so far solutions $x_{\mathrm{bst}}^{\tau}$ , converges, as $\tau \to \infty$ to the optimal set of the problem min $\operatorname{\rho}_{\operatorname{\lambda} x \in X} f(x)$ ; on a closest inspection, this convergence indeed takes place, provided the stepsizes $\gamma_{t} > 0$ satisfy $\gamma_{t} \to 0, t \to \infty$ , and $\textstyle \sum_{t = 1}^{\infty} \gamma_{t} = \infty$

## 5.3.4.6 MD: Optimality

Now let us look what our complexity analysis says in the case of the standard setups.

Ball setup and optimization over the ball. As we remember, in the case of the ball setup one has

$$
\Omega = D_{\| \cdot \|_{2}}(X),
$$

where $D_{\| \cdot \|_{2}}(X) = \operatorname{max}_{x, y \in X} \| x - y \|_{2}$ if the $\| \cdot \|_{2}$ -diameter of X. Consequently, (5.3.24) becomes

$$
f(x^{t}) - \min_{X} f \leq \frac{D_{\| \cdot \|_{2}}(X) L_{\| \cdot \|_{2}}(f)}{\sqrt{T}},\tag{5.3.33}
$$

meaning that the number $N(\epsilon)$ of MD steps needed to solve (CP) within accuracy $\epsilon$ can be bounded as 2

$$
N(\epsilon) \leq \frac{D_{\| \cdot \|_{2}}^{2}(X) L_{\| \cdot \|_{2}}^{2}(f)}{\epsilon^{2}} + 1.\tag{5.3.34}
$$

On the other hand, let $L > 0$ , and let $\mathcal{P}_{\| \cdot \|_{2}, L}(X)$ be the family of all convex problems (CP) with convex Lipschitz continuous, with constant L w.r.t. $\| \cdot \|_{2}$ , objectives. It is known that if X is an n-dimensional Euclidean ball and $n \geq \frac{D_{\| \cdot \|_{2}}^{2}(X) L^{2}}{\epsilon^{2}}$ , then the information-based complexity of the family $\mathcal{P}_{\| \cdot \|_{2}, L}(X)$ is at least $O(1){\frac{D_{\parallel \cdot \parallel_{2}}^{2}(X) L^{\tilde{2}}}{\epsilon^{2}}} ~(\mathrm{cf.~ \(5.1.4)})$ . Comparing this result with (5.3.34), we conclude that

If X is an n-dimensional Euclidean ball, then the complexity of the family $\mathcal{P}_{| | \cdot | |_{2}, L}(X)$ w.r.t. the MD algorithm with the ball setup in the “large-scale case” $n \geq \frac{D_{\| \cdot \|_{2}}^{2}(X) L^{2}}{\epsilon^{2}}$ coincides (within an absolute constant factor) with the information-based complexity of the family.

Entropy/Simplex setup and minimization over the simplex. In the case of Entropy setup we have $\Omega \leq O(1){\sqrt{\ln(n + 1)}}$ , so that (5.3.24) becomes

$$
f(x^{T}) - \min_{X} f \leq \frac{O(1) \sqrt{\ln(n + 1)} L_{\| \cdot \|_{1}}(f)}{\sqrt{T}},\tag{5.3.35}
$$

meaning that in order to solve (CP) within accuracy $\epsilon$ it sufices to carry out

$$
N(\epsilon) \leq \frac{O(1) \ln(n) L_{\| \cdot \|_{1}}^{2}(f)}{\epsilon^{2}} + 1\tag{5.3.36}
$$

MD steps.

On the other hand, let $L > 0$ , and let $\mathcal{P}_{\| \cdot \|_{1}, L}(X)$ be the family of all convex problems (CP) with convex Lipschitz continuous, with constant L w.r.t. $\| \cdot \|_{1}$ , objectives. It is known that if X is the standard n-dimensional simplex $\Delta_{n}$ (or the standard full-dimensional simplex $\Delta_{n}^{+})$ and $\begin{array}{r}{n \geq \frac{L^{2}}{\epsilon^{2}}} \end{array}$ , then the information-based complexity of the family $\mathcal{P}_{\| \cdot \|_{1}, L}(X)$ is at least $\begin{array}{r}{O(1) \frac{L^{2}}{\epsilon^{2}}} \end{array}$ (cf. (5.1.5)). Comparing this result with (5.3.34), we conclude that

If X is the n-dimensional simplex $\Delta_{n}$ (or the full-dimensional simplex $\Delta_{n}^{+})$ , then the complexity of the family $\mathcal{P}_{\| \cdot \|_{1}, L}(X)$ w.r.t. the MD algorithm with the simplex setup in the “large-scale case” $\begin{array}{r}{n \geq \frac{L^{2}}{\epsilon^{2}}} \end{array}$ coincides, within a factor of order of ln $n,$ with the information-based complexity of the family.

Note that the just presented discussion can be word by word repeated when entropy setup is replaced with Simplex setup.

Spectahedron setup and large-scale semidefinite optimization. All the conclusions we have made when speaking about the case of Entropy/Simplex setup and $X = \Delta_{n} \(\mathrm{or} \X = \Delta_{n}^{+})$ remain valid in the case of the spectahedron setup and X defined as the set of all block-diagonal matrices of a given block-diagonal structure contained in $\Delta_{n} = \{x \in \mathbf{S}^{n} : x \succeq 0,{\mathrm{Tr}}(x) = 1\}$ (or contained in $\Delta_{n}^{+} = \{x \in \mathbf{S}^{n} : x \succeq 0, \mathrm{Tr}(x) \leq 1\})$

We see that with every one of our standard setups, the MD algorithm under appropriate conditions possesses dimension independent (or nearly dimension independent) complexity bound and, moreover, is nearly optimal in the sense of Information-based complexity theory, provided that the dimension is large.

Why the standard setups? “The contribution” of $\omega(\cdot)$ to the performance estimate (5.3.24) is in the factor Ω; the less it is, the better. In principle, given X and $\| \cdot \|$ , we could play with $\omega(\cdot)$ to minimize Ω. The standard setups are given by a kind of such optimization for the cases when X is the ball and $\| \cdot \| = \| \cdot \|_{2}$ (“the ball $\mathrm{case}^{\mathfrak{V}})$ , when X is the simplex and $\| \cdot \| = \| \cdot \|_{1}$ (“the entropy $\mathrm{case}^{7})$ , and when X is the $\ell_{1} / \ell_{2}$ ball, or the nuclear norm ball, and the norm $\| \cdot \|$ is the block $\ell_{1}$ norm, respectively, the nuclear norm. We did not try to solve the arising variational problems exactly; however, it can be proved in all three cases that the value of Ω we have reached $(\mathrm{i.e.,} O(1)$ in the ball case, $O({\sqrt{\ln(n)}})$ in the simplex case and the $\ell_{1} / \ell_{2}$ case, and $O({\sqrt{\ln(m)}}$ in the nuclear norm case) cannot be reduced by more than an absolute constant factor.

Adjusting to problem’s geometry. A natural question is: When solving a particular problem (CP), which version of the Mirror Descent method to use? A “theory-based” answer could be “look at the complexity estimates of various versions of MD and run the one with the best complexity.” This “recommendation” usually is of no actual value, since the complexity bounds involve Lipschitz constants of the objective w.r.t. appropriate norms, and these constants usually are not known in advance. We are about to demonstrate that there are cases where reasonable recommendations can be made based solely on the geometry of the domain X of the problem. As an instructive example, consider the case where X is the unit $\| \cdot \|_{p^{-}} \mathrm{ball} \colon$ $X = X^{p} = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^{n} : \| x \|_{p} \leq 1\}$ , where $p \in \{1, 2, \infty\}$

Note that the cases of $p = 1$ and especially $p = \infty{\mathrm{are}}$ “quite practical.” Indeed, the first of them $(p = 1)$ is, essentially, what goes on in problems of $\ell_{1}$ minimization (section 1.3.1); the second $(p = \infty)$ is perhaps the most typical case (minimization under box constraints). The case of $p = 2$ seems to be more of academic nature.

The question we address is: which setup — Ball or Entropy one — to choose<sup>3</sup>.

First of all, we should explain how to process the domains in question via Entropy setup – the latter requires $X$ to be a part of the full-dimensional standard simplex $\Delta_{n}^{+}$ , which is not the case for the domains X we are interested in now. This issue can be easily resolved, specifically, as follows: setting

$$
x_{\rho}[u, v] = \rho(u - v),[u; v] \in \mathbb{R}^{n} \times \mathbb{R}^{n},
$$

we get a mapping from $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$ onto $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ such that the image of $\Delta_{2n}^{+}$ under this mapping covers $X^{p}$ provided that $\rho = \rho_{p} = n^{\gamma_{p}}$ , where $\gamma_{1} = 0, \gamma_{2} = 1 / 2, \gamma_{\infty} = 1$ . It follows that in order to apply to (CP) the MD with Entropy setup, it sufices to rewrite the problem as

$$
\min_{[u; v] \in Y^{p}} g_{p}(u, v) \equiv f(\rho_{p}(u - v)), \quad[Y_{p} =[u; v] \in \Delta_{2n}^{+}: \rho_{p}[u - v] \in X_{p}]
$$

the domain $Y^{p}$ of the problem being a part of $\Delta_{2n}^{+}$
