The complexity bounds of the MD algorithm with both Ball and Entropy setups are of the form ${}^{4 \cdot} N(\epsilon) = \mathcal{C} \epsilon^{- 2},{}^{,}$ where the factor C is independent of $\epsilon,$ although depends on the problem at hand and on the setup we use. In order to understand which setup is more preferable, it sufices to look at the factors $\mathcal{C}$ only. These factors, up to $O(1)$ factors, are listed in following table (where $L_{1}(f)$ and $L_{2}(f)$ stand for the Lipschitz constants of $f$ w.r.t. $\Vert \cdot \Vert_{1^{-}}$ and $\| \cdot \|_{2^{-} \mathrm{{norms}}})$ :

<table><tr><td>Setup</td><td> $X = X^{1}$ </td><td> $X = X^{2}$ </td><td> $X = X^{\infty}$ </td></tr><tr><td>Ball</td><td> $L_{2}^{2}(f)$ </td><td> $L_{2}^{2}(f)$ </td><td> $nL_{2}^{2}(f)$ </td></tr><tr><td>Entropy</td><td> $L_{1}^{2}(f)\ln(n)$ </td><td> $L_{1}^{2}(f)n\ln(n)$ </td><td> $L_{1}^{2}(f)n^{2}\ln(n)$ </td></tr></table>

Now note that for $0 \neq x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ we have $1 \leq{\frac{\| x \|_{1}}{\| x \|_{2}}} \leq{\sqrt{n}}$ , whence

$$
1 \geq \frac{L_{1}^{2}(f)}{L_{2}^{2}(f)} \geq \frac{1}{n}.
$$

With this in mind, the data from the above table suggest that in the case of $p = 1$ (X is the $\ell_{1}$ ball $X^{1})$ , the Entropy setup is more preferable; in all remaining cases under consideration, the preferable setup if the Ball one.

Indeed, when $X = X^{1}$ , the Entropy setup can lose to the Ball one at most by the “small” factor ln(n) and can gain by factor as large as $n / \ln(n)$ ; these two options, roughly speaking, correspond to the cases when subgradients of $f$ have just $O(1)$ significant entries (loss), or, on the contrary, have all entries of the same order of magnitude (gain). Since the potential loss is small, and potential gain can be quite significant, the Entropy setup in the case in question seems to be more preferable than the Ball one. In contrast to this, in the cases of $X = X^{2}$ and $X = X^{\infty}$ even the maximal potential gain associated with the Entropy setup (the ratio of $L_{1}^{2}(f) / L_{2}^{2}(f)$ as small as $1 / n)$ does not lead to an overall gain in the complexity, this is why in these cases we would advice to use the Ball setup.

## 5.3.5 Mirror Descent and Online Regret Minimization

## 5.3.5.1 Online regret minimization: what is it?

In the usual setting, the purpose of a black box oriented optimization algorithm as applied to a minimization problem

$$
\operatorname{Opt} = \min_{x \in X} f(x)
$$

is to find an approximate solution of a desired accuracy $\epsilon$ via calls to an oracle (say, First Order one) representing $f.$ What we are interested in, is the number N of steps (calls to the oracle) needed to build an $\epsilon$-solution, and the overall computational efort in executing these N steps. What we ignore completely, is how “good,” in terms of $f,$ are the search points $x_{t} \in X$ $1 \leq t \leq N - \mathrm{all}$ we want is “to learn” f to the extent allowing to point out an $\epsilon$-minimizer, and the faster is our learning process, the better, no matter how “expensive,” in terms of their non-optimality, are the search points. This traditional approach corresponds to the situation where our optimization is of line: when processing the problem numerically, calling the oracle at a search point does not incur any actual losses. What indeed is used “in reality,” is the computed near-optimal solution, be it an engineering design, a reconstructed image, or a nearoptimal portfolio selection. We are interested in losses incurred by this solution only, with no care of how good “in reality” would be the search points generated in course of the optimization process.

In online optimization, problem’s setting is different: we run an algorithm on the fly, in “real time,” and when calling the oracle at t-th step, the query point being $x_{t},$ , incur “real loss,” in the simplest setting equal to $f(x_{t})$ . What we are interested in, is to make as close to Opt as possible our “properly averaged” loss, in the simplest case – the average loss

$$
L_{N} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{t = 1}^{N} f(x_{t}).
$$

The “horizon” N here can be fixed, in which case we want to make $L_{N}$ as small as possible, or can vary, in which case we want to enforce $L_{N}$ to approach Opt as fast as possible as N grows.

In fact, in online regret minimization it is not even assumed that the objective f remains constant as the time evolves; instead, it is assumed that we are dealing with a sequence of objectives $f_{t}, t = 1, 2,...,$ selected “by nature” from a known in advance family $\mathcal{F}$ of functions on a known in advance set $X \subset \mathbb{R}^{n}$ . At a step $t = 1, 2,...,$ we select a point $x_{t} \in X$ , and “an oracle” provides us with certain information on $f_{t}$ at $x_{t}$ and charges us with “toll” $f_{t}(x_{t})$ . It should be stressed that in this setting, no assumptions on how the nature selects the sequence $\{f_{t}(\cdot) \in \mathcal{F} : t \geq 1\}$ are made. Now our “ideal goal” would be to find a non-anticipative policy (rules for generating $x_{t}$ based solely on the information acquired from the oracle at the first $t - 1$ steps of the process) which enforces our average toll

$$
L_{N} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{t = 1}^{N} f_{t}(x_{t})\tag{5.3.37}
$$

to approach, as $N \to \infty$ , the “ideal” average toll

$$
L_{N}^{*} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{t = 1}^{N} \min_{x \in X} f_{t}(x),\tag{5.3.38}
$$

whatever be the sequence $\{f_{t}(\cdot) \in \mathcal{F} : t \geq 1\}$ selected by the nature. It is absolutely clear that aside of trivial cases (like all functions from $\mathcal{F}$ share common minimizer), this ideal goal cannot be achieved. Indeed, with $L_{N} - L_{N}^{*} \to 0, n \to \infty$ , the average, over time horizon N, of (always nonnegative) non-optimalities $\begin{array}{r}{f_{t}(x_{t}) - \operatorname{min}_{x_{t} \in X} f_{t}(x)} \end{array}$ should go to 0 as $N \to \infty$ , implying that for large N, “near all” of these non-optimalities should be “near-zero.” The latter, with the nature allowed to select $f_{t} \in \mathcal{F}$ in completely unpredictable manner, clearly cannot be guaranteed, whatever be non-anticipative policy used to generate $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots$

To make the online setting with “abruptly varying” f<sub>t</sub>’s meaningful, people compare $L_{N}$ not with its “utopian” lower bound $L_{N}^{*}$ (which can be achieved only by a clairvoyant knowing in advance the trajectory $f_{1}, f_{2}, \ldots)$ , but with a less utopian bound, most notably, with the quantity

$$
\widehat{L}_{N} = \min_{x \in X} \frac{1}{N} \sum_{t = 1}^{N} f_{t}(x).
$$

Thus, we compare the average, on horizon N, toll of a “capable to move” (capable to select $x_{t} \in X$ in a whatever non-anticipative fashion) “mortal” which cannot predict the future with the best average toll of a clairvoyant who knows in advance the trajectory $f_{1}, f_{2}, \ldots$ . selected by the nature, but is unable to move (must use the same action x during all “rounds $\v_{\t} = 1,..., N)$ We arrive at the online regret minimization problem where we are interested in a non-anticipative policy of selecting $x_{t} \in X$ which enforces the associated regret

$$
\Delta_{N} = \sup_{f_{t} \in \mathcal{F}, 1 \leq t \leq N} \left[\frac{1}{N} \sum_{t = 1}^{N} f_{t}(x_{t}) - \min_{x \in X} \frac{1}{N} \sum_{t = 1} f_{t}(x) \right]\tag{5.3.39}
$$

to $_\mathrm{go}$ to 0, the faster the better, as $N \to \infty$

Remark. Whether it is “fair” to compare a “mortal capable to move” with $^{66} a$ handicapped clairvoyant,” this question is beyond the scope of optimization theory, and answer here clearly depends on the application we are interested in. It sufices to say that there are meaningful applications, e.g., in Machine Learning, where online regret minimization makes sense and that even the case where the nature is restricted to select only stationary sequences $f_{t}(\cdot) \equiv f(\cdot) \in \mathcal{F}$ $t = 1, 2, \dots$ (no dificulty with “fairness” at all), making $\Delta_{N}$ small models the meaningful situation when we “learn” the objective f online.

## 5.3.5.2 Online regret minimization via Mirror Descent, deterministic case

Note that the problem of online regret minimization admits various settings, depending on what are our assumptions on X and ${\mathcal{F}}_{:}$ , and what is the information on $f_{t}$ revealed by the oracle at the search point $x_{t}$ . In this section, we focus on the simple case where

1. X is a convex compact set in Euclidean space $E,$ and $(X, E)$ is equipped with proximal setup – a norm $\| \cdot \|$ on $E$ and a compatible with this norm continuously diferentiable on X DGF $\omega(\cdot)$ ;

2. $\mathcal{F}$ is the family of all convex and Lipschitz continuous, with a given constant L w.r.t. $\| \cdot \|$ functions on $X{\mathrm{:}}$ ;

3. the information we get in round t, our search point being $x_{t}.$ , and “nature’s selection” being $f_{t}(\cdot) \in \mathcal{F}$ , is the first order information $f_{t}(x_{t}), f_{t}^{\prime}(x_{t})$ on $f_{t}$ at $x_{t}$ , with the $\| \cdot \|_{*}$ -norm of the taken at $x_{t}$ subgradient $f_{t}^{\prime}(x_{t})$ of $f_{t}(\cdot)$ not exceeding $L.$

Our goal is to demonstrate that Mirror Descent algorithm, in the form presented in section 5.3.4.5, is well-suited for online regret minimization. Specifically, consider algorithm as follows:

1. Initialization: Select stepsizes $\{\gamma_{t} > 0\}_{t \geq 1}$ with $\gamma_{t}$ nonincreasing in t. Select $x_{1} \in X$

2. Step $t = 1, 2, \dots$ . Given $x_{t}$ and a reported by the oracle subgradient $f_{t}^{\prime}(x_{t})$ , of $\| \cdot \|_{*}$ -norm not exceeding $L,$ of $f_{t}$ at $x_{t}.$ , set

$$
x_{t + 1} = \mathrm{Prox}_{x_{t}}(\gamma_{t} f_{t}^{\prime}(x_{t})) := \underset{x \in X}{\operatorname{argmin}} \left[\langle \gamma_{t} f_{t}^{\prime}(x_{t}) - \omega^{\prime}(x_{t}), x \rangle + \omega(x) \right]
$$

and pass to step $t + 1$

Convergence analysis. We have the following straightforward modification of Theorem 5.3.2:

Theorem 5.3.3 In the notation and under assumptions of this section, whatever be a sequence $\{f_{t} \in \mathcal{F} : t \geq 1\}$ selected by the nature, for the trajectory $\{x_{t} : t \geq 1\}$ of search points generated by the above algorithm and for a whatever sequence of weights $\{\lambda_{t} > 0 : t \ge 1\}$ such that $\lambda_{t} / \gamma_{t}$ is nondecreasing in t, it holds for all $N = 1, 2, \ldots$

$$
\frac{1}{\Lambda_{N}} \sum_{t = 1}^{N} \lambda_{t} f_{t}(x_{t}) - \min_{u \in X} \frac{1}{\Lambda_{N}} \sum_{t = 1}^{N} \lambda_{t} f_{t}(u) \leq \frac{\frac{\lambda_{N}}{\gamma_{N}} \Omega^{2} + \sum_{t = 1}^{N} \lambda_{t} \gamma_{t} L^{2}}{2 \Lambda_{N}}\tag{5.3.40}
$$

where Ω is the ω-diameter of X, and

$$
\Lambda_{N} = \sum_{t = 1}^{N} \lambda_{t}.
$$

Postponing for a moment the proof, let us look at the consequences.

Consequences. Let us choose

$$
\gamma_{t} = \frac{\Omega}{L \sqrt{t}}, \lambda_{t} = t^{\alpha},
$$

with $\alpha \geq 0$ . This choice meets the requirements from the description of our algorithm and the premise of Theorem 5.3.3, and results in $\Lambda_{N} \ge O(1)(1 + \alpha)^{- 1} N^{\alpha + 1}$ and $\begin{array}{r}{\sum_{t = 1}^{\tilde{N}} \lambda_{t} \gamma_{t} L^{2} \leq} \end{array}$ $O(1)(1 + \alpha)^{- 1} N^{\alpha + 1 / 2}(\Omega L)$ , provided $N \geq 1 + \alpha$ . As a result, (5.3.40) becomes

$$
\begin{array}{l} \forall(f_{t} \in \mathcal{F}, t = 1, 2,..., N \geq 1 + \alpha): \\ \frac{1}{\Lambda_{N}} \sum_{t = 1}^{N} \lambda_{t} f_{t}(x_{t}) - \min_{u \in X} \frac{1}{\Lambda_{N}} \sum_{t = 1}^{N} \lambda_{t} f_{t}(u) \leq O(1) \frac{(1 + \alpha) \Omega L}{\sqrt{N}}.\end{array}\tag{5.3.41}
$$

We arrive at an $O(1 / \sqrt{N})$ upper bound on a kind of regret (“kind $\mathrm{of}^{\dag}$ stems from the fact that the averaging in the left hand side uses weights proportional to $\lambda_{t}$ rather than equal to each other). Setting $\alpha = 0$ , we get a bound on the “true” N-step regret. Note that the policy of generating the points $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots$ is completely independent of $\alpha,$ so that the bound (5.3.41) contains a “spectrum,” parameterized by $\alpha \geq 0$ , of regret-like bounds on a fixed decision-making policy.

Proof of Theorem 5.3.3. With our current algorithm, relation (5.3.21) becomes

$$
\forall(t \geq 1, u \in X): \gamma_{t} \langle f_{t}^{\prime}(x_{\tau}), x_{t} - u \rangle \leq V_{x_{t}}(u) - V_{x_{t + 1}}(u) + \frac{1}{2} \| \gamma_{\tau} f_{t}^{\prime}(x_{t}) \|_{*}^{2}\tag{5.3.42}
$$

(replace $f$ with $f_{t}$ in the derivation in item $1^{0}$ of the proof of Theorem 5.3.1). Now let us proceed exactly as in the proof of Theorem 5.3.2: multiply both sides in (5.3.42) by $\lambda_{t} / \gamma_{t}$ and sum up the resulting inequalities over $t = 1,..., N$ , arriving at

$$
\begin{array}{rl} &{\forall(u \in X):} \\ &{\sum_{t = 1}^{N} \lambda_{t} \langle f_{t}^{\prime}(x_{t}), x_{t} - u \rangle \leq \sum_{t = 1}^{N} \frac{\lambda_{t}}{\gamma_{t}}[V_{x_{t}}(u) - V_{x_{t + 1}}(u)] + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{t = 1}^{N} \lambda_{t} \gamma_{t} \| f_{t}^{\prime}(x_{t}) \|_{*}^{2}} \\ &{= \frac{\lambda_{1}}{\gamma_{1}} V_{x_{1}}(u) + \underbrace{\left[\frac{\lambda_{2}}{\gamma_{2}} - \frac{\lambda_{1}}{\gamma_{1}} \right]}_{\geq 0} V_{x_{2}}(u) + \underbrace{\left[\frac{\lambda_{3}}{\gamma_{3}} - \frac{\lambda_{2}}{\gamma_{2}} \right]}_{\geq 0} V_{x_{3}}(u) +...+ \underbrace{\left[\frac{\lambda_{N}}{\gamma_{N}} - \frac{\lambda_{N - 1}}{\gamma_{N - 1}} \right]}_{\geq 0} V_{x_{N}}(u)} \\ &{- \frac{\lambda_{N}}{\gamma_{N}} V_{x_{N + 1}}(u) + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{t = 1}^{T} \lambda_{t} \gamma_{t} \| f_{t}^{\prime}(x_{t}) \|_{*}^{2} \leq \frac{\lambda_{N}}{\gamma_{N}} \frac{\Omega^{2}}{2} + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{t = 1}^{N} \lambda_{t} \gamma_{t} \| f_{t}^{\prime}(x_{t}) \|_{*}^{2},} \end{array}
$$

where the concluding inequality is due to $\begin{array}{r}{0 \leq V_{x_{t}}(u) \leq \frac{\Omega^{2}}{2}} \end{array}$ for all t. As a result, taking into account that $\| f_{t}^{\prime}(x_{t}) \|_{*} \leq L$ , we get

$$
\begin{array}{c} \max_{u \in X} \Lambda_{N}^{- 1} \sum_{t = 1}^{N} \lambda_{t} \langle f_{t}^{\prime}(x_{t}), x_{t} - u \rangle \leq \frac{\frac{\lambda_{N}}{\gamma_{N}} \Omega^{2} + \sum_{t = 1}^{N} \lambda_{t} \gamma_{t} L^{2}}{2 \Lambda_{N}} \\ \left[\Lambda_{N} = \sum_{t = 1}^{N} \lambda_{t} \right].\end{array}\tag{5.3.43}
$$

On the other hand, by convexity of $f_{t}$ we have for every $u \in X$

$$
f_{t}(x_{t}) - f_{t}(u) \leq \langle f_{t}^{\prime}(x_{t}), x_{t} - u \rangle,
$$

and thus (5.3.43) implies that

$$
\frac{1}{\Lambda_{N}} \sum_{t = 1}^{N} \lambda_{t} f_{t}(x_{t}) - \min_{u \in X} \frac{1}{\Lambda_{N}} \sum_{t = 1}^{N} \lambda_{t} f_{t}(u) \leq \frac{\frac{\lambda_{N}}{\gamma_{N}} \Omega^{2} + \sum_{t = 1}^{N} \lambda_{t} \gamma_{t} L^{2}}{2 \Lambda_{N}}.
$$

## 5.3.6 Mirror Descent for Saddle Point problems

## 5.3.6.1 Convex-Concave Saddle Point problem

An important generalization of a convex optimization problem (CP) is a convex-concave saddle point problem

$$
\min_{x \in X} \max_{y \in Y} \phi(x, y)\tag{SP}
$$

where

$X \subset{\mathbb{R}}^{n_{x}}, \Y \subset{\mathbb{R}}^{n_{y}}$ are nonempty convex compact subsets in the respective Euclidean spaces (which at this point we w.l.o.g. identified with a pair of $\mathbb{R}^{n} \mathrm{\bar{s}})$

$\phi(x, y)$ is a Lipschitz continuous real-valued cost function on $Z = X \times Y$ which is convex in $x \in X, y \in Y$ being fixed, and is concave in $y \in Y, x \in X$ being fixed.

Basic facts on saddle points. (SP) gives rise to a pair of convex optimization problems

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \mathrm{Opt}(P) & = & \min_{x \in X} \overline{{\phi}}(x) := \max_{y \in Y} \phi(x, y) \\ \mathrm{Opt}(D) & = & \max_{y \in Y} \underline{{\phi}}(y) := \min_{x \in X} \phi(x, y) \end{array}\tag{P}
$$

(D)

(the primal problem (P) requires to minimize a convex function over a convex compact set, the dual problem (D) requires to maximize a concave function over another convex compact set). The problems are dual to each other, meaning that $\mathrm{Opt}(P) = \mathrm{Opt}(D)$ ; this is called strong $\boldsymbol{duality^{4}}$ . Note that strong duality is based upon convexity-concavity of φ and convexity of $X, Y$ (and to a slightly lesser extent – on the continuity of $\phi$ on $Z = X \times Y$ and compactness of the latter domain), while the weak duality $\mathrm{Opt}(P) \ge \mathrm{Opt}(D)$ is a completely general (and simple to verify) phenomenon.

In our case of convex-concave Lipschitz continuous $\phi$ the induced objectives in the primal and the dual problem are Lipschitz continuous as well. Since the domains of these problems are compact, the problems are solvable. Denoting by $X_{*}, \Y_{*}$ the corresponding optimal sets, the set $Z_{*} = X_{*} \times Y_{*}$ admits simple characterization in terms of φ: $Z_{*}$ is exactly the set of saddle points of $\phi$ on $Z = X \times Y$ , that is, the points $(x_{*}, y_{*}) \in X \times Y$ such that

$$
\phi(x, y_{*}) \geq \phi(x_{*}, y_{*}) \geq \phi(x_{*}, y) \forall(x, y) \in Z = X \times Y
$$

(in words: with y set to $y_{*}, \phi$ attains its minimum over $x \in X$ at $x_{*}$ , and with x set to $x_{*}, \phi$ attains its maximum over $y \in Y$ at $y = y_{*})$ . These points are considered as exact solutions to the saddle point problem in question. The common optimal value of (P) and (D) is nothing but the value of $\phi$ at a saddle point:

$$
\operatorname{Opt}(P) = \operatorname{Opt}(D) = \phi(x_{*}, y_{*}) \forall(x_{*}, y_{*}) \in Z_{*}.
$$

The standard interpretation of a saddle point problem is the game where the first player chooses his action $x$ from the set $X.$ his adversary – the second player – chooses his action $y$ in $Y$ , and with a choice $(x, y)$ of the players, the first pays the second the sum $\phi(x, y)$ . Such a game is called antagonistic (since the interests of the players are completely opposite to each other), or a zero sum game (since the sum $\phi(x, y) +[- \phi(x, y)]$ of losses of the players is identically zero). In terms of the game, saddle points $(x_{*}, y_{*})$ are exactly the equilibria: if the first player sticks to the choice $x_{*}$ , the adversary has no incentive to move away from the choice $y_{*},$ , since such a move cannot increase his profit, and similarly for the first player, provided that the second one sticks to the choice $y_{*}$

It is convenient to characterize the accuracy of a candidate $(x, y) \in X \times Y$ to the role of an approximate saddle point by the “saddle point residual”

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \epsilon_{\mathrm{sad}}(x, y) & := & \max_{y^{\prime} \in Y} \phi(x, y^{\prime}) - \min_{x^{\prime} \in X} \phi(x^{\prime}, y) = \overline{{\phi}}(x) - \underline{{\phi}}(y) \\ & = & \left[\overline{{\phi}}(x) - \operatorname{Opt}(P) \right] + \left[\operatorname{Opt}(D) - \underline{{\phi}}(y) \right], \end{array}
$$

where the concluding equality is due to strong duality. We see that the saddle point inaccuracy $\epsilon_{\mathrm{sad}}(x, y)$ is just the sum of non-optimalities, in terms of the respective objectives, of $x$ as a solution to the primal, and $y$ as a solution to the dual problem; in particular, the inaccuracy is nonnegative and is zero if and only if $(x, y)$ is a saddle point of $\phi.$

Vector field associated with (SP). From now on, we focus on problem (SP) with Lipschitz continuous convex-concave cost function $\phi : X \times Y \mathbb{R}$ and convex compact X, Y and assume that $\phi$ is represented by a First Order oracle as follows: given on input a point $z =(x, y) \in$ $Z : = X \times Y$ , the oracle returns a subgradient $F_{x}(z)$ of the convex function $\phi(\cdot, y) : X \to \mathbb{R}$ at the point $x,$ and a subgradient $F_{y}(x, y)$ of the convex function $- \phi(x, \cdot) : Y \mathbb{R}$ at the point $Y$ It is convenient to arrange $F_{x}, F_{y}$ in a single vector

$$
F(z) = \left[F_{x}(z); F_{y}(z) \right] \in \mathbb{R}^{n_{x}} \times \mathbb{R}^{n_{y}}.\tag{5.3.44}
$$

In addition, we assume that the vector field $\{F(z) : z \in Z\}$ is bounded (cf. (5.3.1)).

## 5.3.6.2 Saddle point MD algorithm

The setup for the algorithm is a usual proximal setup, but with the set $Z = X \times Y$ in the role of X and the embedding space $\mathbb{R}^{n_{x}} \times \mathbb{R}^{n_{y}}$ of $Z$ in the role of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ , so that the setup is given by a norm $\| \cdot \|$ on $\mathbb{R}^{n_{x}} \times \mathbb{R}^{n_{y}}$ and a compatible with this norm continuously diferentiable DGF $\omega(\cdot) : Z \to \mathbb{R}$

The MD algorithm for (SP) is given by the recurrence

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} z_{1} :=(x_{1}, y_{1}) & \in & Z, \\ z_{t + 1} :=(x_{t + 1}, y_{t + 1}) & = & \mathrm{Prox}_{z_{t}}(\gamma_{t} F(z_{t})), \\ & & \mathrm{Prox}_{z}(\xi) = \operatorname{argmin}_{w \in Z}[V_{z}(w) + \langle \xi, w \rangle], \\ & & V_{z}(w) = \omega(w) - \langle \omega^{\prime}(z), w - z \rangle - \omega(z) \geq \frac{1}{2} \| w - z \|^{2}, \\ z^{t} & = & \left[\sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau} \right]^{- 1} \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau} z_{\tau}, \end{array}\tag{5.3.45}
$$

where $\gamma_{t} > 0$ are stepsizes, and $z^{t}$ are approximate solutions built in course of t steps.

The saddle point analogy of Theorem 5.3.1 is as follows:

Theorem 5.3.4 For every $\tau \geq 1$ and every $w =(u, v) \in Z,$ one has

$$
\gamma_{\tau} \langle F(z_{\tau}), z_{\tau} - w \rangle \leq V_{z_{\tau}}(w) - V_{z_{\tau + 1}}(w) + \frac{1}{2} \| \gamma_{\tau} F(z_{\tau}) \|_{*}^{2}.\tag{5.3.46}
$$

As a result, for every $t \geq 1$ one has

$$
\epsilon_{\mathrm{sad}}(z^{t}) \leq \frac{\frac{\Omega^{2}}{2} + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau}^{2} \| F(z_{\tau}) \|_{*}^{2}}{\sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau}}.\tag{5.3.47}
$$

In particular, given a number T of iterations we intend to perform and setting

$$
\gamma_{t} = \frac{\Omega}{\| F(z_{t}) \|_{*} \sqrt{T}}, 1 \leq t \leq T,\tag{5.3.48}
$$

we ensure that

$$
\epsilon_{\text{sad}}(z^{T}) \leq \Omega \frac{\sqrt{T}}{\sum_{t = 1}^{T} \frac{1}{\| F(x_{t}) \|_{*}}} \leq \frac{\Omega \max_{t \leq T} \| F(x_{t}) \|_{*}}{\sqrt{T}} \leq \frac{\Omega L_{\| \cdot \|}(F)}{\sqrt{T}}, \quad L_{\| \cdot \|}(F) = \sup_{z \in Z} \| F(z) \|_{*}.\tag{5.3.49}
$$

Proof. $1^{0}$ . (5.3.46) is proved exactly as its “minimization counterpart” (5.3.21), see item $1^{0}$ of the proof of Theorem 5.3.1; on a closest inspection, the reasoning there is absolutely independent of where the vectors $\xi_{t}$ in the recurrence $z_{t + 1} = \operatorname{Prox}_{z_{t}}(\xi_{t})$ come from.

$\mathbf{2}^{0}$ . Summing up relations (5.3.46) over $\tau = 1,..., t.$ , plugging in $F =[F_{x}; F_{y}]$ , dividing both sides of the resulting inequality by $\textstyle \Gamma_{t} = \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau}$ and setting $\nu_{\tau} = \gamma_{\tau} / \Gamma_{t}$ , we get

$$
\sum_{\tau = 1}^{T} \nu_{\tau} \left[\langle F_{x}(z_{t}), x_{t} - u \rangle + \langle F_{y}(z_{t}), y_{t} - v \rangle \right] \leq Q := \Gamma_{t}^{- 1} \left[\frac{\Omega^{2}}{2} + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau}^{2} \| F(z_{\tau}) \|_{*}^{2} \right];\tag{!}
$$

this inequality holds true for all $(u, v) \in X \times Y$ . Now, recalling the origin of $F_{x}$ and $F_{y}$ , we have

$$
\langle F_{x}(x_{t}, y_{t}), x_{t} - u \rangle \geq \phi(x_{t}, y_{t}) - \phi(u, y_{t}), \langle F_{y}(x_{t}, y_{t}), y_{t} - v \rangle \geq \phi(x_{t}, v) - \phi(x_{t}, y_{t}),
$$

so that (!) implies that

$$
\sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \nu_{\tau} \left[\phi(x_{t}, v) - \phi(u, y_{t}) \right] \leq Q := \Gamma_{t}^{- 1} \left[\frac{\Omega^{2}}{2} + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau}^{2} \| F(z_{\tau}) \|_{*}^{2} \right],
$$

## 5.3. MIRROR DESCENT ALGORITHM

which, by convexity-concavity of $\phi,$ yields

$$
\left[\phi(x^{t}, v) - \phi(u, y^{t}) \right] \leq Q := \Gamma_{t}^{- 1} \left[\frac{\Omega^{2}}{2} + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau}^{2} \| F(z_{\tau}) \|_{*}^{2} \right].
$$

Now, the right hand side of the latter inequality is independent of $(u, v) \in Z;$ taking maximum over $(u, v) \in Z$ in the left hand side of the inequality, we get (5.3.47). This inequality clearly implies (5.3.49). ✷

In our course, the role of Theorem 5.3.4 (which is quite useful by its own right) is to be a “draft version” of a much more powerful Theorem 5.5.1, and we postpone illustrations till the latter Theorem is in place.

## 5.3.6.3 Refinement

Similarly to the minimization case, Theorem 5.3.4 admits a refinement as follows:

Theorem 5.3.5 Let $\lambda_{1}, \lambda_{2},...$ . be positive reals such that (5.3.25) holds true, and let

$$
z^{t} = \frac{\sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \lambda_{\tau} z_{\tau}}{\sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \lambda_{\tau}}.
$$

Then $z^{t} \in Z$ , and

$$
\epsilon_{\mathrm{sad}}(z^{t}) \leq \frac{\frac{\lambda_{t}}{\gamma_{t}} \Omega^{2} + \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \lambda_{t} \gamma_{\tau} \| F(z_{\tau}) \|_{*}^{2}}{2 \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \lambda_{\tau}}.\tag{5.3.50}
$$

In particular, with the stepsizes

$$
\gamma_{t} = \frac{\Omega}{\| F(z_{t}) \|_{*} \sqrt{t}}, t = 1, 2, \dots\tag{5.3.51}
$$

and with

$$
\lambda_{t} = \frac{t^{p}}{\| F(z_{t}) \|_{*}}, t = 1, 2, \dots\tag{5.3.52}
$$

where $p > - 1 / 2$ , we ensure $fort = 1, 2,...$ . that

$$
\epsilon_{\mathrm{sad}}(z^{t}) \leq C_{p} \frac{\Omega L_{\| \cdot \|}(F)}{\sqrt{t}}, \quad L_{\| \cdot \|}(F) = \sup_{z \in Z} \| F(z) \|_{*}\tag{5.3.53}
$$

with $C_{p}$ depending solely and continuously on $p > - 1 / 2$

Proof. The inclusion $z^{t} \in Z$ is evident. Processing (5.3.46) in exactly the same fashion as we have processed (5.3.21) when proving Theorem 5.3.2, we get the relation

$$
\begin{array}{c} \sup_{u \in Z} \Lambda_{t}^{- 1} \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \lambda_{\tau} \langle F(z_{t}), z_{t} - u \rangle \leq \frac{\frac{\lambda_{t}}{\gamma_{t}} \Omega^{2} + \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \lambda_{\tau} \gamma_{\tau} \| F(z_{\tau}) \|_{*}^{2}}{2 \Lambda_{t}} \\ \left[\Lambda_{t} = \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \lambda_{\tau} \right] \end{array}
$$

Same as in the proof of Theorem 5.3.4, the left hand side in this inequality upper-bounds $\epsilon_{\mathrm{sad}}(z^{t})$ and we arrive at (5.3.50). The “In particular” part of Theorem is straightforwardly implied by (5.3.50). ✷

## 5.3.7 Mirror Descent for Stochastic Minimization/Saddle Point problems

While what is on our agenda now is applicable to stochastic convex minimization and stochastic convex-concave saddle point problems, in the sequel, to save words, we deal focus on the saddle point case. It makes no harm: convex minimization, stochastic and deterministic alike, is a special case of solving convex-concave saddle point problem, one where Y is a singleton.

## 5.3.7.1 Stochastic Minimization/Saddle Point problems

Let we need to solve a saddle point problem

$$
\min_{x \in X} \max_{y \in Y} \phi(x, y)\tag{SP}
$$

under the same assumptions as above $(\mathrm{i.e.,} X, Y$ are convex compact sets in Euclidean spaces $\mathbb{R}^{n_{x}}, \mathbb{R}^{n_{y}} \mathbf{\Psi} \phi : Z = X \times Y \mathbb{R}$ is convex-concave and Lipschitz continuous), but now, instead of deterministic First Order oracle which reports the values of the associated with $\phi$ vector field $F_{;}$ , see (5.3.44), we have at our disposal a stochastic First Order oracle – a routine which reports unbiased random estimates of $F$ rather than the exact values of F . A convenient model of the oracle is as follows: at t-th call to the oracle, the query point being $z \in Z = X \times Y$ , the oracle returns a vector $G = G(z, \xi_{t})$ which is a deterministic function of z and of t-th realization of oracle’s noise $\xi_{t}$ . We assume the noises $\xi_{1}, \xi_{2},.$ .. to be independent of each other and identically distributed: $\xi_{t} \sim P, t = 1, 2,....$ We always assume that the oracle is unbiased:

$$
\mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim P} \{G(z, \xi)\} =: F(z) =[F_{x}(z); F_{y}(z)] \in \partial_{x} \phi(z) \times \partial_{y}[- \phi(z)]\tag{5.3.54}
$$

(thus, $F_{x}(x, y)$ is a subgradient of $\phi(\cdot, y)$ taken at the point $x,$ while $F_{y}(x, y)$ is a subgradient of $- \phi(x, \cdot)$ taken at the point $y)$ . Besides this, we assume that the second moment of the stochastic subgradient is bounded uniformly in $z \in Z$

$$
\sup_{z \in Z} \mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim P} \{\| G(z, \xi) \|_{*}^{2}\} < \infty,\tag{5.3.55}
$$

Note that when $Y$ is a singleton, our setting recovers the problem of minimizing a Lipschitz continuous convex function over a compact convex set in the case when instead of the subgradients of the objective, unbiased random estimates of these subgradients are available.

## 5.3.7.2 Stochastic Saddle Point Mirror Descent algorithm

It turns out that the MD algorithm admits a stochastic version capable to solve (SP) in the outlined “stochastic environment.” The setup for the algorithm is a usual proximal setup — a norm $\| \cdot \|$ on the space $\mathbb{R}^{n_{x}} \times \mathbb{R}^{n_{y}}$ embedding $Z = X \times Y$ and a compatible with this norm continuously diferentiable DGF $\omega(\cdot)$ for $Z.$ The Stochastic Saddle Point Mirror Descent (SSPMD) algorithm is identical to its deterministic counterpart; it is the recurrence

$$
z_{1} = z_{\omega}, z_{t + 1} = \mathrm{Prox}_{z_{t}}(\gamma_{t} G(z_{t}, \xi_{t})), z^{t} = \left[\sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau} \right]^{- 1} \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau} z_{\tau},\tag{5.3.56}
$$

where $\gamma_{t} > 0$ are deterministic stepsizes. This is nothing but the recurrence (5.3.45), with the only diference that now this recurrence “is $\operatorname{fed}^{\mathrm{,} \mathrm{,}}$ by the estimates $G(z_{t}, \xi_{t})$ of the vectors $F(z_{t})$ participating in (5.3.45). Surprisingly, the performance of SSPMD is, essentially, the same as the performance of its deterministic counterpart:

Theorem 5.3.6 One has

$$
\begin{array}{r} \mathbb{E}_{[\xi_{1}; \dots; \xi_{t}] \sim P \times \dots \times P} \left\{\epsilon_{\mathrm{sad}}(z^{t}) \right\} \leq \frac{7}{2} \frac{\Omega^{2} + \sigma^{2} \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau}^{2}}{\sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau}}.\\ \sigma^{2} = \sup_{z \in Z} \mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim P} \{\| G(z, \xi) \|_{*}^{2}\} \end{array}\tag{5.3.57}
$$

In particular, given a number T of iterations we intend to perform and setting

$$
\gamma_{t} = \frac{\Omega}{\sigma \sqrt{T}}, 1 \leq t \leq T,\tag{5.3.58}
$$

we ensure that

$$
\mathbb{E} \{\epsilon_{\mathrm{sad}}(z^{T})\} \leq \frac{7 \Omega \sigma}{\sqrt{T}}.\tag{5.3.59}
$$

Proof. $1^{0}$ . By exactly the same reason as in the deterministic case, we have for every $u \in Z \colon$ :

$$
\sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau} \langle G(z_{\tau}, \xi_{\tau}), z_{\tau} - u \rangle \leq \frac{\Omega^{2}}{2} + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau}^{2} \| G(z_{\tau}, \xi_{\tau}) \|_{*}^{2}.
$$

Setting

$$
\Delta_{\tau} = G(z_{\tau}, \xi_{\tau}) - F(z_{\tau}),\tag{5.3.60}
$$

we can rewrite the above relation as

$$
\sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau} \langle F(z_{\tau}), z_{\tau} - u \rangle \leq \frac{\Omega^{2}}{2} + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau}^{2} \| G(z_{\tau}, \xi_{\tau}) \|_{*}^{2} + \underbrace{\sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau} \langle \Delta_{\tau}, u - z_{\tau} \rangle}_{D(\xi^{t}, u)},\tag{5.3.61}
$$

where $\xi^{t} =[\xi_{1};...; \xi_{t}]$ . It follows that

$$
\max_{u \in Z} \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau} \langle F(z_{\tau}), z_{\tau} - u \rangle \leq \frac{\Omega^{2}}{2} + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau}^{2} \| G(z_{\tau}, \xi_{\tau}) \|_{*}^{2} + \max_{u \in Z} D(\xi^{t}, u).
$$

As we have seen when proving Theorem 5.3.4, the left hand side in the latter relation is $\geq$ $\begin{array}{rl}{{[\sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau}] \epsilon_{\mathrm{sad}}(z^{t})}} \end{array}$ , so that

$$
\left[\sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau} \right] \epsilon_{\mathrm{sad}}(z^{t}) \leq \frac{\Omega^{2}}{2} + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau}^{2} \| G(z_{\tau}, \xi_{\tau}) \|_{*}^{2} + \max_{u \in Z} D(\xi^{t}, u).\tag{5.3.62}
$$

Now observe that by construction of the method $z_{T}$ is a deterministic function of $\xi^{\tau - 1} \colon z_{\tau} =$ $Z_{\tau}(\xi^{\tau - 1})$ , where $Z_{\tau}$ takes its values in $Z.$ . Due to this observation and to the fact that $\gamma_{\tau}$ are deterministic, taking expectations of both sides in (5.3.62) w.r.t. $\boldsymbol{\xi}^{t}$ we get

$$
\left[\sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau} \right] \mathbb{E} \{\epsilon_{\mathrm{sad}}(z^{t})\} \leq \frac{\Omega^{2}}{2} + \frac{\sigma^{2}}{2} \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau}^{2} + \mathbb{E} \left\{\max_{u \in Z} D(\xi^{t}, u) \right\};\tag{5.3.63}
$$

note that in this computation we bounded E $\{\| G(z_{\tau}, \xi_{\tau}) \|_{*}^{2}\}, \tau \leq t,$ as follows:

$$
\mathbb{E} \left\{\| G(z_{\tau}, \xi_{\tau}) \|_{*}^{2} \right\} = \mathbb{E}_{\xi^{t}} \left\{\| G(Z_{\tau}(\xi^{\tau - 1}), \xi_{\tau}) \|_{*}^{2} \right\} = \mathbb{E}_{\xi^{\tau - 1}} \Bigg \{\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{\xi_{\tau}} \left\{\| G(Z_{\tau}(\xi^{\tau - 1}), \xi_{\tau}) \|_{*}^{2} \right\}}_{\leq \sigma^{2}} \Bigg\} \leq \sigma^{2}.
$$

$\mathbf{2}^{0}$ . It remains to bound $\mathbb{E} \left\{\operatorname{max}_{u \in Z} D(\xi^{t}, u) \right\}$ , which is done in the following two lemmas:

Lemma 5.3.1 For $1 \leq \tau \leq t_{\mathrm{{\scriptsize{i}}}}$ , let $v_{\tau}$ be a deterministic vector-valued function of $\xi^{\tau - 1} \colon v_{\tau} =$ $V_{\tau}(\xi^{\tau - 1})$ taking values in $Z.$ . Then

$$
\mathbb{E} \Bigl \{\mid \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \underbrace{\gamma_{\tau} \langle \Delta_{\tau}, v_{\tau} - z_{1} \rangle}_{\psi_{\tau}} \mid \Bigr\} \leq 2 \sigma \Omega \sqrt{\sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau}^{2}}.\tag{5.3.64}
$$

Proof. Setting $\begin{array}{r}{S_{0} = 0, S_{\tau} = \sum_{s = 1}^{\tau} \gamma_{s} \langle \Delta_{s}, v_{s} - z_{1} \rangle} \end{array}$ , for $\tau \geq 1$ we have:

$$
\mathbb{E} \left\{S_{\tau}^{2} \right\} = \mathbb{E} \left\{S_{\tau - 1}^{2} + 2S_{\tau - 1} \psi_{\tau} + \psi_{\tau}^{2} \right\} \leq \mathbb{E} \left\{S_{\tau - 1}^{2} \right\} + 4 \sigma^{2} \Omega^{2} \gamma_{\tau}^{2},\tag{5.3.65}
$$

where the concluding $\leq$ comes from the following considerations:

a) By construction, $S_{\tau - 1}$ depends solely on $\xi^{\tau - 1}$ , while $\begin{array}{r}{\psi_{\tau} = \gamma_{\tau} \langle G(Z_{\tau}(\xi^{\tau - 1}), \xi_{\tau}) \rangle -} \end{array}$ $F(Z_{\tau}(\xi^{\tau - 1})), V_{\tau}(\xi^{\tau - 1}) \rangle$ . Invoking (5.3.54), the expectation of ψ<sub>τ</sub> w.r.t. ξ<sub>τ</sub> is zero for all $\xi^{\tau - 1}$ , whence the expectation of the product of $S_{\tau - 1}$ (this quantity depends solely of $\xi^{\tau - 1})$ and $\psi_{\tau}$ is zero.

Illustration: Matrix Game and $\ell_{1}$ minimization with uniform fit. “In the nature” there exist “genuine” stochastic minimization/saddle point problems, those where the cost function is given as expectation

$$
\phi(x, y) = \int \Phi(x, y, \xi) dP(\xi)
$$

with eficiently computable integrant $\Phi$ and a distribution P of $\xi$ we can sample from. This is what happens when the actual cost is afected by random factors (prices, demands, etc.). In such a situation, assuming Φ convex-concave and, say, continuously diferentiable in $x, y$ for every ξ, the vector $\begin{array}{r}{G(x, y, \xi) =[\frac{\partial \Phi(x, y, \xi)}{\partial x}; - \frac{\partial \Phi(x, y, \xi)}{\partial y}]} \end{array}$ under minimal regularity assumptions satisfies (5.3.54) and (5.3.55). Thus, we can mimic a stochastic first order oracle for the cost function by generating a realization $\xi_{t} \sim P$ and returning the vector $G(x, y, \xi_{t})$ (t is the serial number of the call to the oracle, $(x, y)$ is the corresponding query point). Consequently, we can solve the saddle point problem by the SSPMD algorithm. Note that typically in a situation in question it is extremely dificult, if at all possible, to compute $\phi$ in a closed analytic form and thus to mimic a deterministic first order oracle for $\phi.$ . We may say that in the “genuine” stochastic saddle point problems, the necessity in stochastic oracle-oriented algorithms, like SSPMD, is genuine as well. This being said, we intend to illustrate the potential of stochastic oracles and associated algorithms by an example of a completely different flavour, where the saddle point problem to be solved is a simply-looking deterministic one, and the rationale for randomization is the desire to reduce its computational complexity.

The problem we are interested in is a bilinear saddle point problem on the direct product of two simplexes:

$$
\min_{x \in \Delta_{n}} \max_{y \in \Delta_{m}} \phi(x, y) := a^{T} x + y^{T} Ax + b^{T} y.
$$

Note that due to the structure of $\Delta_{n}$ and $\Delta_{m}$ , we can reduce the situation to the one where $a = 0, b = 0;$ indeed, it sufices to replace the original A with the matrix

$$
A + \underbrace{[1; \ldots; 1]}_{m} a^{T} + b \underbrace{[1; \ldots; 1]}_{n}^{T}.
$$

By this reason, and in order to simplify notation, we pose the problem of interest as

$$
\min_{x \in \Delta_{n}} \max_{y \in \Delta_{m}} \phi(x, y) := y^{T} Ax.\tag{5.3.75}
$$

This problem arises in several applications, $\mathrm{e.g.}$ , in matrix games and $\ell_{1}$ minimization under $\ell_{\infty}{-} \mathrm{loss}$

Matrix game interpretation of (5.3.75) (this problem is usually even called “matrix game”) is as follows:

There are two players, every one selecting his action from a given finite set; w.l.o.g., we can assume that the actions of the first player form the set $J = \{1,..., n\}$ , and the actions of the second player form the set $I = \{1,...,.m\}$ . If the first player chooses an action $j \in J.$ and the second – an action $i \in I.$ , the first pays to the second $a_{ij}$ where the matrix $A =[a_{ij}]_{\stackrel{1 \leq i \leq m}{1 \leq j \leq n}}$ <sub>,</sub> is known in advance to both the players. What should rational players (interested to reduce their losses and to increase their gains) do?

The answer is easy when the matrix has a saddle point – there exists $(i_{*}, j_{*})$ such that the entry $a_{i_{*}, j_{*}}$ is the minimal one in its row and the maximal one it its column. You can immediately verify that in this case the maximal entry in every column is at least $a_{i *, j *}$ , and the minimal entry in every row is at most $a_{i_{*}, j_{*}}$ , meaning that when the first player chooses some action $j,$ , the second one can take from him at least $a_{i_{*}, j_{*}}$ , and if the second player chooses an action $i,$ the first can pay to the second at most $a_{i_{*}, j_{*}}$ . The bottom line is that rational players should stick to choices $j_{*}$ and $i_{*};$ in this case, no one of them has an incentive to change his choice, provided that the adversary sticks to his choice. We see that if A has a saddle point, the rational players should use its components as their choices. Now, what to do if, as it typically is the case, A has no saddle point? In this case there is no well-defined solution to the game as it was posed – there is no pair $(i_{*}, j_{*})$ such that the rational players will use, as their respective choices, $i_{*}$ and $j_{*}$ . However, there still is a meaningful definition of a solution to a slightly modified game – one in mixed strategies, due to von Neumann and Morgenstern. Specifically, assume that the players play the game not just once, but many times, and are interested in their average, over the time, losses. In this case, they can stick to randomized choices, where at t-th tour, the first player draws his choice $\jmath$ from J according to some probability distribution on $J$ (this distribution is just a vector $x \in \Delta_{n}$ , called mixed strategy of the first player), and the second player draws his choice  according to some probability distribution on I (represented by a vector $y \in \Delta_{m}$ , the mixed strategy of the second player). In this case, assuming the draws independent of each other, the expected per-tour loss of the first player (which is also the expected per-tour gain of the second player) is $y^{T} Ax$ . Rational players would now look for a saddle point of $\phi(x, y) = y^{T} Ax$ on the domain $\Delta_{n} \times \Delta_{m}$ comprised of pairs of mixed strategies, and in this domain the saddle point does exist.

$\ell_{1}$ minimization with $\ell_{\infty}$ fit is the problem $\operatorname{min}_{\xi : \| \xi \|_{1} \le 1} \| B \xi - b \|_{\infty}$ , or, in the saddle point form, min $\begin{array}{r}{\| \xi \|_{1} \le 1 \operatorname{max}_{\| \eta \|_{1} \le 1} \eta^{T}[B \xi - b]} \end{array}$ . Representing $\xi = p - q, \eta = r - s$ with nonnegative $p, q, r, s.$ , the problem can be rewritten in terms of $x =[p; q], y =[r; s]$ , specifically, as

$$
\min_{x \in \Delta_{n}} \max_{y \in \Delta_{m}} \left[y^{T} Ax - y^{T} a \right]
$$

$$
[A = \left[\begin{array}{cc} B & - B \\ - B & B \end{array} \right], a =[b; - b]]
$$

where $n = 2 \mathrm{dim} \xi, m = 2 \mathrm{dim} \eta$ . As we remember, the resulting problem can be represented in the form of (5.3.75).

Problem (5.3.75) is a nice bilinear saddle point problem. The best known so far algorithms for solving large-scale instances of this problem within a medium accuracy find an $\epsilon$-solution $(x_{\epsilon}, y_{\epsilon})$ •

$$
\epsilon_{\mathrm{sad}}(x_{\epsilon}, y_{\epsilon}) \leq \epsilon
$$

in $\begin{array}{r}{O(1) \sqrt{\ln(m) \ln(n)} \frac{\| A \|_{\infty} + \epsilon}{\epsilon}} \end{array}$ steps, where $\| A \|_{\infty}$ is the maximal magnitude of entries in A. A single step requires $O(1)$ matrix-vector multiplications involving the matrices A and $A^{T}$ , plus $O(1)(m + n)$ operations of computational overhead. Thus, the overall arithmetic cost of an $\epsilon$-solution is

$$
\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{det}} = O(1) \sqrt{\ln(m) \ln(n)} \frac{\| A \|_{\infty} + \epsilon}{\epsilon} \mathcal{M}
$$

arithmetic operations $\left(\mathrm{a.o.} \right)$ , where M is the maximum of $m + n$ and the arithmetic cost of a pair of matrix-vector multiplications, one involving A and the other one involving $A^{T}$ . The outlined bound is achieved, $\mathrm{e.g.}$ , by the Mirror Prox algorithm with Simplex setup, see section 5.5.2.

For dense m × n matrices A with no specific structure, the quantity $\mathcal{M}$ is $O(mn)$ , so that the above complexity bound is quadratic in m, n and can became prohibitively large when $m, n$ are really large. Could we do better? The answer is $^{66} \mathrm{yes}^{99} -$ we can replace time-consuming in the large scale case precise matrix-vector multiplication by its computationally cheap randomized version.

A stochastic oracle for matrix-vector multiplication can be built as follows. In order to estimate $Bx,$ we can treat the vector ${\frac{1}{\| x \|_{1}}} \mathrm{abs}[x]$ , where abs $[x]$ is the vector of magnitudes of entries in x, as a probability distribution on the set J of indexes of columns in $B,$ draw from this distribution a random index $\jmath$ and return the vector $G = \| x \|_{1} \mathrm{sign}(x_{\jmath}) \mathrm{Col}_{\jmath}[B]$ . We clearly have

$$
\mathbb{E} \{G\} = Bx
$$

— our oracle indeed is unbiased.

If you think of how could you implement this procedure, you immediately realize that all you need is an access to a generator producing uniformly distributed on [0, 1] random number $\xi;$ the output of the outlined stochastic oracle will be a deterministic function of x and $\xi,$ as required in our model of stochastic oracle. Moreover, the number of operations to build $G$ modulo generating $\xi$ is dominated by dim x operations to generate  and the efort to extract from B a column given its number, which we from now on will assume to be $O(1) m$ , m being the dimension of the column. Thus, the arithmetic cost of calling the oracle in the case of $m \times n$ matrix B is $O(1)(m + n){\mathrm{~ a.o}}$ . (note that for all practical purposes, generating $\xi$ takes just $O(1){\mathrm{~ a.o.}})$ . Note also that the output G of our stochastic oracle satisfies

$$
\| G \|_{\infty} \leq \| x \|_{1} \| B \|_{\infty}, \| B \|_{\infty} = \max_{i, j} | B_{ij} |.
$$

Now, the vector field $F(x, y)$ associated with the bilinear saddle point problem (5.3.75) is

$$
F(x, y) =[F_{x}(y) = A^{T} y; F_{y}(x) = - Ax] = \mathcal{A}[x; z], \mathcal{A} = \left[\begin{array}{cc} & A^{T} \\ - A \end{array} \right].
$$

We see that computing $F(x, y)$ at a point $(x, y) \in \Delta_{n} \times \Delta_{n}$ can be randomized — we can get an unbiased estimate $G(x, y, \xi)$ of $F(x, y)$ at the cost of $O(1)(m + n) ~ a.o.$ , and the estimate satisfies the condition

$$
\| G(x, y, \xi) \|_{\infty} \leq \| A \|_{\infty}.\tag{5.3.76}
$$

Indeed, in order to get $G$ given $(x, y) \in \Delta_{n} \times \Delta_{m}.$ , we treat x as a probability distribution on $\{1,..., n\}$ , draw an index $\jmath$ from this distribution and extract from A the corresponding column $\operatorname{Col}_{\mathcal{I}}[A]$ . Similarly, we treat y as a probability distribution on $\{1,..., m\}$ , draw from this distribution an index ı and extract from $\bar{A}^{T}$ the corresponding column $\mathrm{Col}_{\i}[\dot{A}^{T}]$ . The formula for G is just

$$
G =[\mathrm{Col}_{\iota}[A^{T}]; - \mathrm{Col}_{\jmath}[A]].
$$

## 5.3.7.4 Solving (5.3.75) via Stochastic Saddle Point Mirror Descent.

A natural setup for SSPMD as applied to (5.3.75) is obtained by combining the Entropy setups for $X = \Delta_{n}$ and $Y = \Delta_{m}$ . Specifically, let us define the norm $\| \cdot \|$ on the embedding space $\mathbb{R}^{m -}$ <sup>+</sup>n of $\Delta_{n} \times \Delta_{m}$ as

$$
\|[x; y] \| = \sqrt{\alpha \| x \|_{1}^{2} + \beta \| y \|_{1}^{2}},
$$

and the DGF $\omega(x, y)$ for $Z = \Delta_{n} \times \Delta_{n}$ as

$$
\omega(x, y) =(1 + \delta) \alpha \sum_{j = 1}^{n}(x_{j} + \delta / n) \ln(x_{j} + \delta / n) +(1 + \delta) \beta \sum_{i = 1}^{m}(y_{i} + \delta / m) \ln(y_{i} + \delta / m),[\delta = 10^{- 16}]
$$

where $\alpha, ~ \beta$ are positive weight coeficients. With this choice of the norm and the DGF, we clearly ensure that ω is strongly convex modulus 1 with respect to $\| \cdot \|$ , while the ω-diameter of $Z ={\Delta_{n}} \times{\Delta_{m}}$ is given by

$$
\Omega^{2} = O(1)[\alpha \ln(n) + \beta \ln(m)],
$$

provided that $m, n \geq 3$ , which we assume from now on. Finally, the norm conjugate to $\| \cdot \|$ is

$$
\|[\xi; \eta] \|_{*} = \sqrt{\alpha^{- 1} \| \xi \|_{\infty}^{2} + \beta^{- 1} \| \eta \|_{\infty}^{2}}
$$

$\mathrm{\left(why ? \right)}$ , so that the quantity σ defined in (5.3.57) is, in view of (5.3.76), bounded from above by

$$
\widehat{\sigma} = \| A \|_{\infty} \sqrt{\frac{1}{\alpha} + \frac{1}{\beta}}.
$$

It makes sense to choose $\alpha, \beta$ in order to minimize the error bound (5.3.59), or, which is the same, to minimize Ωσ. One of the optimizers (they clearly are unique up to proportionality) is

$$
\alpha = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\ln(n)}[\sqrt{\ln(n)} + \sqrt{\ln(m)}]}, \beta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\ln(m)}[\sqrt{\ln(n)} + \sqrt{\ln(m)}]},
$$

which results in

$$
\Omega = O(1), \Omega \sigma = O(1) \sqrt{\ln(mn)} \| A \|_{\infty}.
$$

As a result, the eficiency estimate (5.3.59) takes the form

$$
\mathbb{E} \{\epsilon_{\mathrm{sad}}(x^{T}, y^{T})\} \leq \frac{6 \Omega \sigma}{\sqrt{T}} = O(1) \sqrt{\ln(mn)} \frac{\| A \|_{\infty}}{\sqrt{T}}.\tag{5.3.77}
$$

Discussion. The number of steps T needed to make the right hand side in the bound (5.3.77) at most a desired $\epsilon \leq \| A \|_{\infty}$ is

$$
N(\epsilon) = O(1) \ln(mn) \left(\frac{\| A \|_{\infty}}{\epsilon}\right)^{2},
$$

and the total arithmetic cost of these $N(\epsilon)$ steps is

$$
\mathcal{C}_{\text{rand}} = O(1) \ln(mn)(m + n) \left(\frac{\| A \|_{\infty}}{\epsilon}\right)^{2} \text{a.o.}
$$

Recall that for a dense general-type matrix A, to solve (5.3.75) within accuracy $\epsilon$ deterministically costs

$$
\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{det}}(\epsilon) = O(1) \sqrt{\ln(m) \ln(n)} mn \left(\frac{\| A \|_{\infty}}{\epsilon}\right) \text{a.o.}
$$

We see that as far as the dependence of the arithmetic cost of an $\epsilon$-solution on the desired relative accuracy $\delta : = \epsilon / \| A \|_{\infty}$ is concerned, the deterministic algorithm significantly outperforms the randomized one. At the same time, the dependence of the cost on m, n is much better for the randomized algorithm. As a result, when a moderate and fixed relative accuracy is sought and m, n are large, the randomized algorithm by far outperforms the deterministic one.

A remarkable property of the above result is as follows: in order to find a solution of a fixed relative accuracy $\delta,$ the randomized algorithm carries out $O(\ln(mn) \delta^{- 2})$ steps, and at every step inspects $m + n$ entries of the matrix A (those in a randomly selected row and in a randomly selected column). Thus, the total number of data entries inspected by the algorithm in course of building a solution of relative accuracy $\delta$ is $O(\ln(mn)(m + n) \delta^{- 2})$ , which for large m, n is incomparably less than the total number mn of entries in A. We see that our algorithm demonstrates what is called sublinear time behaviour – returns a good approximate solution by inspecting a negligible, for $m = O(n)$ large, and tending to zero as $m ={\cal O}(n) \infty,$ , fraction of problem’s data<sup>5</sup>.

Assessing the quality. Strictly speaking, the outlined comparison of the deterministic and the randomized algorithms for (5.3.75) is not completely fair: with the deterministic algorithm, we know for sure that the solution we end up with indeed is an $\epsilon$-solution to (5.3.75), while with the randomized algorithm we know only that the expected inaccuracy of our (random!) approximate solution is $\leq \epsilon;$ nobody told us that a realization of this random solution $\widehat{z}$ we actually get solves the problem within accuracy about $\epsilon$. If we were able to quantify the actual accuracy of z by computing $\epsilon_{\mathrm{sad}}(\widehat{z})$ , we could circumvent this dificulty as follows: let us choose the number T of steps in our randomized algorithm in such a way that the resulting expected inaccuracy $\mathrm{is} \leq \epsilon / 2$ . After $\widehat{z}$ is built, we compute $\epsilon_{\mathrm{sad}}(\widehat{z})$ ; if this quantity is $\leq \epsilon.$ , we terminate with $\epsilon$-solution to (5.3.75) at hand. Otherwise (this “otherwise” may happen with probability $\leq 1 / 2$ only, since the inaccuracy is nonnegative, and the expected inaccuracy is $\leq \epsilon / 2)$ we rerun the algorithm, check the quality of the resulting solution, rerun the algorithm again when this quality still is worse then $\epsilon,$ and so on, until either an $\epsilon$-solution is found, or a chosen in advance maximum number N of reruns is reached. With this approach, in order to ensure generating an $\epsilon$-solution to the problem with probability at least $1 - \beta$ we need $N = O(\ln(1 / \beta))$ ; thus, even for pretty small $\beta,$ N is just a moderate constant<sup>6</sup>, and the randomized algorithm still can outperform by far its 100%-reliable deterministic counterpart. The dificulty, however, is that in order to compute $\epsilon_{\mathrm{sad}}(\widehat{z})$ , we need to know $F(z)$ exactly, since in our case

$$
\epsilon_{\mathrm{sad}}(x, y) = \max_{i \leq m}[Ax]_{i} - \min_{j \leq n}[A^{T} y]_{j},
$$

and even a single computation of F could be too expensive (and will definitely destroy the sublinear time behaviour). Can we circumvent somehow the dificulty? The answer is positive. Indeed, note that

A. For a general bilinear saddle point problem

$$
\min_{x \in X} \max_{y \in Y} \left[a^{T} x + b^{T} y + y^{T} Ax \right]
$$

the operator F is of a very special structure:

$$
F(x, y) =[A^{T} y + a; - Ax - b] = \mathcal{A}[x; y] + c,
$$

where the matrix $\mathcal{A} = \left[\begin{array}{cc}{\theta} \\{- A} \end{array} \right]$ is skew symmetric;

B. The randomized computation of $F$ we have used in the case of (5.3.75) also is of a very specific structure, specifically, as follows: we associate with $z \in Z = X \times Y$ a probability distribution $P_{z}$ which is supported on $Z$ and is such that if $\zeta \sim P_{z}$ , then $\mathbb{E} \{\zeta\} = z,$ , and our stochastic oracle works as follows: in order to produce an unbiased estimate of $F(z)$ it draws a realization $\zeta$ from $P_{z}$ and returns $G = F(\zeta)$

Specifically, in the case of (5.3.75), $z =(x, y) \in \Delta_{n} \times \Delta_{m}$ , and $P_{x, y}$ is the probability distribution on the mn pairs of vertices $(e_{j}, f_{i})$ of the simplexes $\Delta_{n}$ and $\Delta_{m} \(e_{j}$ are the standard basic orths in $\mathbb{R}^{n}, f_{i}$ are the standard basic orths in $\mathbb{R}^{m})$ such that the probability of a pair $(e_{j}, f_{i})$ is $x_{j} y_{i};$ the expectation of this distribution is exactly z, the expectation of $F(\zeta), \zeta \sim P_{x, y}$ is exactly $F(z)$ . The advantage of this particular distribution $P_{z}$ is that it $\mathrm{^{66} sits^{9}}$ on pairs of highly sparse vectors (just one nonzero entry in every member of a pair), which makes it easy to compute $F$ at a realization drawn from this distribution.

The point is that when A and B are met, we can modify the SSPMD algorithm, preserving its eficiency estimate and making $F(z^{t})$ readily available for every t. Specifically, at a step τ of the algorithm, we have at our disposal a realization $\zeta_{\tau}$ of the distribution $P_{z_{\tau}}$ which we used to compute $G(z_{\tau}, \xi_{\tau}) = F(\zeta_{\tau})$ . Now let us replace the rule for generating approximate solutions, which originally was

$$
z^{t} = \bar{z}^{t} := \left[\sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau} \right]^{- 1} \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau} z_{\tau},
$$

with the rule

$$
z^{t} = \widehat{z}^{t} := \left[\sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau} \right]^{- 1} \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau} \zeta_{\tau}.
$$

since $\zeta_{t} \sim P_{z_{t}}$ and the latter distribution is supported on $Z,$ we still have $z^{t} \in Z$ . Further, we have computed $F(\zeta_{\tau})$ exactly, and since $F$ is Affine, we just have

$$
F(z^{t}) = \left[\sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau} \right]^{- 1} \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau} F(\zeta_{\tau}),
$$

meaning that sequential computing $F(z^{t})$ costs us just additional $O(m + n)$ a.o. per step and thus increases the overall complexity by just a close to 1 absolute constant factor. What is not immediately clear, is why the new rule for generating approximate solutions preserves the eficiency estimate. The explanation is as follows (work it out in full details by yourself): The proof of Theorem 5.3.6 started from the observation that for every $u \in Z$ we have

$$
\sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau} \langle G(z_{\tau}, \xi_{\tau}), z_{\tau} - u \rangle \leq B_{t}(\xi^{t})\tag{!}
$$

with some particular $B_{t}(\xi^{t})$ ; we then verified that the supremum of the left hand side in this inequality in $\begin{array}{r}{u \in Z \mathrm{is} \geq \left\lceil \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau} \right\rceil \epsilon_{\mathrm{sad}}(\bar{z}^{t}) - C_{t}(\xi^{t})} \end{array}$ with certain explicit $C_{t}(\cdot)$ . As a result, we got the inequality

$$
\left[\sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau} \right] \epsilon_{\mathrm{sad}}(\bar{z}^{t}) \leq B(\xi^{t}) + C_{t}(\xi^{t}),\tag{!!}
$$

which, upon taking the expectations, led us to the desired eficiency estimate. Now we should act as follows: it is immediately seen that (!) remains valid and reads

$$
\sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau} \langle F(\zeta_{t}), z_{t} - u \rangle \leq B_{t}(\xi^{t}),
$$

whence

$$
\sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau} \langle F(\zeta_{t}), \zeta_{t} - u \rangle \leq B_{t}(\xi^{T}) + D_{t}(\xi^{t}),
$$

where

$$
D_{t}(\xi^{t}) = \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau} \langle F(\zeta_{t}), \zeta_{t} - z_{t} \rangle,
$$

which, exactly as in the original proof, leads us to a slightly modified version of (!!), specifically, to

$$
\left[\sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau} \right] \epsilon_{\mathrm{sad}}(\widehat{z}^{t}) \leq B_{t}(\xi^{t}) + C_{t}(\xi^{t}) + D_{t}(\xi^{t})
$$

with the same as in the original proof upper bound on $\mathbb{E} \{B_{t}(\xi^{t}) + C_{t}(\xi^{t})\}$ . When taking expectations of the both sides of this inequality, we get exactly the same upper bound on $\mathbb{E} \{\epsilon_{\mathrm{sad}}(\dots)\}$ as in the original proof due to the following immediate observation:

$$
\mathbb{E} \{D_{t}(\xi^{t})\} = 0.
$$

Indeed, by construction, $\zeta_{\tau}$ is a deterministic function of $\xi^{\tau}, \z_{\tau}$ is a deterministic function of $\xi^{\tau - 1}$ , and the conditional, $\xi^{\tau - 1}$ being fixed, distribution of $\zeta_{\tau}$ is $P_{z_{\imath}}$ We now have

$$
\langle F(\zeta_{\tau}), \zeta_{\tau} - z_{\tau} \rangle = \langle \mathcal{A} \zeta_{\tau} + c, \zeta_{\tau} - z_{\tau} \rangle = - \langle \mathcal{A} \zeta_{\tau}, z_{\tau} \rangle + \langle c, \zeta_{\tau} - z_{\tau} \rangle
$$

where we used the fact that $\mathcal{A}$ is skew symmetric. Now, the quantity

$$
- \langle \mathcal{A} \zeta_{\tau}, z_{\tau} \rangle + \langle c, \zeta_{\tau} - z_{\tau} \rangle
$$

is a deterministic function of $\xi^{\tau},$ and among the terms participating in the latter formula the only one which indeed depends on $\xi_{\tau}$ is $\zeta_{\tau}$ . Since the dependence of the quantity on $\zeta_{\tau}$ is Affine, the conditional, $\xi^{\tau - 1}$ being fixed, expectation of it w.r.t. $\xi_{\tau}$ is

$$
\langle \mathcal{A} \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{\xi_{\tau}} \{\zeta_{\tau}\}}_{z_{\tau}}, z_{\tau} \rangle + \langle c, \mathbb{E}_{\xi_{\tau}} \{\zeta_{\tau}\} - z_{\tau} \rangle = - \langle \mathcal{A} z_{\tau}, z_{\tau} \rangle + \langle c, z_{\tau} - z_{\tau} \rangle = 0
$$

(we again used the fact that $\mathcal{A}$ is skew symmetric). Thus, $ { \mathbf { E } } \{  { \langle F ( \zeta _ { \tau } ) , \zeta _ { \tau } - z _ { \tau } \rangle } \} = 0$ 2 whence $\mathbb{E} \{D_{t}(\xi^{t}\} = 0$ as well.

## Operational Exercise 5.3.1 The “covering story” for your tasks is as follows:

There are n houses in a city; i-th house contains wealth $w_{i}$ . A burglar chooses a house, secretly arrives there and starts his business. A policeman also chooses his location alongside one of the houses; the probability for the policeman to catch the burglar is a known function of the distance d between their locations, say, it is $\exp \{- cd\}$ with some coeficient $c > 0$ (you may think, $\mathrm{e.g.}$ , that when the burglary starts, an alarm sounds or 911 is called, and the chances of catching the burglar depend on how long it takes from the policeman to arrive at the scene). This cat and mouse game takes place every night. The goal is to find numerically near-optimal mixed strategies of the burglar, who is interested to maximize his expected “profit” $[1 - \exp \{- cd(i, j)\}] w_{i}$ (i is the house chosen by the burglar, $j$ is the house at which the policeman is located), and of the policeman who has a completely opposite interest.

Remark: Note that the sizes of problems of the outlined type can be really huge. For example, let there be 1000 locations, and 3 burglars and 3 policemen instead of one burglar and one policeman. Now there are about $100^{3} / 3 !$ “locations” of the burglar side, and about $1000^{3} / 3 !$ “locations” of the police side, which makes the sizes of A well above $10^{8}$

The model of the situation is a matrix game where the $n \times n$ matrix A has the entries

$$
[1 - \exp \{- cd(i, j)\}] w_{i},
$$

$d(i, j)$ being the distance between the locations i and $j, \1 \ \leq \i, j \ \leq \n$ . In the matrix game associated with A, the policeman chooses mixed strategy $x \in \Delta_{n}$ , and the burglar chooses a mixed strategy $y \in \Delta_{n}$ Your task is to get an $\epsilon$-approximate saddle point. We assume for the sake of definiteness that the houses are located at the nodes of a square $k \times k \ \mathrm{grid}$ , and $c = 2 / D$ , where D is the maximal distance between a pair of houses. The distance $d(i, j)$ is either the Euclidean distance $\lVert P_{i} - P_{j} \rVert_{2}$ between the locations $P_{i}, P_{j}$ of i-th and j-th houses on the 2D plane, or $d(i, j) = \| P_{i} - P_{j} \|_{1}$ (“Manhattan distance” corresponding to rectangular road network).

Task: Solve the problem within accuracy $\epsilon$ around 1.e-3 for $k = 100 \({\mathrm{i.e.,}} \n = k^{2} = 10000)$ . You may play with

- “profile of wea $.lth^{\prime \prime} ~ w$ . For example, in my experiment reported on Fig. 5.1, I used $w_{i} = \mathrm{max}[p_{i} /(k - 1), q_{i} /(k - 1)]$ , where $p_{i}$ and $q_{i}$ are the coordinates of i-th house (in my experiment the houses were located at the 2D points with integer coordinates $p, q$ varying from 0 to $k - 1)$ ). You are welcome to use other profiles as well.

- distance between houses – Euclidean or Manhattan one (I used the Manhattan distance).
