## 5.3.8 Mirror Descent and Stochastic Online Regret Minimization

## 5.3.8.1 Stochastic online regret minimization: problem’s formulation

Consider a stochastic analogy of online regret minimization setup considered in section 5.3.5, specifically, as follows. We are given

1. a convex compact set X in Euclidean space $E,$ with $(X, E)$ equipped with proximal setup $\mathrm{~ \ - ~ a ~}$ norm $\| \cdot \|$ on E and a compatible with this norm continuously diferentiable on X DGF $\omega(\cdot);$

2. a family $\mathcal{F}$ of convex and Lipschitz continuous functions on $X;$

3. access to stochastic oracle as follows: at t-th call to the oracle, the input to the oracle being a query point $x_{t} \in X$ and a function $f_{t}(\cdot) \in \mathcal{F}$ , the oracle returns vector $G_{t} =$ $G_{t}[f_{t}(\cdot), x_{t}, \xi_{t}]$ and a real $g_{t} = g_{t}[f_{t}(\cdot), x_{t}, \xi_{t}]$ , where for every $tG_{t}[f(\cdot), x, \xi]$ and $g_{t}[f(\cdot), x, \xi]$ are deterministic functions of $f \in{\mathcal{F}}, x \in X$ and a realization $\xi$ of “oracle’s noise.” It is further assumed that

(a) $\left\{\xi_{t} \sim P : t \geq 0 \right\}$ is an i.i.d. sequence of random “oracle noises” (noise distribution $P$ is not known in advance);

(b) $f_{t}(\cdot) \in \mathcal{F}$ is selected “by nature” and depends solely on t and the collection $\xi^{t - 1} =$ $(\xi_{0}, \xi_{1},..., \xi_{t - 1})$ of oracle noises at steps preceding the step t:

$$
f_{t}(\cdot) = F_{t}(\xi^{t - 1}, \cdot),
$$

where $F_{t}(\xi^{t - 1}, x)$ is a legitimate deterministic function of $\xi^{t - 1}$ and $x \in X$ , with $\mathrm{\bar{\cdot} legitimate^{3}}$ meaning that $F_{t}(\xi^{t - 1}, x)$ as a function of x belongs to $\mathcal{F}$ for all $\xi^{t - 1}$ Sequence $\{\cdot F_{t}(\cdot, \cdot) : t \geq 1\}$ is selected by nature prior to our actions. In the sequel, we refer to such a sequence as to nature’s policy.

Finally, we assume that when the stochastic oracle is called at step t, these are we (the decision maker) who inputs to the stochastic oracle the query point $x_{t},$ and this is the nature inputting $f_{t}(\cdot) = F_{t}(\xi^{t - 1}, \cdot)$ ; we do not see $f_{t}(\cdot)$ directly, all we see is the returned by oracle stochastic information $g_{t}[f_{t}(\cdot), x_{t}, \xi_{t}], G_{t}[f_{t}(\cdot), x_{t}, \xi_{t}]$ on $f_{t}$

(c) our actions $x_{1}, \x_{2}, \ldots$ . are yielded by a non-anticipative decision making policy as follows. At step t we have at our disposal the past search points $x_{\tau}, \tau < t,$ along with the answers $g_{\tau}, G_{\tau}$ of the oracle queried at the inputs $(x_{\tau}, F_{\tau}(\xi^{\tau - 1}, \cdot)), 1 \le \tau < t.\x_{t}$ should be a deterministic function of t and of the tuple $\{x_{\tau}, g_{\tau}, G_{\tau} : \tau < t\}$ ; a nonanticipative decision making policy is nothing but the collection of these deterministic functions.

Note that with a non-anticipative decision making policy fixed, the query points $x_{t}$ become deterministic functions of $\xi^{t - 1}, t = 1, 2, \ldots$

Our crucial assumption (which is in force everywhere in this section) is that whatever be $t,$ x and $f(\cdot) \in{\mathcal{F}}_{:}$ , we have

(a)

$$
\mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim P} \{g_{t}[f(\cdot), x, \xi]\} = f(x)\tag{b.1}
$$

$$
\mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim P} \{G_{t}[f(\cdot), x, \xi]\} \in \partial f(x_{t})\tag{5.3.79}
$$

$$
\mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim P} \{\| G_{t}[f(\cdot), x, \xi] \|_{*}^{2}\} \leq \sigma^{2}\tag{b.2}
$$

with some known in advance positive constant $\sigma.$

Finally, we assume that the toll we are paying in round t is exactly the quantity $g_{t}[f_{t}(\cdot), x_{t}, \xi_{t}]$ and that our goal is to devise a non-anticipative decision making policy which makes small, as N grows, the expected regret

$$
\begin{array}{rl} &{\mathbb{E}_{\xi^{N}} \left\{\frac{1}{N} \sum_{t = 1}^{N} g_{t}[F_{t}(\xi^{t - 1}, \cdot), x_{t}, \xi_{t}] \right\} - \inf_{x \in X} \mathbb{E}_{\xi^{N}} \left\{\frac{1}{N} \sum_{t = 1}^{N} g_{t}[F_{t}(\xi^{t - 1}, \cdot), x, \xi_{t}] \right\}} \\{=} &{\mathbb{E}_{\xi^{N}} \left\{\frac{1}{N} \sum_{t = 1}^{N} F_{t}(\xi^{t - 1}, x_{t}) \right\} - \inf_{x \in X} \mathbb{E}_{\xi^{N}} \left\{\frac{1}{N} \sum_{t = 1}^{N} F_{t}(\xi^{t - 1}, x) \right\}} \end{array}\tag{5.3.80}
$$

(the equality here stems from $\left(5.3.79.a \right)$ combined with the facts that $x_{t}$ is a deterministic function of $\xi^{t - 1}$ and that $\xi_{0}, \xi_{1}, \xi_{2}, \ldots \mathrm{arei.i.d.})$ . Note that we want to achieve the outlined goal whatever be nature’s policy, that is, whatever be a sequence $\{F_{t}(\xi^{t - 1}, \cdot) : t \geq 1\}$ of legitimate deterministic functions.

## 5.3.8.2 Minimizing stochastic regret by MD

We have specified the problem of stochastic regret minimization; what is on our agenda now, is to understand how this problem can be solved by Mirror Descent. We intend to use exactly the same algorithm as in section 5.3.5:

1. Initialization: Select stepsizes $\{\gamma_{t} > 0\}_{t \geq 1}$ which are nonincreasing in t and select $x_{1} \in X$

2. Step $t = 1, 2, \ldots$ Given $x_{t}.$ , call the oracle, $x_{t}$ being the query point, pay the corresponding toll $g_{t}.$ observe $G_{t}$ , set

$$
x_{t + 1} = \operatorname{Prox}_{x_{t}}(\gamma_{t} G_{t}) := \underset{x \in X}{\operatorname{argmin}} \left[\langle \gamma_{t} G_{t} - \omega^{\prime}(x_{t}), x \rangle + \omega(x) \right]
$$

and pass to step $t + 1$

Note that with the selected by the nature sequence $\{F_{t}(\xi^{t - 1}, \cdot) : t \geq 1\}$ of legitimate deterministic functions fixed, $x_{t}$ are deterministic functions of $\xi^{t - 1}, t = 1, 2, \ldots$ Note also that the decision making policy yielded by the algorithm indeed is non-anticipative (and even does not require knowledge of tolls $g_{t})$

Convergence analysis. We are about to prove the following straightforward modification of Theorem 5.3.3:

Theorem 5.3.8 In the notation and under assumptions of this section, whatever be nature ${\bf \mathit{\Pi}}_{s}$ policy, that is, whatever be a sequence $\{F_{t}(\cdot, \cdot) : t \geq 1\}$ of legitimate deterministic functions, for the induced by this policy trajectory $\{x_{t} = x_{t}(\xi^{t - 1}) : t \geq 1\}$ of the above algorithm, and for every deterministic sequence $\{\lambda_{t} > 0 : t \ge 1\}$ such that $\lambda_{t} / \gamma_{t}$ is nondecreasing in t, it holds for $N = 1, 2, \ldots$

$$
\begin{array}{rl} &{\mathbb{E}_{\xi^{N}} \left\{\frac{1}{\Lambda_{N}} \sum_{t = 1}^{N} g_{t}[F_{t}(\xi^{t - 1}, \cdot), x_{t}, \xi_{t}] \right\} - \min_{x \in X} \mathbb{E}_{\xi^{N}} \left\{\frac{1}{\Lambda_{N}} \sum_{t = 1}^{N} g_{t}[F_{t}(\xi^{t - 1}, \cdot), x, \xi_{t}] \right\}} \\{\leq} &{\frac{\frac{\lambda_{N}}{\gamma_{N}} \Omega^{2} + \sigma^{2} \sum_{t = 1}^{N} \lambda_{t} \gamma_{t}}{2 \Lambda_{N}}} \end{array}\tag{5.3.81}
$$

Here, same as in Theorem 5.3.3,

$$
\Lambda_{N} = \sum_{t = 1}^{N} \lambda_{t}.
$$

Proof. Repeating word by word the reasoning in the proof of Theorem 5.3.3, we arrive at the relation

$$
\sum_{t = 1}^{N} \lambda_{t} \langle G_{t}[F_{t}(\xi^{t - 1}, \cdot), x_{t}, \xi_{t}], x_{t} - x \rangle \leq \frac{1}{2} \left[\frac{\lambda_{N}}{\gamma_{N}} \Omega^{2} + \sum_{t = 1}^{N} \lambda_{t} \gamma_{t} \| G_{t}[F_{t}(\xi^{t - 1}, \cdot), x_{t}, \xi_{t}] \|_{*}^{2} \right].
$$

which holds true for every $x \in X$ . Taking expectations of both sides and invoking the fact that $\{\xi_{t}\}$ are i.i.d. in combination with (5.3.79.b) and the fact that $x_{t}$ is a deterministic function of $\xi^{t - 1}$ , we arrive at

$$
\mathbb{E}_{\xi^{N}} \left\{\sum_{t = 1}^{N} \lambda_{t} \langle F_{t}^{\prime}(\xi^{t - 1}, x_{t}), x_{t} - x \rangle \right\} \leq \frac{1}{2} \left[\frac{\lambda_{N}}{\gamma_{N}} \Omega^{2} + \sigma^{2} \sum_{t = 1}^{N} \lambda_{t} \gamma_{t} \right],\tag{5.3.82}
$$

where $F_{t}^{\prime}(\xi^{t - 1}, x_{t})$ is a subgradient, taken w.r.t. x, of the function $F_{t}(\xi^{t - 1}, x)$ at $x = x_{t}$ . Since $F_{t}(\xi^{t - 1}, x)$ is convex in $x,$ we have $F_{t}(\xi^{t - 1}, x_{t}) - F_{t}(\xi^{t - 1}, x) \le \langle F_{t}^{\prime}(\xi^{t - 1}, x_{t}), x_{t} - x \rangle$ , and therefore (5.3.82) implies that for all $x \in X$ it holds

$$
\mathbb{E}_{\xi^{N}} \left\{\sum_{t = 1}^{N} \lambda_{t}[F_{t}(\xi^{t - 1}, x_{t}) - F_{t}(\xi^{t - 1}, x)] \right\} \leq \frac{1}{2} \left[\frac{\lambda_{N}}{\gamma_{N}} \Omega^{2} + \sigma^{2} \sum_{t = 1}^{N} \lambda_{t} \gamma_{t} \right],
$$

whence also

$$
\mathbb{E}_{\xi^{N}} \left\{\frac{1}{\Lambda_{N}} \sum_{t = 1}^{N} \lambda_{t} F_{t}(\xi^{t - 1}, x_{t}) \right\} - \inf_{x \in X} \mathbb{E}_{\xi^{N}} \left\{\frac{1}{\Lambda_{N}} \sum_{t = 1}^{N} \lambda_{t} F_{t}(\xi^{t - 1}, x) \right\} \leq \frac{\frac{\lambda_{N}}{\gamma_{N}} \Omega^{2} + \sigma^{2} \sum_{t = 1}^{N} \lambda_{t} \gamma_{t}}{2 \Lambda_{N}}.
$$

Invoking the second representation of the expected regret in (5.3.80), the resulting relation is exactly (5.3.81). ✷

Consequences. Let us choose

$$
\gamma_{t} = \frac{\Omega}{\sigma \sqrt{t}}, \lambda_{t} = t^{\alpha},
$$

with $\alpha \geq 0$ . This choice meets the requirements from the description of our algorithm and from the premise of Theorem 5.3.8, and, similarly to what happened in section 5.3.5, results in

$$
\begin{array}{l} \forall(N \geq \alpha): \\ \mathbb{E}_{\xi^{N}} \left\{\frac{1}{\Lambda_{N}} \sum_{t = 1}^{N} \lambda_{t} F_{t}(\xi^{t - 1}, x_{t}) \right\} - \inf_{x \in X} \mathbb{E}_{\xi^{N}} \left\{\frac{1}{\Lambda_{N}} \sum_{t = 1}^{N} \lambda_{t} F_{t}(\xi^{t - 1}, x) \right\} \leq O(1) \frac{(1 + \alpha) \Omega \sigma}{\sqrt{N}}, \end{array}\tag{5.3.83}
$$

with interpretation completely similar to the interpretation of the bound (5.3.41), see section 5.3.5.

## 5.3.8.3 Illustration: predicting sequences

To illustrate the stochastic regret minimization, consider Predicting Sequence problem as follows:

“The nature” selects a sequence $\{z_{t} : t \geq 1\}$ with terms $z_{t}$ from the d-element set $\mathcal{Z}_{d} = \{1,..., d\}$ . We observe these terms one by one, and at every time t want to predict $z_{t}$ via the past observations $z_{1},..., z_{t - 1}$ . Our loss at step t, our prediction being $\widehat{z}_{t}$ , is $\phi(\widehat{z}^{t}, z_{t})$ , where φ is a given loss function such that $\phi(z, z) = 0, z = 1,..., d.$ and $\phi(z^{\prime}, z) > 0$ when $z^{\prime} \neq z$ . What we are interested in is to make the average, over time horizon $t = 1,..., N$ , loss small.

What was just said is a “high level” imprecise setting. Missing details are as follows. We assume that

1. the nature generates sequences $z_{1}, z_{2}, \ldots$ in a randomized fashion. Specifically, there exists an i.i.d. sequence of “primitive” random variables $\zeta_{t}, t = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$ . observed one by one by the nature, and $z_{t}$ is a deterministic function $Z_{t}(\zeta^{t - 1}){\mathrm{~ of ~}} \zeta^{t - 1}{\mathrm{~ 7 ~}}$ . We refer to the collection $Z^{\infty} = \{Z_{t}(\cdot) : t \geq 1\}$ as to the generation policy.

2. we are allowed for randomized prediction, where the predicted value $\widehat{z}_{t}$ of $z_{t}$ is generated at random according to probability distribution $x_{t} - a$ vector from the probabilistic simplex $X = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^{d} : x \geq 0, \textstyle \sum_{z = 1}^{d} x^{z} = 1\}$ ; an entry $\boldsymbol{x}_{t}^{z}$ in $x_{t}$ is the probability for our randomized prediction to take value $z, z = 1,..., d.$

We impose on $x_{t}$ the restriction to be a deterministic function of $z^{t - 1} \colon x_{t} = X_{t}(z^{t - 1})$ ， and refer to a collection $X^{\infty} = \{X_{t}(\cdot) : t \geq 1\}$ of deterministic functions $X_{t}(z^{t - 1})$ taking values in $X$ as to prediction policy.

Introducing auxiliary sequence η<sub>0</sub>, η<sub>1</sub>, ... of independent of each other and of $\zeta_{t}$ ’s random variables uniformly distributed on [0, 1), we can make our randomized predictions $\widehat{z}_{t} \sim x_{t}$ deterministic functions of $x_{t}$ and $\eta_{t} \colon$

$$
\widehat{z}_{t} = \breve{Z}(x_{t}, \eta_{t}),
$$

where, for a probabilistic vector x and a real $\eta \in[0, 1), \breve{Z}(x, \eta)$ is the integer $z \in \mathcal{Z}_{d}$ uniquely defined by the relation $\textstyle \sum_{\ell = 1}^{z - 1} x^{\ell} \leq \eta < \sum_{\ell = 1}^{z} x^{\ell}$ (think of how would you sample from a probability distribution $x$ on $\{1,..., d\})$ . As a result, setting $\xi_{t} =[\zeta_{t}; \eta_{t}]$ and thinking about the i.i.d. sequence $\xi_{0}, \xi_{1}, \ldots$ as of the input “driving” generation and prediction, the respective policies being $Z^{\infty}$ and $X^{\infty}$ , we see that

$z_{t} \mathrm{' s}$ are deterministic functions of $\xi^{t - 1} =[\zeta^{t - 1}; \eta^{t - 1}]$ , specifically, $z_{t} = Z_{t}(\zeta^{t - 1})$ ;

$\boldsymbol{x}_{t}{}^{\} \mathrm{\boldsymbol{s}}$ are deterministic functions of $z^{t - 1}$ , specifically, $X_{t}(z^{t - 1})$ , and thus are deterministic functions of $\xi^{t - 1} \colon x_{t} = \widetilde{X}_{t}(\xi^{t - 1})$ ;

- predictions $\widehat{z}_{t} \mathrm{: s}$ are deterministic functions of $(\zeta^{t - 1}, \eta_{t})$ and thus – of $(\xi^{t - 1}, \eta_{t}) \colon \widehat{z}_{t} \ =$ $\widehat{Z}_{t}(\xi^{t - 1}, \eta_{t})$

Note that functions $Z_{t}$ are fully determined by generation policy, while functions $\smash{\widetilde{X}}_{t}$ and $\widehat{Z}_{t}$ stem from interaction between the policies for generation and for prediction and are fully determined by these two policies.

Given a generation policy $Z^{\infty} = \{Z_{t}(\cdot) : t \geq 1\}$ , a prediction policy $X^{\infty} = \{X_{t}(\cdot) : t \geq 1\}$ and a time horizon $N_{;}$ we

- quantify the performance of $X^{\infty}$ by the quantity

$$
\mathbb{E}_{\zeta^{N}, \eta^{N}} \left\{\frac{1}{N} \sum_{t = 1}^{N} \phi(\widehat{Z}_{t}(\zeta^{t - 1}, \eta_{t}), Z_{t}(\zeta^{t - 1})) \right\},
$$

that is, by the averaged over the time horizon expected prediction error as quantified by our loss function $\phi,$ and

- define the expected N-step regret associated with $Z^{\infty}, X^{\infty}$ as

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \mathcal{R}_{N}[X^{\infty} | Z^{\infty}] & = & \mathbb{E}_{\zeta^{N}, \eta^{N}} \left\{\frac{1}{N} \sum_{t = 1}^{n} \phi(\widehat{Z}_{t}(\zeta^{t - 1}, \eta_{t}), Z_{t}(\zeta^{t - 1})) \right\} \\ & & - \inf_{x \in X} \mathbb{E}_{\zeta^{N}, \eta^{N}} \left\{\frac{1}{N} \sum_{t = 1}^{N} \phi(\widehat{Z}_{t, x}(\zeta^{t - 1}, \eta_{t}), Z_{t}(\zeta^{t - 1})) \right\}, \end{array}\tag{5.3.84}
$$

where the only yet undefined quantity $\widehat{Z}_{t, x}(\zeta^{t - 1}, \eta_{t})$ is the “stationary counterpart” of $\widehat{Z}_{t}(\zeta^{t - 1}, \eta_{t})$ , that is, $\widehat{Z}_{t, x}(\zeta^{t - 1}, \bar{\eta}_{t})$ is t-th prediction yielded by interaction between the generation policy $Z^{\infty}$ and the stationary prediction policy $X_{x}^{\infty} \ = \ \{x_{t} \equiv x \ : \t \geq \1\}$ Thus, the regret is the excess of the average (over time and “driving input ${\mathfrak{P}}_{} \xi_{0}, \xi_{1}, \ldots \rangle$ prediction error yielded by prediction policy $X^{\infty}$ , generation policy being $Z^{\infty}$ , over the similar average error of the best possible under the circumstances (under generation policy $Z^{\infty})$ stationary $(x_{t} = x, t \ge 1)$ prediction policy.

Put broadly and vaguely, our goal is to build a prediction policy which, whatever be a generation policy, makes the regret small provided N is large.

To achieve our goal, we are about to “translate” our prediction problem to the language of stochastic regret minimization as presented in section 5.3.8.1. A sketch of the translation is as follows. Let $\mathcal{F}$ be the set of $d$ linear functions

$$
f^{\ell}(x) = \sum_{z = 1}^{d} \phi(z, \ell) x^{z}: X \to \mathbb{R}, \ell = 1, \dots, d;
$$

$f^{\ell}(x)$ is just the expected error of the randomized prediction, the distribution of the prediction being $x \in X$ , in the case when the true value to be predicted is \`. Note that $f^{\ell}(\cdot)$ is fully determined by \` and “remembers” \` (since by our assumption on the loss function, when x is the \`-th basic orth $e_{\ell}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , we have $f^{\ell}(e_{\ell}) = 0$ , and $f^{\ell}(x) > 0$ when $x \in X \backslash \{e_{\ell}\})$ . Consequently, we lose nothing when assuming that the nature, instead of generating a sequence $\{z_{t} : t \geq 1\}$ of points from $\mathcal{Z}_{d}.$ , generates a sequence of functions $f_{t}(\cdot) = f^{z_{t}}(\cdot)$ from $\mathcal{F}, t = 1, 2,...;$ with this interpretation, a generation policy $Z^{\infty}$ becomes what was in section 5.3.8.1 called nature’s policy, a policy which specifies t-th selection $f_{t}(\cdot)$ of nature as deterministically depending on $\xi^{t - 1}$ as on a parameter convex (in fact, linear) function $F_{t}(\xi^{t - 1}, \cdot) : X \to \mathbb{R}$

Now, at a step t, after the nature shows us z<sub>t</sub>, we get full information on the function $f_{t}(\cdot)$ selected by the nature at this step, and thus know the gradient of this Affine function; this gradient can be taken as what in the decision making framework of section 5.3.8.1 was called $G_{t}$ . Besides this, after the nature reveals $z_{t}$ , we know which prediction error we have made, and this error can be taken as what in section 5.3.8.1 was called the toll $g_{t}$ . On a straightforward inspection which we leave to the reader, the outlined translation converts the regret minimization form of our prediction problem into the problem of stochastic online regret minimization considered in section 5.3.8.1 and ensures validity of all assumptions of Theorem 5.3.8. As a result, we conclude that

(!) The MD algorithm from section 5.3.8.2 can be straightforwardly applied to the Sequence Prediction problem; with proper proximal setup (namely, the Simplex one) for the probabilistic simplex X and properly selected stepsize policy, this algorithm yields prediction policy $X_{\mathrm{MD}}^{\infty}$ which guarantees the regret bound

$$
\mathcal{R}_{N}[X_{\mathrm{MD}}^{\infty} | Z^{\infty}] \leq O(1) \frac{\sqrt{\ln(d + 1)} \max_{z, \ell} | \phi(z, \ell) |}{\sqrt{N}}.\tag{5.3.85}
$$

whatever be $N = 1, 2, \dots$ and a sequence generation policy $Z^{\infty}$

We see that MD allows to push regret to 0 as $N \to \infty$ at an $O(1 / \sqrt{N})$ rate and uniformly in sequence generation policies of the nature. As a result, when sequence generating policy used by the nature is “well suited” for stationary prediction, i.e., nature’s policy makes small the comparator

$$
\inf_{x \in X} \mathbb{E}_{\zeta^{N}, \eta^{N}} \left\{\frac{1}{N} \sum_{t = 1}^{N} \phi(\widehat{Z}_{t, x}(\zeta^{t - 1}, \eta_{t}), Z_{t}(\zeta^{t - 1})) \right\}\tag{5.3.86}
$$

in (5.3.84), (!) says that the MD-based prediction policy $X_{\mathrm{MD}}^{\infty}$ is good provided N is large. In the examples to follow, we use the simplest possible loss function: $\phi(z, \ell) = 0$ when $z = \ell$ and $\phi(z, \ell) = 1$ otherwise.

Example 1: i.i.d. generation policy. Assume that the nature generates $z_{t}$ by drawing it, independently across $t,$ from some distribution $p$ (let us call this generation policy an i.i.d. one). It is immediately seen that due to the i.i.d. nature of $z_{1}, z_{2},...,$ there is no way to predict $z_{t}$ via $z_{1},..., z_{t - 1}$ too well, even when we know $p$ in advance; specifically, the smallest possible expected prediction error is

$$
\epsilon(p) := 1 - \max_{1 \leq z \leq d} p^{z},
$$

and the corresponding optimal prediction policy is to say all the time that the predicted value of $z_{t}$ is the most probable value $z_{*}$ (the index of the largest entry in $p)$ . Were $p$ known to us in advance, we could use this trivial optimal predictor from the very beginning. On the other hand, the optimal predictor is stationary, meaning that with the generating policy in question, the comparator is equal to $\epsilon(p)$ . As a result, (!) implies that our MD-based predictor policy is “asymptotically optimal” in the i.i.d. case: whatever be an i.i.d. generation policy used by the nature, the average, over time horizon N, expected prediction error of the MD-based prediction can be worse than the best one can get under the circumstances by at most $O(1) \sqrt{\ln(d + 1)} / \sqrt{N}$ A good news is that when designing the MD-based policy, we did not assume that the generation policy is an i.i.d. one; in fact, we made no assumptions on this policy at all!

Example 2: predicting an individual sequence. Note that a whatever individual sequence $z^{\infty} = \{z_{t} : t \geq 1\}$ is given by appropriate generation policy, specifically, a policy where $Z_{t}(\zeta^{t - 1}) \equiv z_{t}$ is independent of $\zeta^{t - 1}$ . For this policy and with our simple loss function, the comparator (5.3.86), as is immediately seen, is

$$
\epsilon_{N}[z^{\infty}] = 1 - \max_{1 \leq z \leq d} \frac{\mathrm{Card}(\{t \leq N : z_{t} = z\})}{N},
$$

that is, it is $\epsilon[p^{N}]$ , where $p^{N}$ is the empirical distribution of $z_{1},..., z_{N}$ . We see that out MDbased predictor behaves reasonably well on individual sequences which are “nearly stationary,” yielding results like: $^{66} if$ the fraction of entries different from 1 in any initial fragment, of length at least $N_{0}$ , of $z^{\infty}$ is at most 0.05, then the percent of errors in the MD-based prediction of the first $N \geq N_{0}$ entries $ofz^{\infty}$ will be at most $0.05 + O(1) \sqrt{\ln(d + 1) / N}.^{\prime}$ Not that much of a claim, but better than nothing!

Of course, there exist “easy to predict” individual sequences (like the alternating sequence $1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2, \ldots)$ where the performance of any stationary predictor is poor; in these cases, we cannot expect much from our MD-based predictor.

## 5.4 Bundle Mirror and Truncated Bundle Mirror algorithms

In spite of being optimal in terms of Information-Based Complexity Theory in the large-scale case, the Mirror Descent algorithm has really poor theoretical rate of convergence, and its typical practical behaviour is as follows: the objective rapidly improves at few first iterations and then the method “gets stuck,” perhaps still far from the optimal value; to get further improvement, one should wait hours, if not days. One way to improve, to some extent, the practical behaviour of the method is to better utilize the first order information accumulated so far. In this respect, the MD itself is poorly organized (cf. comments on SD in the beginning of section 5.2.2): all information accumulated so far is “summarized” in a single entity – the current iterate; we can say that the method is “memoryless.” Computational experience shows that the first order methods for nonsmooth convex optimization which do “have memory,” primarily, the so called bundle algorithms, typically perform much better than the memoryless methods like MD. In what follows, we intend to present a bundle version of MD – the Bundle Mirror (BM) and the Truncated Bundle Mirror (TBM) algorithms for solving the problem

$$
f_{*} = \min_{x \in X} f(x)\tag{CP}
$$

with Lipschitz continuous convex function $f : X \mathbb{R}$ . Note that BM is in the same relation to Bundle Level method from section 5.2.2 as MD is to SD – Bundle Level is just the Euclidean (one corresponding to Ball proximal setup) version of BM.

The assumptions on the problem and the setups for these algorithms are exactly the same as for MD; in particular, X is assumed to be bounded (see Standing Assumption, section 5.3.4.2).

## 5.4.1 Bundle Mirror algorithm

## 5.4.1.1 BM: Description

The setup for BM is the usual proximal setup – a norm $\| \cdot \|$ on Euclidean space $E = \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and a compatible with k · k continuously diferentiable DGF $\omega(\cdot) : X \mathbb{R}$ ;

## The algorithm is a follows:

1. At the beginning of step $t = 1, 2, \dots$ we have at our disposal previous iterates $x_{\tau} \in X$ $1 \leq \tau \leq t$ , along with subgradients $f^{\prime}(x_{\tau})$ of the objective at these iterates, and the current iterate $x_{t} \in X \(x_{1}$ is an arbitrary point of X). As always, we assume that

$$
\left\| f^{\prime} \left(x_{\tau}\right) \right\|_{*} \leq L_{\| \cdot \|}(f),
$$

where $L_{\parallel \cdot \parallel}(f)$ is the Lipschitz constant of $f$ w.r.t. $\| \cdot \|$

## 2. In course of step t, we

(a) compute $f(x_{t}), f^{\prime}(x_{t})$ and build the current model

$$
f_{t}(x) = \max_{\tau \leq t}[f(x_{\tau}) + \langle f^{\prime}(x_{\tau}), x - x_{\tau} \rangle]
$$

of $f$ which underestimates the objective and is exact at the points $x_{1},..., x_{t};$

(b) define the best found so far value of the objective $f^{t} = \mathrm{min}_{\tau \leq t} f(x_{\tau})$

(c) define the current lower bound $f_{t}$ on $f_{*}$ by solving the auxiliary problem

$$
f_{t} = \min_{x \in X} f_{t}(x)
$$

The current gap $\Delta_{t} = f^{t} - f_{t}$ is an upper bound on the inaccuracy of the best found so far approximate solution;

(d) compute the current level $\ell_{t} = f_{t} + \lambda \Delta_{t} \(\lambda \in(0, 1)$ is a parameter)

(e) finally, we set

$$
\begin{array}{rcl}{L_{t}} & = &{\{x \in X: f_{t}(x) \leq \ell_{t}\},} \\{x_{t + 1}} & = &{\mathrm{Prox}_{x_{t}}^{L_{t}}(0) := \operatorname{argmin}_{x \in L_{t}}[\langle - \nabla \omega(x_{t}), x \rangle + \omega(x)]} \end{array}
$$

and loop to step $t + 1$

Note: With Ball setup, we get

$$
\mathrm{Prox}_{x_{t}}^{L_{t}}(0) = \underset{x \in L_{t}}{\operatorname{argmin}} \left[- x_{t}^{T} x + \frac{1}{2} x^{T} x \right] = \underset{x \in L_{t}}{\operatorname{argmin}} \frac{1}{2} \| x - x_{t} \|_{2}^{2}.
$$

i.e., the method becomes exactly the Euclidean Bundle Level algorithm from section 5.2.2.

## 5.4.1.2 Convergence analysis

Convergence analysis of BM is completely similar to the one of Euclidean Bundle Level algorithm and is based on the following

Observation 5.4.1 Let $J = \{s, s + 1,..., r\}$ be a segment of iterations of BM:

$$
\Delta_{r} \geq(1 - \lambda) \Delta_{s}
$$

Then the cardinality of J can be upper-bounded as

$$
\operatorname{Card}(J) \leq \frac{\Omega^{2} L_{\| \cdot \|}^{2}(f)}{(1 - \lambda)^{2} \Delta_{r}^{2}}.\tag{5.4.1}
$$

where Ω is the ω-diameter of $X$ .

(cf. Main observation in section 5.2.2).

From Observation 5.4.1, exactly as in the case of Euclidean Bundle Level, one derives

Corollary 5.4.1 For every $\epsilon$, $0 < \epsilon < \Delta_{1}$ , the number N of steps of BM algorithm before a gap $\leq \epsilon$ is obtained (i.e., before an $\epsilon$-solution to (CP) is found) does not exceed the bound

$$
N(\epsilon) = \frac{\Omega^{2} L_{\| \cdot \|}^{2}(f)}{\lambda(1 - \lambda)^{2}(2 - \lambda) \epsilon^{2}}.\tag{5.4.2}
$$

Verification of Observation 5.4.1: By exactly the same reasons as in the case of Euclidean Bundle Level, observe that

- For t running through a segment of iterations $^{J,}$ the level sets $L_{t} = \{x \in X : f_{t}(x) \leq \ell_{t}\}$ have a point in common, namely, $v \in \mathrm{Argmin}_{x \in X} f_{r}(x)$ ;

- When $t \in J,$ the distances $\gamma_{t} = \| x_{t} - x_{t + 1} \|$ are not too small:

$$
\gamma_{t} \geq \frac{(1 - \lambda) \Delta_{r}}{L_{\| \cdot \|}(f)}.\tag{5.4.3}
$$

Now observe that in our algorithm,

$$
V_{x_{t + 1}}(v) \leq V_{x_{t}}(v) - \frac{1}{2} \gamma_{t}^{2}, t \in J.\tag{5.4.4}
$$

Indeed, we have

$$
x_{t + 1} = \mathrm{Prox}_{x_{t}}^{L_{t}}(0),
$$

which by (5.3.17) as applied with $x = x_{t} \, U = L_{t}, \xi = 0$ (which results in $x_{+} = x_{t + 1})$ results in

$$
V_{x_{t}}(v) - V_{x_{t + 1}}(v) \geq V_{x_{t}}
$$

(recall that $v \in L_{t}$ due to $t \in J)$ . The right hand side in the latter inequality is $\geq \frac{1}{2} \gamma_{t}^{2}$ , and we arrive (5.4.4).

It remains to note that by evident reasons $2V_{x_{s}}(v)) \leq \Omega^{2}$ and $V_{x_{r + 1}}(v) \geq 0$ , so that the conclusion in Observation 5.4.1 is readily given by (5.4.4) combined with (5.4.3).

## 5.4.2 Truncated Bundle Mirror

## 5.4.2.1 TBM: motivation

Main advantage of Bundle Mirror – typical improvement in practical performance due to better utilization of information on the problem acquired so far – goes at a price: from iteration to iteration, the piecewise linear model $f_{t}(\cdot)$ of the objective becomes more and more complex (has more and more linear pieces), implying growing with t computational cost of solving the auxiliary problems arising at iteration t (those of computing $f_{t}$ and of updating $x_{t}$ into $x_{t + 1})$ . In Truncated Bundle Mirror alorithm<sup>8</sup> the “number of linear pieces” responsible for the computational complexity of auxiliary problems is under our full control and can be kept below any desired level. As a result, we can, to some extent, trade of progress in accuracy and computational efort.

## 5.4.2.2 TBM: construction

The setup for the TBM algorithm is exactly the same as for the MD one. As applied to problem (CP), the TBM algorithm works as follows.

## A. The parameters of TBM are

$$
\lambda \in(0, 1), \theta \in(0, 1).
$$

The algorithm generates a sequence of search points, all belonging to $X,$ where the First Order oracle is called, and at every step builds the following entities:

1. the best found so far value of f along with the best found so far search point, which is treated as the current approximate solution built by the method;

2. a (valid) lower bound on the optimal value $f_{*}$ of the problem.

B. The execution is split in subsequent phases. Phase $s, \s = 1, 2,...,$ is associated with prox-center $c_{s} \in X$ and level $\boldsymbol{\ell}_{s} \in \mathbb{R}$ such that

- when starting the phase, we already know what is $f ( c _ { s } ) , f ^ { \prime } ( c _ { s } ) $ ;

$\ell_{s} = f_{s} + \lambda(f^{s} - f_{s})$ , where

$f^{s}$ is the best value of the objective known at the time when the phase starts;

– $f_{s}$ is the lower bound on $f_{*}$ we have at our disposal when the phase starts.

In principle, the prox-center $c_{1}$ corresponding to the very first phase can be chosen in X in an arbitrary fashion; we shall discuss details in the sequel. We start the entire process with computing $f, f^{\prime}$ at this prox-center, which results in

$$
f^{1} = f(c_{1})
$$

and set

$$
f_{1} = \min_{x \in X}[f(c_{1}) + \langle f^{\prime}(x_{1}), x - c_{1} \rangle],
$$

thus getting the initial lower bound on $f_{*}$

C. Now let us describe a particular phase s. Let

$$
\omega_{s}(x) = \omega(x) - \langle \omega^{\prime}(c_{s}), x - c_{s} \rangle;
$$

note that (5.3.3) implies that

$$
\begin{array}{c} \omega_{s}(y) \geq \omega_{s}(x) + \langle \omega_{s}^{\prime}(x), y - x \rangle + \frac{1}{2} \| y - x \|^{2} \quad \forall x, y \in X.\\[\omega_{s}^{\prime}(x) := \omega^{\prime}(x) - \omega^{\prime}(c_{s})] \end{array}\tag{5.4.5}
$$

and that $c_{s}$ is the minimizer of $\omega_{s}(\cdot)$ on $X$ .

The search points $\boldsymbol{x}_{t} ~ = ~ \boldsymbol{x}_{t, s}$ of the phase $s, \t \ = \1, 2,..$ . belong to X and are generated according to the following rules:

1. When generating $x_{t}$ , we already have at our disposal $x_{t - 1}$ and a convex compact set $X_{t - 1} \subset X$ such that

$(o_{t - 1}) \colon X_{t - 1} \subset X$ is of the same Affine dimension as $X.$ , meaning that $X_{t - 1}$ contains a neighbourhood (in X) of a point from the relative interior of $X^{\mathrm{~ 9 ~}}$

and

$$
\begin{array}{ll}(a_{t - 1}) & x \in X \backslash X_{t - 1} \Rightarrow f(x) > \ell_{s}; \\(b_{t - 1}) & x_{t - 1} \in \underset{X_{t - 1}}{\operatorname{argmin}} \omega_{s}.\end{array}\tag{5.4.6}
$$

Here $x_{0} = c_{s}$ and, say, $X_{0} = X$ , which ensures $\left(o_{0} \right)$ and $\left(5.4.6.a_{0} – b_{0} \right)$

2. To update $(x_{t - 1}, X_{t - 1})$ into $(x_{t}, X_{t})$ , we solve the auxiliary problem

$$
\min_{x} \left\{g_{t - 1}(x) \equiv f(x_{t - 1}) + \langle f^{\prime}(x_{t - 1}), x - x_{t - 1} \rangle : x \in X_{t - 1} \right\}.\tag{\((L_{t - 1})\}
$$

Our subsequent actions depend on the results of this optimization:

(a) Let $\tilde{f} \le + \infty$ be the optimal value in $\left(\mathrm{L}_{t - 1} \right)$ (as always, $\tilde{f} = \infty$ means that the problem is infeasible). Observe that the quantity

$$
\widehat{f} = \min[\widetilde{f}, \ell_{s}]
$$

is a lower bound on $f_{*}{:}$ in $X \backslash X_{t - 1}$ we have $f(x) > \ell_{s}$ by $\left(5.4.6.a_{t - 1} \right)$ , while on $X_{t - 1}$ we have $f(x) \geq{\tilde{f}}$ due to the inequality $f(x) \geq g_{t - 1}(x)$ given by the convexity of $f.$ Thus, $f(x) \geq \operatorname{min}[\ell_{s}, \widetilde{f}]$ everywhere on X.

In the case of

$$
\widehat{f} \geq \ell_{s} - \theta(\ell_{s} - f_{s})\tag{5.4.7}
$$

(“significant” progress in the lower bound), we terminate the phase and update the lower bound on $f_{*}$ as

$$
f_{s} \mapsto f_{s + 1} = \widehat{f}.
$$

The prox-center $c_{s + 1}$ for the new phase can, in principle, be chosen in $X$ in an arbitrary fashion (see section 5.4.2.4.2).

(b) When no significant progress in the lower bound is observed, we solve the optimization problem

$$
\min_{x} \left\{\omega_{s}(x): x \in X_{t - 1}, g_{t - 1}(x) \leq \ell_{s} \right\}.\tag{\(\left(\mathbb{P}_{t - 1}\right)\}
$$

This problem is feasible, and moreover, its feasible set is of the same dimension as $X$ Indeed, since $X_{t - 1}$ is of the same dimension as X, the only case when the set $\{x \in X_{t - 1} : g_{t - 1}(x) \leq \ell_{s}\}$ would lack the same property could be the case of $\widetilde{f} = \operatorname{min}_{x \in X_{t - 1}} g_{t - 1}(x) \geq \ell_{s}$ , whence $\widehat{f} = \ell_{s}$ , and therefore (5.4.7) takes place, which is not the case.

When solving $\left(\mathbb{P}_{t - 1} \right)$ , we get the optimal solution $x_{t}$ of this problem and compute $f(x_{t}), f^{\prime}(x_{t})$ . By Fact 5.3.1, for $\omega_{s}^{\prime}(x) : = \omega^{\prime}(x) - \omega^{\prime}(c_{s})$ one has

$$
\langle \omega_{s}^{\prime}(x_{t}), x - x_{t} \rangle \geq 0, \forall(x \in X_{t - 1}: g_{t}(x_{t}) \leq \ell_{s}).\tag{5.4.8}
$$

It is possible that we get a “significant” progress in the objective, specifically, that

$$
f(x_{t}) - \ell_{s} \leq \theta(f^{s} - \ell_{s}).\tag{5.4.9}
$$

In this case, we again terminate the phase and set

$$
f^{s + 1} = f(x_{t});
$$

the lower bound $f_{s + 1}$ on the optimal value is chosen as the maximum of $f_{s}$ and of all lower bounds $\widehat{f}$ generated during the phase. The prox-center $c_{s + 1}$ for the new phase, same as above, can in principle be chosen in X in an arbitrary fashion.

(c) When $\left(\mathbb{P}_{t - 1} \right)$ is feasible and (5.4.9) does not take place, we continue the phase $s,$ choosing as $X_{t}$ an arbitrary convex compact set such that

$$
\underline{{X}}_{t} \equiv \{x \in X_{t - 1}: g_{t - 1}(x) \leq \ell_{s}\} \subset X_{t} \subset \overline{{X}}_{t} \equiv \{x \in X:(x - x_{t})^{T} \omega_{s}^{\prime}(x_{t}) \geq 0\}.\tag{5.4.10}
$$

Note that we are in the case when $\left(\mathbb{P}_{t - 1} \right)$ is feasible and $x_{t}$ is the optimal solution to the problem; as we have claimed, this implies (5.4.8), so that

$$
\emptyset \neq \underline{{X}}_{t} \subset \overline{{X}}_{t},
$$

and thus (5.4.10) indeed allows to choose $X_{t}$ . Since, as we have seen, $X_{t}$ is of the same dimension as $X$ , this property will be automatically inherited by $X_{t},$ , as required by $\left(o_{t} \right)$ . Besides this, every choice of $X_{t}$ compatible with (5.4.10) ensures $\left(5.4.6.a_{t} \right)$ and $\left(5.4.6.b_{t} \right)$ ; the first relation is clearly ensured by the left inclusion in (5.4.10) combined with $\left(5.4.6.a_{t - 1} \right)$ and the fact that $f(x) \geq g_{t - 1}(x)$ , while the second relation $\left(5.4.6.b_{t} \right)$ follows from the right inclusion in (5.4.10) due to the convexity of $\omega_{s}(\cdot)$

## 5.4.2.3 Convergence Analysis

Let us define s-th gap as the quantity

$$
\epsilon_{s} = f^{s} - f_{s}
$$

By its origin, the gap is nonnegative and nonincreasing in s; besides this, it clearly is an upper bound on the inaccuracy, in terms of the objective, of the approximate solution $z^{s}$ we have at our disposal at the beginning of phase s.

The convergence and the complexity properties of the TBM algorithm are given by the following statement.

Theorem 5.4.1 (i) The number $N_{s}$ of oracle calls at a phase s can be bounded from above as follows:

$$
N_{s} \leq \frac{5 \Omega_{s}^{2} L_{\| \cdot \|}^{2}(f)}{\theta^{2}(1 - \lambda)^{2} \epsilon_{s}^{2}}, \Omega_{s} = \sqrt{2 \max_{y \in X}[\omega(y) - \omega(c_{s}) - \langle \omega^{\prime}(c_{s}), y - c_{s} \rangle]} \leq \Omega,\tag{5.4.11}
$$

where Ω is the ω-diameter of X.

(ii) For every $\epsilon > 0$ the total number of oracle calls before the phase s with $\epsilon_{s} \leq \epsilon$ is started $(i.e.$ , before $\epsilon$-solution to the problem is built) does not exceed

$$
N(\epsilon) = c(\theta, \lambda) \frac{\Omega^{2} L_{\| \cdot \|}^{2}(f)}{\epsilon^{2}}\tag{5.4.12}
$$

with an appropriate $c(\theta, \lambda)$ depending solely and continuously on $\theta, \lambda \in(0, 1)$

Proof. (i): Assume that phase s did not terminate in course of N steps. Observe that then

$$
\| x_{t} - x_{t - 1} \| \geq \frac{\theta(1 - \lambda) \epsilon_{s}}{L_{\| \cdot \|}(f)}, \quad 1 \leq t \leq N.\tag{5.4.13}
$$

Indeed, we have $g_{t - 1}(x_{t}) \leq \ell_{s}$ by construction of $x_{t}$ and $g_{t - 1}(x_{t - 1}) = f(x_{t - 1}) > \ell_{s} + \theta(f^{s} - \ell_{s})$ , since otherwise the phase would be terminated at the step $t - 1$ . It follows that $g_{t - 1}(x_{t - 1}) - g_{t - 1}(x_{t}) >$ $\theta(f^{s} - \ell_{s}) = \theta(1 - \lambda) \epsilon_{s}$ . Taking into account that $g_{t - 1}(\cdot)$ , due to its origin, is Lipschitz continuous w.r.t. $\| \cdot \|$ with constant $L_{\parallel \cdot \parallel}(f)$ , (5.4.13) follows.

Now observe that $x_{t - 1}$ is the minimizer of $\omega_{s}$ on $X_{t - 1}$ by $\left(5.4.6.a_{t - 1} \right)$ , and the latter set, by construction, contains $x_{t}$ , whence $\langle x_{t} - x_{t - 1}, \omega_{s}^{\prime}(x_{t - 1}) \rangle \geq 0$ (see (5.4.8)). Applying (5.4.5), we get

$$
\omega_{s}(x_{t}) \geq \omega_{s}(x_{t - 1}) + \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{\theta(1 - \lambda) \epsilon_{s}}{L_{| | \cdot | |}(f)}\right)^{2}, t = 1, \dots, N,
$$

whence

$$
\omega_{s}(x_{N}) - \omega_{s}(x_{0}) \geq \frac{N}{2} \left(\frac{\theta(1 - \lambda) \epsilon_{s}}{L_{\| \cdot \|}(f)}\right)^{2}.
$$

The latter relation, due to the evident inequality max $\omega_{s}(x) - \operatorname{min}_{X} \omega_{s} \leq \frac{\Omega_{s}^{2}}{2}$ (readily given by the definition X of $\Omega_{s}$ and $\omega_{s})$ implies that

$$
N \leq \frac{\Omega_{s}^{2} L_{\| \cdot \|}^{2}(f)}{\theta^{2}(1 - \lambda)^{2} \epsilon_{s}^{2}}.
$$

Recalling the origin of $N$ , we conclude that

$$
N_{s} \leq \frac{\Omega_{s}^{2} L_{\|.\|}^{2}(f)}{\theta^{2}(1 - \lambda)^{2} \epsilon_{s}^{2}} + 1.
$$

All we need in order to get from this inequality the required relation (5.4.11) is to demonstrate that

$$
\frac{\Omega_{s}^{2} L_{\| \cdot \|}^{2}(f)}{\theta^{2}(1 - \lambda)^{2} \epsilon_{s}^{2}} \geq \frac{1}{4},\tag{5.4.14}
$$

which is immediate: let $R = \operatorname{max}_{x \in X} \| x - c_{1} \|$ . We have $\epsilon_{s} \le \epsilon_{1} = f(c_{1}) - \operatorname{min}_{\substack{\mathbf{V}}}[f(c_{1}) +(x - c_{1})^{T} f^{\prime}(c_{1})] \le$ x∈X $RL_{\parallel \cdot \parallel}(f)$ , where the concluding inequality is given by the fact that $\| f^{\prime}(c_{1}) \|_{*} \leq L_{\| \cdot \|}(f)$ . On the other hand, by the definition of $\Omega_{s}$ we have $\frac{\Omega_{s}^{2}}{2} \geq \operatorname{max}_{u \in X} \left[\omega(y) - \langle \omega^{\prime}(c_{s}), y - c_{s} \rangle - \omega(c_{s}) \right]$ and $\omega(y) - \langle \omega^{\prime}(c_{s}), y -$ $c_{s} \rangle - \omega(c_{s}) \geq \frac{1}{2} \Vert y - c_{s} \Vert^{2}$ , whence $\lVert y - c_{s} \rVert \leq \Omega_{s}$ for all $y \in X$ , and thus $R \leq 2 \Omega_{s}$ , whence $\epsilon_{s} \leq L_{\| \cdot \|}(f) R \leq$ $2L_{\parallel \cdot \parallel}(f) \Omega_{s},$ , as required. (i) is proved.

(ii): Assume that $\epsilon_{s} > \epsilon$ at the phases $s = 1, 2,..., S$ , and let us bound from above the total number of oracle calls at these S phases. Observe, first, that the two subsequent gaps $\epsilon_{s}, \epsilon_{s + 1}$ are linked by the relation

$$
\epsilon_{s + 1} \leq \gamma \epsilon_{s}, \gamma = \gamma(\theta, \lambda) := \max[1 - \theta \lambda, 1 -(1 - \theta)(1 - \lambda)] < 1.\tag{5.4.15}
$$

Indeed, it is possible that the phase s was terminated according to the rule ${2 a};$ in this case

$$
\epsilon_{s + 1} = f^{s + 1} - f_{s + 1} \leq f^{s} -[\ell_{s} - \theta(\ell_{s} - f_{s})] =(1 - \theta \lambda) \epsilon_{s},
$$

as required in (5.4.15). The only other possibility is that the phase s was terminated when the relation (5.4.9) took place. In this case,

$$
\epsilon_{s + 1} = f^{s + 1} - f_{s + 1} \leq f^{s + 1} - f_{s} \leq \ell_{s} + \theta(f^{s} - \ell_{s}) - f_{s} = \lambda \epsilon_{s} + \theta(1 - \lambda) \epsilon_{s} =(1 -(1 - \theta)(1 - \lambda)) \epsilon_{s},
$$

and we again arrive at (5.4.15).

From (5.4.15) it follows that $\epsilon_{s} \ge \epsilon \gamma^{s - S}, s = 1,..., S$ , since $\epsilon_{S} > \epsilon$ by the origin of S. We now have

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \sum_{s = 1}^{S} N_{s} & \leq & \sum_{s = 1}^{S} \frac{5 \Omega_{s}^{2} L_{\| \cdot \|}^{2}(f)}{\theta^{2}(1 - \lambda)^{2} \epsilon_{s}^{2}} \leq \sum_{s = 1}^{S} \frac{5 \widehat{\Omega}^{2} L_{\| \cdot \|}^{2}(f) \gamma^{2(S - s)}}{\theta^{2}(1 - \lambda)^{2} \epsilon^{2}} \leq \frac{5 \widehat{\Omega}^{2} L_{\| \cdot \|}^{2}(f)}{\theta^{2}(1 - \lambda)^{2} \epsilon^{2}} \sum_{t = 0}^{\infty} \gamma^{2t} \\ & \equiv & \underbrace{\left[\frac{5}{\theta^{2}(1 - \lambda)^{2}(1 - \gamma^{2})} \right]}_{c(\theta, \lambda)} \frac{\widehat{\Omega}^{2} L_{\| \cdot \|}^{2}(f)}{\epsilon^{2}} \end{array}
$$

and (5.4.12) follows.

## 5.4.2.4 Implementation issues

5.4.2.4.1. Solving auxiliary problems $\left(\mathbf{L}_{t} \right), \left(\mathbb{P}_{t} \right)$ . As far as implementation of the TBM algorithm is concerned, the major issue is how to solve eficiently the auxiliary problems $\left(\mathrm{L}_{t} \right)$ $\left(\mathbb{P}_{t} \right)$ . Formally, these problems are of the same design dimension as the problem of interest; what do we gain when reducing the solution of a single large-scale problem (CP) to a long series of auxiliary problems of the same dimension? To answer this crucial question, observe first that we have control on the complexity of the domain $X_{t}$ which, up to a single linear constraint, is the feasible domain of $\left(\mathrm{L}_{t} \right), \left(\mathbb{P}_{t} \right)$ . Indeed, assume that $X_{t - 1}$ is a part of X given by a finite list of linear inequalities. Then both sets $X_{t}$ and $\overline{{X}}_{t}$ in (5.4.10) also are cut of X by finitely many linear inequalities, so that we may enforce $X_{t}$ to be cut of X by finitely many linear inequalities as well. Moreover, we have full control of the number of inequalities in the list. For example,

A. Setting all the time $X_{t} = \overline{{X}}_{t}$ , we ensure that $X_{t}$ is cut of X by a single linear inequality;

B. Setting all the time $X_{t} = \underline{{X}}_{t}$ , we ensure that $X_{t}$ is cut of X by t linear inequalities (so that the larger is t, the “more complicated” is the description of $X_{t})$ ;

C. We can choose something in-between the above extremes. For example, assume that we have chosen certain m and are ready to work with $X_{t}{}^{\prime} s$ cut of X by at most m linear inequalities. In this case, we could use the policy B. at the initial steps of a phase, until the number of linear inequalities in the description of $X_{t - 1}$ reaches the maximal allowed value m. At the step t, we are supposed to choose $X_{t}$ in-between the two sets

$$
\underline{{X}}_{t} = \{x \in X: h_{1}(x) \leq 0,..., h_{m}(x) \leq 0, h_{m + 1}(x) \leq 0\}, \quad \overline{{X}}_{t} = \{x \in X: h_{m + 2}(x) \leq 0\},
$$

where

– the linear inequalities $h_{1}(x) \leq 0,..., h_{m}(x) \leq 0$ cut $X_{t - 1}$ of $X;$ ;

– the linear inequality $h_{m + 1}(x) \leq 0$ is, in our old notation, the inequality $g_{t - 1}(x) \leq \ell_{s}$ – the linear inequality $h_{m + 2}(x) ~ \leq ~ 0 ~ \mathrm{is}$ , in our old notation, the inequality $\langle x \textrm{-}$ $x_{t}, \omega_{s}^{\prime}(x_{t}) \rangle \geq 0.$

Now we can form a list of m linear inequalities as follows:

- we build m − 1 linear inequalities $e_{i}(x) ~ \le ~ 0$ by aggregating the $m + 1$ inequalities $h_{j}(x) \leq 0, j = 1,..., m + 1$ , so that every one of the e-inequalities is a convex combination of the h-ones (the coeficients of these convex combinations can be whatever we want);

- we set $X_{t} = \{x \in X : e_{i}(x) \leq 0, i = 1,..., m - 1, h_{m + 2}(x) \leq 0\}.$

It is immediately seen that with this approach we ensure (5.4.10), on one hand, and that $X_{t}$ is cut of X by at most m inequalities. And of course we can proceed in the same fashion.

The bottom line is: we always can ensure that $X_{t - 1}$ is cut of X by at most m linear inequalities $h_{j}(x) \le 0, j = 1,..., m$ , where $m \geq 1$ is (any) desirable bound. Consequently, we may assume that the feasible set of $\left(\mathbb{P}_{t - 1} \right)$ is cut of X by $m + 1$ linear inequalities $h_{j}(x) \leq 0, j = 1,..., m + 1$ The crucial point is that with this approach, we can reduce $(\mathrm{L}_{t - 1}),(\mathbb{P}_{t - 1})$ to convex programs with at most $m + 1$ decision variables. Indeed, replacing $\mathbb{R}^{n} \supset X$ with the Affine span of X, we may assume the X has a nonempty interior. By $\left(o_{t - 1} \right)$ this is also the case with the feasible domain $X_{t - 1}$ of the problem

$$
\operatorname{Opt} = \min_{x} \left\{g_{t - 1}(x): x \in X_{t - 1} = \left\{x \in X: h_{j}(x) \leq 0, 1 \leq j \leq m \right\} \right\}\tag{\((L_{t - 1})\}
$$

implying that the linear constraints $h_{j}(x) \leq 0$ (which we w.l.o.g. assume to be nonconstant) satisfy the Slater condition on int X: there exists ${\bar{x}} \in$ int X such that $h_{j}(\bar{x}) < 0, \j \ \leq \m$ Applying Convex Programming Duality Theorem (Theorem D.2.3), we get

$$
\operatorname{Opt} = \max_{\lambda \geq 0} G(\lambda), G(\lambda) = \min_{x \in X}[g_{t - 1}(x) + \sum_{j = 1}^{m} \lambda_{j} h_{j}(x)].\tag{D}
$$

Now, assuming that prox-mapping associated with $\omega(\cdot)$ is easy to compute, it is equally easy to minimize an Affine function over $X \ \mathrm{(why ?)}$ , so that $G(\lambda)$ is easy to compute:

$$
G(\lambda) = g_{t - 1}(x_{\lambda}) + \sum_{j = 1}^{m} \lambda_{j} h_{j}(x_{\lambda}), x_{\lambda} \in \underset{x \in X}{\operatorname{Argmin}}[g_{t - 1}(x) + \sum_{j = 1}^{m} \lambda_{j} h_{j}(x)].
$$

By construction, $G(\lambda)$ is a well defined concave function; its supergradient is given by

$$
G^{\prime}(\lambda) =[h_{1}(x_{\lambda}); \dots; h_{m}(x_{\lambda})]
$$

and thus is as readily available as the value $G(\lambda)$ of G. It follows that we can compute Opt (which is all we need as far as the auxiliary problem $\left(\mathrm{L}_{t - 1} \right)$ is concerned) by solving the m-dimensional convex program (D) by a whatever rapidly converging first order method<sup>10</sup>.

The situation with the second auxiliary problem

$$
\min_{x} \{\omega_{s}(x): x \in X_{t - 1}, g_{t - 1}(x) \leq \ell_{s}\}\tag{\((P_{t - 1})\}
$$

is similar. Here again we are interested to solve the problem only in the case when its feasible domain is full-dimensional (recall that we w.l.o.g. have assumed X to be full-dimensional), and the constraints cutting the feasible domain of X are linear, so that we can write $\left(\mathbb{P}_{t - 1} \right)$ down as the problem

$$
\min_{x} \left\{\omega_{s}(x): h_{j}(x) \leq 0, 1 \leq j \leq m + 1 \right\}
$$

with linear constraints $h_{j}(x) \leq 0, 1 \leq j \leq m + 1$ , satisfying Slater condition on int X. As before, we can pass to the dual problem

$$
\max_{\lambda \geq 0} H(\lambda), H(\lambda) = \min_{x \in X} \left[\omega_{s}(x) + \sum_{j = 1}^{m + 1} \lambda_{j} h_{j}(x) \right].\tag{\((D_{t - 1})\}
$$

Here again, the concave and well defined dual objective $H(\lambda)$ can be equipped with a cheap First Order oracle (provided, as above, that the prox-mapping associated with $\omega(\cdot)$ is easy to compute), so that we can reduce the auxiliary problem $\left(\mathbb{P}_{t - 1} \right)$ to solving a low-dimensional (provided m is not large) black-box-represented convex program by a first order method. Note that now we want to build a high-accuracy approximation to the optimal solution of the problem of actual interest $\left(\mathbb{P}_{t - 1} \right)$ rather than to approximate well its optimal value, and a high-accuracy solution to the Lagrange dual of a convex program not always allows to recover a good solution to the program itself. Fortunately, in our case the objective of the problem of actual interest $\left(P_{t - 1} \right)$ is strongly convex, and in this case a high accuracy solution λ to the dual problem $\left(\mathrm{D}_{t - 1} \right)$ the accuracy being measured in terms of the dual objective $H$ , does produce a high-accuracy solution

$$
x_{\lambda} = \underset{X}{\operatorname{argmin}} \left[\omega_{s}(x) + \sum_{j = 1}^{m + 1} \lambda_{j} h_{j}(x) \right]
$$

to $\left(\mathbb{P}_{t - 1} \right)$ , the accuracy being measured in terms of the distance to the precise solution $x_{t}$ to the latter problem.

The bottom line is that when the “memory depth” m (which is fully controlled by us!) is not too big and the prox-mapping associated with ω is easy to compute, the auxiliary problems arising in the TBM algorithm can be solved, at a relatively low computational cost, via Lagrange duality combined with good high-accuracy first order algorithm for solving black-box-represented low dimensional convex programs.

5.4.2.4.2. Updating prox-centers. In principle, we can select $c_{s} \in X$ in any way we want. Practical experience says that a reasonable policy is to use as $c_{s}$ the best, in terms of the values of $f,$ search point generated so far.

5.4.2.4.3. Accumulating information. The set $X_{t}$ summarizes, in a sense, all the information on $f$ we have accumulated so far and intend to use in the sequel. Relation (5.4.10) allows for a tradeof between the quality (and the volume) of this information and the computational efort required to solve the auxiliary problems $(\mathrm{L}_{t - 1}),(\mathbb{P}_{t - 1})$ . With no restrictions on this efort, the most promising policy for updating $X_{t}$ ’s would be to set $X_{t} = \underline{{X}}_{t - 1}$ (“collecting information with no compression of it”). With this policy the TBM algorithm with the ball setup is basically identical to the Bundle-Level Algorithm of Lemarechal, Nemirovski and Nesterov [34] presented in section 5.2.2; the “truncated memory” version of the latter method (that is, the generic TBM algorithm with ball setup) was proposed by Kiwiel [32]. Aside of theoretical complexity bounds similar to (5.3.34), most of bundle methods (in particular, the Prox-Level one) share the following experimentally observed property: the practical performance of the algorithm is in full accordance with the complexity bound (5.1.2): every n steps reduce the inaccuracy by at least an absolute constant factor (something like 3). This property is very attractive in moderate dimensions, where we indeed are capable to carry out several times the dimension number of steps.

## 5.4.2.5 Illustration: PET Image Reconstruction by MD and TBM

To get an impression of the practical performance of the TBM method, let us look at numerical results related to the 2D version of the PET Image Reconstruction problem.

The model. We process simulated measurements as if they were registered by a ring of 360 detectors, the inner radius of the ring being 1 (Fig. 5.2). The field of view is a concentric circle of the radius 0.9, and it is covered by the 129×129 rectangular grid. The grid partitions the field of view into 10, 471 pixels, and we act as if tracer’s density was constant in every pixel. Thus, the design dimension of the problem (PET<sup>0</sup>) we are interested to solve is $\mathrm{\ddot{J} ust{}^{\prime \prime}} ~ n = 10471$

![Figure 5.2](../../../transcripts/mineru/lectures-modern-convex-optimization/parts/401-600/images/804b586bddd701c1ccfb592a65644ef8da40413c2fc36e2331b46fed76f95c70.jpg)  
Figure 5.2: Ring with 360 detectors, field of view and a line of response

The number of bins (i.e., number m of log-terms in the objective of (PET<sup>0</sup>)) is 39784, while the number of nonzeros among $q_{ij}$ is 3,746,832.

The true image is “black and white” (the density in every pixel is either 1 or 0). The measurement time (which is responsible for the level of noise in the measurements) is mimicked as follows: we model the measurements according to the Poisson model as if during the period of measurements the expected number of positrons emitted by a single pixel with unit density was a given number M.

The algorithm we are using to solve (PET<sup>0</sup>) is the plain TBM method with the simplex setup and the sets $X_{t}$ cut of $X = \Delta_{n}$ by just one linear inequality:

$$
X_{t} = \{x \in \Delta_{n}:(x - x_{t})^{T} \nabla \omega_{s}(x_{t}) \geq 0\}.
$$

The parameters λ, θ of the algorithm were chosen as

$$
\lambda = 0.95, \quad \theta = 0.5.
$$

The approximate solution reported by the algorithm at a step is the best found so far search point (the one with the best value of the objective we have seen to the moment).

The results of two sample runs we are about to present are not that bad.

Experiment 1: Noiseless measurements. The evolution of the best, in terms of the objective, solutions $x^{t}$ found in course of the first t calls to the oracle is displayed at Fig. 5.3 (on pictures, brighter areas correspond to higher density of the tracer). The numbers are as follows. With the noiseless measurements, we know in advance the optimal value in (PET<sup>0</sup>) – it is easily seen that without noises, the true image (which in our simulated experiment we do know) is an optimal solution. In our problem, this optimal value equals to 2.8167; the best value of the objective found in 111 oracle calls is 2.8171 (optimality gap 4.e-4). The progress in accuracy is plotted on Fig. 5.4. We have built totally 111 search points, and the entire computation took 18<sup>0</sup>51<sup>00</sup> on a 350 MHz Pentium II laptop with 96 MB RAM <sup>11</sup>.

With noisy measurements, we have no a priori knowledge of the true optimal value in (PET<sup>0</sup>); in simulated experiments, a kind of orientation is given by the value of the objective at the true image (which is hopefully a close to $f_{*}$ upper bound on $f_{*})$ . 3D PET. As it happened, the TBM algorithm was not tested on actual clinical 3D PET data. However, in late 1990’s we were participating in a EU project on 3D PET Image Recon struction; in this project, among other things, we did apply to the actual 3D clinical data an algorithm which, up to minor details, is pretty close to the MD with Entropy setup as applied to convex minimization over the standard simplex (details can be found in [11]). In the sequel, with slight abuse of terminology, we refer to this algorithm as to MD, and present some experimental data on its the practical performance in order to demonstrate that simple optimization tech niques indeed have chances when applied to really huge convex programs. We restrict ourselves with a single numerical example – real clinical brain study carried out on a very powerful PET scanner. In the corresponding problem (PET<sup>0</sup>), there are n = 2, 763, 635 design variables (this is the number of voxels in the field of view) and about 25,000,000 log-terms in the objective. The

## 5.4.2.6 Alternative: PET via Krylov subspace minimization

The short story we are about to tell is not about First Order algorithms and even not about largescale nonsmooth convex optimization; it is about what can be gained with nontrivial modeling. Consider PET Image Reconstruction problem (PET), and imagine for a moment that there is no observation noise, so that our observation is

$$
y = P \lambda,
$$

where $P$ is a given m×n matrix; assume that m $\gg$ n (there are much more bins than voxels) and $P$ is of rank n (these “size and nondegeneracy” assumptions indeed hold true in PET practice). In this ideal case, image reconstruction reduces to solving the system of linear equations

$$
P^{T} P \lambda = P^{T} y\tag{5.4.16}
$$

with nonsingular matrix, and in principle we could solve it by whatever algorithm of Linear Algebra. In particular, if we do not want to assemble and invert large matrix $P^{T} P_{\cdot}$ , we could use Conjugate Gradients (CG) – algorithm described in every Linear Algebra textbook. The only thing which matters for us now is the “high level” description of the algorithm which states than when started at the origin, k-th approximate solution $\lambda_{k}$ generated by CG is the minimizer of the convex quadratic form

$$
f(\lambda) = \frac{1}{2} \lambda^{T}[P^{T} P] \lambda - \lambda^{T} P^{T} y
$$

one the k-th Krylov subspace of the pair $(P^{T} P, P^{T} y)$ , that is, the linear span

$$
E_{k} = E_{k}(P, y) := \operatorname{Lin} \left\{P^{T} y, \left[P^{T} P \right] P^{T} y; \left[P^{T} P \right]^{2} P^{T} y, \dots, \left[P^{T} P \right]^{k - 1} P^{T} y \right\}
$$

of the first k vectors in the sequence $\{e_{s} =[P^{T} P]^{s - 1} P^{T} y \in{\bf R}^{n}, s = 1, 2, \ldots\}$ There are basically complete results on non-asymptotic rate of convergence of CG expressed in terms of the singular spectrum of $P$ and the norm in which the inaccuracy is measured (usually, norm of the form $\| x \| = \|[P^{T} P]^{\alpha} x \|_{2})$ , but this is not our point here; the point is, that the Krylov subspaces make sense in the case when $y$ is a noisy observation of P λ rather than P λ exactly, and one can take, as an approximate solution to (PET), the minimizer over this subspace of a whatever “meaningful” convex function, and not only the above quadratic form. For example, in (PET) we are minimizing minus log-likelihood of observed y over all nonnegative $\lambda;$ why not to restrict this minimization to the one over nonnegative λ from the Krylov subspace $E_{k}(P, y)$ with somehow selected k? Theoretical justification of this approach, its convergence rates, etc., etc., are completely out of our scope here; all I want is to outline the approach and to illustrate it numerically.

Observe that when k is moderate, the outlined approach is extremely simple computationally all we need is to build generators $g_{1},..., g_{k}$ of $E_{k}(P, y)$ , which requires $k + 1$ multiplications of vectors by $P^{T}$ and k multiplications of vectors by $P;$ restricting candidate solution to be linear combination of the generators, we end up with convex problem of small (provided k is so) design dimension. Thus, one thing for sure – the outlined approach is extremely cheap computationally, provided k is not large. We are about to see how it works numerically. In the “proof of the concept” experiments to be reported, we dealt with 2D PET Image Reconstruction with“just” $n = 5$ , 664 pixels and $m = 18$ , 336 bins; these toy for PET sizes were selected to allow for (PET) $^{66} \mathrm{as} \ \mathrm{is}^{9}$ to be solved in moderate time by commercial Interior Point solver, in order to have benchmark for our results. Along with these Maximum Likelihood recoveries, we built

- Krylov Least Squares recoveries yielded by k iterations of CG as applied to the linear system

$$
[P^{T} P] \lambda = P^{T} y
$$

with unknowns $\lambda;$

- Krylov Maximum Likelihood recoveries obtained by solving with the Ellipsoid method (!) the k-dimensional convex problem

$$
\begin{array}{c}\min_{\mu \in \mathbb{R}^{k}}\left\{\sum_{j = 1}^{n}[\lambda(\mu)]_{j}p_{j} - \sum_{i = 1}^{m}y_{i}\ln \left(\sum_{j = 1}^{m}p_{ij}[\lambda(\mu)]_{j}\right):\lambda(\mu)\geq 0, \| \mu \|_{\infty}\leq M\right\} \\ \left[P =[p_{ij}]_{\substack{i\leq m,\\ j\leq n}}, p_{j} = \sum_{i}p_{ij}, \lambda(\mu) = \sum_{\ell = 1}^{k}\mu_{\ell}g_{\ell}\right] \end{array}
$$

(cf. (PET)); here $M < \infty$ makes the feasible set bounded (and thus Ellipsoid algorithm applicable) and should be selected large enough not to afect the results of optimization.

In our experiments, we used k as small as 10. Typical results of our experiments are illustrated on Fig. 5.8. In these experiments, true tracer’s density $\lambda \geq 0$ was normalized to have $\textstyle \sum_{j} \lambda_{j} \leq 1$ , and matrix $P$ was parameterized by observation time $T$ according to $P = T \bar{P}$ , where $\bar{P}$ corresponds to the case when the expected number of total lines of response emitted by unit amount of traces in unit time is equal to 1; thus, observation time $T$ means equal to $T$ expected total number of registered lines of response per unit amount of tracer.

On Fig. 5.8, we present the values of recovery errors

$$
\epsilon_{1} = \frac{1}{n} \| \lambda - \widehat{\lambda} \|_{1}, \epsilon_{\infty} = \| \lambda - \widehat{\lambda} \|_{\infty}
$$

where λ is the true tracer’s density, and $\widehat{\lambda}$ is the recovered density. Surprisingly, computationally cheap Krylov recoveries — even approximate Least Squares via just 10 steps of CG! — are not worse, and even better, than much more expensive computationally exact Maximum Likelihood recovery. We do not know whether the same phenomenon takes place in 3D PET recovery of practical, and not toy, sizes. However, the outlined approach seems to be worthy of a try in real life applications.

A reader could ask: how happens that high accuracy Maximum Likelihood recovery is, in terms of its closeness to the true image as quantified by $\epsilon_{1}$ and $\epsilon_{\infty},$ not much better, and except for one experiment (“MIRScan”, $T = 10^{8})$ is even worse than its “heavily truncated” Krylov version. Seemingly, the reason is that the problem we are solving is rather ill-posed — the maximal singular value of P is by two orders of magnitude (specifically, by factor ≈ 88.2) larger than its smallest singular value. As a result, “full” Least Squares and Maximum Lilkelihood recoveries are heavily afected by observation noise. While this phenomenon, typical for ill-posed problems, cannot be completely overcome<sup>12</sup>, there are various ways to reduce it by appropriate regularization of the problem in question. One of these ways, well studied in the case of Least Squares recovery, is “regularization by early termination” of the optimization algorithm (say, CG) as applied to the minimization problem at hand. Considering this subject in details is beyond our scope; we, however, do believe that advantages, as demonstrated by the above experiments, of “truncated” Krylov recoveries as compared to the “full Maximum Likelihood” one stem from implici regularization of the ill-posed problem at hand induced by the truncation. To support this guess, we present on Fig. 5.9 the results of additional experiment where the number n of pixels is larger, and the ratio m/n – smaller than in the experiments just reported, resulting in worse than before conditioning of $P;$ “truncation,” same as above, is $k = 10$ . In this experiment the phenomenon we are discussing is essentially more profound that in the preceding experiments: now the recovery errors of Krylov recoveries are significantly smaller than those of the full Maximum Likelihood recovery $(\mathrm{e.g.}$ , Krylov recoveries with $T = 10^{7}$ are more accurate than full Maximum Likelihood recovery with $T = 10^{8})$ , as is clearly seen from pictures, and not from numbers only. Note that disadvantage of full Maximum Likelihood recovery in terms of quality is augmented by unpleasant computational cost which now is by two orders of magnitude larger than the cost of Krylov recoveries.
