## 5.5 Saddle Point representations and Mirror Prox algorithm

## 5.5.1 Motivation

Let us revisit the reasons for our interest in the First Order methods. It stemmed from the fact that when solving large-scale convex programs, applying polynomial time algorithms becomes questionable: unless the matrices of the Newton-type linear systems to be solved at iterations of an IPM possess “favourable sparsity pattern,” a single IPM iteration in the large-scale case becomes too time-consuming to be practical. Thus, we were looking for methods with cheap iterations, and stated that in the case of constrained nonsmooth problems (this is what we deal with in most of applications), the only “cheap” methods we know are First Order algorithms. We then observed that as a matter of fact, all these algorithms are black-box-oriented, and thus obey the limits of performance established by Information-based Complexity Theory, and focused on algorithms which achieve these limits of performance. A bad news here is that the “limits of performance” are quite poor; the best we can get here is the complexity like $N(\epsilon) = O(1 / \epsilon^{2})$ When one tries to understand why this indeed is the best we can get, it becomes clear that the reason is in “blindness” of the black-box-oriented algorithms we use; they utilize only local information on the problem (values and subgradients of the objective) and make no use of a priori knowledge of problem’s structure. Here it should be stressed that as far as Convex Programming is concerned, we nearly always do have detailed knowledge of problem’s structure – otherwise, how could we know that the problem is convex in the first place? The First Order methods as presented so far just do not know how to utilize problem’s structure, in sharp contrast with IPM’s which are fully “structure-oriented.” Indeed, this is the structure of an optimization problem which underlies its setting as an LP/CQP/SDP program, and IPM’s, same as the Simplex method, are quite far from operating with the values and subgradients of the objective and the constraints; instead, they operate directly on problem’s data. We can say that the LP/CQP/SDP framework is a “structure-revealing” one, and it allows for algorithms with fast convergence, algorithms capable to build a high accuracy solution in a moderate number of iterations. In contrast to this, the black-box-oriented framework is “structure-obscuring,” and the associated algorithms, al least in the large-scale case, possess really slow rate of convergence. The bad news here is that the LP/CQP/SDP framework requires iterations which in many applications are prohibitively time-consuming in the large scale case.

Now, for a long time the LP/CQP/SDP framework was the only one which allowed for uti lizing problem’s structure. The situation changed significantly circa 2003, when Yu. Nesterov discovered a “computationally cheap” way to do so. The starting point in his discovery was the well known fact that the disastrous complexity $N(\epsilon) \ge{\cal O}(1 / \epsilon^{2})$ in large-scale nonsmooth convex optimization comes from nonsmoothness; passing from nonsmooth problems (minimiz ing a convex Lipschitz continuous objective over a convex compact domain) to their smooth counterparts, where the objective, still black-box-represented one, has a Lipschitz continuous gradient, reduces the complexity bound to $O(1 / \sqrt \epsilon)$ , and for smooth problems with favourable geometry, this reduced complexity turns out to be nearly- or fully dimension-independent, see section 5.8.1. Now, the “smooth” complexity $O(1 / \sqrt{\epsilon})$ , while still not a polynomial-time one, is a dramatic improvement as compared to its “nonsmooth” counterpart ${\cal O}(1 / \epsilon^{2})$ . All this was known for a couple of decades and was of nearly no practical use, since problems of minimizing a smooth convex objective over a simple convex set (the latter should be simple in order to allow for computationally cheap algorithms) are a “rare commodity”, almost newer met in applications. The major part of Nesterov’s 2003 breakthrough is the observation, surprisingly simple in the hindsight<sup>13</sup>, that

In convex optimization, the typical source of nonsmoothness is taking maxima, and usually a “heavily nonsmooth” convex objective f(x) can be represented as

$$
f(x) = \max_{y \in Y} \phi(x, y)
$$

with a pretty simple (quite often, just bilinear) convex-concave function $\phi$ and simple convex compact set $Y$

As an immediate example, look at the function $\begin{array}{r}{f(x) = \mathrm{max}_{1 \leq i \leq m}[a_{i}^{T} x + b_{i}]^{\14};} \end{array}$ this function can be represented as $\begin{array}{r}{f(x) = \operatorname{max}_{y \in \Delta_{m}} \phi(x, y) = \sum_{i = 1}^{m} y_{i}[a_{i}^{T} x + b_{i}]} \end{array}$ so that both $\phi$ and $Y$ are as simple as they could be...

As a result, the nonsmooth problem

$$
\min_{x \in X} f(x)\tag{CP}
$$

can be reformulated as the saddle point problem

$$
\min_{x \in X} \max_{y \in Y} \phi(x, y)\tag{SP}
$$

with a pretty smooth (usually just bilinear) convex-concave cost function $\phi.$

Now, saddle point reformulation (SP) of the problem of interest (CP) can be used in different ways. Nesterov himself used it to smoothen the function $f.$ Specifically, he assumes (see [47]) that $\phi$ is of the form

$$
\phi(x, y) = x^{T}(Ay + a) - \psi(y)
$$

with convex $\psi,$ , and observes that then the function

$$
f_{\delta}(x) = \max_{y \in Y}[\phi(x, y) - \delta d(y)],
$$

where the “regularizer” $d(\cdot)$ is strongly convex, is smooth (possesses Lipschitz continuous gradient) and is close to $f$ when $\delta$ is small. He then minimizes the smooth function $f_{\delta}$ by his optimal method for smooth convex minimization – one with the complexity $O(1 / \sqrt{\epsilon})$ . Since the Lipschitz constant of the gradient of $f_{\delta}$ deteriorates as $\delta + 0$ , on one hand, and we need to work with small $\delta,$ those of the order of accuracy $\epsilon$ to which we want to solve (CP), on the other hand, the overall complexity of the outlined smoothing method is $O(1 / \epsilon)$ , which still is much better than the “black-box nonsmoo $\cdot h^{\dag}$ complexity ${\cal O}(1 / \epsilon^{2})$ and in fact ${\mathrm{is}},$ in many cases, as good as it could be.

For example, consider the Least Squares problem

$$
\operatorname{Opt} = \min_{x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}: \| x \|_{2} \leq R} \| Bx - b \|_{2},\tag{LS}
$$

where $B$ is an $n \times n$ matrix of the spectral norm $\| B \|$ not exceeding $L.$ This problem can be easily reformulated in the form of (SP), specifically, as

$$
\min_{\| x \|_{2} \leq 1} \max_{\| y \|_{2} \leq 1} y^{T}[Bx - b],
$$

and Nesterov’s smoothing with $\begin{array}{r}{d(y) = \frac{1}{2} y^{T} y} \end{array}$ allows to find an $\epsilon$-solution to the problem in $O(1) \frac{LR}{\epsilon}$ steps, provided that $LR / \epsilon \geq 1;$ each step here requires two matrix-vector multiplications, one involving $B$ and one involving $B^{T}$ . On the other hand, it is known that when $n > LR / \epsilon_{i}$ , every method for solving (LS) which is given in advance b and is allowed to “learn” B via matrix-vector multiplications involving $B$ and $B^{T}$ , needs in the worst (over b and B with $\| B \| \leq L)$ case at least $O(1) LR / \epsilon$ matrix-vector multiplications in order to find an $\epsilon$-solution to (LS). We can say that in the large-scale case complexity of the pretty well structured Least Squares problems (LS) with respect to First Order methods is $O(1 / \epsilon)$ , and this is what Nesterov’s smoothing achieves.

Nesterov’s smoothing is one way to utilize a “nice” (with “good” φ) saddle point representation (SP) of the objective in (CP) to accelerate processing the latter problem. In the sequel, we present another way to utilize (SP) – the Mirror Prox (MP) algorithm, which needs $\phi$ to be smooth (with Lipschitz continuous gradient), works directly on the saddle point problem (SP) and solves it with complexity $O(1 / \epsilon)$ , same as Nesterov’s smoothing. Let us stress that the “fast gradient methods” (this seems to become a common name of the algorithms we have just mentioned and their numerous “relatives” developed in the recent years) do exploit problem’s structure: this is exactly what is used to build the saddle point reformulation of the problem of interest; and since the reformulated problem is solved by black-box-oriented methods, we have good chances to end up with computationally cheap algorithms.

## 5.5.1.1 Examples of saddle point representations

Here we present instructive examples of $\mathrm{^6 \nice^{39} \mathrm{~ - ~} j}$ ust bilinear – saddle point representations of important and “heavily nonsmooth” convex functions. Justification of the examples is left to the reader. Note that the list can be easily extended.

1. $\| \cdot \|_{p^{-}} \mathrm{norm} \colon$

$$
\| x \|_{p} = \max_{y: \| y \|_{q} \leq 1} \langle y, x \rangle, q = \frac{p}{p - 1}.
$$

Matrix analogy: the Shatten p-norm of a rectangular matrix $x \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ is defined as $| x |_{p} = \| \sigma(x) \|_{p},$ where $\sigma(x) =[\sigma_{1}(x);...; \sigma_{\mathrm{min}[m, n]}(x)]$ is the vector of the largest min $[m, n]$ singular values of $x \{\mathrm{(i.e.}}$ ., the singular values which have chances to be nonzero) arranged in the non-ascending order. We have

$$
\forall x \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}: | x |_{p} = \max_{y \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}, | y |_{q} \leq 1} \langle y, x \rangle \equiv \operatorname{Tr}(y^{T} x), q = \frac{p}{p - 1}.
$$

Variation: p-norm of the “positive par $\v{r}^{\prime \prime} \x_{+} =[\mathrm{max}[x_{1}, 0];...; \mathrm{max}[x_{n}, 0]]$ of a vector $x \in$ R<sup>n</sup>:

$$
\| x_{+} \|_{p} = \max_{y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}: y \geq 0, \| y \|_{q} \leq 1} \langle y, x \rangle \equiv y^{T} x, q = \frac{p}{p - 1}.
$$

Matrix analogy: for a symmetric matrix $x \in \mathbf{S}^{n}$ , let $x_{+}$ be the matrix with the same eigenvectors and eigenvalues replaced with their positive parts. Then

$$
| x_{+} |_{p} = \max_{y \in \mathbf{S}^{n}: y \succeq 0, | y |_{q} \leq 1} \langle y, x \rangle = \operatorname{Tr}(yx), q = \frac{p}{p - 1}.
$$

2. Maximum entry $s_{1}(x)$ in a vector x and the sum $s_{k}(x)$ of k maximal entries in a vector $\boldsymbol{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ :

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \forall(x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}, k \leq n): \\ s_{1}(x) & = & \max_{y \in \Delta_{n}} \langle y, x \rangle, \\ & & \Delta_{n} = \{y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}: y \geq 0, \sum_{i} y_{i} = 1\}; \\ s_{k}(x) & = & \max_{y \in \Delta_{n, k}} \langle y, x \rangle, \\ & & \Delta_{n, k} = \{y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}: 0 \leq y_{i} \leq 1 \forall i, \sum_{i} y_{i} = k\} \end{array}
$$

Matrix analogies: maximal eigenvalue $S_{1}(x)$ and the sum of k largest eigenvalues $S_{k}(x)$ of a matrix $x \in \mathbf{S}^{n}$ :

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \forall(x \in \mathbf{S}^{n}, k \leq n): \\ S_{1}(x) & = & \max_{y \in \mathcal{D}_{n}} \langle y, x \rangle \equiv \operatorname{Tr}(yx)), \\ & & \mathcal{D}_{n} = \{y \in \mathbf{S}^{n}: y \succeq 0, \operatorname{Tr}(y) = 1\}; \\ S_{k}(x) & = & \max_{y \in \mathcal{D}_{n, k}} \langle y, x \rangle \equiv \operatorname{Tr}(yx), \\ & & \mathcal{D}_{n, k} = \{y \in \mathbf{S}^{n}: 0 \preceq y \preceq I, \operatorname{Tr}(y) = k\} \end{array}
$$

3. Maximal magnitude $s_{1}(\mathrm{abs}[x])$ of entries in x and the sum $s_{k}(\mathrm{abs}[x])$ of the k largest magnitudes of entries in x:

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \forall(x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}, k \leq n): \\ s_{1}(\mathrm{abs}[x]) & = & \max_{y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}, \| y \|_{1} \leq 1} \langle y, x \rangle; \\ s_{k}(\mathrm{abs}[x]) & = & \max_{y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}: \| y \|_{\infty} \leq 1, \| y \|_{1} \leq k} \langle y, x \rangle \equiv y^{T} x.\end{array}
$$

Matrix analogy: the sum $\Sigma_{k}(x)$ of k maximal singular values of a matrix x:

$$
\begin{array}{rlr} \forall(x \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}, k \leq \min[m, n]): \\ \Sigma_{k}(x) & = & \max_{y \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}: | y |_{\infty} \leq 1, | y |_{1} \leq k} \langle y, x \rangle \equiv \mathrm{Tr}(y^{T} x)).\end{array}
$$

We augment this sample of “raw materials” with calculus rules. We restrict ourselves with bilinear saddle point representations:

$$
f(x) = \max_{y \in Y} \left[\langle y, Ax \rangle + \langle a, x \rangle + \langle b, y \rangle + c \right],
$$

where x runs through a Euclidean space $E_{x}, Y$ is a convex compact subset in a Euclidean space $E_{y}, x \mapsto Ax : E_{x} \to E_{y}$ is a linear mapping, and $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ are inner products in the respective spaces. In the rules to follow, all $Y_{i}$ are nonempty convex compact sets.

1. [Taking conic combinations] Let

$$
f_{i}(x) = \max_{y_{i} \in Y_{i}} \left[\langle y_{i}, A_{i} x \rangle + \langle a_{i}, x \rangle + \langle b_{i}, y_{i} \rangle + c_{i} \right], 1 \leq i \leq m,
$$

and let $\lambda_{i} \geq 0$ . Then

$$
\begin{array}{l} \sum_{i} \lambda_{i} f_{i}(x) \\ = \max_{y =[y_{1}; \ldots; y_{m}] \in Y = Y_{1} \times \ldots \times Y_{m}}[\underbrace{\sum_{i} \lambda_{i} \langle y_{i}, A_{i} x \rangle}_{=: \langle y, Ax \rangle} + \underbrace{\langle \sum_{i} \lambda_{i} a_{i}, x \rangle}_{=: \langle a, x \rangle} + \underbrace{\sum_{i} \lambda_{i} \langle b_{i}, y_{i} \rangle}_{=: \langle b, y \rangle} + \underbrace{\sum_{i} \lambda_{i} c_{i}}_{=: c}].\end{array}
$$

2. [Taking direct sums] Let

$$
f_{i}(x_{i}) = \max_{y_{i} \in Y_{i}} \left[\langle y_{i}, A_{i} x_{i} \rangle + \langle a_{i}, x_{i} \rangle + \langle b_{i}, y_{i} \rangle + c_{i} \right], 1 \leq i \leq m.
$$

Then

$$
\begin{array}{l} f(x \equiv[x^{1};...; x^{m}]) = \sum_{i = 1}^{m} f_{i}(x_{i}) \\ = \max_{y =[y_{1};...; y_{m}] \in Y = Y_{1} \times...\times Y_{m}}[\underbrace{\sum_{i} \lambda_{i} \langle y_{i}, A_{i} x_{i} \rangle}_{=: \langle y, Ax \rangle} + \underbrace{\sum_{i} \lambda_{i} \langle a_{i}, x_{i} \rangle}_{=: \langle a, x \rangle} + \underbrace{\sum_{i} \lambda_{i} \langle b_{i}, y_{i} \rangle}_{=: \langle b, y \rangle} + \underbrace{\sum_{i} \lambda_{i} c_{i}}_{=: c}].\end{array}
$$

3. [Affine substitution of argument] For $x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ , let

$$
f(x) = \max_{y \in Y} \left[\langle y, Ax \rangle + \langle a, x \rangle + \langle b, y \rangle + c \right],
$$

and let $\xi \mapsto P \xi + p$ be an Affine mapping from $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ . Then

$$
g(\xi) := f(P \xi + p) = \max_{y \in Y}[\langle y, AP \xi \rangle + \langle P^{*} a, \xi \rangle + \langle b, y \rangle +[c + \langle a, p \rangle]].
$$

4. [Taking maximum] Let

$$
f_{i}(x) = \max_{y_{i} \in Y_{i}} \left[\langle y_{i}, A_{i} x \rangle + \langle a_{i}, x \rangle + \langle b_{i}, y_{i} \rangle + c_{i} \right], 1 \leq i \leq m.
$$

Then

$$
\begin{array}{l} f(x) := \max_{i} f_{i}(x) \\ = \max_{y =[(\eta_{1}, u_{1}); \ldots;(\eta_{m}, u_{m})] \in Y}[\underbrace{\sum_{i} \langle u_{i}, A_{i} x \rangle + \langle \sum_{i} \eta_{i} a_{i}, x \rangle}_{=: \langle y, Ax \rangle} + \underbrace{\sum_{i} \langle b_{i}, u_{i} \rangle + \sum_{i} c_{i} \eta_{i}\}}_{=: \langle b, y \rangle}], \\ Y = \left\{y =[(\eta_{1}, u_{1}); \ldots;(\eta_{m}, u_{m})]:(\eta_{i}, u_{i}) \in \widehat{Y}_{i}, 1 \leq i \leq m, \sum_{i} \eta_{i} = 1 \right\}, \end{array}
$$

where $\widehat{Y}_{i}$ are the “conic hats” spanned by $Y_{i}{\mathrm{:}}$ :

$$
\widehat{Y}_{i} = \operatorname{cl} \left\{(\eta, u): 0 < \eta \leq 1, \eta^{- 1} u \in Y_{i} \right\} = \{[0, 0]\} \cup \left\{(\eta, u): 0 < \eta \leq 1, \eta^{- 1} u \in Y_{i} \right\}
$$

(the second $^{99} =^{99}$ follows from the compactness of $Y_{i})$ . Here is the derivation:

$$
\begin{array}{l} \max_{i} f_{i}(x) = \max_{\eta \in \Delta_{m}} \sum_{i} \eta_{i} f_{i}(x) \\ = \max_{\eta \in \Delta_{m}, y_{i} \in Y_{i}, 1 \leq i \leq m} \big[\sum_{i} \langle \underbrace{\eta_{i} y_{i}}_{=: u_{i}}, A_{i} x \rangle + \sum_{i} \langle \eta_{i} a_{i}, x \rangle + \sum_{i} \langle b_{i}, \eta_{i} y_{i} \rangle + \sum_{i} \eta_{i} c_{i} \big] \\ = \max_{(\eta_{i}, u_{i}) \in \widehat{Y_{i}}, 1 \leq i \leq m, \sum_{i} \eta_{i} = 1}[[\sum_{i} \langle u_{i}, A_{i} x_{i} \rangle + \langle \sum_{i} \eta_{i} a_{i}, x \rangle] +[\sum_{i} \langle b_{i}, u_{i} \rangle + \sum_{i} c_{i} \eta_{i}]].\end{array}
$$

## 5.5.2 The Mirror Prox algorithm

We are about to present the Mirror Prox algorithm [38] for solving saddle point problem

$$
\min_{x \in X} \max_{y \in Y} \phi(x, y)\tag{SP}
$$

with smooth convex-concave cost function $\phi.$ Smoothness means that $\phi$ is continuously diferentiable on $Z = X \times Y$ , and that the associated vector field (cf. (5.3.44))

$$
F(z =(x, y)) =[F_{x}(x, y) := \nabla_{x} \phi(x, y); F_{y}(x, y) = - \nabla_{y} \phi(x, y)]: Z := X \times Y \to{\bf R}^{n_{x}} \times{\bf R}^{n_{y}}
$$

is Lipschitz continuous on $Z.$

The setup for the MP algorithm as applied to (SP) is the same as for the saddle point Mirror Descent, see section 5.3.6, specifically, we fix a norm $\| \cdot \|$ on the embedding space $\mathbb{R}^{n_{x}} \times \mathbb{R}^{n_{y}}$ of the domain $Z$ of $\phi$ and a DGF ω for this domain. Since $F$ is Lipschitz continuous, we have for properly chosen $L < \infty$

$$
\left\| F(z) - F \left(z^{\prime}\right) \right\|_{*} \leq L \left\| z - z^{\prime} \right\| \forall z, z^{\prime} \in Z.\tag{5.5.1}
$$

The MP algorithm as applied to (SP) is the recurrence

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} z_{1} :=(x_{1}, y_{1}) & = & z_{\omega} := \operatorname{argmin}_{z \in Z} \omega(z), \\ w_{t} :=(\widetilde{x}_{t}, \widetilde{y}_{t}) & = & \mathrm{Prox}_{z_{t}}(\gamma_{t} F(z_{t})) \\ z_{t + 1} :=(x_{t + 1}, y_{t + 1}) & = & \mathrm{Prox}_{z_{t}}(\gamma_{t} F(w_{t})), \\ & & \mathrm{Prox}_{z}(\xi) = \operatorname{argmin}_{w \in Z}[V_{z}(w) + \langle \xi, w \rangle], \\ & & V_{z}(w) = \omega(w) - \langle \omega^{\prime}(z), w - z \rangle - \omega(z) \geq \frac 12 \| w - z \|^{2}, \\ z^{t} & = & \left[\sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau} \right]^{- 1} \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau} w_{\tau}, \end{array}\tag{5.5.2}
$$

where $\gamma_{t}$ are positive stepsizes. This looks pretty much as the saddle point MD algorithm, see (5.3.45); the only diference is in what is called extra-gradient step: what was the updating $z_{t} \mapsto z_{t + 1}$ in the MD, now defines an intermediate point $w_{t}$ , and the actual updating $z_{t} \mapsto z_{t + 1}$ uses, instead of the value of $F$ at $z_{t}.$ , the value of F at this intermediate point. Another diference is that now the approximate solutions $z^{t}$ are weighted sums of the intermediate points $w_{\tau},$ and not of the subsequent prox-centers $z_{T},$ , as in MD. These “minor changes” result in major consequences (provided that $F$ is Lipschitz continuous). Here is the corresponding result:

Theorem 5.5.1 Let convex-concave saddle point problem (SP) be solved by the MP algorithm. Then

(i) For every τ , one has for all $u \in Z$

$$
\gamma_{\tau} \langle F(w_{\tau}), w_{\tau} - u \rangle \leq V_{z_{\tau}}(u) - V_{z_{\tau + 1}}(u) + \underbrace{[\gamma_{\tau} \langle F(w_{\tau}), w_{\tau} - z_{\tau + 1} \rangle - V_{z_{\tau}}(z_{\tau + 1})]}_{},\tag{a}
$$

$$
\delta_{\tau} \leq \gamma_{\tau} \langle F(w_{\tau}) - F(z_{\tau}), w_{\tau} - z_{\tau + 1} \rangle - V_{z_{\tau}}(w_{\tau}) - V_{w_{\tau}}(z_{\tau + 1})\tag{b}
$$

$$
\leq \frac{\gamma_{\tau}^{2}}{2} \| F(w_{\tau}) - F(z_{\tau}) \|_{*}^{2} - \frac{1}{2} \| w_{\tau} - z_{\tau} \|^{2}\tag{c}
$$

(5.5.3)

In particular, in the case of (5.5.1) one has

$$
\gamma_{\tau} \leq \frac{1}{L} \Rightarrow \delta_{\tau} \leq 0,
$$

see (5.5.3.c).

(ii) Let Ω be the ω-diameter of $Z = X \times Y$ . For $t = 1, 2, \dots$ , one has

$$
\epsilon_{\mathrm{sad}}(z^{t}) \leq \frac{\frac{\Omega^{2}}{2} + \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \delta_{\tau}}{\sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau}}.\tag{5.5.4}
$$

In particular, let the stepsizes $\gamma_{\tau}, 1 \leq \tau \leq t$ , be such that $\begin{array}{r}{\gamma_{\tau} \geq \frac{1}{L}} \end{array}$ and $\delta_{\tau} \leq 0$ for all $\tau \leq t$ (by (i), this is definitely so for the stepsizes $\begin{array}{r}{\gamma_{\tau} \equiv \frac{1}{L}} \end{array}$ , provided that (5.5.1) takes place). Then

$$
\epsilon_{\mathrm{sad}}(z^{t}) \leq \frac{\Omega^{2}}{2 \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau}} \leq \frac{\Omega^{2} L}{2t}.\tag{5.5.5}
$$

Proof. ${\bf 1}^{0}$ . To verify (i), let us fix τ and set $\delta = \delta_{\tau}, z = z_{\tau}, \xi = \gamma_{\tau} F(z_{\tau}), w = w_{\tau}, \eta = \gamma_{\tau} F(w_{\tau})$ $z_{+} = z_{\tau + 1}$ . Note that the relations between the entities in question are given by

$$
z \in Z, w = \operatorname{Prox}_{z}(\xi), z_{+} = \operatorname{Prox}_{z}(\eta).\tag{5.5.6}
$$

As we remember, from $w = \mathrm{Prox}_{z}(\xi)$ and $z_{+} = \mathrm{Prox}_{z}(\eta)$ it follows that $w, z_{+} \in Z$ and

$$
(a) \quad \langle \xi - \omega^{\prime}(z) + \omega^{\prime}(w), u - w \rangle \geq 0 \forall u \in Z,
$$

$$
(b) \quad \langle \eta - \omega^{\prime}(z) + \omega^{\prime}(z_{+}), u - z_{+} \rangle \geq 0 \forall u \in Z,
$$

whence for every $u \in Z$ we have

$$
\begin{array}{ll} \langle \eta, w - u \rangle = & \langle \eta, z_{+} - u \rangle + \langle \eta, w - z_{+} \rangle \\ \leq & \langle \omega^{\prime}(z) - \omega^{\prime}(z_{+}), z_{+} - u \rangle + \langle \eta, w - z_{+} \rangle[\text{by}(b)] \\ = &[\omega(u) - \omega(z) - \langle \omega^{\prime}(z), u - z \rangle] -[\omega(u) - \omega(z_{+}) - \langle \omega^{\prime}(z_{+}), u - z_{+} \rangle] \\ & +[\omega(z) - \omega(z_{+}) + \langle \omega^{\prime}(z), z_{+} - z \rangle + \langle \eta, w - z_{+} \rangle] \\ = & V_{z}(u) - V_{z_{+}}(u) +[\langle \eta, w - z_{+} \rangle - V_{z}(z_{+})][\text{we have proved (5.5.3.a)}] \\ \delta : = & \langle \eta, w - z_{+} \rangle - V_{z}(z_{+}) = \langle \eta - \xi, w - z_{+} \rangle - V_{z}(z_{+}) + \langle \xi, w - z_{+} \rangle \\ \leq & \langle \eta - \xi, w - z_{+} \rangle - V_{z}(z_{+}) + \langle \omega^{\prime}(z) - \omega^{\prime}(w), w - z_{+} \rangle[\text{by}(a) \text{with} u = z_{+}] \\ = & \langle \eta - \xi, w - z_{+} \rangle - \omega(z_{+}) + \omega(z) + \langle \omega^{\prime}(z), z_{+} - z \rangle + \langle \omega^{\prime}(z) - \omega^{\prime}(w), w - z_{+} \rangle \\ = & \langle \eta - \xi, w - z_{+} \rangle - \omega(z_{+}) + \omega(z) + \langle \omega^{\prime}(z), z_{+} \rangle - \langle \omega^{\prime}(z), z \rangle \\ & + \langle \omega^{\prime}(z), w \rangle - \langle \omega^{\prime}(z), z_{+} \rangle - \langle \omega^{\prime}(w), w \rangle + \langle \omega^{\prime}(w), z_{+} \rangle \\ = & \langle \eta - \xi, w - z_{+} \rangle +[- \omega(w) + \omega(z) + \langle \omega^{\prime}(z), w \rangle - \langle \omega^{\prime}(z), z \rangle] \\ & +[- \omega(z_{+}) + \omega(w) + \langle \omega^{\prime}(w), z_{+} \rangle - \langle \omega^{\prime}(w), w \rangle] \\ = & \langle \eta - \xi, w - z_{+} \rangle - V_{z}(w) - V_{w}(z_{+})[\text{we have proved (5.5.3.b)}] \\ \leq & \langle \eta - \xi, w - z_{+} \rangle -{\frac{1}{2}}[\| w - z \|^{2} + \| w - z_{+} \|^{2}][bystrongconvexityof \omega] \\ \leq & \| | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | &{\frac{1}{2}} \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \| \|.\end{array}
$$

and we have arrived at $(5.5.3.c)^{15}$ . Thus, (5.5.3) is proved.

Relation (5.5.4) follows from the first inequality in (5.5.3) in exactly the same fashion as (5.3.47) was derived from (5.3.46) when proving Theorem 5.3.4.

All remaining claims in (i) and (ii) are immediate consequences of (5.5.3) and (5.5.4). ✷

Note that (5.5.5) corresponds to $O(1 / \epsilon)$ upper complexity bound.

## 5.5.2.1 Refinement

Same as for various versions of MD, the complexity analysis of $\mathrm{MP}$ can be refined. The corresponding version of Theorem 5.5.1 is as follows.

Theorem 5.5.2 Let positive reals $\lambda_{1}, \lambda_{2}, \ldots$ satisfy (5.3.25). Let convex-concave saddle point problem (SP) be solved by the MP algorithm, and let

$$
z^{t} = \frac{\sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \lambda_{\tau} w_{\tau}}{\sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \lambda_{\tau}}.
$$

Then $z^{t} \in Z$ , and for $t = 1, 2, \dots$ . one has

$$
\epsilon_{\mathrm{sad}}(z^{t}) \leq \frac{\frac{\lambda_{t}}{\gamma_{t}} \frac{\Omega^{2}}{2} + \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \frac{\lambda_{\tau}}{\gamma_{\tau}} \delta_{\tau}}{\sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \lambda_{\tau}},\tag{5.5.7}
$$

with $\delta_{\tau}$ defined by $(5.5.3.a)$

In particular, let $\begin{array}{r}{\gamma_{\tau} \geq \frac{1}{L}} \end{array}$ be such that $\delta_{\tau} \leq 0$ for all $\tau$ (as is the case when $\begin{array}{r}{\gamma_{\tau} \equiv \frac{1}{L}} \end{array}$ and (5.5.1) takes place, see (5.5.3.c)). Then

$$
\epsilon_{\mathrm{sad}}(z^{t}) \leq \frac{\frac{\lambda_{t}}{\gamma_{t}} \Omega^{2}}{2 \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \lambda_{\tau}}.\tag{5.5.8}
$$

Proof. Invoking Theorem 5.5.1, we get (5.5.3). This relation implies for every τ :

$$
\forall(u \in Z): \lambda_{\tau} \langle F(w_{\tau}), w_{\tau} - u \rangle \leq \frac{\lambda_{\tau}}{\gamma_{\tau}}[V_{z_{\tau}}(u) - V_{z_{\tau + 1}}(u)] + \frac{\lambda_{\tau}}{\gamma_{\tau}} \delta_{\tau},
$$

whence, same as in the proof of Theorem 5.3.2, for $t = 1, 2,..$ . we get

$$
\begin{array}{r} \max_{u \in Z} \Lambda_{t}^{- 1} \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \lambda_{\tau} \langle F(w_{\tau}), w_{\tau} - u \rangle \leq \frac{\frac{\lambda_{t}}{\gamma_{t}} \frac{\Omega^{2}}{2} + \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \frac{\lambda_{\tau}}{\gamma_{\tau}} \delta_{\tau}}{\Lambda_{t}}, \\ \Lambda_{t} = \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \lambda_{\tau}.\end{array}
$$

Same as in the proof of Theorem 5.3.4, the latter inequality implies (5.5.7). The latter relation under the premise of Theorem immediately implies (5.5.8). ✷

Incorporating aggressive stepsize policy. The eficiency estimate (5.5.5) in Theorem 5.5.1 is the better the larger are the stepsizes $\gamma_{\tau}$ ; however, this bound is obtained under the assumption that we maintain the relation $\delta_{\tau} \leq 0.$ , and the proof of Theorem suggests that when the stepsizes are greater than the “theoretically safe” value $\begin{array}{r}{\gamma_{\mathrm{safe}} = \frac{1}{L}.} \end{array}$ , there are no guarantees for $\delta_{\tau}$ to stay nonnegative. This does not mean, however, that all we can do is to use the worst-case-oriented stepsize policy $\gamma_{\tau} ~ = ~ \gamma_{\mathrm{safe}}$ . A reasonable “aggressi $\mathrm{ve}^{\mathrm{\gamma}}$ stepsize policy is as follows: we start iteration $\tau$ with a “proposed value $\stackrel{\mathfrak{w}}{,} \gamma_{\tau}^{+} \geq \gamma_{\mathrm{safe}} \operatorname{of} \gamma_{\tau}$ and use $\gamma_{\tau} = \gamma_{\tau}^{+}$ to compute candidate $w_{\tau},$ $z_{T + 1}$ and the corresponding $\delta_{\tau}$ . If $\delta_{\tau} \leq 0$ , we consider our trial successful, treat the candidate $w_{\tau}$ and $z_{\tau + 1}$ as actual ones and pass to iteration $\tau + 1$ , increasing the value of $\gamma^{+}$ by an absolute constant factor: $\gamma_{\tau + 1}^{+} = \theta^{+} \gamma_{\tau}^{+}$ , where $\theta^{+} > 1$ is a parameter of our strategy. On the other hand, if with $\gamma_{\tau} = \gamma_{\tau}^{+}$ we get $\delta_{\tau} > 0$ , we consider the trial unsuccessful, reset $\gamma_{\tau}$ to a smaller value max $[\theta_{-} \gamma_{\tau},$ γ<sub>safe</sub>] $(\theta_{-} \in(0, 1)$ is another parameter of our stepsize policy) and recompute the candidate $w_{\tau}$ and $z_{T + 1}$ with $\gamma_{t}$ set to the new, reduced value. If we still get $\delta_{\tau} > 0.$ , we once again reduce the value of $\gamma_{t}$ and rerun the iteration, proceeding in this fashion until $\delta_{\tau} \leq 0$ is obtained. When it happens, we pass to iteration $\tau + 1$ , now setting $\gamma_{\tau + 1}^{+}$ to the value of $\gamma_{\tau}$ we have reached.

Computational experience shows that with reasonable choice of $\theta_{\pm}$ (our usual choice is $\theta _ { + } = $ $1.2, \theta_{-} = 0.8)$ the aggressive policy outperforms the theoretically safe (i.e., with $\gamma_{t} \equiv \gamma_{\mathrm{safe}})$ one: for the former policy, the “step per oracle call” index defined as the ratio of the quantity $\Gamma_{t} =$ $\scriptstyle \sum_{\tau = 1}^{T}$ γ<sub>τ</sub> participating in the eficiency estimate (5.5.5) to the total number of computations of $F(\cdot)$ in course of $T$ steps (including computations of $F$ at the finally discarded trial intermediate points), where T is the step where we terminate the solution process, usually is essentially larger (for some problems – larger by orders of magnitude) than the similar ratio $\left(\mathrm{i.e., \gamma_{safe} / 2} \right)$ for the safe stepsize policy.

## 5.5.2.2 Typical implementation

In a typical implementation of the MP algorithm, the components X and $Y$ of the domain of the saddle problem of interest are convex compact subsets of direct products of finitely many standard blocks, specifically, Euclidean, $\ell_{1} / \ell_{2}$ and nuclear norm balls. For example, the usual box is the direct product of several segments (and thus – of one-dimensional Euclidean balls), a (standard) simplex is a subset of the $\ell_{1}$ ball (that is, of a specific $\ell_{1} / \ell_{2}$ ball)<sup>16</sup>, a spectahedron is a subset of a specific nuclear norm ball, etc. In the sequel, we assume that X and Y are of the same dimensions as the direct products of standard blocks embedding these two sets. In the case in question, $Z$ is a subset of the direct product $\widehat{Z} = Z_{1} \times...\times Z_{N} \subset E = E_{1} \times...\times E_{N} \(E_{j}$ are the Euclidean spaces embedding $Z_{j})$ of standard blocks $Z_{j}$ and the dimension of Z is equal to the one of ${\widehat{Z}}.$ . Recall that we have associated standard blocks and their embedding spaces with standard proximal setups, see section 5.3.3 The most natural way to get a proximal setup for the saddle point problem in question is to aggregate the proximal setups for separate blocks into a proximal setup $(\omega(\cdot), \parallel \cdot \parallel)$ for ${\widehat{Z}} \subset E.$ , and then to “reduce” this setup onto $Z,$ meaning that we keep the norm $\| \cdot \|$ on the embedding space $E$ (this space is common for $Z \subset{\widehat{Z}}$ and $\widehat{Z})$ intact and restrict the DGF $\omega$ from $\widehat{Z}$ onto Z. The latter is legitimate: since $Z$ and $\widehat{Z} \supset Z$ are of the same dimension, $\omega |_{Z}$ is a DGF for $Z$ compatible with $\| cdot \|$ , and the $\omega |_{Z}.$ -radius of $Z$ clearly does not exceed the quantity

$$
\widehat{\Omega} = \sqrt{2 \Theta}, \Theta = \max_{\widehat{Z}} \omega(\cdot) - \min_{\widehat{Z}} \omega(\cdot).
$$

Now, the simplest way to aggregate the standard proximal setups for the standard blocks $Z_{j}$ into such a setup for $\dot{\hat{Z}}$ is as follows: denoting by $\| \cdot \|_{(j)}$ the norms, and by $\omega_{j}(z_{j}) \textrm{-}$ the DGFs as given by setups for blocks, we equip the embedding space of $\widehat{Z}$ with the norm

$$
\|[z^{1}; \dots; z^{N}] \| = \sqrt{\sum_{j = 1}^{N} \alpha_{j} \| z^{j} \|_{(j)}^{2}},
$$

and equip $\widehat{Z}$ with the DGF

$$
\omega(z^{1}, \dots, z^{N}) = \sum_{j = 1}^{N} \beta_{j} \omega_{j}(z^{j}).
$$

Here $\alpha_{j}$ and $\beta_{j}$ are positive aggregation weights, which we choose in order to end up with a legitimate proximal setup for $Z \subset E$ with the best possible eficiency estimate. The standard recipe is as follows (for justification, see $\left[38 \right])$ ):

Our initial data are the “partial proximal setups” $\| \cdot \|_{(j)}, \omega_{j}(\cdot)$ along with the upper bounds $\Theta_{j}$ on the variations

$$
\max_{Z_{j}} \omega_{j}(\cdot) - \min_{Z_{j}} \omega(\cdot).
$$

Now, the direct product structure of the embedding space of $Z$ allows to represent the vector field $F$ associated with the convex-concave function in question in the “block form”

$$
F(z^{1}, \dots, Z^{N}) =[F_{1}(z); \dots; F_{N}(z)].
$$

Assuming this field Lipschitz continuous, we can find (upper bounds on) the “partial Lipschitz constants” $L_{ij}$ of this field, so that

$$
\forall(i, z =[z^{1}; \dots; z^{N}] \in Z, w =[w^{1}; \dots; w^{n}] \in Z): \| F_{i}(z) - F_{i}(w) \|_{(i, *)} \leq \sum_{j = 1}^{N} \| z^{j} - w^{j} \|_{(j)},
$$

where $\| \cdot \|_{(i, *)}$ are the norms conjugate to $\| \cdot \|_{(i)}$ . W.l.o.g. we assume the bounds $L_{ij}$ symmetric: $L_{ij} = L_{ji}$

In terms of the parameters of the partial setups and the quantities $L_{ij}$ , the aggregation is as follows: we set

$$
\begin{array}{r} M_{ij} = L_{ij} \sqrt{\Theta_{i} \Theta_{j}}, \sigma_{k} = \frac{\sum_{j} M_{kj}}{\sum_{i, j} M_{ij}}, \alpha_{j} = \frac{\sigma_{j}}{\Theta_{j}}, \\ \|[z^{1}; \dots; z^{N}] \|^{2} = \sum_{j = 1}^{N} \alpha_{j} \| z^{j} \|_{(j)}^{2}, \omega(z^{1}, \dots, z^{j}) = \sum_{j = 1}^{N} \alpha_{j} \omega_{j}(z^{j}).\end{array}
$$

which results in

$$
\Theta = \max_{\widehat{Z}} \omega(\cdot) - \min_{\widehat{Z}} \omega(\cdot) \leq 1,
$$

(that is, the ω-radius of Z does not exceed $\sqrt{2})$ . The condition (5.5.1) is now satisfied with

$$
L = \mathcal{L} := \sum_{i, j} L_{ij} \sqrt{\Theta_{i} \Theta_{j}},
$$

and the eficiency estimate (5.5.5) becomes

$$
\epsilon_{\mathrm{sad}}(z^{t}) \leq \mathcal{L} t^{- 1}, t = 1, 2, \dots
$$

Illustration. Let us look at the problem

$$
\operatorname{Opt}_{r, p} = \min_{x \in X = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}: \| x \|_{p} \leq 1\}} \| Bx - b \|_{r},
$$

where B is an $m \times n$ matrix and $p \in \{1, 2\}, r \in \{2, \infty\}$

The problem admits an immediate saddle point reformulation:

$$
\min_{x \in X = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}: \| x \|_{p} \leq 1\}} \max_{y \in Y = \{y \in \mathbb{R}^{m}: \| y \|_{r_{*}} \leq 1\}} y^{T}(Bx - b)
$$

where, as always,

$$
r_{*} = \frac{r}{r - 1}.
$$

We are in the situation of $Z_{1} = X, Z_{2} = Y$ with

$$
F(z^{1} \equiv x, z^{2} \equiv y) = \left[F_{1}(y) = B^{T} y; F_{2}(x) = b - Bx \right].
$$

Besides this, the blocks $Z_{1}, \Z_{2}$ are either unit $\| \cdot \|_{2^{-}} \mathrm{balls}.$ , or unit $\ell_{1}$ balls. The associated quantities $\Theta_{i}, L_{ij}, i, j = 1, 2$ , within absolute constant factors are as follows:

<table><tr><td></td><td> $p = 1$ </td><td> $p = 2$ </td></tr><tr><td> $\Theta_{1}$ </td><td> $\ln(n)$ </td><td> $1$ </td></tr></table>

$$
[L_{ij}]_{i, j = 1}^{2} = \left[\begin{array}{cc} 0 & \| B \|_{p \to r} \\ \| B \|_{p \to r} & 0 \end{array} \right], \quad \| B \|_{p \to r} = \max_{\| x \|_{p} \leq 1} \| Bx \|_{r}.
$$

The matrix norms $\| B \|_{p \to \operatorname{max}[r, 2]}$ , again within an absolute constant factors, are given in the following table:

<table><tr><td></td><td>p=1</td><td>p=2</td></tr><tr><td>r=1</td><td>$ \max_{j\leq n}\|\text{Col}_{j}[B]\|_{2} $</td><td>$ \sigma_{\max}(B) $</td></tr><tr><td>r=2</td><td>$ \max_{j\leq n}\|\text{Col}_{j}[B]\|_{2} $</td><td>$ \sigma_{\max}(B) $</td></tr></table>

where, as always, $\operatorname{Col}_{j}[B]$ is j-th column of matrix B. For example, consider the situations of extreme interest for Compressed Sensing, namely, \` -minimization with $\| \cdot \|_{2^{-}} \mathrm{fit}$ and $\ell_{1}$ minimization with $\ell_{\infty}{-} \mathrm{\mathrm{fit}}$ (that is, the cases $(p = 1, r = 2)$ and $(p = 1, r = \infty)$ , respectively). Here the achievable for MP eficiency estimates (the best known so far in the large scale case, although achievable not only with MP) are as follows:

$\ell_{1}$ -minimization with $\| \cdot \|_{2^{-}} \mathrm{{fit}} !$

$$
\| x^{t} \|_{1} \leq 1 \& \| Bx^{t} - b \|_{2} \leq \min_{\| x \|_{1} \leq 1} \| Bx - x \|_{2} + O(1) \frac{\sqrt{\ln(n)} \max_{j} \| \mathrm{Col}_{j}[B] \|_{2}}{t};
$$

- \`<sub>1</sub>-minimization with $\| \cdot \|_{\infty}{\mathrm{- fit}}$

$$
\| x^{t} \|_{1} \leq 1 \& \| Bx^{t} - b \|_{\infty} \leq \min_{\| x \|_{1} \leq 1} \| Bx - x \|_{\infty} + O(1) \frac{\sqrt{\ln(m) \ln(n)} \max_{i, j} | B_{ij} |}{t};
$$

## 5.6 Summary on Mirror Descent and Mirror Prox Algorithms

The goal of this section is to summarize the numerous preceding results on (non-bundle versions of) Mirror Descent and Mirror Prox algorithms as applied to various problems “with convex structure.” We deliberately make the presentation to follow as self-contained as possible, even at the price of reproducing more or less verbatim some of preceding constructions and proofs.

## 5.6.1 Situation

We fix once for ever a nonempty convex compact subset Z of Euclidean space E (it will serve as the domain of problems we want to solve). We equip $\mathcal{Z}$ with proximal setup $\| \cdot \|, \omega(\cdot)$ , so that $\| \cdot \|$ is a norm on $E$ (its conjugate is denoted $\| \cdot \|_{*})$ and $\omega(z) : \mathcal{Z} \mathbb{R}$ is continuously diferentiable and strongly convex, modulus 1, function:

$$
\langle \omega^{\prime}(z) - \omega^{\prime}(z^{\prime}), z - z^{\prime} \rangle \geq \| z - z^{\prime} \|^{2} \forall z, z^{\prime} \in \mathcal{Z}.\tag{5.6.1}
$$

As a consequence, we arrive at

- Bregman distance from $z^{\prime} \in \mathcal{Z}$ to $z \in { \mathcal { Z } } $

$$
V_{z}(z^{\prime}) = \omega(z^{\prime}) - \omega(z) - \langle z^{\prime} - z, \omega^{\prime}(z) \rangle \geq \frac{1}{2} \| z^{\prime} - z \|^{2}, z, z^{\prime} \in \mathcal{Z};\tag{5.6.2}
$$

- ω-capacity of Z:

$$
\Theta = \max_{z, z^{\prime} \in \mathcal{Z}} V_{z}(z^{\prime});\tag{5.6.3}
$$

and ω-diameter of Z

$$
\Omega = \sqrt{2 \Theta};
$$

note that $\Omega \geq \operatorname{max}_{z, z^{\prime} \in \mathcal{Z}} \| z - z^{\prime} \|$ due to $\begin{array}{r}{V_{x}(z^{\prime}) \geq \frac{1}{2} \| z - z^{\prime} \|} \end{array}$

- Prox-mapping $\operatorname{Prox}_{z}^{U}(\xi) : EU$ centered at $z \in{\mathcal{Z}}$ , where $U$ is a nonempty closed subset of $\mathcal{Z}$ . The mapping is defined by

$$
\operatorname{Prox}_{z}^{U}(\xi) = \underset{u \in U}{\operatorname{argmin}} \left[\langle \xi, u \rangle + V_{z}(u) \right];\tag{5.6.4}
$$

we skip the superscript <sup>U</sup> when $U = \mathcal{Z} \colon \operatorname{Prox}_{z}(\cdot) = \operatorname{Prox}_{z}^{\mathcal{Z}}(\cdot)$ . For this mapping, the Magic relation holds true:

$$
\begin{array}{rl} & z \in \mathcal{Z}, \xi \in E, z_{+} = \mathrm{Prox}_{z}^{U}(\xi) \\ & \Rightarrow \langle \xi, z_{+} - u \rangle \leq \langle \omega^{\prime}(z_{+}) - \omega^{\prime}(z), u - z_{+} \rangle = V_{z}(u) - V_{z_{+}}(u) - V_{z}(z_{+}).\end{array}\tag{5.6.5}
$$

Indeed, the inequality in the declared conclusion is given by optimality conditions stating that $\langle \omega^{\prime}(z_{+}) + \xi - \omega^{\prime}(z), u - z_{+} \rangle \geq 0$ for all $u \in U$ , The subsequent equality is given by the following computation:

$$
\begin{array}{rl} \langle \omega^{\prime}(z_{+}) - \omega^{\prime}(z), u - z_{+} \rangle = &[\omega(u) - \omega(z) - \langle \omega^{\prime}(z), u - z \rangle] \\ & -[\omega(u) - \omega(z_{+}) - \langle \omega^{\prime}(z_{+}), u - z_{+} \rangle] \\ & -[\omega(z_{+}) - \omega(z) - \langle \omega^{\prime}(z), z_{+} - z \rangle] \\ = & V_{z}(u) - V_{z_{+}}(u) - V_{z}(z_{+}).\end{array}
$$

## 5.6.2 Mirror Descent and Mirror Prox algorithms

## 5.6.2.1 First Order oracles and oracle-based algorithms

Algorithms we are interested in operate with oracles providing information on the problem being processed. A general enough for our purposes model of oracle is a “black box” procedure $\mathcal{O};$ at t-th call to this procedure, the input being a query point $z_{t} \in \mathcal{Z}$ , the procedure returns vector $G_{t}(z_{t}, \xi_{t}) \in E$ which is a deterministic function, perhaps depending on $t,$ of the query point and t-th “oracle noise” $\xi_{t}$ , where $\{\xi_{t}, t \ge 1\}$ is a sequence of independent identically distributed realizations of random vector $\xi.$ We assume that for all $t \geq 1$ and $z \in{\mathcal{Z}}$ the random vector $G_{t}(z, \xi)$ has finite expectation and set

$$
g_{t}(z) = \mathbb{E}_{\xi} \left\{G_{t}(z, \xi) \right\}\tag{5.6.6}
$$

In the sequel, we denote by $\xi^{t} =(\xi_{1},..., \xi_{t})$ the sequence of the first t realizations of the oracle’s noise.

We call oracle O stationary, if $G_{t}(\cdot, \cdot) \equiv G(\cdot, \cdot)$ is independent of $t,$ in which case we call $G(\cdot, \cdot)$ the response of O.

An algorithm B associated with oracle O is a procedure which generates subsequent query (a.k.a. search ) points $z_{t} \in \mathcal{Z}, t = 1, 2, \dots -$ those where oracle O is queried — based on information accumulated so far, so that $z_{t}$ is a deterministic function (which one – this depends on B) of the answers $G_{\tau}(z_{\tau}, \xi_{\tau}), 1 \le \tau < t$ , returned by O in the first t − 1 calls to the oracle. As a result, $z_{t}$ is a deterministic function of $\xi^{t - 1}$

$$
z_{t} = Z_{t}(\xi^{t - 1}).
$$

## 5.6.2.2 Mirror Descent Algorithm

In the situation of Section 5.6.1 and given a oracle O as described in Section 5.6.2.1, the MD algorithm operating with oracle O is specified by starting point $z_{1} \in{\mathcal{Z}}$ and deterministic sequence of stepsizes $\{\gamma_{t} > 0\}_{t \geq 1}$ and is given by the recurrence

$$
z_{t + 1} = \mathrm{Prox}_{z_{t}}(\gamma_{t} G_{t}(z_{t}, \xi_{t})), t = 1, 2, \ldots\tag{5.6.7}
$$

As required from an algorithm, the search points $z_{t}$ are deterministic functions of $\xi^{t - 1}$

$$
z_{t} = Z_{t}(\xi^{t - 1}).
$$

The main result on MD algorithm is as follows:

Proposition 5.6.1 $Let,$ in addition to $z_{1}$ and $\{\gamma_{t} > 0\}_{t \geq 1}$ , a deterministic sequence of weights $\lambda_{t} \geq 0$ be given. Assume that

1. for some real $M \geq 0$ and $\sigma \geq 0$ one has

$$
\forall(z \in \mathcal{Z}, t \geq 1): \mathbb{E}_{\xi} \left\{\| G_{t}(z, \xi) - g_{t}(z) \|_{*}^{2} \right\} \leq \sigma^{2}\tag{5.6.8}
$$

and

$$
\forall(z \in \mathcal{Z}, t): \| g_{t}(z) \|_{*} \leq M.\tag{5.6.9}
$$

2. the weights $\lambda_{t} \geq 0$ and the stepsizes $\gamma_{t}$ satisfy

$$
\lambda_{1} / \gamma_{1} \leq \lambda_{2} / \gamma_{2} \leq \lambda_{3} / \gamma_{3} \leq \dots\tag{5.6.10}
$$

Then for every $t \geq 1$ one has

$$
\mathbb{E}_{\xi^{t}} \left\{\left[\max_{z \in \mathcal{Z}} \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \lambda_{\tau} \langle g_{\tau}(z_{\tau}), z_{\tau} - z \rangle \right]_{+} \right\} \leq \frac{\lambda_{t} \Omega^{2}}{2 \gamma_{t}} +[M^{2} + \sigma^{2}] \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \lambda_{\tau} \gamma_{\tau} + 2 \sigma \Omega \sqrt{\sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \lambda_{\tau}^{2}},\tag{5.6.11}
$$

(here, as usual, $[a]_{+} = \operatorname{max}[a, 0]$ is the positive part of a real a).

We shall see in Section 5.6.4 that “esoteric” Proposition 5.6.1 straightforwardly yields all known to us eficiency estimates for all considered so far versions of MD for deterministic and stochastic convex minimization and convex-concave saddle point problems and allows to address much wider families of problems “with convex structure” – convex Nash Equilibrium problems, variational inequalities with monotone operators, and convex equilibrium problems.

Proof of Proposition 5.6.1. Let $z \in \mathcal{Z}, z_{\tau} = Z_{\tau}(\xi^{\tau - 1})$ , and let

$$
\Delta_{t}(\xi^{t}) = G_{t}(z_{t}, \xi_{t}) - g_{t}(z_{t}, \xi_{t}).\tag{5.6.12}
$$

so that

$$
\forall \xi^{t - 1}: \mathbb{E}_{\xi_{t}} \left\{\Delta_{t}(\xi^{t}) \right\} = 0 \& \mathbb{E}_{\xi_{t}} \left\{\| \Delta_{t}(\xi^{t}) \|_{*}^{2} \right\} \leq \sigma^{2}.\tag{5.6.13}
$$

## 5.6.3 Mirror Prox algorithm

So far, we are acquainted with Mirror Prox algorithm for deterministic convex-concave saddle point problems (Section 5.5.2). This algorithm, same as Mirror Descent, admits a version, which we are about to describe, applicable to all problems with convex structure to be defined in Section 5.6.4. In the situation of Section 5.6.1 and given an oracle O as described in Section 5.6.2.1, the MP algorithm operating with O is specified by starting point $z_{1} \in{\mathcal{Z}}$ and deterministic sequence of stepsizes $\{\gamma_{t} > 0\}_{t \geq 1}$ and is given by the recurrence<sup>17</sup>

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} v_{1} & := & z_{1} \in \mathcal{Z} \\ w_{\tau} & = & \mathrm{Prox}_{v_{\tau}}(\gamma_{\tau} G_{2 \tau - 1}(v_{\tau}, \xi_{2 \tau - 1})) \\ v_{\tau + 1} & = & \mathrm{Prox}_{v_{\tau}}(\gamma_{\tau} G_{2 \tau}(w_{\tau}, \xi_{2 \tau})) \end{array}\tag{5.6.22}
$$

The main result on the algorithm is as follows:

Proposition 5.6.2 Let, in addition to $z_{1}$ and $\{\gamma_{t} > 0\}_{t \geq 1}$ , a deterministic sequence of weights $\lambda_{t} \geq 0$ be given. Assume that

1. for some nonnegative M, L, $\sigma$ one has

$$
\begin{array}{l} \forall(\tau \geq 1, z, z^{\prime} \in \mathcal{Z}): \| g_{2 \tau}(z) - g_{2 \tau - 1}(z^{\prime}) \|_{*} \leq M + L \| z - z^{\prime} \|, \\ \forall(\tau \geq 1, z \in \mathcal{Z}): \mathbb{E}_{\xi} \left\{\| G_{\tau}(z, \xi) - g_{t}(z) \|_{*}^{2} \right\} \leq \sigma^{2} \end{array}\tag{5.6.23}
$$

2. the stepsizes $\gamma_{t}$ satisfy

$$
\forall \tau \geq 1: 0 < \gamma_{\tau} \leq \frac{1}{2L},\tag{5.6.24}
$$

3. weights $\lambda_{t}$ and stepsizes $\gamma_{t}$ satisfy

$$
\lambda_{1} / \gamma_{1} \leq \lambda_{2} / \gamma_{2} \leq \lambda_{3} / \gamma_{3} \leq \dots\tag{5.6.25}
$$

Then for every $t = 1, 2, \dots$ one has

$$
\mathbb{E}_{\xi^{2t}} \left\{\left[\max_{z \in \mathcal{Z}} \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \lambda_{\tau} \langle g_{2 \tau}(w_{\tau}), w_{\tau} - z \rangle \right]_{+} \right\} \leq \frac{\lambda_{t} \Omega^{2}}{2 \gamma_{t}} +[2 \sigma^{2} + M^{2}] \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau} \lambda_{\tau} + 2 \sigma \Omega \sqrt{\sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \lambda_{\tau}^{2}}\tag{5.6.26}
$$

We conclude that

$$
\begin{array}{rl} &{\left[\max_{\in \mathcal{Z}} \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \lambda_{\tau} \langle g_{2 \tau}, w_{\tau} - z \rangle \right]_{+} \leq \frac{\lambda_{t}}{2 \gamma_{t}} \Omega^{2} + A_{t}(\xi^{2t}) + \underbrace{\left[\max_{\in \mathcal{Z}} \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \lambda_{\tau} \langle \Delta_{2 \tau}, z - v_{1} \rangle \right]_{+}}_{C_{t}(\xi^{2t})} + R_{t},} \\ &{\quad A_{t}(\xi^{2t}) = 2 \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau} \lambda_{\tau} \left[\| \Delta_{2 \tau - 1} \|_{*}^{2} + \| \Delta_{2 \tau} \|_{*}^{2} + M^{2} \right], R_{t} = | \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \langle \Delta_{2 \tau}, v_{1} - w_{\tau} \rangle |,} \end{array}\tag{5.6.30}

Similarly to items $2^{0} – 4^{0}$ of the proof of Proposition 5.6.1,

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \mathbb{E}_{\xi^{2t}} A_{t}(\xi^{2t}) & \leq & 2[2 \sigma^{2} + M^{2}] \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \gamma_{\tau} \lambda_{\tau}[\mathrm{by(5.6.29)}] \\ \mathbb{E}_{\xi^{2t}} \left\{C_{t}(\xi^{2t}) \right\} & \leq & \sigma \Omega \sqrt{\sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \lambda_{\tau}^{2}}[\mathrm{by(5.6.29)andLemma5.6.1]} \\ R_{t} & \leq & \sigma \Omega \sqrt{\sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} \lambda_{\tau}^{2}}[\mathrm{bythesamereasonsasfor(5.6.21)}] \end{array}

which combines with (5.6.30) to imply (5.6.26).

## 5.6.4 Processing problems with convex structure by Mirror Descent and Mirror Prox algorithms

## 5.6.4.1 Problems with convex structure

We are about to list what we call “problems with convex structure” along with associated (in)accuracy measures. To avoid complications, we always assume the domain of the problem Z to be nonempty convex compact subset of Euclidean space E.

5.6.4.1.A. Convex Minimization. This is the most basic problem of minimizing over Z a Lipschitz continuous convex function f. We identify an instance of this problem with function $f : \mathcal{Z} \to \mathbb{R}$ we need to minimize and associate with this instance the following entities:

- the set $\mathcal{Z}_{*}(f) = \mathrm{Argmin}_{\mathcal{Z}} f(z)$ of minimizers of $f$ on $\mathcal{Z}$ ,

- accuracy measure (“residual in terms of the objective”)

$$
\epsilon_{\mathrm{Min}}[z | f] = f(z) - \min_{u \in \mathcal{Z}} f(u)
$$

quantifying the quality of a candidate solution $u \in{\mathcal{Z}}$ 2

- vector field – a bounded vector-valued function $g^{f}(z) : \mathcal{Z} \to E$ such that

$$
g^{f}(z) \in \partial f(z), z \in \mathcal{Z}
$$

is a subgradient of $f$ at $z,$

- stationary oracle O as defined in Section 5.6.2.1 which represents $f,$ meaning that

$$
g_{\mathcal{O}}(z) \equiv g^{f}(z), z \in \mathcal{Z}
$$

(from now on, for a stationary oracle $\mathcal{O}, g_{\mathcal{O}}(z) ={\bf E}_{\xi} \{G(z, \xi)\} : \mathcal{Z} E, G(\cdot, \cdot)$ being the response of O).

5.6.4.1.B. Convex-concave Saddle Point problem. In this case, $\mathcal{Z} = \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}$ is the direct product of two convex compact sets, and the problem is to find a saddle point (min in $x \in \mathcal{X}$ max in $y \in \mathcal{V})$ of a Lipschitz continuous convex-concave function on $\mathcal{Z}$ . We identify an instance with Lipschitz continuous convex-concave function $f(x, y) : \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}$ the saddle point of which is sought, and associate with this instance the following entities:

- the set $\mathcal{Z}_{*}(f)$ of the saddle points of $f$ on $\mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{V}$ (it is nonempty by Sion-Kakutani Theorem (Theorem D.4.2)),

- accuracy measure (“duality gap”)

$$
\epsilon_{\mathrm{SP}}[(x, y) | f] = \overline{{f}}(x) - \underline{{f}}(x), \overline{{f}}(x) = \max_{y \in \mathcal{Y}} f(x, y), \underline{{f}}(y) = \min_{x \in \mathcal{X}} f(x, y)
$$

quantifying the quality of a candidate solution $(x, y) \in{\mathcal{Z}}$ . Noting that saddle points of $f$ are exactly the pairs $(x_{*}, y_{*})$ of optimal solutions to the optimization problems

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \mathrm{Opt}(P) & = & \min_{x \in \mathcal{X}} \overline{{f}}(x)(P) \\ \mathrm{Opt}(D) & = & \max_{y \in \mathcal{Y}} \underline{{f}}(y)(D) \end{array}
$$

with equal optimal values: $\mathrm{Opt}(P) = \mathrm{Opt}(D)$ , the duality gap at a candidate saddle point $(x, y) \in \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}$ is nothing but the sum of residuals in terms of the respective objectives of x as a candidate solution to (P ) and of $y$ as a candidate solution to (D):

$$
\epsilon_{\mathrm{SP}}[(x, y) | f] =[\overline{{f}}(x) - \operatorname{Opt}(P)] +[\operatorname{Opt}(D) - \underline{{f}}(y)].
$$

- vector field – a bounded vector-valued function $g^{f}(x, y) : \mathcal{Z} \to E$ such that

$$
g^{f}(x, y) =[g_{x}^{f}(x, y); g_{y}^{f}(x, y)] \in \partial_{x} f(x, y) \times \partial_{y}[- f(x, y)],(x, y) \in \mathcal{Z},
$$

that ${\mathrm{is}},$ the x-block in $g^{f}$ is a subgradient of convex function $f(\cdot, y)$ taken at $x,$ and the y-block in $g^{f}$ is a subgradient of the convex function $- f(x, \cdot)$ taken at $y.$ ,

- stationary oracle O as defined in Section 5.6.2.1 which represents $f,$ meaning that

$$
g_{\mathcal{O}}(x, y) \equiv g^{f}(x, y),(x, y) \in \mathcal{Z}.
$$

Remark 5.6.1 Convex minimization is reducible to convex-concave saddle point: setting $\mathcal{X} = \mathcal{Z}$ and specifying Y as a singleton, a Lipschitz continuous convex function $f(z)$ on $\mathcal{Z}$ becomes a convex-concave Lipschitz continuous convex-concave function on $\mathcal{Z} = \mathcal{Z} \times \mathcal{V}$ , and all entities associated with f as an instance of Convex Minimization can be straightforwardly converted into the entities associated with f as a Convex-concave Saddle Point problem. In particular, the residual in terms of the objective of a candidate solution $z \in{\mathcal{Z}}$ to the instance f of Convex Minimization is exactly the same as the duality gap of z considered as a candidate solution to the instance f of Convex-concave Saddle Point.

The above problems are well known to us, which is not the case for problems to follow.

5.6.4.1.C. Convex Nash Equilibrium. Consider the situation where K players are making their choices, the choice of j-th player being a point $x_{j}$ in convex compact subset ${\mathcal{Z}}_{j}$ of Euclidean space $E_{j}$ . The block-vector $z =[z_{1};...; z_{K}]$ of player’s choices specifies the losses of the players, the loss of j-th of them being a given function $f_{j}(z)$ . A Nash Equilibrium is a vector $z^{*} =$ $[z_{1}^{*}; z_{2}^{*};...; z_{K}^{*}] \in \mathcal{Z} : = \mathcal{Z}_{1} \times...\times \mathcal{Z}_{K}$ of choices of the players such that no player can reduce her loss by changing her choice, provided that other players stick to their choices, that is,

$$
z_{j}^{*} \in \underset{z_{j} \in \mathcal{Z}_{j}}{\text{Argmin}} f_{j}(z_{1}^{*};...; z_{j - 1}^{*}; z_{j}; z_{j + 1}^{*};...; z_{K}^{*}), j = 1, 2,..., K.
$$

The Nash Equilibrium problem is to find Nash Equilibrium, given the domain $\mathcal{Z}$ of the problem (along with its representation $\mathcal{Z} = \mathcal{Z}_{1} \times...\times \mathcal{Z}_{K}$ as a direct product of nonempty convex compact sets $\mathcal{Z}_{j})$ and the loss functions $f_{j}(z) : \mathcal{Z} \mathbb{R}$ of the players. From now on we denote j-th block in block-vector $z \in E_{1} \times...\times E_{K}$ by $[z]_{j}$ , so that $[z]_{j} \in E_{j}$ and $z =[[z]_{1};...;[z]_{K}]$ , and denote by $[z]^{j}$ the vector obtained from z by eliminating j-th block (e.g., with $z =[z_{1}; z_{2}; z_{3}],[z]_{2} = z_{2}$ $[z]^{2} =[z_{1}; z_{3}])$ , and refer to j-th loss function both as to $f_{j}(z)$ and as to $f_{j}([z]_{j},[z]^{j})$

From now on, speaking about Nash Equilibrium, we always assume that for all $j$ the functions $f_{j}(z)$ are Lipschitz continuous in $z \in{\mathcal{Z}}$

Nash Equilibrium problem is called convex, if

- for every $j,$ the function $f_{j}([z]_{j},[z]^{j})$ is convex in $[z]_{j} \in{\mathcal{Z}}_{j}$ and concave in $[z]^{j} \in \mathcal{Z}^{j} =$ $\mathcal{Z}_{1} \times \ldots \times \mathcal{Z}_{j - 1} \times \mathcal{Z}_{j + 1} \times \ldots \times \mathcal{Z}_{K}$ , and

- the sum $\textstyle \sum_{j = 1}^{K} f_{j}(z)$ of losses is convex on $\mathcal{Z}$

We shall see in Section 5.6.4.2 that the set of precise solutions to a convex Nash Equilibrium problem, that is, the set of all corresponding Nash equilibria, is nonempty, convex, and closed.

When speaking about K-player Convex Nash Equilibrium, we assume that the convex compact domain $\mathcal{Z}$ of the problem is given as the direct product of $K$ convex compact sets ${\mathcal{Z}}_{j},$ and identify an instance of the problem with the collection $\boldsymbol{f} = \left(f_{1},..., f_{K} \right)$ of players’ loss functions, with $f$ satisfying the above Lipschitz continuity and convexity-concavity assumptions. We associate with such an instance the following entities:

- the set $\mathcal{Z}_{\ast}(f)$ of the corresponding Nash equilibria:

$$
\mathcal{Z}_{*}(f) = \{z^{*} \in \mathcal{Z}:[z^{*}]_{j} \in \underset{z_{j} \in \mathcal{Z}_{j}}{\text{Argmin}} f_{j}(z_{j},[z^{*}]^{j}), j = 1,..., K,
$$

- accuracy measure (“incentive”)

$$
\epsilon_{\mathrm{Nash}}[z | f] = \sum_{j = 1}^{K} \left[f_{j}([z]_{j},[z]^{j}) - \min_{z_{j}^{\prime} \in \mathcal{Z}_{j}} f_{j}(z_{j}^{\prime},[z]^{j}) \right]
$$

The incentive clearly is well-defined and nonnegative on $\mathcal{Z}$ and is zero at a point $z \in{\mathcal{Z}}$ if and only $\operatorname{if} z$ is Nash equilibrium: $z \in \mathcal{Z}_{*}(f)$ . The origin of the name is clear: $\epsilon_{\mathrm{Nash}}[z | f]$ is the total, over players, incentive for player $j$ to deviate from her choice $[z]_{j}$ , provided that all other players $j^{\prime}$ stick to their choices $[z]_{j^{\prime}};$

- vector field $\mathrm{~ \ - ~ a ~}$ bounded vector-valued function $g^{f}(z) =[g_{1}^{f}(z);...; g_{K}^{f}(z)] : \mathcal{Z} E =$ $E_{1} \times \ldots \times E_{K}$ such that

$$
g_{j}^{f}(z) \in \partial_{[z]_{j}} f_{j}([z]_{j},[z]^{j}), j = 1, \dots, K,
$$

that is, j-th block $g_{j}^{f}(z)$ in $g^{f}(z)$ is a subgradient of convex function $f_{j}(\cdot,[z]^{j})$ taken at $[z]_{j}$

- stationary oracle O as defined in Section 5.6.2.1 which represents $f,$ meaning that

$$
g_{\mathcal{O}}(z) \equiv g^{f}(z), z \in \mathcal{Z}.
$$

Remark 5.6.2 Note that the convex-concave saddle point problem is nothing but the “zero sum” two-player convex Nash Equilibrium problem. Indeed, given convex-concave Lipschitz continuous function $h ( z _ { 1 } , z _ { 2 } ) : \mathcal { Z } : = \mathcal { Z } _ { 1 } \times \mathcal { Z } _ { 2 } $ R and setting $f_{1}(z_{1}, z_{2}) = h(z_{1}, z_{2}), f_{2}(z_{1}, z_{2}) = - h(z_{1}, z_{2})$ we, as is immediately seen, get an instance $f =(f_{1}, f_{2})$ of convex Nash Equilibrium problem; the entities associated with h as an instance of Convex-concave Saddle Point problem can be straightforwardly converted into the entities associated with $f$ as an instance of convex Nash Equilibrium, in particular, the vector field remains the same, and $\epsilon_{\scriptscriptstyle \mathrm{SP}}[[z_{1}; z_{2}] | h] = \epsilon_{\scriptscriptstyle \mathrm{Nash}}[[z_{1}; z_{2}] | f]$ Note that the 2-player convex Nash Equilibrium problems f which can be obtained from Convexconcave Saddle Point ones are exactly those for which $f_{1} + f_{2} \equiv 0$

5.6.4.1.D. Monotone Variational Inequality. A vector field $f(z) :{\mathcal{Z}} \to E$ is called monotone, if

$$
\langle f(z) - f \left(z^{\prime}\right), z - z^{\prime} \rangle \geq 0 \forall z, z^{\prime} \in \mathcal{Z}.
$$

Variational Inequality $\operatorname{VI}(f,{\mathcal{Z}})$ associated with $\mathcal{Z}$ and monotone vector field $f \ \mathrm{is}^{18}$

$$
\text{find} z_{*} \in \mathcal{Z}: \langle f(z), z - z_{*} \rangle \geq 0 \forall z \in \mathcal{Z}\tag{\(\operatorname{VI}(f,\mathcal{Z})\}
$$

As we shall see in a while, the vector fields we have associated with already described problems with convex structure (Convex Minimization, Convex-Concave Saddle point, Convex Nash Equilibrium) are monotone, and precise solutions to these problems are exactly the same as the solutions to VI’s associated with these vector fields. This being said, VI’s with monotone operators arise in situations different from those just listed, and therefore deserve the status of a problem with convex structure on their own. An instance of a Monotone VI problem on a (as always, nonempty convex compact) domain Z is a bounded and monotone vector field $f :{\mathcal{Z}} \to E$ , and we associate with such an instance the following entities:

- the set $\mathcal{Z}_{*}(f)$ of the solutions to $\operatorname{VI}(f,{\mathcal{Z}})$

$$
\mathcal{Z}_{*}(f) = \left\{z_{*} \in \mathcal{Z}: \langle f(z), z - z_{*} \rangle \geq 0 \forall z \in \mathcal{Z} \right\};
$$

we will see in a while that $\mathcal{Z}_{\ast}(f)$ is nonempty, convex, and closed;

- accuracy measure (“dual gap function”)

$$
\epsilon_{\mathrm{VI}}[z | f] = \sup_{y \in \mathcal{Z}} \langle f(y), z - y \rangle
$$

This accuracy measure clearly is well-defined and nonnegative on ${\mathcal{Z}},$ and is zero at $z{\mathrm{~ if ~}}$ and only $\mathrm{if} ~ z \in{\mathcal{Z}}_{*}(f)$ ;

- vector field associated with $f$ is $f$ itself;

- stationary oracle O as defined in Section 5.6.2.1 which represents $f,$ meaning that

$$
g_{\mathcal{O}}(z) \equiv f(z), z \in \mathcal{Z}.
$$

5.6.4.1.E. Convex Equilibrium. <sup>19</sup> $\mathrm{An}$ instance of Convex Equilibrium on (nonempty convex compact) domain $\mathcal{Z}$ in Euclidean space $E$ is a function

$$
f(y, z): \mathcal{Z} \times \mathcal{Z} \to \mathbb{R}
$$

with the following properties:

$f(y, z)$ is bounded on $\mathcal{Z} \times \mathcal{Z}$ , uniformly Lipschitz continuous in $y \in{\mathcal{Z}} \colon$

$$
| f(y, z) - f \left(y^{\prime}, z\right) | \leq L_{f} \| y - y^{\prime} \| \forall y, y^{\prime}, z \in \mathcal{Z}
$$

and is convex in $y \in{\mathcal{Z}}$ ;

- one has

$$
f(y, y) + f(z, z) \geq f(y, z) + f(z, y) \forall y, z \in \mathcal{Z}.\tag{5.6.31}
$$

The problem associated with instance $f$ is to find $z_{*}$ such that

$$
z_{*} \in \mathcal{Z} \& f(z, z) - f(z_{*}, z) \geq 0 \forall z \in \mathcal{Z}.\tag{5.6.32}
$$

Example: Let g be a bounded monotone vector field on Z. Setting

$$
f(y, z) = \langle y, g(z) \rangle : \mathcal{Z} \times \mathcal{Z} \to \mathbb{R},
$$

$\mathrm{we,}$ as is immediately seen, get an instance of Convex Equilibrium problem; in particular, for our $f$ one has $f(y, y) + f(z, z) - f(y, z) - f(z, y) = \langle g(y) - g(z), y - z \rangle$ so that the validity of (5.6.31) is exactly the same as the monotonicity of $g.$ Further, for our $f$ relation (5.6.32) reads

$$
z_{*} \in \mathcal{Z} \& \langle z - z_{*}, g(z) \rangle \geq 0 \forall z \in \mathcal{Z},
$$

so that the solutions to our Convex Equilibrium instance are exactly the solutions to $\operatorname{VI}(g,{\mathcal{Z}})$

We associate with an instance f of Convex Equilibrium problem the following entities:

- the set $\mathcal{Z}_{\ast}(f)$ of the precise solutions

$$
\mathcal{Z}_{*}(f) = \{z_{*} \in \mathcal{Z}: f(z, z) - f(z_{*}, z) \geq 0 \forall z \in \mathcal{Z}\};
$$

we will see in a while that $\mathcal{Z}_{*}(f)$ is nonempty, convex, and closed;

- accuracy measure (“equilibrium $\mathrm{gap}^{\dag} \bigr)$

$$
\epsilon_{\text{Equil}}[z | f] = \sup_{y \in \mathcal{Z}}[f(z, y) - f(y, y)]
$$

This accuracy measure clearly is well-defined and nonnegative on $\mathcal{Z},$ , and is zero at $z{\mathrm{~ if ~}}$ and only $\mathrm{if} ~ z \in{\mathcal{Z}}_{*}(f)$ ;

In Example, $\epsilon_{\mathrm{Equil}}[z | f] = \operatorname{sup}_{y \in \mathcal{Z}} \left[\langle z, g(y) \rangle - \langle y, g(y) \rangle \right] = \epsilon_{\mathrm{VI}}[z | g].$

- vector field $g^{f} :{\mathcal{A}} \mathbb{E}$ associated with f is a bounded vector field satisfying the relation

$$
g^{f}(z) \in \partial_{y} |_{y = z} f(y, z),
$$

that is, $g^{f}(z)$ is a subgradient of the convex function $f(y, z)$ of $y \in{\mathcal{Z}}$ taken at $y = z;$

In Example, we can take $g^{f}(\cdot) \equiv g(\cdot)$

- stationary oracle $\mathcal{O}$ as defined in Section 5.6.2.1 which represents $f,$ meaning that

$$
g_{\mathcal{O}}(z) \equiv g^{f}(z), z \in \mathcal{Z}.
$$

Remark 5.6.3 The above Example shows that Monotone Variational Inequality is reducible to Convex Equilibrium.

Remark 5.6.4 The name “Convex Equilibrium” stems from the following observation: Consider an instance $f(z, y) : \mathcal{Z} \times \mathcal{Z} \to \mathbb{R}$ of Convex Equilibrium problem. Then

(i) $Hx_{*} \in{\mathcal{Z}}$ is such that $f(x, x_{*}) \geq f(x_{*}, x_{*})$ for all $x \in{\mathcal{Z}}$ , then $x_{*} \in \mathcal{Z}_{*}(f)$

$$

Now let $x_{*} \in \mathcal{Z}_{*}(f)$ and let f be continuous on ${\mathcal{Z}} \times{\mathcal{Z}}$ Assume, to the contrary of what is claimed in (ii), that $f(\bar{x}, x_{*}) \ < \f(x_{*}, x_{*})$ for some $\bar{x} \in \mathcal{Z};$ ; in particular, $\bar{x} \neq x_{*}$ Now let $z_{\lambda} =(1 - \lambda) x_{*} + \lambda \bar{x}, 0 \leq \lambda \leq 1$ ; note that $z_{\lambda} \in{\mathcal{Z}}$ .
