## 5.6.4.2 Problems with convex structure: basic descriptive results

Basic descriptive results on problems with convex structure as defined above are stated in the following

Theorem 5.6.1 Let us fix a nonempty convex compact domain $\mathcal{Z}$ in Euclidean space $E - the$ domain of all problems with convex structure to follow. Then

(i) Let f be an instance of Convex Equilibrium problem. The solution set $\mathcal{Z}_{\ast}(f)$ of f is nonempty, convex and closed.

(ii) Let g be a bounded monotone vector field on $\mathcal{Z}.$ . The solution set $\mathcal{Z}_{*}(g)$ of $\operatorname{VI}(g,{\mathcal{Z}})$ is nonempty, convex and closed.

(iii) The vector fields $g^{f}$ associated with instances of problems with convex structure on $\mathcal{Z}$ as defined in $5.6.4.1.A - E$ are monotone, and the sets $\mathcal{Z}_{*}(f)$ of precise solutions of the instances are exactly the sets of solutions to $\mathrm{VI}(g^{f},{\mathcal{Z}})$ (and therefore are nonempty, convex and closed by (i)).

(iv) For any candidate solution $z \in{\mathcal{Z}}$ to a Convex Minimization or Convex-concave Saddle Point problem $f,$ inaccuracy of the solution as quantified by the associated accuracy measure (residual in terms of the objective or duality $gap \rangle is \geq$ the inaccuracy, as quantified by dual gap function, of z as a candidate solution to $\operatorname{VI}(g^{f},{\mathcal{Z}})$

For any candidate solution $z \in{\mathcal{Z}}$ to Convex Equilibrium problem f inaccuracy of z as quantified by the Equilibrium gap $is \geq the$ inaccuracy of z, as quantified by the dual gap function, as candidate solution to $\operatorname{VI}(g^{f},{\mathcal{Z}})$

Proof. (i): Consider the function

$$
\underline{{f}}(x) = \inf_{y \in \mathcal{Z}}[f(y, y) - f(x, y)] = - \epsilon_{\text{Equil}}[x | f];
$$

since $f(x, y)$ is bounded and uniformly Lipschitz continuous and is convex in $x \in \mathcal{Z}, \f$ is well defined, concave and continuous on $\mathcal{Z};$ note that $\mathcal{Z}_{\ast}(f) = \{x \in \mathcal{Z} : f(x) \geq 0\}$ , whence $\mathcal{Z}_{\ast}(f)$ is closed and convex. All which remains to prove is that this set is nonempty, that is, that the maximum over $x \in{\mathcal{Z}}$ of the continuous function $f(x){\mathrm{~ is ~}} \geq 0$ . Assuming this is not the case, fo every $x \in{\mathcal{Z}}$ there exists $y_{x} \in \mathcal{Z}$ such that the continuous function $f(y_{x}, y_{x}) - f(u, y_{x})$ of $u \in{\mathcal{Z}}$ is negative at $u = x$ , and therefore is negative in certain neighbourhood $U_{x}$ of x in $\mathcal{Z}.$ . Invoking compactness of $\mathcal{Z},$ we conclude that the resulting covering of $\mathcal{Z}$ admits finite subcovering, that is, there exists $\delta > 0$ and $y_{1},..., y_{N} \in \mathcal{Z}$ such that

$$
\min_{i}[f(y_{i}, y_{i}) - f(x, y_{i})] \leq - \delta \forall x \in \mathcal{Z}.
$$

Consider the function

$$
F(\lambda, x) = \sum_{i} \lambda_{i}[f(y_{i}, y_{i}) - f(x, y_{i})]
$$

and let λ reside in the probabilistic simplex $\Delta, \F$ is convex-concave continuous function on $\Delta \times \mathcal{Z}$ and therefore has a saddle point $\lambda^{*}, x_{*}$ on this set, so that

$$
F \left(\lambda^{*}, x\right) \leq F \left(\lambda^{*}, x_{*}\right) \leq F \left(\lambda, x_{*}\right) \forall \lambda \in \Delta, x \in \mathcal{Z}.
$$

In particular, $F(\lambda^{*}, x_{*}) = \operatorname{min}_{\lambda \in \Delta} \sum_{i} \lambda_{i}[f(y_{i}, y_{i}) - f(x_{*}, y_{i})] = \operatorname{min}_{i}[f(y_{i}, y_{i}) - f(x_{*}, y_{i})] \leq - \delta$ . Thus,

$$
\sum_{i} \lambda_{i}^{*}[f(y_{i}, y_{i}) - f(x, y_{i})] = F(\lambda_{*}, x) \leq F(\lambda^{*}, x_{*}) \leq - \delta \forall x \in \mathcal{Z}.
$$

Now, by (5.6.32) we have $f(y_{i}, y_{i}) - f(x, y_{i}) \geq f(y_{i}, x) - f(x, x)$ for all $x \in{\mathcal{Z}}$ , whence

$$
\sup_{x \in \mathcal{Z}} \sum_{i} \lambda_{i}^{*}[f(y_{i}, x) - f(x, x)] \leq \sup_{x \in \mathcal{Z}} \sum_{i} \lambda_{i}^{*}[f(y_{i}, y_{i}) - f(x, y_{i})] \leq - \delta.
$$

Setting $\bar{y} = \textstyle \sum_{i} \lambda_{i}^{*} y_{i}$ , by convexity of $f(u, v)$ in u we have $\begin{array}{r}{\sum_{i} \lambda_{i}^{*}[f(y_{i}, x) - f(x, x)] \ge f(\bar{y}, x) -} \end{array}$ $f(x, x)$ , and we get

$$
\sup_{x \in \mathcal{Z}}[f(\bar{y}, x) - f(x, x)] \leq \sup_{x \in \mathcal{Z}} \sum_{i} \lambda_{i}^{*}[f(y_{i}, x) - f(x, x)] \leq - \delta,
$$

which is impossible, since the function which we maximize in x in the left hand side is zero when $x = \bar{y}$ ✷

(ii): By Remark 5.6.3, for a bounded monotone $g(\cdot) : \mathcal{Z} \to E$ , the solution set of $\operatorname{VI}(g,{\mathcal{Z}})$ is exactly the same as the solution set of the Convex Equilibrium problem given by $f(y, z) =$ $\langle y, g(z) \rangle$ , so that the set in question is nonempty, convex and closed by (i). ✷

(iii) As far as the claims in (iii) are concerned, Remarks 5.6.1, 5.6.2 say that it sufices to consider the cases of

(iii.a): Convex Nash Equilibrium problem, and

(iii.b): Convex Equilibrium problem.

(iii.a:) Let $\boldsymbol{f} = \left(f_{1},..., f_{K} \right)$ be an instance of Convex Nash Equilibrium problem. Let us start with verifying the monotonicity of $g^{f}$ . Let $x, y \in{\mathcal{Z}}$ , and let $\begin{array}{r}{\bar{x} = \frac{1}{2}[x + y], \Delta = \frac{1}{2}[x - y]} \end{array}$ . To verify that $\langle g^{f}(x) - g^{f}(y), x - y \rangle \geq 0$ is exactly the same as to verify that $\langle g^{f}(\bar{x} + \Delta) - \bar{g}^{f}(\bar{x} - \Delta), \Delta \rangle \geq 0.$ Setting $\begin{array}{r}{F(z) = \sum_{j} f_{j}(z)} \end{array}$ , we have

$$
\langle g^{f}(\bar{x} + \Delta) - g^{f}(\bar{x} - \Delta), \Delta \rangle = \sum_{j}[\underbrace{\langle g_{j}^{f}(\bar{x} + \Delta), \Delta_{j} \rangle} + \underbrace{\langle g_{j}^{f}(\bar{x} - \Delta), - \Delta_{j} \rangle}]
$$

$$
\begin{array}{c} \underset{(a)}{\geq} f_{j}(\bar{x} + \Delta) - f_{j}([\bar{x}]_{j},[\bar{x}]^{j} +[\Delta]^{j}) \quad \underset{(a)}{\geq} f_{j}(\bar{x} - \Delta) - f_{j}([\bar{x}]_{j},[\bar{x}]^{j} -[\Delta]^{j}) \\ \geq \sum_{j}[f_{j}(\bar{x} + \Delta) + f_{j}(\bar{x} - \Delta) -[\underbrace{f_{j}([\bar{x}]_{j},[\bar{x}]^{j} +[\Delta]^{j}) + f_{j}([\bar{x}]_{j},[\bar{x}]^{j} -[\Delta]^{j})}]] \end{array}
$$

$$
\stackrel{\le}{(b)} 2f_{j}(\bar{x})
$$

$$
\geq F(\bar{x} + \Delta) + F(\bar{x} - \Delta) - 2F(\bar{x}) \geq 0,
$$

where $(a)$ is due to convexity of $f_{j}([x]_{j},[x]^{j})$ in $[x]_{j}$ and since $g_{j}^{f}(x) \in \partial_{[x]_{j}} f_{j}([x]_{j},[x]^{j})$ , (b) is due to concavity of $f_{j}([x]_{j},[x]^{j})$ in $[x]^{j}$ , and the concluding $\geq$ is due to convexity of $F.$ . Thus, $g^{f}$ indeed is monotone.

Now let us verify that the solutions of $\operatorname{VI}(g^{f},{\mathcal{Z}})$ are exactly the Nash equilibria. In one direction: let $z_{*}$ be a solution to $\operatorname{VI}(g^{f},{\mathcal{Z}})$ , and let us prove that this is a Nash equilibria. For every $j$ and every $z_{j} \in{\mathcal{Z}}_{j}$ , specifying $z \in{\mathcal{Z}}$ by the relations $[z]_{j} = z_{j},[z]^{j} =[z_{*}]^{j}$

$$
\langle g_{j}^{f}(z_{j},[z_{*}]^{j}), z_{j} -[z_{*}]_{j}) \rangle = \langle g^{f}(z), z - z_{*} \rangle \geq 0,
$$

where the concluding $\geq ~ 0$ is due to the fact that $z_{*}$ solves $\mathrm{VI}(g^{f},{\mathcal{Z}})$ Thus, the Lipschitz continuous convex function $\phi(z_{j}) = f_{j}(z_{j},[z_{*}]^{j})$ of $z_{j} \in{\mathcal{Z}}_{j}$ at every point $z_{j} \in{\mathcal{Z}}_{j}$ admits a subgradient $\phi^{\prime}(z_{j}) = g_{j}^{f}(z_{j},[z_{*}]^{j})$ such that $\langle \phi^{\prime}(z_{j}), z_{j} -[z_{*}]_{j} \rangle \geq 0$ , whence, of course, $[z_{*}]_{j}$ is a minimizer of $\phi$ over $z_{j} \in{\mathcal{Z}}_{j}$ <sup>20</sup> Thus, $[z_{*}]_{j}$ minimizes $f_{j}(\cdot,[z_{*}]^{j})$ over $\mathcal{Z}_{j};$ since $j \le K$ is arbitrary, we conclude that $z_{*}$ is a Nash equilibrium. Vice versa, let $z_{*}$ be a Nash equilibrium; let us prove that then $\langle g^{f}(z), z - z_{*} \rangle \geq 0$ for $\mathrm{every} z \in{\mathcal{Z}}$ . W.l. $\cdot 0.g.$ . it sufices to consider the case of $z \neq z_{*}$ . Note that the monotonicity of $g^{f}$ was proved independently of how the subgradients comprising the value of the field at a point are selected in the corresponding subdiferentials. Since $z_{*}$ is a Nash equilibrium, zeros are legitimate subgradients of the functions $f_{j}(\cdot,[z_{*}]^{j})$ at the points $[z_{*}]_{j}$ , so that replacing the value of $g^{f}$ at $z_{*}$ with zero and keeping the vector field intact at all other points, in particular, at z, we preserve the monotonicity of the field, meaning, in particular, that $\langle g^{f}(z), z - z_{*} \rangle \geq 0$ . (iii.a) is proved.

(iii.b): Let $f(y, z)$ be an instance of Convex Equilibrium problem. Let us first verify that the vector field $g^{f}(z)$ is monotone. Indeed, given $y, z \in{\mathcal{Z}}$ , by convexity of $f(u, v)$ in u and by definition of $g^{f}$ we have

$$
f(z, y) \geq f(y, y) + \langle g^{f}(y), z - y \rangle, f(y, z) \geq f(z, z) + \langle g^{f}(z), y - z \rangle
$$

whence $f(y, y) + f(z, z) - \langle g^{f}(z) - g^{f}(y), z - y \rangle \leq f(z, y) + f(y, z) \leq f(z, y) + f(y, z)$ , implying that $\langle g^{f}(z) - g^{f}(y), z - y \rangle \geq 0$ . as required. Now let us prove that the solutions to the Equilibrium problem are exactly the solutions to $\operatorname{VI}(g^{f},{\mathcal{Z}})$ . By convexity of $f(u, v)$ in u and the origin of $g^{f}$ we have $\langle g^{f}(y), y - z \rangle \geq f(y, y) - f(z, y);$ ; thus, if the latter quantity for some $z = z_{*}$ is nonnegative for all $y \in{\mathcal{Z}}$ , that is, $\operatorname{if} z_{*}$ solves the Equilibrium problem, the quantity $\langle g^{f}(y), y - z_{*} \rangle$ is nonnegative for all $y.$ , that is, $z_{*}$ solves $\operatorname{VI}(g^{f},{\mathcal{Z}})$ . Vice versa, let $z_{*}$ solve $\operatorname{VI}(g^{f},{\mathcal{Z}})$ ; assume, on the contrary to what should be proved, that $z_{*}$ does not solve the Equilibrium problem, so that $f(z_{*}, y) > f(y, y)$ for some $y \in{\mathcal{Z}}$ . Given $\lambda \in(0, 1)$ , let us set $z_{\lambda} = z_{*} + \lambda(y - z_{*})$ . Since $f$ is continuous in the first argument and $f(z_{*}, y) = f(z_{0}, y) > f(y, y)$ , we have $f(z_{\lambda}, y) > f(y, y)$ for some fixed $\lambda \in(0, 1)$ , whence $f(y, z_{\lambda}) < f(z_{\lambda}, z_{\lambda})$ ) due to $f(y, y) + f(z_{\lambda}, z_{\lambda}) \geq f(y, z_{\lambda}) + f(z_{\lambda}, y)$ Since $f(\cdot, z_{\lambda})$ is convex and $f(y, z_{\lambda}) < f(z_{\lambda}, z_{\lambda})$ , we have $\langle g^{f}(z_{\lambda}), y - z_{\lambda} \rangle < 0$ , and since $y - z_{\lambda}$ is a positive multiple of $z_{\lambda} - z_{*}$ , we get $\langle g^{f}(z_{\lambda}), z_{\lambda} - z_{*} \rangle < 0$ , which is the desired contradiction with $z_{*}$ being a solution to $\operatorname{VI}(g^{f},{\mathcal{Z}})$ . The proof of (iii) is complete. ✷

$$
\phi(z_{j}) \geq \phi(\underbrace{[z_{*}]_{j} + \lambda(z_{j} -[z_{*}]_{j})}_{z^{\lambda}}) + \langle \phi^{\prime}(z^{\lambda}), z_{j} - z^{\lambda} \rangle \geq \phi(z^{\lambda}),
$$

with the concluding inequality given by the fact that $\langle \phi^{\prime}(z^{\lambda}), z_{j} - z^{\lambda} \rangle$ is nonnegative multiple of $\langle{\phi}^{\prime}(z^{\lambda}), z^{\lambda} -$ $[z_{*}]_{j} \rangle \ge 0$ , and it remains to look what happens as $\lambda + 0$

(iv): In view of Remark 5.6.1), it sufices to show that the inaccuracy, as quantified by duality gap, of a candidate solution $\boldsymbol{z} =(x, y) \in \mathcal{Z} = \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}$ to a convex-concave saddle point problem f dominates the inaccuracy, as quantified by dual gap function, of z as a candidate solution to $\operatorname{VI}(g^{f},{\mathcal{Z}})$ . Indeed, the vector field associated with $f$ is $[g_{x}^{f}(x, y); g_{y}^{f}(x, y)] \ \in \ \partial_{x} f(x, y) \ \times$ $\partial_{y}[- f(x, y)]$ ], whence

$$
\begin{array}{l} \epsilon_{\mathrm{VI}}[z | f] = \sup_{(u, v) \in \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}} \left[\langle g_{x}^{f}(u, v), x - u \rangle + \langle g_{y}^{f}(u, v), y - v \rangle \right] \\ \leq \sup_{(u, v) \in \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}}[f(x, v) - f(u, v) + f(u, v) - f(u, y)] = \overline{{f}}(x) - \underline{{f}}(y) = \epsilon_{\mathrm{SP}}[z | f] \end{array}
$$

Finally, given a candidate solution z to an instant f of Convex Equilibrium problem and recalling what $g^{f}$ is, we have

$$
\epsilon_{\text{Equil}}[z | f] = \sup_{y \in \mathcal{Z}}[f(z, y) - f(y, y)] \geq \sup_{y \in \mathcal{Z}} \langle g^{f}(y), z - y \rangle = \epsilon_{\text{VI}}[z | g^{f}].
$$

## 5.6.4.3 Problems with convex structure: basic operational results

As stated by Theorem 5.6.1, solving an oracle-represented instance of problem with convex structure can be reduced, modulo quantification of inaccuracy, to solving either Monotone Variational Inequality, or Convex Equilibrium. It turns out that this “unification” captures well the basic proximal type First Order algorithms of (broadly understood) deterministic and stochastic Convex Optimization and the algorithms’ eficiency estimates. From two outlined “unifying options” – Monotone VI and Convex Equilibrium – we select the second, the reason being that while the constructions and eficiency estimates for VI and Equilibrium look completely similar, Equilibrium operates with “more tuf” accuracy measure (Theorem $5.6.1.(\mathrm{iv}))$ and thus provides stronger eficiency estimates.

The main (and in hindsight extremely simple) observation underlying unified constructions and results on First Order algorithms is given by item (i) of the following Theorem:

Theorem 5.6.2 Consider an instance f of Convex Equilibrium problem on (nonempty convex compact) domain Z in Euclidean space $E,$ let O be a stationary oracle representing the instance, the response of the oracle being $G(z, \xi)$ , so that

$$
\mathbb{E}_{\xi} \left\{G(z, \xi) \right\} = g^{f}(z), z \in \mathcal{Z},
$$

where $g^{f}(\cdot)$ is the vector field associated with instance $f.$

Let, next, B be an algorithm operating with O, as described in Section 5.6.2.1, and let $\{z_{t} = Z_{t}(\xi^{t - 1})\}_{t \geq 1}$ be the search trajectory generated by B, so that $z_{t}$ is the query point of t-th call to O. Finally, let positive integer N be given.

(i) Given deterministic collection $\mu = \{\mu_{t} \geq 0, 1 \leq t \leq N\}$ of weights with $\begin{array}{r}{\mathcal{M}_{N} : = \sum_{t = 1}^{N} \mu_{t} >} \end{array}$ 0, let us set

$$
\operatorname{Res}_{N}(\mu, \xi^{N}) = \mathcal{M}_{N}^{- 1} \left[\max_{z \in \mathcal{Z}} \sum_{t = 1}^{N} \mu_{t} \langle g^{f}(z_{t}), z_{t} - z \rangle \right]_{+},\tag{5.6.33}
$$

and specify the approximate solution generated by the algorithm in N calls to O as

$$
z^{N} = z^{N}(\xi^{N}) := \mathcal{M}_{N}^{- 1} \sum_{t = 1}^{N} \mu_{t} z_{t}.\tag{5.6.34}
$$

Then

$$
\forall \xi^{N}: z^{N}(\xi^{N}) \in \mathcal{Z} \& \epsilon_{\text{Equil}}[z^{N}(\xi^{N}) | f] \leq \operatorname{Res}_{N}(\mu, \xi^{N}).\tag{5.6.35}
$$

If, in addition, the Convex Equilibrium instance f in question represents equivalently a K-player Convex Nash Equilibrium problem with loss functions $h_{j}(z), j \ \leq \K$ (see Example in Section $5.6.4.1.E)$ , meaning that $\mathcal{Z} = \mathcal{Z}_{1} \times...\times \mathcal{Z}_{K}$ and

$$
f(y, z) = \langle y, g^{f}(z) \rangle : \mathcal{Z} \times \mathcal{Z} \to \mathbb{R}
$$

where the bounded vector field $g^{f}$ satisfies

$$
g^{f}(z) =[g_{1}^{f}(z); \dots; g_{K}^{f}(z)], g_{j}^{f}(z) \in \partial_{[z]_{j}} h_{j}([z]_{j},[z]^{j}), j \leq K
$$

then, along with (5.6.35), it holds also

$$
\forall \xi^{N}: \epsilon_{\mathrm{Nash}}[z^{N}(\xi^{N}) | h] \leq \operatorname{Res}_{N}(\mu, \xi^{N}).\tag{5.6.36}
$$

(ii) Let B be Mirror Descent algorithm from Section 5.6.2.2 operating with the stationary oracle O in question:

$$
z_{t + 1} = \mathrm{Prox}_{z_{t}}(\gamma_{t} G(z_{t}, \xi_{t})), t = 1, 2, \ldots
$$

where $z_{1} \in{\mathcal{Z}}$ and the sequence of stepsizes $\{\gamma_{t} > 0\}_{t \geq 1}$ are deterministic. Assuming that for some real $M \geq 0$ and $\sigma \geq 0$ and for all $z \in{\mathcal{Z}}$ one has

$$
\left\| g^{f}(z) \right\|_{*} \leq M \& \mathbb{E}_{\xi} \left\{\left\| G(z, \xi) - g^{f}(z) \right\|_{*}^{2} \right\} \leq \sigma^{2},\tag{5.6.37}
$$

and that deterministic weights $\mu = \{\mu_{t} \geq 0, t \leq N\}$ with $\begin{array}{r}{\mathcal{M}_{N} = \sum_{t = 1}^{N} \mu_{t} > 0} \end{array}$ are such that

$$
\mu_{1} / \gamma_{1} \leq \mu_{2} / \gamma_{2} \leq \ldots \leq \mu_{N} / \gamma_{N},
$$

one has

$$
\mathbb{E}_{\xi^{N}} \left\{\operatorname{Res}_{N}(\mu, \xi^{N}) \right\} \leq \mathcal{MD}_{N}[\gamma, \mu] := \mathcal{M}^{- 1} \left[\frac{\mu_{N} \Omega^{2}}{2 \gamma_{N}} +[M^{2} + \sigma^{2}] \sum_{t = 1}^{N} \mu_{t} \gamma_{t} + 2 \sigma \Omega \sqrt{\sum_{t = 1}^{N} \mu_{t}^{2}} \right].\tag{5.6.38}
$$

implying, by (i), that for the approximate solution

$$
z^{N} = z^{N}(\xi^{N}) = \mathcal{M}_{N}^{- 1} \sum_{t = 1}^{N} \mu_{t} z_{t}
$$

one has

$$
z^{N} \in \mathcal{Z} \& \mathbb{E}_{\xi^{N}} \left\{\epsilon_{\text{Equil}}[z^{N}(\xi^{N}) | f] \right\} \leq \mathcal{MD}_{N}[\gamma, \mu].\tag{5.6.39}
$$

(iii) Let N be even: $N = 2S$ , and let B be Mirror Prox algorithm from Section 5.6.3 operating with the stationary oracle O in question:

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} v_{1} & := & z_{1} \in \mathcal{Z} \\ w_{\tau} & = & z_{2 \tau} := \mathrm{Prox}_{v_{\tau}}(\gamma_{\tau} G(v_{\tau}, \xi_{2 \tau - 1})), 1 \leq \tau \leq S, \\ v_{\tau + 1} & = & z_{2 \tau + 1} = \mathrm{Prox}_{v_{\tau}}(\gamma_{\tau} G(w_{\tau}, \xi_{2 \tau})) \end{array}
$$

where $z_{1} \in{\mathcal{Z}}$ and the sequence of stepsizes $\{\gamma_{t} > 0\}_{t \geq 1}$ are deterministic. Assume that for some nonnegative M, L, σ one has

$$
\begin{array}{l} \forall(z, z^{\prime} \in \mathcal{Z}): \| g^{f}(z) - g^{f}(z^{\prime}) \|_{*} \leq M + L \| z - z^{\prime} \|, \\ \forall(z \in \mathcal{Z}): \mathbb{E}_{\xi} \left\{\| G(z, \xi) - g^{f}(\xi) \|_{*}^{2} \right\} \leq \sigma^{2} \end{array}\tag{5.6.40}
$$

and that the stepsizes $\gamma_{t}$ satisfy

$$
\gamma_{\tau} \leq \frac{1}{2L} \forall \tau.
$$

Given deterministic sequence $\lambda = \left\{\lambda_{\tau} \geq 0, 1 \leq \tau \leq S \right\}$ with $\begin{array}{r}{\mathcal{L}_{S} = \sum_{\tau = 1}^{S} \lambda_{\tau} > 0} \end{array}$ such that

$$
\lambda_{1} / \gamma_{1} \leq \lambda_{2} / \gamma_{2} \leq...\lambda_{S} / \gamma_{S},
$$

let us define weights $\mu = \{\mu_{t}, 1 \leq t \leq N\}$ according to

$$
\mu_{2 \tau - 1} = 0, \mu_{2 \tau} = \lambda_{\tau}, 1 \leq \tau \leq S
$$

implying that the approximate solution $z^{N} = z^{N}(\xi^{N})$ as defined by (5.6.34) is

$$
z^{N} = \mathcal{L}_{S}^{- 1} \sum_{\tau = 1}^{S} \lambda_{\tau} w_{\tau}.
$$

Then

$$
\mathbb{E}_{\xi^{N}} \left\{\operatorname{Res}_{N}(\mu, \xi^{N}) \right\} \leq \mathcal{MP}_{N}[\gamma, \lambda] := \mathcal{L}_{S}^{- 1} \left[\frac{\lambda_{S}}{2 \gamma_{S}} \Omega^{2} +[M^{2} + 2 \sigma^{2}] \sum_{\tau = 1}^{S} \gamma_{\tau} \lambda_{\tau} + 2 \sigma \Omega \sqrt{\sum_{\tau = 1}^{S} \lambda_{\tau}^{2}} \right],\tag{5.6.41}
$$

implying, by (i), that for the approximate solution $z^{N}$ one has

$$
z^{N} \in \mathcal{Z} \& \mathbb{E}_{\xi^{N}} \left\{\epsilon_{\text{Equil}}[z^{N}(\xi^{N}) | f] \right\} \leq \mathcal{MP}_{N}[\gamma, \lambda].\tag{5.6.42}
$$

Finally, when the Convex Equilibrium instance f in question represents equivalently a $K \gets$ player Convex Nash Equilibrium problem with loss functions $h_{j}(z), j \le K$ , the equilibrium gap $\epsilon_{\mathrm{Equil}}[z^{N} | f]$ in (5.6.39), (5.6.42) can be replaced with the incentive $\epsilon_{\mathrm{Nash}}[z^{N} | h]$

Proof is immediate.

(i): Since $\nu_{t} = \mu_{t} / \mathcal{M}_{N}$ are nonnegative and sum up to 1, and $z_{t} ~ \in ~ \mathcal{Z}$ , we have $z^{N} =$ $\textstyle \sum_{t - 1}^{N} \nu_{t} z_{t} \in{\mathcal{Z}}$ by convexity of Z. Next, let us fix $\xi^{N}$ and set $\mathrm{Res}_{N} = \mathrm{Res}_{N}(\mu, \xi^{N})$ . We have

$$
\begin{array}{rl} &{\mathrm{Res}_{N} \geq \max_{z \in \mathcal{Z}} \sum_{t = 1}^{N} \nu_{t} \langle g^{f}(z_{t}), z_{t} - z \rangle} \\{\Rightarrow} &{- \mathrm{Res}_{N} \leq \min_{z \in \mathcal{Z}} \sum_{t = 1}^{N} \nu_{t} \langle g^{f}(z_{t}), z - z_{t} \rangle} \\ &{\leq \min_{z \in \mathcal{Z}} \sum_{t = 1}^{N} \nu_{t}[f(z, z_{t}) - f(z_{t}, z_{t})][\mathrm{since} g^{f}(z) \in \partial_{y} |_{y = z} f(y, z)]} \\ &{\leq \inf_{z \in \mathcal{Z}} \sum_{t = 1}^{N} \nu_{t}[f(z, z) - f(z_{t}, z)][\mathrm{by(5.6.31)}]} \\ &{\leq \inf_{z \in \mathcal{Z}}[f(z, z) - f(z^{N}, z)][\mathrm{since} f(y, z) \mathrm{isconvexin} y \mathrm{and} z^{N} = \sum_{t} \nu_{t} z_{t}]} \\{\Rightarrow} &{\epsilon_{\mathrm{Equil}}[z^{N} | f] = \sup_{z \in \mathcal{Z}}[f(z^{N}, z) - f(z, z)] \leq \mathrm{Res}_{N}.} \end{array}
$$

as required in (5.6.35). Now, when f comes from Convex Nash Equilibrium instance $h$ , we have

$$
\begin{array}{rl} &{\mathrm{Res}_{N} \geq \max_{z \in \mathcal{Z}} \sum_{t = 1}^{N} \nu_{t} \langle g^{f}(z_{t}), z_{t} - z \rangle} \\{\Rightarrow} &{- \mathrm{Res}_{N} \leq \min_{z \in \mathcal{Z}} \sum_{t = 1}^{N} \nu_{t} \langle g^{f}(z_{t}), z - z_{t} \rangle} \\ &{= \min_{z \in \mathcal{Z}} \sum_{t = 1}^{N} \nu_{t} \sum_{j} \langle g_{j}^{f}([z_{t}]_{j},[z_{t}]^{j}),[z]_{j} -[z_{t}]_{j} \rangle} \\ &{\leq \min_{z \in \mathcal{Z}} \sum_{t = 1}^{N} \nu_{t} \sum_{j}[h_{j}([z]_{j},[z_{t}]^{j}) - h_{j}(z_{t})][\mathrm{since} g_{j}^{f}(y) \in \partial_{[y]_{j}} h_{j}([y]_{j},[y]^{j})]} \\ &{\leq \min_{z \in \mathcal{Z}} \sum_{j}[h_{j}([z]_{j},[z^{N}]_{j}) - h_{j}(z^{N})][\begin{array}{l} \mathrm{since} h_{j}([x]_{j},[x]^{j}) \mathrm{isconcavein}[x]^{j} \mathrm{and} \\ \sum_{j} h_{j}(u) \mathrm{isconvexin} u \end{array}]} \end{array}
$$

that is,

$$
\epsilon_{\mathrm{Nash}}[z^{N} | h] := \sup_{z \in \mathcal{Z}} \sum_{j} \left[h_{j}(z^{N}) - h_{j}([z]_{j},[z^{N}]^{j}) \right] \leq \operatorname{Res}_{N}.
$$

(i) is proved.

(ii) and (ii) are readily given by Propositions 5.6.1, 5.6.2 as applied to the stationary oracle O in question. ✷

Discussion. The summary of “Summary on MD and $\mathrm{MP^{\ast}}$ suggested by our preceding considerations is as follows (we restrict ourselves to the case of stationary oracle, thus skipping Online minimization):

- MD and MP “do not care and do not know” what is the problem with convex structure they are working on. These algorithms operate with a bounded vector field $g :{\mathcal{Z}} \to E$ represented by (in general, stochastic) oracle, and all (N-step versions of) the algorithms “do carry about” is to generate a sequence $z_{t} = Z_{t}(\xi^{t - 1}), \t \ \leq \N$ of points where O is queried, along with a deterministic sequence of weights $\mu \ : = \ : \{\mu_{t} \ : \geq \ : 0, t \ : \leq \ : N\}$ with $\begin{array}{r}{\mathcal{M}_{t} = \sum_{t = 1}^{N} \mu_{t} > 0} \end{array}$ , resulting in as small as possible expectation of the N-step residual

$$
\mathcal{R}_{N} = \mathbb{E}_{\xi^{N}} \Bigg \{\Big[\underbrace{\max_{z \in \mathcal{Z}} \sum_{t = 1}^{N} \mu_{t} \langle g(z_{t}), z_{t} - z \rangle}_{\mathrm{Res}(g, \xi^{N})} \Big]_{+} \Bigg\}
$$

- The importance of the residual in our intended applications stems from the fact that given an instance $f$ of problem with convex structure, as defined above, one can associate with it a bounded vector field $g^{f}$ such that when specifying an approximate solution to $f$ as

$$
z^{N}(\xi^{N}) = \mathcal{M}^{- 1} \sum_{t = 1}^{N} \mu_{t} z_{t},
$$

we get a point from Z such that

$$
\epsilon[x^{N}(\xi^{N}) | f] \leq \mathrm{Res}(g^{f}, \xi^{N}),
$$

where $\epsilon[z | f]$ is the (in)accuracy measure associated with $f.$ As a result, when operating with stochastic oracle representing $g^{f}$ , small residual means small expected inaccuracy of the approximate solution we end up with.<sup>21</sup>

- Mirror Descent is well suited for processing instances $f$ associated with just bounded vector fields $g^{f}$ . Specifically, in the case of (5.6.37), setting $\begin{array}{r}{\gamma_{t} = \frac{\Omega}{[M + \sigma] \sqrt{t}}} \end{array}$ and $\mu_{t} \equiv 1$ , the upper bound $\mathcal{M} \mathcal{D}_{N}$ on the N-step residual (see (5.6.39)), and thus – on the (expected) inaccuracy of approximate solution $z^{N}$ , becomes

$$
\mathbb{E}_{\xi^{N}} \{\epsilon[z | f]\} \leq O(1) \frac{[M + \sigma] \Omega}{\sqrt{N}},\tag{5.6.43}
$$

in full accordance with what we have seen in the preceding parts of this Lecture when speaking about various versions of MD as applied to deterministic and stochastic convex minimization and convex-concave saddle points.

- Mirror Prox is well suited for processing instances f associated with vector fields $g^{f}$ which are not just bounded, but possess certain (perhaps, partial) smoothness. Specifically, in the case of (5.6.40), setting

$$
\lambda_{\tau} = 1, \tau \leq S, \gamma_{\tau} = \min \left[\frac{\Omega}{(M + \sigma) \sqrt{\tau}}, \frac{1}{2L} \right]
$$

and applying Theorem 5.6.2.(iii), we get

$$
\mathbb{E}_{\xi^{N}} \{\epsilon[z | f]\} \leq O(1) \left[\frac{L \Omega^{2}}{N} + \frac{[M + \sigma] \Omega}{\sqrt{N}} \right].\tag{5.6.44}
$$

In particular, assume that for a given $\sigma \geq 0$ , the second relation in (5.6.40) holds true, and let $g^{f}$ be the sum of two vector fields, $g^{f}(\cdot) = g_{b}(\cdot) + g_{\boldsymbol{q} s}(\cdot)$ , with the first – “nonsmooth” – of variation on $\mathcal{Z}$ bounded by some $M < \infty \colon$

$$
\left\| g_{b}(z) - g_{b} \left(z^{\prime}\right) \right\|_{*} \leq M \forall \left(z, z^{\prime} \in \mathcal{Z}\right)
$$

and the second “smooth” – Lipschitz continuous, with constant $L \mathbf{:}$ :

$$
\| g_{s}(z) - g_{s}(z^{\prime}) \|_{*} \leq L \| z - z^{\prime} \| \forall(z, z^{\prime} \in \mathcal{Z})\tag{\([L < \infty]\}
$$

In this situation our M, L and σ ensure (5.6.40), and (5.6.44) says what are the contributions of the nonsmooth and the smooth components of $g^{f}$ to the upper bound on expected inaccuracy: the contribution of the nonsmooth part is the $O(1 / \sqrt{N})$ -term $O(1) \frac{M \Omega}{\sqrt{N}}$ , and the contribution of the smooth part is the $O(1 / N)$ )-term $O(1) \frac{L \Omega^{2}}{N}$ . On the top of these two contributions, there is a toll $O(1) \frac{\sigma \Omega}{\sqrt{N}}$ for the random noise in the oracle. We cannot say in advance what is the leading term in our inaccuracy bound – it depends on interplay between $M, L, \sigma$ and N. Note that our preceding analysis of MP was by far less detailed.

Note also that our analysis shows that modulo $O(1)$ factors, MP “uniformly dominates” MD, since the validity of (5.6.37) with some M and σ implies the validity of (5.6.40) with the same value of $\sigma,$ twice larger value of M, and $L = 0$ , in which case the right hand side in (5.6.44) is within absolute constant factor of the right hand side in (5.6.43).

Finally, we remark that what was said so far about algorithms processing vector fields in order to achieve small residual and implications for solving problems with convex structure is not restricted to proximal sublinearly converging first order methods like Mirror Descent and Mirror Prox. With minor modifications, the outlined explanation of “what indeed is going on” works also for “fast” black-box oriented algorithms like the Ellipsoid Method, provided the vector field in question is represented by precise deterministic oracle, see [40].

## 5.7 Well-structured monotone vector fields

In the previous Section, we have introduced several types of “problems with convex structure” and have demonstrated that all of them can be posed as Variational Inequalities with monotone vector fields. We have demonstrated that when the domain X of $\operatorname{VI}(F, \mathcal{X})$ is convex compact and F is monotone and bounded on X , the VI can be solved by first order algorithms, e.g., Mirror Descent/Mirror Prox. This being said, we know that in the case of convex minimization, First Order algorithms is something which makes sense to use only when sizes of the minimization problem at hand or lack of its structure make the problem badly suited for processing by interior point polynomial time algorithms. Our current goal is to find “variational inequality analogy” of the notion of K-representable function $1 / \mathrm{set},$ , see Section 2.3.7 in order to be able to solve “well structured” VI’s with monotone operators of moderate sizes to high accuracy by existing polynomial time interior point algorithms.

What follows reproduces Section 4.2 of [31].

Same as in Section $2.3.7,$ from now on we fix a family K of regular cones in Euclidean spaces which contains nonnegative rays, ${\bf L}^{3}$ , and is closed w.r.t. taking finite direct products and passing from a cone K to its dual $\mathbf{K}^{*}$ . Unless otherwise is explicitly stated, all cones below belong to $\kappa$

## 5.7.1 Conic representability of monotone vector fields and monotone VI’s in conic form

## 5.7.1.1 Conic representation of a monotone vector field

Let $F(x) : \mathcal{X} E$ be a monotone and continuous vector field on nonempty convex subset X of Euclidean space E. Consider the set

$$
\mathcal{F}[F, \mathcal{X}] = \{[t; g; x] \in \mathbb{R} \times E \times E: x \in \mathcal{X}, t - \langle g, y \rangle \geq \langle F(y), x - y \rangle \forall y \in \mathcal{X}\}\tag{5.7.1}
$$

and let us make several straightforward observations.

5.7.1.1.A. ${\mathcal{F}}[F,{\mathcal{X}}]$ is a convex set which contains all triples $[\langle F(x), x \rangle; F(x); x], x \in \mathcal{X};$ ; this set is closed provided X is so. Besides this, ${\mathcal{F}}[F,{\mathcal{X}}]$ is t-monotone:

$$
[t; g; x] \in \mathcal{F}[F, \mathcal{X}] \mathrm{and} t^{\prime} \geq t \Rightarrow[t^{\prime}; g; x] \in \mathcal{F}[F, \mathcal{X}].
$$

Indeed, ${\mathcal{F}}[F,{\mathcal{X}}]$ is the intersection of solution set of the system of nonstrict linear constraints

$$
t - \langle g, y \rangle - \langle F(y), x \rangle \geq - \langle F(y), y \rangle, y \in \mathcal{X}
$$

in variables $g, t, x$ (this set is closed and convex) with the convex set $\{[t; g; x] : x \in \mathcal{X}\}$ (which is closed if so is X ). By monotonicity, for every $x \in \mathcal{X}$ we have

$$
\langle F(x), x - y \rangle \geq \langle F(y), x - y \rangle \forall y \in \mathcal{X},
$$

so that $[\langle F(x), x \rangle; F(x); x] \in{\mathcal{F}}[F,{\mathcal{X}}];$ ; and t-monotonicity is evident.

## 5.7.1.1.B. For $\epsilon \geq 0$ let

$$
\mathcal{X}_{*}(\epsilon) = \{[g; t] \in E \times \mathbb{R}: \sup_{y \in \mathcal{X}}[t - \langle g, y \rangle] \leq \epsilon\},\tag{5.7.2}
$$

so that $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{X}}_{*}(\boldsymbol{\epsilon})$ is a nonempty closed convex set. Then for every $\epsilon \geq 0$ , $\epsilon$-solutions to $\operatorname{VI}(F, \mathcal{X})$ —points $x \in \mathcal{X}$ such that

$$
\epsilon_{\mathrm{VI}}[x | F] := \sup_{y \in \mathcal{X}} \langle F(y), x - y \rangle \leq \epsilon
$$

are exactly the points

$$
x: \exists(t, g):[t; g; x] \in \mathcal{F}[F, \mathcal{X}] \text{and}[t; g] \in \mathcal{X}_{*}(\epsilon);\tag{5.7.3}
$$

Indeed, let $x, t, g$ be such that $[t; g; x] \in{\mathcal{F}}[F,{\mathcal{X}}]$ and $[t; g] \in \mathcal{X}_{*}(\epsilon)$ . From the first inclusion it follows that $x \in \mathcal{X}$ and

$$
t - \langle g, y \rangle \geq \langle F(y), x - y \rangle \forall y \in \mathcal{X},
$$

while from the second inclusion it follows that $t - \langle g, y \rangle \leq \epsilon$ for all $y \in \mathcal{X}$ . Taken together, these two relations imply that $x \in \mathcal{X}$ and $\langle F(y), x - y \rangle \leq \epsilon$ for all $y \in{\mathcal{X}}, \operatorname{i.e.,} \epsilon_{\mathrm{VI}}(x | F) \leq \epsilon$ Vice versa, if $x \in \mathcal{X}, \epsilon \geq 0$ , and $\epsilon_{\mathrm{VI}}[x | F] \leq \epsilon$ , then the triple $t = \epsilon, g = 0$ , x clearly belongs to ${\mathcal{F}}[F,{\mathcal{X}}]$ and $[t; g] \in \mathcal{X}_{*}(\epsilon)$

K-representation of $(F, \mathcal{X})$ . Given a continuous monotone vector field $F : \mathcal{X} E$ on a nonempty convex subset X of Euclidean space E, let us call a conic constraint<sup>22</sup>

$$
Xx + Gg + tT + Uu \le_{\mathbf{K}} a\tag{5.7.4}
$$

in variables $t \in \mathbf { R } , g \in E , x \in E $ , and $u \in \mathbb{R}^{k}$ a K-representation of $(F, \mathcal{X})$ , if the set

$$
\mathcal{T} := \{[t; g; x]: \exists u: Xx + Gg + tT + Uu \leq_{\mathbf{K}} a\}\tag{5.7.5}
$$

possesses the following two properties:

(i) T is contained in ${\mathcal{F}}[F,{\mathcal{X}}]$ and, along with the latter set, is “t-monotone:”

$$
[t; g; x] \in \mathcal{T} \text{and} t^{\prime} \geq t \Rightarrow[t^{\prime}; g; x] \in \mathcal{T}
$$

(note that when $\tau \neq \emptyset.$ , t-monotonicity is equivalent to $T \le_{\mathbf{K}} 0)$ ;

and

(ii) T contains the set

$$
\left\{\left[\langle F(x), x \rangle; F(x); x \right], x \in \mathcal{X} \right\}\tag{\([\subset \mathcal{F}[F,\mathcal{X}]]\}
$$

If the set (5.7.5) satisfies (i) and the relaxed version of (ii), specifically,

(ii’) T contains the set

$$
\{[t; F(x); x]: t > \langle F(x), x \rangle, x \in \mathcal{X}\}\tag{\([\subset \mathcal{F}[F,\mathcal{X}]]\}
$$

we say that (5.7.4) is an almost K-representation of $(F, \mathcal{X})$

Let us make an immediate observation:

Remark 5.7.1 In the situation described in the beginning of this section, let X be closed, and let Y be a convex set such that

$$
\operatorname{Conv} \left\{\left[x^{T} F(x); F(x); x \right], x \in \mathcal{X} \right\} \subset \mathcal{Y} \subset \operatorname{cl} \operatorname{Conv} \left\{\left[x^{T} F(x); F(x); x \right], x \in \mathcal{X} \right\}
$$

Then every K-representation of Y represents $(F, \mathcal{X})$

## 5.7.1.2 Conic form of conic-representable monotone VI

Our main observation is as follows:

Proposition 5.7.1 Let $\mathcal{X} \subset E$ be nonempty convex compact given by essentially strictly feasible Krepresentation:

$$
\mathcal{X} = \{x: \exists v: Ax + Bv \le_{\mathbf{L}} b\}, \qquad[\mathbf{L} \in \mathcal{K}],\tag{5.7.6}
$$

so that $\mathcal{X}_{*}(\epsilon)$ , see (5.7.2), by conic quality, admits $\kappa.$ -representation as follows:

$$
\mathcal{X}_{*}(\epsilon) = \{[t; g]: \exists \lambda : A^{T} \lambda + g = 0, B^{T} \lambda = 0, t + b^{T} \lambda \leq \epsilon, \lambda \geq_{\mathbf{L}^{*}} 0\}.\tag{5.7.7}
$$

Let, moreover, $F : \mathcal{X} E$ be a continuous monotone vector field, and let (5.7.4) be an almost $\displaystyle{\mathcal{K}}_{-}$ representation of $(F, \mathcal{X})$ . Then for every $\epsilon > 0$ the system of conic constraints

$$
\begin{array}{rclr} Xx + Gg + tT + Uu & \leq_{\mathbf{K}} & a &(a) \\ A^{T} \lambda + g & = & 0 &(b.1) \\ B^{T} \lambda & = & 0 &(b.2) \\ t + b^{T} \lambda & \leq & \epsilon &(b.3) \\ \lambda & \geq_{\mathbf{L}^{*}} & 0 &(b.4) \end{array}\tag{5.7.8}
$$

in variables $x, g, t, u,$ and λ is feasible, and x-component of any feasible solution belongs to X and is an $\epsilon$-solution to $\operatorname{VI}(F,{\mathcal{X}})$

$$
\epsilon_{\mathrm{VI}}[x | F] := \max_{y \in \mathcal{X}} F^{T}(y)[x - y] \leq \epsilon.
$$

Therefore, finding an $\epsilon$-solution to $\operatorname{VI}(F, \mathcal{X})$ reduces to finding a feasible solution to an explicit feasible K-conic constraint.

When (5.7.4) is a K-representation of $(F, \mathcal{X})$ , the above conclusion holds true for all $\epsilon \geq 0$

Proof. Let us fix $\epsilon > 0,$ and let ¯x solve $\operatorname{VI}(F, X)$ (a solution exists since X is compact). Then $\langle F(\bar{x}), \bar{x} -$ $y \rangle \leq 0$ for all $y \in \mathcal{X}$ due to continuity of F on X . Consequently, given $\epsilon > 0.$ setting $\bar{t} = \langle F(\bar{x}), \bar{x} \rangle$ $\bar{g} = F(\bar{x})$ , we have $[\bar{t} + \epsilon; \bar{g}; \bar{x}] \in \mathcal{X}_{*}(\epsilon)$ , implying by (5.7.7) that there exists λ<sup>¯</sup> such that $t = \bar{t} + \epsilon, g = \bar{g},$ $\lambda = \bar{\lambda}$ solve $\left(5.7.8.b.1 \AA^{- 4} \right)$ . Besides this, by (ii’) there exists ¯u such that $x = \bar{x}, g = \bar{g}, t = \bar{t} + \epsilon, u = \bar{u}$ solve (5.7.8.a). Thus, (5.7.8) is feasible.

Next, if $x, g, t, u, \lambda$ is a feasible solution to (5.7.8), then by (5.7.8.a) one has $[t; g; x] \in \mathcal{T}$ , with T given by (5.7.5), whence [t $; g; x] \in{\mathcal{F}}[F,{\mathcal{X}}]$ , implying that $x \in \mathcal{X}$ , see (5.7.1). Besides this, $\left(5.7.8.b.1 - 4 \right)$ say that $[t; g] \in \mathcal{X}_{*}(\epsilon)$ . Thus, $[t; g; x] \in \mathcal{F}[F, \mathcal{X}]$ and $[t; g] \in \mathcal{X}_{*}(\epsilon)$ , implying by 5.7.1.1.B that $\epsilon_{\mathrm{VI}}[x | F] \leq \epsilon$

Finally, when (5.7.4) is a K-representation of $(F, \mathcal{X})$ , the above reasoning works for $\epsilon = 0$ ✷

## 5.7.2 Calculus of conic representations of monotone vector fields

K-representations of pairs $(F, \mathcal{X})$ (X is a nonempty convex subset of Euclidean space $E, F : \mathcal{X} \to E$ is a continuous monotone vector field) admit a calculus; for verification of claims to follow, see Appendix 5.7.4.

## 5.7.2.1 Raw materials

Raw materials for the calculus of K-representable monotone vector fields include:

1. [Affine monotone vector field] Let K contain all Lorentz cones. Then Affine monotone vector field $F(x) = Ax + a$ on $\mathcal{X} = E = \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is K-represented by conic constraint (cf. [42, Proposition 7.4.3])

$$
t \geq x^{T} \bar{A} x + a^{T} x, g = Ax + a\tag{5.7.9}
$$

in variables $t, g, x,$ , where $\begin{array}{r}{\bar{A} = \frac{1}{2}[A + A^{T}]} \end{array}$

2. [Gradient field of continuously diferentiable K-representable convex function] Let X be nonempty convex compact set, and $f(x) : \mathcal{X} \mathbb{R}$ be continuously diferentiable convex function with $\displaystyle \mathcal{K}_{-}$ representable epigraph,

$$
\{(x, s): s \geq f(x), x \in \mathcal{X}\} = \{(x, s): \exists u: Ax + sp + Qu \leq_{\mathbf{K}} a\},\tag{5.7.10}
$$

the representation being essentially strictly feasible. Then the conic constraint

$$
t \geq s + r, Ax + sp + Qu \leq_{\mathbf{K}} a, r \geq a^{T} \lambda, A^{T} \lambda = g, p^{T} \lambda = - 1, Q^{T} \lambda = 0, \lambda \geq_{\mathbf{K}^{*}} 0\tag{5.7.11}
$$

in variables $t, g, x, s, r, \lambda$ , and u represents $(F(\cdot) : = f^{\prime}(\cdot), \mathcal{X})$ (cf. [42, Proposition 7.4.4]).

3. [Monotone vector field associated with continuously diferentiable K-representable convex-concave function ψ] Let K contain the 3D Lorentz cone, and let $\mathcal{U} \subset \mathbb{R}^{n_{u}}$ and $\mathcal{V} \subset \mathbb{R}^{n_{\tau}}$ be K-representable nonempty compact sets:

$$

(b)

both representations being essentially strictly feasible. Assume that $\psi ( u , v ) : \mathcal { U } \times \mathcal { V } \mapsto $ R is a continuously diferentiable convex-concave function which is K-representable on $\boldsymbol{u} \times \boldsymbol{\nu}$ with essentially strictly feasible representation (see Section 2.3.7.1); that is, ψ admits representation

(b)

[Univariate monotone rational vector field] Let $\mathcal{X} =[a, b] \subset \mathbb{R} \(- \infty < a < b < \infty)$ , and let $\alpha(x)$ and $\beta(x)$ be real algebraic polynomials such that $\beta(x) > 0$ on $\mathcal{X}$ . Suppose that the univariate vector field given on X by the function $\begin{array}{r}{F(x) = \frac{\alpha(x)}{\beta(x)}} \end{array}$ is nondecreasing on $x,$ and that K contain all semidefinite cones. ## 5.7.2.2 Calculus rules

Calculus rules are as follows.

1. [Restriction on a $\kappa.$ -representable set] Let conic constraint

$$
Xx + Gg + tT + Uu \leq_{\mathbf{K}} a\tag{5.7.17}
$$

in variables $t, g, x,$ u represent (almost represent) $(F, \mathcal{X})$ , and let set $y \subset E$ be K-representable:

$$
\mathcal{Y} = \{y \in E: \exists v: Ay + Bv \leq_{\mathbf{L}} b\}\tag{5.7.18}
$$

and have a nonempty intersection ${\mathcal{Z}} = \y \cap \chi$ with X . Denoting by $\bar{F}$ the restriction of F on ${\mathcal{Z}},$ the conic constraint

$$
\{Xx + Gg + tT + Uu \leq_{\mathbf{K}} a, Ax + Bv \leq_{\mathbf{L}} b\}\tag{5.7.19}
$$

in variables t, g, x, u, v represents (resp., almost represent) $({\bar{F}},{\mathcal{Z}})$ (cf. [42, Proposition 7.4.5]).

2. [Direct summation] For $k \leq K$ , let $\mathcal{X}_{k}$ be nonempty convex subsets of Euclidean spaces $E_{k}$ and $F_{k} : \mathcal{X}_{k} E_{k}$ be continuous monotone vector fields, and let

$$
X_{k} x + G_{k} g_{k} + t_{k} T_{k} + U_{k} u_{k} \leq_{\mathbf{K}_{k}} a_{k}, 1 \leq k \leq K\tag{5.7.20}
$$

be K-representations of $(F_{k}, \mathcal{X}_{k})$ . Denote

$$
F([x_{1}; \dots; x_{K}]) =[F_{1}(x_{1}); \dots; F_{K}(x_{K})] \text{and} \mathcal{X} = \mathcal{X}_{1} \times \dots \times \mathcal{X}_{K}.
$$

Then the conic constraint

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} X_{k} x_{k} + G_{k} g_{k} + t_{k} T_{k} + U_{k} u_{k} & \leq_{\mathbf{K}_{k}} & a_{k}, k \leq K \\ t & = & \sum_{k} t_{k} \end{array}\tag{a}
$$

(b)

(5.7.21)

in variables $t, g : =[g_{1};...; g_{K}], x : =[x_{1};...; x_{K}], t_{1},..., t_{K}, u_{1},..., u_{K}$ K-represents $(F, \mathcal{X})$

When conic constraints (5.7.20) almost represent $(F_{k}, \mathcal{X}_{k}), ~(5.7.21)$ almost represents $(F, \mathcal{X})$ (cf. [42, Proposition 7.4.6]).

3. [Taking conic combinations] Let X be a nonempty convex subset of Euclidean space $E,$ and let $F_{1},..., F_{K}$ be continuous monotone vector fields on X with $(F_{k}, \mathcal{X})$ admitting K-representations

$$
X_{k} x + G_{k} g + tT_{k} + U_{k} u_{k} \leq_{\mathbf{K}_{k}} a_{k}, 1 \leq k \leq K.\tag{5.7.22}
$$

Let, further, $\alpha_{k} > 0$ be given, and let

$$
F(x) = \sum_{k} \alpha_{k} F_{k}(x): \mathcal{X} \to E.
$$

The conic constraint

$$
X_{k} x + G_{k} g_{k} + t_{k} T_{k} + U_{k} u_{k} \leq_{\mathbf{K}_{k}} a_{k}, 1 \leq k \leq K\tag{a}
$$

$$
g = \sum_{k} \alpha_{k} g_{k}\tag{b}
$$

(5.7.23)

$$
t = \sum_{k} \alpha_{k} t_{k}\tag{c}
$$

in variables $t, g, x, \{t_{k}, g_{k}, u_{k}, k \le K\}$ is a K-representation of (F, X ).

When (5.7.22) are almost representations of $(F_{k}, \mathcal{X})$ , (5.7.23) is almost representation of $(F, \mathcal{X})$

4. [Affine substitution of variables] Let X be a nonempty convex subset of E, F be a continuous monotone vector field on X, with $(F, \mathcal{X})$ given by K-representation

$$
Xx + Gg + tT + Uu \leq_{\mathbf{K}} a.\tag{5.7.24}
$$

Assume that $\xi \mapsto A \xi + a$ is an Affine mapping from Euclidean space Λ to $E,$ and

$$
\Xi = \{\xi : A \xi + a \in \mathcal{X}\}.
$$

Then vector field $\Phi(\xi) = A^{T} F(A \xi + a) \colon \Xi \Lambda$ is continuous and monotone, and the conic constraint

$$
\tau = t - \langle g, a \rangle, \gamma = A^{T} g, X(A \xi + a) + Gg + tT + Uu \le_{\mathbf{K}} a\tag{5.7.25}
$$

in variables $\tau, \gamma, \xi, g, t.$ , and u represents (Φ, Ξ).

When (5.7.24) nearly represents $(F, \mathcal{X})$ , conic constraint (5.7.25) nearly represents $(\Phi, \Xi)$

## 5.7.3 Illustrations

## 5.7.3.1 “Academic” illustration

Let K contain Lorentz cones, $M \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ be such that $\overline{{{M}}} = \frac 12[M + M^{T}] \succeq 0$ , and let $\mathcal{X} \subset \mathbb{R}_{+}^{n}$ be nonempty and K-representable:

$$
\mathcal{X} = \{x: \exists u_{0}: A_{0} x + B_{0} u_{0} \leq_{\mathbf{K}_{0}} a_{0}\}.\tag{5.7.26}
$$

Suppose that the operator

$$
F(x) = Mx - \left[f_{1}(x); \dots; f_{n}(x) \right]\tag{5.7.27}
$$

is monotone on $x,$ and that functions $f_{i}(x)$ and $- \sum_{i} x_{i} f_{i}(x)$ are K-representable on X :

$$
\{(x, s): x \in \mathcal{X}, s \geq f_{i}(x)\} = \{(x, s): \exists u_{1i}: A_{1i} x + sB_{1i} + C_{1i} u_{1i} \leq_{\mathbf{K}_{1i}} a_{1i}\}\tag{\((a_{i})\}
$$

(5.7.28)

$$
\{(x, s): x \in \mathcal{X}, s \geq - \sum_{i} x_{i} f_{i}(x)\} = \{(x, s): \exists u_{2}: A_{2} x + sB_{2} + C_{2} u_{2} \leq_{\mathbf{K}_{2}} a_{2}\}\tag{b}
$$

Observe, that when $M \succeq \alpha I_{m}$ with $\alpha > 0$ , F definitely is monotone provided that $f(x) : =[f_{1}(x);...; f_{n}(x)]$ is Lipschitz continuous on X with Lipschitz constant w.r.t. $\| \cdot \|_{2}$ bounded with α.

Given $x \in \mathcal{X}$ and $g \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ , let us consider the function

$$
f_{x, g}(y) = g^{T} y + F^{T}(y)(x - y) = - y^{T} \overline{{M}} y + \sum_{i}[g_{i} y_{i} + x_{i}[[My]_{i} - f_{i}(y)] + y_{i} f_{i}(y)]: \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}.
$$

We are in the situation where $x_{i} \geq 0$ for $x \in \mathcal{X}$ , so that

$$
\begin{array}{ll} & \{(y, r): y \in \mathcal{X}, f_{x, g}(y) \geq r\} \\ = & \left\{\begin{array}{c} A_{0} y + B_{0} u_{0} \leq_{\mathbf{K}_{0}} a_{0}, y^{T} \overline{{M}} y - s_{0} \leq 0 \\(y, r): \exists u_{0}, s_{0}, s_{1i}, s_{2}: \quad s_{1i} + f_{i}(y) \leq 0, 1 \leq i \leq n, s_{2} - \sum_{i} y_{i} f_{i}(y) \leq 0 \\ \sum_{i}[g_{i} +[M^{T} x]_{i}] y_{i} - s_{0} + \sum_{i} x_{i} s_{1i} + s_{2} \geq r \end{array} \right\} \\ = & \left\{(y, r): \exists u_{0}, s_{0}, s_{1i}, s_{2}, u_{1i}, u_{2}: \right.\\ & \left.\begin{array}{c} A_{0} y + B_{0} u_{0} \leq_{\mathbf{K}_{0}} a_{0}, y^{T} \overline{{M}} y - s_{0} \leq 0, A_{2} y - s_{2} B_{2} + C_{2} u_{2} \leq_{\mathbf{K}_{2}} a_{2} \\ A_{1i} y - s_{1i} B_{1i} + C_{1i} u_{1i} \leq_{\mathbf{K}_{1i}} a_{1i}, 1 \leq i \leq n \\ \sum_{i}[g_{i} +[M^{T} x]_{i}] y_{i} - s_{0} + \sum_{i} x_{i} s_{1i} + s_{2} \geq r \end{array} \right\} \end{array}
$$

Taking into account that $\overline{{M}} \succeq 0$ , the constraint $y^{T} \overline{{M}} y - s_{0} \leq 0$ can be represented by strictly feasible conic constraint

$$
A_{3} y + s_{0} B_{3} \leq_{\mathbf{K}_{3}} a_{3}
$$

on Lorentz cone ${\bf L}^{3}$ , we get

$$
\begin{array}{c} \max_{y \in \mathcal{X}} f_{x, g}(y) = \sup_{y, u_{0}, s_{0}, s_{1i}, s_{2}, u_{1i}, u_{2}} \Bigg \{\sum_{i}[g_{i} +[M^{T} x]_{i}] y_{i} - s_{0} + \sum_{i} x_{i} s_{1i} + s_{2}: \\ A_{0} y + B_{0} u_{0} \leq_{\mathbf{K}_{0}} a_{0}, A_{3} y + s_{0} B_{3} \leq_{\mathbf{K}_{3}} a_{3} \\ A_{1i} y - s_{1i} B_{1i} + C_{1i} u_{1i} \leq_{\mathbf{K}_{1i}} a_{1i}, 1 \leq i \leq n, A_{2} y - s_{2} B_{2} + C_{2} u_{2} \leq_{\mathbf{K}_{2i}} a_{2} \Bigg\}.\end{array}\tag{5.7.29}
$$

Assume that the system of conic constraints (5.7.29) in variables $y, s_{0}, u_{0}, s_{1i}, s_{2}, u_{1i}$ and $u_{2}$ is essentially strictly feasible. Then, by conic quality,

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \underset{y \in \mathcal{X}}{\max} f_{x, g}(y) & = & \underset{\mu, \nu, \xi_{i}, \eta}{\min} \left\{a_{0}^{T} \mu + a_{3}^{T} \nu + \sum_{i} a_{1i}^{T} \xi_{i} + a_{2}^{T} \eta : \right.\\ & & M^{T} x + g = A_{0}^{T} \mu + A_{3}^{T} \nu + \sum_{i} A_{1i}^{T} \xi_{i} + A_{2}^{T} \eta \\ & & x_{i} + B_{1i}^{T} \xi_{i} = 0, 1 \leq i \leq n, B_{2}^{T} \eta = - 1, B_{3}^{T} \nu = - 1 \\ & & B_{0}^{T} \mu = 0, C_{1i}^{T} \xi_{i} = 0, 1 \leq i \leq n, C_{2}^{T} \eta = 0, \\ & & \mu \geq_{\mathbf{K}_{0}^{*}} 0, \nu \geq_{\mathbf{K}_{3}^{*}} 0, \xi_{i} \geq_{\mathbf{K}_{1i}^{*}} 0, 1 \leq i \leq n, \eta \geq_{\mathbf{K}_{2}^{*}} 0 \end{array}.
$$

Now, recalling what $f_{x, g}(y)$ is, we end up with K-representation of ${\mathcal{F}}[F,{\mathcal{X}}]$

$$
\left.\begin{array}{rcl} \mathcal{F}[F, \mathcal{X}] & := & \left\{[t; g; x]: x \in \mathcal{X}, t - g^{T} y \geq F^{T}(y)[x - y] \forall y \in \mathcal{X} \right\} \\ & = & \left\{[t; g; x]: \exists u_{0}, \mu, \nu, \xi_{i}, \eta : \right.\\ & & \left.\begin{array}{l} t \geq a_{0}^{T} \mu + a_{3}^{T} \nu + \sum_{i} a_{1i}^{T} \xi_{i} + a_{2}^{T} \eta, A_{0} x + B_{0} u_{0} \leq_{\mathbf{K}_{0}} a_{0} \\ M^{T} x + g = A_{0}^{T} \mu + A_{3}^{T} \nu + \sum_{i} A_{1i}^{T} \xi_{i} + A_{2}^{T} \eta \\ x_{i} + B_{1i}^{T} \xi_{i} = 0, 1 \leq i \leq n, B_{2}^{T} \eta = - 1, B_{3}^{T} \nu = - 1 \\ B_{0}^{T} \mu = 0, C_{1i}^{T} \xi_{i} = 0, 1 \leq i \leq n, C_{2}^{T} \eta = 0 \\ \mu \geq_{\mathbf{K}_{0}^{*}} 0, \nu \geq_{\mathbf{K}_{3}^{*}} 0, \xi_{i} \geq_{\mathbf{K}_{1i}^{*}} 0, 1 \leq i \leq n, \eta \geq_{\mathbf{K}_{2}^{*}} 0 \end{array} \right\}, \\ \end{array} \right.
$$

so that the conic constraint

$$
\left[\begin{array}{l} t \geq a_{0}^{T} \mu + a_{3}^{T} \nu + \sum_{i} a_{1i}^{T} \xi_{i} + a_{2}^{T} \eta, A_{0} x + B_{0} u_{0} \leq_{\mathbf{K}_{0}} a_{0} \\ x_{i} + B_{1i}^{T} \xi_{i} = 0, 1 \leq i \leq n, B_{2}^{T} \eta = - 1,, B_{3}^{T} \nu = - 1 \\ B_{0}^{T} \mu = 0, C_{1i}^{T} \xi_{i} = 0, 1 \leq i \leq n, C_{2}^{T} \eta = 0 \\ \mu \geq_{\mathbf{K}_{0}^{*}} 0, \nu \geq_{\mathbf{K}_{3}^{*}} 0, \xi_{i} \geq_{\mathbf{K}_{1i}^{*}} 0, 1 \leq i \leq n, \eta \geq_{\mathbf{K}_{2}^{*}} 0 \end{array} \right]
$$

in variables $t, g, x, u_{0}, \mu, \nu, \xi_{i}$ and η is a K-representation of $(F, \mathcal{X})$

## 5.7.3.2 Nash Equilibrium

The “covering story” for this example is as follows:

$n \geq 2$ retailers intend to enter certain market, say, one of red herrings. To this end they should select their “selling capacities” (say, rent areas at malls) $x_{i}, 1 \leq i \leq n$ , in given ranges $\mathcal{X}_{i} =[0, X_{i}] ~(0 < X_{i} < \infty)$ . With the selections $x =[x_{1};...; x_{n}] \in \mathcal{X} = \mathcal{X}_{1} \times..., \times \mathcal{X}_{n} \subset \mathbb{R}_{+}^{n}$ 2 the monthly loss of the i-th retailer is

$$
\phi_{i}(x) = c_{i} x_{i} - \frac{x_{i}}{\sum_{j = 1}^{K} x_{j} + a} b,
$$

where $c_{i} x_{i}, c_{i} > 0.$ , is the price of the capacity $x_{i}, b > 0$ is the dollar value of the demand on red herrings, and $a > 0$ is the total selling capacity of the already existing retailers; the term ${}^{-} \textstyle \sum_{i = 1}^{\cdot_{i}}{x_{j} + a}^{\textstyle b}$ is the minus the revenue of the i-th retailer under the assumption that the total demand is split between retailers proportionally to their selling capacities.

We want to find is a Nash equilibrium – a point $z^{*} =[z_{1}^{*};...; z_{n}^{*}] \in \mathcal{X}$ such that every one of the functions $\phi_{i}(x_{i}^{*},..., x_{i - 1}^{*}, x_{i}, x_{i + 1}^{*},..., x_{n}^{*})$ attains its minimum over $x_{i} \in{\mathcal{X}}_{i}$ at $x_{i} = x_{i}^{*}$ , so that for the i-th retailer there is no incentive to deviate from capacity $\boldsymbol{x}_{i}^{*}$ provided that all other retailers j stick to capacities $\boldsymbol{x}_{j}^{*}$ , and this is so for all i.

As is immediately seen, the Nash Equilibrium problem in question is convex, meaning that $\phi_{i}(x)$ are convex in $x_{i}$ and concave in $x^{i} =(x_{i},..., x_{i - 1}, x_{i + 1},..., x_{n})$ and, on the top of it, $\textstyle \sum_{i} \phi_{i}(x)$ is convex on X . It is well known (for justification, see, $\mathrm{e.g.,[40])}$ that for such a problem, the vector field

$$
F(x) = \left[\frac{\partial \phi_{1}(x)}{\partial x_{1}}; \frac{\partial \phi_{2}(x)}{\partial x_{2}}; \dots; \frac{\partial \phi_{n}(x)}{\partial x_{n}} \right]: \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}^{n}
$$

is monotone, and that Nash Equilibria are exactly the weak=strong solutions to $\operatorname{VI}(F, \mathcal{X})$ . Specifying $\kappa$ as the family of direct products of Lorentz cones, we are about to demonstrate that $F$ admits an explicit K-representation on $x,$ , allowing to reduce the problem of finding Nash Equilibrium to an explicit Second Order conic problem. This is how the construction goes (to save notation, in what follows we set $b = a = 1$ , which always can be achieved by appropriate scaling of the capacities and loss functions):

1. Observe that all we need is a K-representation $\mathcal{R}(t, g, x, u)$ of $(F,{\mathcal{X}}){\mathrm{-}} \mathbf{a}$ K-conic constraint in variables $t \in \mathbb{R}, g \in \mathbb{R}^{n}, x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and additional variables u—satisfying the requirements specified in Section 5.7.1.1. By Proposition 5.7.1, given $\mathcal{R}_{:}$ , for $\epsilon \geq 0$ we can write down an explicit Kconic constraint $\mathcal{C}_{\epsilon}(t, g, x, u, v)$ in variables $t, g, x$ and additional variables $u, v,$ with the size of the constraint (dimension of the associated cone and the total number of variables) independent of $\epsilon$ such that the constraint is feasible, and the x-component of any feasible solution to the constraint is an $\epsilon$-solution to $\operatorname{VI}(F,{\mathcal{X}})$ :

$$
x \in \mathcal{X} \& \epsilon_{\mathrm{VI}}[x | F] = \max_{y \in \mathcal{X}} F^{T}(y)[x - y] \leq \epsilon.
$$

As a result, finding $\epsilon$-solution to $\operatorname{VI}(F, \mathcal{X})$ reduces to solving an explicit solvable Second Order feasibility conic problem of the size independent of $\epsilon$.

2. Thus, all we need is to find an explicit K-representation of $(F, \mathcal{X})$ . This can be done as follows:

(a) Consider the convex-concave function

$$
\psi(u, v) = - \frac{u}{u + v + 1}: \mathbb{R}_{+}^{2} \to \mathbb{R}
$$

along with the associated monotone vector field

$$
\Phi(u, v) = \left[\frac{\partial \psi(u, v)}{\partial u}; - \frac{\partial \psi(u, v)}{\partial v} \right] = \left[- \frac{v + 1}{(u + v + 1)^{2}}; - \frac{u}{(u + v + 1)^{2}} \right].
$$

Let also $A_{i}$ be $2 \times n$ matrix with i-th column $[1; 0]$ and all remaining columns equal to [0; 1], and let $\begin{array}{r}{G(x) = \nabla \left(\frac{1}{\sum_{j} x_{j} + 1} \right)} \end{array}$ . As is immediately seen, we have

$$
\forall x \in \mathbb{R}_{+}^{n}: \Psi(x) := 2c + \sum_{i = 1}^{n} A_{i}^{T} \Phi(A_{i} x) + G(x) = 2F(x),
$$

so that a K-representation of F is readily given by K-representations of the constant monotone vector ${\mathrm{field}} \equiv c,$ , of $\Phi_{;}$ , and of G via our calculus (rules on Affine substitution of argument and on summation).

A K-representation of the constant vector $\operatorname{field} \equiv c$ is trivial; it is given by the system of linear equalities $t = c^{T} x, g = c$ on variables $(t, g, x) \in \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}^{n} \times \mathbb{R}^{n}$ . A K-representation of the gradient vector field $G(x)$ is given by calculus rule 2 in Section 5.7.2.1; we are in the case where (5.7.10) reads

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \{(x, s): s \geq f(x), x \in X\} & = & \bigg \{(x, s): - x \leq 0, x \leq X :=[X_{1};...; X_{n}], \\ & & \underbrace{- \left[0; \sum_{i} x_{i} - s; \sum_{i} x_{i} + s \right] \leq_{\mathbf{L}^{3}}[2; 1; 1]}_{\Leftrightarrow x + 1 + s \geq 0,} \bigg\}, \\ & &(\sum_{i} x_{i} + 1 + s)^{2} \geq(\sum_{i} x_{i} + 1 - s)^{2} + 4 \\ & \Leftrightarrow & s(\overline{{\sum_{i}}} x_{i} + 1) \geq 1 \end{array}
$$

so that (5.7.11), as seen from immediate computation, reduces to the system of constraints

$$
\underbrace{\underset{\begin{array}{c} t \geq r + s, 0 \leq x \leq X, r \geq \sum_{i} \max[X_{i}(g_{i} + \theta), 0] + \theta - 2 \nu \\ \left[2; \sum_{i} x_{i} + 1 - s; \sum_{i} x_{i} + 1 + s \right] \geq_{\mathbf{L}^{3}} 0, \\ \Leftrightarrow s(\sum_{j} x_{j} + 1) \geq 1 \end{array}}_{\Leftrightarrow s(\sum_{j} x_{j} + 1) \geq 1}}_{\Leftrightarrow \nu^{2} \leq \theta} \underbrace{[2 \nu; \theta - 1; \theta + 1] \geq_{\mathbf{L}^{3}} 0}
$$

in variables $t, g, x, \theta, \nu.$

(b) It remains to find a K-representation of the vector field Φ on a rectangle $\Xi = \mathcal{U} \times \mathcal{V}, \mathcal{U} =[0, U]$ 」， $\mathcal{V} =[0, V]$ with given $U > 0, V > 0$ (they should be large enough in order for $A_{i} x, x \in{\mathcal{X}}$ , to take values in the rectangle).

Let us use the construction described in item 3 of Section 5.7.2.1. By (i) of item 3, the set

$$
\overline{{\mathcal{Z}}} = \left\{(t \in \mathbb{R}, g =[h; e] \in \mathbb{R}^{2}, x =[u; v] \in \Xi): \exists r, s: \begin{array}{l} r \geq \max_{\zeta \in \mathcal{V}} \left[\zeta e + \psi(u, \zeta) \right] \\ s \geq \max_{\omega \in \mathcal{U}} \left[\omega^{T} h - \psi(\omega, v) \right] \\ t \geq r + s \end{array} \right\}
$$

satisfies the relations

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \overline{{\mathcal{Z}}} & \subset & \mathcal{F}[\Phi, \Xi] \\ x \in \mathcal{X}, g = \Phi(x), t \geq x^{T} \Phi(x) & \Rightarrow &[t; g; x] \in \overline{{\mathcal{Z}}}, \end{array}
$$

so that all we need to get a K-representation of Φ is to represent $\overline{{\mathcal{Z}}}$ as a projection onto the plane of $t, g,$ x-variables of the solution set of K-conic constraint in variables $t, g, x$ and additional variables. To this end note that for all $(u, v) \in \Xi = \mathcal{U} \times \mathcal{V}$ one has

$$
\psi(u, v) = \min_{f, t, s, \tau} \left\{fv + t: \underbrace{\left[\begin{array}{l} \tau \geq 0, 1 \geq f \geq 0, s \geq 0, t \leq 1, s + \tau \leq 1 \\[2s; u - f; u + f] \in \mathbf{L}^{3} \\[2(1 - s); t - f; t - f + 2] \in \mathbf{L}^{3} \\[2; u - \tau + 1; u + \tau + 1] \in \mathbf{L}^{3} \end{array} \right]}_{\Leftrightarrow(f, t, s, \tau) \in \Pi_{+}} \right\}\tag{5.7.30}
$$

and

$$
- \psi(u, v) = \min_{f, t, s} \left\{fu + t: \underbrace{\left[\begin{array}{l} 1 \geq f \geq 0, 0 \leq s \leq 1, t \leq 1 \\[2s; v + 1 - f; v + 1 + f] \in \mathbf{L}^{3} \\[2(1 - s); t - 1; t + 1] \in \mathbf{L}^{3} \end{array} \right]}_{\Leftrightarrow(f, t, s) \in \Pi_{-}} \right\},\tag{5.7.31}
$$

see Section 5.7.4.3 for justification. Since $\Pi_{\pm}$ are nonempty convex compact sets, by the Sion-Kakutani Theorem (Theorem D.4.2) one has from (5.7.30):

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \underset{\zeta \in \mathcal{V}}{\max}[\zeta e + \psi(u, \zeta)] & = & \underset{0 \leq \zeta \leq V}{\max} \underset{f, t, s, \tau}{\min} \left\{[f + e] \zeta + t:(f, t, s, \tau) \in \Pi_{+} \right\} \\ & = & \underset{f, t, s, \tau}{\min} \left\{\underset{0 \leq \zeta \leq V}{\max}[f + e] \zeta + t:(f, t, s, \tau) \in \Pi_{+} \right\} \\ & = & \underset{f, t, s, \tau}{\min} \left\{\underset{}{\max[0, V(f + e)] + t:(f, t, s, \tau) \in \Pi_{+}} \right\}, \end{array}
$$

and from (5.7.31):

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \max_{\omega \in \mathcal{U}}[\omega h - \psi(\omega, v)] & = & \max_{0 \leq \omega \leq U} \min_{f, t, s} \left\{[f + h] \omega + t:(f, t, s) \in \Pi_{-} \right\} \\ & = & \min_{f, t, s} \left\{\max_{0 \leq \omega \leq U}[f + h] \omega + t:(f, t, s) \in \Pi_{-} \right\} \\ & = & \min_{f, t, s} \left\{\max[0, U(f + h)] + t:(f, t, s) \in \Pi_{-} \right\}.\end{array}
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{array}{r} \overline{{\mathcal{Z}}} = \Bigg \{(t \in \mathbb{R}, g =[h; e] \in \mathbb{R}^{2}, 0 \leq x :=[u; v] \leq[U; V]): \exists r, s, f_{\pm}, t_{\pm}, s_{\pm}, \tau : \\ t \geq r + s, r \geq \max[0, V(f_{+} + e)] + t_{+}, s \geq \max[0, U(f_{-} + h)] + t_{-} \\(f_{+}, t_{+}, s_{+}, \tau) \in \Pi_{+},(f_{-}, t_{-}, s_{-}) \in \Pi_{-} \Bigg\}.\end{array}
$$

Recalling what are $\Pi_{\pm}$ , we can straightforwardly represent $\overline{{\mathcal{Z}}}$ as projection onto the space of $t, g,$ x-variables of a set given by a K-conic inequality, ending up with an explicit $\displaystyle \mathop{\kappa}_{\scriptscriptstyle -}$ representation of Φ.

Remark 5.7.2 The just outlined construction can be used in the case of a general convex Nash Equilibrium problem where, given n convex compact sets $\mathcal{X}_{i} \subset \mathbb{R}^{k_{i}}$ and n continuously diferentiable functions $\phi _ { i } ( x _ { 1 } , . . . , x _ { n } ) : { \mathcal { X } } : = { \mathcal { X } } _ { 1 } \times . . . \times { \mathcal { X } } _ { n } $ R with $\phi_{i}$ convex in $x_{i},$ concave in $(x_{1},..., x_{i - 1}, x_{i + 1},..., x_{n})$ and such that $\textstyle \sum_{i} \phi_{i}$ is convex, one is looking for Nash Equilibria—points $z^{*} =[z_{1}^{*};...; z_{n}^{*}] \in \mathcal{X}$ such that for every i, the function $\phi_{i}(z_{1}^{*},...,_{i - 1}^{*}, x_{i}, x_{i + 1}^{*},..., x_{n}^{*})$ attains its minimum over $x_{i} \in{\mathcal{X}}_{i}$ at $x_{i} = x_{i}^{*}$ . As it was already mentioned, these equilibria are exactly the weak=strong solutions to $\operatorname{VI}(F,{\mathcal{X}})$ where the monotone vector field $F$ is given by $\begin{array}{r}{F(x_{1},..., x_{n}) = \left\lceil \frac{\partial \phi_{1}(x)}{\partial x_{1}};...; \frac{\partial \phi_{n}(x)}{\partial x_{n}} \right\rceil} \end{array}$ . Observing that the monotone vector fields

$$
F^{i}(x) = \left[- \frac{\partial \phi_{i}(x)}{\partial x_{1}}; \dots; - \frac{\partial \phi_{i}(x)}{\partial x_{i - 1}}; \frac{\partial \phi_{i}(x)}{\partial x_{i}}; - \frac{\partial \phi_{i}(x)}{\partial x_{i + 1}}; \dots; - \frac{\partial \phi_{i}(x)}{\partial x_{n}} \right]
$$

associated with convex-concave functions $\phi_{i}$ and the monotone vector field $\begin{array}{r}{F^{0}(x) = \nabla \left(\sum_{i} \phi_{i}(x) \right)} \end{array}$ are linked to $F$ by the relation $\textstyle 2F = \sum_{i = 0}^{n} F^{i}$ , we see that in order to get a K-representation of $F,$ it sufices to have at our disposal K-representations of $F^{i}, 0 \leq i \leq n$ . These latter representations, in good cases, can be built according to recipes presented in items $2$ and 3 of Section 5.7.2.1.

The latter remark puts in proper perspective the “red herring” illustration which by itself is of no actual interest: setting $\textstyle s = \sum_{i} x_{i} + 1, x \in{\mathcal{X}}$ is a Nash Equilibrium if and only if

$$
c_{i} - \frac{1}{s} + \frac{x_{i}}{s^{2}} = \frac{\partial \phi_{i}(x)}{\partial x_{i}} \left\{\begin{array}{ll} \geq 0, & x_{i} = 0 \\ = 0, & 0 < x_{i} < X_{i} \\ \leq 0, & x_{i} = X_{i}.\end{array} \right.
$$

As a result, finding the equilibrium reduces to solving on the segment $s \in \left[1, \sum_{i} X_{i} + 1 \right]$ the univariate equation

$$
\sum_{i} x_{i}(s) + 1 = s, x_{i}(s) = \left\{\begin{array}{ll} 0, & s(1 - sc_{i}) < 0 \\ s(1 - sc_{i}), & 0 \leq s(1 - sc_{i}) \leq X_{i} \\ X_{i}, & s(1 - sc_{i}) > X_{i}.\end{array} \right.
$$

## 5.7.4 Derivations for Section 5.7.2

## 5.7.4.1 Verification of “raw materials”

1. [Affine monotone vector field] Note first that the symmetric part $\bar{A}$ of $A{\mathrm{~ is ~}} \succeq 0$ due to the monotonicity of $F$ on $E,$ so that (5.7.9) can be rewritten as a conic constraint on a direct product of properly selected Lorentz cone and nonnegative orthant, and this direct product belongs to $\kappa.$ Second, when $t, g, x$ solve (5.7.9), for every $y \in E$ one has $x^{T} Ax = x^{T} \bar{A} x$ , whence

$$
t - y^{T} g = t - y^{T}[Ax + a] = \underbrace{t - x^{T}[Ax + a]}_{= t - x^{T} \bar{A} x - x^{T} a \geq 0} -[y - x]^{T}[Ax + a] \geq[x - y]^{T}[Ax + a] \geq[x - y]^{T}[Ay + a],
$$

that is, $[t; g; x] \in \mathcal{F}[F, E]$ , as required in item (i) of a representation of $(F, E)$ . Furthermore, when $x \in E$ setting $g = F(x) = Ax + a$ and $t = x^{T} F(x) = x^{T}[Ax + a] = x^{T}[\bar{A} x + a]$ , we see that $[t; g; x]$ satisfy (5.7.9), as required in item (ii) of a representation of $(F, E)$

2. [Gradient field of continuously diferentiable K-representable convex function] Let

$$
f_{*}(y) = \sup_{x \in \mathcal{X}}[x^{T} y - f(x)]
$$

be the Fenchel transform of $f \colon$

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} f_{*}(y) & = & \sup_{x \in \mathcal{X}}[x^{T} y - f(x)] = \sup_{x \in \mathcal{X}, s \geq f(x)}[x^{T} y - s] \\ & = & \sup_{x, u}[x^{T} y - s: Ax + sp + Qu \leq_{\mathbf{K}} a] \\ & = & \min_{\lambda} \left\{a^{T} \lambda : A^{T} \lambda = y, p^{T} \lambda = - 1, Q^{T} \lambda = 0, \lambda \geq_{\mathbf{K}^{*}} 0 \right\}[\text{by conic duality}], \end{array}
$$

that is,

$$
r \geq f_{*}(g) \Leftrightarrow \exists \lambda : r \geq a^{T} \lambda, A^{T} \lambda = g, p^{T} \lambda = - 1, Q^{T} \lambda = 0, \lambda \geq_{\mathbf{K}^{*}} 0.\tag{5.7.32}
$$

Next, let

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \mathcal{Z} & = & \{(t, g, x): \exists s, r: s \geq f(x), r \geq f_{*}(g), s + r \leq t\} \\ & = & \left\{(t, g, x): \exists s, r, u, \lambda : \begin{array}{l} t \geq s + r, Ax + sp + Qu \leq_{\mathbf{K}} a \\ r \geq a^{T} \lambda, A^{T} \lambda = g, p^{T} \lambda = - 1, Q^{T} \lambda = 0, \lambda \geq_{\mathbf{K}^{*}} 0 \end{array} \right\} \end{array}\tag{a}
$$

(5.7.33)

(b)

where (5.7.33.b) is due to (5.7.10) and (5.7.32). Thus, $\mathcal{Z}$ is the projection of the solution set of (5.7.11) on the space of $t, g$ , x-variables, and we should check that

(i) $\mathcal{Z} \subset \mathcal{F}[f^{\prime}(\cdot), \mathcal{X}]$ , and

(ii) when $x \in \mathcal{X}, g = f^{\prime}(x)$ , and $t = x^{T} f^{\prime}(x)$ , we have $[t; g; x] \in{\mathcal{Z}}.$

(i): Let $(t, g, x) \in \mathcal{Z}$ . We have $t \geq s + r$ for properly selected $s \geq f(x)$ and $r \geq f_{*}(g)$ , whence for $y \in \mathcal{X}$ it holds

$$
t - g^{T} y \geq f(x) + f_{*}(g) - g^{T} y \geq f(x) - f(y) \geq(x - y)^{T} f^{\prime}(y),
$$

that is, $[t; g; x] \in \mathcal{F}[f^{\prime}(\cdot), \mathcal{X}].\mathrm{~(i) ~}$ is proved.

(ii): Given $x \in \mathcal{X}$ , let us set $g = f^{\prime}(x), t = x^{T} g, s = f(x), r = f_{*}(g)$ . We have

$$
r = f_{*}(g) = \sup_{x^{\prime}} \left\{g^{T} x^{\prime} - f \left(x^{\prime}\right): x^{\prime} \in \mathcal{X} \right\} = g^{T} x - f(x)
$$

(the concluding equality is due to $g \ = \f^{\prime}(x))$ ; thus, $t = r + s$ . Invoking (5.7.33.a), we conclude that $(t, g, x) \in \mathcal{Z}$ . (ii) is proved.
