4. [Univariate monotone rational vector field] For evident reasons, it sufices to consider the case of $\mathcal{X} =[0, 1]$ recall that $\beta(t) > 0$ on $\mathcal{X}.$ . Let degrees of α and $\beta$ be $\mu$ and $\nu,$ respectively, and let

$$
\kappa = \max[\mu, \nu] + 1.
$$

${\bf 1}^{0}.$ Consider the curves

$$
\delta(t) =[tF(t); F(t); t] = \frac{1}{\beta(t)}[t \alpha(t); \alpha(t); t \beta(t)]:[0, 1] \to \mathbb{R}^{3}, \gamma(t) = \frac{1}{\beta(t)} \left[1; t; t^{2};...; t^{\kappa} \right]:[0, 1] \to \mathbb{R}^{\kappa + 1}
$$

For properly selected matrix A we have

$$
\delta(t) = A \gamma(t), 0 \leq t \leq 1,
$$

whence

$$
\mathcal{Y} := \operatorname{Conv} \{\delta(t), 0 \leq t \leq 1\} = A \mathcal{Z}, \mathcal{Z} = \operatorname{Conv} \{\gamma(t), 0 \leq t \leq 1\}.
$$

We intend to build a semidefinite representation (SDR) of Y (i.e., K-representation with K comprised of finite direct products of semidefinite cones). Semidefinite representability (and K-representability in general) of a set is preserved when taking linear images: an SDR

$$
\mathcal{Z} = \{z: \exists u: \mathcal{A}(z, u) \succeq 0\}
$$

[A(z, u) is Affine in [z; u] symmetric matrix]

of $\mathcal{Z}$ implies the representation

$$
\mathcal{Y} := A \mathcal{Z} = \{y: \exists[z; u]: y = Az, \mathcal{A}(z, u) \succeq 0\},
$$

and the system of the right hand side constraints can be written down as a Linear Matrix Inequality in variable y and additional variables $z, u.$ Thus, all we need is to build an SDR of Z.

$2^{0}$ . We shall get SDR of Z from SDR of the “support cone”

$$
\mathcal{P} = \{[p; q] \in \mathbb{R}^{\kappa + 1} \times \mathbb{R}: \min_{z \in \mathcal{Z}} p^{T} z - q \geq 0\} = \{[p; q]: \min_{0 \leq t \leq 1} p^{T} \gamma(t) \geq q\}
$$

of $\mathcal{Z}.$

Given $p =[p_{0}; p_{1};...; p_{\kappa + 1}] \in \mathbb{R}^{\kappa + 1}$ , let, with a slight abuse of notation, $\begin{array}{r}{p(t) = \sum_{i = 0}^{\kappa} p_{i} t^{i}} \end{array}$ be the polynomial with coeficients $p_{i}, 0 \leq i \leq \kappa$ . We have

$$
\begin{array}{l}[p; q] \in \mathcal{P} \Leftrightarrow \frac{p(t)}{\beta(t)} \geq q \forall t \in[0, 1] \\ \Leftrightarrow \frac{(1 + \tau^{2})^{\kappa} p(\tau^{2} /(1 + \tau^{2}))}{(1 + \tau^{2})^{\kappa} \beta(\tau^{2} /(1 + \tau^{2}))} \geq q \forall \tau \in \mathbb{R} \\ \Leftrightarrow \underbrace{(1 + \tau^{2})^{\kappa} p(\tau^{2} /(1 + \tau^{2})) - q(1 + \tau^{2})^{\kappa} \beta(\tau^{2} /(1 + \tau^{2}))}_{=: \pi_{p, q}(\tau)} \geq 0 \forall \tau \in \mathbb{R}.\end{array}
$$

Note that $\pi_{p, q}(\tau)$ is a polynomial of τ of degree $\leq 2 \kappa$ , and the vector $\pi_{p, q}$ of coeficients of polynomia is linear in $[p; q] \colon \pi_{p, q} = P[p; q]$ . We see that $\mathcal{P}$ is the inverse image of the cone $\mathcal{P}_{2 \kappa}$ of coeficients of polynomials of degree ≤ 2κ which are nonnegative on the entire axis:

$$
\mathcal{P} = \{[p; q]: P[p; q] \in \mathcal{P}_{2 \kappa}\}.
$$

As we remember from Lecture 3, the cone $\mathcal{P}_{2 \kappa}$ is the linear image of the semidefinite cone $\mathbf{S}_{+}^{\kappa + 1}$ :

$$
\mathcal{P}_{2\kappa} = \{\pi \in \mathbb{R}^{2\kappa +1}:\exists x =[x_{ij}]_{0\leq i,j\leq \kappa}\in \mathbf{S}_{+}^{\kappa +1}:[\mathcal{Q}x]_{\ell}:= \sum_{\substack{0\leq i,j\leq \kappa,\\ i + j = \ell}}x_{ij} = \pi_{\ell},0\leq \ell \leq 2\kappa\},
$$

and we arrive at a semidefinite representation of $\mathcal{P} \colon$

$$
\mathcal{P} = \{[p; q]: \exists x \in \mathbf{S}^{\kappa + 1}: x \succeq 0 \& \mathcal{Q} x = P[p; q]\}.\tag{5.7.37}
$$

We claim that this representation is essentially strictly feasible. Indeed, let $\bar{p} =[1; 1;...; 1] \in \mathbb{R}^{\kappa + 1}$ and $\bar{q} = 0$ . Then

$$
\pi_{\bar{p}, \bar{q}}(\tau) =(1 + \tau^{2})^{\kappa} \left[1 + \tau^{2} /(1 + \tau^{2}) +[\tau^{2} /(1 + \tau^{2})]^{2} + \dots +[\tau^{2} /(1 + \tau^{2})]^{\kappa} \right] = \sum_{i = 0}^{\kappa} c_{i} \tau^{2i}, c_{i} > 0 \forall i,
$$

implying that with $\bar{x} = \mathrm{Diag} \{c_{0}, c_{1},..., c_{\kappa}\} \in{\bf S}^{\kappa + 1}$ one has

$$
P[\bar{p}; \bar{q}] = \mathcal{Q} \bar{x} \& \bar{x} \succ 0.
$$

That is, ${\bar{p}},{\bar{q}}.$ and ¯x satisfy all constraints in (5.7.37) and strictly satisfy the non-polyhedral constraint $x \succeq 0,$ as required by essentially strict feasibility.

$3^{0}$ . Now we are done: by its origin, $\mathcal{Z}$ is a convex compact set and as such is convex and closed, implying by duality that

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \mathcal{Z} & = & \{z \in \mathbb{R}^{\kappa + 1}: p^{T} z - q \geq 0 \forall[p; q] \in \mathcal{P}\} \\ & = & \left\{z \in \mathbb{R}^{\kappa + 1}: \inf_{p, q, x} \{[p^{T} z - q]: P[p; q] - \mathcal{Q} x = 0, x \succeq 0\} \geq 0 \right\}[\text{by(5.7.37)}] \\ & = & \left\{z \in \mathbb{R}^{\kappa + 1}: \exists \lambda \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \kappa + 1}: P^{T} \lambda =[z; - 1], \mathcal{Q}^{*} \lambda \succeq 0 \right\} \\ & &[\text{by semidefinite duality}; \lambda \mapsto \mathcal{Q}^{*} \lambda : \mathbb{R}^{2 \kappa + 1} \to \mathbf{S}^{\kappa + 1} \\ & & \text{is the conjugate of} x \mapsto \mathcal{Q} x: \mathbf{S}^{\kappa + 1} \to \mathbb{R}^{2 \kappa + 1}], \end{array}
$$

and we arrive at the desired SDR of $\mathcal{Z}.$

## 5.7.4.2 Verification of calculus rules

1. [Restriction on a K-representable set] Let (5.7.17) represent $(F, \mathcal{X})$ . Suppose that [t; g; x] can be augmented by u, v to solve (5.7.19). Then $(t, g, x, u)$ solve (5.7.17), implying that $[t; g; x] \in{\mathcal{F}}[F,{\mathcal{X}}]$ by definition of $\textstyle{\mathcal{K}} -$ representability of $(F, \mathcal{X})$ , and $(x, v)$ solve (5.7.19), implying that $x \in \mathcal{V}$ . Taking together, these inclusions clearly imply that $[t; g; x] \in \mathcal{F}[\bar{F}, \mathcal{Z}].$ , as required in item (i) of the definition of K-representation of $({\bar{F}},{\mathcal{Z}})$ Next, when $x \in{\mathcal{Z}}$ , the triple $[t : = \langle F(x), x \rangle; g : = F(x); x]$ can be augmented by u to solve (5.7.17) (by item (ii) of the definition of K-representation of $(F, \mathcal{X}))$ , and because $x \in \mathcal{V}$ , x can be augmented by v to solve (5.7.18). Thus, $t : = \langle F(x), x \rangle, g : = F(x)$ , x can be augmented by $(u, v)$ to solve (5.7.19), as required in item (ii) of K-representability of $(\bar{F}, Z)$ . Thus, (5.7.19) indeed represents $({\bar{F}},{\mathcal{Z}})$ . A completely similar reasoning shows that if (5.7.17) almost represents $(F, \mathcal{X})$ , then (5.7.19) almost represents $({\bar{F}},{\mathcal{Z}})$

2. [Direct summation] When $x =[x_{1};...; x_{K}] \in \mathcal{X}$ and $g = F(x) =[g_{1};...; g_{K}], g_{k} = F_{k}(x_{k}), t_{k} = \langle x_{k}, g_{k} \rangle$ and $\begin{array}{r}{t = \sum_{k} t_{k} = \dot{\langle g, x \rangle}} \end{array}$ , there exist u<sub>k</sub> such that (5.7.21.a) take place (by item (ii) of the definition of representation as applied to the representations in (5.7.20)), and (5.7.21.b) takes place as well, as required in item (ii) of the definition of a representation of $(F, \mathcal{X})$ On the other hand, when $x =[x_{1};...; x_{K}].$ $g =[g_{1};...; g_{k}]$ , and t can be augmented by $u_{k}$ and $t_{k}$ to solve (5.7.21.a) and (5.7.21.b), we have $[t_{k}; g_{k}; x_{k}] \in$ $\mathcal{F}[F_{k}, \mathcal{X}_{k}], k \leq K$ , whence for every $y =[y_{1};...; y_{K}] \in \mathcal{X}$ it holds

$$
t_{k} - \left\langle g_{k}, y_{k} \right\rangle \geq \left\langle F_{k}(y_{k}), x_{k} - y_{k} \right\rangle, k \leq K.
$$

When summing up the above inequalities over $k,$ we get

$$
t - \langle g, y \rangle \geq \langle F(y), x - y \rangle \forall y \in \mathcal{X},
$$

that is, $[t; g; x] \in \mathcal{F}[F, \mathcal{X}]$ , as required in item (i) of the definition of a representation of $(F, \mathcal{X})$ The above reasoning, with evident modifications, shows the claim in the case of almost representations.

3. [Taking conic combinations] Let $t, g, x$ can be augmented by $u_{k}, t_{k}, g_{k}, k \le K$ to solve (5.7.23). Then $[t_{k}; g_{k}; x] \in \mathcal{F}[\mathcal{F}_{k}, \mathcal{X}]$ , implying that

$$
t_{k} - \langle g_{k}, y \rangle \geq \left\langle F_{k}(y), x - y \right\rangle \forall y \in X;
$$

multiplying both sides by $\alpha_{k}$ and summing up over $k,$ we get

$$
t - \langle g, y \rangle \geq \langle F(y), x - y \rangle \forall y \in X,
$$

that is, $[t; g; x] \in{\mathcal{F}}[F,{\mathcal{X}}]$ . On the other hand, given $x \in \mathcal{X}$ , let us set $g_{k} = F_{k}(x)$ and $t_{k} = \langle F_{k}(x), x \rangle$ Since the k-th conic constraint in (5.7.23) represents $(F_{k}, \mathcal{X})$ , there exist $u_{k}, k \le K$ , such that all relations $\left(5.7.23.a \right)$ take place. Setting $\begin{array}{r}{t = \sum_{k} \alpha_{k} t_{k}, g = \sum_{k} \alpha_{k} g_{k}} \end{array}$ , we, on one hand, satisfy (5.7.23.b-c), and, on the other hand, obtain

$$
t = \sum_{k} \alpha_{k} \langle F_{k}(x), x \rangle = \langle F(x), x \rangle, g = \sum_{k} \alpha_{k} g_{k} = F(x),
$$

the bottom line being that $[\langle F(x), x \rangle; F(x); x]$ can be augmented by $u_{k}, \t_{k}, \g_{k}$ to solve (5.7.23). Thus, (5.7.23) indeed is a K-representation of $(F, \mathcal{X})$

The above reasoning, with evident modifications, works in the case of almost representations.

4. [Affine substitution of variables] Assume that $\tau, \gamma, \xi, g, t,$ u solve (5.7.25). Then $t, g, x : = A \xi + a$ , u satisfy

$$
Xx + Gg + tT + Uu \leq_{\mathbf{K}} a,
$$

implying that $x \in \mathcal{X}$ and

$$
t - \langle g, y \rangle \geq \langle F(y), x - y \rangle \forall y \in \mathcal{X}.
$$

Recall that $x = A \xi + a, x \in \mathcal{X}$ , implies that $\xi \in \Xi.$ Now, when $\eta \in \Xi,$ , setting $y = A \eta + a,$ we have $y \in \mathcal{X}$ and

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \tau - \langle \gamma, \eta \rangle & = & t - \langle g, a \rangle - \langle A^{T} g, \eta \rangle = t - \langle g, y \rangle \geq \langle F(y), x - y \rangle \\ & = & \langle F(A \eta + a), A(\xi - \eta) \rangle = \langle \Phi(\eta), \xi - \eta \rangle, \end{array}
$$

and since $\eta ~ \in ~ \Xi$ is arbitrary, we get $[\tau; \gamma; \xi] \ \in \ \mathcal{F}[\Phi, \Xi]$ , as required in item (i) of the definition of a representation of (Φ, Ξ). On the other hand, when $\xi \in \Xi, \gamma = \Phi(\xi)$ , and $\tau = \langle \Phi(\xi), \xi \rangle$ , setting $x = A \xi + a,$ we get $x \in \mathcal{X}$ . Next, when setting $g = F(x), t = \langle F(x), x \rangle$ , we obtain $\gamma = A^{T} g$ and

$$
\tau = \langle F(x), x - a \rangle = t - \langle g, a \rangle.
$$

Besides this, by the origin of $t, g,$ x and item (ii) of the definition of K-representation, as applied to (5.7.24), there exists u such that $t, g, x, u$ satisfy (5.7.24). The bottom line is that $\xi, \gamma, \tau$ can be augmented by $t, g, u$ to solve (5.7.25), that is, (5.7.25) meets item (ii) of definition of K-representation of $(\Phi, \Xi)$ The above reasoning, with evident modifications, works in the case of almost representations.

## 5.7.4.3 Verifying (5.7.30) and (5.7.31)

A. Let us prove that for all $u \in \mathcal{U} =[0, U], v \in \mathcal{V} =[0, V]$ one has

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \psi(u, v) & = & - \frac{u}{u + v + 1} \\ & = & \min_{f, t, s} \left\{fv + t: 1 \geq f \geq 0, 0 \leq s \leq \sqrt{uf}, s + \frac{1}{u + 1} \leq 1, t - f \geq(1 - s)^{2} - 1, t \leq 1 \right\} \\ & = & \min_{f, t, s; \tau} \left\{\begin{array}{c} 1 \geq f \geq 0, s \geq 0, t \leq 1, \tau \geq 0, s + \tau \leq 1 \\ \underbrace{[2s; u - f; u + f] \in \mathbf{L}^{3}}_{\Leftrightarrow s^{2} \leq uf \text{when} u + f \geq 0} \\ fv + t: \underbrace{[2(1 - s); t - f; t - f + 2] \in \mathbf{L}^{3}}_{\Leftrightarrow(1 - s)^{2} \leq t - f + 1 \text{when} t - f + 2 \geq 0} \\ \underbrace{[2; u - \tau + 1; u + \tau + 1] \in \mathbf{L}^{3}}_{\Leftrightarrow(u + 1) \tau \geq 1 \text{when} u + \tau + 1 \geq 0} \end{array} \right\}.\end{array}
$$

Indeed, for $u \in \mathcal{U}$ and $v \in \mathcal V$ we have

$$
\begin{array}{l} \min_{f, t, s} \left\{fv + t: 1 \geq f \geq 0, 0 \leq s \leq \sqrt{uf}, s + \frac{1}{u + 1} \leq 1, t - f \geq(1 - s)^{2} - 1, t \leq 1 \right\} \\ = \min_{f} \left\{fv + f - 2 \bar{s}(f) + \bar{s}(f)^{2}: 1 \geq f \geq 0, \bar{s}(f) = \min \left[\frac{u}{u + 1}, \sqrt{uf} \right] \right\} \\ = \min \left[\min_{0 \leq f \leq u /(u + 1)^{2}} \left\{fv + f - 2 \sqrt{uf} + uf \right\}, \min_{1 \geq f \geq u /(u + 1)^{2}} \left\{fv + f - \frac{2u}{u + 1} + \frac{u^{2}}{(u + 1)^{2}} \right\} \right] \\ = \min \left[- \frac{u}{u + v + 1}, \frac{u(v + 1) - 2u - u^{2}}{(u + 1)^{2}} \right] = u \min \left[- \frac{1}{v +(u + 1)}, \frac{v -(u + 1)}{(u + 1)^{2}} \right] = \frac{u}{v + u + 1} \min \left[- 1, \frac{v^{2} -(u + 1)^{2}}{(u + 1)^{2}} \right] \\ = \psi(u, v), \end{array}
$$

as claimed.

B. Now let us show that for all $u \in \mathcal{U} =[0, U], v \in \mathcal{V} =[0, V]$

$$
\begin{array}{lll} - \psi(u, v) & := & \frac{u}{u + v + 1} \\ & = & \min_{f, t, s} \left\{fu + t: 1 \geq f \geq 0, 0 \leq s \leq \sqrt{(v + 1) f}, s \leq 1, 1 \geq t \geq(1 - s)^{2} \right\} \\ & = & \min_{f, t, s} \left\{fu + t: \underbrace{\underbrace{[2s; v + 1 - f; v + 1 + f] \in \mathbf{L}^{3}}_{\Leftrightarrow s^{2} \leq(v + 1) f \text{when} v + 1 + f \geq 0}}_{\Leftrightarrow(1 - s)^{2} \leq t} \right\} \end{array}
$$

Indeed, for $u \in \mathcal{U}$ and $v \in \mathcal{Q}$ we have

$$
\begin{array}{l} \min_{f, t, s} \Big \{fu + t: 1 \geq f \geq 0, 0 \leq s \leq \sqrt{(v + 1) f}, s \leq 1, 1 \geq t \geq(1 - s)^{2} \Big\} \\ = \min_{f, s} \Big \{fu +(1 - s)^{2}: 1 \geq f \geq 0, 0 \leq s \leq \sqrt{(v + 1) f}, s \leq 1 \Big\} \\ = \min_{f} \Big \{fu +(1 - \bar{s}(f))^{2}: 1 \geq f \geq 0, \bar{s}(f) = \min[\sqrt{(v + 1) f}, 1] \Big\} \\ = \min \left[\min_{0 \leq f \leq 1 /(v + 1)} \{fu + 1 - 2 \sqrt{(v + 1) f} +(v + 1) f\}, \min_{1 \geq f \geq 1 /(v + 1)} \{fu\} \right] \\ = \min \left[\frac{u}{u + v + 1}, \frac{u}{v + 1} \right] = \frac{u}{u + v + 1} = - \psi(u, v), \end{array}
$$

as claimed.

## 5.8 Fast First Order algorithms for Smooth Convex Minimization

## 5.8.1 Fast Gradient Methods for Smooth Composite minimization

The fact that problem (CP) with smooth convex objective can be solved by a gradient-type algorithm at the rate ${\cal O}(1 / T^{2})$ was discovered by Yu. Nesterov in 1983 (celebrated Nesterov’s optimal algorithm for large-scale smooth convex optimization [43]). A significant more recent development here, again due to Yu. Nesterov [48] is extending of the ${\cal O}(1 / T^{2})$ -converging algorithm from the case of problem (CP) with smooth objective (smoothness is a rare commodity!) to the so called composite case where the objective in (CP) is the sum of a smooth convex component and a nonsmooth “easy to handle” convex component. We are about to present the related results of Yu. Nesterov; our exposition follows [49] (modulo minor modifications aimed at handling inexact proximal mappings).

## 5.8.1.1 Problem formulation

The general problem of composite minimization is

$$
\phi_{*} = \min_{x \in X} \{\phi(x) := f(x) + \Psi(x)\},\tag{5.8.1}
$$

where X is a closed convex set in a Euclidean space E equipped with norm $\| \cdot \|$ (not necessarily the Euclidean one), $\Psi(x) : X \mathbb{R} \cup \{+ \infty\}$ is a lower semicontinuous convex function which is finite on the relative interior of $X,$ and $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ is a convex function. In this section, we focus on the smooth composite case, where $f$ has Lipschitz continuous gradient:

$$
\| \nabla f(x) - \nabla f(y) \|_{*} \leq L_{f} \| x - y \|, \quad x, y \in X;\tag{5.8.2}
$$

here, as always, $\| \cdot \|,$ <sub>∗</sub> is the norm conjugate to $\| \cdot \|$ . Condition (5.8.2) ensures that

$$
f(y) - f(x) - \langle \nabla f(x), y - x \rangle \leq \frac{L_{f}}{2} \| x - y \|^{2} \forall x, y \in X,\tag{5.8.3}
$$

Note that we do not assume here that X is bounded; however, we do assume from now on that (5.8.1) is solvable, and denote by $x_{*}$ an optimal solution to the problem.

## 5.8.1.2 Composite prox-mapping

We assume that X is equipped with DGF $\omega(x)$ compatible with $\| \cdot \|$ . As always, we set

$$
V_{x}(y) = \omega(y) - \omega(x) - \langle \omega^{\prime}(x), y - x \rangle
$$

$$
[x, y \in X]
$$

and denote by $x_{\omega}$ the minimizer of $\omega(\cdot)$ on $X.$

Given a convex lower semicontinuous function $h(x) : X \to \mathbb{R} \cup \{+ \infty\}$ which is finite on the relative interior of $X$ we know from Lemma 5.9.1 that the optimization problem

$$
\operatorname{Opt} = \min_{x \in X} \left\{h(x) + \omega(x) \right\}
$$

is solvable with the unique solution $z = \operatorname{argmin}_{x \in X} \left[h(x) + \omega(x) \right]$ fully characterized by the property

$$
z \in X \& \{\exists h^{\prime}(z) \in \partial_{X} h(z): \langle h^{\prime}(z) + \omega^{\prime}(z), w - z \rangle \geq 0 \forall w \in X\}.
$$

Given $\epsilon \geq 0$ and h as above, let us set

$$
\operatorname{argmin}_{x\in X}^{\epsilon}\left\{h(x) + \omega(x)\right\} = \left\{z\in X:\exists h^{\prime}(z)\in \partial_{X}h(z):\langle h^{\prime}(z) + \omega^{\prime}(z),w - z\rangle \geq -\epsilon \forall w\in X\right\}
$$

Note that for h as above, the set argm $\mathrm{in}_{\substack{x \in X}}^{\epsilon} \left\{h(x) + \omega(x) \right\}$ is nonempty, since it clearly contains the point $\operatorname{argmin}_{x \in X} \left\{h(x) + \omega(x) \right\}$

The algorithm we are about to develop requires the ability to find, given $\xi \in E$ and $\alpha \geq 0.$ , a point from the set

$$
\operatorname{argmin}_{x \in X}^{\epsilon} \left\{\langle \xi, x \rangle + \alpha \Psi(x) + \omega(x) \right\}
$$

where $\epsilon \geq 0$ is construction’s paramete $\mathrm{r^{23}}$ ; we refer to such a computation as to computing within accuracy $\epsilon$ a composite prox-mapping, ξ, α being the arguments of the mapping. The “ideal” situation here is when the composite prox-mapping

$$
(\xi, \alpha) \mapsto \underset{x \in X}{\operatorname{argmin}} \left\{\langle \xi, x \rangle + \alpha \Psi(x) + \omega(x) \right\}
$$

is easy to compute either by an explicit formula, or by a cheap computational procedure, as is the case in the following instructive example.

Example: LASSO. An instructive example of a composite minimization problem where the composite prox-mapping indeed is easy to compute is the LASSO problem

$$
\min_{x \in E} \left\{\lambda \| x \|_{E} + \| A(x) - b \|_{2}^{2} \right\},\tag{5.8.4}
$$

where E is a Euclidean space, $\| \cdot \|_{E}$ is a norm on $E, x \mapsto A(x) : E \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is a linear mapping, $b \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$ ， and $\lambda > 0$ is a penalty coeficient. To represent the LASSO problem in the form of (5.8.1), it sufices to set

$$
f(x) = \| A(x) - b \|_{2}^{2}, \Psi(x) = \| x \|_{E}, X = E.
$$

The most important cases of the LASSO problem are

A. Sparse recovery: $E = \mathbb{R}^{n}, \| \cdot \| = \| \cdot \|_{1}$ or, more generally, $E ={\bf R}^{k_{1}} \times \ldots \times{\bf R}^{k_{n}}$ and $\| \cdot \|$ is the associated block $\ell_{1}$ norm. In this case, thinking of x as of the unknown input to a linear system, and of b as of observed (perhaps, corrupted by noise) output, (5.8.4) is used to carry out a trade of between “model fitting term $\because \| \bar{A(x)} - b \|_{2}^{2}$ and the (block) sparsity of x: usually, the larger is $\lambda,$ the less nonzero entries (in the $\| \cdot \|_{1^{-}} \mathrm{case})$ or nonzero blocks (in the block $\ell_{1} \ \mathrm{case})$ has the optimal solution to (5.8.4), and the larger is the model fitting term.

Note that in the case in question, computing composite prox-mapping is really easy, provided that the proximal setup in use is either

(a) the Euclidean setup, or

(b) the $\ell_{1} / \ell_{2}$ setup with DGF (5.3.11).

Indeed, in both cases computing composite prox-mapping reduces to solving the optimization problem of the form

$$
\min_{x^{j} \in \mathbb{R}^{k_{j}}, 1 \leq j \leq n} \left\{\sum_{j}[\alpha \| x^{j} \|_{2} +[b^{j}]^{T} x^{j}] + \left(\sum_{j} \| x^{j} \|_{2}^{p}\right)^{2 / p} \right\},\tag{5.8.5}
$$

where $\alpha > 0$ and $1 < p \leq 2$ . This problem has a closed form solution (find it!) which can be computed in O(dim E) a.o.

B. Low rank recovery: $E = \mathbf{M}^{\mu \nu}, \parallel \cdot \parallel = \parallel \cdot \parallel_{\mathrm{nuc}}$ is the nuclear norm. The rationale behind this setting is similar to the one for sparse recovery, but now the trade of is between the model fitting and the rank of the optimal solution (which is a block-diagonal matrix) to (5.8.4).

In the case in question, for both the Euclidean and the Nuclear norm proximal setups (in the latter case, one should take $X = E$ and use the DGF (5.3.15)), so that computing composite prox-mapping reduces to solving the optimization problem

$$
\min_{y = \operatorname{Diag} \left\{y^{1}, \dots, y^{n} \right\} \in \mathbf{M}^{\mu \nu}} \left\{\sum_{j = 1}^{n} \operatorname{Tr} \left(y^{j} \left[b^{j} \right]^{T}\right) + \alpha \| \sigma(y) \|_{1} + \left(\sum_{i = 1}^{m} \sigma_{i}^{p}(y)\right)^{2 / p} \right\}, m = \sum_{j} \mu_{j},\tag{5.8.6}
$$

where $b = \mathrm{Diag} \{b^{1},..., b^{n}\} \in{\bf M}^{\mu \nu}, \alpha > 0$ and $p \in(1, 2]$ . Same as in the case of the usual prox-mapping associated with the Nuclear norm setup (see section $5.3.3)$ , after computing the svd of b the problem reduces to the similar one with diagonal $b^{j}{}^{,} s : b^{j} =[\mathrm{Diag} \{\beta_{1}^{j},..., \beta_{\mu_{j}}^{j}\}, 0_{\mu_{j} \times(\nu_{j} - \mu_{j})}^{,}]$ , where $\beta_{k}^{j} \ge 0.$ . By the same symmetry argument as in section 5.3.3, in the case of diagonal $b^{j}, \(5.8.6)$ has an optimal solution with diagonal $y^{j} \mathrm{\tilde{s}}$ . Denoting $s_{k}^{j}, 1 \leq k \leq j$ , the diagonal entries in the blocks $y^{j}$ of this solution, (5.8.6) reduces to the problem

$$
\min_{\{s^{j}_{k}:q\leq j\leq n,1\leq k\leq \mu_{j}\}}\left\{\sum_{\substack{1\leq j\leq n,\\ 1\leq k\leq \mu_{j}}}[s^{j}_{k}\beta^{j}_{k} + \alpha |s^{j}_{k}|] + \left(\sum_{\substack{1\leq j\leq n,\\ 1\leq k\leq \mu_{j}}}|s^{j}_{k}|^{p}\right)^{2 / p}\right\},
$$

which is of exactly the same structure as (5.8.5) and thus admits a closed form solution which can be computed at the cost of $O(m){\mathrm{a.o}}$ . We see that in the case in question computing composite prox-mapping is no more involved that computing the usual prox-mapping and reduces, essentially, to finding the svd of a matrix from $\mathbf{M}^{\mu \nu}$

## 5.8.1.3 Fast Composite Gradient minimization: Algorithm and Main Result

In order to simplify our presentation, we assume that the constant $L_{f} > 0$ appearing in (5.8.2) is known in advance.

The algorithm we are about to develop depends on a sequence $\{L_{t}\}_{t = 0}^{\infty}$ of reals such that

$$
0 < L_{t} \leq L_{f}, t = 0, 1, \dots\tag{5.8.7}
$$

In order to ensure ${\cal O}(1 / t^{2})$ convergence, the sequence should satisfy certain conditions which can be verified online; to meet these conditions, the sequence can be adjusted online. We shall discuss this issue in-depth later.

Let us fix two tolerances $\epsilon \ge 0, \bar{\epsilon} \ge 0$ . The algorithm is as follows:

- Initialization: Set $y_{0} = x_{\omega} : = \operatorname{argmin}_{x \in X} \omega(x), \psi_{0}(w) = V_{x_{\omega}}(w)$ , and select $y_{0}^{+} \in X$ such that $\phi(y_{0}^{+}) \leq \phi(y_{0})$ . Set $A_{0} = 0$

- Step $t = 0, 1, \ldots$ . Given $\psi_{t}(\cdot), y_{t}^{+}$ and $A_{t} \geq 0$

1. Compute

$$
z_{t} \in \operatorname{argmin}_{w \in X}^{\epsilon} \psi_{t}(w).\tag{5.8.8}
$$

2. Find the positive root $a_{t + 1}$ of the quadratic equation

$$
L_{t} a_{t + 1}^{2} = A_{t} + a_{t + 1} \quad \left[\Leftrightarrow a_{t + 1} = \frac{1}{2L_{t}} + \sqrt{\frac{1}{4L_{t}^{2}} + \frac{A_{t}}{L_{t}}} \right]\tag{5.8.9}
$$

and set

$$
A_{t + 1} = A_{t} + a_{t + 1}, \tau_{t} = \frac{a_{t + 1}}{A_{t + 1}}.\tag{5.8.10}
$$

Note that $\tau_{t} \in(0, 1]$

3. Set

$$
x_{t + 1} = \tau_{t} z_{t} +(1 - \tau_{t}) y_{t}^{+}.\tag{5.8.11}
$$

and compute $f(x_{t + 1}), \nabla f(x_{t + 1})$

4. Compute

$$
\hat{x}_{t + 1} \in \underset{w \in X}{\operatorname{argmin}}^{\bar{\epsilon}} \left[a_{t + 1} \left[\langle \nabla f(x_{t + 1}), w \rangle + \Psi(w) \right] + V_{z_{t}}(w) \right].\tag{5.8.12}
$$

5. Set

$$
\begin{array}{rlr}(a) & y_{t + 1} & = \tau_{t} \hat{x}_{t + 1} +(1 - \tau_{t}) y_{t}^{+} \\(b) & \psi_{t + 1}(w) & = \psi_{t}(w) + a_{t + 1}[f(x_{t + 1}) + \langle \nabla f(x_{t + 1}), w - x_{t + 1} \rangle + \Psi(w)].\end{array}\tag{5.8.13}
$$

compute $f(y_{t + 1})$ , set

$$
\delta_{t} = \left[\frac{1}{A_{t + 1}} V_{z_{t}}(\hat{x}_{t + 1}) + \langle \nabla f(x_{t + 1}), y_{t + 1} - x_{t + 1} \rangle + f(x_{t + 1}) \right] - f(y_{t + 1})\tag{5.8.14}
$$

and select somehow $y_{t + 1}^{+} \in X$ in such a way that $\phi(y_{t + 1}^{+}) \leq \phi(y_{t + 1})$

Step t is completed, and we pass to step $t + 1$

The approximate solution generated by the method in course of t steps is $y_{t + 1}^{+}$

In the sequel, we refer to the just described algorithm as to Fast Composite Gradient Method, nicknamed FGM.

Theorem 5.8.1 FGM is well defined and ensures that $z_{t} \in X, \x_{t + 1}, \hat{x}_{t + 1}, y_{t}, y_{t}^{+} \in X$ for all $t \geq 0$ Assuming that (5.8.7) holds true and that $\delta_{t} \geq 0$ for all t (the latter definitely is the case when $L_{t} = L_{f}$ for all t), one has

$$
y_{t}, y_{t}^{+} \in X, \phi(y_{t}^{+}) - \phi_{*} \leq \phi(y_{t}) - \phi_{*} \leq A_{t}^{- 1}[V_{x_{\omega}}(x_{*}) + 2 \epsilon t] \leq \frac{4L_{f}}{t^{2}}[V_{x_{\omega}}(x_{*}) + 2 \epsilon t]\tag{5.8.15}
$$

for $t = 1, 2,$

A step of the algorithm, modulo updates $y_{t} \mapsto y_{t}^{+}$ , reduces to computing the value and the gradient of $f$ at a point, computing the value of $f$ at another point and to computing within accuracy $\epsilon$ two prox mappings.

Comments. Let us look what happens when $\epsilon = 0$ . The ${\cal O}(1 / t^{2})$ eficiency estimate (5.8.15) is conditional, the condition being that the quantities $\delta_{t}$ defined by (5.8.14) are nonnegative for all t and that $0 < L_{t} \leq L_{f}$ for all t. Invoking (5.8.3), we see that at every step t, setting $L_{t} = L_{f}$ ensures that $\delta_{t} \geq 0$ . In other words, we can safely use $L_{t} \equiv L_{f}$ for all t. However, from the description of $A_{t} \mathrm{^{,} s}$ it follows that the less are $L_{t}{\mathrm{' s}}.$ , the larger are $A_{t}{'} s$ and thus the better is the eficiency estimate (5.8.15). This observations suggests more “aggressive” policies aimed at operating with $L_{t}{'} s$ much smaller than $L_{f}.\ \mathrm{A}$ typical policy of this type is as follows: at the beginning of step $t,$ we have at our disposal a trial value $L_{t}^{0} \leq L_{f}$ of $L_{t}$ . We start with carrying out step t with $L_{t}^{0}$ in the role of $L_{t};$ if we are lucky and this choice of $L_{t}$ results in $\delta_{t} \geq 0$ , we pass to step t + 1 and reduce the trial value of $L,$ say, set $L_{t + 1}^{0} = L_{t}^{0} / 2$ If with $L_{t} = L_{t}^{0}$ we get $\delta_{t} < 0$ , we rerun step t with increased value of $L_{t},$ say, with $L_{t} = \operatorname{min}[2L_{t}^{0}, L_{f}]$ or even with $L_{t} = L_{f}$ . If this new value of $L_{t}$ still does not result in $\delta_{t} \geq 0$ , we rerun step t with larger value of $L_{t}.$ , say, with $L_{t} = \mathrm{min}[4L_{t}^{0}, L_{f}]$ , and proceed in this fashion until arriving at $L_{t} \leq L_{f}$ resulting in $\delta_{t} \geq 0$ . We can maintain a whatever upper bound $k \geq 1$ on the number of trials at a step, just by setting $L_{t} = L_{f}$ at k-th trial. As far as the evolution of initial trial values $L_{t}^{0}$ of $L_{t}$ in time is concerned, a reasonable “aggressive” policy could be “set $L_{t + 1}^{0}$ to a fixed fraction (say, 1/2) of the last (the one resulting in $\delta_{t} \geq 0)$ value of $L_{t}$ tested at step $t.\ '$

In spite of the fact that every trial requires some computational efort, the outlined on-line adjustment of $L_{t}{'} s$ usually significantly outperforms the $^{66} \mathrm{safe}^{9}$ policy $L_{t} \equiv L_{f}$

## 5.8.1.4 Proof of Theorem 5.8.1

1<sup>0</sup>. Observe that by construction

$$
\psi_{t}(\cdot) = \omega(\cdot) + \ell_{t}(\cdot) + \alpha_{t} \Psi(\cdot)\tag{5.8.16}
$$

with nonnegative $\alpha_{t}$ and Affine $\ell_{t}(\cdot)$ , whence, taking into account that $\tau_{t} \in(0, 1]$ , the algorithm is well defined and maintains the inclusions $z_{t} \in X, x_{t},{\hat{x}}_{t + 1}, y_{t}, y_{t}^{+} \in X$

Besides this, (5.8.16), (5.8.12) show that computing $z_{t},$ , same as computing $\hat{x}_{t + 1}$ , reduces to computing within accuracy $\epsilon$ composite prox-mappings, and the remaining computational efort at step t is dominated by the necessity to compute $f(x_{t + 1}), \nabla f(x_{t + 1})$ , and $f(y_{t + 1})$ , as stated in Theorem. $2^{0}$ . Observe that by construction

$$
A_{t} = \sum_{i = 1}^{t} a_{i}\tag{5.8.17}
$$

(as always, the empty sum is 0), and

$$
\frac{1}{2 \tau_{t}^{2} A_{t + 1}} = \frac{A_{t + 1}}{2a_{t + 1}^{2}} = \frac{A_{t} + a_{t + 1}}{2a_{t + 1}^{2}} = \frac{L_{t}}{2}, t \geq 0\tag{5.8.18}
$$

(see (5.8.9) and (5.8.10)). Observe also that the initialization rules, (5.8.17.a) and (5.8.13.b) imply that whenever $t \geq 1$ , setting $\lambda_{i}^{t} = a_{i} / A_{t}$ we have

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \psi_{t}(w) & = & \sum_{i = 1}^{t} a_{i}[\langle \nabla f(x_{i}), w - x_{i} \rangle + f(x_{i}) + \Psi(w)] + V_{x_{\omega}}(w) \\ & = & A_{t} \sum_{i = 1}^{t} \lambda_{i}^{t}[\langle \nabla f(x_{i}), w - x_{i} \rangle + f(x_{i}) + \Psi(w)] + V_{x_{\omega}}(w), \\ \sum_{i = 1}^{t} \lambda_{i}^{t} & = & \sum_{i = 1}^{t} \frac{a_{i}}{A_{t}} = 1.\end{array}\tag{5.8.19}
$$

## 3<sup>0</sup>. We need the following simple

Lemma 5.8.1 Let $h : X \to \mathbb{R} \cup \{+ \infty\}$ be a lower semicontinuous convex function which is finite on the relative interior of X, and let

$$
\bar{w} \in \operatorname{argmin}_{x \in X}^{\epsilon} \left\{h(x) + \omega(x) \right\}.
$$

Then for all $w \in X$ we have

$$
h(w) + \omega(w) \geq h(\bar{w}) + \omega(\bar{w}) + V_{\bar{w}}(w) - \epsilon.\tag{5.8.20}
$$

Proof. Invoking the definition of argmin<sup>$\epsilon$</sup>, for some $h^{\prime}(\bar{w}) \in \partial_{X} h(\bar{w})$ we have

$$
\langle h^{\prime}(\bar{w}) + \omega^{\prime}(\bar{w}), w - \bar{w} \rangle \geq - \epsilon \forall w \in X,
$$

implying by convexity that

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \forall w \in X: \\ h(w) + \omega(w) & \geq &[h(\bar{w}) + \langle h^{\prime}(\bar{w}), w - \bar{w} \rangle] + \omega(w) \\ & = &[h(\bar{w}) + \omega(\bar{w}) + \underbrace{\langle h^{\prime}(\bar{w}) + \omega^{\prime}(\bar{w}), w - \bar{w} \rangle}_{\geq - \epsilon}] + V_{\bar{w}}(w), \end{array}
$$

as required.

$4^{0}$ . Denote $\psi_{t}^{*} = \psi_{t}(z_{t})$ . Let us prove by induction that

$$
B_{t} + \psi_{t}^{*} \geq A_{t} \phi(y_{t}^{+}), t \geq 0, B_{t} =(\epsilon + \bar{\epsilon}) t.\tag{\(\left(*_{t}\right)\}
$$

For $t = 0$ this inequality is valid, since by initialization rules $\psi_{0}(\cdot) \geq 0, B_{0} = 0$ , and $A_{0} = 0$ . Suppose that $(*_{t})$ holds true, and let us prove that so is $(*_{t + 1})$

Taking into account (5.8.8) and the structure of $\psi_{t}(\cdot)$ as presented in (5.8.16), Lemma 5.8.1 as applied with $\bar{w} = z_{t}$ and $h(x) = \psi_{t}(x) - \omega(x) = \ell_{t}(x) + \alpha_{t} \Psi(x)$ yields, for all $w \in X$ , the first inequality in the following chain:

$$
\begin{array}{rl} \psi_{t}(w) & \geq \psi_{t}^{*} + V_{z_{t}}(w) - \epsilon \\ & \geq A_{t} \phi(y_{t}^{+}) + V_{z_{t}}(w) - \epsilon - B_{t}[\mathrm{by}(*_{t})] \\ & \geq A_{t}[f(x_{t + 1}) + \langle \nabla f(x_{t + 1}), y_{t}^{+} - x_{t + 1} \rangle + \Psi(y_{t}^{+})] + V_{z_{t}}(w) - \epsilon - B_{t}[\mathrm{since} f \mathrm{isconvex}].\end{array}
$$

Invoking (5.8.13.b), the resulting inequality implies that for all $w \in X$ it holds

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \psi_{t + 1}(w) & \geq & V_{z_{t}}(w) + A_{t} \left[f(x_{t + 1}) + \langle \nabla f(x_{t + 1}), y_{t}^{+} - x_{t + 1} \rangle + \Psi(y_{t}^{+}) \right] \\ & & + a_{t + 1} \left[f(x_{t + 1}) + \langle \nabla f(x_{t + 1}), w - x_{t + 1} \rangle + \Psi(w) \right] - \epsilon - B_{t}.\end{array}\tag{5.8.21}
$$

By (5.8.11) and (5.8.10) we have $A_{t}(y_{t}^{+} - x_{t + 1}) - a_{t + 1} x_{t + 1} = - a_{t + 1} z_{t},$ whence (5.8.21) implies that

$$
\psi_{t + 1}(w) \geq V_{z_{t}}(w) + A_{t + 1} f(x_{t + 1}) + A_{t} \Psi(y_{t}^{+}) + a_{t + 1}[\langle \nabla f(x_{t + 1}), w - z_{t} \rangle + \Psi(w)] - \epsilon - B_{t}\tag{5.8.22}
$$

for all $w \in X$ . Thus,

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \psi_{t + 1}^{*} & = & \min_{w \in X} \psi_{t + 1}(w) \\ & & \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \\ & \geq & \min_{w \in X} \bigl \{\overbrace{V_{z_{t}}(w) + A_{t + 1} f(x_{t + 1}) + A_{t} \Psi(y_{t}^{+}) + a_{t + 1}[\langle \nabla f(x_{t + 1}), w - z_{t} \rangle + \Psi(w)]}^{= h(w) + \omega(w) \text{with convex lower semicondinous} h} \bigr\} - \epsilon - B_{t} \\ & &[\text{by (5.8.22)}] \\ & \geq & V_{z_{t}}(\hat{x}_{t + 1}) + A_{t + 1} f(x_{t + 1}) + A_{t} \Psi(y_{t}^{+}) + a_{t + 1}[\langle \nabla f(x_{t + 1}), \hat{x}_{t + 1} - z_{t} \rangle + \Psi(\hat{x}_{t + 1})] \\ & & \underbrace{- \epsilon - \bar{\epsilon} - B_{t}}_{- B_{t + 1}} \\ & &[\text{by (5.8.12) and Lemma 5.8.1}] \\ & = & V_{z_{t}}(\hat{x}_{t + 1}) + \underbrace{[A_{t} + a_{t + 1}]}_{= A_{t + 1} \text{by (5.8.10)}} \bigl[\underbrace{\frac{A_{t}}{A_{t} + a_{t + 1}} \Psi(y_{t}^{+}) + \frac{a_{t + 1}}{A_{t} + a_{t + 1}} \Psi(\hat{x}_{t + 1})}_{\geq \Psi(y_{t + 1}) \text{by (5.8.13.a) and (5.8.10); recall that} \Psi \text{is convex}} + A_{t + 1} f(x_{t + 1}) + a_{t + 1} \langle \nabla f(x_{t + 1}), \hat{x}_{t + 1} - z_{t} \rangle - B_{t + 1} \\ & \geq & V_{z_{t}}(\hat{x}_{t + 1}) + A_{t + 1} f(x_{t + 1}) + a_{t + 1} \langle \nabla f(x_{t + 1}), \hat{x}_{t + 1} - z_{t} \rangle + A_{t + 1} \Psi(y_{t + 1}) - B_{t + 1} \end{array}
$$

that is,

$$
\psi_{t + 1}^{*} \geq V_{z_{t}}(\hat{x}_{t + 1}) + A_{t + 1} f(x_{t + 1}) + a_{t + 1} \langle \nabla f(x_{t + 1}), \hat{x}_{t + 1} - z_{t} \rangle + A_{t + 1} \Psi(y_{t + 1}) - B_{t + 1}.\tag{5.8.23}
$$

Now note that $\hat{x}_{t + 1} - z_{t} =(y_{t + 1} - x_{t + 1}) / \tau_{t}$ by (5.8.11) and (5.8.13.a), whence (5.8.23) implies the first inequality in the following chain:

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \psi_{t + 1}^{*} & \geq & V_{z_{t}}(\hat{x}_{t + 1}) + A_{t + 1} f(x_{t + 1}) + \frac{a_{t + 1}}{\tau_{t}} \langle \nabla f(x_{t + 1}), y_{t + 1} - x_{t + 1} \rangle + A_{t + 1} \Psi(y_{t + 1}) - B_{t + 1} \\ & = & V_{z_{t}}(\hat{x}_{t + 1}) + A_{t + 1} f(x_{t + 1}) + A_{t + 1} \langle \nabla f(x_{t + 1}), y_{t + 1} - x_{t + 1} \rangle + A_{t + 1} \Psi(y_{t + 1}) - B_{t + 1} \\ & &[\text{by (5.8.10)}] \\ & = & A_{t + 1} \Big[\frac{1}{A_{t + 1}} V_{z_{t}}(\hat{x}_{t + 1}) + f(x_{t + 1}) + \langle \nabla f(x_{t + 1}), y_{t + 1} - x_{t + 1} \rangle + \Psi(y_{t + 1}) \Big] - B_{t + 1} \\ & = & A_{t + 1}[\phi(y_{t + 1}) + \delta_{t}] - B_{t + 1}[\text{by (5.8.14)}] \\ & \geq & A_{t + 1} \phi(y_{t + 1}) - B_{t + 1}[\text{since we are in the case of} \delta_{t} \geq 0] \\ & \geq & A_{t + 1} \phi(y_{t + 1}^{+}) - B_{t + 1}[\text{since} \phi(y_{t + 1}^{+}) \leq \phi(y_{t + 1})].\end{array}
$$

The inductive step is completed.

5<sup>0</sup>. Observe that $V_{z_{t}}(\hat{x}_{t + 1}) \geq \frac{1}{2} \| \hat{x}_{t + 1} - z_{t} \|^{2}$ and that $\hat{x}_{t + 1} - z_{t} =(y_{t + 1} - x_{t + 1}) / \tau_{t}$ , implying that $\begin{array}{r}{V_{z_{t}}(\hat{x}_{t + 1}) \geq \frac{1}{2 \tau_{t}^{2}} \Vert y_{t + 1} - x_{t + 1} \Vert^{2}} \end{array}$ , whence

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \delta_{t} & = & \left[\frac{1}{A_{t + 1}} V_{z_{t}}(\hat{x}_{t + 1}) + \langle \nabla f(x_{t + 1}), y_{t + 1} - x_{t + 1} \rangle + f(x_{t + 1}) \right] - f(y_{t + 1})[\text{by (5.8.14)}] \\ & \geq & \left[\frac{1}{2A_{t + 1} \tau_{t}^{2}} \| y_{t + 1} - x_{t + 1} \|^{2} + \langle \nabla f(x_{t + 1}), y_{t + 1} - x_{t + 1} \rangle + f(x_{t + 1}) \right] - f(y_{t + 1}) \\ & = & \frac{L_{t}}{2} \| y_{t + 1} - x_{t + 1} \|^{2} + \langle \nabla f(x_{t + 1}), y_{t + 1} - x_{t + 1} \rangle + f(x_{t + 1}) - f(y_{t + 1})[\text{by (5.8.18)}] \end{array}
$$

whence $\delta_{t} \geq 0$ whenever $L_{t} = L_{f}$ by (5.8.3), as claimed.

${\bf 6}^{0}$ . We have proved inequality $(*_{t})$ for all $t \geq 0$ . On the other hand,

$$
\psi_{t}^{*} = \min_{w \in X} \psi_{t}(x) \leq \psi_{t}(x_{*}) \leq A_{t} \phi_{*} + V_{x_{\omega}}(x_{*}),
$$

where the concluding inequality is due to (5.8.19). The resulting inequality taken together with $(*_{t})$ yields

$$
\phi(y_{t}^{+}) \leq \phi_{*} + A_{t}^{- 1}[V_{x_{\omega}}(x_{*}) + B_{t}], t = 1, 2, \dots\tag{5.8.24}
$$

Now, from $A_{0} = 0,(5.8.9)$ and (5.8.10) it immediately follows that if $L_{t} \leq L$ for some L and all t and if ${\bar{A}}_{t}$ are given by the recurrence

$$
\bar{A}_{0} = 0; \bar{A}_{t + 1} = \bar{A}_{t} + \left[\frac{1}{2L} + \sqrt{\frac{1}{4L^{2}} + \frac{\bar{A}_{t}}{L}} \right],\tag{5.8.25}
$$

then $A_{t} \geq \bar{A}_{t}$ for all t. It is immediately seen that (5.8.25) implies that $\begin{array}{r}{\bar{A}_{t} \geq \frac{t^{2}}{4L}} \end{array}$ for all $t^{\24}$ . Taking into account that $L_{t} \leq L_{f}$ for all t by Theorem’s premise, the bottom line is that $\begin{array}{r}{\bar{\boldsymbol{A}}_{t} \geq \frac{t^{2}}{4L_{f}}} \end{array}$ for all $t,$ which combines with $\left(5.8.24 \right)$ to imply (5.8.15). ✷

## 5.8.2 “Universal” Fast Gradient Methods

A conceptual shortcoming of the Fast Composite Gradient Method FGM presented in section 5.8.1 is that it is “tuned” to composite minimization problems (5.8.1) with smooth (with Lipschitz continuous gradient) functions $f.$ We also know what to do when f is convex and just Lipschitz continuous; here we can use Mirror Descent. Note that Lipschitz continuity of the gradient of a convex function f and

Lipschitz continuity of f itself are “two extremes” in characterizing function’s smoothness; they can be linked together by “in-between” requirements for the gradient $f^{\prime}$ of $f$ to be H¨older continuous with a given H¨older exponent $\kappa \in[1, 2]$ :

$$
\| f^{\prime}(x) - f^{\prime}(y) \|_{*} \leq L_{\kappa} \| x - y \|^{\kappa - 1}, \forall x, y \in X.\tag{5.8.26}
$$

Inspired by Yu. Nesterov’s recent paper [50], we are about to modify the algorithm from section 5.8.1 to become applicable to problems of composite minimization (5.8.1) with functions f of smoothness varying between the outlined two extremes. It should be stressed that the resulting algorithm does not require a priori knowledge of smoothness parameters of f and adjusts itself to the actual level of smoothness as characterized by H¨older scale.

While inspired by [50], the algorithm to be developed is not completely identical to the one proposed in this reference; in particular, we still are able to work with inexact prox mappings.

## 5.8.2.1 Problem formulation

We continue to consider the optimization problem

$$
\phi_{*} = \min_{x \in X} \{\phi(x) := f(x) + \Psi(x)\},\tag{5.8.1}
$$

where

1. X is a closed convex set in a Euclidean space E equipped with norm $\| \cdot \|$ (not necessarily the Euclidean one). Same as in section 5.8.1, we assume that X is equipped with distance-generating function $\omega(x)$ compatible with $\| \cdot \|$

2. $\Psi(x) : X \mathbb{R} \cup \{+ \infty\}$ is a lower semicontinuous convex function which is finite on the relative interior of X,

3. $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ is a convex Lipschitz function satisfying, for some $\kappa \in[1, 2], L \in(0, \infty)$ , and a selection $f^{\prime}(\cdot) : X \to E$ of subgradients, the relation

$$
\forall(x, y \in X): f(y) \leq f(x) + \langle f^{\prime}(x), y - x \rangle + \frac{L}{\kappa} \| y - x \|^{\kappa}.\tag{5.8.27}
$$

Observe that in section 5.8.1 we dealt with the case $\kappa = 2$ of the outlined situation. Note also that a sufficient (necessary and sufficient when $\kappa = 2)$ condition for (5.8.27) is H¨older continuity of the gradient of $f,{\mathrm{i.e.}}$ , the relation (5.8.26).

It should be stressed that the algorithm to be built does not require a priori knowledge of κ and L.

From now on we assume that (5.8.1) is solvable and denote by x<sub>∗</sub> an optimal solution to this problem.

In the sequel, we continue to use our standard “prox-related” notation $x_{\omega}, V_{x}(y)$ , same as the notation

$$
\operatorname{argmin}_{x \in X}^{\epsilon} \left\{h(x) + \omega(x) \right\} = \left\{z \in X: \exists h^{\prime}(z) \in \partial_{X} h(z): \langle h^{\prime}(z) + \omega^{\prime}(z), w - z \rangle \geq - \epsilon \forall w \in X \right\}
$$

see $\mathrm{p.}$ 511.

The algorithm we are about to develop requires the ability to find, given $\xi \in E$ and $\alpha \geq 0$ , a point from the set

$$
\operatorname{argmin}_{x \in X}^{\nu} \left\{\langle \xi, x \rangle + \alpha \Psi(x) + \omega(x) \right\}
$$

where $\nu \geq 0$ is construction’s parameter.

## 5.8.2.2 Algorithm and Main Result

The Fast Universal Composite Gradient Method, nicknamed FUGM, we are about to consider is aimed at solving (5.8.1) within a given accuracy $\epsilon > 0$ ; we will refer to $\epsilon$ as to target accuracy of FUGM. On the top of its target accuracy $\epsilon$, FUGM is specified by three other parameters

$$
\nu \geq 0, \bar{\nu} \geq 0, \underline{{L}} > 0.
$$

The method works in stages. The stages difer from each other only in their numbers of steps; for stage $s, s = 1, 2, \ldots$ , this number is $N_{s} = 2^{s}$

Single Stage. N-step stage of FUGM is as follows.

- Initialization: Set $y_{0} = x_{\omega} : = \operatorname{argmin}_{x \in X} \omega(x), \psi_{0}(w) = V_{x_{\omega}}(w)$ , and select $y_{0}^{+} \in X$ such that $\phi(y_{0}^{+}) \leq \phi(y_{0})$ . Set $A_{0} = 0$

- Outer step $t = 0, 1,..., N - 1$ . Given $\psi_{t}(\cdot), y_{t}^{+} \in X$ and $A_{t} \geq 0$

1. Compute

$$
z_{t} \in \operatorname{argmin}_{w \in X}^{\nu} \psi_{t}(w).\tag{5.8.28}
$$

2. Inner Loop: Set $L_{t, 0} = \underline{{L}}.$ . For $\mu = 0, 1,...,$ carry out the following computations.

(a) Set $L_{t, \mu} = 2^{\mu} L_{t, 0};$

(b) Find the positive root $a_{t + 1, \mu}$ of the quadratic equation

$$
L_{t, \mu} a_{t + 1}^{2} = A_{t} + a_{t + 1, \mu} \quad \left[\Leftrightarrow a_{t + 1, \mu} = \frac{1}{2L_{t, \mu}} + \sqrt{\frac{1}{4L_{t, \mu}^{2}} + \frac{A_{t}}{L_{t, \mu}}} \right]\tag{5.8.29}
$$

and set

$$
A_{t + 1, \mu} = A_{t} + a_{t + 1, \mu}, \tau_{t, \mu} = \frac{a_{t + 1, \mu}}{A_{t + 1, \mu}}.\tag{5.8.30}
$$

Note that $\tau_{t, \mu} \in(0, 1]$

(c) Set

$$
x_{t + 1, \mu} = \tau_{t, \mu} z_{t} +(1 - \tau_{t, \mu}) y_{t}^{+}.\tag{5.8.31}
$$

and compute $f(x_{t + 1, \mu}), f^{\prime}(x_{t + 1, \mu})$

(d) Compute

$$
\hat{x}_{t + 1, \mu} \in \underset{w \in X}{\operatorname{argmin}}^{\bar{\nu}} \left[a_{t + 1, \mu} \left[\langle f^{\prime}(x_{t + 1, \mu}), w \rangle + \Psi(w) \right] + V_{z_{t}}(w) \right].\tag{5.8.32}
$$

(e) Set

$$
y_{t + 1, \mu} = \tau_{t, \mu} \hat{x}_{t + 1, \mu} +(1 - \tau_{t, \mu}) y_{t}^{+},\tag{5.8.33}
$$

compute $f(y_{t + 1, \mu})$ and then compute

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \delta_{t, \mu} & = & \left[\frac{L_{t, \mu}}{2} \| y_{t + 1, \mu} - x_{t + 1, \mu} \|^{2} + \langle f^{\prime}(x_{t + 1, \mu}), y_{t + 1, \mu} - x_{t + 1, \mu} \rangle + f(x_{t + 1, \mu}) \right] \\ & & - f(y_{t + 1, \mu}).\end{array}\tag{5.8.34}
$$

(f ) If $\delta_{t, \mu} < - \frac{\epsilon}{N}$ , pass to the step $\mu + 1$ of Inner loop, otherwise terminate Inner loop and set

$$
\begin{array}{rclrclrcl} L_{t} & = & L_{t, \mu}, \qquad a_{t + 1} & = & a_{t + 1, \mu}, \qquad A_{t + 1} & = & A_{t + 1, \mu}, \qquad \tau_{t} & = & \tau_{t, \mu}, \\ x_{t + 1} & = & x_{t + 1, \mu}, \qquad y_{t + 1} & = & y_{t + 1, \mu}, \qquad \delta_{t} & = & \delta_{t, \mu}, \\ \psi_{t + 1}(w) & = & \psi_{t}(w) + a_{t + 1} \left[f(x_{t + 1}) + f^{\prime}(x_{t + 1}), w - x_{t + 1} \right\rangle + \Psi(w)] \end{array}\tag{5.8.35}
$$

3. Select somehow $y_{t + 1}^{+} \in X$ in such a way that $\phi(y_{t + 1}^{+}) \leq \phi(y_{t + 1})$ Step t is completed. If $t < N - 1$ , pass to outer step $t + 1$ , otherwise terminate the stage and output $y_{N}^{+}$

## Main result on the presented algorithm is as follows:

Theorem 5.8.2 Let function f in (5.8.1) satisfy (5.8.27) with some $L \in(0, \infty)$ and $\kappa \in[1, 2]$ . As a result $of$ an N-step stage $\boldsymbol{S_{N}}$ of FUGM we get a point $y_{N}^{+} \in X$ such that

$$
\phi(y_{N}^{+}) - \phi_{*} \leq \epsilon + A_{N}^{- 1} V_{x_{\omega}}(x_{*}) +[\nu + \bar{\nu}] NA_{N}^{- 1}.\tag{5.8.36}
$$

Furthermore,

$$
\begin{array}{ll}(a) & \underline{{L}} \leq L_{t} \leq \max[\underline{{L}}, 2L^{\frac{2}{\kappa}}[N / \epsilon]^{\frac{2 - \kappa}{\kappa}}], 0 \leq t \leq N - 1, \\(b) & A_{N} \geq \left(\sum_{\tau = 0}^{N - 1} \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{L_{\tau}}}\right)^{2}, \end{array}\tag{5.8.37}
$$

Besides this, the number of steps of Inner loop at every outer step of $\boldsymbol{S_{N}}$ does not exceed

$$
M(N) := 1 + \log_{2} \left(\max \left[1, 2 \underline{{L}}^{- 1} L^{\frac{2}{\kappa}}[N / \epsilon]^{\frac{2 - \kappa}{\kappa}} \right]\right).\tag{5.8.38}
$$

For proof, see the concluding subsection of this section.

Remark 5.8.1 Along with the outlined “aggressive” stepsize policy, where every Inner loop of a stage is initialized by setting $L_{t, 0} = \underline{{L}},$ one can consider a “safe” stepsize policy where $L_{0, 0} = \underline{{L}}$ and $L_{t, 0} = L_{t - 1}$ for $t > 0$ . Inspecting the proof of Theorem 5.8.2 it is immediately seen that with the safe stepsize policy, (5.8.36) and (5.8.37) remain true, and the guaranteed bound on the total number of Inner loop steps at a stage (which is $NM(N)$ for the aggressive stepsize policy) becomes $N + M(N)$

Assume from now on that

We have at our disposal a valid upper bound Θ<sub>∗</sub> on $V_{x_{\omega}}(x_{*})$

Corollary 5.8.1 Let function f in (5.8.1) satisfy (5.8.27) with some $L \in(0, \infty)$ and $\kappa \in[1, 2]$ , and let

$$
N_{*}(\epsilon) = \max \left[2 \frac{\sqrt{L \Theta_{*}}}{\sqrt{\epsilon}}, \left(\frac{8^{\frac{\kappa}{2}} L \Theta_{*}^{\frac{\kappa}{2}}}{\epsilon}\right)^{\frac{2}{3 \kappa - 2}} \right].\tag{5.8.39}
$$

Whenever $N \geq N_{*}(\epsilon)$ , the N -step stage $\boldsymbol{S_{N}}$ of the algorithm ensures that

$$
A_{N}^{- 1} V_{x_{\omega}}(x_{*}) \leq A_{N}^{- 1} \Theta_{*} \leq \epsilon.\tag{5.8.40}
$$

In turn, the on-line verifiable condition

$$
A_{N}^{- 1} \Theta_{*} \leq \epsilon\tag{5.8.41}
$$

implies, by (5.8.36), the relation

$$
\phi(y_{N}^{+}) - \phi_{*} \leq 2 \epsilon +[\nu + \bar{\nu}] NA_{N}^{- 1}.\tag{5.8.42}
$$

In particular, with exact prox-mappings $(i.e.$ , with $\nu = \bar{\nu} = 0)$ it takes totaly at most $\mathrm{Ceil}(N^{*}(\epsilon))$ outer steps to ensure (5.8.41) and thus to ensure the error bound

$$
\phi(y_{N}^{+}) - \phi_{*} \leq 2 \epsilon.
$$

Postponing for a moment Corollary’s verification, let us discuss its consequences, for the time being – in the case $\nu = \bar{\nu} = 0$ of exact prox-mappings (the case of inexact mappings will be discussed in section 5.8.3).

Discussion. Corollary 5.8.1 suggests the following policy of solving problem (5.8.1) within a given accuracy $\epsilon > 0 :$ we run FUGM with somehow selected L and $\nu = \bar{\nu} = 0$ stage by stage, starting with a single-step stage and increasing the number of steps N by factor 2 when passing from a stage to the next one. This process is continued until at the end of the current stage the condition (5.8.41) (which is on-line verifiable) takes place. When it happens, we terminate; by Corollary 5.8.1, at this moment we have at our disposal a feasible 2$\epsilon$-optimal solution to the problem of interest. On the other hand, the total, over all stages, number of Outer steps before termination clearly does not exceed twice the number of Outer steps at the concluding stage, that is, invoking Corollary 5.8.1, it does not exceed

$$
N^{*}(\epsilon) := 4 \mathrm{Ceil}(N_{*}(\epsilon)).
$$

As about the total, over all Outer steps of all stages, number M of Inner Loop steps (which is the actual complexity measure of FUGM), it, by Theorem 5.8.2, can be larger than $N^{*}(\epsilon)$ by at most a logarithmic in $\underline{{L}}, L, 1 / \epsilon$ factor. Moreover, when “safe” stepsize policy is used, see Remark 5.8.1, we have by thi Remark

$$
M \leq \sum_{s \geq 0: 2^{s - 1} \leq N_{*}(\epsilon)}[2^{s} + M(2^{s})] \leq N^{*}(\epsilon) + \mathcal{M}, \mathcal{M} := \sum_{s \geq 0: 2^{s - 1} \leq N_{*}(\epsilon)} M(2^{s})
$$

with $M(N)$ given by (5.8.38). It is easily seen that for small $\epsilon$ the “logarithmic complexity term” M is negligible as compared to the “leading complexity term” $N^{*}(\epsilon)$

Further, setting $\overline{{L}} = \operatorname{max}[\underline{{L}}, L]$ and assuming $\epsilon \leq \overline{{L}} \Theta_{*}^{\kappa / 2}$ , we clearly have

$$
N^{*}(\epsilon) \leq O(1) \left(\frac{\overline{{L}} \Theta_{*}^{\frac{\kappa}{2}}}{\epsilon}\right)^{\frac{2}{3 \kappa - 2}}.\tag{5.8.43}
$$

Thus, our principal complexity term is expressed in terms of the true and unknown in advance smoothness parameters $(L, \kappa)$ and is the better the better is smoothness (the larger is κ and the smaller is $L)$ . In the “most smooth case” $\kappa = 2$ , we arrive at $\begin{array}{r}{N^{*}(\epsilon) = O(1) \sqrt{\frac{\overline{{L}} \Theta_{*}}{\epsilon}}} \end{array}$ , which, basically, is the complexity bound for the Fast Composite Gradient Method FGM from section 5.8.1. In the “least smooth case” $\kappa = 1$ , we get $\begin{array}{r}{N^{*}(\epsilon) = O(1) \frac{\overline{{L}} \sqrt{\Theta_{*}}}{\epsilon^{2}}} \end{array}$ , which, basically, is the complexity bound of Mirror Descent<sup>25</sup> Note that while in the nonsmooth case the complexity bounds of FUGM and MD are “nearly the same,” the methods are essentially different, and in fact FUGM exhibits some theoretical advantage over MD: the complexity bound of FUGM depends on the maximal deviation L of the gradients of $f$ from each other, the deviation being measured in $\| \cdot \|_{*}$ , while what matters for MD is the Lipschitz constant, taken w.r.t. $\| \cdot \|_{*},$ of $f,$ that is, the maximal deviation of the gradients of f from zero; the latter deviation can be much larger than the former one. Equivalently: the complexity bounds of MD are sensitive to adding to the objective a linear form, while the complexity bounds of FUGM are insensitive to such a perturbation.

Proof of Corollary 5.8.1. The first inequality in (5.8.40) is evident. Now let $N \geq N_{*}(\epsilon)$ . Consider two possible cases, I and II, as defined below.

Case I: $2L^{\frac{2}{\kappa}}[N / \epsilon]^{\frac{2 - \kappa}{\kappa}} \geq L$ . In this case, (5.8.37.a) ensures the first relation in the following chain:

$$
\begin{array}{rl} & L_{t} \leq 2L^{\frac{2}{\kappa}}[N / \epsilon]^{\frac{2 - \kappa}{\kappa}}, 0 \leq t \leq N - 1 \\ \Rightarrow & A_{N} \geq \left(2^{- 3 / 2} L^{- \frac{1}{\kappa}} N^{1 - \frac{2 - \kappa}{2 \kappa}} \epsilon^{\frac{2 - \kappa}{2 \kappa}}\right)^{2} \quad[\text{by (5.8.37.b)}] \\ & = \frac{1}{8L^{\frac{2}{\kappa}}} N^{\frac{3 \kappa - 2}{\kappa}} \epsilon^{\frac{2 - \kappa}{\kappa}} \\ & \geq \frac{1}{8L^{\frac{2}{\kappa}}} \left[\left(\frac{8^{\frac{\kappa}{2}} L \Theta_{*}^{\frac{\kappa}{2}}}{\epsilon}\right)^{\frac{2}{3 \kappa - 2}} \right]^{\frac{3 \kappa - 2}{\kappa}} \epsilon^{\frac{2 - \kappa}{\kappa}} \quad[\text{by(5.8.39) andduetoN\geq N_{*}(\epsilon)}] \\ & = \frac{1}{8L^{\frac{2}{\kappa}}} 8L^{\frac{2}{\kappa}} \Theta_{*} \epsilon^{\frac{2 - \kappa}{\kappa} - \frac{2}{\kappa}} = \Theta_{*} / \epsilon, \end{array}
$$

and the second inequality in (5.8.40) follows.

Case II: $2L^{\frac{2}{\kappa}}[N / \epsilon]^{\frac{2 - \kappa}{\kappa}} < L$ . In this case, (5.8.37.a) ensures the first relation in the following chain:

$$
\begin{array}{ll} & L_{t} \leq \underline{{L}}, 0 \leq t \leq N - 1 \\ \Rightarrow & A_{N} \geq \frac{N^{2}}{4 \underline{{L}}} \quad[\text{by (5.8.37.b)}] \\ & \geq \Theta_{*} / \epsilon \quad[\text{by (5.8.39) and due to} N \geq N_{*}(\epsilon)] \end{array}
$$

and the second inequality in (5.8.40) follows.

## 5.8.2.3 Proof of Theorem 5.8.2

${\bf 0}^{0}$ . By (5.8.27) we have

$$
\delta_{t, \mu} \geq \frac{L_{t, \mu}}{2} \| y_{t + 1, \mu} - x_{t + 1, \mu} \|^{2} - \frac{L}{\kappa} \| y_{t + 1, \mu} - x_{t + 1, \mu} \|^{\kappa} \geq \min_{r \geq 0} \left[\frac{L_{t, \mu}}{2} r^{2} - \frac{L}{\kappa} r^{\kappa} \right].\tag{5.8.44}
$$

Assuming $\kappa = 2$ , we see that $\delta_{t, \mu}$ is nonpositive whenever $L_{t, \mu} \geq L,$ so that in the case in question Inner loop is finite, and

$$
L_{t} \leq \max[\underline{{L}}, 2L].\tag{5.8.45}
$$

When $\kappa \in[1, 2)$ , (5.8.44) after straightforward calculation implies that whenever

$$
L_{t, \mu} \geq L^{\frac{2}{\kappa}}[N / \epsilon]^{\frac{2 - \kappa}{\kappa}},
$$

we have $\delta_{t, \mu} \geq - \frac{\epsilon}{N}$ . Consequently, in the case in question Inner loop as finite as well, and

$$
L_{t} \leq \max[\underline{{L}}, 2L^{\frac{2}{\kappa}}[N / \epsilon]^{\frac{2 - \kappa}{\kappa}}],\tag{5.8.46}
$$

Note that by (5.8.45) the resulting inequality holds true for $\kappa = 2$ as well.

The bottom line is that FUGM is well defined and maintains the following relations:

$$
\overline{{(a.1)}} \quad \underline{{L}} \leq L_{t} \leq \max[\underline{{L}}, 2L^{\frac{2}{\kappa}}[N / \epsilon]^{\frac{2 - \kappa}{\kappa}}],
$$

$$
(a.2) a_{t + 1} = \frac{1}{2L_{t}} + \sqrt{\frac{1}{4L_{t}^{2}} + \frac{A_{t}}{L_{t}}}[\Leftrightarrow L_{t} a_{t + 1}^{2} = A_{t} + a_{t + 1}],
$$

(a.3) $\begin{array}{r}{A_{t + 1} = \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t + 1} a_{\tau},} \end{array}$

(a.4) $\begin{array}{r}{\tau_{t} = \frac{a_{t + 1}}{A_{t + 1}} \in(0, 1],} \end{array}$

(a.5) $\begin{array}{r}{\frac{1}{\tau_{t}^{2} A_{t + 1}} = L_{t} \quad[\mathrm{by}(a.2 – 4)];} \end{array}$

(b.1) $\overline{{\psi_{0}(\boldsymbol{w}) = V_{\boldsymbol{x}_{\omega}}(\boldsymbol{w})}},$

$$
\psi_{t + 1}(w) = \psi_{t}(w) + a_{t + 1} \left[f(x_{t + 1}) + f^{\prime}(x_{t + 1}), w - x_{t + 1} \right\rangle + \Psi(w)]\tag{5.8.47}
$$

(c.1) $z_{t} \in \operatorname{argmin}^{\nu} \psi_{t}(w);$

(c.2) $x_{t + 1} = \tau_{t} z_{t} +(1 - \tau_{t}) y_{t}^{+},$

$$
\hat{x}_{t + 1} \in \operatorname{argmin}^{\tilde{\nu}} \left[a_{t + 1} \left[\langle f^{\prime}(x_{t + 1}), w \rangle + \Psi(w) \right] + V_{z_{t}}(w) \right],
$$

(c.4) $y_{t + 1} = \tau_{t} \hat{x}_{t + 1} +(1 - \tau_{t}) y_{t}^{+};$

$$
\frac{L_{t}}{2} \| y_{t + 1} - x_{t + 1} \|^{2} + \langle f^{\prime}(x_{t + 1}), y_{t + 1} - x_{t + 1} \rangle + f(x_{t + 1}) - f(y_{t + 1}) \geq - \frac{\epsilon}{N}
$$

(e) $\overline{{y_{t}^{+} \in X \ \& \ \phi(y_{t}^{+}) \leq \phi(y_{t}).}}$

and, on the top of it, the number M of steps of Inner loop does not exceed

$$
M(N) := 1 + \log_{2} \left(\max \left[1, 2 \underline{{L}}^{- 1} L^{\frac{2}{\kappa}}[N / \epsilon]^{\frac{2 - \kappa}{\kappa}} \right]\right).\tag{5.8.48}
$$

$1^{0}$ . Observe that by (5.8.47.b) we have

$$
\psi_{t}(\cdot) = \omega(\cdot) + \ell_{t}(\cdot) + \alpha_{t} \Psi(\cdot)\tag{5.8.49}
$$

with nonnegative $\alpha_{t}$ and Affine $\ell_{t}(\cdot)$ , whence, taking into account that $\tau_{t} \in(0, 1]$ , the algorithm maintains the inclusions $z_{t} \in X, x_{t},{\hat{x}}_{t + 1}, y_{t}, y_{t}^{+} \in X$

$2^{0}$ . Observe that by (5.8.47.a.2-4) we have

$$
A_{t} = \sum_{i = 1}^{t} a_{i}\tag{5.8.50}
$$

(as always, the empty sum is 0) and

$$
\frac{1}{2 \tau_{t}^{2} A_{t + 1}} = \frac{A_{t + 1}}{2a_{t + 1}^{2}} = \frac{A_{t} + a_{t + 1}}{2a_{t + 1}^{2}} = \frac{L_{t}}{2}, t \geq 0.\tag{5.8.51}
$$

Observe also that (5.8.47.b1-2) and (5.8.50) imply that whenever $t \geq 1$ , setting $\lambda_{i}^{t} = a_{i} / A_{t}$ we have

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \psi_{t}(w) & = & \sum_{i = 1}^{t} a_{i}[\langle f^{\prime}(x_{i}), w - x_{i} \rangle + f(x_{i}) + \Psi(w)] + V_{x_{\omega}}(w) \\ & = & A_{t} \sum_{i = 1}^{t} \lambda_{i}^{t}[\langle f^{\prime}(x_{i}), w - x_{i} \rangle + f(x_{i}) + \Psi(w)] + V_{x_{\omega}}(w), \\ \sum_{i = 1}^{t} \lambda_{i}^{t} & = & \sum_{i = 1}^{t} \frac{a_{i}}{A_{t}} = 1.\end{array}\tag{5.8.52}
$$

$\mathbf{3^{0}}.$ Denote $\psi_{t}^{*} = \psi_{t}(z_{t})$ . Let us prove by induction that

$$
B_{t} + \psi_{t}^{*} \geq A_{t} \phi(y_{t}^{+}), \quad t \geq 0, B_{t} =(\nu + \bar{\nu}) t + \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} A_{\tau} \frac{\epsilon}{N}.\tag{\(\left(*_{t}\right)\}
$$

For $t = 0$ this inequality is valid, since by initialization rules $\psi_{0}(\cdot) \geq 0, B_{0} = 0$ , and $A_{0} = 0$ . Suppose that $(*_{t})$ holds true for some $t \geq 0,$ , and let us prove that so is $\left(*_{t + 1} \right)$

Taking into account $\left(5.8.47.c.1 \right)$ and the structure of $\psi_{t}(\cdot)$ as presented in (5.8.49), Lemma 5.8.1 as applied with $\bar{w} = z_{t}$ and $h(x) = \psi_{t}(x) - \omega(x) = \ell_{t}(x) + \alpha_{t} \Psi(x)$ ) yields, for all $w \in X$ , the first inequality in the following chain:

$$
\begin{array}{rl} \psi_{t}(w) & \geq \psi_{t}^{*} + V_{z_{t}}(w) - \nu \\ & \geq A_{t} \phi(y_{t}^{+}) + V_{z_{t}}(w) - \nu - B_{t}[\mathrm{by}(*_{t})] \\ & \geq A_{t}[f(x_{t + 1}) + \langle f^{\prime}(x_{t + 1}), y_{t}^{+} - x_{t + 1} \rangle + \Psi(y_{t}^{+})] + V_{z_{t}}(w) - \nu - B_{t}[\mathrm{since} f \mathrm{isconvex}].\end{array}
$$

Invoking (5.8.47.b.2), the resulting inequality implies that for all $w \in X$ it holds

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \psi_{t + 1}(w) & \geq & V_{z_{t}}(w) + A_{t} \left[f(x_{t + 1}) + \langle f^{\prime}(x_{t + 1}), y_{t}^{+} - x_{t + 1} \rangle + \Psi(y_{t}^{+}) \right] \\ & & + a_{t + 1} \left[f(x_{t + 1}) + \langle f^{\prime}(x_{t + 1}), w - x_{t + 1} \rangle + \Psi(w) \right] - \nu - B_{t}.\end{array}\tag{5.8.53}
$$

By $\left(5.8.47.c.2 \right)$ and (5.8.47.a.4-5) we have $A_{t}(y_{t}^{+} - x_{t + 1}) - a_{t + 1} x_{t + 1} = - a_{t + 1} z_{t}$ , whence (5.8.53) implies that

$$
\psi_{t + 1}(w) \geq V_{z_{t}}(w) + A_{t + 1} f(x_{t + 1}) + A_{t} \Psi(y_{t}^{+}) + a_{t + 1}[\langle f^{\prime}(x_{t + 1}), w - z_{t} \rangle + \Psi(w)] - \nu - B_{t}\tag{5.8.54}
$$

for all $w \in X$ . Thus,

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \psi_{t + 1}^{*} & = & \min_{w \in X} \psi_{t + 1}(w) \\ & & \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad[by(5.8.54)] \\ & \geq & \min_{w \in X} \bigl \{\overbrace{V_{z_{t}}(w) + A_{t + 1} f(x_{t + 1}) + A_{t} \Psi(y_{t}^{+}) + a_{t + 1}[\langle f^{\prime}(x_{t + 1}), w - z_{t} \rangle + \Psi(w)]}^{= h(w) + \omega(w) \text{with convex lower semicontinuous} h} \bigr\} - \nu - B_{t} \\ & &[by(5.8.47.c.3) andLemma5.8.1] \\ & \geq & V_{z_{t}}(\hat{x}_{t + 1}) + A_{t + 1} f(x_{t + 1}) + A_{t} \Psi(y_{t}^{+}) + a_{t + 1}[\langle f^{\prime}(x_{t + 1}), \hat{x}_{t + 1} - z_{t} \rangle + \Psi(\hat{x}_{t + 1})] \\ & & - \nu - \bar{\nu} - B_{t} \\ & &[by(5.8.47.c.3) andLemma5.8.1] \\ & = & V_{z_{t}}(\hat{x}_{t + 1}) + \underbrace{[A_{t} + a_{t + 1}]}_{= A_{t + 1} by(5.8.47.a.3)} \bigl[\underbrace{\frac{A_{t}}{A_{t} + a_{t + 1}} \Psi(y_{t}^{+}) + \frac{a_{t + 1}}{A_{t} + a_{t + 1}} \Psi(\hat{x}_{t + 1})}_{\geq \Psi(y_{t + 1}) by(5.8.47.c.4) and(5.8.47.a.2 - 3); recallthat \Psi isconvex}] \\ & & + A_{t + 1} f(x_{t + 1}) + a_{t + 1} \langle f^{\prime}(x_{t + 1}), \hat{x}_{t + 1} - z_{t} \rangle - \nu - \bar{\nu} - B_{t} \\ & \geq & V_{z_{t}}(\hat{x}_{t + 1}) + A_{t + 1} f(x_{t + 1}) + a_{t + 1} \langle f^{\prime}(x_{t + 1}), \hat{x}_{t + 1} - z_{t} \rangle + A_{t + 1} \Psi(y_{t + 1}) - \nu - \bar{\nu} - B_{t} \end{array}
$$

that is,

$$
\psi_{t + 1}^{*} \geq V_{z_{t}}(\hat{x}_{t + 1}) + A_{t + 1} f(x_{t + 1}) + a_{t + 1} \langle f^{\prime}(x_{t + 1}), \hat{x}_{t + 1} - z_{t} \rangle + A_{t + 1} \Psi(y_{t + 1}) - \nu - \bar{\nu} - B_{t}.\tag{5.8.55}
$$

Now note that

$$
\hat{x}_{t + 1} - z_{t} =(y_{t + 1} - x_{t + 1}) / \tau_{t}\tag{5.8.56}
$$

by (5.8.47.c), whence (5.8.55) implies the first inequality in the following chain:

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \psi_{t + 1}^{*} & \geq & V_{z_{t}}(\hat{x}_{t + 1}) + A_{t + 1} f(x_{t + 1}) + \frac{a_{t + 1}}{\tau_{t}} \langle f^{\prime}(x_{t + 1}), y_{t + 1} - x_{t + 1} \rangle + A_{t + 1} \Psi(y_{t + 1}) - \nu - \bar{\nu} - B_{t} \\ & = & V_{z_{t}}(\hat{x}_{t + 1}) + A_{t + 1} f(x_{t + 1}) + A_{t + 1} \langle f^{\prime}(x_{t + 1}), y_{t + 1} - x_{t + 1} \rangle + A_{t + 1} \Psi(y_{t + 1}) - \nu - \bar{\nu} - B_{t} \\ & &[\text{by (5.8.47.a.4)}] \\ & = & A_{t + 1} \left[\frac{1}{A_{t + 1}} V_{z_{t}}(\hat{x}_{t + 1}) + f(x_{t + 1}) + \langle f^{\prime}(x_{t + 1}), y_{t + 1} - x_{t + 1} \rangle + \Psi(y_{t + 1}) \right] - \nu - \bar{\nu} - B_{t} \\ & = & A_{t + 1} \left[\phi(y_{t + 1}) + \left[\frac{1}{A_{t + 1}} V_{z_{t}}(\hat{x}_{t + 1}) + f(x_{t + 1}) + \langle f^{\prime}(x_{t + 1}, y_{t + 1} - x_{t + 1} \rangle - f(y_{t + 1}) \right] \right] \\ & & - \nu - \bar{\nu} - B_{t} \\ & \geq & A_{t + 1} \left[\phi(y_{t + 1}) + \left[\frac{1}{2A_{t + 1}} \| \hat{x}_{t + 1} - z_{t} \|^{2} + f(x_{t + 1}) + \langle f^{\prime}(x_{t + 1}, y_{t + 1} - x_{t + 1} \rangle - f(y_{t + 1}) \right] \right] \\ & & - \nu - \bar{\nu} - B_{t} \\ & = & A_{t + 1} \phi(y_{t + 1}) \\ & & + A_{t + 1} \left[\frac{1}{2 \tau_{t}^{2} A_{t + 1}} \| x_{t + 1} - y_{t + 1} \|^{2} + f(x_{t + 1}) + \langle f^{\prime}(x_{t + 1}, y_{t + 1} - x_{t + 1} \rangle - f(y_{t + 1}) \right] \\ & & - \nu - \bar{\nu} - B_{t}[\text{by (5.8.56)}] \\ & = & A_{t + 1} \left[\phi(y_{t + 1}) + \left[\frac{L_{t}}{2} \| x_{t + 1} - y_{t + 1} \|^{2} + f(x_{t + 1}) + \langle f^{\prime}(x_{t + 1}, y_{t + 1} - x_{t + 1} \rangle - f(y_{t + 1}) \right] \right] \\ & & - \nu - \bar{\nu} - B_{t}[\text{by (5.8.47.a.5)}] \\ & \geq & A_{t + 1} \phi(y_{t + 1}) - A_{t + 1} \frac{\epsilon}{N} - \nu - \bar{\nu} - B_{t}[\text{by (5.8.47.d)}] \\ & = & A_{t + 1} \phi(y_{t + 1}) - B_{t + 1}[\text{see(*_{t})}] \\ & \geq & A_{t + 1} \phi(y_{t + 1}^{+}) - B_{t + 1}[\text{by (5.8.47.e)}].\end{array}
$$

The inductive step is completed.

$4^{0}$ . We have proved inequality $(*_{t})$ for all $t \geq 0$ . On the other hand,

$$
\psi_{t}^{*} = \min_{w \in X} \psi_{t}(x) \leq \psi_{t}(x_{*}) \leq A_{t} \phi_{*} + V_{x_{\omega}}(x_{*}),
$$

where the concluding inequality is due to (5.8.52). The resulting inequality taken together with $(*_{t})$ yields

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \phi(y_{t}^{+}) - \phi_{*} & \leq & A_{t}^{- 1}[V_{x_{\omega}}(x_{*}) + B_{t}] \\ & = & A_{t}^{- 1} V_{x_{\omega}}(x_{*}) + A_{t}^{- 1} \sum_{\tau = 1}^{t} A_{\tau} \frac{\epsilon}{N} + A_{t}^{- 1}[\nu + \bar{\nu}] t \\ & \leq & A_{t}^{- 1} V_{x_{\omega}}(x_{*}) + \epsilon \frac{t}{N} + A_{t}^{- 1}[\nu + \bar{\nu}] t, t = 1, 2,..., N, \end{array}\tag{5.8.57}
$$

where the concluding $\leq$ is due to $A_{\tau} \le A_{t}$ for $\tau \leq t$

$\mathbf{5}^{0}$ . From $A_{0} = 0$ and (5.8.47.a.2) by induction in t it follows that

$$
A_{t} \geq \underbrace{\left(\sum_{\tau = 0}^{t - 1} \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{L_{\tau}}}\right)^{2}}_{=: \bar{A}_{t}}.\tag{5.8.58}
$$

Indeed, (5.8.58) clearly holds true for $t = 0$ . Assuming that the relation holds true for some t and invoking (5.8.47.a.2), we get

$$
\begin{array}{rl} & A_{t + 1} = A_{t} + a_{t + 1} \geq \bar{A}_{t} + \sqrt{\bar{A}_{t} / L_{t}} + \frac{1}{2L_{t}} \geq \left[\sum_{\tau = 0}^{t - 1} \frac{1}{\sqrt{L_{\tau}}} \right]^{2} + 2 \left[\sum_{\tau = 0}^{t - 1} \frac{1}{\sqrt{L_{\tau}}} \right] \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{L_{t}}} + \frac{1}{4L_{t}} \\ & = \left[\sum_{\tau = 0}^{t} \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{L_{\tau}}} \right]^{2} = \bar{A}_{t + 1}^{2}, \end{array}
$$

completing the induction.

Bottom line. Combining (5.8.47.a.1), (5.8.57), (5.8.58) and taking into account (5.8.48), we arrive at Theorem 5.8.2. ✷

## 5.8.3 From Fast Gradient Minimization to Conditional Gradient

## 5.8.3.1 Proximal and Linear Minimization Oracle based First Order algorithms

First Order algorithms considered so far heavily utilize proximal setups; to be implementable, these algorithms need the convex compact domain X of convex problem

$$
\mathrm{Opt} = \min_{x \in X} f(x)\tag{CP}
$$

to be proximal friendly – to admit a continuously diferentiable strongly convex (and thus nonlinear!) DGF $\omega(\cdot)$ with easy to minimize over X linear perturbations $\omega(X) +(\xi, x) \^{26}$ . Whenever this is the case, it is easy to minimize over X linear forms $\langle \xi, x \rangle$ (indeed, minimizing such a form over X within a whatever high accuracy reduces to minimizing over X the sum $\omega(x) + \alpha \langle \xi, x \rangle$ with large α). The inverse conclusion is, in general, not true: it may happen that X admits a computationally cheap Linear Minimization Oracle $\mathbf{(LMO) - a}$ procedure capable to minimize over X linear forms, while no DGFs leading to equally computationally cheap proximal mappings are known. The important for applications examples include:

1. nuclear norm ball $X \subset \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ playing crucial role in low rank matrix recovery: with all known proximal setups, computing prox-mappings requires computing full singular value decomposition of an $n \times n$ matrix. At the same time, minimizing a linear form over $\bar{X}$ requires finding just the pair of leading singular vectors of an $n \times n$ matrix x (why?) The latter task can be easily solved by Power method $\lfloor 27$ For n in the range of few thousands and more, computing the leading singular vectors is by order of magnitude cheaper, progressively as n grows, than the full singular value decomposition.

2. spectahedron $X \ = \ \{x \in \mathbf{S}^{n} : x \succeq 0, \mathrm{Tr}(x) = 1\}$ “responsible” for Semidefinite Programming. Situation here is similar to the one with nuclear norm ball: with all known proximal setups, computing a proximal mapping requires full eigenvalue decomposition of a symmetric $n \times n$ matrix, while minimizing a linear form over X reduces to approximating the leading eigenvector of such a matrix; the latter task can be achieved by Power method and is, progressively in $n,$ much cheaper computationally than full eigenvalue decomposition.

3. Total Variation ball X in the space of $n \times n$ images $(n \times n$ arrays with zero mean). Total Variation of an $n \times n$ image x is

$$
\operatorname{TV}(x) = \sum_{i = 1}^{n - 1} \sum_{j = 1}^{n} | x_{i + 1, j} - x_{i, j} | + \sum_{i = 1}^{n} \sum_{j = 1}^{n - 1} | x_{i, j + 1} - x_{i, j} |
$$

and is a norm on the space of images (the discrete analogy of $L_{1}$ norm of the gradient of a function on a 2D square); convex minimization over TV balls and related problems (like LASSO problem (5.8.4) with the space of images in the role of E and $\mathrm{TV}(\cdot)$ in the role of $\| \cdot \|_{E})$ plays important role in image reconstruction. Computing the simplest – Euclidean – prox mapping on TV ball in the space of $n \times n$ images requires computing Euclidean projection of a point onto large-scale polytope cut of $O(1) n^{2} \ell_{1}$ ball by $O(1) n^{2}$ homogeneous linear equality constraints; for n of practical interest (few hundreds), this problem is quite time consuming. In contrast, it turns out that minimizing a linear form over TV ball requires solving a special Maximum Flow problem [28], and this turns out to be by order of magnitudes cheaper than metric projection onto TV ball.

Full svd for n = 8192 takes 475.6 sec!
