The outlined and some other generic large-scale problems of convex minimization inspire investigating the abilities to solve problems (CP) on LMO - represented domains X – convex compact domains equipped by Linear Minimization Oracles. As about the objective $f,$ we still assume that it is given by First Order Oracle.

## 5.8.3.2 Conditional Gradient algorithm

The only classical optimization algorithm capable to handle convex minimization over LMO-represented domain is Conditional Gradient Algorithm (CGA ) invented as early as in 1956 by Frank and Wolfe [23]. CGA does not work when the function $f$ in (CP) possesses no smoothness beyond Lipschitz continuity, so in the sequel we impose some “nontrivial smoothness” assumption. More specifically, we consider the same composite minimization problem

$$
\phi_{*} = \min_{x \in X} \{\phi(x) := f(x) + \Psi(x)\},\tag{5.8.1}
$$

as in the previous sections, and assume that

- X is a convex and compact subset in Euclidean space E equipped with a norm $\| \cdot \|,$

- Ψ is convex lower semicontinuous on X and is finite on the relative interior of X function, and

- f is convex and continuously diferentiable on X function satisfying, for some $L < \infty$ and $\kappa \in(1, 2]$ (note that $\kappa > 1 !)$ relation (5.8.27):

$$
\forall(x, y \in X): f(y) \leq f(x) + \langle f^{\prime}(x), y - x \rangle + \frac{L}{\kappa} \| y - x \|^{\kappa}.
$$

Composite LMO and Composite Conditional Gradient algorithm. We assume that we have at our disposal a Composite Linear Minimization Oracle (CLMO) – a procedure which, given on input a linear form $\langle \xi, x \rangle$ on the embedding X Euclidean space $E$ and a nonnegative α, returns a point

$$
\operatorname{CLMO}(\xi, \alpha) \in \underset{x \in X}{\operatorname{Argmin}} \left\{\langle \xi, x \rangle + \alpha \Psi(x) \right\}.\tag{5.8.59}
$$

The associated Composite Conditional Gradient Algorithm (nicknamed in the sequel CGA ) as applied to (5.8.1) generates iterates $x_{t} \in X, t = 1, 2,...,$ as follows:

1. Initialization: $x_{1}$ is an arbitrary points of X.

2. Step $t = 1, 2,...;$ Given $x_{t},$ we

- compute $f^{\prime}(x_{t})$ and call CLMO to get the point

$$
x_{t}^{+} = \operatorname{CLMO}(f^{\prime}(x_{t}), 1) \qquad[\in \underset{x \in X}{\operatorname{Argmin}}[\ell_{t}(x) := f(x_{t}) + \langle f^{\prime}(x_{t}), x - x_{t} \rangle + \Psi(x)]\tag{5.8.60}
$$

- compute the point

$$
\widehat{x}_{t + 1} = x_{t} + \gamma_{t}(x_{t}^{+} - x_{t}), \gamma_{t} = \frac{2}{t + 1}\tag{5.8.61}
$$

- take as $x_{t + 1}$ a (whatever) point in X such that $\phi(x_{t + 1}) \leq \phi(\widehat{x}_{t + 1})$

The convergence properties of the algorithm are summarized in the following simple statement going back to [23]:

Theorem 5.8.3 Let Composite CGA be applied to problem (5.8.1) with convex f satisfying (5.8.27) with some $\kappa \in(1, 2]$ , and let D be the k · k-diameter of X. Denoting by φ the optimal value in (5.8.1), for all $t \geq 2$ one has

$$
\epsilon_{t} := \phi(x_{t}) - \phi_{*} \leq \frac{2LD^{\kappa}}{\kappa(3 - \kappa)} \gamma_{t}^{\kappa - 1} = \frac{2 \kappa LD^{\kappa}}{\kappa(3 - \kappa)(t + 1)^{\kappa - 1}}.\tag{5.8.62}
$$

Proof. Let

$$
\ell_{t}(x) = f(x_{t}) + \langle f^{\prime}(x_{t}), x - x_{t} \rangle + \Psi(x).
$$

We have

$$
\begin{array}{ll} & \epsilon_{t + 1} := \phi(x_{t + 1}) - \phi_{*} \leq \phi(\widehat{x}_{t + 1}) - \phi_{*} = \phi(x_{t} + \gamma_{t}(x_{t}^{+} - x_{t})) - \phi_{*} \\ = & \ell_{t}(x_{t} + \gamma_{t}(x_{t}^{+} - x_{t}) +[f(x_{t} + \gamma_{t}(x_{t}^{+} - x_{t})) - f(x_{t}) - \langle f^{\prime}(x_{t}), \gamma_{t}(x_{t}^{+} - x_{t})] - \phi_{*} \\ \leq & \big[(1 - \gamma_{t}) \underbrace{\ell(x_{t})}_{= \phi(x_{t})} + \gamma_{t} \ell(x_{t}^{+}) - \phi_{*} \big] + \frac{L}{\kappa}[\gamma_{t} D]^{\kappa} \\ &[\text{since} \ell_{t}(\cdot) \text{is convex and due to (5.8.27); note that} \| \gamma_{t}(x_{t}^{+} - x_{t}) \| \leq \gamma_{t} D] \\ = & \big[(1 - \gamma_{t}) \underbrace{[\phi(x_{t}) - \phi_{*}]}_{\epsilon_{t}} + \gamma_{t}[\ell(x_{t}^{+}) - \phi_{*}] \big] + \frac{L}{\kappa}[\gamma_{t} D]^{\kappa} \\ = &(1 - \gamma_{t}) \epsilon_{t} + \frac{L}{\kappa}[\gamma_{t} D]^{\kappa} + \gamma_{t}[\ell(x_{t}^{+}) - \phi_{*}] \\ \leq &(1 - \gamma_{t}) \epsilon_{t} + \frac{L}{\kappa}[\gamma_{t} D]^{\kappa} \\ &[\text{since} \ell_{t}(x) \leq \phi(x) \text{for all} x \in X \text{and} \ell(x_{t}^{+}) = \min_{x \in X} \ell_{t}(x)] \end{array}
$$

We have arrived at the recurrent inequality for the residuals $\epsilon_{t} = \phi(x_{t}) - \phi_{*} \colon$

$$
\epsilon_{t + 1} \leq(1 - \gamma_{t}) \epsilon_{t} + \frac{L}{\kappa}[\gamma_{t} D]^{\kappa}, \gamma_{t} = \frac{2}{t + 1}, t = 1, 2, \dots\tag{5.8.63}
$$

Let us prove by induction in $t \geq 2$ that for $t = 2, 3, \ldots$ it holds

$$
\epsilon_{t} \leq \frac{2LD^{\kappa}}{\kappa(3 - \kappa)} \gamma_{t}^{\kappa - 1}\tag{\(\left(*_{t}\right)\}
$$

The base $t ~ = ~ 2$ is evident: from (5.8.63) it follows that $\epsilon_{2} ~ \le ~ \frac{LD^{\kappa}}{\kappa}$ , and the latter quantity is $\begin{array}{r}{\le \frac{2LD^{\kappa}}{\kappa(3 - \kappa)} \gamma_{2}^{\kappa - 1} = \frac{2^{\kappa} LD^{\kappa}}{\kappa(3 - \kappa)}^{28}} \end{array}$ . Assuming that $(*_{t})$ holds true for some $t \geq 2$ , we get from (5.8.63) the first inequality in the following chain:

$$
\begin{array}{rl} &{\epsilon_{t + 1} \leq \frac{2LD^{\kappa}}{\kappa(3 - \kappa)}[\gamma_{t}^{\kappa - 1} - \gamma_{t}^{\kappa}] + \frac{LD^{\kappa}}{\kappa} \gamma_{t}^{\kappa}} \\ &{= \frac{2LD^{\kappa}}{(3 - \kappa) \kappa}[\gamma_{t}^{\kappa - 1} -[1 - \frac{3 - \kappa}{2}] \gamma_{t}^{\kappa}] = \frac{2LD^{\kappa}}{(3 - \kappa) \kappa} 2^{\kappa - 1}[(t + 1)^{-(\kappa - 1)} +(1 - \kappa)(t + 1)^{- \kappa}]} \\ &{\leq \frac{2LD^{\kappa}}{(3 - \kappa) \kappa} 2^{\kappa - 1}(t + 2)^{- \kappa - 1},} \end{array}
$$

where the concluding inequality in the chain is the gradient inequality for the convex function $u^{1 - \kappa}$ of $u > 0$ . We see that the validity of $(*_{t})$ for some t implies the validity of $\left(*_{t + 1} \right)$ ; induction, and thus the proof of Theorem 5.8.3, is complete. ✷

## 5.8.3.3 Bridging Fast and Conditional Gradient algorithms

Now assume that we are interested in problem (5.8.1) in the situation considered in section 5.8.2, so that X is a convex subset in Euclidean space E with a norm k · k, and X is equipped with a compatible with this norm DGF ω. From now on, we make two additional assumptions:

A. X is a compact set, and for some known $\Upsilon < \infty$ one has

$$
\forall(z \in X, w \in X): | \langle \omega^{\prime}(z), w - z \rangle | \leq \Upsilon.\tag{5.8.64}
$$

Remark: For all standard proximal setups described in section 5.3.3, one can take as Υ the quantity ${\cal O}(1) \Theta.$ , with Θ defined in section 5.3.2.

B. We have at our disposal a Composite Linear Minimization Oracle (5.8.59).

Lemma 5.8.2 Under assumptions A, B, let

$$
\epsilon = \Upsilon, \bar{\epsilon} = 3 \Upsilon.
$$

Then for every $\xi \in E, \alpha \ge 0$ and every $z \in X$ one has

$$
\begin{array}{ll}(a) & \text{CLMO}(\xi, \alpha) \in \underset{x \in X}{\operatorname{argmin}}^{\epsilon} \left\{\langle \xi, x \rangle + \alpha \Psi(x) + \omega(x) \right\}, \\(b) & \text{CLMO}(\xi, \alpha) \in \underset{x \in X}{\operatorname{argmin}}^{\bar{\epsilon}} \left\{\langle \xi, x \rangle + \alpha \Psi(x) + V_{z}(x) \right\}.\end{array}
$$

Proof. Given $\xi \in E, \alpha > 0, z \in X$ , and setting $w = \mathrm{CLMO}(\xi, \alpha)$ , we have Lemma 5.9.1 $w \in X$ and for some $\Psi^{\prime}(w) \in \partial_{X} \Psi(w)$ one has

$$
\langle \xi + \alpha \Psi^{\prime}(w), x - w \rangle \geq 0 \forall x \in X.
$$

Consequently,

$$
\forall x \in X: \langle \xi + \alpha \Psi^{\prime}(w) + \omega^{\prime}(w), x - w \rangle \geq \langle \omega^{\prime}(w), x - w \rangle \geq - \Upsilon,
$$

whence $w \in \operatorname{argmin}^{\epsilon} \left\{\langle \xi, x \rangle + \alpha \Psi(x) + \omega(x) \right\}$ . Similarly, x∈X

$$
\begin{array}{l} \forall x \in X: \langle \xi + \alpha \Psi^{\prime}(w) + \omega^{\prime}(w) - \omega^{\prime}(z), x - w \rangle \geq \langle \omega^{\prime}(w) - \omega^{\prime}(z), x - w \rangle \\ \geq - \Upsilon + \langle \omega^{\prime}(z), w - x \rangle = - \Upsilon + \langle \omega^{\prime}(z), w - z \rangle + \langle \omega^{\prime}(z), z - x \rangle \geq - 3 \Upsilon.\end{array}
$$

whence $w \in \underset{x \in X}{\operatorname{argmin}}^{\bar{\epsilon}} \left.\left.\xi, x \right.+ \alpha \Psi(x) + V_{z}(w) \right.$ . The case of $\alpha = 0$ is completely similar (redefine Ψ as identically zero and α as 1). ✷

Combining Lemma 5.8.2 and Theorem 5.8.1, we arrive at the following

Corollary 5.8.2 In the situation described in section 5.8.1.1 and under assumptions A, B, consider the implementation of the Fast Composite Gradient Method (5.8.8) – (5.8.14) where (5.8.8) is implemented as

$$
z_{t} = \mathrm{CLMO}(\nabla \ell_{t}(\cdot), \alpha_{t})\tag{5.8.65}
$$

(see (5.8.16)), and (5.8.12) is implemented as

$$
\hat{x}_{t + 1} = \mathrm{CLMO}(a_{t + 1} \nabla f(x_{t + 1}), a_{t + 1})\tag{5.8.66}
$$

(which, by Lemma 5.8.2, ensures (5.8.8), (5.8.12) with $\epsilon = \Upsilon, \bar{\epsilon} = 3 \Upsilon)$ . Assuming that (5.8.7) holds true and that $\delta_{t} \geq 0$ for all t (the latter definitely is the case when $L_{t} = L_{f}$ for all t), one has

$$
y_{t}, y_{t}^{+} \in X, \phi(y_{t}^{+}) - \phi_{*} \leq \phi(y_{t}) - \phi_{*} \leq A_{t}^{- 1}[V_{x_{\omega}}(x_{*}) + 4 \Upsilon t] \leq \frac{4L_{f}}{t^{2}}[V_{x_{\omega}}(x_{*}) + 4 \Upsilon t]\tag{5.8.67}
$$

for $t = 1, 2, \ldots$ where, as always, $x_{*}$ is an optimal solution to (5.8.1) and $x_{\omega}$ is the minimizer of $\omega(\cdot)$ on X.

A step of the algorithm, modulo updates $y_{t} \mapsto y_{t}^{+}$ , reduces to computing the value and the gradient of f at a point, computing the value of f at another point and to computing two values of Composite Linear Minimization Oracle, with no computations of the values and the derivatives of ω(·) at all.

Discussion. Observe that (5.8.64) clearly implies that $V_{x_{\omega}}(x_{*}) \leq \Upsilon$ , which combines with (5.8.67) to yield the relation

$$
\phi(y_{t}^{+}) - \phi_{*} \leq O(1) \frac{L_{f} \Upsilon}{t}, t = 1, 2, \dots\tag{5.8.68}
$$

On the other hand, under the premise of Corollary 5.8.2, we have at our disposal a Composite LMO for X and the function f in (5.8.1) is convex and satisfies (5.8.27) with $L = L_{f}$ and $\kappa = 2,$ , see (5.8.2). As a result, we can solve the problem of interest (5.8.1) by CGA ; the resulting eficiency estimate, as stated by Theorem 5.8.3 in the case of $L = L_{f}, \kappa = 2.$ , is

$$
\phi(x_{t}) - \phi_{*} \leq O(1) \frac{L_{f} D^{2}}{t},\tag{5.8.69}
$$

where D is the k · k-diameter of X. Assuming that

$$
\Upsilon \leq \alpha(X) D^{2}\tag{5.8.70}
$$

for properly selected $\alpha(X) \geq 1$ , the eficiency estimate (5.8.68) is by at most factor $O(1) \alpha(X)$ worse than the CGA eficiency estimate (5.8.69), so that for moderate $\alpha(X)$ the estimates are “nearly the same.” This is not too surprising, since FGM with imprecise proximal mappings given by (5.8.65), (5.8.66) is, basically, LMO-based rather than proximal algorithm. Indeed, with on-line tuning of $L_{t}{'} s$ , the implementation of FGM described in Corollary 5.8.2 requires operating with $\omega(z_{t}), \omega^{\prime}(z_{t})$ , and $\omega \big(\hat{x}_{t + 1} \big)$ solely in order to compute $\delta_{t}$ when checking whether this quantity is nonnegative. We could avoid the necessity to work with ω by computing $\| \widehat{x}_{t + 1} - z_{t} \|$ in order to build the lower bound

$$
\bar{\delta}_{t} = \left[\frac{1}{2A_{t + 1}} \| \widehat{x}_{t + 1} - z_{t} \|^{2} + \langle \nabla f(x_{t + 1}), y_{t + 1} - x_{t + 1} \rangle + f(x_{t + 1}) \right] - f(y_{t + 1})
$$

on $\delta_{t}$ , and to use this bound in the role of $\delta_{t}$ when updating $L_{t}{'} s$ (note that from item $5^{0}$ of the proof of Theorem 5.8.1 it follows that $\bar{\delta}_{t} \geq 0$ whenever $L_{t} = L_{f})$ . Finally, when both the norm $\| \cdot \|$ and $\omega(\cdot)$ are dificult to compute, we can use the of-line policy $L_{t} = L_{f}$ for all t, thus avoiding completely the necessity to check whether $\delta_{t} \geq 0$ and ending up with an algorithm, let it be called FGM-LMO, based solely on Composite Linear Minimization Oracle and never “touching” the DGF ω (which is used solely in the algorithm’s analysis). The eficiency estimate of the resulting algorithm is within $O(1) \alpha(X)$ factor of the one of CGA .

Note that in many important situations (5.8.70) indeed is satisfied with “quite moderate” $\alpha(X)$ . For example, for the Euclidean setup one can take $\alpha(X) = 1$ . For other standard proximal setups presented in section 5.3.3, except for the Entropy one, $\alpha(X)$ just logarithmically grows with the dimension of X.

An immediate question is, what, if any, do we gain when passing from simple and transparent CGA to much more sophisticated FGM-LMO. The answer is: as far as theoretical eficiency estimates are concerned, nothing is gained. Nevertheless, “bridging” proximal Fast Composite Gradient Method and LMO-based Conditional Gradients possesses some “methodological value.” For example, FGM-LMO replaces the precise composite prox mapping

$$
(\xi, z) \mapsto \underset{x \in X}{\operatorname{argmin}} \left[\langle \xi, x \rangle + \alpha \Psi(x) + V_{z}(x) \right]
$$

with its “most crude” approximation

$$
(\xi, z) \mapsto \operatorname{CLMO}(\xi, \alpha) \in \underset{x \in X}{\operatorname{Argmin}} \left[\langle \xi, x \rangle + \alpha \Psi(x) \right].
$$

which ignores Bregman distance $V_{z}(x)$ at all. In principle, one could utilize a less crude approximation of the composite prox mapping, “shifting” the CGA eficiency estimate $O(LD^{2} / t)$ towards the $O(LD^{2} / t^{2})$ eficiency estimate of FGM with precise proximal mappings – the option we here just mention rather than exploit in depth.

## 5.8.3.4 LMO-based implementation of Fast Universal Gradient Method

The above “bridging” of FGM and CGA as applied to Composite Minimization problem (5.8.1) with convex and “fully smooth” f (one with Lipschitz continuous gradient) can be extended to the case of less smooth $f^{\prime} s,$ , with FUGM in the role of FGM. Specifically, with assumptions A, B in force, let us look at Composite Minimization problem (5.8.1) with convex f satisfying the smoothness requirement (5.8.27) with some $L > 0$ and $\kappa \in(1, 2]$ (pay attention to $\kappa > 1 !)$

By Lemma 5.8.2, setting

$$
\nu = \Upsilon, \bar{\nu} = 3 \Upsilon.
$$

we ensure that for every $\xi \in E, \alpha \ge 0$ and every $z \in X$ one has

$$
\begin{array}{ll}(a) & \text{CLMO}(\xi, \alpha) \in \underset{x \in X}{\operatorname{argmin}}^{\nu} \left\{\langle \xi, x \rangle + \alpha \Psi(x) + \omega(x) \right\}, \\(b) & \text{CLMO}(\xi, \alpha) \in \underset{x \in X}{\operatorname{argmin}}^{\bar{\nu}} \left\{\langle \xi, x \rangle + \alpha \Psi(x) + V_{z}(x) \right\}.\end{array}\tag{5.8.71}
$$

Therefore we can consider the implementation of FUGM (in the sequel referred to as FUGM-LMO) where the target accuracy is a given $\epsilon$, the parameters ν and ¯ν are specified as $\nu = \Upsilon, \bar{\nu} = 3 \Upsilon$ , and

$z_{t}$ is defined according to

$$
z_{t} = \mathrm{CLMO}(\nabla \ell_{t}(\cdot), \alpha_{t}).
$$

with $\ell_{t}(\cdot), \alpha_{t}$ defined in (5.8.49);

$\hat{x}_{t + 1, \mu}$ is defined according to

$$
\hat{x}_{t + 1, \mu} = \mathrm{CLMO}(a_{t + 1, \mu} f^{\prime}(x_{t + 1, \mu}), a_{t + 1, \mu}).
$$

By (5.8.71), this implementation ensures (5.8.28), (5.8.32).

Let us upper-bound the quantity $[\nu + \bar{\nu}] NA_{N}^{- 1}$ appearing in (5.8.36) and (5.8.42).

Lemma 5.8.3 Let assumption A take place, and let FUGM-LMO be applied to Composite Minimization problem (5.8.1) with convex function f satisfying the smoothness condition (5.8.27) with some $L \in(0, \infty)$ and $\kappa \in(1, 2]$ . When the number of steps N at a stage of the method satisfies the relation

$$
N \geq N^{\#}(\epsilon) := \max \left[\frac{16L \Upsilon}{\epsilon}, 2^{\frac{5 \kappa}{2(\kappa - 1)}} \left(\frac{L \Upsilon^{\frac{\kappa}{2}}}{\epsilon}\right)^{\frac{1}{\kappa - 1}} \right]\tag{5.8.72}
$$

one has

$$
[\nu + \bar{\nu}] NA_{N}^{- 1} \leq \epsilon.
$$

Proof. We have $A_{N}^{- 1} N[\nu + \bar{\nu}] = 4 \Upsilon A_{N}^{- 1} N$ . Assuming $N \geq N^{\#}(\epsilon)$ , consider the same two cases as in the proof of Corollary 5.8.1. Similarly to this proof,

— in Case I we have

$$
\begin{array}{rl} & A_{N} \geq \frac{1}{8L^{\frac{2}{\kappa}}} N^{\frac{3 \kappa - 2}{\kappa}} \epsilon^{\frac{\kappa - 2}{\kappa}} \\ \Rightarrow & 4A_{N}^{- 1} N \Upsilon \leq 32 \Upsilon L^{\frac{2}{\kappa}} N^{\frac{2(1 - \kappa)}{\kappa}} \epsilon^{\frac{\kappa - 2}{\kappa}} \leq \epsilon[\text{due to} N \geq 2^{\frac{5 \kappa}{2(\kappa - 1)}} \left(\frac{L \Upsilon^{\frac{\kappa}{2}}}{\epsilon}\right)^{\frac{1}{\kappa - 1}}]; \end{array}
$$

— in Case II we have

$$
\begin{array}{rl} & A_{N} \geq \frac{N^{2}}{4L} \\ \Rightarrow & 4A_{N}^{- 1} N \Upsilon \leq 16 \frac{L \Upsilon}{N} \leq \epsilon[\text{due to} N \geq \frac{16L \Upsilon}{\epsilon}].\end{array}
$$

Combining Corollary 5.8.1, Lemma 5.8.3 and taking into account that the quantity Υ participating in assumption A can be taken as $\Theta,$ participating in Corollary 5.8.1 (see Discussion after Corollary 5.8.2), we arrive at the following result:

Corollary 5.8.3 Let assumption A take place, and let FUGM-LMO be applied to Composite Minimization problem (5.8.1) with convex function f satisfying, for some $L \in(0, \infty)$ and $\kappa \in(1, 2]$ , the smoothness condition (5.8.27). The on-line verifiable condition

$$
4A_{N}^{- 1} N \Upsilon \leq \epsilon\tag{5.8.73}
$$

ensure that the result $y_{N}^{+}$ of N -step stage $\boldsymbol{S_{N}}$ of FUGM-LMO satisfies the relation

$$
\phi(y_{N}^{+}) - \phi_{*} \leq 3 \epsilon.
$$

Relation (5.8.73) definitely is satisfied when

$$
N \geq N(\epsilon) := \max[N_{\#}(\epsilon), N^{\#}(\epsilon)],
$$

where

$$
N_{\#}(\epsilon) = \max \left[2 \frac{\sqrt{L} \Upsilon}{\sqrt{\epsilon}}, \left(\frac{8^{\frac{\kappa}{2}} L \Upsilon^{\frac{\kappa}{2}}}{\epsilon}\right)^{\frac{2}{3 \kappa - 2}} \right]\tag{5.8.74}
$$

(cf. (5.8.39)) and $N^{\#}(\epsilon)$ is given by (5.8.72).

Remarks. I. Note that FUGM-LMO does not require computing $\omega(\cdot)$ and $\omega^{\prime}(\cdot)$ and operates solely with $\mathrm{CLMO}(\cdot, \cdot)$ , First Order oracle for $f,$ and the Zero Order oracle for $\| \cdot \|$ (the latter is used to compute $\delta_{t, \mu}$ , see (5.8.34)). Assuming κ and L known in advance, we can further avoid the necessity to compute the norm k · k and can skip, essentially, the Inner loop. To this end it sufices to carry out a single step $\mu = 0$ of the Inner loop with $L_{t, 0}$ set to $L^{\frac{2}{\kappa}}[N / \epsilon]^{\frac{2 - \kappa}{\kappa}}$ and to skip computing $\delta_{t, 0} \mathrm{~ - ~}$ the latter quantity automatically is $\ge - \epsilon / N$ , see item $\mathbf{1}^{0}$ in the proof of Theorem 5.8.2, p. 521.

II. It is immediately seen that for small enough values of $\epsilon > 0$ , we have $N^{\#}(\epsilon) \geq N_{\#}(\epsilon)$ , so that the total, over all stages, number of outer steps before $\epsilon$-solution is built is upper-bounded by $O(1) N^{\#}(\epsilon);$ with “safe” stepsize policy, see Remark 5.8.1, and small $\epsilon$ the total, over all stages, number of Inner steps also is upper-bounded by $O(1) N^{\#}(\epsilon)$ . Note that in the case of (5.8.70) and for small enough $\epsilon > 0$ , we have

$$
N^{\#}(\epsilon) \leq[O(1) \alpha(X)]^{\frac{\kappa}{2(\kappa - 1)}} \left(\frac{LD^{\kappa}}{\epsilon}\right)^{\frac{1}{\kappa - 1}},
$$

implying that the complexity bound of FUGM-LMO for small $\epsilon$ is at most by factor $[O(1) \alpha(X)]^{\frac{\kappa}{2(\kappa - 1)}}$ worse that the complexity bound for CGA as given by (5.8.62). The conclusions one can make from these observations are completely similar to those related to FGM-LMO, see p. 528.

## 5.9 Appendix: Some proofs

## 5.9.1 A useful technical lemma

Lemma 5.9.1 Let X be a closed convex domain in Euclidean space $E, \ :(\parallel \cdot \parallel, \omega(\cdot))$ be a proximal setup for X, let Ψ $: X \to \mathbb{R} \cup \{+ \infty\}$ be a lower semicontinuous convex function which is finite on the relative interior of $X$ , and let $\phi(\cdot) : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be a convex continuously diferentiable function.The minimizer $z_{+}$ of the function $\omega(w) + \phi(w) + \Psi(w)$ on X exists and is unique, and there exists $\Psi^{\prime} \in \partial \Psi(z_{+})$ such that

$$
\langle \omega^{\prime}(z_{+}) + \phi^{\prime}(z_{+}) + \Psi^{\prime}, w - z_{+} \rangle \geq 0 \forall w \in X.\tag{5.9.1}
$$

If $\Psi(\cdot)$ is diferentiable at $z_{+}$ , one can take $\Psi^{\prime} = \nabla \Psi(z_{+})$

Proof. Let us set $\widehat \omega(w) = \omega(w) + \phi(w)$ . Since $\phi$ is continuously diferentiable and convex on $X.$ , ω possesses the same convexity and smoothness properties as $\omega,$ specifically, ω is continuously diferentiable and strongly convex, with modulus 1 w.r.t. $\| \cdot \|_{;}$ , on $X$

To prove existence and uniqueness of $z_{+}$ , let us set

$$
X^{+} = \{(x, t) \in E \times \mathbb{R}: x \in X, t \geq \Psi(x)\}, f(x, t) = \widehat{\omega}(x) + t: X^{+} \to \mathbb{R}.
$$

$X^{+}$ is a closed convex set (since X is closed and convex, and $\Psi$ is convex, lower semicontinuous, and finite on the relative interior of X), and f is a continuously diferentiable convex function on x. Besides this, the level sets $X_{a}^{+} = \{(x, t) \in X^{+} : f(x, t) \leq a\}$ are bounded for every $a \in \mathbb{R}$

Indeed, selecting ${\bar{x}} \in$ rint X and selecting somehow $g \in \partial_{X} \Psi(\bar{x})$ , we have

$$
\begin{array}{l} \forall((x, t) \in X^{+}): \\ f(x, t) \geq \widehat{\omega}(x) + \Psi(x) \geq \bar{f}(x) := \widehat{\omega}(\bar{x}) + \Psi(\bar{x}) + \langle \widehat{\omega}^{\prime}(\bar{x}) + g, x - \bar{x} \rangle + \frac{1}{2} \| x - \bar{x} \|^{2} \end{array}
$$

It follows that when $(x, t) \in X_{a}^{+}$ , we have $x \in X_{a} : = \{x \in X :{\bar{f}}(x) \leq a\}$ . The set $X_{a}$ clearly is bounded, and therefore $\Psi(x) \geq \Psi({\bar{x}}) + \langle g, x -{\bar{x}} \rangle \geq a^{\prime} \in \mathbb{R}$ for some $a^{\prime} \in \mathbb{R}$ and all $x \in X_{a}$ Assuming, on the contrary to what should be proved, that $X_{a}^{+}$ is unbounded, there exists an unbounded sequence $(x_{i}, t_{i}) \in X_{a}^{+}$ ; since $x_{i} \in X_{a}.$ the sequence $\{x_{i}\}$ is bounded, whence the sequence $\{t_{i}\}$ is unbounded; the latter sequence is below bounded due to $t_{i} \geq \Psi(x_{i}) \geq a^{\prime}$ implying that $\{t_{i}\}$ is not bounded from above. Passing to a subsequence, we can assume that $t_{i} \to \infty$ , whence $a \geq f(x_{i}, t_{i}) = \widehat{\omega}(x_{i}) + t_{i}.$ , which is a desired contradiction: the right hand side in the latter inequality goes to ∞ as $i \to \infty$ due to the fact that $t_{i} \to \infty, i \to \infty$ while the sequence $\{\widehat{\omega}(x_{i})\}$ is bounded along with the sequence $\{x_{i}\}$

Since $X^{+}$ is closed and the level sets of $f$ are bounded, $f$ achieves its minimum at some point $(z_{+}, t_{+}) \in X^{+};$ by evident reasons, $ t _ { + } = \Psi ( z _ { + } )$ , and $z_{+}$ is a minimizer of $F(x) : = \widehat{\omega}(x) + \Psi(x)$ on $X.$ , so that such a minimizer does exist; its uniqueness is readily given by strong convexity of $F(x)$ (implied by strong convexity of $\widehat{\omega}$ and convexity of Ψ). By optimality condition we have

$$
\forall(x, t) \in X^{+}: \langle \widehat{\omega}^{\prime}(z_{+}), x - z_{+} \rangle + t - t_{+} \geq 0,
$$

whence

$$
\forall x \in X: \Psi(x) - \Psi(z_{+}) + \langle \widehat{\omega}^{\prime}(z_{+}), x - z_{+} \rangle \geq 0
$$

implying that $\Psi^{\prime} : = - \widehat{\omega}^{\prime}(z_{+}) \in \partial_{X} \Psi(z_{+})$ , so that $\Psi^{\prime} + \omega^{\prime}(z_{+}) + \phi^{\prime}(z_{+}) = \Psi^{\prime} + \widehat{\omega}^{\prime}(z_{+}) = 0$ , implying that $\left(5.9.1 \right)$ holds true. Finally, assuming that Ψ has a derivative at $z_{+}$ , the convex function $\Psi(x) + \omega(x) + \phi(x)$ which achieves its minimum on $X{\mathrm{~ at ~}} z_{+}$ is diferentiable at $z_{+}$ , the derivative being $\nabla \Psi(z_{+}) + \omega^{\prime}(z_{+}) +$ $\psi^{\prime}(z_{+})$ , and validity of (5.9.1) with $\Psi = \nabla \Psi(z_{+})$ is readily given by optimality conditions. ✷

## 5.9.2 Justifying Ball setup

Justification of Ball setup is trivial.

## 5.9.3 Justifying Entropy setup

For $x \in \Delta_{n}^{+}$ and $h \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ , setting $z_{i} =(x_{i} + \delta / n) /(1 + \delta)$ , so that $0 < z \in \Delta_{n}^{+} z_{i}$ , we have

$$
\sum_{i} | h_{i} | = \sum_{i}[| h_{i} | / \sqrt{z_{i}}] \sqrt{z_{i}} \leq \sqrt{\sum_{i} h_{i}^{2} / z_{i}} \sqrt{\sum_{i} z_{i}} \leq \sqrt{\sum_{i} h_{i}^{2} / z_{i}} = \sqrt{h^{T} \omega^{\prime \prime}(x) h},
$$

that is,

$$
h^{T} \omega^{\prime \prime}(x) h \geq \| h \|_{1}^{2},
$$

which immediately implies that ω is strongly convex, with modulus 1, w.r.t. $\| \cdot \|_{1}$

Now let us upper-bound Θ. Given $x, x^{\prime} \in \Delta_{n}^{+}$ and setting $y_{i} = x_{i} + \delta / n, y_{i}^{\prime} = x_{i} 6 \prime + \delta / n$ , we have

$$
\begin{array}{l} V_{x}(x^{\prime}) =(1 + \delta)[\sum_{i} y_{i}^{\prime} \ln(y_{i}^{\prime}) - \sum_{i} y_{i} \ln(y_{i}) - \sum_{i}[y_{i}^{\prime} - y_{i}][1 + \ln(y_{i})]] \\ =(1 + \delta)[\sum_{i}[y_{i} - y_{i}^{\prime}] + \sum_{i} y_{i}^{\prime} \ln(y_{i}^{\prime} / y_{i})] \leq(1 + \delta)[1 + \sum_{i} y_{i}^{\prime} \ln((1 + \delta / n) n / \delta)] \\ \leq(1 + \delta)[1 +(1 + \delta) \ln(2n / \delta)], \end{array}
$$

and (5.3.8) follows. When justifying Entropy setup, the only not completely trivial task is to check that $\begin{array}{r}{\omega(x) = \sum_{i = 1}^{n} x_{i} \ln(x_{i})} \end{array}$ is strongly convex, modulus 1, w.r.t. $\| \cdot \|_{1}$ , on the set $\Delta^{o} = \{x \in \Delta_{n}^{+} : x > 0\}$ . An evident sufficient condition for this is the relation

$$
D^{2}(x)[h, h] := \frac{d^{2}}{dt^{2}} \big |_{t = 0} \omega(x + th) \geq \kappa \| h \|^{2} \quad \forall(x, h: x > 0, \sum_{i} x_{i} \leq 1)\tag{5.9.2}
$$

(why?) To verify (5.9.2), observe that for $x \in \Delta^{o}$ we have

$$
\| h \|_{1}^{2} = \left[\sum_{i} | h_{i} | \right]^{2} = \left[\sum_{i} \frac{| h_{i} |}{\sqrt{x_{i}}} \sqrt{x_{i}} \right]^{2} \leq \left[\sum_{i} x_{i} \right] \left[\sum_{i} \frac{h_{i}^{2}}{x_{i}} \right] = h^{T} \omega^{\prime \prime}(x) h.
$$

## 5.9.4 Justifying $\ell_{1} / \ell_{2}$ setup

All we need is given by the following two claims:

Theorem 5.9.1 Let $E = \mathbb{R}^{k_{1}} \times \ldots \times \mathbb{R}^{k_{n}}, \parallel \cdot \parallel$ be the $\ell_{1} / \ell_{2}$ norm on $E,$ and let Z be the unit ball of the norm $\| \cdot \|$ . Then the function

$$
\omega(x =[x^{1};...; x^{n}]) = \frac{1}{p \gamma} \sum_{j = 1}^{n} \| x^{j} \|_{2}^{p}, p = \left\{\begin{array}{ll} 2, & n \leq 2 \\ 1 + \frac{1}{\ln n}, & n \geq 3 \end{array} \right., \gamma = \left\{\begin{array}{ll} 1, & n = 1 \\ 1 / 2, & n = 2 \\ \frac{1}{\operatorname{e} \ln(n)}, & n > 2 \end{array} : Z \to \mathbb{R} \right.\tag{5.9.3}
$$

is a continuously diferentiable DGF for $Z$ compatible with $\| \cdot \|$ . As a result, whenever $X \subset Z$ is a nonempty closed convex subset of $Z,$ the restriction $\omega \big |_{X}$ of ω on X is DGF for X compatible with $\| \cdot \|$ and the $\omega \big |_{X}$ -radius of X can be bounded as

$$
\Omega \leq \sqrt{2 e \ln(n + 1)}.\tag{5.9.4}
$$

Corollary 5.9.1 Let E and $\| \cdot \|$ be as in Theorem 5.9.1. Then the function

$$
\widehat{\omega}(x =[x^{1}; \dots; x^{n}]) = \frac{n^{(p - 1)(2 - p) / p}}{2 \gamma} \left[\sum_{j = 1}^{n} \| x^{j} \|_{2}^{p} \right]^{\frac{2}{p}}: E \to \mathbb{R}\tag{5.9.5}
$$

with $p, \gamma$ given by (5.9.3) is a continuously diferentiable DGF for E compatible with $\| \cdot \|$ . As a result, whenever X is a nonempty closed subset of E, the restriction ${\widehat{\omega}}{\big \vert}_{X}$ of ω onto X is a DGF for X compatible with $\| \cdot \|$ . When, in addition, $X \subset \{x \in E : \| x \| \leq R\}$ with $R < \infty$ , the ${\widehat{\omega}}{\big |}_{X}$ -radius of X can be bounded as

$$
\Omega \leq O(1) \sqrt{\ln(n + 1)} R.\tag{5.9.6}
$$

## 5.9.4.1 Proof of Theorem 5.9.1

We have for $x =[x^{1};...; x^{n}] \in Z^{\prime} = \{x \in Z : x^{j}[x] \neq 0 \forall j\},{\mathrm{and ~}} h =[h^{1};...; h^{n}] \in E \colon$ :

$$
\begin{array}{l} \gamma D \omega(x)[h] = \sum_{j = 1}^{n} \| x^{j} \|_{2}^{p - 2} \langle x^{j}, h^{j} \rangle \\ \gamma D^{2} \omega(x)[h, h] = -(2 - p) \sum_{j = 1}^{n} \| x^{j} \|_{2}^{p - 4}[\langle x^{j}, h^{j} \rangle]^{2} + \sum_{j = 1}^{n} \| x^{j} \|_{2}^{p - 2} \| h^{j} \|_{2}^{2} \\ \geq \sum_{j = 1}^{n} \| x^{j} \|_{2}^{p - 2} \| h^{j} \|_{2}^{2} -(2 - p) \sum_{j = 1}^{n} \| x^{j} \|_{2}^{p - 4} \| x^{j} \|_{2}^{2} \| h^{j} \|_{2}^{2} \\ \geq(p - 1) \sum_{j = 1}^{n} \| x^{j} \|_{2}^{p - 2} \| h^{j} \|_{2}^{2} \\ \Rightarrow \left[\sum_{j} \| h^{j} \|_{2} \right]^{2} = \left[\sum_{j = 1}^{n}[\| h^{j} \|_{2} \| x^{j} \|_{2}^{\frac{p - 2}{2}}] \| x^{j} \|_{2}^{\frac{2 - p}{2}} \right]^{2} \leq \left[\sum_{j = 1}^{n} \| h^{j} \|_{2}^{2} \| z^{j} \|_{2}^{p - 2} \right] \left[\sum_{j = 1}^{n} \| x^{j} \|_{2}^{2 - p} \right] \\ \Rightarrow \left[\sum_{j} \| h^{j} \|_{2} \right]^{2} \leq \left[\sum_{j = 1}^{n} \| x^{j} \|_{2}^{2 - p} \right] \frac{\gamma}{p - 1} D^{2} \omega(x)[h, h] \end{array}
$$

Setting $t_{j} = \| x^{j} \|_{2} \geq 0$ , we have $\textstyle \sum_{j} t_{j} \leq 1$ , whence due to $0 \leq 2 - p \leq 1$ it holds $\begin{array}{r}{\sum_{j} t_{j}^{2 - p} \le n^{p - 1}} \end{array}$ . Thus,

$$
\left[\sum_{j} \| h^{j} \|_{2} \right]^{2} \leq n^{p - 1} \frac{\gamma}{p - 1} D^{2} \omega(x)[h, h]\tag{5.9.7}
$$

while

$$
\max_{x \in Z} \omega(x) - \min_{x \in Z} \omega(x) \leq \frac{1}{\gamma p}\tag{5.9.8}
$$

With $p, \gamma$ as stated in Theorem 5.9.1, when $n \geq 3$ we get $\begin{array}{r}{\frac{\gamma}{p - 1} n^{p - 1} = 1} \end{array}$ , and similarly for $n = 1, 2.$ Consequently,

$$
\forall(x \in Z^{\prime}, h =[h^{1};...; h^{n}]): \left[\sum_{j = 1}^{n} \| h^{j} \|_{2} \right]^{2} \leq D^{2} \omega(x)[h, h].\tag{5.9.9}
$$

Since $\omega(\cdot)$ is continuously diferentiable and the complement of $Z^{\prime}$ in $Z$ is the union of finitely many proper linear subspaces of E, (5.9.9) implies that ω is strongly convex on $Z,$ modulus 1, w.r.t. the $\ell_{1} / \ell_{2}$ norm $\| \cdot \|$ . Besides this, we have

$$
\frac{1}{\gamma p} \left\{\begin{array}{ll} = \frac{1}{2}, & n = 1 \\ = 1, & n = 2 \\ \leq e \ln(n), & n \geq 3 \end{array} \right\} \leq O(1) \ln(n + 1).
$$

which combines with (5.9.8) to imply (5.9.4).

## 5.9.4.2 Proof of Corollary 5.9.1

Let

$$
w(x =[x^{1}; \dots; x^{n}]) = \frac{1}{\gamma p} \sum_{j = 1}^{n} \| x^{j} \|_{2}^{p}: E := \mathbb{R}^{k_{1}} \times \dots \times \mathbb{R}^{k_{n}} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\tag{5.9.10}
$$

with $\gamma, p$ given by (5.9.3); note that $p \in(1, 2]$ . As we know from Theorem 5.9.1, the restriction of $w(\cdot)$ onto the unit ball of $\ell_{1} / \ell_{2}$ norm $\| \cdot \|$ is continuously diferentiable and strongly convex, modulus 1, w.r.t. $\| \cdot \|.$ Besides this, $w(\cdot)$ clearly is nonnegative and positively homogeneous of the degree p: $w(\lambda x) \equiv | \lambda |^{p} w(x)$ Note that the outlined properties clearly imply that $w(\cdot)$ is convex and continuously diferentiable on the entire E. We need the following simple

Lemma 5.9.2 Let H be a Euclidean space, $\| \cdot \|_{H}$ be a norm (not necessary the Euclidean one), on $H$ and let $Y_{H} = \{y \in H : \| y \|_{H} \leq 1\}$ . Let, further, $\zeta : H \mathbb{R}$ be a nonnegative continuously diferentiable function, absolutely homogeneous of a degree $p \in(1, 2]$ , and strongly convex, modulus 1, w.r.t. $\| \cdot \|_{H}$ , on $Y_{H}$ . Then the function

$$
\widehat{\zeta}(y) = \zeta^{2 / p}(y): H \to \mathbb{R}
$$

is continuously diferentiable homogeneous of degree 2 and strongly convex, modulus

$$
\beta = \frac{2}{p} \left[\min_{y: \| y \|_{H} = 1} \zeta^{2 / p - 1}(y) \right],
$$

w.r.t. $\| \cdot \|_{H}$ , on the entire $H$

Proof. The facts that $\widehat{\zeta}(\cdot)$ is continuously diferentiable convex and homogeneous of degree 2 function on H is evident, and all we need is to verify that the function is strongly convex, modulus $\beta,$ , w.r.t k · k<sub>H</sub> :

$$
\langle \widehat{\zeta}^{\prime}(y) - \widehat{\zeta}^{\prime}(y^{\prime}), y - y^{\prime} \rangle \geq \beta \| y - y^{\prime} \|_{H}^{2} \forall y, y^{\prime}.\tag{5.9.11}
$$

It is immediately seen that for a continuously diferentiable function ${\widehat{\zeta}},$ the target property is local: to establish (5.9.11), it sufices to verify that every $\bar{y} \in H \backslash \{0\}$ admits a neighbourhood $U$ such that the inequality in (5.9.11) holds true for al $y, y^{\prime} \in U$ . By evident homogeneity reasons, in the case of homogeneous of degree 2 function ${\widehat{\zeta}},$ to establish the latter property for every $\bar{y} \in H \backslash \{0\}$ is the same as to prove it in the case of $\| \bar{y} \|_{H} = 1 - \epsilon$ , for any fixed $\epsilon \in(0, 1 / 3)$ Thus, let us fix an $\epsilon \in(0, 1)$ and $\bar{y} \in H$ with $\lVert \bar{y} \rVert_{H} = 1 - \epsilon.$ , and let $U = \{y^{\prime} : \| y^{\prime} - \bar{y} \|_{H} \leq \epsilon / 2\}$ , so that $U$ is a compact set contained in the interior of $Y_{H}$ . Now let $\phi(\cdot)$ be a nonnegative $\mathrm{C}^{\infty}$ function on $H$ which vanishes outside of $Y_{H}$ and has unit integral w.r.t. the Lebesgue measure on H. For $0 < r \leq 1$ , let us set

$$
\phi_{r}(y) = r^{- \dim H} \phi(y / r), \zeta_{r}(\cdot) =(\zeta * \phi_{r})(\cdot), \widehat{\zeta}_{r}(\cdot) = \zeta_{r}^{2 / p}(\cdot),
$$

where ∗ stands for convolution. As $r + 0$ , the nonnegative $\mathrm{C}^{\infty}$ function $\zeta_{r}(\cdot)$ converges with the first order derivative, uniformly on $U,$ , to $\zeta(\cdot)$ , and $\widehat{\zeta_{r}}(\cdot)$ converges with the first order derivative, uniformly on $U, \mathrm{to} \widehat{\zeta}(\cdot)$ . Besides this, when $r < \epsilon / 2$ , the function $\zeta_{r}(\cdot)$ is, along with $\zeta(\cdot)$ , strongly convex, modulus 1, w.r.t. $\| \cdot \|_{H}$ on $U$ (since $\zeta_{r}^{\prime}(\cdot)$ is the convolution of $\zeta^{\prime}(\cdot)$ and $\phi_{r}(\cdot))$ . Since $\zeta_{r} ~ \mathrm{is} ~ \mathrm{C}^{\infty}$ , we conclude that when $r < \epsilon / 2$ , we have

$$
D^{2} \zeta_{r}(y)[h, h] \geq \| h \|_{H}^{2} \forall(y \in U, h \in H),
$$

whence also

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} D^{2} \widehat{\zeta_{r}}(y)[h, h] & = & \frac{2}{p} \left(\frac{2}{p} - 1\right) \zeta_{r}^{2 / p - 2}(y)[D \zeta_{r}(y)[h]]^{2} + \frac{2}{p} \zeta_{r}^{2 / p - 1}(y) D^{2} \zeta_{r}[h, h] \\ & \geq & \frac{2}{p} \zeta_{r}^{2 / p - 1}(y) \| h \|_{H}^{2} \forall(h \in H, y \in U).\end{array}
$$

It follows that when $r < \epsilon / 2.$ , we have

$$
\begin{array}{c} \langle \widehat{\zeta_{r}}(y) - \widehat{\zeta_{r}^{\prime}}(y^{\prime}), y - y^{\prime} \rangle \geq \beta_{r}[U] \| y - y^{\prime} \|_{H}^{2} \forall y, y^{\prime} \in U, \\ \beta_{r}[U] = \frac{2}{p} \min_{u \in U} \zeta_{r}^{2 / p - 1}(u).\end{array}
$$

As $r + 0, \widehat{\zeta}_{r}^{\prime}(\cdot)$ uniformly on $U$ converges to $\widehat{\zeta^{\prime}}(\cdot)$ , and $\beta_{r}[U]$ converges to $\begin{array}{r}{\beta[U] = \frac{2}{p} \underset{uU}{\operatorname{min}} \zeta^{2 / p - 1}(u) \ge} \end{array}$ $(1 - 3 \epsilon / 2)^{2 - p} \beta$ (recall the origin of $\beta$ and U and note that ζ is absolutely homogeneous of degree $p)$ , and we arrive at the relation

$$
\langle \widehat{\zeta}^{\prime}(y) - \widehat{\zeta}^{\prime}(y^{\prime}), y - y^{\prime} \rangle \geq(1 - 3 \epsilon / 2)^{2 - p} \beta \| y - y^{\prime} \|_{H}^{2} \forall y, y^{\prime} \in U.
$$

As we have already explained, the just established validity of the latter relation for every $U = \{y \ :$ $\| y - \bar{y} \|_{H} \le \epsilon / 2\}$ and every $\bar{y}, \| \bar{y} \|_{H} = 1 - \epsilon$ implies that $\widehat{\zeta}$ is strongly convex, modulus $(1 - 3 \epsilon / 2)^{2 - p} \beta.$ on the entire H. Since $\epsilon > 0$ is arbitrary, Lemma 5.9.2 is proved. ✷

B. Applying Lemma 5.9.2 to E in the role of $H,$ , the $\ell_{1} / \ell_{2}$ norm $\| \cdot \|$ in the role of $\| \cdot \|_{H}$ and the function $w(\cdot)$ given by (5.9.10) in the role of $\zeta,$ we conclude that the function $\widehat{w}(\cdot) \equiv w^{2 / p}(\cdot)$ is strongly convex, modulus $\begin{array}{r}{\beta = \frac{2}{p} \left[\operatorname{min}_{y} \{w(y) : y \in E, \lVert y \rVert = 1\} \right]^{2 / p - 1}} \end{array}$ , w.r.t. $\| \cdot \|$ , on the entire space $E,$ , whence the function $\beta^{- 1} w(z)$ is continuously diferentiable and strongly convex, modulus 1, w.r.t. $\| \cdot \|$ , on the entire $E.$ This observation, in view of the evident relation $\textstyle{\beta ={\frac{2}{p}}(n^{1 - p} \gamma^{- 1} p^{- 1})^{2 / p - 1}}$ and the origin of $\gamma, p,$ immediately implies all claims in Corollary 5.9.1. ✷

## 5.9.5 Justifying Nuclear norm setup

All we need is given by the following two claims:

$$
m = \sum_{j = 1}^{n} \mu_{j}.
$$

Theorem 5.9.2 Let $\boldsymbol{\mu} =(\mu_{1},..., \mu_{n})$ and $\nu =(nu_{1},..., \nu_{n})$ be collections of positive reals such that $\mu_{j} \leq \nu_{j}$ for all j, and let

With $E = \mathbf{M}^{\mu \nu}$ and $\| \cdot \| = \| \cdot \|_{\mathrm{nuc}}$ , let $Z = \{x \in E : \| x \|_{\mathrm{nuc}} \leq 1\}$ . Then the function

$$
\omega(x) = \frac{4 \sqrt{e} \ln(2m)}{2^{q}(1 + q)} \sum_{i = 1}^{m} \sigma_{i}^{1 + q}(x): Z \to \mathbb{R}, q = \frac{1}{2 \ln(2m)},\tag{5.9.12}
$$

is continuously diferentiable DGF for Z compatible with $\| \cdot \|_{\mathrm{nuc}}$ , so that for every nonempty closed convex subset X of Z, the function $\omega \big |_{X}$ is a DGF for X compatible with $\| \cdot \|_{\mathrm{nuc}}$ . Besides this, the $\omega \big |_{X}$ radius of X can be bounded as

$$
\Omega \leq 2 \sqrt{2 \sqrt{e} \ln(2m)} \leq 4 \sqrt{\ln(2m)}.\tag{5.9.13}
$$

Corollary 5.9.2 Let $\mu, \nu, m, E, \parallel \cdot \parallel$ be as in Theorem 5.9.2. Then the function

$$
\widehat{\omega}(x) = 2 e \ln(2m) \left[\sum_{j = 1}^{m} \sigma_{j}^{1 + q}(x) \right]^{\frac{2}{1 + q}}: E \rightarrow \mathbb{R}, q = \frac{1}{2 \ln(2m)}\tag{5.9.14}
$$

is continuously diferentiable DGF for $Z = E$ compatible with $\| \cdot \|_{\mathrm{nuc}},$ , so that for every nonempty closed convex set $X \subset E$ , the function ${\widehat{\omega}}{\big \vert}_{X}$ is a DGF for X compatible with $\| \cdot \|_{\mathrm{nuc}}$ . Besides this, if X is bounded, the ${\widehat{\omega}}{\big \vert}_{X}$ radius of X can be bounded as

$$
\Omega \leq O(1) \sqrt{\ln(2 \mu)} R,\tag{5.9.15}
$$

where $R < \infty$ is such that $X \subset \{x \in E : \| x \|_{\mathrm{nuc}} \leq R\}$

## 5.9.5.1 Proof of Theorem 5.9.2

A. As usual, let $\mathbf{S}^{n}$ be the space of n × n symmetric matrices equipped with the Frobenius inner product; for $y \in \mathbf{S}^{n}$ , let $\lambda(y)$ be the vector of eigenvalues of y (taken with their multiplicities in the non-ascending order), and let $| y |_{1} = \| \lambda(y) \|_{1}$ be the trace norm.

Lemma 5.9.3 Let $N \geq M \geq 2$ , and let F be a linear subspace in $\mathbf{S}^{N}$ such that every matrix $y \in F$ has at most M nonzero eigenvalues. Let $\begin{array}{r}{q = \frac{1}{2 \ln(M)}} \end{array}$ , so that $0 < q < 1$ , and let

$$
\widehat{\omega}(y) = \frac{4 \sqrt{e} \ln(M)}{1 + q} \sum_{j = 1}^{N} | \lambda_{j}(y) |^{1 + q}: \mathbf{S}^{N} \to \mathbb{R}.
$$

The function $\widehat{\omega}(\cdot)$ is continuously diferentiable, convex, and its restriction on the set $Y_{F} = \{y \in F$ $| y |_{1} \le 1\}$ is strongly convex, modulus 1, w.r.t. | · |<sub>1</sub>.

Proof. ${\bf 1}^{0}$ . Let $0 < q < 1$ . Consider the following function of $y \in \mathbf{S}^{N}$

$$
\chi(y) = \frac{1}{1 + q} \sum_{j = 1}^{N} | \lambda_{j}(y) |^{1 + q} = \operatorname{Tr}(f(y)), f(s) = \frac{1}{1 + q} | s |^{1 + q}.\tag{5.9.16}
$$

${\bf 2}^{0}$ . Function $f(s)$ is continuously diferentiable on the axis and twice continuously diferentiable outside of the origin; consequently, we can find a sequence of polynomials $f_{k}(s)$ converging, as $k \infty$ , to $f$ along with their first derivatives uniformly on every compact subset of R and, besides this, converging to $f$ uniformly along with the first and the second derivative on every compact subset of $\mathbb{R} \backslash \{0\}$ . Now let $y, h \in{\bf S}^{N}$ , let $y = u \mathrm{Diag} \{\lambda\} u^{T}$ be the eigenvalue decomposition of $y,$ and let $h = u \widehat{h} u^{T}$ . For a polynomial $\textstyle p(s) = \sum_{k = 0}^{K} p_{k} s^{k}$ , setting $\begin{array}{r}{P(w) = \mathrm{Tr}(\sum_{k = 0}^{K} p_{k} w^{k}) : \mathbf{S}^{N} \to \mathbb{R}} \end{array}$ , and denoting by γ a closed contour in C encircling the spectrum of y, we have

$$
\begin{array}{ll}(a) & P(y) = \mathrm{Tr}(p(y)) = \sum_{j = 1}^{N} p(\lambda_{j}(y)) \\(b) & DP(y)[h] = \sum_{k = 1}^{K} kp_{k} \mathrm{Tr}(y^{k - 1} h) = \mathrm{Tr}(p^{\prime}(y) h) = \sum_{j = 1}^{N} p^{\prime}(\lambda_{j}(y)) \widehat{h}_{jj} \\(c) & D^{2} P(y)[h, h] = \frac{d}{dt} \big |_{t = 0} DP(y + th)[h] = \frac{d}{dt} \big |_{t = 0} \mathrm{Tr}(p^{\prime}(y + th) h) \\ & = \frac{d}{dt} \big |_{t = 0} \frac{1}{2 \pi \imath} \oint_{\gamma} \mathrm{Tr}(h(zI -(y + th))^{- 1}) p^{\prime}(z) dz = \frac{1}{2 \pi \imath} \oint_{\gamma} \mathrm{Tr}(h(zI - y)^{- 1} h(zI - y)^{- 1}) p^{\prime}(z) dz \\ & = \frac{1}{2 \pi \imath} \oint_{\gamma} \sum_{i, j = 1}^{N} \widehat{h}_{ij}^{2} \frac{p^{\prime}(z)}{(z - \lambda_{i}(y))(z - \lambda_{j}(y))} dz = \sum_{i, j = 1}^{n} \widehat{h}_{ij}^{2} \Gamma_{ij}, \\ & \Gamma_{ij} = \left\{\begin{array}{ll} \frac{p^{\prime}(\lambda_{i}(y)) - p^{\prime}(\lambda_{j}(y))}{\lambda_{i}(y) - \lambda_{j}(y)}, & \lambda_{i}(y) \neq \lambda_{j}(y) \\ p^{\prime \prime}(\lambda_{i}(y)), & \lambda_{i}(y) = \lambda_{j}(y) \end{array} \right.\end{array}
$$

We conclude from $(a, b)$ that as $k \infty$ , the real-valued polynomials $F_{k}(\cdot) = \operatorname{Tr}(f_{k}(\cdot))$ on $\mathbf{S}^{N}$ converge, along with their first order derivatives, uniformly on every bounded subset of ${\bf S}^{N}$ , and the limit of the sequence, by (a), is exactly $\chi(\cdot)$ . Thus, $\chi(\cdot)$ is continuously diferentiable, and (b) says that

$$
D \chi(y)[h] = \sum_{j = 1}^{N} f^{\prime}(\lambda_{j}(y)) \widehat{h}_{jj}.\tag{5.9.17}
$$

Besides this, $(a - c)$ say that if $U$ is a closed convex set in ${\bf S}^{N}$ which does not contain singular matrices, then $F_{k}(\cdot)$ , as $k \infty,$ converge along with the first and the second derivative uniformly on every compact subset of $U_{i}$ , so that $\chi(\cdot)$ is twice continuously diferentiable on $U.$ , and at every point $y \in U$ we have

$$
D^{2} \chi(y)[h, h] = \sum_{i, j = 1}^{N} \widehat{h}_{ij}^{2} \Gamma_{ij}, \Gamma_{ij} = \left\{\begin{array}{ll} \frac{f^{\prime}(\lambda_{i}(y)) - f^{\prime}(\lambda_{j}(y))}{\lambda_{i}(y) - \lambda_{j}(y)}, & \lambda_{i}(y) \neq \lambda_{j}(y) \\ f^{\prime \prime}(\lambda_{i}(y)), & \lambda_{i}(y) = \lambda_{j}(y) \end{array} \right.\tag{5.9.18}
$$

and in particular $\chi(\cdot)$ is convex on $U.$

${\bf 3}^{0}$ . We intend to prove that $(i) \chi(\cdot)$ is convex, and (ii) its restriction on the set $Y_{F}$ is strongly convex, with certain modulus $\alpha > 0$ , w.r.t. the trace norm $| \cdot |_{1}$ . Since $\chi$ is continuously diferentiable, all we need to prove (i) is to verify that

$$
\langle \chi^{\prime}(y^{\prime}) - \chi^{\prime}(y^{\prime \prime}), y^{\prime} - y^{\prime \prime} \rangle \geq 0\tag{\( \left(*\right)\}
$$

for a dense in ${\bf S}^{N} \times{\bf S}^{N}$ set of pairs $(y^{\prime}, y^{\prime \prime}), \mathrm{e.g.}$ , those with nonsingular $y^{\prime} - y^{\prime \prime}$ . For a pair of the latter $\mathrm{type}.$ , the polynomial $q(t) = \mathrm{Det}(y^{\prime} + t(y^{\prime \prime} - y^{\prime}))$ of $t \in \mathbb{R}$ is not identically zero and thus has finitely many roots on [0, 1]. In other words, we can find finitely many points $t_{0} = 0 < t_{1} <...< t_{n} = 1$ such that all “matrix intervals” $\Delta_{i} =(y_{i}, y_{i + 1}), y_{k} = y^{\prime} + t_{k}(y^{\prime \prime} - y^{\prime}), 1 \le i \le n - 1$ , are comprised of nonsingular matrices. Therefore χ is convex on every closed segment contained in one of $\Delta_{i}{^{\mathrm{{\sc ~}}} \mathrm{{s},}}$ and since $\chi$ is continuously diferentiable, (∗) follows.

$4^{0}$ . Now let us prove that with properly defined $\alpha > 0$ one has

$$
\langle \chi^{\prime}(y^{\prime}) - \chi^{\prime}(y^{\prime \prime}), y^{\prime} - y^{\prime \prime} \rangle \geq \alpha | y^{\prime} - y^{\prime \prime} |_{1}^{2} \forall y^{\prime}, y^{\prime \prime} \in Y_{F}\tag{5.9.19}
$$

Let $\epsilon > 0$ , and let $Y^{\epsilon}$ be a convex open in $Y = \{y : | y |_{1} \leq 1\}$ neighbourhood of $Y_{F}$ such that for all $y \in Y^{\epsilon}$ at most M eigenvalues of y are of magnitude $> \epsilon.$ . We intend to prove that for some $\alpha_{\epsilon} > 0$ one has

$$
\langle \chi^{\prime}(y^{\prime}) - \chi^{\prime}(y^{\prime \prime}), y^{\prime} - y^{\prime \prime} \rangle \geq \alpha_{\epsilon} | y^{\prime} - y^{\prime \prime} |_{1}^{2} \forall y^{\prime}, y^{\prime \prime} \in Y^{\epsilon}.\tag{5.9.20}
$$

Same as above, it sufices to verify this relation for a dense in $Y^{\epsilon} \times Y^{\epsilon}$ set of pairs $y^{\prime}, y^{\prime \prime} \in Y^{\epsilon}$ , e.g., for those pairs $y^{\prime}, y^{\prime \prime} \in Y^{\epsilon}$ for which $y^{\prime} - y^{\prime \prime}$ is nonsingular. Defining matrix intervals $\Delta_{i}$ as above and taking into account continuous Differentiability of $\chi_{i}$ , it sufices to verify that if $y \in \Delta_{i}$ and $h = y^{\prime} - y^{\prime \prime}$ , then $D^{2} \chi(y)[h, h] \geq \alpha_{\epsilon} | h |_{1}^{2}$ . To this end observe that by (5.9.18) all we have to prove is that

$$
D^{2} \chi(y)[h, h] = \sum_{i, j = 1}^{N} \widehat{h}_{ij}^{2} \Gamma_{ij} \geq \alpha_{\epsilon} | h |_{1}^{2}.\tag{#}
$$

$5^{0}$ . Setting $\lambda_{j} = \lambda_{j}(y)$ , observe that $\lambda_{i} \neq 0$ for all i due to the origin of y. We claim that if $y.$ $| \lambda_{i} | \geq | \lambda_{j} |;$ then $\Gamma_{ij} \ge q | \lambda_{i} |^{q - 1}$ . Indeed, the latter relation definitely holds true when $\lambda_{i} = \lambda_{j}$ . Now, if $\lambda_{i}$ and $\lambda_{j}$ are of the same sign, then $\begin{array}{r}{\Gamma_{ij} = \frac{| \lambda_{i} |^{q} - | \lambda |_{j}^{q}}{| \lambda_{i} | - | \lambda_{j} |} \geq q | \lambda_{i} |^{q - 1}} \end{array}$ , since the derivative of the concave (recall that $0 < q \le 1)$ function $t^{q}$ of $t > 0$ is positive and nonincreasing. $\operatorname{If} \lambda_{i}$ and $\lambda_{j}$ are of different signs, then $\begin{array}{r}{\Gamma_{ij} = \frac{| \lambda_{i} |^{q} + | \lambda_{j} |^{q}}{| \lambda_{i} | + | \lambda_{j} |} \ge | \lambda_{i} |^{q - 1}} \end{array}$ due to $| \lambda_{j} |^{q} \geq | \lambda_{j} | | \lambda_{i} |^{q - 1}$ , and therefore $\Gamma_{ij} \geq q | \lambda_{i} |^{q - 1}$ . Thus, our claim is justified.

W.l.o.g. we can assume that the positive reals $\mu_{i} = | \lambda_{i} |, i = 1,..., N$ , form a nondecreasing sequence, so that, by above, $\Gamma_{ij} \geq q \mu_{j}^{q - 1}$ when $i \le j$ . Besides this, at most M of $\mu_{j}$ are $\geq \epsilon,$ since $y^{\prime}, y^{\prime \prime} \in \bar{Y}^{\epsilon}$ and therefore $y \in Y^{\epsilon}$ by convexity of $Y^{\epsilon}$ . By the above,

$$
D^{2} \chi(y)[h, h] \geq 2q \sum_{i < j \leq N} \widehat{h}_{ij}^{2} \mu_{j}^{q - 1} + q \sum_{j = 1}^{N} \widehat{h}_{jj}^{2} \mu_{j}^{q - 1},
$$

or, equivalently by symmetry of ${\widehat{h}},$ if

$$
h^{j} = \left[\begin{array}{ccccc} & & & \widehat{h}_{1j} \\ & & & \widehat{h}_{2j} \\ & & & \vdots \\ \widehat{h}_{j1} & \widehat{h}_{j2} & \dots & \widehat{h}_{jj} \end{array} \right]
$$

and $H_{j} = \| h^{j} \|_{\mathrm{Fro}}$ is the Frobenius norm of $h^{j}$ , then

$$
D^{2} \chi(y)[h, h] \geq q \sum_{j = 1}^{N} H_{j}^{2} \mu_{j}^{q - 1}.\tag{5.9.21}
$$

Observe that $h^{j}$ are of rank $\leq 2$ , whence $| h^{j} |_{1} \leq \sqrt{2} \| h^{j} \|_{\mathrm{Fro}} = \sqrt{2} H_{j}$ , so that

$$
\begin{array}{rl} &{| h |_{1}^{2} = | \widehat{h} |_{1}^{2} \leq \left(\sum_{j = 1}^{N} | h^{j} |_{1}\right)^{2} \leq 2 \left(\sum_{j = 1}^{N} H_{j}\right)^{2} = 2 \left(\sum_{j}[H_{j} \mu_{j}^{(q - 1) / 2}] \mu_{j}^{(1 - q) / 2}\right)^{2}} \\ &{\leq 2 \left(\sum_{j = 1}^{N} H_{j}^{2} \mu_{j}^{q - 1}\right) \left(\sum_{j = 1}^{N} \mu_{j}^{1 - q}\right)} \\ &{\leq(2 / q) D^{2} \chi(y)[h, h] \left(\sum_{j = 1}^{N} \mu_{j}^{1 - q}\right)[\text{by (5.9.21)}]} \\ &{\leq(2 / q) D^{2} \chi(y)[h, h] \left((N - M) \epsilon^{1 - q} +[M^{- 1} \sum_{j = N - M + 1}^{N} \mu_{j}]^{1 - q} M\right)} \\ &{[\text{dueto0 < q < 1and \mu_{j} \leq\epsilon, j\leq N - M}]} \\ &{\leq(2 / q) D^{2} \chi(y)[h, h] \left((N - M) \epsilon^{1 - q} + M^{q}\right)[\text{since \sum_{j} \mu_{j} \leq 1duetoy\in Y^{\epsilon}\subset\{y:|y|_{1}\leq 1\}},} \end{array}
$$

and we see that (#) holds true with $\alpha_{\epsilon} = \frac{q}{2[(N - M) \epsilon + M^{q}]}$ . As a result, with the just defined $\alpha_{\epsilon}$ relation (5.9.20) holds true, whence (5.9.19) is satisfied with $\begin{array}{r}{\alpha = \operatorname{lim}_{\epsilon \to + 0} \alpha_{\epsilon} = \frac{q}{2} M^{- q}} \end{array}$ , that is, $\chi$ is continuously diferentiable convex function which is strongly convex, modulus α, w.r.t. $| \cdot |_{1}$ , on $Y_{F}$ . Recalling the definition of $q,$ we see that $\widehat{\omega}(\cdot) = \alpha^{- 1} \chi(\cdot)$ , so that $\widehat{\omega}$ satisfies the conclusion of Lemma 5.9.3. ✷

B. We are ready to prove Theorem 5.9.2. Under the premise and in the notation of Theorem, let

$$
N = \sum_{j} \mu_{j} + \sum_{j} \nu_{j}, M = 2 \sum_{j} \mu_{j} = 2m, \mathcal{A} x = \frac{1}{2} \left[\begin{array}{cc} & x \\ x^{T} & \end{array} \right] \in \mathbf{S}^{N}[x \in E = \mathbf{M}^{\mu \nu}].\tag{5.9.22}
$$

Observe that the image space $F$ of A is a linear subspace of $\mathbf{S}^{N}$ , and that the eigenvalues of $y = Ax$ are the 2m reals $\pm \sigma_{i}(x) / 2, 1 \le i \le m$ , and $N - M$ zeros, so that $\| x \|_{\mathrm{nuc}} \equiv |{\mathcal{A}} x |_{1}$ and $M, F$ satisfy the premise of Lemma 5.9.3. Setting

$$
\omega(x) = \widehat{\omega}(\mathcal{A} x) = \frac{4 \sqrt{e} \ln(2m)}{2^{q}(1 + q)} \sum_{i = 1}^{m} \sigma_{i}^{1 + q}(x), q = \frac{1}{2 \ln(2m)},
$$

and invoking Lemma 5.9.3, we see that ω is a convex continuously diferentiable function on E which, due to the identity $\| x \|_{\mathrm{nuc}} \equiv |{\mathcal{A}} x |_{1}$ , is strongly convex, modulus 1, w.r.t. $\| \cdot \|_{\mathrm{nuc}}$ , on the $\| \cdot \|_{\mathrm{nuc}}$ -unit ball $Z$ of $E$ . This function clearly satisfies (5.9.13). ✷

## 5.9.5.2 Proof of Corollary 5.9.2

Corollary 5.9.2 is obtained from Theorem 5.9.2 in exactly the same fashion as Corollary 5.9.1 was derived from Theorem 5.9.1, see section 5.9.4.
