# Solutions to Selected Exercises

## 6.1 Exercises for Lecture 1

## 6.1.1 Around Theorem on Alternative

Exercise 1.4, 1) and 3) Derive the following statements from the General Theorem on Alternative:

1. [Gordan’s Theorem on Alternative] One of the inequality systems

$$
\text{(I)} \quad Ax < 0, x \in \mathbb{R}^{n},
$$

$$
\text{(II)} \quad A^{T} y = 0, 0 \neq y \geq 0, y \in \mathbb{R}^{m},
$$

(A being an $m \times n$ matrix, x are variables in (I), y are variables in (II)) has a solution if and only if the other one has no solutions.

Solution: By GTA, (I) has no solutions if and only if a weighted sum $[A^{T} y]^{T} x \Omega 0$ , with $y \geq 0$ and $\Omega = " < "$ when $y \ne 0$ and $\Omega = " \leq "$ when $y = 0$ , is a contradictory inequality, which happens if $\Omega = " < "$ and $A^{T} y = 0$ . Thus, $Ax < 0$ has no solutions if there exists nonzero $y \geq 0$ such that $A^{T} y = 0$ ✷

## 3. [Motzkin’s Theorem on Alternative] The system

$$
Sx < 0, Nx \leq 0
$$

in variables x has no solutions if and only if the system

$$
S^{T} \sigma + N^{T} \nu = 0, \sigma \geq 0, \nu \geq 0, \sigma \neq 0
$$

in variables $\sigma, \nu$ has a solution.

Solution: Same as above, non-existence of solutions to the first system is equivalent to existence of nonnegative weights $\sigma, \nu$ such that the inequality $[S^{\overset{\cdot}{T}} \sigma + N^{T} \overset{\cdot}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}]^{\widehat{T}}$ xΩ0 with $\Omega = " < "$ when $\sigma \neq 0$ and $\Omega = " \leq "$ when $\sigma = 0$ is contradictory. The only one of these two options which can take place is that $S^{T} \sigma + N^{T} \nu = 0$ and $\sigma \neq 0$ ✷

## 6.1.2 Around cones

Exercise 1.8.2-3) 2) Let K be a cone in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ and u 7→ Au be a linear mapping from certain $\mathbb{R}^{k}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ with trivial null space and such that ImA ∩ int $\mathbf{K} \neq \varnothing$ . Prove that the inverse image of K under the mapping – the set

$$
A^{- 1}(\mathbf{K}) = \{u \mid Au \in \mathbf{K}\}
$$

– is a cone in $\mathbb{R}^{k}$ . Prove that the cone dual to $A^{- 1}(\mathbf{K})$ is the image of K<sub>∗</sub> under the mapping $\lambda \mapsto A^{T} \lambda \colon$

$$
\left(A^{- 1}(\mathbf{K})\right)_{*} = \left\{A^{T} \lambda \mid \lambda \in \mathbf{K}_{*} \right\}.
$$

Solution: The fact that $A^{- 1}(K)$ is a cone is evident. Let us justify the announced description of the cone dual to $A^{- 1}(\mathbf{K})$ . If $\lambda \in \mathbf{K}_{*}.$ , then $A^{T} \lambda$ clearly belongs to $(A^{- 1}(\mathbf{K}))_{*}$

$$
u \in A^{- 1}(\mathbf{K}) \Rightarrow Au \in \mathbf{K} \Rightarrow \lambda^{T}(Au) =(A^{T} \lambda)^{T} u \geq 0.
$$

Now let us prove the inverse implication: if $c \in(A^{- 1}(\mathbf{K}))$ <sub>∗</sub>, then $c = A^{T} \lambda$ for some $\lambda \in \mathbf{K},$ <sub>∗</sub>. To this end consider the conic problem

$$
\min_{x} \left\{c^{T} x \mid Ax \geq_{\mathbf{K}} 0 \right\}.
$$

The problem is strictly feasible and below bounded $\mathrm{(why ?)}$ , so that by the Conic Duality Theorem the dual problem

$$
\max_{\lambda} \left\{0^{T} \lambda \mid A^{T} \lambda = c, \lambda \geq_{\mathbf{K}_{*}} 0 \right\}
$$

is solvable, Q.E.D.

3) Let K be a cone in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $y = Ax$ be a linear mapping from $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ onto $\mathbb{R}^{N}$ (i.e., the image of A is the entire $\mathbb{R}^{N})$ . Assume that $\mathrm{Null}(A) \cap \mathbf{K} = \{0\}$

Prove that then the image of K under the mapping A – the set

$$
A \mathbf{K} = \{Ax \mid x \in \mathbf{K}\}
$$

is a cone in $\mathbb{R}^{N}$

Prove that the cone dual to AK is

$$
(A \mathbf{K})_{*} = \{\lambda \in \mathbb{R}^{N} \mid A^{T} \lambda \in \mathbf{K}_{*}\}.
$$

Demonstrate by example that if in the above statement the assumption $\mathrm{Null}(A) \cap \mathbf{K} = \{0\}$ is weakened to $\operatorname{Null}(A) \cap$ int $\mathbf{K} = \mathbb{\varnothing}$ , then the image of K under the mapping A may happen to be non-closed.

Solution: Let us temporarily set $B = A^{T}$ (note that B has trivial null space, since A is an onto mapping) and

$$
\mathbf{L} = \{\lambda \in \mathbb{R}^{N} \mid B \lambda \in \mathbf{K}_{*}\}.
$$

Let us prove that the image of B intersects the interior of $\mathbf{K}_{*}$ . Indeed, otherwise we could separate the convex set int K<sub>∗</sub> from the linear subspace Im B: there would exist $x \neq 0$ such that

$$
\inf_{\mu \in \mathrm{int} \mathbf{K}_{*}} x^{T} \mu \geq \sup_{\mu \in \mathrm{Im} B} x^{T} \mu,
$$

whence $x \in(\mathbf{K}_{*})_{*} = \mathbf{K}$ and $x \in(\operatorname{Im} B)^{\perp} = \operatorname{Null}(A)$ , which is impossible.

It remains to apply to the cone K<sub>∗</sub> and the mapping B the rule on inverse image (rule 2)): according to this rule, the set L is a cone, and its dual cone is the image of $(\mathbf{K}_{*})_{*} = \mathbf{K}$ under the mapping $B^{T} = A$ . Thus, $A(\mathbf{K})$ indeed is a cone – namely, the cone dual to L, whence the cone dual to $A(\mathbf{K})$ is L.

“Demonstrate by example...”: When the 3D ice-cream cone is projected onto its tangent plane, the projection is the open half-plane plus a single point on the boundary of this half-plane, which is not a closed set.

Exercise 1.9 Let A be a $m \times n$ matrix of full column rank and K be a cone in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$

1. Prove that at least one of the following facts always takes place:

(i) There exists a nonzero $x \in$ Im A which is $\ge \mathbf{\mathbf{\mathbf{\mathbf{K}}}} 0;$

(ii) There exists a nonzero $\lambda \in \operatorname{Null}(A^{T})$ which is $\geq_{\mathbf{K}_{*}} 0.$

Geometrically: given a primal-dual pair of cones $\mathbf{K}, \mathbf{K}_{*}$ and a pair $L, L^{\perp}$ of linear subspaces which are orthogonal complements of each other, we either can find a nontrivial ray in the intersection $L \cap \mathbf{K}$ , or in the intersection $L^{\perp} \cap \mathbf{K}_{*}$ , or both.

2. Prove that the “strict” version of (ii) takes place $({\mathrm{i.e.}}$ , there exists $\lambda \in \operatorname{Null}(A^{T})$ which is ${>} \mathbf{\mathbf{\mathbf{\mathbf{\mathbf{\mathbf{\mathbf{K}}}}}}}$ 0) if and only if (i) does not take place, and vice versa: the strict version of (i) takes place if and only if (ii) does not take place.

Geometrically: if K, K is a primal-dual pair of cones and $L, L^{\perp}$ are linear subspaces which are orthogonal complements of each other, then the intersection L ∩ K is trivial (is the singleton {0}) if and only if the intersection $L^{\perp}$ ∩ int K<sub>∗</sub> is nonempty.

Solution: 1): Assuming that (ii) does not take place, note that $A^{T} \mathbf{K},$ is a cone in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ (Exercise 1.8), and the dual of this latter cone is the inverse image of K under the mapping A. Since the dual must contain nonzero vectors, (i) takes place.

2): Let $e >_{\mathbf{K}_{*}} 0.$ . Consider the conic problem

$$
\max_{\lambda, t} \left\{t \mid A^{T} \lambda = 0, \lambda - te \geq_{\mathbf{K}_{*}} 0 \right\}.
$$

Note that this problem is strictly feasible, and the strict version of (ii) is equivalent to the fact that the optimal value in the problem $\mathrm{is} > 0,$ . Thus, (ii) is not valid if and only if the optimal value in our strictly feasible maximization conic problem $\mathrm{is} \leq 0$ . By Conic Duality Theorem this is the case if and only if the dual problem

$$
\min_{z, \mu} \left\{0 \mid Az + \mu = 0, \mu^{T} e = 1, \mu \geq_{\mathbf{K}} 0 \right\}
$$

is solvable with optimal value equal to 0, which clearly is the case if and only if the intersection of ImA and K is not the singleton {0}.

## 6.1.3 Feasible and level sets of conic problems

Exercise 1.15 Let the problem

$$
\min \left\{c^{T} x \mid Ax - b \geq_{\mathbf{K}} 0 \right\}\tag{CP}
$$

be feasible (A is of full column rank). Then the following properties are equivalent to each other:

(i) the feasible set of the problem is bounded;

(ii) the set of primal slacks $K = \{y \ge_{\bf K} 0, y = Ax - b\}$ is bounded

(iii) Im $A \cap \mathbf{K} = \{0\}$

(iv) the system of vector inequalities

$$
A^{T} \lambda = 0, \lambda >_{\mathbf{K}_{*}} 0
$$

is solvable.

Corollary. The property of (CP) to have bounded feasible set is independent of the particular value of b such that (CP) is feasible!

Solution: $(i) \Leftrightarrow(\mathrm{ii})$ : this is an immediate consequence of A being of full column rank.

$(\mathrm{ii}) \Rightarrow(\mathrm{iii})$ : If there exists $0 \neq y = Ax \ge_{\bf K} 0$ , then the set of primal slacks contains, along with any of its points ${\bar{y}},$ the entire ray $\{\bar{y} + ty \mid t > 0\}$ , so that the set of primal slacks is unbounded (recall that it is nonemp $\mathrm{{y} - \left(CP \right)}$ is feasible!). Thus, (iii) follows from (ii) (by contradiction).

$(\mathrm{iii}) \Rightarrow(\mathrm{iv})$ : see Exercise 1.9.2).

$(\mathrm{iv}) \Rightarrow(\mathrm{ii}){:}$ let λ be given by (iv). For all primal slacks $y = Ax - b \in \mathbf{K}$ one has $\lambda^{T} y =$ $\begin{array}{r}{\dot{\lambda}^{T}[Ax - \dot{b}] =(A^{T} \lambda)^{T} \dot{x} - \lambda^{T} \dot{b} = \lambda^{T} b,} \end{array}$ , and it remains to use the result of Exercise 1.7.2).

Exercise 1.16 Let the problem

$$
\min \left\{c^{T} x \mid Ax - b \geq_{\mathbf{K}} 0 \right\}\tag{CP}
$$

be feasible (A is of full column rank). Prove that the following two conditions are equivalent to each other:

(i) (CP) has bounded level sets

(ii) The dual problem

$$
\max \left\{b^{T} \lambda \mid A^{T} \lambda = c, \lambda \geq_{\mathbf{K}_{*}} 0 \right\}
$$

is strictly feasible.

Corollary. The property of (CP) to have bounded level sets is independent of the particular value of b such that (CP) is feasible!

Solution: $(i) \Rightarrow(\mathrm{ii})$ : Consider the linear vector inequality

$$
\begin{array}{c} \bar{A} x \equiv \binom{Ax}{- c^{T} x} \geq_{\bar{\mathbf{K}}} 0 \\ \bar{\mathbf{K}} = \{(x, t) | x \geq_{\mathbf{K}} 0, t \geq 0\} \end{array}
$$

If ¯x is a solution of this inequality and x is a feasible solution to (CP), then the entire ray $\{x + t{\bar{x}} \mid t \geq 0\}$ is contained in the same level set of (CP) as x. Consequently, in the case of (i) the only solution to the inequality is the trivial solution $\bar{x} = 0$ . In other words, the intersection of Im $\bar{A}$ with $\bar{\bf K}$ is trivial $- \ \{0\}$ . Applying the result of Exercise 1.9.2), we conclude that the system

$$
\bar{A}^{T} \binom{\lambda}{\mu} \equiv A^{T} \lambda - \mu c = 0, \binom{\lambda}{\mu} >_{\bar{\mathbf{K}}_{*}} 0
$$

is solvable; $\operatorname{if} \(\lambda, \mu)$ solves the latter system, then $\lambda >_{\bf K_{*}} 0$ and $\mu > 0$ , so that $\mu^{- 1} \lambda$ is a strictly feasible solution to the dual problem.

$\mathrm{(ii)} \Rightarrow \mathrm{(i)} \colon \mathrm{If} \ \lambda >_{\mathbf{K}_{*}}$ 0 is feasible for the dual problem and x is feasible for (CP), then

$$
\lambda^{T}(Ax - b) = \left(A^{T} \lambda\right)^{T} x - \lambda^{T} b = c^{T} x - \lambda^{T} b.
$$

We conclude that if x runs through a given level set $\mathcal{L}$ of (CP), the corresponding slacks $y = Ax - b$ belong to a set of the form $\{y \ge_{\mathbf{K}} 0, \lambda^{T} y \le \mathrm{const}\}$ . The sets of the latter type are bounded in view of the result of Exercise 1.7.2) (recall that $\lambda >_{\mathbf{K}_{*}} 0)$ . It remains to note that in view of A being of full column rank boundedness of the image of $\mathcal{L}$ under the mapping $x \mapsto Ax - b$ implies boundedness of ${\mathcal{L}}.$

## 6.2 Exercises for Lecture 2

## 6.2.1 Optimal control in discrete time linear dynamic system

Consider a discrete time linear dynamic system

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} x(t) & = & A(t) x(t - 1) + B(t) u(t), t = 1, 2,..., T; \\ x(0) & = & x_{0}.\end{array}\tag{S}
$$

Here:

- t is the (discrete) time;

$\boldsymbol{x}(t) \in \mathbb{R}^{l}$ is the state vector: its value at instant t identifies the state of the controlled plant;

$u(t) \in \mathbb{R}^{k}$ is the exogenous input at time instant $t; \{u(t)\}_{t = 1}^{T}$ is the control;

- For every $t = 1,..., T, A(t)$ is a given $l \times l,$ and $B(t) - a$ given $l \times k$ matrices.

A typical problem of optimal control associated with (S) is to minimize a given functional of the trajectory $x(\cdot)$ under given restrictions on the control. As a simple problem of this type, consider the optimization model

$$
\min_{x} \left\{c^{T} x(T) \mid \frac{1}{2} \sum_{t = 1}^{T} u^{T}(t) Q(t) u(t) \leq w \right\},\tag{OC}
$$

where Q(t) are given positive definite symmetric matrices.

Exercise 2.1.1-3) 1) Use (S) to express $x(T)$ via the control and convert (OC) in a quadratically constrained problem with linear objective w.r.t. the u-variables.

Solution: From (S) it follows that

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} x(1) & = & A(1) x_{0} + B(1) u(1); \\ x(2) & = & A(2) x(1) + B(2) u(2) \\ & = & A(2) A(1) x_{0} + B(2) u(2) + A(2) B(1) u(1); \\ \dots \\ x(T) & = & A(T) A(T - 1)...A(1) x_{0} + \sum_{t = 1}^{T} A(T) A(T - 1)...A(t + 1) B(t) u(t) \\ & \equiv & A(T) A(T - 1)...A(1) x_{0} + \sum_{t = 1}^{T} C(t) u(t), \\ & & C(t) = A(T) A(T - 1)...A(t + 1) B(t); \end{array}
$$

Consequently, (OC) is equivalent to the problem

$$
\min_{u(\cdot)} \left\{\sum_{t = 1}^{T} d_{t}^{T} u(t) \mid \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i = 1}^{T} u^{T}(t) Q(t) u(t) \leq w \right\} \quad[d_{t} = C^{T}(t) c]\tag{\(^{*} \)}
$$

2) Convert the resulting problem to a conic quadratic program

Solution:

$$
\begin{array}{lll} \text{minimize} & \sum_{t = 1}^{T} d_{t}^{T} u(t) \\ \text{s.t.} & \\ & \left(\begin{array}{ccc} 2^{1 / 2} Q^{1 / 2}(t) u(t) & \geq_{\mathbf{L}^{k}} & 0, t = 1,..., T \\ 1 - s(t) & & \\ 1 + s(t) & & \\ \end{array} \right) \\ & \sum_{t = 1}^{T} s(t) & \leq w, \end{array}
$$

the design variables are $\{u(t) \in \mathbb{R}^{k}, s(t) \in \mathbb{R}\}_{t = 1}^{T}$

3) Pass to the resulting problem to its dual and find the optimal solution to the latter problem. Solution: The conic dual is

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \text{maximize} & - w \omega - \sum_{t = 1}^{T}[\mu(t) + \nu(t)] \\ \text{s.t.} & & \\ & 2^{1 / 2} Q^{1 / 2}(t) \xi(t) & = d_{t}, t = 1, \dots, T \\ & &[\Leftrightarrow \xi(t) = 2^{- 1 / 2} Q^{- 1 / 2}(t) d_{t}] \\ & - \omega - \mu(t) + \nu(t) & = 0, t = 1, \dots, T \\ & &[\Leftrightarrow \mu(t) = \nu(t) - \omega] \\ & \sqrt{\xi^{T}(t) \xi(t) + \mu^{2}(t)} & \leq \nu(t), t = 1, \dots, T, \end{array}
$$

the variables are $\{\xi(t) \in \mathbb{R}^{k}, \mu(t), \nu(t), \omega \in \mathbb{R}\}$ . Equivalent reformulation of the dual problem is

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \text{minimize} & w \omega + \sum_{t = 1}^{T}[2 \nu(t) - \omega] \\ \text{s.t.} & \sqrt{a_{t}^{2} +(\nu(t) - \omega)^{2}} & \leq \nu(t), t = 1,..., T \\ & &[a_{t}^{2} = 2^{- 1} d_{t}^{T} Q^{- 1}(t) d_{t}] \end{array}
$$

or, which is the same,

$$
\begin{array}{ll} \text{minimize} & w \omega + \sum_{t = 1}^{T}[2 \nu(t) - \omega] \\ \text{s.t.} & \omega(2 \nu(t) - \omega) \geq a_{t}^{2}, t = 1, \dots, T \end{array}
$$

or, which is the same,

$$
\min_{\omega} \left\{w \omega + \omega^{- 1} \left(\sum_{t = 1}^{T} a_{t}^{2}\right) | \omega > 0 \right\}.
$$

It follows that the optimal solution to the dual problem is

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \omega_{*} & = & \sqrt{w^{- 1}(\sum_{i = 1}^{T} a_{t}^{2})}; \\ \nu_{*}(t) & = & \frac{1}{2}[a_{t}^{2} \omega_{*}^{- 1} + \omega_{*}], t = 1, \dots, T; \\ \mu_{*}(t) & = & \nu_{*}(t) - \omega_{*} \\ & = & \frac{1}{2}[a_{t}^{2} \omega_{*}^{- 1} - \omega_{*}], t = 1, \dots, T.\end{array}
$$

## 6.2.2 Around stable grasp

Recall that the Stable Grasp Analysis problem is to check whether the system of constraints

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \| F^{i} \|_{2} & \leq & \mu(f^{i})^{T} v^{i}, i = 1, \dots, N \\(v^{i})^{T} F^{i} & = & 0, i = 1, \dots, N \\ \sum_{i = 1}^{N}(f^{i} + F^{i}) + F^{\mathrm{ext}} & = & 0 \\ \sum_{i = 1}^{N} p^{i} \times(f^{i} + F^{i}) + T^{\mathrm{ext}} & = & 0 \end{array}\tag{SG}
$$

in the 3D vector variables $F^{i}$ is or is not solvable. Here the data are given by a number of 3D vectors, namely,

- vectors $v^{i} -$ unit inward normals to the surface of the body at the contact points;

## 6.2. EXERCISES FOR LECTURE 2

- contact points $p^{i}$ ;

- vectors f<sup>i</sup> – contact forces;

- vectors $F^{\mathrm{ext}}$ and $T^{\mathrm{ext}}$ of the external force and torque, respectively.

$\mu > 0$ is a given friction coeficient; we assume that $f_{i}^{T} v^{i} > 0$ for all i.

Exercise 2.2 Regarding (SG) as the system of constraints of a maximization program with trivial objective, build the dual problem.

Solution:

$$
\begin{array}{rlrl} & \text{minimize} & \sum_{i = 1}^{N} \mu[(f^{i})^{T} v^{i}] \phi_{i} - \left[\sum_{i = 1}^{N} f^{i} + F^{\mathrm{ext}} \right]^{T} \Phi - \left[\sum_{i = 1}^{N} p^{i} \times f^{i} + T^{\mathrm{ext}} \right]^{T} \Psi \\ & \text{s.t.} & \Phi_{i} + \sigma_{i} v^{i} + \Phi - p^{i} \times \Psi & = 0, i = 1,..., N \\ & & \| \Phi_{i} \|_{2} & \leq \phi_{i}, i = 1,..., N, \\ & &[\Phi, \Phi_{i}, \Psi \in \mathbb{R}^{3}, \sigma_{i}, \phi_{i} \in \mathbb{R}] \end{array}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{c} \min_{\sigma_{i} \in \mathbb{R}, \Psi, \Phi \in \mathbb{R}^{3}} \Bigg \{\sum_{i = 1}^{N} \mu[(f^{i})^{T} v^{i}] \| p^{i} \times \Psi - \Phi - \sigma_{i} v^{i} \|_{2} - F^{T} \Phi - T^{T} \Psi \Bigg\}, \\ F = \sum_{i = 1}^{N} f^{i} + F^{\mathrm{ext}}, T = \sum_{i = 1}^{N} p^{i} \times f^{i} + T^{\mathrm{ext}} \end{array}
$$

m

## 6.3 Exercises for Lecture 3

## 6.3.1 Around positive semidefiniteness, eigenvalues and $\succeq$-ordering

## 6.3.1.1 Criteria for positive semidefiniteness

Exercise 3.2 [Diagonal-dominant matrices] Let $A =[a_{ij}]_{i, j = 1}^{m}$ be a symmetric matrix satisfying the relation

$$
a_{ii} \geq \sum_{j \neq i} | a_{ij} |, i = 1, \dots, m.
$$

Prove that A is positive semidefinite.

Solution: Let e be an eigenvector of A and λ be the corresponding eigenvalue. We may assume that the largest, in absolute value, of coordinates of e is equal to 1. Let i be the index of this coordinate; then

$$
\lambda = a_{ii} + \sum_{j \neq i} a_{ij} e_{j} \geq a_{ii} - \sum_{j \neq i} | a_{ij} | \geq 0.
$$

Thus, all eigenvalues of A are nonnegative, so that A is positive semidefinite.

## 6.3.1.2 Variational description of eigenvalues

Exercise 3.7 Let $f_{*}$ be a closed convex function with the domain Dom $f_{*} \subset \mathbb{R}_{+}$ , and let $f$ be the Legendre transformation of $f_{*}$ . Then for every pair of symmetric matrices $X, Y$ of the same size with the spectrum of X belonging to Dom f and the spectrum of Y belonging to Dom $f_{*}$ one has

$$
\lambda(f(X)) \geq \lambda \left(Y^{1 / 2} XY^{1 / 2} - f_{*}(Y)\right).\tag{*}
$$

Solution: By continuity reasons, it sufices to prove $(*)$ in the case of $Y \mathrm{im0 \Delta \left(why ? \right)}$ . Let m be the size of $X$ , let $k \in \{1,..., m\}$ , let $\mathcal{E}_{k}$ be the family of linear subspaces of ${\mathbb{R}}^{m}$ of codimension $k - 1$ , and let $E \in{\mathcal{E}}_{k}$ be such that

$$
e \in E \Rightarrow e^{T} Xe \leq \lambda_{k}(X) e^{T} e
$$

(such an $E$ exists by the Variational characterization of eigenvalues as applied to $X)$ . Let also $F = Y^{- 1 / 2} E$ ; the codimension of $F,$ , same as the one of $E_{i}$ , is $k - 1$ . Finally, let $g_{1}, \ldots$ g<sub>m</sub>

## 6.3. EXERCISES FOR LECTURE 3

be an orthonormal system of eigenvectors of Y , so that $Yg_{j} = \lambda_{j}(Y) g_{j}$ . We have

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} h \in F, h^{T} h = 1 & \Rightarrow \\ h^{T}[Y^{1 / 2} XY^{1 / 2} - f_{*}(Y)] h & = &(\underbrace{Y^{1 / 2} h}_{\in E})^{T} X(Y^{1 / 2} h) - \sum_{j = 1}^{m} f_{*}(\lambda_{j}(Y))(g_{j}^{T} h)^{2} \\ & \leq & \lambda_{k}(X)(Y^{1 / 2} h)^{T}(Y^{1 / 2} h) - \sum_{j = 1}^{m} f_{*}(\lambda_{j}(Y))(g_{j}^{T} h)^{2} \\ & &[\text{since} Y^{1 / 2} h \in E] \\ & = & \lambda_{k}(X)(h^{T} Yh) - \sum_{j = 1}^{m} f_{*}(\lambda_{j}(Y))(g_{j}^{T} h)^{2} \\ & = & \lambda_{k}(X) \sum_{j = 1}^{m} \lambda_{j}(Y)(g_{j}^{T} h)^{2} - \sum_{j = 1}^{m} f_{*}(\lambda_{j}(Y))(g_{j}^{T} h)^{2} \\ & = & \sum_{j = 1}^{m}[\lambda_{k}(X) \lambda_{j}(Y) - f_{*}(\lambda_{j}(Y))](g_{j}^{T} h)^{2} \\ & \leq & \sum_{j = 1}^{m} f(\lambda_{k}(X))(g_{j}^{T} h)^{2} \\ & &[\text{since} f =(f_{*})_{*}] \\ & = & f(\lambda_{k}(X)) \\ & &[\text{since} \sum_{j}(g_{j}^{T} h)^{2} = h^{T} h = 1] \\ & = & \lambda_{k}(f(X)) \\ & &[\text{since} f(\cdot) \text{is nonincreasing due to Dom f_* \subset R_+}] \end{array}
$$

We see that there exists $F \in{\mathcal{E}}_{k}$ such that

$$
\max_{h \in F: h^{T} h = 1} h^{T}[Y^{1 / 2} XY^{1 / 2} - f_{*}(Y)] h \leq \lambda_{k}(f(X)).
$$

From Variational characterization of eigenvalues it follows that

$$
\lambda_{k}(Y^{1 / 2} XY^{1 / 2} - f_{*}(Y)) \leq \lambda_{k}(f(X)).
$$

Exercise 3.9,(iv) [Trace inequality] Prove that whenever A, $B \in \mathbf{S}^{m}$ , one has

$$
\lambda^{T}(A) \lambda(B) \geq \operatorname{Tr}(AB).
$$

Solution: Denote $\lambda = \lambda(A)$ , and let $A = V^{T} \mathrm{Diag}(\lambda) V$ be the spectral decomposition of A. Setting $\hat{B} = VBV^{T}$ , note that $\lambda(\hat{B}) = \lambda(B)$ and $\mathrm{Tr}(AB) = \mathrm{Tr}(\mathrm{Diag}(\lambda) \hat{B})$ . Thus, it sufices to prove the Trace inequality in the particular case when A is a diagonal matrix with the diagonal $\lambda = \lambda(A)$ . Denoting by $\mu$ the diagonal of B and setting

$$
\sigma^{0} = 0; \sigma^{k} = \sum_{i = 1}^{k} \mu_{i}, k = 1, \dots, m,
$$

we have

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \operatorname{Tr}(AB) & = & \sum_{i = 1}^{m} \lambda_{i} \mu_{i} \\ & = & \sum_{i = 1}^{m} \lambda_{i}(\sigma^{i} - \sigma^{i - 1}) \\ & = & - \lambda_{1} \sigma^{0} + \sum_{i = 1}^{m - 1}(\lambda_{i} - \lambda_{i + 1}) \sigma^{i} + \lambda_{m} \sigma^{m} \\ & = & \sum_{i = 1}^{m - 1}(\lambda_{i} - \lambda_{i + 1}) \sigma^{i} + \lambda_{m} \operatorname{Tr}(B) \\ & \leq & \sum_{i = 1}^{m - 1}(\lambda_{i} - \lambda_{i + 1}) \sum_{j = 1}^{i} \lambda_{j}(B) + \lambda_{m} \sum_{j = 1}^{m} \lambda_{j}(B) \\ & &[\text{since} \lambda_{i} \geq \lambda_{i + 1} \text{and in view of Exercise 3.9.(iii)}] \\ & = & \sum_{i = 1}^{m} \lambda_{i} \lambda_{i}(B) \\ & = & \lambda^{T}(A) \lambda(B).\end{array}
$$

Exercise 3.11.3) Let $X$ be a symmetric $n \times n$ matrix partitioned into blocks in a symmetric, w.r.t. the diagonal, fashion:

$$
X = \left(\begin{array}{cccc} X_{11} & X_{12} &...& X_{1m} \\ X_{12}^{T} & X_{22} &...& X_{2m} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ X_{1m}^{T} & X_{2m}^{T} &...& X_{mm} \end{array} \right)
$$

so that the blocks $X_{ii}$ are square. Let also $g : \mathbb{R} \mathbb{R} \cup \{+ \infty\}$ be convex function on the real line which is finite on the set of eigenvalues of $X,$ and let $\mathcal{F}_{n} \subset \mathbf{S}^{n}$ be the set of all $n \times n$ symmetric matrices with all eigenvalues belonging to the domain of $g.$ . Assume that the mapping

$$
Y \mapsto g(Y): \mathcal{F}_{n} \to \mathbf{S}^{n}
$$

is $\succeq$-convex:

$$
g \left(\lambda^{\prime} Y^{\prime} + \lambda^{\prime \prime} Y^{\prime \prime}\right) \preceq \lambda^{\prime} g \left(Y^{\prime}\right) + \lambda^{\prime \prime} g \left(Y^{\prime \prime}\right) \quad \forall \left(Y^{\prime}, Y^{\prime \prime} \in \mathcal{F}_{n}, \lambda^{\prime}, \lambda^{\prime \prime} \geq 0, \lambda^{\prime} + \lambda^{\prime \prime} = 1\right).
$$

Prove that

$$
(g(X))_{ii} \succeq g(X_{ii}), i = 1, \dots, m,
$$

where the partition of $g(X)$ into the blocks $(g(X))_{ij}$ is identical to the partition of X into the blocks $X_{ij}$

Solution: Let $\boldsymbol{\epsilon} =(\epsilon_{1},..., \epsilon_{m})$ with $\epsilon_{j} = \pm 1$ , and let $U_{\epsilon} = \left(\begin{array}{ccccc}{{\epsilon_{1} I_{n_{1}}}} &{{}} &{{}} &{{}} &{{}} \\{{}} &{{\epsilon_{2} I_{n_{2}}}} &{{}} &{{}} &{{}} \\{{}} &{{}} &{{\ddots}} &{{}} &{{}} \\{{}} &{{}} &{{}} &{{}} &{{\epsilon_{m} I_{n_{m}}}} \end{array} \right),$

where $n_{i}$ is the row size of $X_{ii}$ . Then $U_{\epsilon}$ are orthogonal matrices and one clearly has

$$
D(X) \equiv \left(\begin{array}{cccc} X_{11} & & & \\ & X_{22} & & \\ & & \ddots & \\ & & & X_{mm} \end{array} \right) = \frac{1}{2^{m}} \sum_{\epsilon : \epsilon_{i} = \pm 1, i = 1, \ldots, m} U_{\epsilon}^{T} XU_{\epsilon}.
$$

We have

$$
\begin{array}{cc} D(X) = \frac{1}{2^{m}} \underset{\epsilon : \epsilon_{i} = \pm 1, i = 1, \ldots, m}{\sum} U_{\epsilon}^{T} XU_{\epsilon} \\ \Downarrow &[\text{since g is\succeq - convex}] \\ g(D(X)) \preceq \frac{1}{2^{m}} \underset{\epsilon : \epsilon_{i} = \pm 1, i = 1, \ldots, m}{\sum} g(U_{\epsilon}^{T} XU_{\epsilon}) \\ \Updownarrow \\ g(D(X)) \preceq \frac{1}{2^{m}} \underset{\epsilon : \epsilon_{i} = \pm 1, i = 1, \ldots, m}{\sum} U_{\epsilon}^{T} g(X) U_{\epsilon} \\ \Downarrow \\ g(D(X)) \preceq D(g(X)).\end{array}
$$

Exercise 3.16 Let $\boldsymbol{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$ , and let $X_{+}[x]$ be the set of all vectors $x^{\prime}$ dominated by a vector form X [x]:

$$
X_{+}[x] = \{y \mid \exists z \in X[x]: y \leq z\}.
$$

1) Prove that $X_{+}[x]$ is a closed convex set.

2) Prove the following characterization of $X_{+}[x] \colon$

$X_{+}[x]$ is exactly the set of solutions of the system of inequalities $S_{j}(y) \leq S_{j}(x), j = 1,..., m$ in variables $y,$ where $S_{j}(\cdot)$ is the sum of $j$ largest entries in a vector.

Solution: 1) is evident – $X_{+}[x]$ admits evident polyhedral representation and as such is polyhedral (see Section $\mathrm{B.2.4})$ , and therefore is convex and closed.

2) In one direction: if $y \le z = \pi x$ for some double-stochastic x, then $S_{j}(y) \le S_{j}(z)$ , and the latter quantity is $\leq S_{j}(x)$ , see (3.8.1) in Section 3.8.1.3. In the opposite direction: let $S_{j}(y) \leq S_{j}(x), 1 \leq j \leq m$ . Let us decrease the smallest entry in x by $\delta = S_{m}(x) - S_{m}(y) \geq 0$ and keep remaining entries in x intact, thus arriving at a vector $x^{\prime}$ . Clearly, $S_{j}(x^{\prime}) = S_{j}(x) \geq$ $S_{j}(y)$ for $j < m$ and $S_{m}(y) = S_{m}(x^{\prime})$ . By Majorization Principle (Section $3.8.1.4) \y = \pi x^{\prime}$ for some double-stochastic π, and since $x^{\prime} \leq x$ , we have $\pi x^{\prime} \leq \pi x$ and therefore $y \le \pi x$ ✷

## Exercise 3.17 Derive Proposition 3.2.2 from the result of Exercise 3.16.2).

Solution: All we need to prove is that under the premise of Proposition 3.2.2 one has

$$
t \geq g(\sigma_{1}(X),..., \sigma_{k}(X) \Leftrightarrow \exists x_{1},..., x_{k}: \left\{\begin{array}{ll} x_{1} \geq x_{2} \geq...\geq x_{k} \geq 0, g(x) \leq t \\ \Sigma_{j}(X) \leq x_{1} +...+ x_{j}, 1 \leq j \leq k \end{array} \right.
$$

In one direction: if $g(\sigma(X)) \leq t.$ where $\sigma(X) =[\sigma_{1}(X);...; \sigma_{k}(x)]$ , the relations to the right of ⇔ are satisfied by $x_{j} ~ = ~ \sigma_{j}(X), ~ j ~ \le ~ k$ . In the opposite direction: if x be such that $x_{1} \geq x_{2} \geq...\geq x_{k} \geq 0$ with $g(x) \leq t$ and $\Sigma_{j}(X) \leq x_{1} + \ldots + x_{j}, j \leq k.$ . Then $S_{j}(\sigma(X)) \leq S_{j}(x), j \leq k$ , implying by the result of Exercise 3.16.2) that $0 \leq \sigma(X) \leq \pi x$ for some double-stochastic π. Since g is ≥-nondecreasing on $\mathbb{R}_{+}^{k}$ , we have $g(\sigma(X)) \leq g(\pi x)$ and the latter quantity $\mathrm{is} \leq g(x) \leq t$ since g is permutationally symmetric and convex, see (3.8.1) in Section 3.8.1.3. ✷

## 6.3.1.3 Cauchy’s inequality for matrices

The standard Cauchy’s inequality says that

$$
\left| \sum_{i} x_{i} y_{i} \right| \leq \sqrt{\sum_{i} x_{i}^{2}} \sqrt{\sum_{i} y_{i}^{2}}\tag{3.8.2}
$$

for reals $x_{i}, y_{i}, i = 1,..., n;$ this inequality is exact in the sense that for every collection $x_{1},..., x_{n}$ there exists a collection $y_{1},..., y_{n}$ with $\sum_{i}{\bar{y}}_{i}^{2} ={\bar{1}}$ which makes (3.8.2) an equality.

Exercise 3.18 (i) Prove that whenever $X_{i}, Y_{i} \in \mathbf{M}^{p, q}$ , one has

$$
\sigma \left(\sum_{i} X_{i}^{T} Y_{i}\right) \leq \lambda \left(\left[\sum_{i} X_{i}^{T} X_{i} \right]^{1 / 2}\right) \| \lambda \left(\sum_{i} Y_{i}^{T} Y_{i}\right) \|_{\infty}^{1 / 2}\tag{*}
$$

where $\sigma(A) = \lambda([AA^{T}]^{1 / 2})$ is the vector of singular values of a matrix A arranged in the non-ascending order.

Prove that for every collection $X_{1},..., X_{n} \in \mathbf{M}^{p, q}$ there exists a collection $Y_{1},..., Y_{n} \in \mathbf{M}^{p, q}$ with $\sum_{i} Y_{i}^{T} Y_{i} = I_{q}$ which makes (∗) an equality.

(ii) Prove the following “matrix version” of the Cauchy inequality: whenever $X_{i}, Y_{i} \in \mathbf{M}^{p, q}$ , one has

$$
\left| \sum_{i} \operatorname{Tr} \left(X_{i}^{T} Y_{i}\right) \right| \leq \operatorname{Tr} \left(\left[\sum_{i} X_{i}^{T} X_{i} \right]^{1 / 2}\right) \| \lambda \left(\sum_{i} Y_{i}^{T} Y_{i}\right) \|_{\infty}^{1 / 2},\tag{**}
$$

and for every collection $X_{1},..., X_{n} \in \mathbf{M}^{p, q}$ there exists a collection $Y_{1},..., Y_{n} \in \mathbf{M}^{p, q}$ with $\sum_{i} Y_{i}^{T} Y_{i} = I_{q}$ which makes (∗∗) an equality.

Solution: (i): Denote $P ={\left(\sum_{i} X_{i}^{T} X_{i} \right)}^{1 / 2}, Q = \sum_{i} Y_{i}^{T} Y_{i} \(X_{i}, Y_{i} \in \mathbf{M}^{p, q})$ . We should prove

that

$$
\sigma(\sum_{i} X_{i}^{T} Y_{i}) \leq \lambda(P) \| \lambda(Q) \|_{\infty}^{1 / 2},
$$

or, which is the same,

$$
\sigma(\sum_{i} Y_{i}^{T} X_{i}) \leq \lambda(P) \| \lambda(Q) \|_{\infty}^{1 / 2}.
$$

By the Variational description of singular values, it sufices to prove that for every $k =$ $1, 2,..., p$ there exists a subspace $L_{k} \subset \mathbb{R}^{q}$ of codimension $k - 1$ such that

$$
\forall \xi \in L_{k}: \| \left(\sum_{i} Y_{i}^{T} X_{i}\right) \xi \|_{2} \leq \| \xi \|_{2} \lambda_{k}(P) \| \lambda(Q) \|_{\infty}^{1 / 2}.\tag{\( \left(*\right)\}
$$

Let $e_{1},..., e_{q}$ be the orthonormal eigenbasis of P : $Pe_{i} = \lambda_{i}(P) e_{i}$ , and let $L_{k}$ be the linear span of $e_{k}, e_{k + 1},..., e_{q}$ . For $\xi \in L_{k}$ one has

$$
\begin{array}{rl}{| \eta^{T} \left(\sum_{i} Y_{i}^{T} X_{i}\right) \xi |} &{\leq \sum_{i} \| Y_{i} \eta \|_{2} \| X_{i} \xi \|_{2} \leq \sqrt{\sum_{i} \| Y_{i} \eta \|_{2}^{2}} \sqrt{\sum_{i} \| X_{i} \xi \|_{2}^{2}}} \\ &{= \sqrt{\eta^{T} \left(\sum_{i} Y_{i}^{T} Y_{i}\right) \eta} \sqrt{\xi^{T} \left(\sum_{i} X_{i}^{T} X_{i}\right) \xi}} \\ &{\leq \left(\| \lambda(Q) \|_{\infty} \| \eta \|_{2}^{2}\right)^{1 / 2} \left(\lambda_{k}^{2}(P) \| \xi \|_{2}^{2}\right)^{1 / 2} = \| \lambda(Q) \|_{\infty}^{1 / 2} \lambda_{k}(P) \| \eta \|_{2} \| \xi \|_{2},} \end{array}
$$

whence

$$
\| \left(\sum_{i} Y_{i}^{T} X_{i}\right) \xi \|_{2} = \max_{\eta : \| \eta \|_{2} = 1} \eta^{T} \left(\sum_{i} Y_{i}^{T} X_{i}\right) \xi \leq \lambda_{k}(P) \| \lambda(Q) \|_{\infty}^{1 / 2} \| \xi \|_{2},
$$

as required in (\*).

To make $(^{*})$ equality, assume that $P \succ 0$ (the case of singular $P$ is left to the reader), and let $Y_{i} = X_{i} P^{- 1}$ . Then

$$
\sum_{i} Y_{i}^{T} Y_{i} = P^{- 1} \left(\sum_{i} X_{i}^{T} X_{i}\right) P^{- 1} = I
$$

and

$$
\sum_{i} X_{i}^{T} Y_{i} = \left(\sum_{i} X_{i}^{T} X_{i}\right) P^{- 1} = P,
$$

so that (\*) becomes equality.

$( \mathrm { i } ) { \Rightarrow } ( \mathrm { i i } ) $ : it sufices to prove that if $A \in \mathbf{M}^{p, p}$ , then

$$
| \operatorname{Tr}(A) | \leq \| \sigma(A) \|_{1}.\tag{**}
$$

Indeed, we have $A = U \Lambda V$ , where $U, V$ are orthogonal matrices and Λ is a diagonal matrix with the diagonal $\sigma(A)$ . Denoting by $e_{i}$ the standard basic orths in $\mathbb{R}^{p},$ , we have

$$
| \mathrm{Tr}(A) | = | \mathrm{Tr}(U^{T} AU) | = | \mathrm{Tr}(\Lambda(VU)) | = | \sum_{i} e_{i}^{T} \Lambda(VU) e_{i} | \leq \sum_{i} | \sigma_{i}(A) e_{i}^{T}(VU) e_{i} | \leq \sum_{i} \sigma_{i}(A),
$$

as required in (\*\*).

Here is another exercise of the same flavour:

Exercise 3.19 For nonnegative reals $a_{1},..., a_{m}$ and a real $\alpha > 1$ one has

$$
\left(\sum_{i = 1}^{m} a_{i}^{\alpha}\right)^{1 / \alpha} \leq \sum_{i = 1}^{m} a_{i}.
$$

Both sides of this inequality make sense when the nonnegative reals $a_{i}$ are replaced with positive semidefinite $n \times n$ matrices $A_{i}$ . What happens with the inequality in this case?

Consider the following four statements (where $\alpha > 1$ is a real and $m, n > 1)$

$$
\forall(A_{i} \in \mathbf{S}_{+}^{n}): \quad \left(\sum_{i = 1}^{m} A_{i}^{\alpha}\right)^{1 / \alpha} \preceq \sum_{i = 1}^{m} A_{i}.
$$

2)

$$
\forall(A_{i} \in \mathbf{S}_{+}^{n}): \quad \lambda_{\max} \left(\left(\sum_{i = 1}^{m} A_{i}^{\alpha}\right)^{1 / \alpha}\right) \leq \lambda_{\max} \left(\sum_{i = 1}^{m} A_{i}\right).
$$

3)

$$
\forall(A_{i} \in \mathbf{S}_{+}^{n}): \quad \operatorname{Tr} \left(\left(\sum_{i = 1}^{m} A_{i}^{\alpha}\right)^{1 / \alpha}\right) \leq \operatorname{Tr} \left(\sum_{i = 1}^{m} A_{i}\right).
$$

4)

$$
\forall(A_{i} \in \mathbf{S}_{+}^{n}): \quad \operatorname{Det} \left(\left(\sum_{i = 1}^{m} A_{i}^{\alpha}\right)^{1 / \alpha}\right) \leq \operatorname{Det} \left(\sum_{i = 1}^{m} A_{i}\right).
$$

Among these 4 statements, exactly 2 are true. Identify and prove the true statements.

Solution: The true statements are 2) and 3).

2) is an immediate consequence of the following

Lemma 6.3.1 Let $A_{i} \in \mathbf{S}_{+}^{n}, i = 1,..., m$ , and let $\alpha > 1$ . Then

$$
\lambda_{j} \left(\left(\sum_{i = 1}^{m} A_{i}^{\alpha}\right)^{1 / \alpha}\right) \leq \lambda_{j}^{\frac{1}{\alpha}} \left(\sum_{i = 1}^{m} A_{i}\right) \lambda_{1}^{1 - \frac{1}{\alpha}} \left(\sum_{i = 1}^{m} A_{i}\right).
$$

(here, as always, $\lambda_{j}(B)$ are eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix B arranged in the nonascending order).

Proof. Let $B = \sum_{i = 1}^{m} A_{i}^{\alpha}, A = \sum_{i = 1}^{m} A_{i}$ . Since $\lambda_{j}(B^{1 / \alpha}) = \left(\lambda_{j}(B) \right)^{1 / \alpha}$ , we should prove that

$$
\lambda_{j}(B) \leq \lambda_{j}(A) \lambda_{1}^{\alpha - 1}(A)\tag{6.3.1}
$$

By the Variational description of eigenvalues, it sufices to verify that for every $j \le n$ there exists a linear subspace $L_{j}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ of codimension $j - 1$ such that

$$
\xi^{T} B \xi \leq \lambda_{j}(A) \lambda_{1}^{\alpha - 1}(A) \quad \forall(\xi \in L_{j}, \| \xi \|_{2} = 1).\tag{6.3.2}
$$

Let $e_{1},..., e_{n}$ be an orthonormal eigenbasis of $\boldsymbol{A} \left(\boldsymbol{A} \boldsymbol{e}_{j} = \lambda_{j}(\boldsymbol{A}) \boldsymbol{e}_{j} \right)$ , and let $L_{j}$ be the linear span of the vectors $e_{j}, e_{j + 1},..., e_{n}$ . Let $\xi \in L_{j}$ be a unit vector. We have

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \sum_{i} \xi^{T} A_{i}^{\alpha} \xi & = & \sum_{i} \xi^{T} A_{i} \underbrace{[A_{i}^{\alpha - 1} \xi]}_{\eta_{i}} \\ & \leq & \sum_{i}(\xi^{T} A_{i} \xi)^{1 / 2}(\eta_{i}^{T} A_{i} \eta_{i})^{1 / 2} \qquad[\text{since} A_{i} \succeq 0] \\ & \leq & \left(\sum_{i} \xi^{T} A_{i} \xi\right)^{1 / 2} \left(\sum_{i} \eta_{i}^{T} A_{i} \eta_{i}\right)^{1 / 2} \qquad[\text{Cauchy's inequality}] \\ & = & \left(\xi^{T} A \xi\right)^{1 / 2} \left(\sum_{i} \xi^{T} A_{i}^{2 \alpha - 1} \xi\right)^{1 / 2} \\ & \leq & \left(\xi^{T} A \xi\right)^{1 / 2} \left(\sum_{i} \lambda_{1}^{2 \alpha - 2}(A_{i}) \xi^{T} A_{i} \xi\right)^{1 / 2} \\ & \leq & \left(\max_{i} \lambda_{1}(A_{i})\right)^{\alpha - 1} \sum_{i} \xi^{T} A_{i} \xi \\ & \leq & \lambda_{1}^{\alpha - 1}(A) \lambda_{j}(A) \qquad[\text{since} \| \xi \|_{2} = 1 \text{and} \xi \in L_{j}] \end{array}
$$

as required in (6.3.2).

3) is less trivial than 2). Let us look at the $(nm) \times(nm)$ square matrix

$$
Q = \left(\begin{array}{ccc} A_{1}^{\alpha / 2} & & \\ A_{2}^{\alpha / 2} & & \\ \vdots & & \\ A_{m}^{\alpha / 2} & & \end{array} \right)
$$

(as always, blank spaces are filled with zeros). Then

$$
Q^{T} Q = \left(\begin{array}{cc} B \equiv \sum_{i} A_{i}^{\alpha} & \\ \hline \end{array} \right),
$$

so that $\mathrm{Tr}([Q^{T} Q]^{1 / \alpha}) = \mathrm{Tr}(B^{1 / \alpha})$ . Since the eigenvalues of $Q^{T} Q$ are exactly the same as eigenvalues of $X = QQ^{T}$ , we conclude that

$$
X = \left(\begin{array}{cccc} A_{1}^{\alpha} & A_{1}^{\alpha / 2} A_{2}^{\alpha / 2} & \dots & A_{1}^{\alpha / 2} A_{m}^{\alpha / 2} \\ A_{2}^{\alpha / 2} A_{1}^{\alpha / 2} & A_{2}^{\alpha} & \dots & A_{2}^{\alpha / 2} A_{m}^{\alpha / 2} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ A_{m}^{\alpha / 2} A_{1}^{\alpha / 2} & A_{m}^{\alpha / 2} A_{2}^{\alpha / 2} & \dots & A_{m}^{\alpha} \end{array} \right).
$$

Applying the result of Exercise 3.11.1) with $F(Y) = - \mathrm{Tr}(Y^{1 / \alpha})$ , we get

$$
[\mathrm{Tr}(B^{1 / \alpha}) =] \quad \mathrm{Tr}(X^{1 / \alpha}) = - F(X) \leq - F(\left(\begin{array}{ccc} A_{1}^{\alpha} & & \\ & \ddots & \\ & & A_{m}^{\alpha} \end{array} \right)) = \sum_{i = 1}^{m} \mathrm{Tr}(A_{i}),
$$

as required.

## 6.3.2 $\succeq$-convexity of some matrix-valued functions

Exercise 3.21.4-6) 4): Prove that the function

$$
F(x) = x^{1 / 2}: \mathbf{S}_{+}^{m} \to \mathbf{S}_{+}^{m}
$$

is $\succeq$-concave and $\succeq - \mathrm{monotone}$

Solution: Since the function is continuous on its domain, it sufices to verify that it is $\succeq -$ monotone and $\succeq$ -concave on int $\mathbf{S}_{+}^{m}$ , where the function is smooth.

Diferentiating the identity

$$
F(x) F(x) = x\tag{*}
$$

in a direction h and setting $F(x) = y, DF(x)[h] = dy$ , we get

$$
ydy + dyy = h.
$$

Since $y \succ 0,$ , this Lyapunov equation admits an explicit solution:

$$
dy = \int_{0}^{\infty} \exp \{- ty\} h \exp \{- ty\} dt,
$$

and we see that $dy \succeq 0$ whenever $h \succeq 0;$ applying Exercise 3.20.4), we conclude that $F$ $\succeq$-monotone.

Diferentiating (\*) twice in a direction h and denoting $d^{2} y = D^{2} F(x)[h, h]$ , we get

$$
yd^{2} y + d^{2} yy + 2(dy)^{2} = 0,
$$

whence, same as above,

$$
d^{2} y = - \int_{0}^{\infty} \exp \{- ty\}(dy)^{2} \exp \{- ty\} dt \preceq 0;
$$

applying Exercise 3.20.3), we conclude that $F{\mathrm{~ is ~}} \succeq - \mathrm{concave}.$

5): Prove that the function

$$
F(x) = \ln x: \operatorname{int} \mathbf{S}_{+}^{m} \to \mathbf{S}^{m}
$$

is $\succeq$-monotone and $\succeq - \mathrm{concave}$

Solution: The function $x^{1 / 2} : \mathbf{S}_{+}^{m} \mathbf{S}_{+}^{m}$ is $\succeq$-monotone and $\succeq$-concave by Exercise 3.21.4). Applying Exercise 3.20.6), we conclude that so are the functions $x^{1 / 2^{k}}$ for all positive integer k. It remains to note that

$$
\ln x = \lim_{k \to \infty} 2^{k} \left[x^{1 / 2^{k}} - I \right]
$$

and to use Exercise 3.20.7).

6): Prove that the function

$$
F(x) = \left(Ax^{- 1} A^{T}\right)^{- 1}: \operatorname{int} \mathbf{S}_{+}^{n} \to \mathbf{S}^{m},
$$

with matrix A of rank m is $\succeq$-concave and $\succeq$-monotone.

Solution: Since A is of rank m, the function $F(x)$ clearly is well-defined and $\succ 0$ when $x \succ 0$ To prove that F is $\succeq$-concave, it sufices to verify that the set

$$
\{(x, Y) \mid x, Y \succ 0, Y \preceq(Ax^{- 1} A^{T})^{- 1}\}
$$

is convex, which is nearly evident:

$$
\begin{array}{lll} \{(x, Y) \mid x, Y \succ 0, Y \preceq(Ax^{- 1} A^{T})^{- 1}\} & = & \{(x, Y) \mid x, Y \succ 0, Y^{- 1} \succeq Ax^{- 1} A^{T}\} \\ & = & \{(x, Y) \mid x, Y \succ 0, \left(\begin{array}{cc} Y^{- 1} & A \\ A^{T} & x \end{array} \right) \succeq 0\} \\ & = & \{(x, Y) \mid x, Y \succ 0, x \succeq A^{T} YA\}.\end{array}
$$

To prove that F is $\succeq$-monotone, note that ${\mathrm{if ~}} 0 \preceq x \preceq x^{\prime}$ , then $0 \prec(x^{\prime})^{- 1} \preceq x^{- 1}$ , whence $0 \prec$ $A(x^{\prime})^{- 1} A^{T} \preceq Ax^{- 1} A^{T}$ , whence, in turn, $F(x) =(Ax^{- 1} A^{T})^{- 1} \preceq(A(x^{\prime})^{- 1} A^{T})^{- 1} = F(x^{\prime})$

## 6.3.3 Around Lovasz capacity number

Exercise 3.28 Let Γ be an n-node graph, and $\sigma(\Gamma)$ be the optimal value in the problem

$$
\min_{\lambda, \mu, \nu} \left\{\lambda : \left(\begin{array}{cc} \lambda & - \frac{1}{2}(e + \mu)^{T} \\ - \frac{1}{2}(e + \mu) & A(\mu, \nu) \end{array} \right) \succeq 0 \right\},\tag{Sh}
$$

where $e =(1,..., 1)^{T} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}, A(\mu, \nu) = \mathrm{Diag}(\mu) + Z(\nu)$ , and $Z(\nu)$ is the matrix as follows:

- the dimension of ν is equal to the number of arcs in Γ, and the coordinates of ν are indexed by these arcs;

- the diagonal entries of $Z,$ same as the of-diagonal entries of $Z$ corresponding to “empty” cells $ij$ (i.e., with i and $j$ non-adjacent) are zeros;

- the of-diagonal entries of $Z$ in a pair of symmetric “non-empty” cells $ij, ji$ are equal to the coordinate of ν indexed by the corresponding arc.

Prove that $\sigma(\Gamma)$ is nothing but the Lovasz capacity Θ(Γ) of the graph.

Solution. In view of (3.8.3) all we need is to prove that $\sigma(\Gamma) \geq \Theta(\Gamma)$

Let $(\lambda, \mu, \nu)$ be a feasible solution to (Sh); we should prove that there exists x such that $(\lambda, x)$ is a feasible solution to the Lovasz problem

$$
\min_{\lambda, x} \left\{\lambda : \lambda I_{n} - \mathcal{L}(x) \succeq 0 \right\}\tag{L}
$$

Setting $\begin{array}{r}{y = \frac{1}{2}(e + \mu)} \end{array}$ , we see that

$$
\left(\begin{array}{cc} \lambda & - \frac{1}{2}(e + \mu)^{T} \\ - \frac{1}{2}(e + \mu) & Z(\nu) + \mathrm{Diag}(\mu) \end{array} \right) = \left(\begin{array}{cc} \lambda & - y^{T} \\ - y & Z(\nu) + 2 \mathrm{Diag}(y) - I_{n} \end{array} \right) \succeq 0.
$$

The diagonal entries of $Z = Z(\nu)$ are zero, while the diagonal entries of $Z + 2{\mathrm{Diag}}(y) - I_{n}$ must be nonnegative; we conclude that $y > 0$ . Setting $Y = \mathrm{Diag}(y)$ , we have

$$
\left(\begin{array}{cc} \lambda & - y^{T} \\ - y & Z + 2Y - I_{n} \end{array} \right) \succeq 0 \Rightarrow \left(\begin{array}{cc} 1 & \\ & Y^{- 1} \end{array} \right) \left(\begin{array}{cc} \lambda & - y^{T} \\ - y & Z + 2Y - I_{n} \end{array} \right) \left(\begin{array}{cc} 1 & \\ & Y^{- 1} \end{array} \right) \succeq 0,
$$

i.e.,

$$
\left(\begin{array}{cc} \lambda & - e^{T} \\ - e & Y^{- 1} ZY^{- 1} + 2Y^{- 1} - Y^{- 2} \end{array} \right) \succeq 0,
$$

whence by the Schur Complement Lemma

$$
\lambda \left[Y^{- 1} ZY^{- 1} + 2Y^{- 1} - Y^{- 2} \right] - ee^{T} \succeq 0,
$$

$^{\mathrm{or,}}$ which is the same,

$$
\lambda I_{n} - \left[ee^{T} - \lambda Y^{- 1} ZY^{- 1} \right] \succeq \lambda(I_{n} - 2Y^{- 1} + Y^{- 2}) = \lambda(I_{n} - Y^{- 1})^{2}.
$$

We see that $\lambda I_{n} - \left\lceil ee^{T} - \lambda Y^{- 1} ZY^{- 1} \right\rceil \succeq 0;$ ; it remains to note that the matrix in the brackets clearly is $\mathcal{L}(x)$ for certain x.

## 6.3.4 Around operator norms

Exercise 3.35.

1) Let $T \subset \mathbb{R}^{n}$ be a convex compact set with a nonempty interior, and

$$
\mathbf{T} = \operatorname{cl} \left\{\left[x; t \right] \in \mathbb{R}^{n} \times \mathbb{R}: t > 0, t^{- 1} x \in T \right\}
$$

be the closed conic hull of T . Prove that $T$ is a regular cone such that

$$
T = \{x:[x; 1] \in \mathbf{T}\},
$$

and the cone dual to T is

$$
\mathbf{T}_{*} = \{[g; s]: s \geq \phi_{T}(- g)\},
$$

where

$$
\phi_{T}(y) = \max_{x \in T} x^{T} y
$$

is the support function of T .

Solution: The only not completely evident claim is the one about the dual cone. We have

$$
[y; s] \in \mathbf{T}_{*} \Leftrightarrow y^{T} x + st \geq 0 \forall[x; t] \in \mathbf{T} \Leftrightarrow y^{T} x + s \geq 0 \forall x \in T \Leftrightarrow - \phi_{T}(- y) + t = \min_{x \in T} y^{T} x + t \geq 0
$$

2) Let $T$ be a convex compact subset of $\mathbb{R}_{+}^{m}$ with int $T \neq \emptyset$ , and let

$$
X[T] = \{X \in \mathbf{S}_{+}^{m}: \mathrm{Dg}(X) \in T\},
$$

where, as always, $\operatorname{Dg}(X)$ is the vector of diagonal entries of matrix X. Prove that $X[T]$ is a convex compact subset of $\mathbf{S}_{+}^{n}$ , the closed conic hull of $X[T]$ is the regular cone

$$
\mathbf{X}[T] = \{(X, t) \in \mathbf{S}_{+}^{m} \times \mathbb{R}:[\mathrm{Dg}(X); t] \in \mathbf{T}\},
$$

where T is the closed conic hull of $T,$ , and the cone dual to $\mathbf{X}[T]$ is

$$
\mathbf{X}_{*}[T] = \{Y \in \mathbf{S}^{m}: \exists h \in \mathbb{R}^{m}: \operatorname{Diag} \{h\} + Y \succeq 0, r \geq \phi_{T}(h)\},
$$

with the same $\phi_{T}(\cdot)$ as in 1).

Solution: all claims, except for the description of $\mathbf{X}_{*}[T]$ , are evident. Now, the cone dual to $\mathbf{X}[T]$ lives in the space $\mathbf{S}^{m} \times \mathbb{R}$ , and $(Y, r)$ belongs to this dual cone if and only if $\mathrm{Tr}(YX) + r \geq 0$ whenever $X \succeq 0$ and $\operatorname{Dg}(X) \in T$ , that is, if and only if

$$
\operatorname{Opt}(Y) := \min \left\{\operatorname{Tr}(YX): X \succeq 0, \mathrm{Dg}(X) \in T \right\} \geq - r.
$$

Now, by 1), Opt(Y ) is the optimal value in the conic problem

$$
\min_{X} \left\{\operatorname{Tr}(YX): X \succeq 0,[\mathrm{Dg}(X); 1] \in \mathbf{T} \right\}\tag{\( \left(*\right)\}
$$

and under assumptions of 2), the feasible set of this problem is compact and with a nonempty interior, implying that the optimal value in question is equal to the one of the dual problem. By 1), the dual problem is as follows: we equip the constraint $X \succeq 0$ with Lagrange multiplier $Z \succeq 0$ , and the constraint $[\mathrm{Dg}(X); 1] \in \mathbf{T}$ with the Largange multiplier $[g; s] \in \mathbf{T}_{*}$ , that is, with $\phi_{T}(- g) \leq s$ . Aggregating the constraints of $(*)$ with these Lagrange multipliers, we get the inequality

$$
\operatorname{Tr}(ZX) + \sum_{i} X_{ii} g_{i} \geq - s;
$$

to get the dual problem, we impose on $Z$ and $[g; s]$ aside of the above conic constraints, the requirement for the left hand side in the aggregated inequality to be equal to $\operatorname{Tr}(YX)$ identically in $X \in \mathbf{S}^{m}$ , and maximize under these restrictions the right hand side −s of the aggregated inequality. Thus,

$$
\operatorname{Opt}(Y) = \max_{Z,[g; s]} \left\{- s: Y = Z + \operatorname{Diag} \{g\}, Z \succeq 0, s \geq \phi_{T}(- g) \right\} = - \min_{[g; s]} \left\{\phi_{T}(- g): Y \succeq \operatorname{Diag} \{g\} \right\},
$$

and

$$
\mathbf{X}_{*}[T] = \left\{Y \in \mathbf{S}^{m}: \operatorname{Opt}(Y) + r \geq 0 \right\} = \left\{Y: \exists h: \operatorname{Diag} \{h\} + Y \succeq 0, r \geq \phi_{T}(h) \right\},
$$

as claimed.

3) Under the premise and in the notation of Theorem 3.4.3, let $T$ posses a nonempty interior. Prove that

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} s_{*}(A) & = & - \min_{u} \left\{\phi_{T}(- u): A \succeq \mathrm{Diag} \{u\} \right\} \\ s^{*}(A) & = & \min_{w} \left\{\phi_{T}(w): \mathrm{Diag} \{w\} \succeq A \right\} \end{array}\tag{a}
$$

(!)

(b)

Solution: We have by results of 1), 2):

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} s_{*}(A) & := & \min_{X} \{\mathrm{Tr}(AX): X \succeq 0, \mathrm{Dg}(X) \in T\} = \min_{X} \{\mathrm{Tr}(AX):[X; 1] \in \mathbf{X}[T]\} \\ & = & \max_{r} \{- r:[A; r] \in \mathbf{X}_{*}[T]\}[\text{conic duality}] \\ & = & - \min_{u} \{\phi_{T}(- u): A \succeq \mathrm{Diag} \{u\}\}[\text{by 2})] \end{array}
$$

and

$$
\begin{array}{lll} s^{*}((A) & := & \max_{X} \{\mathrm{Tr}(AX): X \succeq 0, \mathrm{Dg}(X) \in T\} = \max_{X} \{\mathrm{Tr}(AX):[X; 1] \in \mathbf{X}[T]\} \\ & = & \min_{r} \left\{r:[- A; - r] \in \mathbf{X}_{*}[T] \right\}[\text{conic duality}] \\ & = & \min_{w} \left\{\phi_{T}(w): \mathrm{Diag} \{w\} \succeq A \right\}[\text{by 2})] \end{array}
$$

4) In the situation of 3), let matrix A from 3) be of special structure: $A = \left[{\frac{\partial B}{B^{T}}} \right]$ with $p \times q$ matrix B. Prove that in this case

a. One has $s^{*}(A) = - s_{*}(A)$ and $m^{*}(A) = - m_{*}(A)$

b. One has $\begin{array}{r}{m^{*}(A) = \operatorname{max}_{x \in{\mathcal{T}}} \left| x^{T} Ax \right| \leq s^{*}(A) = \operatorname{min}_{h} \left\{\phi_{T}(h) : \operatorname{Diag} \{h\} \succeq A \right\} \leq \frac{\pi}{4 - \pi} m^{*}(A)} \end{array}$

c. Derive from Theorem 3.4.3 the following “partial refinement” of Theorem 3.4.6:

Theorem 3.8.1 Consider a special case of the situation considered in Theorem 3.4.6, specifically, the one where in $(3.4.29) \K = \dim z, \z^{T} R_{k} z = z_{k}^{2}, \k \leq K$ , and similarly L = dim w and $w^{T} S_{\ell} w = w_{\ell}^{2}, \ell \le L$ . Then the eficiently computable upper bound

$$
\overline{{\Phi}}_{\pi \to \theta}(C) = \min_{\lambda \geq 0, \mu \geq 0} \left\{\phi_{\mathcal{R}}(\lambda) + \phi_{\mathcal{S}}(\mu): \left[\begin{array}{cc} \mathrm{Diag} \{\mu\} & \frac{1}{2} Q^{T} CP \\ \hline \frac{1}{2} P^{T} C^{T} Q & \mathrm{Diag} \{\lambda\} \end{array} \right] \succeq 0 \right\}\tag{a}
$$

(3.8.9)

(cf. (3.4.30)) on the operator norm $\Phi_{\pi \to \theta}(C) = \operatorname{max}_{x : \pi(x) \leq 1} \theta(Cx)$ of a matrix C is tight within absolute constant factor:

$$
\Phi_{\pi \to \theta}(C) \leq \overline{{\Phi}}_{\pi \to \theta}(C) \leq \frac{\pi}{4 - \pi} \Phi_{\pi \to \theta}(C),\tag{3.8.10}
$$

cf. (3.4.31).

Solution: In the situation of Theorem 3.4.3, alternating in whatever fashion signs of entries of $x \in \tau$ keeps $x$ in $\tau$ , so that when $x =[x_{1};...; x_{n}] \in{\mathcal{T}}$ , vector $x^{\prime}$ obstained from x by multiplying the first p entries by $- 1$ belongs to $\tau$ as well. Since $x^{T} Ax = -[x^{\prime}]^{T} Ax^{\prime}.$ , we conclude that the set of values of $x^{T} Ax$ at points of $\tau$ is symmetric w.r.t. the origin, so that $m_{*}(A) = - m^{*}(A)$ . Next, with our $^{a,}$ the matrices $\mathrm{Diag} \{z\} + A$ and $\operatorname{Diag} \{z\} - A$ simultaneously are or are not positive semidefinite. It follows that w is feasible for (!.a) if and only if $u = - w$ is feasible for (!.b), implying that $s_{*}(A) = - s^{*}(A)$ , as claimed in 4.a.

In 4.b, the first equality is readily given by the definition of $m^{*}$ combined with the second equalaity in 4.a, and the second equality is (!.b), while the inequalities are exactly what is stated by Theorem 3.4.3 in the situation of 4.a.

To justify 4.c, note that under the premise of Theorem 3.8.1 the operator norm $\Phi_{\pi \to \theta}(C)$ of C is nothing but the quantity

$$
\max_{[w; z]} \left\{[w; z]^{T} \left[\begin{array}{cc} & B \\ \hline B^{T} & \end{array} \right][w; z]: \exists r \in \mathcal{R}, s \in \mathcal{S}: w_{\ell}^{2} \leq s_{\ell}, \ell \leq L, z_{k}^{2} \leq r_{k}, k \leq K \right\}, B = \frac{1}{2} Q^{T} CP.
$$

Setting $\mathcal{T} = \mathcal{S} \times \mathcal{R}$ , we find ourselves under the premise of Theorem 3.4.3 with $A =$ $\left[{\frac{\left| B \right.}{\left.B^{T} \right|}} \right]$ , and $\Phi_{\pi \to \theta}(B)$ is nothing but what in this Theorem was called $m^{*}(A)$ . From comparing (3.8.9.a) with (!.a), we conclude that ${\overline{{\Phi}}}_{\pi \to \theta}(C)$ is nothing but $s^{*}(A)$ . With these observations, (3.8.10) becomes nothing but the already proved 4.b. ✷

## 6.3.5 Around S-Lemma

For notation in what follows, see section 3.8.7 in Lecture 3.

## 6.3.5.1 A straightforward proof of the standard S-Lemma

Exercise 3.49.3) Given data $A, B$ satisfying the premise of (SL.B), define the sets

$$
Q_{x} = \{\lambda \geq 0: x^{T} Bx \geq \lambda x^{T} Ax\}.
$$

Prove that every two sets $Q_{x^{\prime}}, Q_{x^{\prime \prime}}$ have a point in common.

Solution: The case when $x^{\prime}, x^{\prime \prime}$ are collinear is trivial. Assuming that $x^{\prime}, x^{\prime \prime}$ are linearly independent, consider the quadratic forms on the 2D plane:

$$
\alpha(z) =(sx^{\prime} + tx^{\prime \prime})^{T} A(sx^{\prime} + tx^{\prime \prime}), \beta(z) =(sx^{\prime} + tx^{\prime \prime})^{T} B(sx^{\prime} + tx^{\prime \prime}), z =(s, t)^{T}.
$$

By their origin, we have

$$
\alpha(z) \geq 0, z \neq 0 \Rightarrow \beta(z) > 0.\tag{!}
$$

All we need is to prove that there exists $\lambda \geq 0$ such that $\beta(z) \geq \lambda \alpha(z)$ for all $z \in \mathbb{R}^{2};$ ; such a λ clearly is a common point of $Q_{x^{\prime}}$ and $\boldsymbol{Q}_{\boldsymbol{x}^{\prime \prime}}$

As it is well-known from Linear Algebra, we can choose a coordinate system in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ in such a way that the matrix α of the form $\alpha(\cdot)$ in these coordinates, let them be called $u, v,$ is diagonal:

$$
\alpha = \left(\begin{array}{cc} a & 0 \\ 0 & b \end{array} \right);
$$

let also

$$
\beta = \left(\begin{array}{cc} p & r \\ r & q \end{array} \right)
$$

be the matrix of the form $\beta(\cdot)$ in the coordinates $u, v$ . Let us consider all possible combinations of signs of $^{a,}$ b:

$a \ge 0, b \ge 0.$ . In this case, $\alpha(\cdot)$ is nonnegative everywhere, whence by $(!) \beta(\cdot) \geq 0$ Consequently, $\beta(\cdot) \geq \lambda \alpha(\cdot)$ with $\lambda = 0$

- $a < 0, b < 0.$ . In this case the matrix of the quadratic form $\beta(\cdot) - \lambda \alpha(\cdot)$ is

$$
\left(\begin{array}{cc} p + \lambda | a | & r \\ r & q + \lambda | b | \end{array} \right).
$$

This matrix clearly is positive definite for all large enough positive $\lambda,$ so that here again $\beta(\cdot) \geq \lambda \alpha(\cdot)$ for properly chosen nonnegative λ.

$a = 0, b < 0$ . In this case $\alpha(1, 0) = 0$ (the coordinates in question are $u, v)$ , so that by (!) $p > 0$ . The matrix of the form $\beta(\cdot) - \lambda \alpha(\cdot)$ is

$$
\left(\begin{array}{cc} p & r \\ r & q + \lambda | b | \end{array} \right),
$$

and since $p > 0$ and $| b | > 0$ , this matrix is positive definite for all large enough positive λ. Thus, here again $\beta(\cdot) \geq \lambda \alpha(\cdot)$ for properly chosen $\lambda \geq 0$

$a < 0, b = 0.$ This case is completely similar to the previous one.

3) is proved.

## 6.3.5.2 S-Lemma with a multi-inequality premise

Exercise 3.50 Demonstrate by example that if $x^{T} Ax, x^{T} Bx, x^{T} Cx$ are three quadratic forms with symmetric matrices such that

$$
\begin{array}{c} \exists \bar{x}: \bar{x}^{T} A \bar{x} > 0, \bar{x}^{T} B \bar{x} > 0 \\ x^{T} Ax \geq 0, x^{T} Bx \geq 0 \Rightarrow x^{T} Cx \geq 0, \end{array}\tag{6.3.3}
$$

then not necessarily there exist $\lambda, \mu \geq 0$ such that $C \succeq \lambda A + \mu B.$

A solution:

$$
A = \left(\begin{array}{cc} \lambda^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & - 1 \end{array} \right), \quad B = \left(\begin{array}{cc} \mu \nu & 0.5(\mu - \nu) \\ 0.5(\mu - \nu) & - 1 \end{array} \right), \quad C = \left(\begin{array}{cc} \lambda \mu & 0.5(\mu - \lambda) \\ 0.5(\mu - \lambda) & - 1 \end{array} \right)
$$

With a proper setup, $\mathrm{e.g.}$

$$
\lambda = 1.100, \quad \mu = 0.818, \quad \nu = 1.344,
$$

the above matrices satisfy both (3.8.19) and (3.8.20).

Exercise 3.55 Let $n \geq 3$

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} f(x) & = & \theta_{1} x_{1}^{2} - \theta_{2} x_{2}^{2} + \sum_{i = 3}^{n} \theta_{i} x_{i}^{2}: \mathbb{R}^{n} \to \mathbb{R}, \\ & & \theta_{1} \geq \theta_{2} \geq 0, \theta_{1} + \theta_{2} > 0, - \theta_{2} \leq \theta_{i} \leq \theta_{1} \forall i \geq 3; \\ Y & = & \{x: \| x \|_{2} = 1, f(x) = 0\}.\end{array}
$$

1) Let $x \in Y$ . Prove that x can be linked in $Y$ by a continuous curve with a point $x^{\prime}$ such that the coordinates of $x^{\prime}$ with indices $3, 4,..., n$ vanish.

Proof: It sufices to build a continuous curve $\gamma(t) \in Y, 0 \leq t \leq 1$ , of the form

$$
\gamma(t) =(x_{1}(t), x_{2}(t), tx_{3}, tx_{4}, \dots, tx_{n})^{T}, 0 \leq t \leq 1
$$

which passes through x as $t = 1$ . Setting $s = \sum_{i = 3}^{n} \theta_{i} x_{i}^{2} = \theta_{2} x_{2}^{2} - \theta_{1} x_{1}^{2}$ and $g^{2} = d^{T} d =$ $1 - x_{1}^{2} - x_{2}^{2}$ , we should verify that one can define continuous functions $x_{1}(t), x_{2}(t)$ of $t \in[0, 1]$ satisfying the system of equations

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{rcl} \theta_{1} x_{1}^{2}(t) - \theta_{2} x_{2}^{2}(t) + t^{2} s & = & 0 \\ x_{1}^{2}(t) + x_{2}^{2}(t) + t^{2} g^{2} & = & 1 \end{array} \right.
$$

along with the “boundary conditions”

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} x_{1}(1) & = & x_{1}; \\ x_{2}(1) & = & x_{2}.\end{array}
$$

Substituting $v_{1}(t) = x_{1}^{2}(t), v_{2}(t) = x_{2}^{2}(t)$ and taking into account that $\theta_{1}, \theta_{2} \geq 0, \theta_{1} + \theta_{2} > 0$ we get

$$
\begin{array}{rcl}(\theta_{1} + \theta_{2}) v_{1}(t) & = & \theta_{2}(1 - t^{2} g^{2}) - t^{2} s \\ & = & \theta_{2}(1 - t^{2} g^{2} - t^{2}(\theta_{2} x_{2}^{2} - \theta_{1} x_{1}^{2}) \\ & = & \theta_{2}(1 - t^{2}[g^{2} + x_{2}^{2}]) + t^{2} \theta_{1} x_{1}^{2} \\ & = & \theta_{2}(1 - t^{2}[1 - x_{1}^{2}]) + t^{2} \theta_{1} x_{1}^{2}; \\(\theta_{1} + \theta_{2}) v_{2}(t) & = & \theta_{1}(1 - t^{2} g^{2}) + t^{2} s \\ & = & \theta_{1}(1 - t^{2} g^{2}) + t^{2}(\theta_{2} x_{2}^{2} - \theta_{1} x_{1}^{2}) \\ & = & \theta_{1}(1 - t^{2}[g^{2} + x_{1}^{2}]) + t^{2} \theta_{2} x_{2}^{2} \\ & = & \theta_{1}(1 - t^{2}[1 - x_{2}^{2}]) + t^{2} \theta_{2} x_{2}^{2}.\end{array}
$$

We see that $v_{1}(t), v_{2}(t)$ are continuous, nonnegative and equal $x_{1}^{2}, x_{2}^{2}$ , respectively, as $t = 1$ Taking $x_{1}(t) = \kappa_{1} v_{1}^{1 / 2}, x_{2}(t) = \kappa_{2} v_{2}^{1 / 2}(t)$ with properly chosen $\kappa_{i} = \pm 1, i = 1, 2$ , we get the required curve $\gamma(\cdot)$

2) Prove that there exists a point $z^{+} =(z_{1}, z_{2}, z_{3}, 0, 0,..., 0)^{T} \in Y$ such that

$$
\text{(i)} z_{1} z_{2} = 0;
$$

(ii) given a point $u =(u_{1}, u_{2}, 0, 0,..., 0)^{T} \in Y$ , you can either (ii.1) link u by continuous curves in $Y$ both to $z^{+}$ and to $\bar{z}^{+} =(z_{1}, z_{2}, - z_{3}, 0, 0,..., 0)^{T} \in Y$ , or (ii.2) link u both to $z^{-} =(- z_{1}, - z_{2}, z_{3}, 0, 0,..., 0)^{T}$ and $\bar{z}^{-} =(- z_{1}, - z_{2}, - z_{3}, 0, 0,..., 0)^{T}$ (note that $z^{+} = - \bar{z}^{-}, \bar{z}^{+} = - z^{-})$

Proof: Recall that $\theta_{1} \geq \theta_{2} \geq 0$ and $\theta_{1} + \theta_{2} > 0$ . Consider two possible cases: $\theta_{2} = 0$ and $\theta_{2} > 0.$

Case of $\theta_{2} = 0 \colon$ In this case it sufices to set $z^{+} =(0, 1, 0, 0,..., 0)^{T}$ . Indeed, the point clearly belongs to Y and satisfies (i). Further, if $u \in Y$ is such that $u_{3} = \ldots = u_{n} = 0$ , then from $\theta_{2} = 0$ and the definition of $Y$ it immediately follows that $u_{1} = 0, u_{2} = \pm 1$ . Thus, either u coincides with $z^{+} = \bar{z}^{+}$ , or u coincides with $z^{-} = \bar{z}^{-}$ ; in both cases, (ii) takes place.

$$
\theta_{2} > 0:
$$

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \tau & = & \min \left[\frac{\theta_{1}}{\theta_{1} - \theta_{3}}; \frac{\theta_{2}}{\theta_{2} + \theta_{3}} \right]; \\[\text{note that} \tau > 0 \text{due to} \theta_{1}, \theta_{2} > 0 \text{and} - \theta_{2} \leq \theta_{3} \leq \theta_{1}] \\ z_{1} & = & \sqrt{(\theta_{1} + \theta_{2})^{- 1}(\theta_{2} - \tau[\theta_{2} + \theta_{3}])}; \\ z_{2} & = & \sqrt{(\theta_{1} + \theta_{2})^{- 1}(\theta_{1} - \tau[\theta_{1} - \theta_{3}])}; \\ z_{3} & = & \sqrt{\tau}; \\ z^{+} & = &(z_{1}, z_{2}, z_{3}, 0, 0,..., 0)^{T}.\end{array}
$$

It is immediately seen that $z^{+}$ is well-defined and satisfies (i). Now let us verify that $z^{+}$ satisfies (ii) as well. Let $u \ = \(u_{1}, u_{2}, 0, 0,..., 0)^{T} \ \in \Y$ , and let the vector-function $z(t)$ $0 \leq t \leq \sqrt{\tau}$ , be defined by the relations

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} z_{1}(t) & = & \sqrt{(\theta_{1} + \theta_{2})^{- 1}(\theta_{2} - t^{2}[\theta_{2} + \theta_{3}])}; \\ z_{2}(t) & = & \sqrt{(\theta_{1} + \theta_{2})^{- 1}(\theta_{1} - t^{2}[\theta_{1} - \theta_{3}])}; \\ z_{3}(t) & = & t; \\ z_{i}(t) & = & 0, i = 4,..., n.\end{array}
$$

It is immediately seen that $z(\cdot)$ is well-defined, continuous, takes its values in $Y$ and that $z(\sqrt{\tau}) = z^{+}$ . Now, z(0) is the vector

$$
\bar{u} \equiv(\sqrt{\frac{\theta_{2}}{\theta_{1} + \theta_{2}}}, \sqrt{\frac{\theta_{1}}{\theta_{1} + \theta_{2}}}, 0, 0,..., 0)^{T};
$$

from $u \in Y, u_{3} =...= u_{n} = 0$ it immediately follows that $| u_{i} | = | \bar{u}_{i} |, i = 1, 2$ . Now consider four possible cases:

$$
(+) u_{1} = \bar{u}_{1}, u_{2} = \bar{u}_{2}
$$

$$
(- -) u_{1} = - \bar{u}_{1}, u_{2} = - \bar{u}_{2}
$$

$$
\left(+ -\right) u_{1} = \bar{u}_{1}, u_{2} = - \bar{u}_{2}
$$

$$
(- +) u_{1} = - \bar{u}_{1}, u_{2} = \bar{u}_{2}
$$

- In the case of (++) the continuous curve $\gamma(t) \equiv z(t) \in Y, 0 \leq t \leq \sqrt{\tau}$ , links u with $z^{+}$ , while the continuous curve $\bar{\gamma}(t) =(z_{1}(t), z_{2}(t), - z_{3}(t), 0, 0,..., 0)^{T} \in Y$ links u with $\bar{z}^{+}$ , so that (ii.1) takes place;

- In the case of (−−) the continuous curve $\gamma(t) \equiv - z(t) \in Y, 0 \leq t \leq \sqrt{\tau}$ , links u with $\bar{z}^{-} = - z^{+}$ , while the continuous curve $\bar{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}(t) \ : = \ :(- z_{1}(t), - z_{2}(t), z_{3}(t), 0, 0,..., 0)^{T} \in \ : Y$ links u with $z^{-} = - \bar{z}^{+}$ , so that (ii.2) takes place;

- In the case of (+−) the continuous curves $\gamma(t) \equiv(z_{1}(t), - z_{2}(t), z_{3}(t), 0, 0,..., 0)^{T} \in Y$ and $\bar{\gamma}(t) =(z_{1}(t), - z_{2}(t), - z_{3}(t), 0, 0,..., 0)^{T}, 0 \leq t \leq \sqrt{\tau}$ , link u either with both points of the pair $(z^{+}, \bar{z}^{+})$ , or with both points of the pair $(z^{-}, \bar{z}^{-})$ , depending on whether $z_{1} = 0 \mathrm{or} z_{1} \neq 0, z_{2} = 0$ (note that at least one of these possibilities does take place due to $z_{1} z_{2} = 0, \sec{\mathrm{(i)}})$ . Thus, in the case in question at least (ii.1) or (ii.2) does hold.

- In the case of (−+) the continuous curves $\gamma(t) \equiv(- z_{1}(t), z_{2}(t), z_{3}(t), 0, 0,..., 0)^{T} \in{\cal Y}$ and $\bar{\gamma}(t) =(z_{1}(t), - z_{2}(t), - z_{3}(t), 0, 0,..., 0)^{T}, 0 \leq t \leq \sqrt{\tau},$ link u either with both points of the pair $(z^{-}, \bar{z}^{-})$ , or with both points of the pair $(z^{+}, \bar{z}^{+})$ , depending on whether $z_{1} = 0 \mathrm{or} z_{1} \neq 0, z_{2} = 0$ , so that here again (ii.1) or (ii.2) does hold.

3) Conclude from 1-2) that Y satisfies the premise of Proposition 3.8.1 and thus complete the proof of Proposition 3.8.3.

Proof: Let $z^{+}$ be given by 2), and let $x, x^{\prime} \in Y$ . By 1), we can link in $Y$ the point x with a point $v =(v_{1}, v_{2}, 0, 0,..., 0)^{T} \in Y$ , and the point $x^{\prime}$ with a point $v^{\prime} =(v_{1}^{\prime}, v_{2}^{\prime}, 0, 0,..., 0)^{T} \in Y$ If for both $u = v$ and $u = v^{\prime} \ \mathrm{(ii.1)}$ holds, then we can link both $v, v^{\prime}$ by continuous curves with $z^{+};$ ; thus, both $x, x^{\prime}$ can be linked in $Y$ with $z^{+}$ as well. We see that both $x, x^{\prime}$ can be linked in $Y$ with the set $\{z^{+}; - z^{+}\}$ , as required in the premise of Proposition 3.8.1. The same conclusion is valid if for both $u = v, u = v^{\prime}$ (ii.2) holds; here both x and $x^{\prime}$ can be linked in $Y$ with $z^{-}$ , and the premise of Proposition 3.8.1 holds true.

Now consider the case when for one of the points $u = v, u = v^{\prime}$ , say, for $u = v$ , (ii.1) holds, while for the other one (ii.2) takes place. Here we can link in Y the point v (and thus – the point x) with the point $z^{+}$ , and we can link in $Y$ the point $v^{\prime}$ (and thus – the point $x^{\prime})$ with the point $\bar{z}^{-} = - z^{+}$ . Thus, we can link in $Y$ both x and $x^{\prime}$ with the set $\{z^{+}; - z^{+}\}$ , and the premise of Proposition 3.8.1 holds true. Thus, $Y$ satisfies the premise of Proposition 3.8.1.

Exercise 3.56.2) Let $A_{i}, i = 1, 2, 3$ , satisfy the premise of (SL.D). Assuming $A_{1} = I$ , prove that the set

$$
H_{1} = \left\{\left(v_{1}, v_{2}\right)^{T} \in \mathbb{R}^{2} \mid \exists x \in \mathbf{S}^{n - 1}: v_{1} = f_{2}(x), v_{3} = f_{3}(x) \right\}
$$

is convex.

Proof: Let $\ell = \{(v_{1}, v_{2})^{t} \in \mathbb{R}^{2} \ | \pv_{1} + qv_{2} + r = 0\}$ be a line in the plane; we should prove that $W = X_{1} \cap \ell$ is a convex, or, which is the same, connected set (Exercise 3.52). There is nothing to prove when $W = \emptyset$ . Assuming $W \neq \emptyset$ , let us set

$$
f(x) = rf_{1}(x) + pf_{2}(x) + qf_{3}(x).
$$

It is immediately seen that $f$ is a homogeneous quadratic form on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ , and that

$$
W = F(Y),
$$

where

$$
\begin{array}{c} F(x) = \binom{f_{2}(x)}{f_{3}(x)}, \\ Y \equiv \{x \in S^{n - 1}: f(y) = 0\} = - Y.\end{array}
$$

By Proposition 3.8.3, the image $Z$ of the set Y under the canonical projection $S^{n - 1} \to \mathbb{P}^{n - 1}$ is connected; since $F$ is even, $W = F(\boldsymbol{Y})$ is the same as $G(Z)$ for certain continuous mapping $G : Z \to \mathbb{R}^{2}$ (Proposition 3.8.2). Thus, W is connected by (C.2).

We have proved that $Z_{1}$ is convex; the compactness of $Z_{1}$ is evident.

Exercise 3.57 Demonstrate by example that (SL.C) not necessarily remains valid when skipping the assumption $^{6} n \geq 3^{5}$ in the premise.

A solution: The linear combination

$$
A + 0.005B - 1.15C
$$

of the matrices built in the solution to Exercise 3.50 is positive definite.

Exercise 3.58.1) Let $A, B, C$ be three $2 \times 2$ symmetric matrices such that the system of inequalities $x^{T} Ax \ge 0, x^{T} Bx \ge 0$ is strictly feasible and the inequality $x^{T} Cx$ is a consequence of the system. 1) Assume that there exists a nonsingular matrix Q such that both the matrices $QAQ^{\dot{T}}$ and $QBQ^{T}$ are diagonal. Prove that then there exist $\lambda, \mu \geq 0$ such that $C \succeq \lambda A + \mu B$

Solution: W.l.o.g. we may assume that the matrices A, B themselves are diagonal. The case when at least one of the matrices A, B is positive semidefinite is trivially reducible to the usual S-Lemma, so that we can assume that both matrices A and B are not positive semidefinite. Since the system of inequalities $x^{T} Ax > 0, x^{T} Bx > 0$ is feasible, we conclude that the determinants of the matrices A, B are negative. Applying appropriate dilatations of the coordinate axes, swapping, if necessary, the coordinates and multiplying A, B by appropriate positive constants we may reduce the situation to the one where $\overset{\vartriangle}{\boldsymbol{x}^{T}} \boldsymbol{A} \boldsymbol{x} = \boldsymbol{x}_{1}^{2} - \boldsymbol{x}_{2}^{2}$ and either

(a) $x^{T} Bx = \theta^{2} x_{1}^{2} - x_{2}^{2}$

or

(b) $x^{T} Bx = - \theta^{2} x_{1}^{2} + x_{2}^{2}$ with certain $\theta > 0.$

Case of (a): Here the situation is immediately reducible to the one considered in S-Lemma. Indeed, in this case one of the inequalities in the system $x^{T} Ax \ge 0, x^{T} Bx \ge 0$ is a consequence of the other inequality of the system; thus, a consequence $x^{T} Cx$ of the system is in fact a consequence of a properly chosen single inequality from the system; thus, by S-Lemma either $C \succeq \lambda A$ , or $C \succeq \lambda B$ with certain $\lambda \geq 0$

Case of (b): Observe, first, that $\theta < 1$ , since otherwise the system $x^{T} Ax \ge 0, x^{T} Bx \ge 0$ is not strictly feasible. When $\theta < 1$ , the solution set of our system is the union of the following four angles $D^{+ +}, D^{+ -}, D^{--}, D^{- +}$

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} D^{+ +} & = & \{x \mid x_{1} \geq 0, \theta x_{1} \leq x_{2} \leq x_{1}\}; \\ D^{+ -} & = & \text{reflection of} D^{+ +} \text{w.r.t.the} x_{1} \text{-axis;} \\ D^{- -} & = & - D^{+ +}; \\ D^{- +} & = & \text{reflection of} D^{+ +} \text{w.r.t.the} x_{2} \text{-axis.} \end{array}
$$

Now, the case when C is positive semidefinite is trivial – here $C \succeq 0{\times} A{+} 0{\times} B$ . Thus, we may assume that one eigenvalue of C is negative; the other should be nonnegative, since otherwise $x^{T} Cx < 0$ whenever x $\neq 0$ , while we know that $x^{T} Cx \geq 0$ at the (nonempty!) solution set of the system $x^{T} Ax > 0, x^{T} Bx > 0$ . Since one eigenvalue of C is negative, and the other one is nonnegative, the set $X_{C} = \{x \mid x^{T} Cx \geq 0\}$ is the union of an certain angle D (which can reduce to a ray) and the angle $- D$ . Since the inequality $x^{T} Cx \geq 0$ is a consequence of the system $x^{T} Ax \geq 0, x^{T} Bx \geq 0$ , we have $D \cup(- D) \supset D^{+ +} \cup D^{+ -} \cup D^{--} \cup D^{- +}$ . Geometry says that the latter inclusion can be valid only when D contains two “neighbouring”, w.r.t. the cyclic order, of the angles $D^{+ +}, D^{+ -}, D^{--}, D^{- +},$ ; but in this case the inequality $x^{T} Cx$ is a consequence of an appropriate single inequality from the pair $x^{T} Ax \ge 0, x^{T} Bx \ge 0$ Namely, when $D \supset D^{+ +} \cup D^{+ -}{\mathrm{~ or ~}} D \supset D^{--} \cup D^{- +}, X_{C}$ contains the solution set of the inequality $x^{T} Bx \geq 0$ , while in the cases of $D \supset D^{+ -} \cup D^{--}$ and of $D \supset D^{- +} \cup D^{+ +} X_{C}$ contains the solution set of the inequality $x^{T} Ax \geq 0$ . Applying the usual S-Lemma, we conclude that in the case of (b) there exist $\lambda, \mu \geq 0$ (with one of these coeficients equal to 0) such that $C \succeq \lambda A + \mu B$

Solution: As explained in the Hint, it sufices to consider the case of ${\bf K} ={\bf L}^{k}$ . Let $x =$ $(u, t) \in$ int ${\bf L}^{k}$ , and let $s =(v, \tau) = - \nabla L_{k}(x)$ . We should prove that $s \in$ int ${\bf L}^{k}$ and that $\nabla L_{k}(s) = - x.$ . By (4.3.1), one has

$$
v = - \frac{2}{t^{2} - u^{T} u} u, \quad \tau = \frac{2}{t^{2} - u^{T} u} t
$$

$$
\begin{array}{c} \tau \geq 0 \text{and} \tau^{2} - v^{T} v = \frac{4}{t^{2} - x^{T} x} > 0 \\ \Downarrow \end{array}
$$

$$
s \in \operatorname{int} \mathbf{L}^{k};
$$

$$
- \nabla L_{k}(s) = \binom{- \frac{2}{\tau^{2} - v^{T} v} v}{\frac{2}{\tau^{2} - v^{T} v} \tau} = \left(\begin{array}{cc} \frac{2}{4} & \frac{2}{t^{2} - u^{T} u} u \\ \frac{2}{4} & \frac{2}{t^{2} - u^{T} u} t \end{array} \right) = \binom{u}{t}.
