## 6.4.2 Scalings of canonical cones

Exercise 4.4.1) Prove that

1) Whenever $e \in \mathbb{R}^{k - 1}$ is a unit vector and $\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ , the linear transformation

$$
L_{\mu, e}: \quad \binom{u}{t} \mapsto \binom{u -[\mu t -(\sqrt{1 + \mu^{2}} - 1) e^{T} u] e}{\sqrt{1 + \mu^{2}} t - \mu e^{T} u}\tag{*}
$$

maps the cone ${\bf L}^{k}$ onto itself. Besides this, transformation (∗) preserves the “space-time interval” $x^{T} J_{k} x \equiv$ $- x_{1}^{2} -...- x_{k - 1}^{2} + x_{k}^{2} \colon$

$$
[L_{\mu, e} x]^{T} J_{k}[L_{\mu, e} x] = x^{T} J_{k} x \quad \forall x \in \mathbb{R}^{k}
$$

$$
[\Leftrightarrow L_{\mu, e}^{T} J_{k} L_{\mu, e} = J_{k}]
$$

and $L_{\mu, e}^{- 1} = L_{\mu, - e}$

Solution: Let $x ={\binom{u}{t}} \in \mathbf{L}^{k}$ . Denoting $s \equiv \binom{v}{\tau} = L_{\mu, e} x.$ , we have

$$
v = u -[\mu t -(\sqrt{1 + \mu^{2}} - 1) e^{T} u] e, \quad \tau = \sqrt{1 + \mu^{2}} t - \mu e^{T} u
$$

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \tau & = & \sqrt{1 + \mu^{2}} t - \mu e^{T} u \geq \sqrt{1 + \mu^{2}} t - \mu \| u \|_{2} \geq 0[\text{since} t \geq \| u \|_{2}, \| e \|_{2} = 1] \\ \tau^{2} - v^{T} v & = &(1 + \mu^{2}) t^{2} - 2 \mu \sqrt{1 + \mu^{2}} te^{T} u + \mu^{2}(e^{T} u)^{2} \\ & & - u^{T} u -[\mu t -(\sqrt{1 + \mu^{2}} - 1) e^{T} u]^{2} \\ & & + 2(e^{T} u)[\mu t -(\sqrt{1 + \mu^{2}} - 1) e^{T} u] \\ & = & t^{2} - u^{T} u[\text{just arithmetic!}] \end{array}
$$

Thus, $x \in \mathbf{L}^{k} \Rightarrow L_{\mu, e} x \in \mathbf{L}^{k}$ . To replace here ⇒ with ⇔, it sufices to verify (a straightforward computation!) that

$$
L_{\mu, e}^{- 1} = L_{\mu, - e},
$$

so that both $\scriptstyle L_{\mu, e}$ and its inverse map ${\bf L}^{k}$ onto itself.

## 6.4.3 Dikin ellipsoid

Exercise 4.8 Prove that if K is a canonical cone, K is the corresponding canonical barrier and $X \in \operatorname{int} \mathbf{K}$ , then the Dikin ellipsoid

$$
W_{X} = \{Y \mid \| Y - X \|_{X} \leq 1\}[\| H \|_{X} = \sqrt{\langle[\nabla^{2} K(X)] H, H \rangle_{E}}]
$$

is contained in K.

Hint: Note that the property to be proved is “stable w.r.t. taking direct products”, so that it sufices to verify it in the cases of ${\bf K} ={\bf L}^{k}$ and $\mathbf{K} = \mathbf{S}_{+}^{k}$ . Further, use the result of Exercise 4.7 to verify that the Dikin ellipsoid “conforms with scalings”: the image of $W_{X}$ under a scaling Q is exactly $W_{\Omega X}$ . Use this observation to reduce the general case to the one where $X = e(\mathbf{K})$ is the central point of the cone in question, and verify straightforwardly that $W_{e(\mathbf{K})} \subset \mathbf{K}$

Solution: According to Hint, it sufices to verify the inclusion $W_{X} \subset \mathbf{K}$ in the following two particular cases:

$$
\mathrm{A} \colon \mathbf{K} = \mathbf{S}_{+}^{k}, X = I_{k};
$$

$$
\text{B:} \mathbf{K} = \mathbf{L}^{k}, X = \binom{0_{k - 1}}{\sqrt{2}}.
$$

Note that in both cases $\nabla^{2} K(X)$ is the unit matrix, so that all we need to prove is that the unit ball, centered at our particular X, is contained in our particular K.

A: We should prove that if $\| H \|_{F} \leq 1$ , then $I + H \succeq 0$ , which is evident: the moduli of eigenvalues of H are $\leq \| H \|_{F} \leq 1$ , so that all these eigenvalues are $\geq - 1$

B: We should prove that if $du \in \mathbb{R}^{k - 1}$ , dt $\mathbf{\Xi} \in \textbf{R}$ satisfy $dt^{2} + du^{T} du \leq 1$ , then the point $\left({\overset{0_{k - 1}}{\sqrt{2}}} \right) + \left({\overset{\bar{du}}{dt}} \right) = \left({\overset{du}{\sqrt{2}}} + dt \right)$ belongs to ${\bf L}^{k}$ . In other words, we should verify that ${\sqrt{2}} + dt \geq 0$ (which is evident) and that $({\sqrt{2}} + dt)^{2} - du^{T} du \geq 0$ . Here is the verification of the latter statement:

$$
\begin{array}{rcl}(\sqrt{2} + dt)^{2} - du^{T} du & = & 2 + 2 \sqrt{2} dt + dt^{2} - du^{T} du \\ & = & 1 + 2 \sqrt{2} dt + 2dt^{2} +(1 - dt^{2} - du^{T} du) \\ & \geq & 1 + 2 \sqrt{2} dt + 2dt^{2} \\ & = &(1 + \sqrt{2} dt)^{2} \geq 0.\end{array}[\text{since} dt^{2} + du^{T} du \leq 1]
$$

Exercise 4.9.2,4) Let K be a canonical cone:

$$
\mathbf{K} = \mathbf{S}_{+}^{k_{1}} \times \dots \times \mathbf{S}_{+}^{k_{p}} \times \mathbf{L}^{k_{p + 1}} \times \dots \times \mathbf{L}^{k_{m}} \subset E = \mathbf{S}^{k_{1}} \times \dots \times \mathbf{S}^{k_{p}} \times \mathbb{R}^{k_{p + 1}} \times \dots \times \mathbb{R}^{k_{m}},\tag{Cone}
$$

and let $X \in \operatorname{int} \mathbf{K}.$ Prove that

2) Whenever $Y \in \mathbf{K}$ , one has

$$
\langle \nabla K(X), Y - X \rangle_{E} \leq \theta(K).
$$

4) The conic cap $\mathbf{K}_{X}$ is contained in the $\| \cdot \|_{X^{-}} \mathrm{ball}$ , centered at X, of the radius $\theta(K)$

$$
Y \in \mathbf{K}_{X} \Rightarrow \| Y - X \|_{X} \leq \theta(K).
$$

Solution to 2), 4): According to the Hint, it sufices to verify the statement in the case when $X = e(\mathbf{K})$ is the central point of $\mathbf{K};$ in this case the Hessian $\nabla^{2} K(X)$ is just the unit matrix, whence, by Proposition 4.3.1, $\nabla K(X) = - X$

2): We should prove that if $Y \in \mathbf{K}$ , then $\langle \nabla K(X), Y - X \rangle_{E} \leq \theta(K)$ . The statement clearly is “stable w.r.t. taking direct products”, so that it sufices to prove it in the cases of $\mathbf{K} = \mathbf{S}_{+}^{k}$ and ${\bf K} ={\bf L}^{k}$

In the case of ${\bf K} ={\bf S}_{+}^{k}$ what should be proved is

$$
\forall H \in \mathbf{S}_{+}^{k}: \quad \operatorname{Tr}(I_{k} - H) \leq k,
$$

which is evident.

In the case of ${\bf K} ={\bf L}^{k}$ what should be proved is

$$
\forall \left(\binom{u}{t}: \| u \|_{2} \leq t\right) \quad \sqrt{2}(\sqrt{2} - t) \leq 2,
$$

which again is evident.

4): We should prove that $\mathrm{~ f ~} X = e({\bf K}), \langle - \nabla K(X), X - Y \rangle_{E} \geq 0$ and $Y \in \mathbf{K}$ , then $\| Y - X \|_{E} \leq$ $\theta(K)$

Let $Y \in \mathbf{K}$ be such that $\langle - \nabla K(X), X - Y \rangle_{E} \geq 0$ , i.e., such that $\langle X, X - Y \rangle_{E} \geq 0$ . We may think of Y as of a collection of a block-diagonal symmetric positive semidefinite matrix H with diagonal blocks of the sizes $k_{1},..., k_{p}$ and $m - p$ vectors ${\binom{u_{i}}{t_{i}}} \in \mathbf{L}^{k_{i}}, i = p + 1,..., m$ (see (Cone)); the condition $\langle X, X - Y \rangle_{E} \geq 0$ now becomes

$$
\operatorname{Tr}(\underbrace{I - H}_{D}) + \sum_{i = p + 1}^{m} \sqrt{2}(\sqrt{2} - t_{i}) \geq 0.\tag{*}
$$

We now have, denoting by $D_{j}$ the eigenvalues of D and by $n = \sum_{i = 1}^{p} k_{i}$ the row size of $D;$

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \| X - Y \|_{X}^{2} & = & \| X - Y \|_{E}^{2} = \mathrm{Tr}((I - H)^{2}) + \sum_{i = p + 1}^{m} \left((\sqrt{2} - t_{i})^{2} + u_{i}^{T} u_{i}\right) \\ & = & \sum_{j = 1}^{n} D_{j}^{2} + \sum_{i = p + 1}^{m} \left(2 - 2 \sqrt{2} t_{i} + t_{i}^{2} + u_{i}^{T} u_{i}\right) \\ & \leq & \sum_{j = 1}^{n} D_{j}^{2} + \sum_{i = p + 1}^{m} \left(2 - 2 \sqrt{2} t_{i} + 2t_{i}^{2}\right) \\ & &[\text{sinceu_{i}^{T} u_{i}} \leq t_{i}^{2}] \\ & = & \sum_{j = 1}^{n} D_{j}^{2} + \sum_{i = p + 1}^{m} \left(1 +(1 - \sqrt{2} t_{i})^{2}\right).\end{array}
$$

Denoting $q = m - p, D_{n + i} = 1 - \sqrt{2} t_{p + i}, i = 1,..., q,$ , we come to the relation

$$
\| X - Y \|_{X}^{2} = q + \sum_{j = 1}^{n + q} D_{j}^{2},\tag{6.4.1}
$$

while (∗) and relations $H \succeq 0, t_{i} \geq 0$ imply that

$$
\begin{array}{c} D_{j} \leq 1, j = 1,..., n + q; \\ \sum_{j = 1}^{n + q} D_{j} \geq - q.\end{array}\tag{6.4.2}
$$

Let A be the maximum of the right hand side in (6.4.1) over $D_{j}{}^{\circ} s$ satisfying (6.4.2), and let $D^{*} =(D_{1}^{*},..., D_{n + q}^{*})^{T}$ be the corresponding maximizer (which clearly exists – (6.4.2) defines a compact set!). In the case of $n + q = 1$ we clearly have $A = 1 + q$ . Now let $n + q > 1$ . We claim that among n+q coordinates of $D^{*}, n + q - 1$ are equal 1, and the remaining coordinate equals $\mathrm{to \ -}(n + 2q - 1)$ . Indeed, if there were at least two entries in $D^{*}$ which are less than 1, then subtracting from one of them a small enough in absolute value $\delta \neq 0$ and adding the same $\delta$ to the other coordinate, we preserve the feasibility of the perturbed point w.r.t. (6.4.2), and, with properly chosen sign of δ, increase $\sum_{j} D_{j}^{2}$ , which is impossible. Thus, at least $n + q - 1$ coordinates of $D^{*}$ are equal to 1; among the points with this property which satisfy (6.4.2) the one with the largest $\sum_{j} D_{j}^{2}$ clearly has the remaining coordinate equal to $1 - n - 2q$ , as claimed.

From our analysis it follows that

$$
A = \left\{\begin{array}{ll} q + 1, & n + q = 1 \\ q +(n + q - 1) +(n + 2q - 1)^{2} =(n + 2q - 1)(n + 2q), & n + q > 1 \end{array}; \right.
$$

recalling that $\theta(K) = n + 2q$ and taking into account (6.4.1) and the origin of A, we get

$$
\| X - Y \|_{X} \leq \theta(K),
$$

as claimed.

## 6.4.4 More on canonical barriers

Exercise 4.11, second statement Prove that if K is a canonical cone, K is the associated canonical barrier, X ∈ int K and ${\cal H} \in{\bf K},{\cal H} \ne 0$ , then

$$
\inf_{t \geq 0} K(X + tH) = - \infty.\tag{*}
$$

Derive from this fact that

(!!) Whenever N is an Affine plane which intersects the interior of K, K is below bounded on the intersection $\mathcal{N} \cap \mathbf{K}$ if and only if the intersection is bounded.

Solution: as explained in Hint, it sufices to verify $(*)$ in the particular case when X is the central point of K. It is also clear that (∗) is stable w.r.t. taking direct products, so that we can restrict ourselves with the cases of $\dot{\mathbf{K}} = \mathbf{S}_{+}^{k}$ and ${\bf K} ={\bf L}^{k}$

Case of ${\bf K} ={\bf S}_{+}^{k}, X = e({\bf S}_{+}^{k}) = I_{k}.$ : Denoting by $H_{i} \geq 0$ the eigenvalues of H and noting that at least one of $\overline{{H_{i} \mathrm{\is > 0}}}$ due to $\overline{{H}} \neq 0$ , we have for $t > 0$ :

$$
K(X + tH) = - \ln \operatorname{Det} \left(I_{k} + tH\right) = - \sum_{i = 1}^{k} \ln \left(1 + tH_{i}\right)\rightarrow - \infty, t \rightarrow \infty.
$$

Case of ${\bf K} ={\bf L}^{k}, X = e({\bf L}^{k}) = \left(\begin{array}{c}{{0_{k - 1}}} \\{{\sqrt 2}} \end{array} \right)$ : Setting $H ={\binom{u}{s}}$ , we have $s \geq \| u \|_{2}$ and $s > 0$ due to $\overline{{H \neq 0}}$ . For $\overline{{t > 0}}$ we have

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} K(X + tH) & = & - \ln((\sqrt{2} + ts)^{2} - t^{2} u^{T} u) = - \ln(2 + 2 \sqrt{2} ts + t^{2}(s^{2} - u^{T} u)) \\ & \leq & - \ln(2 + 2 \sqrt{2} ts) \to - \infty, t \to \infty.\end{array}
$$

To derive (!!), note that if $U = \mathcal{N} \cap \mathbf{K}$ is bounded, then K is below bounded on U just in view of convexity of K (moreover, from the fact that $K$ is a barrier for K it follows that $K$ attains its minimum on U). It remains to prove that if U is unbounded, then K is not below bounded on U. If U is unbounded, there exists a nonzero direction $H \in \mathbf{K}$ which is parallel to $\mathcal{N}$ (take as H a limiting point of the sequence $\| Y_{i} - X \|_{2}^{- 1}(Y_{i} - X)$ , where $Y_{i} \in U$ $\| Y_{i} \|_{2} \to \infty{\mathrm{~ as ~}} i \to \infty$ , and X is a once for ever fixed point from $U)$ . By (∗), K is not below bounded on the ray $\{X + tH \mid t \geq 0\}$ , and this ray clearly belongs to U. Thus, $K$ is not below bounded on $U.$ ✷

## 6.4.5 Around the primal path-following method

Exercise 4.15 Looking at the data in the table at the end of Section 4.5.3, do you believe that the corresponding method is exactly the short-step primal path-following method from Theorem 4.5.1 with the stepsize policy (4.5.12)?

Solution: The table cannot correspond to the indicated method. Indeed, we see from the table that the duality gap along the 12-iteration trajectory is reduced by factor about $10^{6}$ since the duality gap in a short-step method is nearly inverse proportional to the value of the penalty, the latter in course of our 12 iterations should be increased by factor of order of $10^{5} - 10^{6}$ . In our case $\theta(K) = 3$ , and the policy (4.5.12) increases the penalty at an iteration by the factor $(1 + 0.1 / \sqrt{3}) \approx 1.0577;$ with this policy, in 12 iterations the penalty would be increased by $1.0577^{12} < 2 \cdot$ , which is very far from $10^{5} !$

## 6.4.6 An infeasible start path-following method

Exercise 4.18 Consider the problem

$$
\max_{X} \left\{\langle \widetilde{C}, Y \rangle_{\widetilde{E}} \mid Y \in(\mathcal{M} + R) \cap \widetilde{\mathbf{K}} \right\}.\tag{Aux}
$$

where

$$
\widetilde{\mathbf{K}} = \mathbf{K} \times \mathbf{K} \times \underbrace{\mathbf{S}_{+}^{1}}_{= \mathbb{R}_{+}} \times \underbrace{\mathbf{S}_{+}^{1}}_{= \mathbb{R}_{+}}
$$

(K is a canonical cone),

$$
\mathcal{M} = \left\{\left(\begin{array}{c} U \\ V \\ s \\ r \end{array} \right) \Big | \begin{array}{c} U + rB \in \mathcal{L}, \\ V - rC \in \mathcal{L}^{\perp}, \\ \langle C, U \rangle_{E} - \langle B, V \rangle_{E} + s = 0 \end{array} \right\}
$$

is a linear subspace in the space $\widetilde{E}$ where the cone $\widetilde{\bf K}$ lives, and

$$
C \in \mathcal{L}, \quad B \in \mathcal{L}^{\perp}.
$$

It is given that the problem (Aux) is feasible. Prove that the feasible set of $(\mathrm{Aux})$ is unbounded.

Solution: According to the Hint, we should prove that the linear space $\mathcal{M}^{\perp}$ does not intersect int K .

Let us compute $\mathcal{M}^{\perp}$ . A collection $\left(\stackrel{\xi}{\eta} \right), \xi, \eta \in E, s, r \in{\bf S}^{1} ={\bf R}$ is in $\mathcal{M}^{\perp}$ if and only if the linear equation in variables $X, S, \sigma, \tau$

$$
\langle X, \xi \rangle_{E} + \langle S, \eta \rangle_{E} + \sigma s + \tau r = 0
$$

is a corollary of the system of linear equations

$$
X + \tau B \in \mathcal{L}, \quad S - \tau C \in \mathcal{L}^{\perp}, \quad \langle X, C \rangle_{E} - \langle S, B \rangle_{E} + \sigma = 0;
$$

by Linear Algebra, this is the case if and only if there exist $U \in \mathcal{L}^{\bot}, V \in \mathcal{L}$ and a real λ such that

$$
\begin{array}{rcl}(a) & \xi & = U + \lambda C, \\(b) & \eta & = V - \lambda B, \\(c) & s & = \lambda, \\(d) & r & = \langle U, B \rangle_{E} - \langle V, C \rangle_{E}.\end{array}\tag{Pr}
$$

we have obtained a parameterization of $\mathcal{M}^{\perp}$ via the “parameters” $U, V, \lambda$ running through, respectively, $\mathcal L^{\perp}, \mathcal L$ and R. Now assume, on contrary to what should be proved, that the intersection of $\mathcal{M}^{\perp}$ and int $\widetilde{\bf K}$ is nonempty. In other words, assume that there exist $U \in{\mathcal{L}}^{\perp}$ $V \in{\mathcal{L}}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$ which, being substituted in $(\mathrm{Pr})$ , result in a collection $(\xi, \eta, s, r)$ such that $\xi \in \mathbf{\Xi}$ int $\mathbf{K}, \eta \in \mathrm{int} \mathbf{K}, s > 0, r > 0.$ From $(\mathrm{Pr}.c)$ it follows that $\lambda > 0;$ since $(\mathrm{Pr})$ is homogeneous, we may normalize our $U, V, \lambda$ to make $\lambda = 1$ , still keeping $\xi \in \mathbf{\Xi}$ int $\mathbf{K}, \eta \in$ int K, $s > 0, r > 0$ . Assuming $\lambda = 1$ and taking into account that $U, B \in \mathcal{L}^{\bot}, V, C \in \mathcal{L}$ , we get from $\left(\operatorname{Pr}.a - b \right)$

$$
\langle \xi, \eta \rangle_{E} = \langle C, V \rangle_{E} - \langle B, U \rangle_{E};
$$

adding this equality to $(\mathrm{Pr}.d)$ , we get

$$
\langle \xi, \eta \rangle_{E} + r = 0,
$$

which is impossible, since both $r > 0$ and $\langle \xi, \eta \rangle_{E} > 0$ (recall that the cone K is self-dual and $\xi, \eta \in \operatorname{int} \mathbf{K})$ . We have come to the desired contradiction. ✷

Exercise 4.19 Let ${\bar{X}},{\bar{S}}$ be a strictly feasible pair of primal-dual solutions to the primal-dual pair of problems

$$
\min_{X} \left\{\langle C, X \rangle_{E} \mid X \in(\mathcal{L} - B) \cap \mathbf{K} \right\}
$$

$$
\max_{S} \left\{\langle B, S \rangle_{E} \mid S \in(\mathcal{L}^{\perp} + C) \cap \mathbf{K} \right\}\tag{P}
$$

(D)

so that there exists $\gamma \in(0, 1]$ such that

$$
\begin{array}{rclr} \gamma \| X \|_{E} & \leq & \langle \bar{S}, X \rangle_{E} & \forall X \in \mathbf{K}, \\ \gamma \| S \|_{E} & \leq & \langle \bar{X}, S \rangle_{E} & \forall S \in \mathbf{K}.\end{array}
$$

Prove that if $\begin{array}{r}{Y = \left(\begin{array}{c}{X} \\{S} \\{\sigma} \\{\tau} \end{array} \right)} \end{array}$ is feasible for $(\mathrm{Aux})$ , then

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \| Y \|_{\widetilde{E}} & \leq & \alpha \tau + \beta, \\ & & \alpha = \gamma^{- 1} \left[\langle \bar{X}, C \rangle_{E} - \langle \bar{S}, B \rangle_{E} \right] + 1, \\ & & \beta = \gamma^{- 1} \left[\langle \bar{X} + B, D \rangle_{E} + \langle \bar{S} - C, P \rangle_{E} + d \right].\end{array}\tag{6.4.3}
$$

Solution: We have $\bar{X} = \bar{U} - B, \bar{U} \in \mathcal{L}, \bar{S} = \bar{V} + C, \bar{V} \in \mathcal{L}^{\perp}$ . Taking into account the constraints of $(\mathrm{Aux})$ , we get

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \langle \bar{U}, S - \tau C - D \rangle_{E} & = & 0 \Rightarrow \\ \langle \bar{U}, S \rangle_{E} & = & \langle \bar{U}, \tau C + D \rangle_{E} \Rightarrow \\ \langle \bar{X}, S \rangle_{E} & = & - \langle B, S \rangle_{E} + \langle \bar{U}, \tau C + D \rangle_{E}, \\ \langle \bar{V}, X + \tau B - P \rangle_{E} & = & 0 \Rightarrow \\ \langle \bar{V}, X \rangle_{E} & = & \langle \bar{V}, - \tau B + P \rangle_{E} \Rightarrow \\ \langle \bar{S}, X \rangle_{E} & = & \langle C, X \rangle_{E} + \langle \bar{V}, - \tau B + P \rangle_{E}, \\ & \Rightarrow \\ \langle \bar{X}, S \rangle_{E} + \langle \bar{S}, X \rangle_{E} & = &[\langle C, X \rangle_{E} - \langle B, S \rangle_{E}] + \tau[\langle \bar{U}, C \rangle_{E} - \langle \bar{V}, B \rangle_{E}] \\ & & +[\langle \bar{U}, D \rangle_{E} + \langle \bar{V}, P \rangle_{E}] \\ & = & d - \sigma + \tau[\langle \bar{U}, C \rangle_{E} - \langle \bar{V}, B \rangle_{E}] +[\langle \bar{U}, D \rangle_{E} + \langle \bar{V}, P \rangle_{E}] \end{array}
$$

whence

$$
\gamma \left[\| X \|_{E} + \| S \|_{E} \right] + \sigma \leq \tau \left[\langle \bar{U}, C \rangle_{E} - \langle \bar{V}, B \rangle_{E} \right] + \left[\langle \bar{U}, D \rangle_{E} + \langle \bar{V}, P \rangle_{E} + d \right],
$$

and (6.4.3) follows (recall that $\langle C, B \rangle_{E} = 0)$

Exercise 4.23 Let K be a canonical cone, let the primal-dual pair of problems

$$
\min_{X} \left\{\langle C, X \rangle_{E} \mid X \in(\mathcal{L} - B) \cap \mathbf{K} \right\}\tag{P}
$$

$$
\max_{S} \left\{\langle B, S \rangle_{E} \mid S \in(\mathcal{L}^{\perp} + C) \cap \mathbf{K} \right\}\tag{D}
$$

be strictly primal-dual feasible and be normalized by $\langle C, B \rangle_{E} = 0$ , let $(X_{*}, S_{*})$ be a primal-dual optimal solution to the pair, and let X, S “$\epsilon$-satisfy” the feasibility and optimality conditions for (P), (D), i.e.,

$$
(a) \quad X \in \mathbf{K} \cap(\mathcal{L} - B + \Delta X), \| \Delta X \|_{E} \leq \epsilon,
$$

$$
(b) \quad S \in \mathbf{K} \cap(\mathcal{L}^{\perp} + C + \Delta S), \| \Delta S \|_{E} \leq \epsilon,
$$

$$
(c) \quad \langle C, X \rangle_{E} - \langle B, S \rangle_{E} \leq \epsilon.
$$

Prove that

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \langle C, X \rangle_{E} - \mathrm{Opt}(\mathbb{P}) & \leq & \epsilon(1 + \| X_{*} + B \|_{E}), \\ \mathrm{Opt}(\mathrm{D}) - \langle B, S \rangle_{E} & \leq & \epsilon(1 + \| S_{*} - C \|_{E}).\end{array}
$$

Solution: We have $S - C - \Delta S \in{\mathcal{L}}^{\perp}, X_{*} + B \in{\mathcal{L}}$ , whence

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} 0 & = & \langle S - C - \Delta S, X_{*} + B \rangle_{E} \\ & = & \underbrace{\langle S, X_{*} \rangle_{E}}_{\geq 0: X_{*}, S \in \mathbf{K} = \mathbf{K}_{*}} - \text{Opt(P)} + \langle S, B \rangle_{E} + \langle - \Delta S, X_{*} + B \rangle_{E} \\ & & \Rightarrow \\ - \text{Opt(P)} & \leq & - \langle S, B \rangle_{E} + \langle \Delta S, X_{*} + B \rangle_{E} \leq - \langle S, B \rangle_{E} + \epsilon \| X_{*} + B \|_{E}.\end{array}
$$

Combining the resulting inequality and (c), we get the first of the inequalities to be proved; the second of them is given by “symmetric” reasoning.

# Prerequisites from Linear Algebra and Analysis

Regarded as mathematical entities, the objective and the constraints in a Mathematical Programming problem are functions of several real variables; therefore before entering the Optimization Theory and Methods, we need to recall several basic notions and facts about the spaces $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ where these functions live, same as about the functions themselves. The reader is supposed to know most of the facts to follow, so he/she should not be surprised by a “cooking book” style which use below.

## A.1 Space $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ : algebraic structure

Basically all events and constructions to be considered will take place in the space $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ of n-dimensional real vectors. This space can be described as follows.

## A.1.1 A point in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$

A point in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ (called also an n-dimensional vector) is an ordered collection $x =(x_{1},..., x_{n})$ of n reals, called the coordinates, or components, or entries of vector x; the space $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ itself is the set of all collections of this type.

## A.1.2 Linear operations

$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ is equipped with two basic operations:

- Addition of vectors. This operation takes on input two vectors $x =(x_{1},..., x_{n})$ and $y =(y_{1},..., y_{n})$ and produces from them a new vector

$$
x + y =(x_{1} + y_{1}, \dots, x_{n} + y_{n})
$$

with entries which are sums of the corresponding entries in x and in $y.$

- Multiplication of vectors by reals. This operation takes on input a real λ and an n-dimensional vector $x =(x_{1},..., x_{n})$ and produces from them a new vector

$$
\lambda x =(\lambda x_{1}, \dots, \lambda x_{n})
$$

with entries which are λ times the entries of $x.$

The as far as addition and multiplication by reals are concerned, the arithmetic of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ inherits most of the common rules of Real Arithmetic, like $x + y = y + x,(x + y) + z = x +(y + z),(\lambda + \mu)(x + y) =$ $\lambda x + \mu x + \lambda y + \mu y, \lambda(\mu x) =(\lambda \mu) x$ , etc.

## A.1.3 Linear subspaces

Linear subspaces in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are, by definition, nonempty subsets of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ which are closed with respect to addition of vectors and multiplication of vectors by reals:

$$
L \subset \mathbb{R}^{n} \text{is a linear subspace} \Leftrightarrow \left\{\begin{array}{c} L \neq \emptyset; \\ x, y \in L \Rightarrow x + y \in L; \\ x \in L, \lambda \in \mathbb{R} \Rightarrow \lambda x \in L.\end{array} \right.
$$

## A.1.3.A. Examples of linear subspaces:

1. The entire $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ ;

2. The trivial subspace containing the single zero vector $0 =(0,..., 0) \^{1)}$ ; (this vector/point is called also the origin)

3. The set $\{x \in \mathbb{R}^{n} : x_{1} = 0\}$ of all vectors x with the first coordinate equal to zero.

The latter example admits a natural extension:

4. The set of all solutions to a homogeneous $({\mathrm{i.e.}}$ , with zero right hand side) system of linear equations

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{rcl} & a_{11} x_{1} + \ldots + a_{1n} x_{n} & = 0 \\ x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}: & a_{21} x_{1} + \ldots + a_{2n} x_{n} & = 0 \\ & \ldots \\ & a_{m1} x_{1} + \ldots + a_{mn} x_{n} & = 0 \end{array} \right\}\tag{A.1.1}
$$

always is a linear subspace in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ . This example is “generic”, that is, every linear subspace in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the solution set of a (finite) system of homogeneous linear equations, see Proposition A.3.6 below.

5. Linear span of a set of vectors. Given a nonempty set X of vectors, one can form a linear subspace Lin(X), called the linear span of $X;$ this subspace consists of all vectors x which can be represented as linear combinations $\sum_{i = 1}^{N} \lambda_{i} x_{i}$ of vectors from X (in $\sum_{i = 1}^{N} \lambda_{i} x_{i}, N$ is an arbitrary positive integer, $\lambda_{i}$ are reals and $x_{i}$ belong to X). Note that

Lin(X) is the smallest linear subspace which contains $X \colon ifL$ is a linear subspace such that $L \supset X$ , then $L \supset L(X){\mathrm{~(why ?) ~}}$

The “linear span” example also is generic:

Every linear subspace in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the linear span of an appropriately chosen finite set of vectors from $\mathbb{R}^{n}$

(see Theorem A.1.2.(i) below).

A.1.3.B. Sums and intersections of linear subspaces. Let $\{L_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha \in I}$ be a family (finite or infinite) of linear subspaces of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ . From this family, one can build two sets:

1. The sum $\sum_{\alpha} L_{\alpha}$ of the subspaces $L_{\alpha}$ which consists of all vectors which can be represented as finite sums of vectors taken each from its own subspace of the family;

2. The intersection $\bigcap_{\alpha} L_{\alpha}$ of the subspaces from the family.

Theorem A.1.1 Let $\{L_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha \in I}$ be a family of linear subspaces of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ . Then

(i) The sum $\sum_{\alpha} L_{\alpha}$ of the subspaces from the family is itself a linear subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ ; it is the smallest of those subspaces of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ which contain every subspace from the family;

(ii) The intersection $\bigcap_{\alpha} L_{\alpha}$ of the subspaces from the family is itself a linear subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{n},$ it is the largest of those subspaces of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ which are contained in every subspace from the family.

## A.1.4 Linear independence, bases, dimensions

A collection $X = \{x^{1},..., x^{N}\}$ of vectors from $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ is called linearly independent, if no nontrivial (i.e., with at least one nonzero coeficient) linear combination of vectors from X is zero.

Example of linearly independent set: the collection of n standard basic orths $e_{1} =(1, 0,..., 0)$ 2 $e_{2} =(0, 1, 0,..., 0),..., e_{n} =(0,..., 0, 1)$

Examples of linearly dependent sets: $\left(1 \right) X = \{0\}; \left(2 \right) X = \{e_{1}, e_{1}\}; \left(3 \right) X = \{e_{1}, e_{2}, e_{1} + e_{2}\}$

A collection of vectors $f^{1},..., f^{m}$ is called a basis in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ , if

1. The collection is linearly independent;

2. Every vector from $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ is a linear combination of vectors from the collection $({\mathrm{i.e.}}$ , Lin $\{f^{1},..., f^{m}\} =$ R<sup>n</sup>).

Example of a basis: The collection of standard basic orths $e_{1},..., e_{n}$ is a basis in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ Examples of non-bases: (1) The collection $\{e_{2},..., e_{n}\}$ . This collection is linearly independent, but not every vector is a linear combination of the vectors from the collection; (2) The collection $\{e_{1}, e_{1}, e_{2},..., e_{n}\}$ . Every vector is a linear combination of vectors form the collection, but the collection is not linearly independent.

Besides the bases of the entire $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ , one can speak about the bases of linear subspaces:

A collection $\{f^{1},..., f^{m}\}$ of vectors is called a basis of a linear subspace $L,$ if

1. The collection is linearly independent,

2. $L = \operatorname{Lin} \{f^{1},..., f^{m}\}$ , i.e., all vectors $f^{i}$ belong to $L_{:}$ and every vector from $L$ is a linear combination of the vectors $f^{1},..., f^{m}$

In order to avoid trivial remarks, it makes sense to agree once for ever that

An empty set of vectors is linearly independent, and an empty linear combination of vectors $\sum_{i \in \emptyset} \lambda_{i} x_{i}$ equals to zero.

With this convention, the trivial linear subspace $L = \{0\}$ also has a basis, specifically, an empty set of vectors.

Theorem A.1.2 (i) Let L be a linear subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ . Then L admits a (finite) basis, and all bases of L are comprised of the same number of vectors; this number is called the dimension of L and is denoted by dim (L).

We have seen that $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ admits a basis comprised of n elements (the standard basic orths). From (i) it follows that every basis of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ contains exactly n vectors, and the dimension of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ is n.

(ii) The larger is a linear subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ , the larger is its dimension: if $L \subset L^{\prime}$ are linear subspaces of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ , then dim $(L) \leq \dim \left(L^{\prime} \right)$ , and the equality takes place if and only if $L = L^{\prime}$

We have seen that the dimension of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ is $n;$ according to the above convention, the trivial linear subspace {0} of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ admits an empty basis, so that its dimension is 0. Since $\{0\} \subset$ $L \subset \mathbb{R}^{n}$ for every linear subspace L of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ , it follows from (ii) that the dimension of a linear subspace in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ is an integer between 0 and n.

(iii) Let L be a linear subspace in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ . Then

(iii.1) Every linearly independent subset $of$ vectors from L can be extended to a basis of $L;$

(iii.2) From every spanning subset X for $L \mathrm{~ - ~} i.e.$ , a set X such that $\operatorname{Lin}(X) = L - one$ can extract a basis of L.

It follows from (iii) that

– every linearly independent subset of L contains at most dim (L) vectors, and if it contains exactly dim (L) vectors, it is a basis of $L;$

– every spanning set for L contains at least dim (L) vectors, and if it contains exactly dim (L) vectors, it is a basis of L.

(iv) Let L be a linear subspace in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ , and $f^{1},..., f^{m}$ be a basis in L. Then every vector $x \in L$ admits exactly one representation

$$
x = \sum_{i = 1}^{m} \lambda_{i}(x) f^{i}
$$

as a linear combination of vectors from the basis, and the mapping

$$
x \mapsto(\lambda_{1}(x),..., \lambda_{m}(x)): L \to \mathbb{R}^{m}
$$

is a one-to-one mapping of L onto $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ which is linear, i.e. for every $i = 1,..., m$ one has

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \lambda_{i}(x + y) & = & \lambda_{i}(x) + \lambda_{i}(y) \quad \forall(x, y \in L); \\ \lambda_{i}(\nu x) & = & \nu \lambda_{i}(x) \quad \forall(x \in L, \nu \in \mathbb{R}).\end{array}\tag{A.1.2}
$$

The reals $\lambda_{i}(x), i = 1,..., m$ , are called the coordinates of $x \in L$ in the basis $f^{1},..., f^{m}$

$\mathrm{E.g.}$ , the coordinates of a vector $x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ in the standard basis $e_{1},..., e_{n}$ of ${\mathbb{R}}^{n} \mathrm{~ - ~}$ the one comprised of the standard basic orths – are exactly the entries of x.

(v) [Dimension formula] Let $L_{1}, L_{2}$ be linear subspaces of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ . Then

$$
\dim \left(L_{1} \cap L_{2}\right) + \dim \left(L_{1} + L_{2}\right) = \dim \left(L_{1}\right) + \dim \left(L_{2}\right).
$$

Important convention. When speaking about adding n-dimensional vectors and multiplying them by reals, it is absolutely unimportant whether we treat the vectors as the column ones, or the row ones, or write down the entries in rectangular tables, or something else. However, when matrix operations (matrix-vector multiplication, transposition, etc.) become involved, it is important whether we treat our vectors as columns, as rows, or as something else. For the sake of definiteness, from now on we treat all vectors as column ones, independently of how we refer to them in the text. For example, when saying fo the first time what a vector is, we wrote $x =(x_{1},..., x_{n})$ , which might suggest that we were speaking abou row vectors. We stress that it is not the case, and the only reason for using the notation $x =(x_{1},..., x_{n})$

instead of the “correct” one $\begin{array}{r}{\boldsymbol{x} = \left[\begin{array}{c}{x_{1}} \\{\vdots} \\{x_{n}} \end{array} \right]} \end{array}$ is to save space and to avoid ugly formulas like $f(\left[\begin{array}{c}{x_{1}} \\{\vdots} \\{x_{n}} \end{array} \right])$

when speaking about functions with vector arguments. After we have agreed that there is no such thing as a row vector in this textbook, we can use (and do use) without any harm whatever notation we want.
