## A.6.7 Higher order derivatives

Let $f : \mathbb{R}^{n} \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be a mapping which is well-defined and diferentiable at every point x from an open set U. The Jacobian of this mapping $J(x)$ is a mapping from $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ to the space $\mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ matrices, i.e., is a mapping taking values in certain $\mathbb{R}^{M} \mathbf{\Phi}(M = mn)$ ). The derivative of this mapping, if it exists, is called the second derivative of $f;$ it again is a mapping from $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ to certain $\mathbb{R}^{M}$ and as such can be diferentiable, and so on, so that we can speak about the second, the third, ... derivatives of a vector-valued function of vector argument. A sufficient condition for the existence of k derivatives of $f$ in $U$ is that $f$ is $\mathrm{C}^{k}$ in $U,$ i.e., that all partial derivatives of $f$ of orders $\leq k$ exist and are continuous everywhere in $U$ (cf. Theorem A.6.1).

We have explained what does it mean that f has k derivatives in $U;$ note, however, that according to the definition, highest order derivatives at a point x are just long vectors; say, the second order derivative of a scalar function $f \ \mathrm{of} \2$ variables is the Jacobian of the mapping $x \mapsto f^{\prime}(x) : \mathbb{R}^{2} \to \mathbb{R}^{2},{\mathrm{i.e.}}$ , a mapping from $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2} = \mathbb{R}^{4};$ ; the third order derivative of $f$ is therefore the Jacobian of a mapping from $\mathbb{R}^{\bar{2}}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{4}, \mathrm{i.e.}$ , a mapping from $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{4 \times 2} = \mathbb{R}^{8}$ , and so on. The question which should be addressed now is: What is a natural and transparent way to represent the highest order derivatives?

The answer is as follows:

(<sub>∗</sub>) Let $f : \mathbb{R}^{n} \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be $\mathrm{C}^{k}$ on an open set $U \subset \mathbb{R}^{n}$ . The derivative of order $\ell \leq k$ of $f,$ taken at a point $x \in U$ , can be naturally identified with a function

$$
D^{\ell} f(x)[\Delta x^{1}, \Delta x^{2}, \dots, \Delta x^{\ell}]
$$

of \` vector arguments $\Delta x^{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}, i = 1,..., \ell,$ and taking values in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ . This function is linear in every one of the arguments $\Delta x^{i}$ , the other arguments being fixed, and is symmetric with respect to permutation of arguments $\Delta x^{1},..., \Delta x^{\ell}$

In terms of $f,$ the quantity $D^{\ell} f(x)[\Delta x^{1}, \Delta x^{2},..., \Delta x^{\ell}]$ (full name: “the $_{\ell - th}$ derivative (or diferential) of f taken at a point x along the directions $\Delta x^{1},..., \Delta x^{\ell}{}^{\mathsf{3}})$ is given by

$$
D^{\ell} f(x)[\Delta x^{1}, \Delta x^{2}, \dots, \Delta x^{\ell}] = \frac{\partial^{\ell}}{\partial t_{\ell} \partial t_{\ell - 1} \dots \partial t_{1}} \big |_{t_{1} = \dots = t_{\ell} = 0} f(x + t_{1} \Delta x^{1} + t_{2} \Delta x^{2} + \dots + t_{\ell} \Delta x^{\ell}).\tag{A.6.7}
$$

The explanation to our claims is as follows. Let $f : \mathbb{R}^{n} \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be $\mathrm{C}^{k}$ on an open set $U \subset \mathbb{R}^{n}$

1. When $\ell = 1, ~(*)$ says to us that the first order derivative of $f,$ taken at $x,$ is a linear function $Df(x)[\Delta x^{1}]$ of $\Delta x^{1} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ , taking values in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ , and that the value of this function at every $\Delta x^{1}$ is given by the relation

$$
Df(x)[\Delta x^{1}] = \frac{\partial}{\partial t_{1}} \big |_{t_{1} = 0} f(x + t_{1} \Delta x^{1})\tag{A.6.8}
$$

(cf. (A.6.2)), which is in complete accordance with what we already know about the derivative.

2. To understand what is the second derivative, let us take the first derivative $Df(x)[\Delta x^{1}]$ , let us temporarily fix somehow the argument $\Delta x^{1}$ and treat the derivative as a function of x. As a function of $x, \ \Delta x^{1}$ being fixed, the quantity $Df(x)[\Delta x^{1}]$ is again a mapping which maps U into $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ and is diferentiable by Theorem A.6.1 (provided, of course, that $k \geq 2)$ . The derivative of this mapping is certain linear function of $\Delta x \equiv \Delta x^{2} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ , depending on x as on a parameter; and of course it depends on $\Delta x^{1}$ as on a parameter as well. Thus, the derivative of $Df(x)[\Delta x^{1}]$ in x is certain function

$$
D^{2} f(x)[\Delta x^{1}, \Delta x^{2}]
$$

of $x \in U$ and $\Delta x^{1}, \Delta x^{2} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and taking values in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ . What we know about this function is that it is linear in $\Delta x^{2}$ . In fact, it is also linear in $\Delta x^{1}$ , since it is the derivative in $x$ of certain function (namely, of $Df(x)[\Delta x^{1}])$ ) linearly depending on the parameter $\Delta x^{1}$ , so that the derivative of the function in x is linear in the parameter $\Delta x^{1}$ as well (diferentiation is a linear operation with respect to a function we are diferentiating: summing up functions and multiplying them by real constants, we sum up, respectively, multiply by the same constants, the derivatives). Thus, $D^{2} f(x)[\Delta x^{1}, \Delta x^{2}]$ is linear in $\Delta x^{1}$ when x and $\Delta x^{2}$ are fixed, and is linear in $\Delta x^{2}$ when x and $\Delta x^{1}$ are fixed. Moreover, we have

$$
\begin{array}{rcll} D^{2} f(x)[\Delta x^{1}, \Delta x^{2}] & = & \frac{\partial}{\partial t_{2}} \Big |_{t_{2} = 0} Df(x + t_{2} \Delta x^{2})[\Delta x^{1}] &[\mathrm{cf.}(\mathrm{A.6.8})] \\ & = & \frac{\partial}{\partial t_{2}} \Big |_{t_{2} = 0} \frac{\partial}{\partial t_{1}} \Big |_{t_{1} = 0} f(x + t_{2} \Delta x^{2} + t_{1} \Delta x^{1}) &[\mathrm{by}(\mathrm{A.6.8})] \\ & = & \frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial t_{2} \partial t_{1}} \Bigg |_{t_{1} = t_{2} = 0} f(x + t_{1} \Delta x^{1} + t_{2} \Delta x^{2}) \end{array}\tag{A.6.9}
$$

as claimed in $\mathrm{(A.6.7)}$ for $\ell = 2$ . The only piece of information about the second derivative which is contained in ( ) and is not justified yet is that $D^{2} f(x)[\Delta x^{1}, \Delta x^{2}]$ is symmetric in $\Delta x^{1}, \Delta x^{2};$ ;

but this fact is readily given by the representation (A.6.7), since, as they prove in Calculus, if a function $\phi$ possesses continuous partial derivatives of orders $\le \ell$ in a neighbourhood of a point, then these derivatives in this neighbourhood are independent of the order in which they are taken; it follows that

$$
\begin{array}{llll} D^{2} f(x)[\Delta x^{1}, \Delta x^{2}] & = & \left.\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial t_{2} \partial t_{1}} \right|_{t_{1} = t_{2} = 0} \underbrace{f(x + t_{1} \Delta x^{1} + t_{2} \Delta x^{2})}_{\phi(t_{1}, t_{2})} &[(\mathrm{A.6.9})] \\ & = & \left.\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial t_{1} \partial t_{2}} \right|_{t_{1} = t_{2} = 0} \phi(t_{1}, t_{2}) \\ & = & \left.\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial t_{1} \partial t_{2}} \right|_{t_{1} = t_{2} = 0} f(x + t_{2} \Delta x^{2} + t_{1} \Delta x^{1}) \\ & = & D^{2} f(x)[\Delta x^{2}, \Delta x^{1}] &[\text{the same (A.6.9)}] \end{array}
$$

3. Now it is clear how to proceed: to define $D^{3} f(x)[\Delta x^{1}, \Delta x^{2}, \Delta x^{3}]$ , we fix in the second order derivative $D^{2} f(x)[\Delta x^{1}, \bar{\Delta{x}^{2}}]$ the arguments $\Delta x^{1}, \Delta x^{2}$ and treat it as a function of x only, thus arriving at a mapping which maps $U$ into $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ and depends on $\Delta x^{1}, \Delta x^{2}$ as on parameters (linearly in every one of them). Diferentiating the resulting mapping in x, we arrive at a function $D^{3}{\dot{f}}(x)[\Delta x^{1}, \Delta x^{2}, \Delta x^{3}]$ which by construction is linear in every one of the arguments $\Delta x^{1}, \Delta x^{2}$ $\Delta x^{3}$ and satisfies $(\mathrm{A}.6.7){\vdots}$ ; the latter relation, due to the Calculus result on the symmetry of partial derivatives, implies that $D^{3} f(x)[\Delta x^{1}, \Delta x^{2}, \Delta x^{3}]$ is symmetric in $\Delta x^{1}, \Delta x^{2}, \Delta x^{3}$ . After we have at our disposal the third derivative $D^{3} f.$ , we can build from it in the already explained fashion the fourth derivative, and so on, until k-th derivative is defined.

Remark A.6.2 Since $D^{\ell} f(x)[\Delta x^{1},..., \Delta x^{\ell}]$ is linear in every one of $\Delta x^{i}$ , we can expand the derivative in a multiple sum:

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \Delta x^{i} = \sum_{j = 1}^{n} \Delta x_{j}^{i} e_{j} \\ \Downarrow \\ D^{\ell} f(x)[\Delta x^{1},..., \Delta x^{\ell}] & = & D^{\ell} f(x)[\sum_{j_{1} = 1}^{n} \Delta x_{j_{1}}^{1} e_{j_{1}},..., \sum_{j_{\ell} = 1}^{n} \Delta x_{j_{\ell}}^{\ell} e_{j_{\ell}}] \\ & = & \sum_{1 \leq j_{1},..., j_{\ell} \leq n} D^{\ell} f(x)[e_{j_{1}},..., e_{j_{\ell}}] \Delta x_{j_{1}}^{1}...\Delta x_{j_{\ell}}^{\ell} \end{array}\tag{A.6.10}
$$

What is the origin of the coeficients $\phi^{\ell} f(x)[e_{j_{1}},..., e_{j_{\ell}}] ?$ According to (A.6.7), one has

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} D^{\ell} f(x)[e_{j_{1}}, \dots, e_{j_{\ell}}] & = & \left.\frac{\partial^{\ell}}{\partial t_{\ell} \partial t_{\ell - 1} \dots \partial t_{1}} \right|_{t_{1} = \dots = t_{\ell} = 0} f(x + t_{1} e_{j_{1}} + t_{2} e_{j_{2}} + \dots + t_{\ell} e_{j_{\ell}}) \\ & = & \frac{\partial^{\ell}}{\partial x_{j_{\ell}} \partial x_{j_{\ell - 1}} \dots \partial x_{j_{1}}} f(x).\end{array}
$$

so that the coeficients in (A.6.10) are nothing but the partial derivatives, of order \`, of $f.$

Remark A.6.3 An important particular case of relation (A.6.7) is the one when $\Delta x^{1} = \Delta x^{2} =...= \Delta x^{\ell};$ let us call the common value of these \` vectors d. According to (A.6.7), we have

$$
D^{\ell} f(x)[d, d,..., d] = \frac{\partial^{\ell}}{\partial t_{\ell} \partial t_{\ell - 1}...\partial t_{1}} \bigg |_{t_{1} =...= t_{\ell} = 0} f(x + t_{1} d + t_{2} d +...+ t_{\ell} d).
$$

This relation can be interpreted as follows: consider the function

$$
\phi(t) = f(x + td)
$$

of a real variable t. Then (check it!)

$$
\phi^{(\ell)}(0) = \frac{\partial^{\ell}}{\partial t_{\ell} \partial t_{\ell - 1} \ldots \partial t_{1}} \bigg |_{t_{1} = \ldots = t_{\ell} = 0} f(x + t_{1} d + t_{2} d + \ldots + t_{\ell} d) = D^{\ell} f(x)[d, \ldots, d].
$$

In other words, $D^{\ell} f(x)[d,..., d]$ is what is called \`-th directional derivative of $f$ taken at x along the direction $d;$ to define this quantity, we pass from function $f$ of several variables to the univariate function $\phi(t) = f(x + td)$ – restrict $f$ onto the line passing through x and directed by $d -$ and then take the “usual” derivative of order \` of the resulting function of single real variable t at the point $t = 0$ (which corresponds to the point x of our line).

Representation of higher order derivatives. k-th order derivative $D^{k} f(x)[\cdot,..., \cdot]$ of a $\mathrm{C}^{k}$ function $f : \mathbf { R } ^ { n } $ Rm is what it is – it is a symmetric k-linear mapping on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ taking values in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ and depending on x as on a parameter. Choosing somehow coordinates in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ , we can represent such a mapping in the form

$$
D^{k} f(x)[\Delta x_{1},..., \Delta x_{k}] = \sum_{1 \leq i_{1},...i_{k} \leq n} \frac{\partial^{k} f(x)}{\partial x_{i_{k}} \partial x_{i_{k - 1}}...\partial x_{i_{1}}}(\Delta x_{1})_{i_{1}}...(\Delta x_{k})_{i_{k}}.
$$

We may say that the derivative can be represented by k-index collection of m-dimensional vectors $\frac{\partial^{k} f(x)}{\partial x_{i_{k}} \partial x_{i_{k - 1}}...\partial x_{i_{1}}}$ . This collection, however, is a dificult-to-handle entity, so that such a representation does not help. There is, however, a case when the collection becomes an entity we know to handle; this is the case of the second-order derivative of a scalar function $(k = 2, m = 1)$ . In this case, the collection in question is just a symmetric matrix $\begin{array}{r}{H(x) = \left[\frac{\partial^{2} f(x)}{\partial x_{i} \partial x_{j}} \right]_{1 \leq i, j \leq n}} \end{array}$ . This matrix is called the Hessian of $f$ at x. Note that

$$
D^{2} f(x)[\Delta x_{1}, \Delta x_{2}] = \Delta x_{1}^{T} H(x) \Delta x_{2}.
$$

## A.6.8 Calculus of $\mathbf{C}^{k}$ mappings

The calculus of $\mathrm{C}^{k}$ mappings can be summarized as follows:

Theorem A.6.3 (i) Let U be an open set in R<sup>n</sup>, $f_{1}(\cdot), f_{2}(\cdot) : \mathbb{R}^{n} \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be $\mathrm{C}^{k}$ in $U$ , and let real-valued functions $\lambda_{1}(\cdot), \lambda_{2}(\cdot)$ be $\mathrm{C}^{k}$ in U. Then the function

$$
f(x) = \lambda_{1}(x) f_{1}(x) + \lambda_{2}(x) f_{2}(x)
$$

is $\mathrm{C}^{k}$ in $U$

(ii) Let U be an open set in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ , V be an open set in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ , let a mapping $f : \mathbb{R}^{n} \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be $\mathrm{C}^{k}$ in $U$ and such that $f(x) \in V \for \x \in U$ , and, finally, let a mapping $g : \mathbb{R}^{m} \mathbb{R}^{p}$ be $\mathrm{C}^{k}$ in $V.$ Then the superposition

$$
h(x) = g(f(x))
$$

is $\mathrm{C}^{k}$ in $U.$ .

Remark A.6.4 For higher order derivatives, in contrast to the first order ones, there is no simple “chain $\mathrm{rule}^{\prime \prime}$ for computing the derivative of superposition. For example, the second-order derivative of the superposition $h(x) = g(f(x))$ of two $\mathrm{C^{2}}.$ -mappings is given by the formula

$$
Dh(x)[\Delta x^{1}, \Delta x^{2}] = Dg(f(x))[D^{2} f(x)[\Delta x^{1}, \Delta x^{2}]] + D^{2} g(x)[Df(x)[\Delta x^{1}], Df(x)[\Delta x^{2}]]
$$

(check it!). We see that both the first- and the second-order derivatives of $f$ and $g$ contribute to the second-order derivative of the superposition $h.$

The only case when there does exist a simple formula for high order derivatives of a superposition is the case when the inner function is Affine: if $f(x) = Ax + b$ and $h(x) = g(f(x)) = g(Ax + b)$ with a $\mathrm{C}^{\ell}$ mapping $^{g,}$ then

$$
D^{\ell} h(x)[\Delta x^{1},..., \Delta x^{\ell}] = D^{\ell} g(Ax + b)[A \Delta x^{1},..., A \Delta x^{\ell}].\tag{A.6.11}
$$

## A.6.9 Examples of higher-order derivatives

Example 1: Second-order derivative of an Affine function $f(x) = a + b^{T} x$ is, of course, identically zero. Indeed, as we have seen,

$$
Df(x)[\Delta x^{1}] = b^{T} \Delta x^{1}
$$

is independent of $x,$ and therefore the derivative of $Df(x)[\Delta x^{1}]$ in $x,$ which should give us the second derivative $D^{2} f(x)[\Delta x^{1}, \Delta x^{2}]$ , is zero. Clearly, the third, the fourth, etc., derivatives of an Affine function are zero as well.

Example 2: Second-order derivative of a homogeneous quadratic form $f(x) = x^{T} Ax$ (A is a symmetric $n \times n$ matrix). As we have seen,

$$
Df(x)[\Delta x^{1}] = 2x^{T} A \Delta x^{1}.
$$

Diferentiating in x, we get

$$
D^{2} f(x)[\Delta x^{1}, \Delta x^{2}] = \lim_{t \to + 0} t^{- 1} \left[2(x + t \Delta x^{2})^{T} A \Delta x^{1} - 2x^{T} A \Delta x^{1} \right] = 2(\Delta x^{2})^{T} A \Delta x^{1},
$$

so that

$$
\boxed{D^{2} f(x)[\Delta x^{1}, \Delta x^{2}] = 2(\Delta x^{2})^{T} A \Delta x^{1}}
$$

Note that the second derivative of a quadratic form is independent of $x;$ consequently, the third, the fourth, etc., derivatives of a quadratic form are identically zero.

Example 3: Second-order derivative of the log-det barrier $F(X) = \ln \operatorname{Det}(X)$ . As we have seen, this function of an $n \times n$ matrix is well-defined and diferentiable on the set U of matrices with positive determinant (which is an open set in the space $\mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ of $n \times n$ matrices). In fact, this function is $\mathrm{C}^{\infty}$ in U. Let us compute its second-order derivative. As we remember,

$$
DF(X)[\Delta X^{1}] = \operatorname{Tr}(X^{- 1} \Delta X^{1}).\tag{A.6.12}
$$

To diferentiate the right hand side in X, let us first find the derivative of the mapping $G(X) = X^{- 1}$ which is defined on the open set of non-degenerate $n \times n$ matrices. We have

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} DG(X)[\Delta X] & = & \underset{t \to + 0}{\lim} t^{- 1} \left[(X + t \Delta X)^{- 1} - X^{- 1} \right] \\ & = & \underset{t \to + 0}{\lim} t^{- 1} \left[(X(I + tX^{- 1} \Delta X))^{- 1} - X^{- 1} \right] \\ & = & \underset{t \to + 0}{\lim} t^{- 1} \left[(I + t \underbrace{X^{- 1} \Delta X}_{Y})^{- 1} X^{- 1} - X^{- 1} \right] \\ & = & \left[\underset{t \to + 0}{\lim} t^{- 1} \left[(I + tY)^{- 1} - I \right] \right] X^{- 1} \\ & = & \left[\underset{t \to + 0}{\lim} t^{- 1} \left[I -(I + tY) \right](I + tY)^{- 1} \right] X^{- 1} \\ & = & \left[\underset{t \to + 0}{\lim}[- Y(I + tY)^{- 1}] \right] X^{- 1} \\ & = & - YX^{- 1} \\ & = & - X^{- 1} \Delta XX^{- 1} \end{array}
$$

and we arrive at the important by its own right relation

$$
\boxed{D(X^{- 1})[\Delta X] = - X^{- 1} \Delta XX^{- 1}, \quad[X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}, \operatorname{Det}(X) \neq 0]}
$$

which is the “matrix extension” of the standard relation $(x^{- 1})^{\prime} = - x^{- 2}, x \in \mathbb{R}$

Now we are ready to compute the second derivative of the log-det barrier:

$$
\begin{array}{rl}{F(X) = \ln \mathrm{Det}(X)} & \\{\Downarrow} & \\{DF(X)[\Delta X^{1}] = \mathrm{Tr}(X^{- 1} \Delta X^{1})} & \\{\Downarrow} & \\{D^{2} F(X)[\Delta X^{1}, \Delta X^{2}]} &{= \lim_{t \to + 0} t^{- 1} \left[\mathrm{Tr}((X + t \Delta X^{2})^{- 1} \Delta X^{1}) - \mathrm{Tr}(X^{- 1} \Delta X^{1}) \right]} \\ &{= \lim_{t \to + 0} \mathrm{Tr} \left(t^{- 1}(X + t \Delta X^{2})^{- 1} \Delta X^{1} - X^{- 1} \Delta X^{1}\right)} \\ &{= \lim_{t \to + 0} \mathrm{Tr} \left(\left[t^{- 1}(X + t \Delta X^{2})^{- 1} - X^{- 1} \right] \Delta X^{1}\right)} \\ &{= \mathrm{Tr} \left([- X^{- 1} \Delta X^{2} X^{- 1}] \Delta X^{1}\right),} \end{array}
$$

and we arrive at the formula

$$
\boxed{D^{2} F(X)[\Delta X^{1}, \Delta X^{2}] = - \operatorname{Tr}(X^{- 1} \Delta X^{2} X^{- 1} \Delta X^{1}) \quad[X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}, \operatorname{Det}(X) > 0]}
$$

Since $\mathrm{Tr}(AB) = \mathrm{Tr}(BA)$ (check it!) for all matrices $A, B$ such that the product $AB$ makes sense and is square, the right hand side in the above formula is symmetric in $\Delta X^{1}, \Delta X^{2}$ , as it should be for the second derivative of $\mathrm{a ~ C^{2}}$ function.

## A.6.10 Taylor expansion

Assume that $f : \mathbb{R}^{n} \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is $\mathrm{C}^{k}$ in a neighbourhood U of a point ¯x. The Taylor expansion of order k of $f,$ built at the point ¯x, is the function

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} F_{k}(x) & = & f(\bar{x}) + \frac{1}{1 !} Df(\bar{x})[x - \bar{x}] + \frac{1}{2 !} D^{2} f(\bar{x})[x - \bar{x}, x - \bar{x}] \\ & & + \frac{1}{3 !} D^{2} f(\bar{x})[x - \bar{x}, x - \bar{x}, x - \bar{x}] + \ldots + \frac{1}{k !} D^{k} f(\bar{x})[\underbrace{x - \bar{x}, \ldots, x - \bar{x}}_{k \text{times}}] \end{array}\tag{A.6.13}
$$

We are already acquainted with the Taylor expansion of order 1

$$
F_{1}(x) = f(\bar{x}) + Df(\bar{x})[x - \bar{x}]
$$

– this is the Affine function of x which approximates “very well” $f(x)$ in a neighbourhood of ${\bar{x}},$ namely, within approximation error $\bar{o}(\left| x - \bar{x} \right|)$ . Similar fact is true for Taylor expansions of higher order:

Theorem A.6.4 Let $f : \mathbb{R}^{n} \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be $\mathrm{C}^{k}$ in a neighbourhood $of \bar{x}.$ , and let $F_{k}(x)$ be the Taylor expansion of $f$ at x¯ of degree k. Then

(i) $F_{k}(x)$ is a vector-valued polynomial of full degree $\leq k \(i.e.,$ every one of the coordinates of the vector $F_{k}(x)$ is a polynomial $ofx_{1},..., x_{n},$ and the sum of powers $ofx_{i} \stackrel{,}{s}$ in every term of this polynomial does not exceed $k)$ ;

(ii) $F_{k}(x)$ approximates $f(x)$ in a neighbourhood of x¯ up to a remainder which is $\bar{o}(| x - \bar{x} |^{k})$ as $x \to \bar{x}.$

For every $\epsilon > 0$ , there exists $\delta > 0$ such that

$$
| x - \bar{x} | \leq \delta \Rightarrow | F_{k}(x) - f(x) | \leq \epsilon | x - \bar{x} |^{k}.
$$

$F_{k}(\cdot)$ is the unique polynomial with components of full degree $\leq k$ which approximates $f$ up to a remainder which is $\bar{o}(| x - \bar{x} |^{k})$

(iii) The value and the derivatives of $F_{k}$ of orders $1, 2,..., k$ , taken at ${\bar{x}},$ are the same as the value and the corresponding derivatives of f taken at the same point.

As stated in Theorem, $F_{k}(x)$ approximates $f(x)$ for x close to ¯x up to a remainder which is $\bar{o}(| x - \bar{x} |^{k})$ In many cases, it is not enough to know that the reminder is $^{\mathfrak{a}} \bar{o}(| x - \bar{x} |^{k})^{\mathfrak{d}} \mathrm{~ - ~}$ we need an explicit bound on this remainder. The standard bound of this type is as follows:

Theorem A.6.5 Let k be a positive integer, and let $f : \mathbb{R}^{n} \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be $\mathrm{C}^{k + 1}$ in a ball $B_{r} = B_{r}(\bar{x}) = \{x \in$ $\mathbb{R}^{n} : | x -{\bar{x}} | < r\}$ of a radius $r > 0$ centered at a point x¯. Assume that the directional derivatives $of$ order $k + 1$ , taken at every point of $B_{r}$ along every unit direction, do not exceed certain $L < \infty.$

$$
\left| D^{k + 1} f(x)[d, \dots, d] \right| \leq L \quad \forall(x \in B_{r}) \forall(d, | d | = 1).
$$

Then for the Taylor expansion $F_{k}$ of order $k$ of $f$ taken at x¯ one has

$$
| f(x) - F_{k}(x) | \leq \frac{L | x - \bar{x} |^{k + 1}}{(k + 1) !} \quad \forall(x \in B_{r}).
$$

Thus, in a neighbourhood of ¯x the remainder of the k-th order Taylor expansion, taken at ${\bar{x}},$ is of order of $L | x -{\bar{x}} |^{k + 1}$ , where $L$ is the maximal (over all unit directions and all points from the neighbourhood) magnitude of the directional derivatives of order $k + 1$ of $f.$

## A.7 Symmetric matrices

Let ${\mathbf{S}}^{m}$ be the space of symmetric $m \times m$ matrices, and $\mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ be the space of rectangular $m \times n$ matrices with real entries. From the viewpoint of their linear structure $({\mathrm{i.e.}}$ , the operations of addition and multiplication by reals) ${\mathbf{S}}^{m}$ is nothing but the arithmetic linear space $\mathbb{R}^{m(m + 1) / 2}$ of dimension $\frac{m(m{+} 1)}{2}$ by arranging the elements of a symmetric $m \times m$ matrix $X$ in a single column, say, in the row- $- \mathrm{by}.$ -row order, you get a usual $m^{2}.$ -dimensional column vector; multiplication of a matrix by a real and addition of matrices correspond to the same operations with the “representing vector $\mathrm{(s)^{\dag}}$ . When X runs through ${\bf{S}}^{m}$ the vector representing $X$ runs through $ \iota ( m + 1 ) / 2$ -dimensional subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{m^{2}}$ consisting of vectors satisfying the “symmetry condition” – the coordinates coming from symmetric to each other pairs of entries in X are equal to each other. Similarly, ${\bf M}^{m, n}$ as a linear space is just $\mathbb{R}^{mn}$ , and it is natural to equip ${\bf M}^{m, n}$ with the inner product defined as the usual inner product of the vectors representing the matrices:

$$
\langle X, Y \rangle := \sum_{i = 1}^{m} \sum_{j = 1}^{n} X_{ij} Y_{ij} = \operatorname{Tr}(XY^{T}) \quad \left[= \sum_{i = 1}^{m} \sum_{j = 1}^{n} Y_{ij} X_{ij} = \operatorname{Tr}(YX^{T}) \right]
$$

Here Tr stands for the trace – the sum of diagonal elements of a (square) matrix. With this inner product (called the Frobenius inner product), $\mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ becomes a legitimate Euclidean space, and we may use in connection with this space all notions based upon the Euclidean structure, $\mathrm{e.g.}$ , the (Frobenius) norm of a matrix

$$
\| X \|_{2} = \sqrt{\langle X, X \rangle} = \sqrt{\sum_{i = 1}^{m} \sum_{j = 1}^{n} X_{ij}^{2}} = \sqrt{\mathrm{Tr}(X^{T} X)},
$$

and likewise the notions of orthogonality, orthogonal complement of a linear subspace, etc. The same applies to the space ${\bf{S}}^{m}$ equipped with the Frobenius inner product; of course, the Frobenius inner product of symmetric matrices can be written without the transposition sign:

$$
\langle X, Y \rangle = \operatorname{Tr}(XY), X, Y \in \mathbf{S}^{m}.
$$

The following simple fact is very useful:

Proposition A.7.1 Let $X, Y$ be rectangular matrices such that XY makes sense and is square. $Then_{;}$ $\operatorname{Tr}(YX)$ also makes sense and

$$
\operatorname{Tr}(XY) = \operatorname{Tr}(YX).
$$

Proof. In order for $XY$ make sense and be square, the sizes of the matrices should be $m \times n \(\mathrm{for} \X)$ and $n \times m$ (for Y ) with some m and n, We now have

$$
\operatorname{Tr}(XY) = \sum_{i = 1}^{m} \sum_{j = 1}^{n} X_{ij} Y_{ji}, \operatorname{Tr}(YX) = \sum_{j = 1}^{n} \sum_{i = 1}^{m} Y_{ji} X_{ij},
$$

that is, both quantities are the same.

Another equally simple and useful fact is:

Proposition A.7.2 If $X, Y \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ , the Frobenius inner product of X and Y is equal to the Frobenius inner product of $X^{T}$ and $Y^{T}$ :

$$
\operatorname{Tr}(XY^{T}) = \operatorname{Tr}([X^{T}][Y^{T}]^{T}).
$$

Besides $this,$ when U is orthonormal n n matrix: $U^{T} U = I_{n};$ the Frobenius inner product of UX and $UY$ is the same as the Frobenius inner product of X and Y :

$$
\operatorname{Tr}(XY^{T}) = \operatorname{Tr}([UX][UY]^{T}).
$$

Proof. We have $\mathrm{Tr}([X^{T}][Y^{T}]^{T}) = \mathrm{Tr}(X^{T} Y) = \mathrm{Tr}([X^{T} Y]^{T}] = \mathrm{Tr}(Y^{T} X) = \mathrm{Tr}(XY^{T})$ , where the concluding inequality is by Proposition A.7.1. Similarly, when U is orthonormal, we have

$$
\operatorname{Tr}([UX][UY]^{T}) = \operatorname{Tr}(UXY^{T} X^{T} U^{T}) = \operatorname{Tr}(XY^{T}[U^{T} U]) = \operatorname{Tr}(XY^{T}),
$$

with the second equality given by the same Proposition $\mathrm{A.7.1}$ , and the third – by the fact that $U^{T} U =$ $UU^{T} = I_{n}$ for all orthonormal $n \times n$ matrices $U$ ✷

## A.7.1 Main facts on symmetric matrices

Here, we will focus on the space ${\bf{S}}^{m}$ of symmetric matrices. We start with the following most important property of these matrices.

Theorem A.7.1 [Eigenvalue decomposition] An $n \times n$ matrix A is symmetric if and only if it admits an orthonormal system of eigenvectors, $i.e.,$ there exist orthonormal basis $\{e_{1}, \ldots, e_{n}\}$ such that

$$
Ae_{i} = \lambda_{i} e_{i}, i = 1, \dots, n,\tag{A.7.1}
$$

holds for some reals $\lambda_{i}$

In connection with Theorem A.7.1, it is worthy to recall the following notions and facts:

## A.7.1.1 Eigenvectors and eigenvalues

Definition A.7.1 [Eigenvector and Eigenvalue] An eigenvector of an n n matrix A is a nonzero vector e (real or complex) such that Ae = λe holds for some (real or complex) scalar λ. This scalar is called the eigenvalue of A corresponding to the eigenvector e.

Eigenvalues of A are exactly the roots of the characteristic polynomial of A given by

$$
\pi(z) = \mathrm{Det}(zI - A) = z^{n} + b_{1} z^{n - 1} + b_{2} z^{n - 2} + \ldots + b_{n}.
$$

In the sequel, we denote by $\sigma(A)$ the spectrum of A, i.e., the set of all reals which are eigenvalues of the matrix. To avoid misunderstanding, let us stress that $\sigma(A)$ has as many points as many distinct eigenvalues A has and “pays no attention” to the multiplicities of these eigenvalues; for example, $\sigma(I_{n}) =$ <sub>{</sub><sup>1</sup><sub>}</sub><sup>.</sup>

Theorem A.7.1 states, in particular, that for a symmetric matrix A, all eigenvalues are real, and the corresponding eigenvectors can be chosen to be real and to form an orthonormal basis in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$

## A.7.1.2 Eigenvalue decomposition of a symmetric matrix

We will give an alternative characterization of symmetric matrices. To this end, we start with a definition and a fact that are important on their own.

Definition A.7.2 [Orthogonal matrix] An $n \times n$ matrix U is called orthogonal $ifU^{- 1} = U^{T}$

There are several equivalent characterizations of orthogonal matrices. An n n matrix U is orthogonal if and only if any (and all) of the following holds:

$U^{- 1} = U^{T},$

$U^{T} U = I,$

$UU^{T} = I,$

the columns of U form an orthonormal basis in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$

the rows of U form an orthonormal basis in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$

Theorem A.7.1 admits an equivalent reformulation as follows (check the equivalence!).

Theorem A.7.2 An $n \times n$ matrix A is symmetric if and only if it can be represented in the form

$$
A = U \Lambda U^{T},\tag{A.7.2}
$$

where

U is an orthogonal matrix,

Λ is the diagonal matrix with the diagonal entries $\lambda_{1}, \ldots, \lambda_{n}$

Representation (A.7.2) with orthogonal U and diagonal Λ is called the eigenvalue decomposition of A. In such a representation,

the columns of U form an orthonormal system of eigenvectors of A, and

<sub>•</sub> the diagonal entries in Λ are the eigenvalues of A corresponding to these eigenvectors.

## A.7.1.3 Vector of eigenvalues

When speaking about eigenvalues $\lambda_{i}(A)$ of a symmetric $n \times n$ matrix A, we always arrange them in the non-increasing order:

$$
\lambda_{1}(A) \geq \lambda_{2}(A) \geq \dots \geq \lambda_{n}(A).
$$

Moreover, we use $\b \lambda(A) \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ to denote the vector of eigenvalues of A taken in the above order. We let $\lambda_{\mathrm{max}}(A)$ (and respectively $\lambda_{\mathrm{min}}(A)$ correspond to the largest (smallest) eigenvalue of A.

## A.7.1.4 Freedom in eigenvalue decomposition

It is important to note that in the eigenvalue decomposition (A.7.2), a part of the data Λ, U is uniquely defined by A, while the other data admit certain “freedom.” Specifically, the sequence $\lambda_{1}, \ldots, \lambda_{n}$ of eigenvalues of A $({\mathrm{i.e.}}$ , diagonal entries of Λ) is exactly the sequence of roots of the characteristic polynomial of A (every root is repeated according to its multiplicity) and thus is uniquely defined by A (provided that we arrange the entries of the sequence in the non-increasing order). On the other hand, it is possible that the columns of U are not uniquely defined by A. What is uniquely defined, are the linear spans $E(\lambda)$ of the columns of U corresponding to all eigenvalues equal to certain λ, and such a linear span is nothing but the spectral subspace $\{x : \Ax = \lambda x\}$ of A corresponding to the eigenvalue λ. Given a $A \in \mathbf{S}^{n}$ , there are as many spectral subspaces of A as the number of different eigenvalues of A. Moreover, the spectral subspaces corresponding to different eigenvalues of a given symmetric matrix are orthogonal to each other, and their sum is the entire space. When building an orthogonal matrix U for the eigenvalue decomposition (A.7.2), one chooses an orthonormal eigenbasis in the spectral subspace corresponding to the largest eigenvalue and makes the vectors of this basis the first columns in U, then chooses an orthonormal basis in the spectral subspace corresponding to the second largest eigenvalue and makes the vectors from this basis the next columns of U, and so on.

## A.7.1.5 “Simultaneous” decomposition of commuting symmetric matrices

Given a number of symmetric matrices $A_{1}, \ldots, A_{k} \in \mathbf{S}^{n}$ , it is useful to know when they commute with each other, $\mathrm{i.e., ~} A_{i} A_{j} = A_{j} A_{i}$ for all $i, j$ . It turns out that there is a complete characterization of this property given as follows.

Proposition A.7.3 The matrices $A_{1}, \ldots, A_{k} \in \mathbf{S}^{n}$ commute with each other $(A_{i} A_{j} = A_{j} A_{i}$ for all $i, j)$ if and only if they can be “simultaneously diagonalized,” i.e., there exist a single orthogonal matrix U and diagonal matrices $\Lambda_{1}, \ldots, \Lambda_{k}$ such that

$$
A_{i} = U \Lambda_{i} U^{T}, i = 1, \dots, k.
$$

The proof of Proposition A.7.3 relies on two simple facts that are important by their own rights. We state these facts next.

Proposition A.7.4 Let $A, B \in \mathbf{S}^{n}$ be commuting and λ be a real eigenvalue of A. Then, the spectral subspace $E = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^{n} : \Ax = \lambda x\}$ of A corresponding to λ is invariant for B $(i.e., Be \in E$ for every $e \in E)$

Indeed, For $e \in E$ we have $A(Be) = B(Ae) = B(\lambda e) = \lambda(Be),{\mathrm{that ~ is ~}} Be \in E{\mathrm{.}}$

Proposition A.7.5 If A is an $n \times n$ matrix and L is an invariant subspace of $A \(i.e., \L$ is a linear subspace such that $Ae \in L$ whenever $e \in L)$ , then the orthogonal complement $L^{\perp} ~ ofL$ is invariant for the matrix $A^{T}$ . In particular, $ifA$ is symmetric and L is invariant subspace of A, then $L^{\perp}$ is an invariant subspace of $A^{T}$ as well.

Indeed, when L is invariant for $A, x \in L^{\bot}$ if and only if $x^{T} y$ for all $y \in L$ . Therefore for $x \in L^{\perp}$ one has

$$
y \in L \Rightarrow Ay \in L \Rightarrow 0 = x^{T} Ay =(A^{T} x)^{T} y,
$$

implying that $A^{T} x \in L^{\perp}$

Proof of Proposition A.7.3. The fact that when the matrices are simultaneously diagonizable, then they commute, is evident: for diagonal $D, \E$ and orthogonal U we have $[U^{T}{\bar{D}} U][{\breve{U}}^{T} EU] \ =$ $U^{T} D[U^{T} U] EU \ = \U^{T} DEU,$ and similarly $[U^{T} EU][U^{T} DU] ~ = ~ U^{T} EDU;$ ; it remains to note that $ED \ = \DE$ In the opposite direction, let us carry out induction in the number oK of commuting symmetric matrices. There is nothing to prove when $k = 1$ , or, more precisely, the case of $k = 1$ is covered by the results on eigenvalue decomposition of symmetric matrix. Inductive step: Assuming the statement valid for some k and given $k + 1$ commuting matrices $A_{1},..., A_{k + 1}$ , let $\lambda_{1},..., \lambda_{s}$ be distinct eigenvalues of $A_{k + 1}$ , and $E_{1},..., E_{s}$ be the corresponding spectral subspaces of $A_{k + 1}$ , that is, restricted onto $S_{\ell}.$ , the mapping $x \mapsto A_{k + 1} x$ acts as multiplication buy $\lambda_{\ell}.$ . By Proposition $\mathrm{A.7.4}$ , subspaces $E_{\ell}$ are invariant for matrices $A_{1},..., A_{k}$ . Applying inductive hypothesis, for every $\ell \leq s$ there exists an orhonormal basis in $E_{l}$ with basic vectors being eigenvalues of every one of $A_{1},..., A_{k};$ besides this, these vectors, as all vectors from $E_{\ell}.$ , are eigenvectors of $A_{k + 1}$ . the union, over $\ell \leq s$ of vectors from these orthonormal bases form an orthonormal basis in the entire space, and in this basis all matrices $A_{1},..., A_{k + 1}$ become diagonal. ✷

## A.7.2 Variational characterization of eigenvalues

To put what follows into a proper perspective, let us ask ourselves the following simple question: for a vector x with coordinates $x_{1},..., x_{n}$ , let $x^{(k)}$ be the k-th largest of the coordinates – the one which will be at k-th place when the entries in x are rearranged in the non-ascending order. For example, for $x =[2; 1; 2]$ we have $x^{(1)} = 2, x^{(2)} = 2, x^{(3)} = 1$ . Now the question is how to characterize $x^{(k)}$ without referring to rearranging the entries in x. The answer is as follows. Let us think about n stones with the weights $x_{1}, x_{2},..., x_{n}$ . Then $x^{(k)}$ can be described as follows: let us somehow throw away from the collection of our n stones $k - 1$ of them and look at the largest weight, w, of the remaining stones; this weight depends on which $k - 1$ of the stones were thrown away. Now let us take the minimum of the weights w we can get in this fashion over all possible ways to select $k - 1$ stones to throw away; this minimum is exactly $x^{(k)}$ . By the way, it is immediately self-evident that when $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $y \geq x,$ then $y^{(k)} \geq x^{(k)}$ for every $k \leq n$ . However, even self-evident facts need proof, and here is the proof: when increasing entries $x_{i}$ in x to $y_{i} \mathrm{\dot{s}}$ (which precisely corresponds to increasing the weights of every one of our stones) we clearly cannot decrease the above w’s (that is, the largest of the weights in groups obtained by throwing away a particular collection of $k - 1$ stones). And since none of the w’s decrease, their minimum does not decrease as well.

Variational characterization of eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix is the extremely useful matrix version of the elementary considerations above.

Theorem A.7.3 [Variational Characterization of Eigenvalues (VCE)] For any $A \in \mathbf{S}^{n}$ , we have

$$
\lambda_{\ell}(A) = \min_{E \in \mathcal{E}_{\ell}} \max_{x \in E, x^{T} x = 1} x^{T} Ax, \quad \ell = 1, \ldots, n,\tag{A.7.3}
$$

where $\mathcal{E}_{\ell}$ is the family of all linear subspaces in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ of the dimension $n - \ell + 1$

Based on VCE, in order to get the largest eigenvalue $\lambda_{1}(A)$ , we maximize the quadratic form $x^{T} Ax$ over the unit sphere $S = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^{n} : \x^{T} x = 1\}$ and the maximum is exactly $\lambda_{1}(A)$ . To get the second largest eigenvalue $\lambda_{2}(A)$ , we act as follows: we choose a linear subspace $E$ of dimension $n - 1$ and maximize the quadratic form $x^{T}$ Ax over the cross-section of S by this subspace; the maximum value of the form depends on $E_{\mathrm{{i}}}$ , and we minimize this maximum over linear subspaces $E$ of the dimension $n - 1;$ the resulting value is exactly $\lambda_{2}(A)$ ). To get $\lambda_{3}(A)$ , we replace in the latter construction subspaces of the dimension $n - 1$ by those of the dimension $n - 2$ , and so on. In particular, the smallest eigenvalue $\lambda_{n}(A)$ is just the minimum, over all linear subspaces E of the dimension $n - n + 1 = 1$ , i.e., over all lines passing through the origin, of the quantities $x^{T}$ Ax, where $x \in E$ has unit norm $(x^{T} x = 1)$ . In other words, $\lambda_{n}(A)$ is just the minimum of the quadratic form $x^{T}$ Ax over the unit sphere S.

Proof of the VCE. Let $e_{1}, \ldots, e_{n}$ be an orthonormal eigenbasis of $A.$ , i.e., ${\cal A} e_{\ell} = \lambda_{\ell}({\cal A}) e_{\ell}$ and $e_{\ell}$ are unit vectors for all $1 \leq \ell \leq n$ . For $1 \leq \ell \leq n$ , let

$$
F_{\ell} := \operatorname{Lin} \left\{e_{1}, \dots, e_{\ell} \right\}, \quad \text{and} \quad G_{\ell} := \operatorname{Lin} \left\{e_{\ell}, e_{\ell + 1}, \dots, e_{n} \right\}.
$$

Finally, for $x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ , let $\xi(x)$ be the vector of coordinates of x in the orthonormal basis $e_{1}, \ldots, e_{n}$ . Note that

$$
x^{T} x = \xi(x)^{T} \xi(x),
$$

since $\{e_{1}, \ldots, e_{n}\}$ is an orthonormal basis, and that

$$
x^{T} Ax = x^{T} A \sum_{i = 1}^{n} \xi_{i}(x) e_{i} = x^{T} \sum_{i = 1}^{n} \lambda_{i}(A) \xi_{i}(x) e_{i} = \sum_{i = 1}^{n} \lambda_{i}(A) \xi_{i}(x) \underbrace{(x^{T} e_{i})}_{\xi_{i}(x)} = \sum_{i = 1}^{n} \lambda_{i}(A) \xi_{i}^{2}(x).\tag{A.7.4}
$$

Now, consider a fixed \` such that $1 \leq \ell \leq n$ , and set $E = G_{\ell}$ . Note that $E$ is a linear subspace of the dimension $n - \ell + 1$ . Moreover, from (A.7.4), we deduce that

$$
x^{T} Ax = \sum_{i = \ell}^{n} \lambda_{i}(A) \xi_{i}(x)^{2}
$$

holds for any $x \in E$ . Therefore,

$$
\max_{x} \{x^{T} Ax: x \in E, x^{T} x = 1\} = \max_{\xi} \{\sum_{i = \ell}^{n} \lambda_{i}(A) \xi_{i}^{2}: \sum_{i = \ell}^{n} \xi_{i}^{2} = 1\} = \max_{\ell \leq i \leq n} \lambda_{i}(A) = \lambda_{\ell}(A).
$$

Thus, for appropriately chosen $E \in{\mathcal{E}}_{\ell}.$ , the inner maximum in the right hand side of (A.7.3) equals to $\lambda_{\ell}(A)$ . Hence, we have

$$
\min_{E \in \mathcal{E}_{\ell}} \max_{x \in E, x^{T} x = 1} x^{T} Ax \leq \lambda_{\ell}(A).
$$

It remains to prove the reverse inequality. To this end, consider a linear subspace E of the dimension $n - \ell + 1$ and observe that its intersection with the linear subspace $F_{\ell}$ of the dimension \` is nontrivial (indeed, dim $E +$ dim $F_{\ell} =(n - \ell + 1) + \ell > n$ , so that dim $(E \cap F) > 0$ by the Dimension formula). Consider any unit vector $y \in E \cap F_{\ell}$ . Since y is a unit vector from $F_{\ell}$ , it admits a representation of the form,

$$
y = \sum_{i = 1}^{\ell} \eta_{i} e_{i} \quad \mathrm{with} \quad \sum_{i = 1}^{\ell} \eta_{i}^{2} = 1,
$$

whence, by (A.7.4),

$$
y^{T} Ay = \sum_{i = 1}^{\ell} \lambda_{i}(A) \eta_{i}^{2} \geq \min_{1 \leq i \leq \ell} \lambda_{i}(A) = \lambda_{\ell}(A).
$$

Since $y \in E$ , we conclude that

$$
\max_{x \in E, x^{T} x = 1} x^{T} Ax \geq y^{T} Ay \geq \lambda_{\ell}(A).
$$

Since $E$ is an arbitrary subspace form $\mathcal{E}_{\ell}.$ , we conclude that the right hand side in (A.7.3) is $\geq \lambda_{\ell}(A)$ . ✷

Our reasoning in the proof of the VCE uses the relation (A.7.4) which is a simple and useful byproduct. Therefore, we state it formally as a corollary.

Corollary A.7.1 For any $A \in \mathbf{S}^{n}$ , the quadratic form $x^{T}$ Ax is exactly equal to the weighted sum of squares of the coordinates $\xi_{i}(x)$ of x taken with respect to an orthonormal eigenbasis of A. Moreover, the weights in this sum are exactly the eigenvalues of A. That is,

$$
x^{T} Ax = \sum_{i} \lambda_{i}(A) \xi_{i}^{2}(x).
$$

## A.7.3 Corollaries of the VCE

VCE admits a number of extremely important corollaries as follows:

## A.7.3.1 Eigenvalue characterization of positive (semi)definite matrices

Definition A.7.3 [Positive definite matrix] A matrix A is called positive definite (notation: $A \succ 0)$ , if it is symmetric and $\mathit{x}^{T} Ax > 0$ holds for all x $\neq 0$

Definition A.7.4 [Positive semidefinite matrix] A matrix A is called positive semidefinite (notation: $A \succeq 0)$ , if it is symmetric and $x^{T} Ax \geq 0$ holds for all x.

Based on VCE we arrive at the following eigenvalue characterization of positive (semi)definite matrices.

Proposition A.7.6 A symmetric matrix A is positive semidefinite if and only if its eigenvalues are nonnegative. Moreover, A is positive definite if and only if all eigenvalues of A are positive.

Proof. Indeed, A is positive definite (positive semidefinite) if and only if the minimum value of $x^{T} Ax$ over the unit sphere is positive (nonnegative). Recall also that by VCE, the minimum value of $x^{T} Ax$ over the unit sphere is exactly the minimum eigenvalue of A. ✷

## A.7.3.2 -Monotonicity of the vector of eigenvalues

We write $A \succeq B \left(A \succ B \right)$ to express that A, B are symmetric matrices of the same size such that $A - B$ is positive semidefinite (respectively, positive definite).

Proposition A.7.7 Consider A, $B \in{\bf S}^{n}.~ IfA \succeq B$ , then $\lambda(A) \geq \lambda(B)$ . Also, if $A \succ B$ , then $\lambda(A) >$ $\lambda(B)$

Proof. Indeed, when $A \succeq B$ , then, of course,

$$
\max_{x \in E: x^{T} x = 1} x^{T} Ax \geq \max_{x \in E: x^{T} x = 1} x^{T} Bx
$$

for every linear subspace $E,$ , whence

$$
\lambda_{\ell}(A) = \min_{E \in \mathcal{E}_{\ell}} \max_{x \in E: x^{T} x = 1} x^{T} Ax \geq \min_{E \in \mathcal{E}_{\ell}} \max_{x \in E: x^{T} x = 1} x^{T} Bx = \lambda_{\ell}(B), \ell = 1, \ldots, n,
$$

i.e., $\lambda(A) \geq \lambda(B)$ . The case of $A \succ B$ can be considered similarly.

## A.7.3.3 Eigenvalue Interlacement Theorem

This is an extremely important result, and we formulate it as follows.

Theorem A.7.4 [Eigenvalue Interlacement Theorem] For $A \in \mathbf{S}^{n}$ , let $\bar{A}$ be the angular $(n - k) \times(n - k)$ submatrix of A. Then, for every $\ell \leq n - k_{\mathrm{:}}$ , the \`-th eigenvalue of $\bar{A}$ separates the \`-th and the $(\ell + k) - th$ eigenvalues of A:

$$
\lambda_{\ell}(A) \succeq \lambda_{\ell}(\bar{A}) \succeq \lambda_{\ell + k}(A).\tag{A.7.5}
$$

Proof. Recall that by VCE,

$$
\lambda_{\ell}(\bar{A}) = \min_{E \in \bar{\mathcal{E}}_{\ell}} \max_{x \in E: x^{T} x = 1} x^{T} Ax,
$$

where $\bar{\mathcal{E}}_{\ell}$ is the family of all linear subspaces of the dimension $n - k - \ell + 1$ contained in the linear subspace $\{x \in \mathbb{R}^{n} : \x_{n - k + 1} = x_{n - k + 2} = \ldots = x_{n} = 0\}$ . Since $\bar{\mathcal{E}}_{\ell} \subset \mathcal{E}_{\ell + \vert \vert}$ , we have

$$
\lambda_{\ell}(\bar{A}) = \min_{E \in \bar{\mathcal{E}}_{\ell}} \max_{x \in E: x^{T} x = 1} x^{T} Ax \geq \min_{E \in \mathcal{E}_{\ell + \parallel}} \max_{x \in E: x^{T} x = 1} x^{T} Ax = \lambda_{\ell + k}(A).
$$

We have proved the left inequality in (A.7.5). Applying this inequality to the matrix $- A$ , we get

$$
- \lambda_{\ell}(\bar{A}) = \lambda_{n - k - \ell}(- \bar{A}) \geq \lambda_{n - \ell}(- A) = - \lambda_{\ell}(A),
$$

or, which is the same, $\lambda_{\ell}(\bar{A}) \leq \lambda_{\ell}(A)$ . This then proves the first inequality in (A.7.5).

## A.7.4 Spectral norm and Lipschitz continuity of vector of eigenvalues

## A.7.4.1 Spectral and induced norms of matrices

A useful example of a norm (to refresh your memory on what a norm is, see Section A.4) is the spectral norm of an $m \times n$ matrix A:

$$
\| A \| = \max_{x: \| x \|_{2} \leq 1} \| Ax \|_{2},
$$

The spectral norm is indeed a special case of the induced norm of a linear mapping. $x \mapsto y = Ax : E \to F$ where E and F are (finite-dimensional) linear spaces equipped with norms $\| \cdot \|_{E}$ and $\| \cdot \|_{F}$ respectively. The norm $\| A \|_{F, E}$ of A induced by these two norms is

$$
\| A \|_{F, E} = \max_{x} \{\| Ax \|_{F}: \| x \|_{E} \leq 1\}.
$$

The definition of induced norm immediately imply (check it!) that, first, for all $x \in E, y \in F$ one has

$$
\| Ax \|_{F} \leq \| A \|_{F, E} \| x \|_{E},
$$

and, second, the latter inequality is equality for properly selected nonzero $x \in E$ . In other words, the induced norm is the largest “amplification fact $\mathrm{{; or}^{\prime \prime} \mathrm{~ - ~} the}$ largest factor by which the norm $\| \cdot \|_{F}$ of Ax can be larger than the norm $\| \cdot \|_{E}$ of x.

Clearly, when $E = \mathbb{R}^{n}, F = \mathbb{R}^{m}$ , and $\| \cdot \|_{E}, \| \cdot \|_{F}$ are the standard Euclidean norms on the respective spaces, the induced norm of A is exactly the spectral norm of A.

Proposition A.7.8 (i) Let E and F be finite-dimensional linear spaces. The induced norm $\| \cdot \|_{F, E}$ is indeed a norm on the space $\operatorname{Lin}(E, F)$ of linear mappings from E to $F.$

(ii) Let $E, F, G$ be finite-dimensional linear spaces equipped with respective norms $\| \cdot \|_{E}, \| \cdot \|_{F}, \| \cdot \|_{G}$ and let $y = Ax : E \to F$ and $z = By : F \to G$ be linear mappings. Then,

$$
\| BA \|_{G, E} \leq \| B \|_{G, F} \| A \|_{F, E}.
$$

Proof. (i): Homogeneity and positivity of $\| \cdot \|_{F, E}$ are evident. Triangle inequality is given by the following computation:

$$
A, B \in \operatorname{Lin}(E, F) \Rightarrow \|[A + B] x \|_{F} = \| Ax + Bx \|_{F} \leq \| Ax \|_{F} + \| Bx \|_{F} \leq[\| A \|_{F, E} + \| B \|_{F, E}] \| x \|_{E}.
$$

(ii): For every $x \in E$ one has $\lVert BAx \rVert_{G} \leq \lVert B \rVert_{G, F} \lVert Ax \rVert_{F} \leq \lVert B \rVert_{G, F} \lVert A \rVert_{F, E} \lVert x \rVert_{E}.$

We also have the following useful properties of the spectral norm $\| \cdot \|$ on $\mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$

Proposition A.7.9 (i) For any $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ , we have $\begin{array}{r}{\| A \| = \operatorname{max}_{x, y} \{y^{T} Ax : \| x \|_{2} \leq 1, \ \| y \|_{2} \leq 1\}} \end{array}$ whence also $\| A \| = \| A^{\acute{T}} \|$

(ii) For any $A \in \mathbf{S}^{n}$ , we have $\| A \| = \operatorname{max} \{| \lambda_{\operatorname{max}}(A) |, | \lambda_{\operatorname{min}}(A) |\}$ . Moreover, for any $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ we have

$$
\| A \|^{2} = \| A^{T} A \| = \lambda_{\max}(A^{T} A) = \lambda_{\max}(AA^{T}) = \| AA^{T} \| = \| A^{T} \|^{2}.
$$

Proof. (i): We have $\| Ax \|_{2} = \operatorname{max}_{y : \| y \|_{2} \leq 1} y^{T}$ Ax by Cauchy inequality (Theorem A.4.1), implying that $\operatorname{max}_{\boldsymbol{x} : \| \boldsymbol{x} \|_{2} \le 1} \| \boldsymbol{A} \boldsymbol{x} \|_{2} = \operatorname{max}_{\boldsymbol{x}, \| \boldsymbol{x} \|_{2} \le 1 \atop y, \| \boldsymbol{y} \|_{2} \le 1}{y^{T}} \boldsymbol{A} \boldsymbol{x}.$

(ii): Let $A = U \mathrm{Diag} \{\lambda\} U^{T}$ be the eigenvalue decomposition of symmetric matrix A, Then $y^{T} Ax \ =$ $\begin{array}{r}{[U^{T} y]^{T} \mathrm{Diag} \{\lambda\}[U^{T} x]} \end{array}$ with orthogonal $U_{i}$ whence

$$
\max_{\substack{x, \| x\|_{2}\leq 1\\ y, \| y\|_{2}\leq 1}}y^{T}Ax = \max_{\substack{u, \| u\|_{2}\leq 1\\ v, \| v\|_{2}\leq 1}}v^{T}\text{Diag}\{\lambda\} u = \max_{\substack{u, \| u\|_{2}\leq 1\\ v, \| v\|_{2}\leq 1}}\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}u_{i}v_{i}\leq[\max_{i}|\lambda_{i}|]\max_{\substack{u, \| u\|_{2}\leq 1\\ v, \| v\|_{2}\leq 1}}\sum_{i}|u_{i}v_{i}|\leq \max_{i}|\lambda_{i}|
$$

(concluding  is due to Cauchy inequality), and $y^{T} Ax = \operatorname{max}_{i} \left| \lambda_{i} \right|$ when x is the unit norm eigenvector of A corresponding to the maximum magnitude eigenvalue, $\lambda_{i_{*}}$ , of A, and $y = \mathrm{sign}(\lambda_{i_{*}}) x$ . Thus, when A is symmetric, we do have $\lVert A \rVert = \operatorname{max}_{i} \left| \lambda_{i}(A) \right|$

For an arbitrary matrix A we have

$$
\| A \|^{2} = \max_{x: \| x \|_{2} \leq 1} \| Ax \|_{2}^{2} = \max_{x: \| x \|_{2} \leq 1} x^{T}[A^{T} A] x = \lambda_{\max}(A^{T} A),
$$

where the concluding equality is given by the variational characterization of the largest eigenvalue of symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $A^{T} A$ (Theorem A.7.3). Besides this, $\| A^{T} A \| = \lambda_{\operatorname{max}}(A^{T} A)$ due to the already proved “symmetric” part of (ii). Thus, $\| A \| = \sqrt{\| A^{T} A \|} = \sqrt{\lambda_{\operatorname{max}}(A^{T} A)}$ , Recalling that $\| A \| = \| A^{T} \|$ , we complete the verification of (ii). ✷

## A.7.4.2 Lipschitz continuity of the vector of eigenvalues

Another useful consequence of VCE is the Lipschitz continuity of the vector of eigenvalues of a matrix as a function of the matrix:

Proposition A.7.10 The vector-valued function $A \mapsto \lambda(A) : \mathbf{S}^{n} \to \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is Lipschitz continuous, Specifically, denoting by $\| \cdot \|$ the spectral norm, for all $k \leq n$ , we have

$$
\left| \lambda_{k}(A) - \lambda_{k} \left(A^{\prime}\right) \right| \leq \left\| A - A^{\prime} \right\| \quad \forall \left(A, A^{\prime} \in \mathbf{S}^{n}\right).
$$

Proof. $\mathrm{By}$ VCE, denoting $\mathcal{E}_{\|}$ the family of all subspaces of codimension $k - 1$ in ${\mathbb{R}}^{m}$ , we have

$$
\lambda_{k}(A) = \min_{E \in \mathcal{E}_{\parallel}} \max_{e \in E: \| e \|_{2} = 1} e^{T} Ae,
$$

and the right hand side clearly is Lipschitz continuous, with constant 1 w.r.t. $\| \cdot \|$ , function of $A^{\mathrm{~ 6 ~}}$ ✷

We also have the following immediate consequence of Proposition A.7.10.

Proposition A.7.11 Let S be a subset $of \mathbb{R}^{n}$ , and be the set of all matrices $A \in \mathbf{S}^{n}$ with $\lambda(A) \in S$ Whenever S is open, or closed, or bounded, so is $\boldsymbol{s}$

## A.7.5 Functions of symmetric matrices

Let A be a symmetric m  m matrix, and f be a real-valued function defined on a subset of real line containing the spectrum $\sigma(A)$ of A. We define the $m \times m$ symmetric matrix $f(A)$ as follows:

Let $\sigma(A) : = \{\mu_{1}, \dots, \mu_{s}\}$ , and let $\mathbb{R}^{m} = E_{1} + \ldots + E_{s}$ be the decomposition of $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ into the sum of mutually orthogonal spectral subspaces of A, i.e., $E_{i} : = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^{m} : Ax = \lambda_{i} x\}$ . The matrix $f(A)$ has every one of $E_{i}$ invariant, and $x \in E_{i}$ implies $Ax = f(\mu_{i}) x$ for all $i \leq s.$

Equivalently: given an eigenvalue decomposition $A = U \mathrm{Diag} \{\lambda_{1}, \dots, \lambda_{m}\} U^{T}$ of A, one has $f(A) = U \mathrm{Diag} \{f(\lambda_{1}), \ldots, f(\lambda_{m})\} U^{T}$

From this definition it follows immediately that $f(A) = g(A)$ whenever f and g coincide with each other on the spectrum of A.

Moreover, it is immediately seen (check it!) that the resulting “calculus of functions of (fixed) symmetric matrix $A^{\mathfrak{s}}$ obeys very natural rules:

1. $f(\cdot) \mapsto f(A)$ is a mapping from the algebra $\mathbb{R}(\sigma(A))$ of real-valued functions on the subset $\sigma(A)$ of the real axis into the space ${\mathbf{S}}^{m}$ of m  m symmetric matrices which preserves linear operations and multiplication. That is, for any $f_{1}, \ldots, f_{k} \in \mathbb{R}(\sigma(A))$ and any $a_{1}, \dotsc, a_{k} \in \mathbb{R}$ , we have

$$
[a_{1} f_{1}(\cdot) + \dots + a_{k} f_{k}(\cdot)](A) = a_{1} f_{1}(A) + \dots + a_{k} f_{k}(A) \quad \text{and} \quad[f_{1}(\cdot) \cdot f_{2}(\cdot)](A) = f_{1}(A) f_{2}(A).
$$

In particular, all matrices of the form $f(A), f \in \mathbb{R}(\sigma(A))$ commute with each other.

2. When $f(\cdot) \equiv 1$ , one has $f(A) = I_{m}$ , and when $f(x) \equiv x$ , one has $f(A) = A$ . More generally, whenever f is a real algebraic polynomial

$$
f(x) = a_{0} + \sum_{i = 1}^{k} a_{i} x^{i},
$$

we have

$$
f(A) = a_{0} I_{n} + \sum_{i = 1}^{k} a_{i} A^{i}.
$$

3. The mapping $f(\cdot) f(A)$ “preserves nonnegativity,” i.e., the matrix $f(A)$ is positive semidefinite whenever $f(\cdot)$ is nonnegative on $\sigma(A)$

4. When a sequence $f_{i}(\cdot) \in \mathbb{R}(\sigma(A))$ pointwise on $\sigma(A)$ converges to $f(\cdot)$ as $i \infty$ , the matrices $f_{i}(A)$ converge to $f(A)$ as $i \to \infty$

Illustration: Square root of a positive semidefinite matrix. When A is positive semidefinite matrix, its matrix square root $A^{1 / 2}$ is, by definition, $f(A)$ , where $f(\mu) = \mu^{1 / 2}$ is the usual square root on the nonnegative ray. From the above rules, it follows that $A^{1 / 2}$ is symmetric, positive semidefinite, and it squares to A: $[\dot{A^{1 / 2}}]^{2} = A$

Similarly to the arithmetic square root of a nonnegative real a – the unique nonnegative real which squares to $^{a,}$ the square root $A^{1 / 2}$ of a positive semidefinite matrix A is the unique positive semidefinite matrix which squares to A.

Proposition A.7.12 Let A be a positive semidefinite $m \times m$ matrix, and B be a positive semidefinite matrix such that $B^{2} = A$ . Then $\bar{B =} A^{1 / 2}$

Proof. When $B^{2} = A$ , B clearly commutes with A, implying by Proposition A.7.3 that the matrices admit simultaneous diagonalization:

$$
A = U \mathrm{Diag} \{\lambda_{1}, \dots, \lambda_{m}\} U^{T}, B = U \mathrm{Diag} \{\upsilon_{1}, \dots, \upsilon_{m}\} U^{T}
$$

with some orthonormal matrix U. Thus, the relation $A = B^{2}$ reads

$$
\begin{array}{l} U \text{Diag} \{\lambda_{1}, \ldots, \lambda_{m}\} U^{T} =(U \text{Diag} \{\upsilon_{1}, \ldots, \upsilon_{m}\} U^{T})(U \text{Diag} \{\upsilon_{1}, \ldots, \upsilon_{m}\} U^{T}) \\ = U \text{Diag} \{\upsilon_{1}, \ldots, \upsilon_{m}\} \underbrace{(U^{T} U)}_{= I_{m}} \text{Diag} \{\upsilon_{1}, \ldots, \upsilon_{m}\} U^{T} = U \text{Diag} \{\upsilon_{1}^{2}, \ldots, \upsilon_{m}^{2}\} U^{T}, \end{array}
$$

whence $\lambda_{i} = v_{i}^{2}$ . Besides this, B is positive semidefinite, implying that $v_{i} \geq 0$ . The bottom line is that $v_{i} = \lambda_{i}^{1 / 2}$ for all i, that is, $B = A^{1 / 2}$ ✷

Proposition A.7.13 Let $f(x)$ be a continuously diferentiable real-valued function on an interval $(a, b) =$ $\{s : a \leq s \leq b\}$ $(- \infty \leq a < b \leq + \infty)$ of the real axis. The function $\phi(X) = \operatorname{Tr}(f(X))$ is continuously diferentiable on the open set ${\mathcal{D}} \of \ \mathbf{S}^{m}$ comprised by all matrices with spectrum from (a, b), and

$$
\left.\frac{d}{dt} \right|_{t = 0} \phi(X + tH) = \mathrm{Tr}(f^{\prime}(X) H) \quad \forall X \in \mathcal{D}, h \in \mathbf{S}^{m}.
$$

In other words, $\phi(\cdot)$ is continuously diferentiable on the open set and its gradient, taken $w.r.t.$ the Frobenius Euclidean structure on ${\bf S}^{M}, is \nabla \phi(X) = f^{\prime}(X)$

Proof. Let us start with the case when $\begin{array}{r}{f(x) = \sum_{i = 0}^{k} a_{i} x^{k}} \end{array}$ is an algebraic polynomial. In this case the matrix-valued function $f(X) : \mathbf{S}^{m} \mathbf{S}^{m}$ clearly is infinitely many times diferentiable, and for all $X, H \in \mathbf{S}^{m}$ one has

$$
\left.\frac{d}{dt} \right|_{t = 0} f(X + tH) = \sum_{i = 0}^{k} a_{i} \sum_{j = 1}^{i} X^{j - 1} HX^{i - j},
$$

whence

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac{d}{dt} \bigg |_{t = 0} \phi(X + tH) = \frac{d}{dt} \bigg |_{t = 0} \mathrm{Tr}(f(X + tH)) \\ \mathrm{Tr} \left(\frac{d}{dt} \bigg |_{t = 0} f(X + tH)\right)[\text{since} \mathrm{Tr}(Z) \text{is a linear function of} Z] \\ = \mathrm{Tr} \left(\sum_{i = 0}^{k} a_{i} \sum_{j = 1}^{i} X^{j - 1} HX^{i - j}\right) = \sum_{i = 0}^{k} a_{i} \sum_{j = 1}^{i} \mathrm{Tr} \left(X^{j - 1} HX^{i - j}\right) \\ = \sum_{i = 0}^{k} a_{i} \sum_{j = 1}^{i} \mathrm{Tr}(HX^{i - 1})[\text{since for square matrices} P, Q \text{of the same size one has} \mathrm{Tr}(PQ) = \mathrm{Tr}(QP), \text{see Proposition A.7.1}] \\ = \mathrm{Tr} \left(H[\sum_{i = 0}^{k} a_{i} iX^{i - 1}]\right) = \mathrm{Tr}(Hf^{\prime}(X)).\end{array}
$$

Next, is open by Proposition A.7.11. Now let f be continuously diferentiable real-valued function on interval $(a, b) \subset \mathbb{R}$ , and $f_{t}(x), t = 1, 2,...,$ be polynomials such that $f_{t}(\cdot)$ and $f_{t}^{\prime}(\cdot)$ converge as $t \infty,$ uniformly on every segment $[a^{\prime}, b^{\prime}] \subset(a, b)$ , to $f(\cdot)$ and $f^{\prime}(\cdot)$ , respectively; it is well known that such a sequence exists. Taking into account that the spectral norm (maximum of magnitudes of eigenvalues) of $g(X)$ is upper-bounded by the uniform norm of $g(\cdot)$ on $\sigma(X)$ , we immediately conclude that as $t \to \infty$ the functions $\phi_{t}(x) = \mathrm{Tr}(f_{t}(X))$ , uniformly on closed and bounded subsets of ${\mathcal{D}},$ converge to $\phi(X)$ , and the gradients $\nabla \phi_{t}(X) = f_{t}^{\prime}(X)$ converge uniformly on closed and bounded subsets of to $f^{\prime}(X)$ . By the standard results of Analysis, it follows that $\phi(\cdot)$ is continuously diferentiable on $\mathcal{D},$ the gradient being $\nabla \phi(X) = f^{\prime}(X)$ ✷

## A.8 Positive semidefinite matrices and positive semidefinite cone

## A.8.1 Positive semidefinite matrices.

Recall that an $n \times n$ matrix A is called positive semidefinite (notation: $A \succeq 0)$ , if A is symmetric and produces nonnegative quadratic form:

$$
A \succeq 0 \iff \{A = A^{T} \quad \text{and} \quad x^{T} Ax \geq 0 \quad \forall x\}.
$$

A is called positive definite (notation: $A \succ 0)$ , if it is positive semidefinite and the corresponding quadratic form is positive outside the origin:

$$
A \succ 0 \iff \{A = A^{T} \quad \text{and} \quad x^{T} Ax > 0 \quad \forall x \neq 0\}.
$$

The class of positive semidefinite matrices play an important role in mathematics. Thus, we next list a number of equivalent definitions of a positive semidefinite matrix.

Theorem A.8.1 For any $A \in \mathbf{S}^{n}$ , the following properties of A are equivalent to each other:

(i) $A \succeq 0,$

(ii) $\lambda(A) \geq 0$

(iii) $A = D^{T} D$ for certain rectangular matrix $D$

(iv) $A = \Delta^{T} \Delta$ for certain upper triangular $n \times n$ matrix $\Delta$ ,

(v) $A = B^{2}$ for certain symmetric matrix $B_{i}$

(vi) $A = B^{2}$ for certain $B \succeq 0.$

Moreover, for any $A \in \mathbf{S}^{n}$ , we also have the following properties equivalent to each other:

(i<sup>0</sup>) $A \succ 0$

(ii<sup>0</sup>) $\lambda(A) > 0$

(iii<sup>0</sup>) $A = D^{T} D$ for certain rectangular matrix D of rank $n,$

(iv<sup>0</sup>) $A = \Delta^{T} \Delta$ for certain nonsingular upper triangular $n \times n$ matrix $\Delta$

(v<sup>0</sup>) $A = B^{2}$ for certain nonsingular symmetric matrix $B_{i}$

(vi<sup>0</sup>) $A = B^{2}$ for certain $B \succ 0$

Proof. $\mathrm{(i)} \longleftrightarrow \mathrm{(ii)}$ : This equivalence is given by Proposition $\mathrm{A.7.6}$

$(\mathrm{ii}){\Rightarrow}(\mathrm{vi})$ : Suppose that we are in the case of (ii). Let $A = U \Lambda U^{T}$ be the eigenvalue decomposition of A, so that U is orthogonal and Λ is diagonal with nonnegative diagonal entries $\lambda_{i}(A)$ (as we are in the case of (ii)). Let $\Lambda^{1 / 2}$ be the diagonal matrix with the diagonal entries $\lambda_{i}^{1 / 2}(A)$ . Note that $(\Lambda^{1 / 2})^{2} = \Lambda$ Then, the matrix $B = U \Lambda^{1 / 2} U^{T}$ is symmetric with nonnegative eigenvalues $\lambda_{i}^{1 / 2}(A)$ , and thus $B \succeq 0$ by Proposition A.7.6. Moreover,

$$
B^{2} = U \Lambda^{1 / 2} \underbrace{U^{T} U}_{= I} \Lambda^{1 / 2} U^{T} = U(\Lambda^{1 / 2})^{2} U^{T} = U \Lambda U^{T} = A,
$$

## A.8. POSITIVE SEMIDEFINITE MATRICES AND POSITIVE SEMIDEFINITE CONE 621

as required in $\left(\mathrm{vi} \right)$

$(\mathrm{vi}){\Rightarrow}(v)$ : Evident.

(v) (iv): Suppose $A = B^{2}$ with certain symmetric B. Let $b_{i}$ be the i-th column of B for all $i \leq n$ Applying the Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization process (see proof of Theorem $\mathrm{A.2.3(iii)})$ , we can find an orthonormal system of vectors $u_{1}, \ldots, u_{n}$ and lower triangular matrix L such that

$$
b_{i} = \sum_{j = 1}^{i} L_{ij} u_{j},
$$

or, which is the same, $B^{T} = LU$ , where U is the orthogonal matrix with the rows $u_{1}^{T}, \ldots, u_{n}^{T}$ . Then, we have $A = B^{2} = B^{T}(B^{T})^{T} = LUU^{T} L^{T} = LL^{T}$ . Recalling that L is a lower triangular matrix, we see that $A = \Delta^{T} \Delta$ , where the matrix $\Delta = L^{T}$ is upper triangular.

$(\mathrm{iv}){\Rightarrow}(\mathrm{iii})$ : Evident.

(iii)<sub>⇒</sub>(i): If $A = D^{T} D$ , then $x^{T} Ax =(Dx)^{T}(Dx) \geq 0$ for all $x.$ .

We have proved the equivalence of the properties $\mathrm{(i) ~ - ~(vi)}$ . Slightly modifying the reasoning (do it yourself!), one can prove the equivalence of the properties $\mathrm{(i^{\prime}) -(vi^{\prime})}$ ✷

Remark A.8.1 (i) [Checking positive semidefiniteness] Given matrix $A \in \mathbf{S}^{n}$ , we can check whether it is positive semidefinite by a purely algebraic finite algorithm (the so called Lagrange diagonalization of a quadratic form) which requires at most $O(n^{3})$ arithmetic operations. Positive definiteness of a matrix can be checked also by the Cholesky factorization algorithm which finds the decomposition in $(\mathrm{iv}^{\prime})$ , if it exists, in approximately $\scriptstyle{\frac{1}{6}} n^{3}$ arithmetic operations.

There exists another useful algebraic criterion (Sylvester’s criterion) for positive semidefiniteness of a matrix. According to this criterion, a symmetric matrix A is positive definite if and only if all of its angular minors are positive, and A is positive semidefinite if and only if all its principal minors are nonnegative. For example, a symmetric $2 \times 2$ matrix $A ={\left[\begin{array}{ll}{a} &{b} \\{b} &{c} \end{array} \right]}$ is positive semidefinite if and only if $a \ge 0, c \ge 0$ , and $\operatorname{Det}(A) : = ac - b^{2} \geq 0$ . Another consequence is that when $A \succeq 0$ , one has $A_{ii} A_{jj} \geq A_{ij}^{2}$ since the principal $2 \times 2$ minors of A should be nonnegative.

(ii) [Square root of a positive semidefinite matrix] By the first chain of equivalences in Theorem A.8.1, a symmetric matrix A is $\succeq 0$ if and only if A is the square of a positive semidefinite matrix B. The latter matrix is uniquely defined by $A \succeq 0$ and is called the square root of A (notation: $A^{1 / 2})$ , see Section A.7.5.

## A.8.2 The positive semidefinite cone

When adding symmetric matrices and multiplying them by reals, we add, respectively multiply by reals, the corresponding quadratic forms. Hence, we arrive at the following basic fact.

Proposition A.8.1 Let $A, B \in \mathbf{S}^{n}$ be positive semidefinite. Then, $A + B$ is also positive semidefinite. For any $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}_{+}$ , the matrix αA is also positive semidefinite.

This fact is also the same as the following one stated in Section B.1.4.

Proposition A.8.2 The set of $n \times n$ positive semidefinite matrices form a cone $\mathbf{S}_{+}^{n}$ in the Euclidean space $\mathbf{S}^{n}$ of symmetric n n matrices based on the Euclidean structure being given by the Frobenius inner product $\begin{array}{r}{\langle A, B \rangle = \operatorname{Tr}(AB) = \sum_{i, j} A_{ij} B_{ij}} \end{array}$

The cone $\mathbf{S}_{+}^{n}$ is called the positive semidefinite cone of size n. It is immediately seen that the semidefinite cone $\mathbf{S}_{+}^{n} \mathrm{is} \ \mathrm{\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle..}{good} \mathrm{\uparrow}}$ (regular, see Section 1.4.2). Specifically, it satisfies the following properties:

$\mathbf{S}_{+}^{n}$ is closed: the limit of a converging sequence of positive semidefinite matrices is positive semidefinite.

- $\mathbf{S}_{+}^{n}$ is pointed: the only $n \times n$ matrix A such that both A and A are positive semidefinite is the n n matrix of all zeros.

$\mathbf{S}_{+}^{n}$ possesses a nonempty interior (subset comprised by all interior points of $\mathbf{S}_{+}^{n})$ which is exactly the set of positive definite matrices.

Note that the relation $A \succeq B$ means exactly that $A - B \in \mathbf{S}_{+}^{n}$ , while $A \succ B$ is equivalent to $A - B \in \operatorname{int} \mathbf{S}_{+}^{n}$ The “matrix inequalities” ${\mathit{\Sigma}}^{\prime} A \succeq B \left(A \succ B \right)$ match the standard properties of the usual scalar inequalities, $\mathrm{e.g.}$

$$
A \succeq B, B \succeq A \Rightarrow A = B
$$

$$
A \succeq B, B \succeq C \Rightarrow A \succeq C
$$

$$
A \succeq B, C \succeq D \Rightarrow A + C \succeq B + D
$$

$$
A \succeq B, \lambda \geq 0 \Rightarrow \lambda A \succeq \lambda B
$$

$$
A_{i} \succeq B_{i}, A_{i} \rightarrow A, B_{i} \rightarrow B \text{as} i \rightarrow \infty \Rightarrow A \succeq B
$$

with evident modifications when $\succeq$ is replaced with $\succ$ , like

$$
A \succeq B, C \succ D \Rightarrow A + C \succ B + D,
$$

etc. Along with these standard properties of inequalities, the inequali $\mathrm{\Delta ty ~ ucceq ~}$ possesses the following nice additional property.

Fact A.8.1 For any A, $B \in \mathbf{S}^{n}$ such that $A \succeq B$ , and for any $V \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times m}$ , we always have

$$
V^{T} AV \succeq V^{T} BV.
$$

Another important property of the positive semidefinite cone is that its dual cone is equal to the cone itself, i.e., the positive semidefinite cone is self-dual.

Theorem A.8.2 A matrix X has nonnegative Frobenius inner products with all positive semidefinite matrices $if$ and only $ifX$ itself is positive semidefinite.

Proof. We first prove the $ { \mathbf { \hat { \rho } } } _ { \mathrm { 1 f } }  { \mathbf { \vec { \rho } } } _ { \mathrm { 1 f } } ^ { \mathrm { 9 } }$ part: Assume that $X \succeq 0.$ , and let us prove that then $\mathrm{Tr}(XY) \geq 0$ for every $Y \succeq 0$ . Using the eigenvalue decomposition of X, we can write it as

$$
X = \sum_{i = 1}^{n} \lambda_{i}(X) e_{i} e_{i}^{T},
$$

where $e_{i}$ are the orthonormal eigenvectors of X. Then, we arrive at

$$
\begin{array}{rl} \mathrm{Tr}(XY) & = \mathrm{Tr} \left(\left(\sum_{i = 1}^{n} \lambda_{i}(X) e_{i} e_{i}^{T}\right) Y\right) = \sum_{i = 1}^{n} \lambda_{i}(X) \mathrm{Tr}(e_{i} e_{i}^{T} Y) \\ & = \sum_{i = 1}^{n} \lambda_{i}(X) \mathrm{Tr}(e_{i}^{T} Ye_{i}), \end{array}\tag{A.8.1}
$$

where the last equality is given by Proposition A.7.1. Recall that $e_{i} s$ are just vectors, and thus $\mathrm{Tr}(e_{i}^{T} Ye_{i}) = e_{i}^{T} Y \bar{e}_{i}$ . Also, as $Y \succeq 0$ , we have $e_{i}^{T} Ye_{i} \geq 0$ for all i. Moreover, since $X \succeq 0$ by P.7.5, we have $\lambda_{i}(X) \geq 0$ , and thus we conclude

$$
\mathrm{Tr}(XY) = \sum_{i = 1}^{n} \lambda_{i}(X) \mathrm{Tr}(e_{i}^{T} Ye_{i}) \geq 0.
$$

In order to prove the “only $\mathrm{if}^{\dag}$ part, suppose that X is such that $\mathrm{Tr}(XY) \geq 0$ for all matrices $Y \succeq 0$ Note that for every vector y, the matrix $\bar{Y} = yy^{T}$ is positive semidefinite (Theorem A.8.1.(iii)). Then, for any $y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ we have $\begin{array}{r}{0 \le \mathrm{Tr}(Xyy^{T}) = \mathrm{Tr}(y^{T} Xy) = y^{T} Xy} \end{array}$ , where the first equality follows from Proposition A.7.1. Thus, $X \succeq 0$ as desired. ✷

Graphical illustration. The single-dimensional positive semidefinite cone $\mathbf{S}_{1}^{n}$ is just the nonnegative ray, i.e.,

$$
\mathbf{S}_{+}^{1} = \{x \in \mathbb{R}: x \geq 0\}.
$$
