A trivial example of a lower semicontinuous function is a continuous one. Note, however, that a semicontinuous function is not obliged to be continuous; what it is obliged, is to make only “jumps down”. $\mathrm{E.g.}$ , the function

$$
f(x) = \left\{\begin{array}{ll} 0, & x \neq 0 \\ a, & x = 0 \end{array} \right.
$$

is lower semicontinuous if $a \leq 0 \mathrm{~(?)} \.$ jump down at $x = 0$ or no jump at all”), and is not lower semicontinuous if $a > 0 \ \mathrm{(" jump \up ")}$

The following statement links lower semicontinuity with the geometry of the epigraph:

Proposition C.6.1 A function f defined on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ and taking values from $\scriptstyle \mathbb{R} \cup \{+ \infty\}$ is lower semicontinuous $if$ and only if its epigraph is closed $(e.g.$ , due to its emptiness).

I shall not prove this statement, same as most of other statements in this Section; the reader definitely is able to restore (very simple) proofs I am skipping.

An immediate consequence of the latter proposition is as follows:

Corollary C.6.1 The upper bound

$$
f(x) = \sup_{\alpha \in \mathcal{A}} f_{\alpha}(x)
$$

of arbitrary family of lower semicontinuous functions is lower semicontinuous.

[from now till the end of the Section, if the opposite is not explicitly stated, “a function” means “a function defined on the entire $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ and taking values in $\mathbb{R} \cup \{+ \infty\}^{\mathfrak{N}}]$

Indeed, the epigraph of the upper bound is the intersection of the epigraphs of the functions forming the bound, and the intersection of closed sets always is closed. ✷

Now let us look at convex lower semicontinuous functions; according to our general convention, “convex” means “satisfying the convexity inequality and finite at least at one point”, or, which is the same, “with convex nonempty epigraph”; and as we just have seen, “lower semicontinuous” means “with closed epigraph”. Thus, we are interested in functions with closed convex nonempty epigraphs; to save words, let us call these functions proper.

What we are about to do is to translate to the functional language several constructions and results related to convex sets. In the usual life, a translation (e.g. of poetry) typically results in something less rich than the original; in contrast to this, in mathematics this is a powerfu source of new ideas and constructions.

“Outer description” of a proper function. We know that a closed convex set is intersection of closed half-spaces. What does this fact imply when the set is the epigraph of a proper function $f ?$ First of all, note that the epigraph is not a completely arbitrary convex set: it has a recessive direction $e =(1, 0) \mathrm{~ - ~ the}$ basic orth of the t-axis in the space of variables $t \in \mathbb{R}, x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ where the epigraph lives. This direction, of course, should be recessive for every closed half-space

$$
(*) \quad \Pi = \{(t, x): \alpha t \geq d^{T} x - a\} \quad[| \alpha | + | d | > 0]
$$

containing Epi(f) (note that what is written in the right hand side of the latter relation, is one of many universal forms of writing down a general nonstrict linear inequality in the space where the epigraph lives; this is the form the most convenient for us now). Thus, e should be a recessive direction of $\Pi \supset \operatorname{Epi}(f);$ as it is immediately seen, recessivity of e for Π means exactly that $\alpha \geq 0$ . Thus, speaking about closed half-spaces containing $\operatorname{Epi}(f)$ , we in fact are considering some of the half-spaces (\*) with $\alpha \geq 0$

Now, there are two essentially different possibilities for α to be nonnegative – (A) to be positive, and (B) to be zero. In the case of (B) the boundary hyperplane of Π is “vertical” – it is parallel to $e,$ and in fact it “bounds” only $x - \Pi$ is comprised of all pairs $(t, x)$ with x belonging to certain half-space in the x-subspace and t being arbitrary real. These “vertical” subspaces will be of no interest for us.

The half-spaces which indeed are of interest for us are the “nonvertical” ones: those $\mathrm{gi}$ ven by the case $\mathrm{(A)}$ , i.e., with $\alpha > 0$ . For a non-vertical half-space Π, we always can divide the inequality defining Π by α and to make $\alpha = 1$ . Thus, a “nonvertical” candidate to the role of a closed half-space containing $\operatorname{Epi}(f)$ always can be written down as

$$
(* *) \quad \Pi = \{(t, x): t \geq d^{T} x - a\},
$$

i.e., can be represented as the epigraph of an Affine function of $x.$

Now, when such a candidate indeed is a half-space containing $\operatorname{Epi}(f) ?$ The answer is clear: it is the case $if$ and only if the Affine function $d^{T} x - a$ everywhere in $\mathbb{R}^{n} \is \ \leq \f(\cdot) \ - \ \mathrm{as}$ we shall say, “is an Affine minorant of $f^{\ast}$ ; indeed, the smaller is the epigraph, the larger is the function. If we knew that $\operatorname{Epi}(f) ~ -$ which definitely is the intersection of all closed half-spaces containing $\operatorname{Epi}(f) - is$ in fact the intersection of already nonvertical closed $half_{-}$ spaces containing $\operatorname{Epi}(f)$ , or, which is the same, the intersection of the epigraphs of all Affine minorants of $^{\cdot} f,$ we would be able to get a nice and nontrivial result:

(!) a proper convex function is the upper bound of Affine functions – all its Affine minorants.

(indeed, we already know that it is the same – to say that a function is an upper bound of certain family of functions, and to say that the epigraph of the function is the intersection of the epigraphs of the functions of the family).

(!) indeed is true:

Proposition C.6.2 A proper convex function $f$ is the upper bound of all its $affune$ minorants. Moreover, at every point ${\bar{x}} \in$ ri Dom $f$ from the relative interior of the domain $_{f \f}$ is even not the upper bound, but simply the maximum of its minorants: there exists an Affine function $f_{\bar{x}}(x)$ which $is \leq f(x)$ everywhere in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ and is equal to $f$ at $x = \bar{x}$

Proof. I. We start with the “Moreover” part of the statement; this is the key to the entire statement. Thus, we are about to prove that if $\bar{x} \in \operatorname{riDom} f.$ , then there exists an Affine function $f_{\bar{x}}(x)$ which is everywhere $\leq f(x)$ , and at $x = \bar{x}$ the inequality becomes an equality. $\mathrm{I.1^{0}}$ First of all, we easily can reduce the situation to the one when Dom $f$ is full-dimensional. Indeed, by shifting $f$ we may make the Affine span $\operatorname{Aff}(\operatorname{Dom} f)$ of the domain of $f$ to be a linear subspace $L$ in $\mathbb{R}^{n};$ restricting $f$ onto this linear subspace, we clearly get a proper function on $L.$ . If we believe that our statement is true for the case when the domain of $f$ is full-dimensional, we can conclude that there exists an Affine function

$$
d^{T} x - a \quad[x \in L]
$$

on $\underline{{L}} \(d \in L)$ such that

$$
f(x) \geq d^{T} x - a \quad \forall x \in L; f(\bar{x}) = d^{T} \bar{x} - a.
$$

The Affine function we get clearly can be extended, by the same formula, from $L$ on the entire $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ and is a minorant of $f$ on the entire $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ – outside of $L \supset$ Dom $f ~ f$ simply is + ! This minorant on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ is exactly what we need.

$\mathrm{I.2^{0}}$ . Now let us prove that our statement is valid when Dom f is full-dimensional, so that x¯ is an interior point of the domain of $f.$ Let us look at the point $y =(f({\bar{x}}),{\bar{x}})$ . This is a point from the epigraph of $f,$ and I claim that it is a point from the relative boundary of the epigraph. Indeed, if $y$ were a relative interior point of $\operatorname{Epi}(f)$ , then, taking $y^{\prime} = y + e,$ we would get a segment $[y^{\prime}, y]$ contained in $\operatorname{Epi}(f)$ ; since the endpoint $y$ of the segment is assumed to be relative interior for $\operatorname{Epi}(f)$ , we could extend this segment a little through this endpoint, not leaving $\operatorname{Epi}(f)$ ; but this clearly is impossible, since the t-coordinate of the new endpoint would be $< f(\bar{x})$ , and the x-component of it still would be ${\bar{x}}.$

Thus, $y$ is a point from the relative boundary of $\operatorname{Epi}(f)$ . Now I claim that $y^{\prime}$ is an interior point of $\operatorname{Epi}(f)$ . This is immediate: we know from Theorem C.4.1 that $f$ is continuous at ${\bar{x}},$ so that there exists a neighbourhood $U$ of ¯x in Af(Dom $f) = \mathbb{R}^{n}$ such that $f(x) \leq f(\bar{x} + 0.5)$ whenever $x \in U$ , or, in other words, the set

$$
V = \{(t, x): x \in U, t > f(\bar{x}) + 0.5\}
$$

is contained in $\operatorname{Epi}(f)$ ; but this set clearly contains a neighbourhood of $y^{\prime}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{n + 1}$

Now let us look at the supporting linear form to $\operatorname{Epi}(f)$ at the point y of the relative boundary of $\operatorname{Epi}(f)$ . This form gives us a linear inequality on $\mathbb{R}^{n + 1}$ which is satisfied everywhere on $\operatorname{Epi}(f)$ and becomes equality at $y;$ besides this, the inequality is not equality identically on $\operatorname{Epi}(f)$ , it is strict somewhere on $\operatorname{Epi}(f)$ . Without loss of generality we may assume that the inequality is of the form

$$
(+) \quad \alpha t \geq d^{T} x - a.
$$

Now, since our inequality is satisfied at $y^{\prime} = y + e$ and becomes equality at $(t, x) = y$ , α should be $\geq 0;$ it cannot be $0_{;}$ since in the latter case the inequality in question would be equality also at $y^{\prime} \in \operatorname{int} \operatorname{Epi}(f)$ . But a linear inequality which is satisfied at a convex set and is equality at an interior point of the set is trivial – coming from the zero linear form (this is exactly the statement that a linear form attaining its minimum on a convex set at a point from the relative interior of the set is constant on the set and on its Affine hull).

Thus, inequality $(+)$ which is satisfied on $\operatorname{Epi}(f)$ and becomes equality at $y$ is an inequality with $\alpha > 0$ . Let us divide both sides of the inequality by $\alpha;$ we get a new inequality of the form

$$
(\ &) \quad t \geq d^{T} x - a
$$

(I keep the same notation for the right hand side coeficients – we never will come back to the old coeficients); this inequality is valid on $\operatorname{Epi}(f)$ and is equality at $y =(f({\bar{x}}),{\bar{x}})$ . Since the inequality is valid on $\operatorname{Epi}(f)$ , it is valid at every pair $(t, x)$ with $x \in$ Dom $f$ and $t = f(x)$

$$
(\#) f(x) \geq d^{T} x - a \forall x \in \operatorname{Dom} f;
$$

so that the right hand side is an Affine minorant of $f$ on Dom $f$ and therefore – on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ $(f = + \infty$ outside Dom $f !)$ . It remains to note that $(\#)$ is equality at ${\bar{x}},$ since $(\&)$ is equality at $y.$ ✷

II. We have proved that if $\mathcal{F}$ if the set of all Affine functions which are minorants of $f,$ then the function

$$
\bar{f}(x) = \sup_{\phi \in \mathcal{F}} \phi(x)
$$

is equal to $f$ on ri Dom $f$ (and at $x$ from the latter set in fact sup in the right hand side can be replaced with max); to complete the proof of the Proposition, we should prove that $\bar{f}$ is equal to $f$ also outside ri Dom $f.$

$\mathrm{II.1^{0}}$ . Let us first prove that $\bar{f}$ is equal to $f$ outside cl Dom $f,$ or. which is the same, prove that $\bar{f}(x) = + \infty$ outside cl Dom $f.$ This is easy: is ¯x is a point outside cl Dom $f,$ it can be strongly separated from Dom $f,$ see Separation Theorem (ii) (Theorem B.2.9). Thus, there exists $z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ such that

$$
z^{T} \bar{x} \geq z^{T} x + \zeta \quad \forall x \in \operatorname{Dom} f \quad[\zeta > 0].\tag{C.6.1}
$$

Besides this, we already know that there exists at least one Affine minorant of $f,$ or, which is the same, there exist a and d such that

$$
f(x) \geq d^{T} x - a \quad \forall x \in \operatorname{Dom} f.\tag{C.6.2}
$$

Let us add to (C.6.2) inequality (C.6.1) multiplied by positive weight $\lambda;$ we get

$$
f(x) \geq \phi_{\lambda}(x) \equiv(d + \lambda z)^{T} x +[\lambda \zeta - a - \lambda z^{T} \bar{x}] \quad \forall x \in \mathrm{Dom} f.
$$

This inequality clearly says that $\phi_{\lambda}(\cdot)$ is an Affine minorant of $f$ on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ for every $\lambda > 0$ The value of this minorant at $x = \bar{x}$ is equal to $d^{T} \bar{x} - a + \lambda \zeta$ and therefore it goes to + as $\lambda \to + \infty$ . We see that the upper bound of Affine minorants of $f$ at ¯x indeed is $+ \infty,$ , as claimed.

II. $.2^{0}$ . Thus, we know that the upper bound $\bar{f}$ of all Affine minorants of $f$ is equal to $f$ everywhere on the relative interior of Dom $f$ and everywhere outside the closure of Dom $f;$ all we should prove that this equality is also valid at the points of the relative boundary of Dom $f.$ . Let $\bar{x}$ be such a point. There is nothing to prove $\mathrm{if} \ \bar{f}(\bar{x}) = + \infty$ , since by construction $\bar{f}$ is everywhere $\leq f.$ . Thus, we should prove that if $\bar{f}(\bar{x}) = c < \infty$ , then $f({\bar{x}}) = c.$ . Since $\bar{f} \le f$ everywhere, to prove that $f({\bar{x}}) = c$ is the same as to prove that $f({\bar{x}}) \leq c.$ This is immediately given by lower semicontinuity of $f \colon$ let us choose $x^{\prime} \in \operatorname{riDom} f$ and look what happens along a sequence of points $x_{i} \in[x^{\prime},{\bar{x}})$ converging to ¯x. All the points of this sequence are relative interior points of Dom f (Lemma B.1.1), and consequently

$$
f(x_{i}) = \bar{f}(x_{i}).
$$

Now, $x_{i} =(1 - \lambda_{i}) \bar{x} + \lambda_{i} x^{\prime}$ with $\lambda_{i} \to + 0$ as $i \infty;$ since $\bar{f}$ clearly is convex (as the upper bound of a family of Affine and therefore convex functions), we have

$$
\bar{f}(x_{i}) \leq(1 - \lambda_{i}) \bar{f}(\bar{x}) + \lambda_{i} \bar{f}(x^{\prime}).
$$

Putting things together, we get

$$
f(x_{i}) \leq(1 - \lambda_{i}) \bar{f}(\bar{x}) + \lambda_{i} f(x^{\prime});
$$

as $i \infty, x_{i} \bar{x}$ , and the right hand side in our inequality converges to $\bar{f}(\bar{x}) = c;$ since $f$ is lower semicontinuous, we get $f(\bar{x}) \leq c$ ✷

We see why “translation of mathematical facts from one mathematical language to another” – in our case, from the language of convex sets to the language of convex functions – may be fruitful: because we invest a lot into the process rather than run it mechanically.

Closure of a convex function. We got a nice result on the “outer description” of a proper convex function: it is the upper bound of a family of Affine functions. Note that, vice versa, the upper bound of every family of Affine functions is a proper function, provided that this upper bound is finite at least at one point (indeed, as we know from Section C.2.1, upper bound of every family of convex functions is convex, provided that it is finite at least at one point; and Corollary C.6.1 says that upper bound of lower semicontinuous functions (e.g., Affine ones – they are even continuous) is lower semicontinuous).

Now, what to do with a convex function which is not lower semicontinuous? The similar question about convex sets – what to do with a convex set which is not closed – can be resolved very simply: we can pass from the set to its closure and thus get a “normal” object which is very “close” to the original one: the “main part” of the original set – its relative interior – remains unchanged, and the “correction” adds to the set something relatively small – the relative boundary. The same approach works for convex functions: if a convex function $f$ is not proper (i.e., its epigraph, being convex and nonempty, is not closed), we can “correct” the function – replace it with a new function with the epigraph being the closure of $\operatorname{Epi}(f)$ To justify this approach, we, of course, should be sure that the closure of the epigraph of a convex function is also an epigraph of such a function. This indeed is the case, and to see it, it sufices to note that a set $G$ in $\mathbb{R}^{n + 1}$ is the epigraph of a function taking values in $\mathbb{R} \cup \{+ \infty\}$ if and only if the intersection of G with every vertical line $\{x = \mathrm{const}, t \in \mathbb{R}\}$ is either empty, or is a closed ray of the form $\{x = \mathrm{const}, t \ge \bar{t} > - \infty\}$ . Now, it is absolutely evident that if $G$ is the closure of the epigraph of a function $f,$ that its intersection with a vertical line is either empty, or is a closed ray, or is the entire line (the last case indeed can take place – look at the closure of the epigraph of the function equal to $-{\frac{1}{x}}$ for $x > 0$ and $+ \infty$ for $x \leq 0)$ . We see that in order to justify our idea of “proper correction” of a convex function we should prove that if $f$ is convex, then the last of the indicated three cases – the intersection of cl $\operatorname{Epi}(f)$ with a vertical line is the entire line – never occurs. This fact evidently is a corollary of the following simple

Proposition C.6.3 A convex function is below bounded on every bounded subset of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$

Proof. Without loss of generality we may assume that the domain of the function f is full-dimensional and that 0 is the interior point of the domain. According to Theorem C.4.1, there exists a neighbourhood $U$ of the origin – which can be thought of to be a centered at the origin ball of some radius $r > 0 ~ \AA^{-}$ where $f$ is bounded from above by some $C.$ Now, if $R > 0$ is arbitrary and x is an arbitrary point with $| x | \le R$ , then the point

$$
y = - \frac{r}{R} x
$$

belongs to $U,$ and we have

$$
0 = \frac{r}{r + R} x + \frac{R}{r + R} y;
$$

since $f$ is convex, we conclude that

$$
f(0) \leq \frac{r}{r + R} f(x) + \frac{R}{r + R} f(y) \leq \frac{r}{r + R} f(x) + \frac{R}{r + R} c,
$$

and we get the lower bound

$$
f(x) \geq \frac{r + R}{r} f(0) - \frac{r}{R} c
$$

for the values of $f$ in the centered at 0 ball of radius $R.$

Thus, we conclude that the closure of the epigraph of a convex function $f$ is the epigraph of certain function, let it be called the closure cl f of $\cdot_{f.}$ Of course, this latter function is convex (its epigraph is convex – it is the closure of a convex set), and since its epigraph is closed, cl f is proper. The following statement gives direct description of cl $f$ in terms of $f \colon$

Proposition C.6.4 Let $f$ be a convex function and cl $f$ be its closure. Then

(i) For every x one has

$$
\operatorname{cl} f(x) = \lim_{r \to + 0} \inf_{x^{\prime}: \| x^{\prime} - x \|_{2} \leq r} f(x^{\prime}).
$$

In particular,

$$
f(x) \geq \operatorname{cl} f(x)
$$

for all x, and

$$
f(x) = \operatorname{cl} f(x)
$$

whenever $x \in$ ri Dom $f,$ same as whenever x $\notin$ cl Dom $f.$

Thus, the “correction” $f \mapsto \operatorname{cl} f$ may vary $f$ only at the points $fr$ om the relative boundary $of$ Dom $f,$

$$
\operatorname{Dom} f \subset \operatorname{Dom} \operatorname{cl} f \subset \operatorname{cl} \operatorname{Dom} f,
$$

whence also

$$
\operatorname{ri} \operatorname{Dom} f = \operatorname{ri} \operatorname{Dom} \operatorname{cl} f.
$$

(ii) The family of Affine minorants of cl $f$ is exactly the family of Affine minorants of $f,$ so that

$$
\operatorname{cl} f(x) = \sup \left\{\phi(x): \phi \text{is an affine minorant of} f \right\},
$$

and the sup in the right hand side can be replaced with max whenever $x \in$ ri Dom cl $f =$ ri Dom $f.$

[“so that” comes from the fact that cl $f$ is proper and is therefore the upper bound of its Affine minorants]

## C.6.2 Subgradients

Let $f$ be a convex function, and let $x \in$ Dom $f.$ It may happen that there exists an Affine minorant $d^{T} x - a$ of $f$ which coincides with $f$ at x:

$$
f(y) \geq d^{T} y - a \quad \forall y, \quad f(x) = d^{T} x - a.
$$

From the equality in the latter relation we get $\boldsymbol{a} = d^{T} \boldsymbol{x} - f(\boldsymbol{x})$ , and substituting this representation of a into the first inequality, we get

$$
f(y) \geq f(x) + d^{T}(y - x) \quad \forall y.\tag{C.6.3}
$$

Thus, if $f$ admits an Affine minorant which is exact at $x,$ , then there exists d which gives rise to inequality (C.6.3). Vice versa, if d is such that (C.6.3) takes place, then the right hand side of (C.6.3), regarded as a function of $y,$ is an Affine minorant of $f$ which is exact at x.

Now note that (C.6.3) expresses certain property of a vector $d.$ A vector satisfying, for a given x, this property – i.e., the slope of an exact at x Affine minorant of $f$ – is called a subgradient of $f$ at $x,$ and the set of all subgradients of $f$ at x is denoted $\partial f(x)$

Subgradients of convex functions play important role in the theory and numerical methods of Convex Programming – they are quite reasonable surrogates of gradients. The most elementary properties of the subgradients are summarized in the following statement:

Proposition C.6.5 Let f be a convex function and x be a point from Dom f. Then

(i) $\partial f(x)$ is a closed convex set which for sure is nonempty when $x \in$ ri Dom $f$

(ii) $Ifx \in$ int Dom f and f is diferentiable at $x,$ then $\partial f(x)$ is the singleton comprised of the usual gradient of f at x.

Proof. (i): Closedness and convexity of $\partial f(x)$ are evident – (C.6.3) is an infinite system of nonstrict linear inequalities with respect to $d,$ , the inequalities being indexed by $y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ Nonemptiness of $\partial f(x)$ for the case when $x \in$ ri Dom f – this is the most important fact about the subgradients – is readily given by our preceding results. Indeed, we should prove that if $x \in$ ri Dom $f,$ then there exists an Affine minorant of $f$ which is exact at x. But this is an immediate consequence of Proposition C.6.4: part $(i)$ of the proposition says that there exists an Affine minorant of $f$ which is equal to cl $f(x)$ at the point $x,$ and part (i) says that $f(x) = \operatorname{cl} f(x)$

(ii): If x  int Dom $f$ and $f$ is diferentiable at $x,$ then $\nabla f(x) \in \partial f(x)$ by the Gradient Inequality. To prove that in the case in question $\nabla f(x)$ is the only subgradient of $f$ at $x_{i}$ , note that if $d \in \partial f(x)$ , then, by definition,

$$
f(y) - f(x) \geq d^{T}(y - x) \quad \forall y
$$

Substituting $y - x = th$ , h being a fixed direction and t being $> 0$ , dividing both sides of the resulting inequality by t and passing to limit as $t + 0$ , we $\mathrm{get}$

$$
h^{T} \nabla f(x) \geq h^{T} d.
$$

This inequality should be valid for all h, which is possible if and only if $d = \nabla f(x)$ ✷

Proposition C.6.5 explains why subgradients are good surrogates of gradients: at a point where gradient exists, it is the only subgradient, but, in contrast to the gradient, a subgradient exists basically everywhere (for sure in the relative interior of the domain of the function). E.g., let us look at the simple function

$$
f(x) = | x |
$$

on the axis. It is, of course, convex (as maximum of two linear forms x and x). Whenever $x \neq 0, f$ is diferentiable at x with the derivative +1 for $x > 0$ and 1 for $x < 0$ . At the point $x = 0 \f$ is not diferentiable; nevertheless, it must have subgradients at this point (since 0 is an interior point of the domain of the function). And indeed, it is immediately seen that the subgradients of $| x |$ at $x = 0$ are exactly the reals from the segment $[- 1, 1]$ . Thus,

$$
\partial | x | = \left\{\begin{array}{ll} \{- 1\}, & x < 0 \\[- 1, 1], & x = 0 \\ \{+ 1\}, & x > 0 \end{array} \right..
$$

Note also that if $x$ is a relative boundary point of the domain of a convex function, even $\mathrm{~ a ~} \ \mathrm{\stackrel{\scriptscriptstyle ~ 4 \ell}{good} ~}$ one, the set of subgradients of $f$ at x may be empty, as it is the case with the function

$$
f(y) = \left\{\begin{array}{ll} - \sqrt{y}, & y \geq 0 \\ + \infty, & y < 0 \end{array}; \right.
$$

it is clear that there is no non-vertical supporting line to the epigraph of the function at the point $(0, f(0))$ , and, consequently, there is no Affine minorant of the function which is exact at $x = 0$

A significant – and important – part of Convex Analysis deals with subgradient calculus – with the rules for computing subgradients of “composite” functions, like sums, superpositions, maxima, etc., given subgradients of the operands. These rules extend onto nonsmooth convex case the standard Calculus rules and are very nice and instructive; the related considerations, however, are beyond our scope.

## C.6.3 Legendre transformation

Let $f$ be a convex function. We know that $f \{^{} \mathrm{basically}}^{,}$ is the upper bound of all its Affine minorants; this is exactly the case when $f$ is proper, otherwise the corresponding equality takes place everywhere except, perhaps, some points from the relative boundary of Dom $f.$ Now, when an Affine function $d^{T} x - a$ is an Affine minorant of $f ?$ It is the case if and only if

$$
f(x) \geq d^{T} x - a
$$

for all $x \mathrm{\o ~} \mathrm{or}$ , which is the same, if and only if

$$
a \geq d^{T} x - f(x)
$$

for all $x.$ . We see that if the slope d of an Affine function $d^{T} x - a$ is fixed, then in order for the function to be a minorant of $f$ we should have

$$
a \geq \sup_{x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}}[d^{T} x - f(x)].
$$

The supremum in the right hand side of the latter relation is certain function of $d;$ this function is called the Legendre transformation of $f$ and is denoted $f^{*}$ :

$$
f^{*}(d) = \sup_{x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}}[d^{T} x - f(x)].
$$

Geometrically, the Legendre transformation answers the following question: given a slope d of an Affine function, i.e., given the hyperplane $t = d^{T} x$ in $\mathbb{R}^{n + 1}$ , what is the minimal “shift down” of the hyperplane which places it below the graph of $f ?$

From the definition of the Legendre transformation it follows that this is a proper function. Indeed, we loose nothing when replacing sup $[d^{T} x - f(x)]$ by sup $[d^{T} x - \bar{f}(x)]$ , so that x∈<sup>Rn</sup> x∈Dom f

the Legendre transformation is the upper bound of a family of Affine functions. Since this bound is finite at least at one point (namely, at every d coming form Affine minorant of $f;$ we know that such a minorant exists), it is a convex lower semicontinuous function, as claimed. The most elementary (and the most fundamental) fact about the Legendre transformation is its symmetry:

Proposition C.6.6 Let f be a convex function. Then twice taken Legendre transformation of f is the closure cl f of $f.$

$$
(f^{*})^{*} = \operatorname{cl} f.
$$

In particular, if f is proper, then it is the Legendre transformation of its Legendre transformation (which also is proper).

Proof is immediate. The Legendre transformation of $f^{*}$ at the point x is, by definition,

$$
\sup_{d \in \mathbb{R}^{n}}[x^{T} d - f^{*}(d)] = \sup_{d \in \mathbb{R}^{n}, a \geq f^{*}(d)}[d^{T} x - a];
$$

the second sup here is exactly the supremum of all Affine minorants of $f$ (this is the origin of the Legendre transformation: $a \geq f^{*}(d)$ if and only if the Affine form $d^{T} x - a$ is a minorant of $f)$ . And we already know that the upper bound of all Affine minorants of $f$ is the closure of $f.$ ✷

The Legendre transformation is a very powerful tool – this is a “global” transformation, so that local properties of $f^{*}$ correspond to global properties of $f.\ \mathrm{E.g.}$ ，

$d = 0$ belongs to the domain of $f^{*}$ if and only if $f$ is below bounded, and if it is the case, then $f^{*}(0) = - \operatorname{inf} f;$

if $f$ is proper, then the subgradients of $f^{*}$ at $d = 0$ are exactly the minimizers of $f$ on $\mathbb{R}^{n};$ ;

Dom $f^{*}$ is the entire $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ if and only if $f(x)$ grows, as $\|{x} \|_{2} \to \infty$ , faster than $\Vert{x} \Vert_{2}$ there exists a function $r(t) \to \infty$ , as $t \to \infty$ such that

$$
f(x) \geq r(\| x \|_{2}) \quad \forall x,
$$

etc. Thus, whenever we can compute explicitly the Legendre transformation of $f,$ we get a lot of “global” information on $f.$ Unfortunately, the more detailed investigation of the properties of Legendre transformation is beyond our scope; I simply list several simple facts and examples:

From the definition of Legendre transformation,

$$
f(x) + f^{*}(d) \geq x^{T} d \quad \forall x, d.
$$

Specifying here f and $f^{*},$ , we get certain inequality, $\mathrm{e.g.}$ , the following one: [Young’s Inequality] $ifp$ and q are positive reals such that $\textstyle{\frac{1}{p}} +{\frac{1}{q}} = 1$ , then

$$
\frac{| x |^{p}}{p} + \frac{| d |^{q}}{q} \geq xd \quad \forall x, d \in \mathbb{R}
$$

(indeed, as it is immediately seen, the Legendre transformation of the function $| x |^{p} / p$ is $| d |^{q} / q)$

Consequences. Very simple-looking Young’s inequality gives rise to a very nice and useful H¨older inequality:

Let $1 \leq p \leq \infty$ and let q be such ${\begin{array}{l}{{\frac{1}{p}} +{\frac{1}{q}} = 1 \(p = 1 \Rightarrow q = \infty, p = \infty \Rightarrow q = 1)} \end{array}}$ . For every two vectors $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ one has

$$
\sum_{i = 1}^{n} | x_{i} y_{i} | \leq \| x \|_{p} \| y \|_{q}\tag{C.6.4}
$$

Indeed, there is nothing to prove if p or $q$ is $\infty$ – if it is the case, the inequality becomes the evident relation

$$
\sum_{i} | x_{i} y_{i} | \leq(\max_{i} | x_{i} |)(\sum_{i} | y_{i} |).
$$

Now let $1 < p < \infty,$ , so that also $1 < q < \infty$ . In this case we should prove that

$$
\sum_{i} | x_{i} y_{i} | \leq(\sum_{i} | x_{i} |^{p})^{1 / p}(\sum_{i} | y_{i} |^{q})^{1 / q}.
$$

There is nothing to prove if one of the factors in the right hand side vanishes; thus, we can assume that $x \neq 0$ and $y \ne 0$ . Now, both sides of the inequality are of homogeneity degree 1 with respect to x (when we multiply x by t, both sides are multiplied by $| t |)$ , and similarly with respect to $y.$ Multiplying x and y by appropriate reals, we can make both factors in the right hand side equal to 1: $\| x \|_{p} = \| y \|_{p} = 1$ . Now we should prove that under this normalization the left hand side in the inequality is $\leq 1$ , which is immediately given by the Young inequality:

$$
\sum_{i} | x_{i} y_{i} | \leq \sum_{i}[| x_{i} |^{p} / p + | y_{i} |^{q} / q] = 1 / p + 1 / q = 1.
$$

Note that the H¨older inequality says that

$$
| x^{T} y | \leq \| x \|_{p} \| y \|_{q};\tag{C.6.5}
$$

when $p = q = 2$ , we get the Cauchy inequality. Now, inequality (C.6.5) is exact in the sense that for every x there exists y with $\| y \|_{q} = 1$ such that

$$
x^{T} y = \| x \|_{p}[= \| x \|_{p} \| y \|_{q}];
$$

it sufices to take

$$
y_{i} = \| x \|_{p}^{1 - p} | x_{i} |^{p - 1} \mathrm{sign}(x_{i})
$$

(here $x \ne 0;$ ; the case of $x = 0$ is trivial – here y can be an arbitrary vector with $\| y \|_{q} = 1)$

Combining our observations, we come to an extremely important, although simple, fact:

$$
\| x \|_{p} = \max \{y^{T} x: \| y \|_{q} \leq 1\}[\frac{1}{p} + \frac{1}{q} = 1].\tag{C.6.6}
$$

It follows, in particular, that $\| x \|_{p}$ is convex (as an upper bound of a family of linear forms), whence

$$
\| x^{\prime} + x^{\prime \prime} \|_{p} = 2 \| \frac{1}{2} x^{\prime} + \frac{1}{2} x^{\prime \prime} \|_{p} \leq 2(\| x^{\prime} \|_{p} / 2 + \| x^{\prime \prime} \|_{p} / 2) = \| x^{\prime} \|_{p} + \| x^{\prime \prime} \|_{p};
$$

this is nothing but the triangle inequality. Thus, $\| x \|_{p}$ satisfies the triangle inequality; it clearly possesses two other characteristic properties of a norm – positivity and homogeneity. Consequently, $\| \cdot \|_{p}$ is a norm – the fact that we announced twice and have finally proven now.

The Legendre transformation of the function

$$
f(x) \equiv - a
$$

is the function which is equal to a at the origin and is + outside the origin; similarly, the Legendre transformation of an Affine function $\bar{d}^{T} x - a$ is equal to a at $d = \bar{d}$ and is $+ \infty$ when d $\neq \bar{d};$

The Legendre transformation of the strictly convex quadratic form

$$
f(x) = \frac{1}{2} x^{T} Ax
$$

(A is positive definite symmetric matrix) is the quadratic form

$$
f^{*}(d) = \frac{1}{2} d^{T} A^{- 1} d
$$

The Legendre transformation of the Euclidean norm

$$
f(x) = \| x \|_{2}
$$

is the function which is equal to 0 in the closed unit ball centered at the origin and is + outside the ball.

The latter example is a particular case of the following statement:

Let $\lVert x \rVert$ be a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ , and let

$$
\| d \|_{*} = \sup \{d^{T} x: \| x \| \leq 1\}
$$

be the conjugate $to \parallel \cdot \parallel$ norm.

Exercise C.1 Prove that $\| \cdot \|_{*}$ is a norm, and that the norm conjugate to $\| \cdot \|_{*}$ is the original norm $\| \cdot \|$

Hint: Observe that the unit ball of $\| \cdot \|_{:}$ is exactly the polar of the unit ball of $\| \cdot \|$

The Legendre transformation of $\lVert x \rVert$ is the characteristic function of the unit ball of the conjugate norm, i.e., is the function of d equal to 0 when $\| d \|_{*} \leq 1$ and $i s \mathrm{\Omega} + \infty$ otherwise.

E. $\mathrm{g.,(C.6.6)}$ says that the norm conjugate to $\| \cdot \|_{p}, 1 \leq p \leq \infty,{\mathrm{is ~}} \| \cdot \|_{q}, 1 / p + 1 / q = 1;$ consequently, the Legendre transformation of p-norm is the characteristic function of the unit $\| \cdot \|_{q}{\mathrm{- ball}}$

# Convex Programming, Lagrange Duality, Saddle Points

## D.1 Mathematical Programming Program

A (constrained) Mathematical Programming program is a problem as follows:

$$
\text{(P)} \quad \min \left\{f(x): x \in X, \quad g(x) \equiv(g_{1}(x),..., g_{m}(x)) \leq 0, h(x) \equiv(h_{1}(x),..., h_{k}(x)) = 0 \right\}.\tag{D.1.1}
$$

The standard terminology related to (D.1.1) is:

[domain] X is called the domain of the problem

[objective] f is called the objective

[constraints] $g_{i}, i = 1,..., m, \mathrm{are}$ called the (functional) inequality constraints; $h_{j}, j = 1,..., k,$ are called the equality constraints<sup>1)</sup>

In the sequel, if the opposite is not explicitly stated, it always is assumed that the objective and the constraints are well-defined on X.

[feasible solution] a point $x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is called a feasible solution to (D.1.1), if $x \in X, g_{i}(x) \leq 0,$ $i = 1,..., m.$ , and $h_{j}(x) = 0, j = 1,..., k.$ i.e., if x satisfies all restrictions imposed by the formulation of the problem

[feasible set] the set of all feasible solutions is called the feasible set of the problem

– [feasible problem] a problem with a nonempty feasible set (i.e., the one which admits feasible solutions) is called feasible (or consistent)

– [active constraints] an inequality constraint $g_{i}(\cdot) \leq 0$ is called active at a given feasible solution x, if this constraint is satisfied at the point as an equality rather than strict inequality, i.e., if

$$
g_{i}(x) = 0.
$$

A equality constraint $h_{i}(x) = 0$ by definition is active at every feasible solution x.

[optimal value] the quantity

$$
f^{*} = \left\{\begin{array}{ll} \inf_{x \in X: g(x) \leq 0, h(x) = 0} f(x), & \text{the problem is feasible} \\ + \infty, & \text{the problem is infeasible} \end{array} \right.
$$

is called the optimal value of the problem

– [below boundedness] the problem is called below bounded, if its optimal value is $> - \infty$ , i.e., if the objective is below bounded on the feasible set

<sub>•</sub> [optimal solution] a point $x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is called an optimal solution to (D.1.1), if $x$ is feasible and $f(x) \leq f(x^{\prime})$ for any other feasible solution, i.e., if

$$
x \in \operatorname{Argmin}_{x^{\prime} \in X: g(x^{\prime}) \leq 0, h(x^{\prime}) = 0} f(x^{\prime})
$$

– [solvable problem] a problem is called solvable, if it admits optimal solutions

– [optimal set] the set of all optimal solutions to a problem is called its optimal set

To solve the problem exactly means to find its optimal solution or to detect that no optimal solution exists.

## D.2 Convex Programming program and Lagrange Duality Theorem

A Mathematical Programming program (P) is called convex (or Convex Programming program), if

$X$ is a convex subset of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$

$f, g_{1},..., g_{m}$ are real-valued convex functions on $X$

there are no equality constraints at all.

Note that instead of saying that there are no equality constraints, we could say that there are constraints of this type, but only linear ones; this latter case can be immediately reduced to the one without equality constraints by replacing $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ with the Affine subspace given by the (linear) equality constraints.

## D.2.1 Convex Theorem on Alternative

The simplest case of a convex program is, of course, a Linear Programming program – the one where $X = \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and the objective and all the constraints are linear. We already know what are optimality conditions for this particular case – they are given by the Linear Programming Duality Theorem. How did we get these conditions?

We started with the observation that the fact that a point $x^{*}$ is an optimal solution can be expressed in terms of solvability/unsolvability of certain systems of inequalities: in our now terms, these systems are

$$
x \in G, f(x) \leq c, g_{j}(x) \leq 0, j = 1, \dots, m\tag{D.2.1}
$$

and

$$
x \in G, f(x) < c, g_{j}(x) \leq 0, j = 1,..., m;\tag{D.2.2}
$$

here c is a parameter. Optimality of $x^{*}$ for the problem means exactly that for appropriately chosen c (this choice, of course, is $c = f(x^{*}))$ the first of these systems is solvable and $x^{*}$ is its solution, while the second system is unsolvable. Given this trivial observation, we converted the “negative” part of it – the claim that (D.2.2) is unsolvable – into a positive statement, using the General Theorem on Alternative, and this gave us the LP Duality Theorem.

Now we are going to use the same approach. What we need is a “convex analogy” to the Theorem on Alternative – something like the latter statement, but for the case when the inequalities in question are given by convex functions rather than the linear ones (and, besides it, we have a “convex inclusion” $x \in X)$ .

It is easy to guess the result we need. How did we come to the formulation of the Theorem on Alternative? The question we were interested in was, basically, how to express in an afirmative manner the fact that a system of linear inequalities has no solutions; to this end we observed that if we can combine, in a linear fashion, the inequalities of the system and get an obviously false inequality like $0 \leq - 1$ , then the system is unsolvable; this condition is certain afirmative statement with respect to the weights with which we are combining the original inequalities.

Now, the scheme of the above reasoning has nothing in common with linearity (and even convexity) of the inequalities in question. Indeed, consider an arbitrary inequality system of the type (D.2.2):

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \text{(I)}: & \\ f(x) & < & c \\ g_{j}(x) & \leq & 0, j = 1,..., m \\ x & \in & X; \end{array}
$$

all we assume is that X is a nonempty subset in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $f, g_{1},..., g_{m}$ are real-valued functions on X. It is absolutely evident that

if there exist nonnegative $\lambda_{1},..., \lambda_{m}$ such that the inequality

$$
f(x) + \sum_{j = 1}^{m} \lambda_{j} g_{j}(x) < c\tag{D.2.3}
$$

has no solutions in X, then (I) also has no solutions.

Indeed, a solution to (I) clearly is a solution to (D.2.3) – the latter inequality is nothing but a combination of the inequalities from (I) with the weights 1 (for the first inequality) and $\lambda_{j}$ (for the remaining ones).

Now, what does it mean that (D.2.3) has no solutions? A necessary and sufficient condition for this is that the infimum of the left hand side of (D.2.3) in $x \in X{\mathrm{~ is ~}} \geq c.$ . Thus, we come to the following evident

Proposition D.2.1 [sufficient condition for insolvability of (I)] Consider a system (I) with arbitrary data and assume that the system

(II) :

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \inf_{x \in X} \left[f(x) + \sum_{j = 1}^{m} \lambda_{j} g_{j}(x) \right] & \geq & c \\ \lambda_{j} & \geq & 0, j = 1,..., m \end{array}
$$

with unknowns $\lambda_{1},..., \lambda_{m}$ has a solution. Then (I) is infeasible.

Let us stress that this result is completely general; it does not require any assumptions on the entities involved.

The result we have obtained, unfortunately, does not help us: the actual power of the Theorem on Alternative (and the fact used to prove the Linear Programming Duality Theorem) is not the suficiency of the condition of Proposition for infeasibility of (I), but the necessity of this condition. Justification of necessity of the condition in question has nothing in common with the evident reasoning which gives the suficiency. The necessity in the linear case $(X = \mathbb{R}^{n}, f, g_{1},..., g_{m}$ are linear) can be established via the Homogeneous Farkas Lemma. Now we shall prove the necessity of the condition for the convex case, and already here we need some additional, although minor, assumptions; and in the general nonconvex case the condition in question simply is not necessary for infeasibility of (I) [and this is very bad – this is the reason why there exist dificult optimization problems which we do not know how to solve eficiently].

The just presented “preface” explains what we should do; now let us carry out our plan. We start with the aforementioned “minor regularity assumptions”.

Definition D.2.1 [Slater Condition] Let $X \subset \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $g_{1},..., g_{m}$ be real-valued functions on X. We say that these functions satisfy the Slater condition on X, if there exists x in the relative interior of X such that $g_{j}(x) < 0, j = 1,..., m$

An inequality constrained program

$$
\min \left\{f(x): g_{j}(x) \leq 0, j = 1,..., m, x \in X \right\}\tag{IC}
$$

$(f, g_{1},..., g_{m}$ are real-valued functions on $X)$ is called to satisfy the Slater condition, if $g_{1},..., g_{m}$ satisfy this condition on $X$

Definition D.2.2 [Relaxed Slater Condition] Let $X \subset \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $g_{1},..., g_{m}$ be real-valued functions on $X,$ We say that these functions satisfy the Relaxed Slater condition on $X, if,$ after appropriate reordering of $g_{1},..., g_{m},$ for properly selected $k \in \{0, 1,..., m\}$ the functions $g_{1},..., g_{k}$ are Affine, and there exists x in the relative interior of X such that $g_{j}(x) \leq 0, 1 \leq j \leq k_{\cdot}$ , and $g_{j}(x) < 0, k + 1 \leq j \leq m$

An inequality constrained problem (IC) is called to satisfy the Relaxed Slater condition, $ifg_{1},..., g_{n}$ satisfy this condition on X.

Clearly, the validity of Slater condition implies the validity of the Relaxed Slater condition (in the latter, we should set $k = 0)$ . We are about to establish the following fundamental fact:

Theorem D.2.1 [Convex Theorem on Alternative]

Let $X \subset \mathbb{R}^{n}$ be convex, let $f, g_{1},..., g_{m}$ be real-valued convex functions on X, and let $g_{1},..., g_{m}$ satisfy the Relaxed Slater condition on X. Then system (I) is solvable if and only if system (II) is unsolvable.

## D.2.1.1 Cone constrained case

We shall obtain Theorem D.2.1 as a particular case of Convex Theorem on Alternative in Cone Constrained form dealing with convex system (I) in cone constrained form:

$$
f(x) < c, \overline{{g}}(x) := Ax - b \leq 0, \widehat{g}(x) \in - \mathbf{K}, x \in X,\tag{D.2.4}
$$

where

$X$ is a nonempty convex set in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ , and $f : X \mathbb{R}$ is convex,

${\bf K} \subset{\bf R}^{\nu}$ is a regular cone, regularity meaning that K is closed, convex, possesses a nonempty interior, and is pointed, that is $\mathbf{K} \cap[- \mathbf{K}] = \{0\}$

${\widehat{g}}(x) : Z \to \mathbb{R}^{\nu}$ is K-convex, meaning that whenever x, $y \in X$ and $\lambda \in[0, 1]$ , we have

$$
\lambda \widehat{g}(x) +(1 - \lambda) \widehat{g} - \widehat{g}(\lambda x +(1 - \lambda) y) \in \mathbf{K}.
$$

Note that in the simplest case of ${\bf K} ={\bf R}_{+}^{\nu}$ (nonnegative orthant is a regular cone!) K-convexity means exactly that $\widehat g$ is a vector function with convex on X components.

Given a regular cone ${\bf K} \subset{\bf R}^{\nu}$ , we can associate with it K-inequality between vectors of $\mathbb{R}^{\nu}$ saying that $a \in \mathbb{R}^{\nu}$ is K-greater then or equal to $b \in \mathbb{R}^{\nu}$ (notation: $A \geq_{\bf K} b,$ or, equivalently, $\boldsymbol{b} \le_{\mathbf{K}} \boldsymbol{a})$ when $a - b \in \mathbf{K}$ :

$$
a \geq_{\mathbf{K}} b \Leftrightarrow b \leq_{\mathbf{K}} a \Leftrightarrow a - b \in \mathbf{K}
$$

For example, when ${\bf K} ={\bf R}_{+}^{\nu}$ is nonnegative orthant, $\geq \mathbf{\mathbf{\mathbf{\mathbf{\mathbf{\mathbf{\mathbf{\mathbf{K}}}}}}}}$ is the standard coordinate-wise vector inequality $\geq \textit{a} \geq \textit{b}$ means that every entry of a is greater than or equal to, in the standard arithmetic sense, the corresponding entry in b. K- vector inequality possesses all algebraic properties of $\geq :$

1. it is a partial order on $\mathbb{R}^{\nu}$ , meaning that the relation $a \ge \mathbf{\kappa}$ b is

reflexive: $a \ge \mathbf{\kappa}$ a for all a

anti-symmetric: $a \ge \mathbf{\kappa} b$ and $b \ge \mathbf{\kappa} a$ if and only if $a = b$

transitive: is $a \ge_{\bf K} l$ b and $b \geq_{\mathbf{K}} c,$ then $a \ge \mathbf{\kappa} c$

2. is compatible with linear operations, meaning that

-inequalities can be summed up: is $a{\ge} \mathbf{\kappa} b$ and $c{\ge}_{\bf K} d,$ , then $a + c{\ge}{\bf{\scriptscriptstyle K}} b + d$

multiplied by nonnegative reals: if $a{\ge} \mathbf{\kappa} b$ and λ is a nonnegative real, then $\lambda a{\geq}_{\mathbf{K}} \lambda b$

3. is compatible with convergence, meaning that one can pass to sidewise limits in $\geq \mathbf{\mathbf{\mathbf{\mathbf{K}}^{-}}}$ inequality:

<sub>•</sub> if $a_{t} \ge_{\mathbf{K}} b_{t}, t = 1, 2,...,$ and $a_{t} \to a$ and $b_{t} \to b$ as $t \to \infty$ , then $a{\ge} \mathbf{\kappa} b$

4. gives rise to strict version $>_{\mathbf{K}}$ of $\geq \mathbf{\mathbf{\mathbf{\mathbf{\mathbf{\mathbf{\mathbf{K}}}}}}}.$ -inequality: $a >_{\mathbf{K}} b$ (equivalently: $b <_{\mathbf{K}} a)$ meaning that $a - b \in$ int K. The strict K-inequality possesses the basic properties of the coordinate-wise $>,$ specifically

$> \mathbf{\mathbf{\mathbf{\mathbf{\mathbf{\mathbf{\mathbf{\mathbf{\mathbf \Lambda}}}}}}}}$ is stable: if a $> \mathbf{\mathbf{\mathbf{\mathbf{\mathbf{\mathbf{\mathbf{\mathbf{\mathbf \Lambda}}}}}}}}$ b and $a^{\prime}, \b^{\prime}$ are close enough to a, b respectively, then $a^{\prime} >_{\bf K} b^{\prime}$

<sub>•</sub> if $a >_{\bf K} b, \lambda$ is a positive real, and $c{\ge} \mathbf{{K}} d,$ , then $\lambda a >_{\bf K} \lambda b$ and $a + c >_{\mathbf{K}} b + d$

In summary, the arithmetics of $\le_{\mathbf{K}}$ and $< \mathbf{\kappa}$ inequalities is completely similar to the one of the usual $\geq$ and $>$ .

Exercise D.1 Verify the above claims

Since 1990’s, it was realized that as far as nonlinear Convex Optimization is concerned, it is extremely convenient to consider, along with the usual Mathematical Programming form

$$
\begin{array}{c} \min_{x \in X} \left\{g_{0}(x): g(x) :=[g_{1}(x);...; g_{m}(x)] \leq 0, 1 \leq i \leq m, h_{j}(x) = 0, j \leq k \right\} \\[X \colon \text{convex set}; g_{i}(x): X \to \mathbb{R}, 0 \leq i \leq m \colon \text{convex}; h_{j}(x), j \leq k \colon \text{affine}] \end{array}
$$

of a convex problem, where nonlinearity “sits” in $g_{i} \mathrm{\dot{s}}$ and $1 / \mathrm{or}$ non-polyhedrality of $X,$ the cone constrained form where the nonlinearity $\mathrm{^{6} sits^{5}}$ in $\leq -$ the usual coordinate-wise $\leq$ is replaced with $\le_{\mathbf{K}}$ , K being a regular cone. The resulting convex program in cone constrained form reads

$$
\min_{x \in X} \left\{f(x): \overline{{g}}(x) := Ax - b \leq 0, \underbrace{\widehat{g}(x) \leq_{\mathbf{K}} 0}_{\Leftrightarrow \widehat{g}(x) \in - \mathbf{K}} \right\}\tag{D.2.5}
$$

where (cf. (D.2.4) X is convex set, $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ is convex function, ${\bf K} \subset{\bf R}^{\nu}$ is a regular cone, and ${\widehat{g}} : X \to \mathbb{R}^{\nu}$ is K-convex. Note that K-convexity of $\widehat g$ is our new notation takes the quite common for us form

$$
\forall(x, y \in X, \lambda \in[0, 1]): \widehat{g}(\lambda x +(1 - \lambda) y)) \le_{\mathbf{K}} \lambda \widehat{g}(x) +(1 - \lambda) \widehat{g}(y).
$$

Note also that when K is nonnegative orthant, (D.2.5) recovers the Mathematical Programming form of a convex problem.

It turns out that with “cone constrained approach” to Convex Programming, we loose nothing when restricting ourselves with $X = \mathbb{R}^{n}$ , linear $f(x)$ , and Affine ${\widehat{g}}(x)$ ; this specific version of (D.2.5) is called “conic problem” (to be considered in more details later). It makes sense also to speak about a “less extreme” cone constrained form of a convex program, specifically, one presented in (D.2.5); we call problems of this form “convex problems in cone constrained form,” reserving the words “conic problems” for problems (D.2.5) with $X = \mathbb{R}^{n}$ , linear $f$ and Affine ${\widehat{g}}.$

What we have done so far in this section can be naturally extended to the cone constrained case. Specifically, (in what follows $X \subset \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is a nonempty set, ${\bf K} \subset{\bf R}^{\nu}$ is a regular cone, $f$ is a real-valued function on X, and ${\widehat{g}}(\cdot)$ is a K-convex mapping from X into R<sup>ν</sup>)

1. Instead of feasibility/infeasibility of system (I) we can speak about feasibility/infeasibility of system of constraints

(ConI) :

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} f(x) & < & c \\ \overline{{g}}(x) := Ax - b & \leq & 0 \\ \widehat{g}(x) & \leq_{\mathbf{K}} & 0[\Leftrightarrow \widehat{g}(x) \in - \mathbf{K}] \\ x & \in & X \end{array}
$$

in variables x. Denoting by K<sub>∗</sub> the cone dual to K, a sufficient condition for infeasibility of (ConI) is solvability of system of constraints

(ConII) :

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} \inf_{x \in X} \left[f(x) + \overline{{\lambda}}^{T} \overline{{g}}(x) + \widehat{\lambda}^{T} \widehat{g}(x) \right] & \geq & c \\ \overline{{\lambda}} & \geq & 0 \\ \widehat{\lambda} & \geq_{\mathbf{K}_{*}} & 0[\Leftrightarrow \widehat{\lambda} \in \mathbf{K}_{*}] \end{array}
$$

in variables $\lambda =({\overline{{\lambda}}},{\widehat{\lambda}})$

Indeed, given a feasible solution $\overline{{\lambda}}, \widehat{\lambda}$ to (ConII) and “aggregating” the constraints in (ConI) with weights $1,{\overline{{\lambda}}},{\widehat{\lambda}} \left({\mathrm{i.e.}} \right.$ , taking sidewise inner products of constraints in (ConI) and weights and summing up the results), we arrive at the inequality

$$
f(x) + \overline{{{{\lambda}}}}^{T} \overline{{{{g}}}}(x) + \widehat{\lambda}^{T} \widehat{g}(x) < c
$$

which due to $\overline{{\lambda}} \geq 0$ and $\widehat{\lambda} \in{\bf K}.$ <sub>∗</sub> is a consequence of (ConI) – it must be satisfied at every feasible solution to (ConI). On the other hand, the aggregated inequality contradicts the first constraint in (ConII), and we conclude that under the circumstances (ConI) is infeasible.

2. “Cone constrained” version of Slater/Relaxed Slater condition is as follows: we say that the system of constraints

$$
\overline{{g}}(x) := Ax - b \leq 0 \& \widehat{g}(x) \leq_{\mathbf{K}} 0\tag{S}
$$

in variables x satisfies

— Slater condition on $X$ , if there exists ${\bar{x}} \in$ rint X such that $\overline{{g}}(\bar{x}) < 0$ and $\widehat{g}(\bar{x}){<}_{\bf K} 0 \(\mathrm{i.e.,} \ \widehat{g}(\bar{x}) \in$ int $\mathbf{K})$

— Relaxed Slater condition on X, if there exists ${\bar{x}} \in$ rint X such that $\overline{{g}}(\bar{x}) \leq 0$ and $\widehat g(\bar{x}) <_{\bf K} 0$ We say that convex optimization problem in cone constrained form – problem of the form

(ConIC)

$$
\min_{x \in X} \{f(x): \overline{{g}}(x) := Ax - b \leq 0, \widehat{g}(x) \leq_{\mathbf{K}} 0\}
$$

satisfies Slater/Relaxed Slater condition, if the system of its constraints satisfies this condition on X.

Note that in the case of ${\bf K} ={\bf R}_{+}^{\nu}$ , (ConI) and (ConII) become, respectively, (I) and (II), and the cone constrained versions of Slater/Relaxed Slater condition become the usual ones.

The cone constrained version of Theorem D.2.1 reads as follows:

## Theorem D.2.2 [Convex Theorem on Alternative in Cone Constrained Form]

Let ${\bf K} \subset{\bf R}^{\nu}$ be a regular cone, let $X \subset \mathbb{R}^{n}$ be convex, and let $f$ be real-valued convex function on $X$ ${\overline{{g}}}(x) = Ax - b$ be Affine, and ${\widehat{g}}(x) : X \to \mathbb{R}^{\nu}$ be K-convex. Let also system (S) satisfy Relaxed Slater condition on X. Then system (ConI) is solvable $if$ and only if system (ConII) is unsolvable.

Note: “In reality” (ConI) may have no polyhedral part ${\overline{{g}}}(x) : = Ax - b \leq 0$ and/or no “general part” ${\widehat{g}}(x){\leq}_{\mathbf{K}} 0;$ ; absence of one or both of these parts leads to self-evident modifications in (ConII). To unify our forthcoming considerations, it is convenient to assume that both these parts are present. This assumption is for free: it is immediately seen that in our context, in absence of one or both of g-constraints in (ConI) we lose nothing when adding artificial polyhedral part $\overline{{g}}(x) : = 0^{T} x - 1 \leq 0$ instead of missing polyhedral part, and/or artificial general part $\widehat{g}(x) : = 0^{T} x - 1{\leq} \mathbf{{\kappa}} 0$ with ${\bf K} ={\bf R}_{+}$ instead of missing general part. Thus, we lose nothing when assuming from the very beginning that both polyhedral and general parts are present.

It is immediately seen that Convex Theorem on Alternative (Theorem D.2.1) is a special case of the latter Theorem corresponding to the case when K is a nonnegative orthant.

Proof of Theorem D.2.2. The first part of the statement – “if (ConII) has a solution, then (ConI) has no solutions” – has been already verified. What we need is to prove the inverse statement. Thus, let us assume that (ConI) has no solutions, and let us prove that then (ConII) has a solution.

$$

satisfies $\mathrm{Opt}(P) \geq 0$ , and our goal is to show that (ConII) is feasible.

\mathbf{1}^{0}.\text{Let} Y = \{x \in X: \overline{{g}}(x) \leq 0\} = \{x \in X: Ax - b \leq 0\},
$$

$$
\begin{array}{rcl} S & = & \{t =[t_{0}; t_{1}] \in \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}^{\nu}: t_{0} < 0, t_{1} \leq_{\mathbf{K}} 0\}, \\ T & = & \{t =[t_{0}; t_{1}] \in \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}^{\nu}: \exists x \in Y: f(x) \leq t_{0}, \widehat{g}(x) \leq_{\mathbf{K}} t_{1}\}, \end{array}

so that $S$ and $T$ are nonempty (since (P ) is feasible by (D.2.6)) non-intersecting (since $\mathrm{Opt}(P) \geq 0)$ convex (since X and $f$ are convex, and ${\widehat{g}}(x)$ is K-convex on X) sets. By Separation Theorem (Theorem B.2.9) S and $T$ can be separated by an appropriately chosen linear form α. Thus,

$$

$$

and the form is non-constant on $S \cup T$ , implying that $\alpha \neq 0$ We clearly have $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}_{+} \times \mathbf{K}_{*}$ , since otherwise ${\mathrm{sup}}_{t \in S} \alpha^{T} t$ would be + . Since $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}_{+} \times \mathbf{K}_{*}$ , the left hand side in (D.2.7) is 0 (look what S is), and therefore (D.2.7) reads

Indeed, the point $\bar{t} =[\bar{t}_{0}; \bar{t}_{1}]$ with the components $\bar{t}_{0} ~ = ~ f(0)$ and $\bar{t}_{1} = \widehat{g}(0)$ belongs to $T,$ so that by (D.2.8) it holds $\alpha_{0} \hat{t}_{0} + \alpha_{1}^{T} \hat{t}_{1} \ge 0$ . h(x) = f(x) + \bar{\alpha}_{1}^{T} \widehat{g}(x).

3<sup>0</sup>.1. Consider the convex sets

$$
S = \{[x; \tau] \in \mathbb{R}^{n} \times \mathbb{R}: x \in X, \overline{{g}}(x) := Ax - b \leq 0, \tau < 0\}, T = \{[x; \tau] \in \mathbb{R}^{n} \times \mathbb{R}: x \in X, \tau \geq h(x)\}.

These sets clearly are nonempty and do not intersect (since the x-component $x$ of a point from $S \cap T$ would satisfy the premise and violate the conclusion in (D.2.9)). By Separation Theorem, there exists $[e; \alpha] \neq 0$ such that

$$
\sup_{[x; \tau] \in S}[e^{T} x + \alpha \tau] \leq \inf_{[x; \tau] \in T}[e^{T} x + \alpha \tau].
$$

Taking into account what $S$ is, we have $\alpha \geq 0$ (since otherwise the left hand side in the inequality would be $+ \infty)$ . With this in mind, the inequality reads

$$
\sup_{x} \left\{e^{T} x: x \in X, \overline{{g}}(x) \leq 0 \right\} \leq \inf_{x} \left\{e^{T} x + \alpha h(x): x \in X \right\}.\tag{D.2.10}
$$

$\mathbf{3^{0}.2}$ . We need the following fact:

Lemma D.2.1 Let $X \subset \mathbb{R}^{n}$ be a convex set with $0 \in$ int X, $g(x) = Ax + a$ be such that $g(0) \leq 0$ , and $d^{T} x + \delta$ be an Affine function such that

$$
x \in X, g(x) \leq 0 \Rightarrow d^{T} x + \delta \leq 0.
$$

Then there exists $\mu \geq 0$ such that

$$
d^{T} x + \delta \leq \mu^{T} g(x) \forall x \in X.
$$

Note that when $X = \mathbb{R}^{n}$ , Lemma D.2.1 is nothing but Inhomogeneous Farkas Lemma. Proof of Lemma D.2.1. Consider the cones

$$
M_{1} = \operatorname{cl} \left\{\left[x; t \right]: t > 0, x / t \in X \right\}, M_{2} = \left\{y =[x; t]: Ax + ta \leq 0 \right\}.
$$

$M_{2}$ is a polyhedral cone, and $M_{1}$ is a closed convex cone with a nonempty interior (since the point [0; 1] belongs to int $M_{1}$ due to $0 \in \operatorname{int} X);$ ; moreover, [int $M_{1}] \cap M_{2} \neq \emptyset$ (since the point $\left[0; 1 \right] \in$ int $M_{1}$ belongs to $M_{2}$ due to $g(0) \leq 0)$ . Observe that the linear form $f^{T}[x; t] : = \mathbf{\bar{\Gamma}} \mathbf{\bar{\Gamma}} \mathbf{\bar{{x}}} + t \delta$ is nonpositive on $M_{1} \cap M_{2}$ , that is, $(- f) \in[M_{1} \cap M_{2}]_{*}$ , where, as usual, $M_{*}$ is the cone dual to a cone M.

Indeed, let $[z; t] \in M_{1} \cap M_{2}$ , and let $y_{s} =[z_{s}; t_{s}] =(1 - s) y + s[0; 1]$ . Observe that $y_{s} \in M_{1} \cap M_{2}$ when $0 \leq s \leq 1$ . When $0 < s \le 1$ , we have $t_{s} > 0.$ and $y_{s} \in M_{1}$ implies that $w_{s} : = z_{s} / t_{s} \in \mathrm{cl} X$ (why?), while $y_{s} \in M_{2}$ implies that $g(w_{s}) \leq 0$ Since 0  int X, $w_{s} \in$ cl X implies that $\theta w_{s} \in X$ for all $\theta \in[0, 1)$ , while $g(0) \leq 0$ along with $g(w_{s}) \leq 0$ implies that $g(\theta w_{s}) \leq 0$ for $\theta \in[0, 1)$ . Invoking the premise of Lemma, we conclude that

$$
d^{T}(\theta w_{s}) + \delta \leq 0 \forall \theta \in[0, 1],
$$

whence $d^{T} w_{s} + \delta \leq 0$ , or, which is the same, $f^{T} y_{s} \leq 0$ . As $s + 0$ , we have $f^{T} y_{s} \to f^{T}[z; t]$ , implying that $f^{T}[z; t] \leq 0$ , as claimed.

Thus, $M_{1}, M_{2}$ are closed cones such that [int $M_{1}] \cap M_{2} \neq \emptyset$ and $f \in[M_{1} \cap M_{2}] *$ . Applying to $M_{1}, M_{2}$ the Dubovitski-Milutin Lemma (Proposition B.2.7), we conclude that $[M_{1} \cap M_{2}] * =$ $(M_{1})_{*} +(M_{2}),$ <sub>∗</sub>. Since $- f \in[M_{1} \cap M_{2}] *$ , there exist $\psi \in(M_{1})$ and $\phi \in(M_{2})$ such that $[d; \delta] = - \phi - \psi$ . The inclusion $\phi \in(M_{2})$ <sub>∗</sub> means that the homogeneous linear inequality $\phi^{T} y \ge 0$ is a consequence of the system $[A, a] y ~ \leq ~ 0$ of homogeneous linear inequalities; by Homogeneous Farkas Lemma (Lemma B.2.1), it follows that identically in x it holds $\check{\phi^{T}}[x; 1] = - \mu^{T} g(x)$ ), with some nonnegative $\mu.$ Thus,

$$
\forall x \in E: d^{T} x + \delta =[d; \delta]^{T}[x; 1] = \mu^{T} g(x) - \psi^{T}[x; 1],
$$

and since $[x; 1] \in M_{1}$ whenever $x \in X$ , we have $\psi^{T}[x; 1] \geq 0, x \in X$ , so that $\mu$ satisfies the requirements stated in the lemma we are proving.

$\mathbf{3^{0}.3}$ . Recall that we have seen that in (D.2.10), $\alpha \geq 0$ . We claim that in fact $\alpha > 0$

Indeed, assuming $\alpha = 0$ and setting $\begin{array}{r}{a = \operatorname{sup}_{x} \left\{e^{T} x : x \in X, \overline{{g}}(x) \leq 0 \right\}} \end{array}$ , (D.2.10) implies that $a \in \mathbb{R}$ and

$$
\{\forall(x \in X, \overline{{g}}(x) \leq 0): e^{T} x - a \leq 0\} \& \{\forall x \in X: e^{T} x \geq a\}.\tag{D.2.11}
$$

By Lemma D.2.1, the first of these relations implies that for some nonnegative $\mu$ it holds

$$

$\mathbf{3^{0}.4}.$ . Thus, α in (D.2.10) is strictly positive; replacing e with $\alpha^{- 1} e,$ we can assume that (D.2.10) holds true with $\alpha = 1$ . Setting $\begin{array}{r}{a = \operatorname{sup}_{x} \left\{e^{T} x : x \in X, \overline{{g}}(x) \leq 0 \right\}} \end{array}$ , (D.2.10) reads

$$
\forall(x \in X): h(x) + e^{T} x \geq a,
$$

while the definition of a along with Lemma D.2.1 implies that there exists $\mu \geq 0$ such that

\forall x \in X: e^{T} x - a \leq \mu^{T} \overline{{g}}(x).

Combining these relations, we conclude that

Recalling that $h(x) = f(x) + \bar{\alpha}_{1}^{T} \widehat{g}(x)$ with $\bar{\alpha}_{1} \in \mathbf{K},$ <sub>∗</sub> and setting $\overline{{\lambda}} = \mu, \widehat{\lambda} = \bar{\alpha}_{1}$ , we get $\overline{{{\lambda}}} \geq 0, \widehat{\lambda} \in{\bf K},$ ∗ while by (D.2.12) it holds
